This is one of my favourite games. To be sure, it's not always a high-octane experience - there is a lot of walking across barren, quasi-British countryside (looks more like Suffolk than anywhere else). You'll spend a fair amount of time alone, poking around deserted villages. However, I happen to enjoy that kind of atmosphere - and there's plenty of atmosphere.
When things do get dicey though, they really do. While you might stand a fair chance vs 1 or even 2 robots if you've found weaponry enough, more than that and you're taking your life in your hands. The robots are not at all easy to escape once they've got a bead on you and if you do manage to escape them by crawling through a wheat field and then sprinting through some woods you'll really feel like you earned it, not that you just outwitted a dull AI.
So it's much like war - long periods of quiet boringness (which actually really sets up the mood) with sudden bursts of frantic activity. Often you'll find yourself gazing through your binoculars at a collectible guarded by robots, trying to fathom out the best way to outwit or destroy them. You certainly won't succeed by just charging in.
To have any hope of success you'll really need to find the device that detects nearby pieces - you can start with this by default if you choose the right character mode. If you don't, it'll be very hard going until you do. I played this game a lot before that particular feature was added in and the dectector improved the game exponentially. Before that it was perfectly possible to walk right by a piece and miss it, despite the tell-tale smoke and you could spend hours scouring the same island trying to find it.
Not one for you if you're seeking constant thrills then, but if you're feeling like playing a slow-burning and rewarding experience this is an excellent choice.

Balanced and fair, if a bit short on content/variety, freemium turn-based strategy game with solid depth to it's mechanics. Not recommended for those without much strategy experience/love, as the game's tactics are sort of left to the player to learn- advanced concepts like controlling the pace of turns, unit harassment/blocking, etc are present here.
Real money purchases consist of cosmetics and 2/3 of the game's 'decks', which are sets of units you use to battle. I wish these were a bit more customizable, the decks are a static number of 'cards' that summon units, give them an upgrade, or have an immediate impact on the battle. The first deck is free, and a f2p player will be using one deck for their sessions. Annoying since I fall into that category (budget of $0, literally) but the decks are balanced quite well even in 'competitive' matches (the game is new and deceptively simple, so there isn't much of a 'scene' here)
Also, developer is very friendly and non-malicious. This is no cash grab or lackluster effort, but a polished and scrappy little foray into competitive strategy by a young developer simply trying his hand. Give it a try if you fit the audience, it'll be a good bit of fun.

Introduction:
DoTE is an interesting take on Tower Defense, coupled with what should be turn-based RPG, Rouge-like squad combat.
Initially i was gonna give this one a pass, considering i dislike the turn-based aspect. But here the combat itself is done in real-time, so i thought id give it a go.
The only turn-based aspect to this title, is in essence; the opening of doors. Once you open a door, you are commiting your turn. Resources wont generate in real-time, instead they will increase based on each turn (door opened). Though i may have very little experience in the case of turn-based games (never played FTL, for instance), i would say that this game is as close as ill get to enjoying one.
Graphics:
The pixel art style here is done very well, especially on the characters. The environments are nice too, each varying style of floor have their own theme. Though maybe they are slightly *too* static, in places. Admittedly there are some animated effects that compliment rooms, like blinking rats, candles and toxic/electro-magnetic 'aura's' (which in the case of the last two; play into the game mechanics).
Idle and movement character animations were very well-done and add a lot of flavour to the style. I was hoping for more variation in attack animations for each Hero, though. Yet at the same time i will say that they are more than adequate.
The UI/menu presentation is of its own style and its non-obtrusive and easy on the eyes. Players are given the option between a large/small UI/HUD based on their own personal preference.
Audio:
Whoever did the music, has really nailed the atmosphere for this game. Probably one of the best aspects to this game, i think. The sound effects themselves are adequate, nothing bad about them, nor is there anything overly impressive about them either. There is no spoken dialogue, yet there are text based conversations between Heroes.
Gameplay:
To put it simply; its turn-based tower defense with real-time combat. You move, in real-time, your group of up to 4 Heroes through a procedurally generated dungeon. Enemies/monsters wont have a chance at spawning until you open a door, so its important to plan before opening too many doors. You can place Minor/Major modules (Automated Weapons/Resources) which is where this game gets its Tower Defense tag from. To expand on that, the player is constantly having to choose between risk/reward. For instance; do i save my resources for the next floor? Or do i increase the amount of weaponry (Minor Modules) i have in this current floor, to aid my Heroes? Its quite risky hanging onto your resources and hoping your Heroes will get the job done, on their own. Yet if it pays off, come the next floor (or many after, due to an overabundance of resources), if you manage to succeed.
There have been many times where ive lost a Hero or two, because i attempted to hoard my resources. This is by far the most challenging aspect of the game for me. As im constantly trying to ensure i use 'just enough' Minor/Major Modules to keep my neck above the water, so i can bank enough resources for the next floor.
The combat itself, which was an important aspect for me buying this game, doesnt give you direct control of your Heroes attacks. Rather you have real-time control of their movements and their attacks are automatic, if in the same room as enemies.
A wide variety of strategies can be deployed based on your Hero setup and/or your preferred play-style. This gives the player the sense that he/she can beat this game in a variety of ways. Which is a good thing. For instance, you could level up your Heroes and Tactical HUD Modules to increase their stats and effectiveness in combat. Alternatively you could research Minor Modules which come in the form of base defense weaponry, focus on accumulating more science points and upgrading those weapons further. That wont necessarily increase your Heroes stats in combat, but will increase their chances if they occupy the same room.
Both of those strategies will require quite differing tactics in order to succeed. I tend to use the latter and got as far as attempting to hoard enough resources so i could afford the former. That lead to my eventual death on the 11th floor.
Narrative:
This game definitely has its own edge in humour. Which is mainly played out through small story arcs that happen between certain Heroes if they are grouped together. Some of the dialogue/bio's got a few chuckles out of me alright, especially the midget who is obsessed with his disparity in height, so much so that he has worked his muscles and upper-body strength to the point where he can wield over-sized weaponry. Inbetween levels, in the elevator, he said something to another Hero that made me lose it. Ill omit that considering i believe it belongs in the game, not this review. ;)
If certain Heroes are grouped together for enough time (ie. levels/floors), their dialogue will eventually lead to an end in their story which will have either a positive or negative effect on both of them. This gives the narratives a purpose, as in, its not just tacked on. Its complimentary.
Overall:
A solid offering. I was pleasantly surprised at how much i ended up enjoying this game. Initially i was very aprehensive as i really dont like turn-based games, but i believe that DoTE should appeal to both fans of turn-based games, and those who arent but have an interest in tower defense with squad based combat. Ive clocked like 33 hours so far and i havent beaten the Dungeon yet, so in regards to longevity i do believe this title should fulfill that aspect for most people.
Personally i dont really care for rating systems, so i wont attempt to do one here. +Recommended. :P

Dungeon of the Endless is an immersive and highly strategic game. It's tons of fun and definitely worth a buy.
Video Review:
What is it?
Dungeon of the Endless is a tower defense, rouge like, roleplaying game. That is a bit long winded, so I'll break these down a bit. You play as a goup of adventurers who have crash landed on an ancient planet. You're goal is to get off of the planet by getting to the elevator on each level and powering it up. In order to do this you have to search through rooms, kill enemies, and loot awsome stuff. Every few rooms you explore, there will be a wave of enemies that tries to either kill you or destroy your power crystal. You have to defend this crystal (you need it to power the elevator). In order to do this, you power up the derelict rooms that you've searched and build towers to kill the waves of enemies.
How hard can this be (you might ask)? Quite hard. The limiting factor in all of this is the four rescources you have to manage; industry, tech, food, and dust. Industry builds towers. Food heals and upgrades your heroes. Tech gets you new towers. Dust allows you to power more rooms. You get a certain amount of each of these every turn based upon how many large rescource producing towers you have.
You also unlock characters and new escape pods as you go through the game. These will give you new options to start the game with.
Pros:
-Amazing soundtrack. From the start menu this music draws you into the world of Dungeon of the Endless.
-Streamline gameplay. Everything is quick and easy to do in the game (the hard part is getting the strategy down).
-Great visuals. All of the characters have great personality that is expressed even through their movements. For instance,
Cons:
-There is no way to zoom out without entering the tactical view. This isn't terrible, but it would be great to be able to see the entire network in it's full color.
This game is great and I'll be playing the heck out of it for quite a while. It is definitely worth picking up, and is worth way more than the current price.
DLC: Is the Crystal Pack worth it?
That is a question. I havn't purchased it, and I'm going to give it some time before I really decide wether or not to pick it up. All that the DLC adds in game is one character and an escape pod. I'd recommend picking up the game first and then upgrading it if you get hooked (which you're likely to).

Im major roguelike fan. My favourites include Risk of Rain, Faster Than Light and One Way Heroics, so i have some experience on the genre. But yeah, let's get to the point:
In Dungeon of The Endless your goal is to escape the Underground Lab whilst defending yourself with heroes and different turrets. You start humbly, but as you make your way closer to the entrance, you'll recruit new heroes, and unlock new turrets to keep them alive. But as you grow stronger, enemies grow outright brutal, in strength, variety and sheer numbers...
The game is a masterpiece. I'd recommend it to anyone who's into roguelikes, towerdefence or dungeon crawling. If you're into 2 or more of those categories, you should have alredy bought the game just to see what you're missing.
Here are the pros and cons of the game:
+ Art style is unique and pretty.
+ Music is great.
+ Gameplay is innovative and fresh.
+ Glitches are extremely rare.
+ The story is interesting (if you care to search for it), as are the interactions between playable characters (heroes).
+ Amazing replayability.
+ Micromanagement. Doing one thing over and over might get you trough couple floors, but after that the enemies will slaughter you. So it's important to keep in mind what kind of enemies the floor in question hosts, and what turrets work on them.
- Some of the heroes would need some balancing work. (Im looking at you, Max and Josh)
- The luck factor. As with all roguelikes, sometimes the game just kills you without giving you even slightest chance. This becomes apparent, when you're on the last level, and game refuses to give you any Dust (resource required to power your defences), and then steamrolling you with first big enemy wave.
Long story short, I still love the game. 130+ hours played, and I have yet to clear the Sanitary pod (hard mode). Update, Sanitary Pod cleared with around 140 hours.

Since I just reviewed INSIDE, I thought maybe I also should review the OG - LIMBO.
I don't like platformers.

-thus-
I shouldn't like this game.
Yet LIMBO is a masterpiece. There's not much I can say about LIMBO that hasn't already been said. LIMBO has a uniquely beautiful, spooky and mysterious art style. It has a dark, brooding, ethereal and dreamlike music track that communicates effectively with the player. Interesting puzzles that aren't too hard for the non-twitch gamer but are effectively in conveying the story. The controls are responsive and consistent. There's simply nothing here that's not exceptionally well done. This game surrounds very tight and well-honed-honed gameplay with incredible atmosphere and a emotional but still ambiguous story. It's one of those games that you can point to when someone says "games aren't art". You don't realize how magical this game is until you experience it for yourself. Screenshots, Let's Plays and other forms of media simply don't do it justice.

At first glance, Beyond Good and Evil came off to me as a product of its time- a game that hasn't aged all too well. It has that sort of GameCube/PS2 mid-era vibe where they might've been good back then, but has unfortunately lost some of the charm it once had. However, I can say without a doubt that Beyond Good and Evil is an outstanding game easily worth whatver cheap price you can pick it up for. The humor, story, and largely varied gameplay styles of Beyond Good and Evil shine in their own unique ways every time you face a challenge, and very rarely loses that charm. The only downside to this PC version of the game is that for my personal experience, there were a number of graphical errors and other quirks. However, even with these problems, Beyond Good and Evil is worth your time. Let's hope Beyond Good and Evil 2 doesn't fall into a No Man's Sky situation...

Beyond Good and Evil is a very solid game even with its gameplay flaws, players will find a very well written story to go along with the atomospheric environment. You control Jade, a photographer/journalist who lives in an orphanage in the world of Hillys which is under attack by a race called the DomZ. That's all I'll say without spoiling anything.
The PC version, not gonna lie, is a mess, out of the box there are problems with widescreen compatibility, texture flickering and audio/video desynchronization. With some guides and help online, I've managed to resolve the widescreen and texture flickering issue but a/v desync on cut-scenes was left unresolved. That issue gets annoying but it didn't affect gameplay thankfully.
Combat is about average, there are a lot of frustrating moments where combat was definetly not viable against certain encounters. In short combat is very simplistic and clunky at the same time, don't expect a deep combat system like Bayonetta or DMC.

Cuphead - A game that has been anticipated for so long, shown at many E3 conventions, but it was hard for the developers. I wasn't part of this hype train, but when the game came out with a very good price tag and people were playing it, I thought to myself, "why not?"
And I have to say, this was definitely worth the years and years of waiting!
Cuphead is wonderful! It pretty much nails every aspect this game has to offer.
You play as Cuphead (or Mugman for Player 2), and your objective is to get the soul contracts of many bosses in Inkwell Isle to try and not get sent to Hell after failing a shady deal with the Devil himself.
This game plays excellently! The run and gun mechanics are very well done and makes for a great experience. The parry technique is brilliant. The game is mostly composed of boss battles that you have to defeat to progress forward. Alongside them are the run and gun levels, where you have to reach the goal, defeating mini-bosses along the way. Boss fights are either on the ground or you fight them in a plane, the latter which is also done nicely. You can buy new types of weapons and get passive abilities to help you.
Cuphead has one of the best collection of bosses I have ever seen in a video game. They range from giant sentient vegetables, a blue blob, and a clown to a queen bee, a dragon, and a mermaid that is at least 100 times the size of Cuphead. Each one plays differently to each other, which will mean changing tactics to find the best way to defeat them. They are also brilliantly drawn and designed, which brings some memorable experiences.
Speaking of which, the best thing about Cuphead is the sound and visuals. They are a joy to witness. The game is stylised to be like the rubberband animated cartoons from the 1930s, and it is superb. The animations are super slick, the backgrounds are gorgeous, the characters are designed brilliantly, and the soundtrack consists of amazingly composed jazz. In fact, when you load the game, you are greeted with a barbershop quartet singing the summary of the game's simple story, and it always brings a smile to my face.
Cuphead is something that will be hard to match. It is a breath of fresh air that is great to witness. Even with the hundreds of times I have died, I still carry on, because I have not seen anything quite like it.
So, long story short, go play it!

This game is obscure, even for a 4X. We all know our Civilizations or Dominions or Alpha Centauris, but I barely know anyone who's heard of this, let alone played it. That being said, this game could be described a rough diamond. The game has some glaring balance issues, and it's a good bit glitchy at times, but the gameplay is solid and rewarding.
Every game begins like any Civilization game, where you found your capital city and then start to explore the world. However, instead of your standard units like Civilization has, you have customized units that you can design yourself. You also have heroes, which are specialty one-man armies that will join your cause from time to time.
If you've played Age of Wonders III, the combat is remarkably similar. When you enter battle, both factions are placed on the opposite side of the battlefield, and you move them into play until they're in range to strike.
The world itself is incredibly detailed. On almost every playthrough, I'll run into a quest or monster that I've never seen before, and every game spawns one of four special areas of the map where you can fight boss-type monsters and aquire extremely rare treasure. Every game brings something new.
PROS:
- Incredibly varied worlds
- Good combat system
- Lots of "fluff"
- Wide variety of artifacts and weapons
- Useful character creator
CONS:
- Some factions just plain suck
- Game can be glitchy, particularly when loading saves
- Soundtrack's rather forgettable
FINAL VERDICT

I am simply dumbfounded by the positive reviews for this game.  This game is an ongoing tragedy in what not to do as a game developer.  From the very beginning (in its first incarnation as Elemental: War of Magic) this game was doomed to failure.  From its horrid UI, to it's uninspired gameplay, vintage 1990's graphics, and abysmal balance--the game plays more like a college student's unfinished Unity 3D project than anything else.  How it has garnered fans of any kind is beyond me.
I've always enjoyed games such as: Master of Magic, Disciples, Heroes of Might and Magic, and Age of Wonders, so, as a longtime supporter of Stardock/Bred Wardell, I was looking forward to their foray into the realm of Fantasy 4x.  One word sums up my experience:  Disappointment.  For the life of me, I don't understand how a game developer that produced Galactic Civilizations could produce something so unpolished and uninspired like Elemental/Fallen Enchantress.  It's like they didn't even research the genre--they just looked at Master of Magic and said, "Well, we can do better than that!".  The only problem with that point of view is that other/better developers had already made better fantasy 4x games, and had been pushing the genre forward for nearly a decade.
Fallen Enchantress is a failed attempt at saving an aborted development project, nothing more.  A new development director was hired to rework the UI and add (i.e., "tack on") some new features--things like distict races, unique abilites, etc.--things that should have already been part of the initial design--in a desperate attempt to save an already-doomed game.  For some people, this was enough.  Gamers unfamiliar with the fantasy 4x genre liked what they saw, while veterans of the genre just asked the question:  "Why?  Why try to save this game?  Just let it go already."
There are no bright spots with this game--not when you look around at all of the other, better fantasy 4x games that are out there.  As already mentioned, the main flaw with this game is that Stardock developed it in a vacuum, in isolation, and thought they were doing something monumental.  If this were the 1980s/early 1990s, they might have actually pulled it off.  Unfortunately, this game game out in the 2010+ era of PC games, and, quite frankly, PC gamers deserve better than this lukewarm dalliance with hubris.
Also, if you actually compared this game to the Civilization series ..... shame on you.

This is an interesting one. I got this game out of curiousity, despite not being to keen on zombies, and I had a lot of fun with it. Let me start by saying if you ARE a zombie fan, this is the DEFINITIVE zombie survival experience. Its got everything, getting bit, zombie hordes, barricading houses and scrounging for food, building up a fort, getting food poisoning, getting the flu, hell, you can even die of hypothermia in the winter.
The best part is the zombie costomization: for those of you who, like me, prefer sprinters, you can have sprinters. You can have zombies that rot, zombie juggernauts with rediculous health and damage, none-infectious zombies, horde zombies or loner zombies, hell, even blind zombies like the clickers from the Last of Us. Or... Deaf zombies with eagle-vision.
(If you do decide you want sprinters, decrease the spawn rate to 0.01 OR 0.05ish, and it will be balanced.)
Hell, a game without zombies is still fun. You can make the weather harsh and food scarce for a sort of post apocolyptic last man on earth sort of thing. With the promise of NPC survivors coming soon, you could also potentially have a Hunger Games esk man vs man survival thing without the zombies. And indeed, with zombies, there will be fully dynamic NPC survivors who, like you, are just trying to survive. (Though this feature has not yet been added and I dont recommend getting the game based on this as you never know what will happen, I have faith, the studio doesn't look like its going to abandon the game any time soon.
One of this games biggest pros is yoyr characters weakness. In this game, you dont play as a badass parkour master, or a machinegun totting zombie murderer, you just play as a typical guy (or girl) armed with nothing but your wits and a few perks. Guns are rare, and dont ensure survival at all when you have them, and you'll find yourself fighting off hunger and thirst, especially when the dynamic power and water goes down and refrigerator no longer work, making your character weak.
You'll stave off panic attacks by reading books or watching TV (keep the volume down, zombies are attracted to sound,) you can avoid urban areas and become a forest dweller where there are fewer zombies, (or not, you can change it in the sandbox mode), you can farm, build, cut down trees, etc.
The building system doesn't work like Minecraft, so dont worry. You can only carry a few logs at a time, adding just a little bit more to your defensive wall every day, this can take months.
Best of all - its permadeath. So, unlike other zombie games, there is a massive sense of tension. You never know if, when you wake up in the morning, it'll be your last.
Pros:
Excellent sense of danger and hopelessness: Your going to die eventually, everyone does. When you depart the safety of your mega fortress, complete with thirty defensive walls and barricades everywhere to scrounge for food in Muldrough, you feel a perfect sense of dread. All it takes is one screw up, and thats it, your trapped in the top floor of a house, with ahordes of zombies pouring in, bashing down the door, and you realize all that work - all those hours you put in - its all about to vanish. And thats... Perfect.
Great survival mechanics: The mechanics are not simplified into punching trees and placing blocks, like every other generic survival game these days. It is by far the most realistic survival game I have ever seen.
Costomization: You can costomize everything. You can have a game that starts off with next to no zombies, then has hundreds everywhere within a week, you can have everything overgrown and decaying, or prestine as though the zombies attacked just yesterday. I once played as the human Flash - my exp gains were multiplied by 999, allowing me to put so much xp into running speed that I broke and game and sprinted down roads at super speed. Or just play without zombies.
Sort of exploration: The map has plenty of interesting locations to creep through, especially in the bigger town of West Point. But the explorations strong point is the sense of danger, with zombies lurking in the bathrooms of houses, hordes waiting just outside the laundromat your picking clean for the slightest crack or bump, etc.
Realism: This game is hardcore. One of the best things about it though is that it kind of manages to be nood friendly at the same time. There are plenty of common sense things that the game has in it - if you play it thinking of what you would actually do in a zombie infested countryside, rather then thinking of how the mechanics work, you'll find the game works quite logically. Healthier foods, like fruit, sandwiches, water, etc. are more nutritious then just filling up on chocolate bars from the nearest corner store, sleeping in an open room with the doors locked and windows wide open will kill you really fast, and all it takes is one bad injury and your character will die of blood loss, an infection, etc.
Cons:
Repetitive: Even if you can make them your own special zombies, they are still the blind and deaf weakling super slow none-infectious shamblers the whole way through. It would be nice if we could have some other options then just zombies - kind of what I'm hoping the NPC update will do.
Weird, unfinished map: The map hurts my OCD. For some reason, it just sort of ends in place, turning into voide. The parts of the map that are concrete are fantastic, dont get me wrong, I jus think the game desperately needs a more solid barrier. Like a wall, a river, anything
Map too small: I know the team is small and its just an indie game, but I feel like this game desperately needs a bigger map. Actually, not really bigger, the size isn't the problem, just add more things along the country roads, more, smaller little neighborhoods out in the woods. The updates coming out may add Fort Knox and a new city area, which is good.
I got kind of bored with it: The sheer loneliness is good, in theory, but when all you've got to do day after day is scavange and run from zombies, it can kind of get boring.
OVERALL, the game has really good potential. I will be paying close attention - when the NPCs come out, the experienc eshould become far more varied, and with more map coming out and all that - I have incredibly high hopes. If your in to zombies, GET IT. If not, you may get bored with it, but its still worth a shot. 7.5 out of 10, I think.

When I first saw what Stardock wanted to do with Fallen Enchantress, I became excited. All those video diaries about the lore of the world, the customization options, and the options for what you could do made me very excited for the game! Then I paid $40 for a complete mess of a game that, aside from being buggy, was very much a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥project that did not live up to my expectations. I gave up on that, but then I heard of the "expansion" to a bad game with a great concept: Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes! Although it looked like the exact same game for the exact same price, it couldn't be completely the same, right? They probably had to change EVERYTHING to fix it, essentially creating a new game, right? Nope. As far as I'm aware, there is no difference except for maybe a new faction and maybe a new map. As such, here are the reasons why not to give Stardock any more money ever.
1). Tedious city building.
To me, this game looked very much like a customizable game of Civilization that, considering the modders of the popular Fall from Heaven mod for Civ IV were working on this, I expected it to play like Civilization. However, although some aspects of city building are similar to the Civ series, it falls considerably short of it. Settling of cities can only be on certain places, and those places start with a predetermined Food, Production, and Mana. Once you place your city, there is no way to work the surrounding land to enhance them. Instead, you gain more "resources" by building outposts next to resources (iron, crystal, and mana) and then build upgrades on those resources. Your cities do not take part in this process, instead being used solely for unit production. Although you can build buildings to "improve" your cities, they never really seem to improve them that much. The game decided to follow "a lot of a little is a lot" making city progression a very long and tedious task that does not factor in units or later buildings, meaning they take FOREVER to build.
2). Pointless Unit customization.
In the game, you start off with a hero and a settler. You can explore and complete quests with your hero, and found a city with your settlers. Once your city is founded, you are allowed to customize units much like you can customize your hero. At first this sounds really cool; the possibilities are seemingly endless with the amount of equipment you can give your troops to improve them. But then you realize that equiping a troop with horses doesn't make them cavalry, or that equiping them with spears doesn't make them spearmen. Instead, the game simplifies combat to three basic unit types: Ranged, melee, magic. As you can guess, each type dictates how each unit attacks, either from range with a bow or magic, or up close with a variety of melee weapons. Although each weapon has a unique "attribute" that gives them additional functionality, these attributes hardly matter during battle. The only thing that matters is how hard each weapon hits, which leads me to my next point.
3). Simplistic, boring, unbalanced combat.
The game was trying to go for a hybrid between TurnBasedStrategy and TurnBasedTactics. In this case, combat takes place on a relatively small grid (reminiscent of chess) with environmental textures that add nothing to said grid. Both teams start on opposite sides of the grid and must kill each other. This is typically how combat works in TurnBasedStrategies(like Tactics Ogre or FFTactics), however, it is not handled well. The only variety of the combat grid involves the textures, so every battle will essentially play out the same way. Mix that with units that have no range limits, and early battles become a slogfest that is determined by how many ranged units you have/can kill quickly. The most complex tactic is which unit to focus fire on. There is no positioning/elevation advantage, useful abilities, unit variety advantage, or change in AI behavior. The AI have a suicidal mentality, and why wouldn't they? It doesn't matter if they die while targetting a single unit, they are only there to be a pawn in the great battle of attrition. If this sounds like the game is challenging, don't fall for it. This only affects early game, late game is a cake walk due to how OP troops become. Troops, unlike heroes, can be upgraded in SIZE, meaning that more soldiers will be in that troop. This increases the health and damage of the troop unit with each additional member. This means that troops will EASILY out perform any amount of heroes at any level with any equipment. These essentially godly units can only be countered by other godly units, which are...never made. Once you reach the max level of equipment, its smooth sailing.
4). All around lack of variety.
Overall, there is very little variety in gameplay. All the possibilities of the game are quickly exhausted after a few hours. The only victory condition I am aware of is conquest, making the game easily beaten and done with. There is no point to unit variety, so unless you want to create a challenge for yourself, there is no reason to change it up. With no random map generation, Stardock has resorted to selling map pack DLC for maps that add no actual variety or unique experiences to the game. Aside from singleplayer random game, there is a "story/campaign" that apparently tells a lore driven story of...something. I have played the campaign and found it very similar to a random game with extra random scenarios. It is apparent that the developers wanted the antagonist faction to be an overwhelming superpower that the player had no chance of standing up against, but I felt no sense of ugency to complete the story objectives. The final objective is for you to bring your hero into a portal and fight demons as a final resort to stop the "invasion"(or something), but I found myself conquering their unneccessarily large quanitity of cities with ease(once again, late game cakewalk). However, stepping into the portal is a completely different story. Apparently your hero forgots to bring his army, because its him against max level demons. As you would expect, he gets easily slaughtered. This HUGE difficulty spike is artificial and unfair, as there is no way of preparing for it. Apparently the only way to win is to use magic the scenario GIVES YOU, meaning there is no way to prepare or create a solution.
In conclusion, if you like the premise of a customizable TBS/T game that is probably easily modded(?), then this game is right up your alley. It is VERY rough and definitely needs a modder's touch, but the core concepts are there and, in the end, that's all you can hope for...*cries*

My lack of time in the game is mainly down to the start. It has a fairly decent basic tutorial, that takes you through the general concepts and mechanics. Project Zomboid is somewhat of a hidden gem. This game, though in development for over 6 years, is still not released due to multiple setbacks during development. However, what is here is something very enjoyable. You may see bad reviews, but these stem from the very long development cycle.
I have probably spent over 100 hours in this game, when including time before it came on steam. It has lots of great aspects   which set it apart from the competition. However, there are still places which could be improved. Some pros and cons:
Positive:
+Lots of detal put into systems such as Nutrition, Farming, and Zombification. More recently, they have included passive effects from dead bodies.
+RPG elements which improve the more you use certain skills. If you don't do something often, you won't level up in that area. Along with this, they have many different skills you can learn, and some which are affected by how you play.
+Sound direciton is very good, helping to create a suspenseful atmosphere.
+Very large map which spans over multiple cities, a prison, small communities, and more. Eventually, they are supposed to add larger cities to the game.
+Large modding community on official forum and on the steam workshop.
+Zombies being attracted to sounds, smells, and other things they player may do. You have to be careful with your actions, otherwise you may wake up to a horde outside your window.
+Lots of customization on how you want the apocalypse to play out. Do you want the power to go out/water to shut off at the start, or have it random in the near future. Do you want to have old school zombies, or 28 Days Later olympic runners?
+Local Co-op allows for you to play with friends at home, without needing them to own the game also. Especially in this era of games, this is something to be applauded.
Positive/Negative:
+-Basic storytelling, which provides enough material to roleplay. However, you wont get answers on why the apocalypse happened or details like that.
+-Graphics are not bad, but may be lacking to some consumers.
Negative:
-No NPCs as of yet, though they have been one of the major points since the beginning of development.
-Slow development cycle, shown with their 6+ years before this.
-Animation update has been teased for more than a full year, with no release date in sight. This has been holding back most future systems, such as NPCs mentioned above.
-Multiplayer is present, although there is no server browser (at the time of writing this). Port Forwarding is the only way to play, and as such can be a pain at times.
Overall, it is easily one of the best Early Access games I've played. It is one of the most in depth  zombie survival game I've seen. Their work shows that they're determined to make one of the best zombie games on the market, and that they aren't going to rush an unfinished product out the door. If you are willing to wait a while for updates to come out, then this is a purchase I don't think you'll regret.

In short: If you like watching progress bars this may be for you.  There seem to be a bunch of folks who really enjoy this game a lot, but it wasn't for me.
I knew going in that this is an extremely detailed zombie survival game with a huge range of possibilities.  I'm OK with that, and I generally appreciate games that make some nod toward realistic world building (zombies notwithstanding, of course.)  My issue with this game is that it's just not fun.  I only played for an hour or so before I surrendered to the fact that it is just boring, plain and simple.  (I was playing offline, so steam doesn't track time properly; I actually had to play the silly thing again for online just so it would let me post a review.)
The biggest issues I have are with the times required to do anything.  I actually like that it takes 5-10 seconds to fill a water bottle or a few seconds to dig some bit of electronics out of a cabinet.  What I don't care for is things like a baseball bat that takes 10 seconds to pick up, 20 more seconds to store in a backpack, 20 seconds to remove from the backpack, and finally 10 seconds to store in a cupboard when you get home.  If you find a nice collection of goods or equipment to bring home, you're going to spend a huge amount of time just waiting for progress bars to progress while you move items around in your inventory.  There needs to be a middle ground between the time required to deal with inventory tasks (looting, moving things around, etc) being meaningful and being wasted.  As it is, I felt like the game was more about watching progress bars than it was about zombies or survival.
The book system is another offender in this way.  I was unable to actually read an entire book (Basic Cooking, mind you, not Rocket Surgery Level XVIII) because I'm not willing to wait 10 real minutes for a progress bar to complete in a video game.  220 pages at 2-3 seconds per page is a long time to wait while doing nothing fun.  Not surprisingly but higher skill level volumes have more pages still, so yay?  At first I was even more unhappy since the progress bar completely restarts whenever you move or do any action at all.  It appears that you completely restart the book but it does record partial progress (there's a small tooltip that shows how many pages you've read.)  I will say that recipes (plans for an electronic timer, let's say) are learned much more quickly (fewer pages, presumably) so that this isn't a problem for them.
Just moving around and fighting are clunky as well.  Whack a zombie in the head with a baseball bat (you've got to be holding the RMB while you click the LMB, because reasons!) and it falls over.  If it doesn't fall in just the right direction (maybe within 15° off of your current view direction) or if it stumbles back a step before falling then your followup smacks are going to miss.  Gotta take a half step closer and adjust your angle slightly.  Whoops, you stepped on it instead, now you're swinging at the dirt past its head.  Perhaps ranged combat it less frustrating, but I never got there.
If the exploration aspect of that game were lacking while the rest of the game (survival, crafting, etc) compensated for it, that could work, but as it stands, neither part of the game is worth it.  It's a game that is essentially sorting through inventories and watching progress bars broken up by a mildly frustrating game of exploration and zombie fighting.  I guess you die eventually, but I couldn't be bothered to get that far before quitting.

Im major roguelike fan. My favourites include Risk of Rain, Faster Than Light and One Way Heroics, so i have some experience on the genre. But yeah, let's get to the point:
In Dungeon of The Endless your goal is to escape the Underground Lab whilst defending yourself with heroes and different turrets. You start humbly, but as you make your way closer to the entrance, you'll recruit new heroes, and unlock new turrets to keep them alive. But as you grow stronger, enemies grow outright brutal, in strength, variety and sheer numbers...
The game is a masterpiece. I'd recommend it to anyone who's into roguelikes, towerdefence or dungeon crawling. If you're into 2 or more of those categories, you should have alredy bought the game just to see what you're missing.
Here are the pros and cons of the game:
+ Art style is unique and pretty.
+ Music is great.
+ Gameplay is innovative and fresh.
+ Glitches are extremely rare.
+ The story is interesting (if you care to search for it), as are the interactions between playable characters (heroes).
+ Amazing replayability.
+ Micromanagement. Doing one thing over and over might get you trough couple floors, but after that the enemies will slaughter you. So it's important to keep in mind what kind of enemies the floor in question hosts, and what turrets work on them.
- Some of the heroes would need some balancing work. (Im looking at you, Max and Josh)
- The luck factor. As with all roguelikes, sometimes the game just kills you without giving you even slightest chance. This becomes apparent, when you're on the last level, and game refuses to give you any Dust (resource required to power your defences), and then steamrolling you with first big enemy wave.
Long story short, I still love the game. 130+ hours played, and I have yet to clear the Sanitary pod (hard mode). Update, Sanitary Pod cleared with around 140 hours.
Rating:
9.5/10
Don't buy this, it's more addicting than drugs.

Overall, Dungeon of the Endless artistic direction, in terms of both visuals and sound, is a great wee marriage, One that (Despite its pixelated art style) still manages to feel very up-to-date, which brings the game to life. Beautiful.

I didn't plan to write a review yet but due to the recent "scandal", I think that the time is right for me do so. Once Story Mode is out and the thousandth hour has been logged, I might decide to write an update.
Hinterlands has been recieving a log of critism recently due to the mysterious countdown they left on the "The Long Dark" website but in all honesty no promises were ever made so any dissappointment felt by people was due solely to speculation on their part. Hinterlands deserves to be forgiven for trying to increase public interest in their project. After all, a project of this magnitude requires a lot of reasources and having more people purchase the game would certainly help.
Now, on to the technicalities.
Pros:
- The mechanics are very unforgiving and mistakes will likely cost you, sometimes more, sometimes less.
- Equally so, prudent action will likely be rewarded and any perceivable success in the game will be the result of your ability spot and exploit opportunities.
- There is a ballanced amount of randomization which is central in testing your ability to make decisions during challenging situations.
- There are many ways to play the game that can result in success. It depends on the risks that you are willing to take and the sacrifices that you are willing to make.
- Due to the nature of the game, curveballs will be thrown at you. No matter how well established you are, you will find yourself cold, tired, hungry, thristy, and surrounded by danger. Sweat will be running down your face and goosebumps will be covering your body as you grit your teeth looking for a way out of your current FUBAR.
- There are several difficulty modes to cater to your experience level but be advised; if the dificulty that you choose is too low, then you will only get bored.
- The game is well maintained and updated. There are delays, which are frequent, but this is a good thing. The developers have never in my experience, released a half-arsed update.
Cons:
- The way that the game currently autosaves means that playing requires a lot of time. It might change in the future but this is how it is now.
- Since the game is still in development, there are bugs and glitches that can spoil your experience.
- In its current stage of development, the only longterm playable mode is sandbox. If you want this game for story mode, wait for story mode's release before you purchase it.
- I have a particular gripe with the hardest difficulty: "Interloper". To be honest, it's playable and I do like it but because part of the difficulty is created by restricting content, I choose not to since I want to have access to all available content, especially those I've not encountered yet. In my opinion, difficulty should be created by adding content and not restricting it, this incentivises players to challenge themselves in order to experience more.
P.S. If you want to purchase this game, purchase it for what it is now and what the developers expressed it to become. Do not purchase in the hopes that you can somehow influence the developers to make the game how you want is to be.

In the Long Dark (sandbox mode at the time of this review) you will face the elements and nature in order to survive. But how is this different than any other survival game out there? Well, the best word i can come up with is "contemplation" this is a game that will make you stop harvesting a carcass or collecting wood and will make you just look at your surroundings, watching the sunset, hearing the wind or listening for crows or deer.
As for mechanics, like any other survival game you will be struggling with hunger, thirst, the cold and energy. in order to keep in shape you will have to be constantly exploring, always on the move, hunting with a bow, rifle or snares, harvesting berries and mushrooms, melting and boiling snow in order to drink (or just find a decent soda can), changing clothes or craft your own. you will come across several shelters, from abandoned houses to power plants and yet none of these will feels like home because resources will start to be less and less and so you will have to move and find the next shelter, this is if you don’t find yourself in the middle of  a snowstorm or mist and lose yourself and fall into and icy river.
On a final note get this game if:
• if you like survival games
• if you like immersive games
• if you like pretty games with unique art-style
• if you like to support developers which actually make good games
Start your journey, survive or succumb into the long dark.

Being a player who have played most of the Survival games outthere, I can easily say that TLD hits the spot.
The tense feeling when you are out in the wild, long away from any kind of shelter. The howling from wolves nearby, ready to tear you to shreds, while you, shaking from freezing, crawl through the snow, hiding behind the trees, in the hope that those wolves won't see or hear you.
All this, while you constantly have to maintain some kind of directional feeling - am I going north, south, east or west? Where am I, and where can I find shelter and new supplies. The long, dark night is closing in on you, and your view is steady but surely becomming worse.
Your body is shaking even more now. The howls are getting closer. You look in your inventory in search of something that can keep you warm. But alas. Only a couple of branches. You know that if you light these, the wolves will see you.
What do you do?
Tbh, I love the feeling of surviving in this game. Sure, it is a sandbox at the moment, but nothing beats that feeling when you rummage through a shelf, and find a bandage or some type of food! It truly feels like you are living on the premises of the nature - and that you really have to fight in order to survive. Nothing is given to you. You have to take it. Have to use your brains. Everything you do, you have to think about. Do I use this last match to keep me warm, or do I save it to warm up some food for when I get hungry? Do I destroy these mittens to make some makeshift bandages or do I keep them to keep me warm?
Try it out guys. If you enjoy any type of survival games where you have to have at least a bit of brain - then this is the one. :)

The game does not feel well balanced. I understand the challenge of balancing different playstyles with potency and all of those variables. This game just does not feel like it does it well.
I won my first game and only game at this stage. The pirate deck felt like it had received a lot more lovin than the Order deck. A melee unit that is slow as molasses and knocks the enemy away from himself after one hit? Really they could not think of a better way to handle that mechanic when it takes one action to move and one action to attack. You have 5 total actions every turn? How about making it so he pushes enemies within melee range away after his turn.
The pirates are all about speed and control. Which is fine, but after one game it feels like they got the love. Their Dr does a passive 10% heal each round to any friendly units in range. The Monk gives a bonus when you actively heal a unit.
In a game that actions are critical those passives are worth gold and can be an overpowering factor.
They gave the pirates a unit that fires a cannon for 4 squares with splash but can only move one square. The Alchemist can fire for 3 squares and move one square. They hit for equal damage.
On paper it sounds good, in reality the cannon troop has the advantage due to the range variable. There are very few units with movement that can close the distance quickly enough to not use 2 actions doing so.
The Capt Hooks ability can propel him in a straight line to an enemy. 7 squares, not a problem.
The spear guy can drag guys into his reach.
Boatswain can move 4 squares.
They can leave it like that, but the pirates should have reduced health and armor to compensate for the benefit in movement. I am talking about more than 10%.

I might be doing those two missions slighlty wrong to get the 3 stars, but when each mission is designed so that only one way works it can lead to problems if anything changes.

Since I have lots of time, I might as well put a detailed review.
Gameplay:
The first thing I look in a game that I haven't played yet is the gameplay. Gameplay is, in my opinion, the most important part of a game. Without it, it's not a game, atleast for me. Now the gameplay is perfect. The addition of plasmids makes the gameplay very interesting. With the use of plasmids, you can throw out fire out your hand, shoot out bees, freeze opponents, etc. With this in mind, the plasmids is a reason why the gameplay excels. The gunplay is good and all, but the plasmids are the best things in terms of gameplay, atleast for me.
Story:
Now since the game is set after the civil war of Rapture, you are given little context of what life was like in Rapture before the Cvili War that destroyed Rapture. However, the use of voice diaries to find out what was life like in Rapture added in terrffic insight of the pre-Civil War era of Rapture. However, the story of the game is also terrfic with an excellent plot twist that will be as comparable as Darth Vader's reveal in "The Empire Strikes Back". *wink* *wink*
Music:
The music is terrific. It fits the mood well and yeah. That's all I have to say. Really lackluster compared to the other two. :(
Atmosphere:
This is the reason why I love the game so much. It has a sense of mystery that cannot be topped. It also has a sense of horror that I love. Coming from a guy who doesn't like horror games, it's horror isn't too much like the scariest games you know but enough to make you crap your pants. Especially the first scene with the Splicers. That was scary.
Graphics:
They're good. I'm not the guy who thinks good graphics makes a good game. But they're pretty good.
Conclusion:
This game is an absolute masterpiece. From the very beginning until the very end, this game never made me regret buying it. Everything in this game is perfect. From the music to the gameplay to the atmosphere to the story. IT'S PERFECT.

In other reviews you can easily come across with the abbreviation of FNaF. This means this game has had an influence on many other; in fact, one might say it is a genre-defining video game. The fact that it all comes from a guy called Scott Cawthon is commendable.
The game takes place in a pizzeria where our protagonist fulfills the role of a security guard. At night our job is to monitor the various rooms in the pizza place via security cameras. Controls and gameplay are easy and simplistic - we cannot control our character nor are we able to move from one place to another. We can simply switch between the cameras and while we are not looking at any screen we can check the doors on the left-hand and right-hand side of our small office to see if anybody wants to come in.
And this is where the game gets interesting. Cute little animatronics bears are stored in the place (for daily children entertainment purposes) who become murderers at night. Slowly (but surely) they start moving towards us and one of them showing up at our doorstep is inevitable. Closing the doors on each side is a possibility as well as switching on the lights in the corridors / hallways but these all drain our precious power meter.
Every night we have to survive from midnight till 6 AM. Since we are bound to our chair I believe the game is terrifying. The sense of loneliness, inability to move in order to escape and the constant fear that something will suddenly jump at you is just terrifying. It is a horror game in its true sense - there's no blood in it; the animatronics suddenly pop-up in front of us and the screen goes distorted then black. A loud scream accompanies every encounter and we can survive none of them. If the power is drained completely we'll lose for sure; if we leave a door open for too long and not check the hallways we are doomed.
Replayability is great since every encounter is different. If you are attacked at 2 AM on the third night and you have to repeat don't expect the same path taken by the same bear at the same time. Every night a guy calls us giving us some tips on how to survive - I like the explanation of the bears' free-roaming mode as a means for their engines not to get locked up. Graphics are simplistic but they serve their purpose - this isn't exactly the game you'll use to test the latest features a GeForce Titan has to offer.
In roughly 4 years the game has already spawned 4 sequels. There are spin-offs, novels and even an oncoming film adaptation. Hush Interactive's The Dolls and Shut Eye have already borrowed the concept of FNaF. To be honest there's not much else to input here - this is a unique horror game with some great jumpscares and it requires patience to be completed. Amongst all the zombie shooters this is a novelty for the genre.

---The Final Encounter in my game I find the final piece on a Peninsula on the center island with no robots in sight and as I enter the field where the standing stones are, two squads of robots appear on my left and right so i crouch and crawl as far as I can between them before one spots me. then I booked it sprinting across the field jumping over bushes hearing bullets missing me and getting hit by several of them. I make it to the stone and place the final part and the game ends the camera panning out showing a dozen enemies surrounding the stones firing a barrage of bullets and I breath a sigh of relief, I've done it.
What a beautiful way to spend the day. Running in the wide open England countryside. Open fields, birds flying, oh and of course the robotic gentlemen set on turning your head into a trophy. Sir you are being hunted, created by Big Robot Ltd. It combines the tense gameplay of survival games with a cartoon like animated look makes quite a fun combination jumping from humor to horror. The premise is given by your butler Mr.Walters telling the player that the experiment has gone wrong  and you're stuck on the archipelago and that you must collect pieces of the device and bring them back to the standing stones which is where the player spawns in order to return home for dinner and that's all the story you get. Before beginning the game there are options to be chosen before starting your play through. The games starts with your selection of playing as Sir, or Madam purely an aesthetic choice affecting nothing but the dialog spoken to you by Mr.Walters. Once you start a new game then the player chooses their "profession" which is their starting loadout and the choice entirely depends on how difficult you want the game to be. Aristocrat is the default choice and begins your game with no equipment except for some rags and is the ideal choice for players looking for a challenge. Other options vary your equipment greatly such as the inventor loadout which has a scanner which can be used to locate device pieces and Officer loadout which gives the player a revolver and rifle right from the start. Once that's done then the player will be allowed to customize their world by choosing the setting of the other 4 islands you will be going through. The center island at the start of the game will also be the same rural setting every time which are large fields, forests, and small groups of houses but the other 4 islands you'll be visiting can have there biomes changed to Castle- fields with castle ruins that can be used for cover, Industrial- large structures and much more housing making it ripe for finding items but can many more robots walking around , Fens- marshlands with canals and plenty of tall grass to hide in., and Mountains- Massive forests and very large hills with plenty of space to keep away from robots but also few homes. From there the difficulty can be left at the default which does increase over time and based on the progress the player makes but can be adjusted at the start to suit your play style whether you want a casual run or a nerve wracking one. Your mission is to collect all 17 pieces of the device and return them to the center island to the standing stones. They'll be spread all over the 5 islands and your inventory menu will allow you to keep track of how many pieces remain on which islands and how many total you've returned. The only thing giving away their position is the smoke rising from their craters. Also now and again you'll see strange floating sprites going across the landscape to the device pieces and they'll serve as a guide you may see only one or as many as 5 at a given time so it's definitely worth keeping an eye out for them. Once you've spawned in you'll receive some basic instruction of how to play but for the most part the player must figure out how this world works on their own. That is a very poor aspect of the game for various reasons one, in regard to the various enemies that'll be faced of which there are plenty you get no information on them so when the player comes across a new foe they'll be unsure of how to face them and the only way to know is to go head to head with them which is not something you should be doing in a survival game. Speaking of the hunters which are the very first enemy encountered is the most basic and will be most often seen thin, looking dapper and carrying shotguns these machines will be your most common foe. They'll be patrolling the islands usually one or two will be guarding a device piece and they can even roam in packs they have an almost random behavior so it can be tough to tell where one can be moving next or when it'll turn around. Beyond just movement they're random with their behavior with each other  interacting with themselves in random ways sometimes they'll have a short conversation about taxes or show each  other some trophies they may also argue and fight other groups until one side is dead. The way the player will approach these machines will entirely depend on what's present in their inventory if the player has rocks and bottles they can toss them to cause a distraction. If they have weapons they can sneak in close and try to take them on with a hatchet or shotgun. If the player has nothing to use then they may employ a slow stealth approach to avoid being spotted or if they're desperate they can sprint past them and hope they don't land any shots. The way your spotted is dependent on your level of visibility shown on the bottom left corner of your screen if you're running through an open field it'll be pretty easy for the robots to see but if you're crouched in some tall grass unmoving then you're practically invisible. Should the player be damaged in anyway your health will recover slowly provided you have a decent amount of vitality which you keep maintained by constantly eating food that you find in the environment such as mints, cured ham, and a jar marmalade. This is a Terraria-like game, so if you do/do not like terraria, expect your feelings toward this to be similar.
That said, it's not a clone, so don't set it aside if you've already played Terraria.
One notable aspect of this game (though like many other things, it is still in development) is the spellcrafting system.  You can create spells using a base spell type and several spell attributes, depending on the spell type (duration, speed, power, size, etc).  It almost reminds me of Morrowind's spellcrafting, but on Planet Centauri you cannot combine multiple spell types into a single spell (at least as it stands now).  The main downside to magic right now is that it seems fairly underpowered unless you are in sudden death mode (where it is extremely overpowered)
Another interesting part of the game, and possibly my favorite part as the game CURRENTLY stands is the summoning system.  It's fairly similar to pokemon...
1. You capture a creature by throwing a soul gem at it, and can then summon the creature by throwing the same soul gem.
2. If the creature dies, it is unsummoned and must regain full HP before it can be summoned again.
3. Creatures in gems will slowly regain HP, and will regain HP faster if they are not KO'd.
4. You can only have one creature summoned at a time.
When capturing a creature, the chance of success depends MOSTLY on the soul gem's level (currently 1 to 4) and the creature's type.  I'm not sure if other things factor in, such as the creature's level (# of buffs) or prefix (does not always correspond to level; in reckless mode normal monsters are all max level).  If the soul gem has more than a 0% chance of capturing the monster, it will make a lower pitch sound on contact, or if it has a 0% chance, it will make a higher pitch sound.
Planet Centauri still has a lot of work to be done on it, but is already interesting enough for me, at least, to have over 100 hours of gameplay time.  I like to experiment a lot though, so most people won't get that many hours out of it yet.  If all you plan to do is finish the quests/kill all the bosses, it will be pretty short until more content is released (depending on your skill).  Check out their website to see the myriad of other aspects they plan to add to the game!
*** This is currently my most anticipated game, so good job Permadeath!  Keep up the good work! ***

Red Faction: Armageddon is the Fourth game in the Red Faction series and the first game of the series I have played. The game is played in third-person, both as a single player campaign and in multiplayer mode. The story revolves around Terraforming operations on Mars and hostile Martian creatures who attack your Terraformer. The environment is destructible which is a departure from a lot of shooter-type games, and makes Red Faction particularly fun to play. Visually speaking, Red Faction: Armageddon seems pretty average for a shooter, though it was released in 2011. The story doesn't seem all that deep, but you do get to blow stuff up and rampage out, so I suppose like a hollywood movie, if you can't win them over with story, just add explosions. I give it a thumbs up, though I think there are better Shooters out there with more depth.

After playing this game, I have played all the RF games, and I can now tell you which one is the worst. It's NOT Red Faction: Armageddon. The worst RF game goes to Red Faction II. Seriously, Armageddon is better than I thought it would be. The story is ok somewhat, but it's better than in RF:G. You play as Darius Mason, grandson of Alec Mason from RF:G, and he has more personality than his grandfather. He can be hilarious at times, especially when interacting with his S.A.M. (Situational Awareness Module) A.I. The theme of revolution is still here, although not as it was in previous games, you'll see what I mean. The campaign last for roughly 15 hours.
As for gameplay, it's really fun. Geo-Mod is still here. My main gripe is the removal of open-world. That's really a step back. It could easily have been implemented here. An underground open-world? That would have been great. But I like the new weapons such as the Magnet Gun. It allows you to latch magnets between two objects making one move towards the other. Upgrades are nice too. Taking out the baddies is really fun. What I really didn't like is how the game holds your hand. Not only do you have an objective marker, but also an arrowed path telling you where to go, leaving no room to find where to go on your own. I feel like I haven't played enough of this game to be super in-depth, but I have played enough to tell you it's good.
+Great atmosphere (visuals/audio)
+Awesome art style
+Both intense and calm gameplay (one minute you're warming up tomato soup, the next you're fending for your life against wolves). Also, very immersive.
+Cozy Gameplay (As in it's nice to hang out by a fireplace, munching on salty crackers and drinking non-potable water.)
+Good balance of risk and reward
~It's slow; it takes a while to get things going, and it won't be particularly easy along the way.
~Games can be very long; not a good or bad thing, but the sandbox mode is kind of a slow-burn. Endless survival is the name of the game. And that can be fairly addictive in itself.
Cons: None really come to mind.
You'll manage hunger, thirst, fatigue and body temperature, as well your health should you sustain injuries, and select which garments you'll  don as you attempt to brave the cold. A dynamic weather system keeps things interesting, and you'll have to plan your days accordingly so you don't starve or freeze, have time to seek out resources and so you can keep your eyes open long enough to run back to your dwellings should night fall. That is, unless you want to forge onwards in the dead of night, risking an unwelcome encounter with wolves or...other...things.
The game has a relatively steep learning curve at first, but it doesn't take long to get a hang of what you're doing. If you like survival, crafting, a bit of fighting and scavenging, resource management and Canada, this game is for you.

A 2D hybrid strategic tower defense game with resource management elements where you guide your hero towards the surface of the dungeon as you protect the crystal that is your only hope of salvation. Comes highly recommended to fans of tower defense and rough-lite games since death is permanent and every level is randomized.
Game Detail
Name: Dungeons of The Endless
Developer: Amplitude Studio [Endless Space, Endless Legends]
Genre: Tower Defense, Resource Management, Rogue-lite
Personal Score: Hard but is cushion enough to never blame the game but instead each mistake is yours alone.
From Amplitude Studios, maker of such fine strategy games Endless Space and Endless Legends comes a game that does not match their portfolio at all, Dungeon of The Endless; a rogue-lite 2D dungeon escaping game with a dash of tower defense and resource management where every resources count and the RNG hates you.
Despite being their first foray into this genre they took what works and throws out what doesnt and in the end we are left with a compact,clean and functional game where the RNG actually adds level of fun instead of pure hate and grind. Read on.
You are a prisoner sent to a new world where it shall be your duty to colonize it but just above the planet your prisoncraft explodes plunging you straight towards the planet below and stright into the bowels of an Endless Underground Complex.
Will you escape towards the surface? Or will you perish along with the others?
2D retro style graphics that is from the 90s style not the horrible 80s one. That means delicious looking bits of colourful pixel where it is detailed enough for us to know what we are looking at yet vague enough for us to assume a little bit.
Included within the game is an album that fills up as you accomplish objectives showing short bio about the characters and monster as if it is written by a mysterious omni-present being. Beautifully done stuff overall.
Fans of the Endless series rejoice for once again Amplitude has included within your game directory the soundtrack for the game as they have always done. Melodious and well crafted music flows along as chiptune version of their usual fare brighthens up your day in the dark dungeons or in situation where all hopes are lost, carries you forward to the next game.
You start the game in your chosen escape pod with 2 heroes inside and as you progress through the game, more escape pods for your future session that has their own pros and cons to consider although the starting pod is the most balance thankfully.
The gameplay is fundamentally about you defending a crystal as you open doors after doors that each count as a turn and watch in horror as your supplies dwindle, the monster kills you and a myriad of other things. The crystal serve 3 function, providing you with dust so you can power up rooms and make sure nothing spawns there and as the power souce you need to escape from the current floor you are in once you found the exit. Its destruction means the end of the game session and even minor damage can easily set you back in precious Dust which does not carry over to the enxt floor.
Protecting your crystal are heroes that you control up to a maximum party of 4. They can be hired with Food if you happen to find them in the dungeon and you start the game with a few of thems. Each hero are vaguely divided into several classes with the hard hitting bruiser and the fast speedster serving as an example. Conversely their class type also reflects upon their stats and equipment allowed. A trickster type simply would not be able to carry weapons with them but they serve as an important utility with their myriad of skills.
As you open doors which serve as a turn indicator, monsters and other random events can happen to you and without spoiling things the theme of the floor often reflects on the danger that lies behind these doors. Enemies are divided into several sub-types that have different priority with an anti hero monster will target the hero, an anti-crystal will go straight for the crystal and boss enemy will destroy everything in their wake. They only ever spawn in dark unpowered rooms but considering doors and room outnumber your Dust resources by several magnitude you often find yourself being swarm by them the moment you open doors.
To help you with that the game allows you to build modules and turrets to help lessen the diffculity a bit. Turrets and modules uses your precious industry point and science point to for both research and building purposes. Many types of turrets do not attack but give buffs and debuffs instead but sad to say any turrets you have built will be lost when you reach the next floor. Modules make you industry, science and food points respectively but their cost goes up as you place more but more efficient module can be research.... at the cost of more resource point.
Industry point serves as your base building points and the occasional random room where you gamble it for goodies, science points are spent at artifacts room for researching new modules and turrets and lastly food points are used to heal, level up and recruit more heroes. But the little wrench in the whole things are the merchants, randomly spawning in rooms they demand one of your resource point for items that are useful for your hero but the thing is they will sometimes charge in Dust , your most precious resource used to power up rooms to stop monster spawn.
More heroes are unlock along with new escape pods as you play through the game.
Once again Amplitude Studios produce the same minimalist game with the same great quality soundtrack as they have always been known for and it sure is great. Death while harsh is still cushioned confortably by the game so even the loss of 2 of your heroes does not spell doom for your game session. Overall a great rouge-lite game.
Final Verdict: Do it. Buy it.

Industy point is your greatest weakness early on, try to upgrade its module and carefully watch where you are spending but by late game you are swimming in dough.
Merchants sell items.... they also buy. So while you can only save 4 junks to carry to the next floor it might be wish to hold on to them should you find a merchant who can buy it from you.
The most badass hero often gets targeted first otherwise the game defaults to first come first serve in regard to the enemy ai so use it to your advantage.
Easy is misleading, choose Too Easy First to familiarize yourself with the game.
Lastly my name is Chlorique Queas and thank you for reading my review of Dungeons of The Endless.

A child care worker becomes a vigilante reporter entrenched in a plot to reveal a planet-wide conspiracy involving missing furry creatures in Beyond Good and Evil, a stealth-action hybrid adventure. Joining you for your adventure are a stubborn pig mechanic, a genius artificial intelligence, and a strictly by-the-book soldier turned double agent. This game features a mid-sized open world environment whose boundaries gradually expand as Jade (that’s you) unlocks vehicular and item upgrades giving you access to new areas.
Early on in BG&E, you are given a camera which becomes a huge part of the overall gameplay. First, it provides you with a means of income by photographing rare species for the planet’s naturalist society to study. Each photo earns you a fair share of cash and the society will send you a pearl for each full roll of photos. You’ll eventually get an upgrade that lets you shoot discs in camera mode which will be invaluable for solving certain puzzles, distracting enemies, or removing small pests from a safe distance. As you unravel the planet-wide conspiracy, your camera will be needed to secure picture evidence of wrong doing as well as pictographic keys to submit for decryption.
Of course, secret military installations won’t just let Jade waltz in to take incriminating photos, meaning stealth will be the word of the day. Stealth sections are fairly challenging, while having just the right amount of forgiveness. Many enemies can be tricked into abandoning their post or eliminated, however there are also sections where detection will result in a near-instant lasery death and you will be forced to study patterns of movement to find the optimal time to sneak past. For when stealth is not an option, Jade is capable of fending for herself with very fluid combat controls and acrobatics.  This game throws a considerable number of puzzles at you as well, many will require careful observation to find the obvious or not so obvious route to victory.
In between all the stealth action and subterfuge, you will need to collect Pearls, the game’s “black market” currency. Pearls are often found in secure locations, boss monsters, or even given to Jade as part of the game’s plot and are spent at the Mamago Garage in exchange for vehicle upgrades necessary for advancing the story. By the way, vehicles are also an important part of this game, with various racing and chasing segments required to get pearls or access new areas of the game.
Beyond Good and Evil is an amazingly well-rounded gem of a game that has aged quite well thanks to the simplistic art style with its colorful palette. The musical score is also very well done and VA cast are just the right amount of quirky needed for making memorable characters. The game camera can be a bit wonky at times but this is often solved by going into first person mode as a workaround. The PC port of this game does not have native controller support, but that’s also easily remedied by using 3rd party software such as controller companion.
Taking it all in, I found myself having loads of fun despite this being my second play-through of the game. I highly recommend Beyond Good and Evil to everyone. The only way you could not enjoy this game would be if you are anti-fun.
