Sir is one of those games you would either love or hate. This game is so unique that I had a hard time pin-pointing what this game does well.
Sir is a survival stealth game. Your task is to gather all teleporter pieces from five island and gather them into one place. The longer the time passes or the more teleporter pieces you collect, the more foes you will encounter.
First off, I ADORE the soundtrack and the visual design. If it was a war game, it would be boring as hell, but because it goes for highly exaggerated world that looks like other people think Britain looks like it's suprisingly solid. It's great, atmospheric and overall good design. However if you don't like depressing grim colors for 2 hours of gameplay on one save, this isn't the game for you, cause it might look dull to some (this comes from a guy who plays cute games with tons of colours.)
The stealth in this game is very solid. If you get out from a predicament somehow, it really feels like it was your doing. The game is punishing, but just enough that you don't want to give up. Each hour of gameplay gives you more to work with.
There are two features that were a real lifesaver for me. Custom world generation and Multiplayer! With the first one, you can create much more interesting worlds with more decorations and stuff than the default generators, however you need to be quite careful with sliders. The second feature is hit or miss. There aren't many servers (but I host one in my free time), so you might not encounter as many players. If you do, you're in for a great ride. Basically you have to escape the island competing with other players in doing the same. There's PvP, loot and trading! Find a friend, have a battle or form an alliance.
What are the flaws? This game feels a bit incomplete, but every now and then I encounter a new item that got me really excited thanks to custom world generation. For some reason the default one isn't so generous with them. When I found a Thingometer and a Mysterious Talisman, they really enchanced the game.
World generation can be really poor too. Unless you're playing on custom generated worlds, they might be really boring. I would like this game to support modding, so I can add more structures to spawn, more items to create and more enemies to fight! I'm a modder type of guy.
Set up a server, be patient and you'll be rewarded for it. However for the standard price it's not worth it. I would wait for a sale below -50% to really make it worth your money.

Each player draws 6 cards then has 5 moves from which they must deploy, move, cast spells, heal, etc. You can use all your moves on single unit if you chose which makes it quite a bit different than other tactical map type of games. There are 3 factions to chose from each with their own unique units and challenges. The presentation of the game is a bit cartoony which can be deceptive in that there is a more difficult challenge here than the graphics would seem to suggest.
So each faction has its own Deck (3) each set up and seemingly balanced so that you will not be at an advantage or disadvantage to your opponent. The biggest complaint I have (and i can see I am not alone) is that there is 2nd set of cards called power cards you can access at anytime for one use per turn and up to ten times a game. These cards are one time use (as in forever) and although it seems you can unlock a solid amount of them for free intitially you can also flop out the wallet as needed to get a huge stack of them to play with. I really can not say if this is really unbalancing enough to declare this a free to play but pay to win title but I felt like this game was designed to be a "perfect" tactical boardgame in the vein of chess. To clarify by perfect boardgame I mean that if you make mathmatically better decisions you will win over an opponent possessing the same resources. Obviosly having the power cards spoils this aspect which i feel is pretty disappointing.
However the missions which are really more like tactical puzzlers are outstanding and should provide you with a good solid challenge for no-cost at all.
Hopefully the model changes a little bit and the PVP portion of this game catches up a good bit.
I recommend if you like tactical combat or puzzle games and do not mind slow pacing. Give PVP a shot for yourself but for the time being I will be ignoring it for the single player missions.

Star Wars Empire at War and it's expansion Forces of Corruption (included in the Gold Pack) are a must buy for a Star Wars fan looking for a worthy RTS to soak some hours into.
I may not have many hours on my Steam copy, but I assure you I played this all the time on my old PC back when it came out. You could say it was my childhood pc game.
In this game you can play a story campaign of all 3 factions: Empire, Rebellion and the Zann Consortium. The Empire and Rebellion ones take place before and during A New Hope. (You need to run the Empire at War Gold Edtion game to play this) The Consortium campaign takes place after this. (You need to run the Forces of Corruption game to play this) I'm putting this behind it as it's a bit unclear to newer players.
But the game really shines in the next part of the game: Galactic Conquest. This is where you will put most of your hours in. A real-time sandbox campaign with the goal to take over the Star Wars Galaxy. You can do this with the 3 factions listed above. As the Empire you can build the Super Star Destroyer: Executor and the best of all... the Death Star! (Death Star I in EaW and Death Star II in FoC) I really enjoy playing as the Empire with all its technical marvels. But beware even your greatest piece of technological terror has a weakness... and others are desperate to exploit it!
But the conquest works as follows: you have an X amount of starting systems, which you can upgrade with bigger space stations and build bases on to increase income, your army or build it into an impenatrable fortress. To capture a planet one must first destroy the fleet and station in orbit, then you must prepare your troops for a ground assault. After winning both battles the planet is yours! I would get this game for this sandbox experience alone.
And then there's Skirmish, the mode where you can play on a vast selection of space and ground maps with all the units available in the Galactic Conquest mode (except the big ones like the Executor and Death Stars). Here you start with a space station (in space) or a ground base with pre-built buildings and defences which you can upgrade (on the ground). The focus here is more on epic battles than on base building, you can still put down turrets, repair and healing stations.
I played this less, but it's still good fun.
And then you have multiplayer! Yes! Since a few months ago, Disney gave the all-clear to the developers from back in 2006 to release new updates to the game! In the first patch they added Multiplayer which was gone for quite some time after GameSpy got shut down, it's now integrated into Steam! Furthermore they fixed bugs and crashes that were still present in the game. And best of all they made installing mods quicker and easier with the addition of the Steam Workshop!
And then we come to the final part of this review.. the mods! The mods for this game are amazing, from mods that add new units and maps to enormous overhauls that change the setting from Galactic Civil War to the Clone Wars era! This means that when the base game starts getting old, you can just download a nice mod from the Workshop or Moddb and get a whole new experience!
I played tons of Republic at War, Phoenix Rising with my CD copy. Now I found new ones like Battlefront Commander and Awakening of the Rebellion.
So should you get this game? Well I think you know the answer by now. The game is very stable, yes some crashes here and there but thats mostly when playing mods. The game has plenty of content worth of 100s of hours. Great community and modding community with amazing mods.
I'm grateful to the devs for making this game. If you are a Star Wars fan and like strategy and RTS? Yes get it now! As Darth Vader said many times: "It is your destiny..."
Also, a few sentences that will describe the experience of playing this game:
- We will crush this Rebellion with one swift stroke!
- Everything that has transpired has done so according to my design....
- General, prepare your troops for a surface attack!
- Lord Vader, you may start your landing. The shield will be down in moments.
- It's a TRAP!
- Intensify forward firepower! IT'S TOO LATE! *explodes*
- They came from behind! *explodes*
Great fun, simple strategy and is ageing well. Superb that it's been updated to remove Gamespy.

IE in GB1 the fear of a large black murderous voodoo cult where every black person in the story is involved taps into racist fears that the American population have had and yet again portrays black people in a negative light.
MILD SPOILER ALERTS: So the plot that reincarnated people of the past are 'chosen ones' and supior aristocratic blood lines wasn't one I warmed to but it worked in a B movie kind of way much like GB1 worked similarly. The relationship was based on BBCs Sherlock as were the 'analyse' feature where Malachi like Sherlock analyses people at first glance. The relationship between the 2 men and Malachi being a savant is clearly based on this to. The bit were our genius rewires an electrical circuit without first turning the power off wasn't thought through.

There are strong themes of sexism and mysoginy in the way women are judged throughout the story. Yes I know the writer is a woman, but sometimes women judge other women more harshly. I was also a little uneasy with the middled aged men marrying teenage girls.
The puzzles are generally logical and nowhere near as nigh on impossible as the puzzles in Gabriel Knight puzzles. I prefer this, some people prefer HARD puzzles though so if this is you maybe this isn't the game for you.
Graphically I've seen negative comments. For me I think it's a beautiful looking game but I don't play the latest games so it probably is dated, that doesn't bother me but it may bother others.
So for me it's not far off Gabriel Knight 1 in terms of quality.

One of the keys to a good puzzle game is creating something that feels new, but also has an air of familiarity. It is a feat rooted in simple and intuitive design, a form which conjures the thought that, surely, someone must have had the idea already.
Thomas Bowker's LYNE does exactly this. And, no matter how hard we wrack our brains, we can't think of another game that does what it does. Or, at least, none that do it as well.
As the name suggests, the simple goal of LYNE is to draw a continuous line that links shapes of the same type together.
The basic grid pattern upon which the puzzles play of allow for movement along the eight ordinal directions. To complete each stage, you simply trace the desired line between each point. The only initial complication is that you can't visit the same shape twice, or allow lines to overlap.
The game's minimalist visual design, and panpipe soundtrack, provide a meditative feel to these early puzzles. But it doesn't take long for LYNE to completely destroy this illusion of calm.
The first level of difficulty introduces additional shapes, requiring two or three lines to be drawn to link each type of shape. At first this doesn't present any major challenge, but as the grid of symbols increases in number, so too do the opportunities for confusion.
The games deceptive simplicity is part of LYNE's appeal. Restricted grid sizes mean that you always feel the solution is just within reach. Then, just when you think you've nailed it, you realise its slipped through your fingers.
LYNE's final complication comes in the form of junctions, which require a certain number of connections to other shapes to be completed. These - combined with the multiple shapes and intricacies of later stages - form beautiful circuit-styled patterns once the solution is found.
With hundreds of puzzles in the initial game, and additional daily challenges, LYNE offers a brilliant dose of puzzling fun, one which is ideal for anyone who enjoys solving logic-based problems

If you like brainteasing games in a quiet atmosphere without any rush, LYNE is made for you (and let's be honest, the price is really fair for the quality of the game, especially during sales)!

Recommend Purchase: Defnitely Yes!
Pro's:
-Lot's of customization for unique structures and crafts.
-Monster Capturing and Taming System (Capture, level, evolve, and battle monsters, I call it "The Pokemon Mechanic")
-Clear Character Progression (eat food)
-Outstanding spell system allows for crafting unique and custom spells for a nearly endless amount of options.
-Upgradeable gear (through sheer upgrades, random traits, and runes)
-"Challenges" offer a simple way to complete tasks and give a tutorial, AND end goals (like quests).
-Beautiful, and refreshing animations and original artwork
-ABSOLUTELY STUNNING DEV RESPONSE TIME
Con's:
-Can't wait for more to come
-Resolution takes a bit of fidgeting (All resolutions are TINY, and the "zoom" features causes UI overlays)
-Some crafting takes extraordinarily rare materials for simple crafts (Maybe not rare, but not easy to mass produce. I.E. Batwings, and Flowers to create potions)
-Still very early, so gameplay at the time I tested it, is roughly short, as there are only two bosses, and the first of which is rather easy. Also, there are only 8 different armor sets, and no visual pieces for chest/legs. Again, this isn't a bad thing, considering the dev communication! They even allow for player suggestions, and ask what features to impliment next, with short turn around times!)
Let's start by saying this: I've played A LOT of voxel-y type games, and some of the best are (IMO) Creativerse, Minecraft, Terraria. That being said, they all seem to lack minor things to bring gamers of all sorts together! This game, bridges that gap. It is a crafting/building game, with STRONG rpg elements, lots of pre-fabricated structures to explore, and hundreds of visual customization options that allow exceedingly unique builds. It plays VERY similar to Terraria, however, you can capture and tame monsters, level them up, and evolve them, and eventually battle other players. This alone makes pvp enjoyable, more so than a star cannon rocket-fest that is Terraria PVP. You can permanently increase HP and SP by creating and finding different foods, which gives reward to searching for new foods. Gear can be crafted and upgraded up through (I think) 7 levels of rarity, and runes can be added for unique effects (like spawn chickens when you attack, or increased damage/crit chance, etc...). You don't randomly wait on NPC's to spawn, but you go "rescue" them, and assign them a job. They then performing crafting tasks for you, while using less materials, and saving you a lot of time and effort. You can even assign them to be a guard, and equip them. The devs even mentioned that eventually you will be able to hire a recruit to follow you into the depths of hell!
tl;dr
Great game, great potential, lots of room to grow, wonderful devs, and a sure favorite for voxel fans.

This is a fun singleplayer survival sandbox, that's it.
The Long Dark ticked all my interests when I first stumbled upon it. And I thought it had the most honest and unique approach to Early Access; They wanted to make a sandbox to test mechanics for a story driven game. Basically you weren't going to be spoiling anything about the story if you bought in early but could experience the rules of the universe being built. I thought that was novel and I bit. At the time a "survival sandbox" isn't something that was on my radar as something I wanted to play, but it turned out I could get plenty of enjoyment out of it. Still, it was the idea of a storymode with some structure to these mechanics that I was after and the long wait for what I wanted of The Long Dark began. I kept tabs on the progress but didn't over indulge. The grass was surely greener on the other side of that storymode hill. And there were other games to play in the meantime. I was happily patient and enjoyed poking my head in when real world blizzards kept me indoors.
Months turned to years. Announcements turned into announcements of announcements. Early Access turned into xBox Insider and GOG InDev. Cash flowed and creator's dreams perhaps got more grandiose and seemingly endlessly re-imagined. The perils of success. A fawning cult following, myself included, sang it's praises along the way helping it get a perhaps overstated legend status in the gaming world. User-interfaces turned into radial menus and into UIs anew. Many a thesaurus were worn to their bindings titling things. But we got there. Storymode released and once again The Long Dark bounded up the charts and onto harddrives the world over.
An uninteresting cinematic introduction gets you to the beginning of your struggle. Tedium and extremely linear days greet you early in storymode gameplay. There is one way to do things. Immersion breaking oversights like one and half plane's worth of wreckage or non-campfire flames providing no heat are immediate. Magical floating text telling you that you don't need something yet soon follow. The simple idea of a battered and injured beginning just isn't presented in a cohesive manner. The game slowly tries to blossom open to give you some semblance of control and freedom. But you are consistently bombarded with artificial hindrances from fetch quests to conveniently placed wolves. Which lets be honest, they are just zombie placeholders despite the common saying of "survival without the zombies" TLD is tagged with. Always were and now as artificial barriers it cannot be denied. Toss in sorely lacking dialogue presented in text conversation akin to something with a much deeper story. And a "trust" system that just seems like a way to pad gameplay time. A lot of it really feels like padding time early on, maybe to even get to the coveted 2hr threshold. Other things too, like an extra step in making tea that ironically takes even more tweets to explain to the wide audience. All in all that jump in quality from the desolate 'hardcore' solo survival to NPCs, broad appeal play, and abysmal story dialogue writing gets quite stark. I can't quite put my finger on all the specifics but the best way I can sum it up is that the all encompassing atmosphere just isn't there at all. Dud. Weird transitions too. I just don't know. Doesn't work.
I have accepted (my) reality that this is a survival sandbox though. And I'm content with that. But in the coming weeks articles will be written praising artistic this or brutal survival story adventure that or 10/10 something or another. And people will come snooping around based on the storymode just as I did years ago when it was presented as a much simpler idea. So on that selling point of the storymode I would weigh lots of caution. Especially at the new price points. Take a step back and consider what kind of experience you are actually after. I look forward to enjoying this as a singleplayer survival sandbox without waiting for something. Its probably best to rip that bandage off quickly too! Because if I had felt like storymode delivered anything worthwhile Id still be in for months (years?) worth of more waiting as the episodic delivery is only two parts of five at the moment. Something being overlooked or understated in much of the media I've read covering the release.
So the short of it; I heavily caution and warn a closer look if you're here for solely for storymode. Satisfying survival sandbox meandering is there to be had outside of storymode but with the price its well worth a wait for a drop.
PS: Like others have said in reviews, I do wish to add a congratulations to Hinterland for whatever that's worth.

Dungeon of Endless is a fantastic rogue-like game. the pixel art style in games is getting old, however it doesnt take away from this title. Starting out with 2 heroes ,you must travel through a maze-like dungeon consisting of, I believe 12 levels to reach the exit.  Along the way you must build machines at way points you find ,to produce industry,science,and food. these are all used to build defenses,level up your heroes.and unlock technology. Finding items along the way to equip in your heroes inventory is rewarding.Finding and unlocking additional heroes along the way is satisfying as well. Traversing the dungeon is done by unlocking doors, each door unlocked may reveal a treasure chest, merchant,monsters,heroes,resource bonuses, Dust,or nothing. Dust is collected by opening some rooms and by defeating monsters. Dust is required to power a room. you can only buid machines and defenses in rooms that are powered. Some rooms are powered by themselves,however you may not power a room if it is not  connected to a room powered between it and yout starting point. Thhere is a technology that will allow this, but the cost is expensive. You will rarely have enough Dust to power every room. Unpowered rooms will spawn monsters that will attack you ,your technology or your crystal. The Crystal is always in the room you start in. once you find the exit, one of your heroes must carry the crystal. Of course carrying the crystal will severly cripple that heroes speed. you must defend the helpless hero as he/she makes thier way to the exit room. once there any heros in the exit room with the crystal may exit that floor and continue to progrees the dundeon, While you take unspent resources with you ,finding Dust seems to diminish as you reach the final handful of levels. The levels and items are procedurally-generated ,making  for worth playing again and again. Leveling up your heroes is fun and unlocks new abilities. I had a bit of a hard time learning the game. I did have to watch some play throughs before understanding what was really required to be successful. Once you grasp  the resources, how to get them, and what they are useful for  the game actually plays quite simple. While it plays simple Dungeon of Endless is hard and tense at times. You will die often and have to start over, however unlocking new heroes for your next playthrough is rewarding even in defeat. 4/5

When I first was introduced to the game I had some suspicions of the game but as I've played for a couple of hours with friends I thought I would write a review on how the game works and the overall feel of the game with two bulleted lists. First off I would commend the developers of Red Orchestra 2/Rising Sun for the amount of effort into designing and replicating what the gruling war looked, sounded and felt like. The game is practicly a simulation of a real life war except not the same era of combat we are used to. While in game you either pick to be either a Russian, German, American, or Japanese solider in the team select screen though Americans are fighting the Japanese and Russians are fighting Germans. The game depicts battles from the Russian-European Theater and Pacific Theater. In game once a team has been picked you go into a loadout screen where you pick a class, each class varies by team or map but mostly they are all the same except for gun loadouts that change according to which team you initially pick before you start the game. once in game you are then expected to capture or defend objectives and kill other players depending on what gamemode you are playing on. Most of the time when you enter a server the game settings are set to realism, meaning if you if you get shot in the torso or head you will most likely be killed instantaneously, if you are shot in the arm or leg you can most likely patch yourself up and keep moving but you never know. Also the game has a slight learning curve meaning when you first enter the game for your very first time be expected to die a lot, seriously you'll get ♥♥♥♥ing destroyed. It takes time to learn how to play the game so play quite a bit and eventually you'll get better at the game. the realism factor keeps coming into play as there will be a limited HUD system that you can access by pressing the T key on your keyboard.
In game its scary period, you never know when someone is going to snipe or kill you there will be times where you just die for no reason at all and you'll be behind cover
and you'll just be dead. However when you get your first kill things will ease up on you and you'll get the hang of the game play. the graphics are great for a game from 2011 better than most FPS games from 2011 actually. One thing I dislike about the game is the respawn times, sometimes I want to get back into the fray very quickly and it kills my patience when I have to wait 10 to 15 seconds to respawn. Other than that the game has my recommendation.

You should definitely pick up this FPS if you have the money its a great game that would be wonderful to have in your Steam collection. - Biggest Boss signing off

Well, I gave this the thumbs up because I enjoyed parts of it, and it was infinitely better than Bioshock Infinite. But it was still a disappointment in many ways, especially for someone who loved Deus Ex, System Shock, Vampire TM Bloodlines and so on. I'll list some of my disappointments in order.
First, the release of the game many years ago. I was so excited as a System Shock fan. Back then all my games were on disc - I hated online activation, DRM, Steam etc (I'm obviously a bit more mellow now). The game came and there were two problems - online activation, which annoyed me and was a real hassle, since I was on dial-up back then, and it hadn't been mentioned in the pre-order; and the game hardly ran on my PC anyway, just a few frames per second. I tried for a while, and it got to the silly bit where you find a massive hypodermic needle full of scary liquid, and immediately stick it in your arm like a total idiot. I shouted "WTF!", uninstalled, and sent it back to Amazon and got a refund. It was many, many years before I eventually played Bioshock all the way through.
Even if I replay the game now, that bit when you find your first plasmid annoys the hell out of me. You find a massive needle filled with glowing chemicals and immediately stick it in your arm! An intensely stupid moment. Why would anyone dropped into a terrifying environment inject themselves with an unknown substance? Oh yes, because it is actually the red keycard that unlocks the door, I should have realised that Bioshock was the follow-up to Doom, just prettier...
The inventory system was incredibly dumbed down. Everything you search in the world can contain up to three items, regardless of container size. Bodies, pockets, huge chests, even dead opponents with no pockets to carry anything ... And since you can't carry anything but guns and ammunition it's mostly pointless - you pick it all up anyway if possible. It's a far cry from System Shock 2 where you would need peace and time to safely search - or you might grab things and run, to examine at a safe point later, because everything might help, you're scavenging for your life not double tapping for teeny boosts. Give me the clunky System Shock 2 or Deus Ex inventories any day.
Related to items are the guns. There is no need to make weapon choices, or hard decisions between a better gun with no ammo and a worse one but with a stack of bullets - in Bioshock you lug them all around. Though you are strangely unable to carry an apple.
The whole plasmid thing, altering genes via an injection: that was a letdown. It happens in a second across your whole body, and you can suddenly shoot fireballs – no sense of bodily corruption, gradual changes, like a magic pill. In fact, the whole upgrades thing falls apart if you think about it: gain “Adam” and spend it for powers at a vending machine; splicers tearing the city apart for Adam, yet they don’t vandalise the machines for the Adam people have spent, and the unbought powers. Gene tonics give upgrades, in a bottle, like a tonic, so presumably you drink them – yet can swap them out for others and store them in a vending machine – how? Regurgitate into an empty bottle to create space for another? It really makes no sense. It also misses out on the whole chance to make a world of choice where each bodily change is irreversible, you live with it, and if you keep splicing you get more powerful but also corrupted physically and mentally. They could have limited choices, once you go down a route of particular combinations it rules out others, but the ones you choose get more powerful – that would be great for replayability (rather than just ending up with a huge range of powers and guns that are clunky to switch between on the fly). Instead they just become the equivalent of magic spells, hammer away at them, represented by icons of bottles.
The plot had some good elements, some average elements, and some silly ones. The “sacrifice” bit people talk about – that was pretty weak, I thought, when you realise that you become a Big Daddy just to get through a door. Surely if I’d looked around enough I’d find a Red Keycard? And the only bit of the transformation that might have been permanent could have been the implausible voice-box alteration, but I couldn’t take the machinery that did it seriously. I’m sure open-throat surgery with no painkillers would be more gruesome and traumatic than “Whirr, whirr, ting!, goal achieved, time to move on.”
I think part of the problem was that the teaser trailers was so misleading. It made the game look so exciting and scary, massive scale, interactive and reactive, a huge city to explore; the injections were a bit more believable (in size) and horrible. The actual game we got does not feel like that trailer. The game is not part of the legacy of the immersive sims I mentioned earlier. I remember it mainly for the setting and the creatures you meet, but always feeling constrained, restricted. The true Bioshock game has yet to be made.

I've owned the game for a few years now and haven't played it much.  I bought the game when they had NPCs.  Then they removed NPCs and decided to work on things to make it more "realistic."  I feel as that the developers can't see the forest through the trees anymore.  People have been clamoring for NPC's and the devs continue  to work on other things which the majority of users don't care about.
Now they're looking at "caloric intake" as a factor to consider during the zombie apocalypse.  Is it a good idea.  Yes.  But is it more important than what the majority of users want?  No.
The devs were so focused on having a realistic "radio" system.  They spent months working on radio broadcasts.  Then they spend months working on radios for the player in multiplayer.  They have to create walkie talkies. It's it a good idea. Yes.  Should it take priority over what the majority of users want (NPCs).  No.
The fanbase wanted cars.  Developers don't think it's a priority.  It was ignored.  So modders created cars.   The fan base wanted more firearms.  Developers didn't thin it was a priority.  It was ignored.  So modders created firearms.  I could go on and on about how the developers just ignore what the majority of the fans want.
Did I mention there is still no in game map available?  No map of the area since the game was created.  Some guy had to create a map of both play areas so you can have a vague idea of where you are.  You have to alt tab to the map website and figure out where you are.  Oh, it's realistic.  But is it fun?  Nope.  If they wanted to be "realistic" they could allow GPS technology with google maps for the first few months of the zombie apocalypse and then have it shut off . . .
Also, the zomboid fanbase is rabid.  You say anything against the developers they pounce on you like a bunch of . . . zombies.  I'm sure I'll get a good amount of flame from the zomboid acolytes from my review as it is forbidden to be critical unless you are punished.
Other problems - my game is constantly stuck on "updating workshop content" in an endless loop.  Uninstalled the game, deleted the folder.  Verified game cache before I did this.  Nothing works.  By the way, the game is super boring without mods.
Now on the plus side -
The developers give weekly regular updates as to what is happening with the game.  Not actual software updates. They just tell you what they are working on.
They are more active with their fans (i.e. they actually interact with them) more than the developers of the Fun Dumps, Seven Days to Payout game.  And team zomboid releases more updates to the game than those knuckleheads, even though team zomboid has a development team which is only a fraction of the Fun Dumps.
The graphics are decent and proof of concept ideas are great.  Looking forward to seeing them implementing the new running and side strafing system.  The new 3d models will be good. But nothing has happened yet.
Multiplayer is okay fun.  But it's ridiculous trying to find anyone.  No way to find them with the games build in map.  You have to say, "oh I'm near the quickie mart in muldrah."  Which one?  The partially burned out one.  I don't know where that is.  Well, good luck survivor.  If you do know where it's you'll have to go on foot because you started on the other map.
So, as it is I wouldn't recommend the game in its' present state.  They need to listen to their fans and include the NPCs.  It's been years now  developers.  If you don't care about income then just keep going this route and doing your own thing.  And probably a few things will happen.  You'll close your doors because you can't support development on the game because nobody will buy it.  Or another developer will make a similar game with the features the fans want.
Edit -
It is now 10/14/17.  Developers have put cars in the game but instead of working on the NPC's they decided to continue their pattern of inane micromanagment.   I see they are now working on cars breaking down and having to salvage parts to get the car running again.  They are working on tons of little things that really don't add value to the game.  Check out the developers notes and you'll see what I mean.
They had NPC's when the game came out.  The fans (see below) are saying they are working on NPC's.  From the time they removed the NPC's to now . . . how many years has that been?  Three years?  Four years?  Developers make complete games in that time period.  What's the holdup??
Last time I checked, developers are in the business to make money by selling their product or service. They listen to what their customers want (called "marketing research") and focus their efforts in that direction. That's not what this developer has done.    They treat the development of this game as something they are making for their own personal satisfaction, rather than to satisfy customers and make sales.
To the people who posted below, here are my general thoughts.  An in-game map (with a GPS or whatever technological magic) might not be realistic but it would add to the fun factor.  You may disagree but don't you think it should be an option for gamers?  If you don't want to use it, the developers could have a checkbox to toggle it off.   There was obviously a demand for a map.  And because the developers couldn't or wouldn't make the map in a timely manner, a customer had to do it for them.  And now maps are in the game.  Yet another example how misguided this developer is in thier business plan (or lack thereof).
Priorities - Vehicles - took them a year (at least from this post) to put them in.  NPC's were initially in and then removed.   Why is is that they can create something from scratch (vehicles) in a year and yet can't complete something they had once before and then removed?  Answer?  It's not a priority for them, even though it's a priority for their customers.  It would be interesting to have a poll on Steam by the developers to see what they should be putting their energy in next.  List NPC's as an option (not "what color should the cabbage in the fridge be?" which is their usual micromanagment mode).  Keep the poll open for two weeks and get some feedback.  When NPC's are selected, see if they continue to move at glacial pace or instead put some coal in the fire to get the train moving.
Also interesting to note that they removed Steam customer's ability to comment on their weekly "updates"  section (if you can call them updates).  I suspect due to the amount of criticism they are receiving from the people who bought their game and the direction they are taking it,  they redirect ed comments to their website so they can moderate and delete them.  Sorry developers, no amount of damage control will stop this ship from sinking unless you change your course.

It's a great game if you get it on sale. This is a multiplayer only game with a bit of a story that develops while the hunters are getting dropped into the fight. It does offer a single player mode where you fight against bots to practice your hunter or monster skills. As much as I love this game, it's a great game if you get it on sale. The multiplayer is great and keeps you on your toes the entire time when you are fighting a great team, and that is where this game shines. To get the best of evolve, you want to fight good hunters or a good monster. I have never played a game where the multiplayer action is as nail biting as this.
The DLC content is completely optional. If you cannot purchase the monsters or hunters, it doesn't mean you cannot play with them. You will be able to fight alongside all the DLC characters. Most of the DLC content is cosmetic skins for the exception of playable hunters and monsters which I agree, should have been part of the package. That is why you should purchase this game on sale. Plenty of sites where you can get it at lower prices.
There are also plenty of weekend events that take place almost every weekend that the developers put out. You will get skins for your characters if the challenges they put forth are completed as a community which inlcudes the console community as well.
TLDR: PROS: Buy it on sale. Multiplayer is amazing and jam packed with action. Developers are involved. Plenty of DLC cosmetics for sale.
CONS: Playable characters and monsters DLC has to be paid for, when it should have been part of the game to begin with.

Bitter, crushing disappointment.
I loved the Gabriel Knight series of games, as well as Jane Jensen's early forays into adventure games like KQ6 - so I had at least moderate hopes for this game. I got it I believe as part of a kickstarter as well as the GK1 Remake, which is another story.
This game made me realize just how important the vibe of a game is to the player as well as the writing. Gabriel Knight was beautifully written (and admittedly a little hammy from a not so rose tinted perspective) - but it had ATMOSPHERE. Through the myriad of jerky animation and excruciatingly annoying voice acting - this game felt lifeless, cheap. I couldn't get past the first few screens. The interface was also painful. I had to turn it off.
And the thing that frustrates me most - is that the team behind Moebius seem to see all of this as less important than the writing itself. They crush criticism on their forums, and hide behind a screen of people who are able to let nostalgia light their gaming fire.
Well guess what, guys? I'd prefer pay whomever owns the rights to the original Gabriel Knight and buy it again, than play either this or GK2014. Because they both suffer from a huge lack of quality control. The original Gabriel Knight may be low resolution and 20 odd years old, but it was a beautifully crafted piece of storytelling from the ground up. You may say that budget is an issue - then make smaller projects so you can produce higher quality content. Because until I see something of a higher calibre, I'm never spending my money on anything Pinkerton Road makes again - and will actively campaign against it.

This is a commercial failure with top-of-the-line writing by one of the industry's most veteran adventure creators. If ever there was proof that the mainstream market has given up on this genre, it's that this wasn't one of its year's top sellers. I can't recommend it enough. A brilliant story, solid acting, fun puzzles, investigation mechanics... if none of that means anything to you, just quietly go back to Doom.

Moebius: Empire Rising is a dramatic point-and-click adventure game in the style of Jane Jensen's earlier titles, such as the Gabriel Knight series.
You play Malachi Rector, a New York antiques dealer who also happens to be a non-violent psychopath with exceptional analytical abilities. Early in the game you're contacted by the head of a mysterious organisation and asked to investigate a murder in Venice. What you uncover leads Malachi through a life-changing journey across the world to discover more about the Moebius theory, and friendship.
The graphics in Moebius: Empire Rising are a weird mix.
Backgrounds are generally great and the mix of hand-painted and photographed textures and images is usually quite well done, with a few notable exceptions (e.g. the wedding photo in the Billionaire's house looks rather odd). Dynamic lighting in the final scenes is also rather good, although the water reflection effects caused significant slowdown for me.
The character models, though, are odd, with some strange animations and facial expressions, and limbs and joints that look rather unnatural in some scenes.
The game has a certain offbeat graphical charm, but I've found myself laughing out loud a few times at some of the scripted scenes that are supposed to be the most dramatic.
Music is used to great effect, and sounds are acceptable. The game is fully spoken, and it's mostly done extremely well, but Malachi's accent is all over the place; I assume it's supposed to be British, but some of the words are pronounced in a distinctly American manner.
Moebius: Empire Rising plays like a traditional point-and-click adventure game, similar to Jane Jensen's earlier games. With Malachi's antiques business, complete with a very organised female assistant, I felt like I was playing as an alternate-universe Gabriel Knight, although Malachi is nowhere near as charming and likeable as Gabriel was.
The puzzles in Moebius are not as interesting as Jensen's earlier games, though, and consist mainly of very obvious "use this item there" solutions. Sometimes you'll find an object that you know you'll need later, but the game won't let you pick it up until you've done something else, so there's some backtracking required, but it's only a minor annoyance.
Overall, the actual gameplay seems to take a back seat to the story, which is fine in an adventure game like this. The addition of Malachi's smartphone seemed like it would be a good one at the beginning of the game, but in the end it was only really used as a way to provide the player with very limited in-game information and a reminder of progress; I found myself ignoring it most of the time. I do have to wonder why Malachi needed a flashlight in one section, though: I don't think I've seen a modern smartphone without a flashlight app.
There are a few points in the game where Malachi freezes, preventing you from doing anything for up to 30 seconds or so, but these were only a minor annoyance; the game always came back eventually. The game also features some timed quick-time event sequences, which are terrible and have no place in an otherwise-traditional point-and-click adventure like this one. I'm not even sure what I did differently to succeed rather than fail at one of these events (Walker on Malachi's balcony); it was more luck than skill.
Steam Achievements are integrated into the game, but as seems to be inevitable with point-and-click adventure games on Steam, it's likely that you'll miss some of them unless you're using a guide. Since this type of game has a completely linear story, it has next to no replayability, so I don't really like this approach; I don't want to spoil the game by using a guide, but I'm not going to play through it all again just to get missed achievements. It's not unique to Moebius, though, by any means.
Pros:
+ Interesting story
+ Solid writing and high production values
+ Mostly great voice acting
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Timed events don't really work
- Some funky character animations
- Overly dramatic parts of the story just come off as amusing
- Puzzles are a bit disappointing
- Malachi's accent is not quite believable
Moebius: Empire Rising is a solid point-and-click adventure game in the traditional style, with an interesting story from one of the masters of the genre. Unfortunately some of the most dramatic moments fall a bit flat, but if you enjoyed Jensen's earlier work then this should keep you interested, too.

The one thing that can be said about Cuphead is that it's a 'beautiful' game. Yes, it is beautiful in its visuals, gameplay, character/boss/level design and else, but its beauty, I felt, reaches beyond a mere composition of its elements. The game is definitely challenging and will leave your hands sweaty and aching after most bosses, but (with the exception of a couple bosses perhaps) it is not THAT hard to the point it will keep you down and frustrated. Rather than an overbearing sense of challenge and difficulty branded across it, what Cuphead does is tease you very, very thoroughly with every stage of a level, so that the true goal becomes 'figuring out' all the challenges it throws at you and beating a boss is just a very tasty cherry at the top. Ultimately, I found Cuphead to be the kind of treat that isn't meant to be a super-frustrating challenge, at the end of which comes an unearthly relief and satisfaction, but rather a cherishing and refreshing experience that reminds you that YOU can get better at challenges you encounter, as long as you throw your head at it enough times.
A list of pros/cons would make such a piece of heart huge injustice. Therefore, my only con is that in some levels, some elements on the screen and especially FOREGROUND elements (looking at you, damn Junkyard Robot) can be highly distracting and will definitely frustrate any player with the slightest of attention deficit problem. Otherwise, 10/10 genuinely.

Cuphead is a fun thrilling third-person shooter with the majority being boss battles and some platformer levels. The difficulty isn't easy, even in Simple Mode; the difficulty doesn't change and bosses are only shorter, so this game isn't for you if you can't keep up with the game's pace. (Actually, the game doesn't even let you progress if you play the bosses in Simple Mode.) However, the controls are fluent and gameplay is great. All the levels require memorizing how to dodge/counter a boss's attacks or safely get through a platforming level. In the Regular Mode for boss levels there are usually three main stages, and they always have different attack patterns. All the bosses stages are very creative and I applaud the developers for this. Every boss comes off as original even if based on something else, such as the cat that resembles Tom from Tom and Jerry. (Is that technically a spoiler?) For both the boss and platformer levels, there's no checkpoints, making you get it in just one try. The platformer levels are literally run and gun, so run, shoot, jump, and dash your way to the goal! You could also play as a Pacifist in the platformer levels by not killing any enemies. Every time I lose a level I have the urge to play it again and again until I succeed, which makes this game super addictive and a great time-consumer. The artstyle is exactly like "rubber hose animation" used in cartoons from the 1930's. All the traditional hand drawn cel animations and watercolor backgrounds in this game were done by the creators and their animation crew, so this game took a lot of time, effort, and dedication to make. Then there's the music! Cuphead's OST (Original Soundtrack) was composed by big band recording sessions, creating the original jazz recordings and other themes of music the game's description mentions. All the music works great with all the levels! Like the visuals, Cuphead's soundtrack is just like the times it captures so well. This game's price is currently $21.99 CAD and let me tell you, this price is a bargain considering this game's visuals looks so beautiful and is just super fun to play (with the vibe of feeling like I'm immersed into a cartoon). Yes, the game may be short, but beating any level can take a very long time. You can have multiple playthroughs because this game isn't one that gets old after one playthrough, so you can play this again in the more challenging Expert Mode after completing it normally if you think you're good enough! Or try co-op mode! I do recommend using a controller (I use a PS4 controller but whatever works for you) because it feels better than with the keyboard. This game has full controller support. And for local co-op, all you have to do for that is open the game, open your game file, and then connect your controller, simple.
Difficult, but not impossible. A controller is highly recommended.

I haven't reviewed many games, but I've logged more hours into this game than any other in my library so far, including Skyrim. It's a very detailed strategy game that includes Civilization style kingdom/empire building from a starting date (after a world-shattering cataclysm) until you achieve one of multiple possible victories over the competition. Similarities to Civilization include focusing research to unlock new city improvements, resources, units, and abilities; expanding your country through exploration or conquest; making trade agreements, treaties, and war with other factions; and turn-based actions for all levels of the game.
However, this game also includes a lot of plot. There are some default scenarios you can play to see what the underlying relationship is between each of the sovereigns. Even if you choose to just do a custom map or pre-set map without a scenario, you are able to control a soverign character and heroes s/he recruits to complete quests, explore the map, and level up customized ability trees. This comes into play into the larger faction planning because leveling these characters unlocks abilities and bonuses that can boost any other aspect of the game and can lead to extremely powerful units that can trounce through ordinary enemies. There's not as many factions as similar games, but the bonuses are fairly unique to each sovereign and allow for enough variation that trying different game types is a good way to learn new strategies.
The fantasy theme is also very fun. There was a lot of effort and creative writing with the incredible number of quests and lore that is inlcuded in each game. The DLC adds even more.
Overall, I just haven't gotten bored with this game. It's a lot of fun and worth the full price, though I did find it on sale when I purchased it. That said, if I had played a demo beforehand, I would have gladly paid the full price if no sale was offered. I had no qualms about paying for DLC, each of the ones I have so far were worth it.

It's funny how this game is nearly 15 years old now, but feels more relevant than ever. Beyond Good & Evil is basically a game about journalism, and how important a role it plays in society. Playing it in 2017, it was almost eerie to see how relevant it felt to current events. That theme and the way its presented throughout the story feels like unique territory for gaming, making this a really special game. On that merit alone, I'd recommend this to anyone who's interested in seeing how a big studio game can effectively tackle real world issues like any other art form.
Though, it's important to know what you're getting into. This game is from 2003, and it really shows. While playing it, I couldn't stop noticing all of the outdated trends of the era used here. There's obligatory stealth, arbitrary, collecting, generic Zelda-esque action, and goofy PS2-platformer humor that doesn't quite mesh with the game's tone (it feels like someone shoved Ratchet & Clank's jokes into a completely different game). None of it is purely bad, but it certainly doesn't age well making certain sections of it a slog. It's also a very buggy game (again, as you may expect). In one of the biggest cutscenes in the game, the dialogue track completely cut out for me, so I missed a pretty major section.
If all of that sounds like it'd drive you crazy, then I wouldn't recommend it. But I still maintain that there's enough value in this to warrant checking it out. I think it's one of the more effective studio games I've played in terms of how meaningful it feels. This should be at the center of a video game museum, showcasing how the medium of games can do more than simply entertain us.

Short Version: Overall, this game is not worth its price tag. Absolutely wait for a sale if you really want this game.
Long Version:
Well, storymode finally came out after about three years of waiting. So props to Hinterland for finally being able to get two out of five episodes of storymode out. The episodes themselves are okay and maybe it's because I waited for so long, but they feel underwhelming in a way.
The pacing felt off in the beginning. It felt like that the devs were just throwing things in your face way too quickly instead fleshing it out and giving you a little more backstory into what is going on in a well paced way. Though, you do find out what is going on through flashbacks; however, they felt a little rushed and unemotional. They almost seemed out of place whenever they appeared. Also, do expect the beginning of the episode to be a little boring since it’s mainly just tutorial type stuff.
Once you get past the beginning though, then it starts to feel better. You don’t feel as restrained by some invisible entity, it’s more freeing.
However, it gets soured pretty quickly when you encounter wolves and don’t have much to defend yourself with. This game touts itself as being free of zombies, but the wolves in this game are very much like zombies. They’re overly aggressive under the excuse that the apocalypse turned them that way. They show up far too frequently and are a nuisance to deal with, especially after being attacked by one only to have it come back ten seconds later and kill you.
Besides trying to avoid wolves, you are also trying to make sure that you don’t starve and become dehydrated. Sounds simple and normal for a survival game. Too bad the eating and drinking in this game is incredibly unbalanced. You could take 4 pounds of meat from a deer, cook it all, eat it, and then still be hungry. You could also drink to your heart’s delight, then rest in a warm bed for the night, and wake up dehydrated. Food and thirst drain way too quickly. Also there is not enough food around because your tools for harvesting meat from deer degrade too quickly, making it hard to keep a stockpile of food around.
After about twenty minutes of trying to keep your character fed and quenched, it gets so tiring because all you want to do is make progress, but all your character can do is moan and groan about being hungry and thirsty. It gets in the way of progress too much and begins to feel like micromanaging.
This is especially a problem when

I’m finding it really difficult to get through episode one because of how frustrating the wolves are, how tedious eating and drinking is, and just how generally boring this story mode is.
General/Sandbox:
I realize that I liked this game a lot better when everything was much simpler; when I didn’t have to worry about intestinal parasites, hypothermia, frostbite, etc. That was when the game was most fun for me because I didn’t feel like I was trying to micromanage everything, I could make progress and have fun while doing so. The atmosphere was great and exploring felt satisfying. As of now, it feels like a chore to play. Things that have bothered me in the game are:
-	Items degrade too quickly
-	Food and thirst drain too quickly
-	Wolves are a nuisance rather than a threat
-	Too many overly aggressive zombie-like wolves
-	Repetitive
-	Restrictive with what you can do (no sleeping on the floor without a bedroll, no fire indoors)
-	Backpack weight issue (clothes you wear still count towards being in your backpack)
-	Clothes take away running speed
-	Bad UI design (you’ll be navigating/loooking at menus more than exploring at certain points in the game)
-	Breathing effect at night/in the dark is really distracting and makes it hard to see
-       No jumping (wouldn't be so bad if the character could also lift their leg over a three inch ledge or log. You'll get stuck on the terrain often, especially on itty bitty clumps of snow)
Which is such a shame because the game was great and fun, but it slowly lost its charm over time.
The game is decent, but Hinterland is constantly lying to its customers. Eternal delays, lack of content and a misty future for this super hyped game. DO NOT BUY

text:
November 20, 1942
Modern Day Volgograd (Stalingrad)
Mortar shells rang in the frigid air. Artyom, Evgeny, and Sergei were huddled near a rock inside of a mortar hole. They each clutched rifles in their shivering hands. There was no emotion in their eyes. None but fear. Fear was what drove them to run through this blood-spattered, cold and unforgiving hell, and fear was what made them kill young men, young men who probably did not differ much from them.
They were the last remnants of their squadron, with the rest being gunned down in the the advance. The counter-offensive was in full storm, and the 3 were in a woeful spot. Alone in enemy territory, they stayed on alert inside of the mortar hole. Bodies of their comrades were littered, just metres away from the hole. If they dared to retrieve them, a swift bullet would be the reaction from the Germans, who had setup a machine gun post near the hole.
Eventually, after a few brief minutes of relative quiet (or what you would call quiet when your ears rang and artillery thundered miles away) they relaxed. Evgeny, the old seargent, took out a few cigarettes, and passed them around. Relieved, young Artyom and Sergei took them with gratitude, thanking him. They each lit their cigarettes over Evgeny's lighter. Smoking them, their minds calmed. It seemed that the Germans had thought all their number was wiped out, and were not going to send in an advance party to check the hole. For Evgeny, who realized it first, it seemed that atleast they would not be killed by advancing Germans for the moment. They all depended on their comrades in the back to come and rescue them now. And patience was soon wearing thin among the 3.
Whispering to not attract the attention of the Germans, Artyom started asking about Sergei's family, for lack of anything better to do.
"So, what was home like?" he asked.
Thinking back, 16 year old Sergei thought dreamily of his house on the hill, his brother who would run in the woods with him, the warm food served by mom, and the foolish things he did growing up.
"Well, I was born in Chelyabinsk, in the Urals. I grew up with my mother, father, and older brother. My father worked in the nearby factory, and me and my brother would play in the forest, chasing each other, throwing rocks at squirrels, and seeing who could climb the tallest trees. Our house was a cottage on a hill, with dozens of neighbours around us. The neighbours would sometimes join us when we played tag, or chased girls in the streets. But it all changed, soon. The houses were being emptied for suitable soldiers. The commisars said that they were being driven to fight "The Evil Fascist Scum", who they said were out for our homes, and it would be a most glorious way to help Comrade Stalin if we fought them. Everyone who looked 15 or older were taken, sometimes forcefully. My brother was one of them."
Sergei struggled to say any more. He held back tears in his eyes as he thought of his older brother.
"Dmitry was a tall, foreboding figure, but he was as kind. He wasn't the type of person to go to war and kill. But he got recruited nonetheless. I have not heard from him since, but I fear the worst."
He paused. He could speak no more.
"And what about you, Artyom? What was your home like?"
Artyom was contemplating memories, but right as he was about to say a word, a mortar round landed right near them, and a piece of steel shrapnel chopped off his head. Blood pooled around the headless body, and Sergei stumbled back, terrified.
"Artyom!?!?"
"GET DOWN!!" yelled Evgeny.
Shells started to strike left and right of the large mortar hole, creating scattered smaller ones.
Sergei and Evgeny ducked with their hands above their heads. The sound rang in their ears, like thunder and lightning.
Evgeny thought about his wife and kids in Leningrad. He knew that he would probably never see them again. He had accepted this long ago. But now, in the storm of artillery, he could sense that the end was near.
Sergei could not remove the image of headless Artyom as he ducked and hoped that by some magic, the explosions would stop.
They didn't.
November 21, 1942
The squadron was moving up, now that the machine gun post had been bombed. They charged, bayonets out, into the Germans. Rifle fire mowed down many, leaving them to scream in the dirt and snow. Infront of the machine guns, was a mortar hole. Much of them dived into the mortar hole, to see 3 dead bodies. One has headless, with his head rolling around on the other side of the hole. Another died clutching his head, only to have a shrapnel round slice straight into it. The other one was lying, motionless, rifle in hand, and a photo of his wife in the other.
10/10 will never look at AI Sergei, Evgeny and Artyom the same again.

Moebius: Empire Rising is a classic PnC-adventure.
Good:
Story: The story of Moebius is pretty decent overall.
Voice acting: The voice acting, is solid, I have nothing to criticize here.
Bad:
Gameplay:
You can die in this adventure game. But considering that there is neither autosave nor checkpoints this was a bad design decision.
There is a game mechanic that lets you analyze characters (and sometimes objects). This mechanic is supposed to give you clues. But often those analyses can only be solved by guessing, so it creates just as many problems as it solves.
Often you can pick up objects only after some event. Therefore you have to explore the locations multiple times, which is rather annoying.
Bugs:
A variety of bugs make the game pretty annoying. The game also freezes quite often and crashes sometimes.
Graphics: Oh dear, oh dear, oh dear. Prerendered backgrounds might have been acceptable ten years ago, but not anymore. The 3D character models aren't great either.
However, the biggest problems are the animations. They are not only ugly and hideous. Moebius has managed to reach a new low that I did not even know existed: sometimes the animations fail to make their point and communicate something completely different than intended, like making characters look evil or surprised when they are clearly not. The eyes are completely mishandled, instead the characters move their noses all the times when talking!

This could have been a fantastic game - and to some high degree, it is. It has many positive elements that make it stand out and be a great gaming experience, which is why I am definitely recommending it anyway. Coming from the team that created the Gabriel Knight series, this was more or less expected.
The characters are good, the plot is good. There is variety in settings and puzzles, there are some really nice dialogues,  beautiful ambience and gorgeous music throughout. The main hero travels to several parts of the world, after accepting a complicated mission that involves several riddles. While at it, he meets an ally, who seems to be connected to him in more than one ways. Their relationship is extremely interesting, and in particular when interwoven with the - imaginary but very well-developed - theory that runs through the story. Said theory brings together influential people from the past and specific individuals from the contemporary world. The parts where you have to examine several characters and match them with those historical personalities are wonderful.
Like in all purely Adventure games, you have to do lots of research, talk to people, carry out sub-missions, combine info and reach conclusions. You also have to collect important items and use them when necessary so as to move on. All this is very well-organized, although some of the dialogues, especially with people that do not play crucial part of the plot, may feel sometimes like they drag out too long.
On the technical side, the characters (especially the main hero) seem to have a bit of awkward movement, but personally I didn't mind this much because it didn't affect the gameplay in any way. There are a few really serious issues however that make the game frustrating without reason and lower its overall quality.
There is one puzzle at some point that you have to solve; it is based on cryptology and you are supposed to figure out the various options, rule out those that do not fit and solve the puzzle with the one option that is suitable. All this is OK when you play the game for the first time, but what about when you want to replay it? You have to go through the whole chore again, even though you already know which is the correct option and answer. You have to search again, find all the options, rule them out and stick with the correct one. As if this wasn't enough, if you try to use directly the correct option, the game locks the puzzle and you can neither reset it nor cancel it. The only solution is to use a previous save, assuming you have one.
Personally I found this issue extremely serious for a game of this class. A game designer should always keep in mind that their game may have replay value for a player; and if a player goes through a game for a second or third time, they already know what to do and they should be given the option to do just that. I have played lots of games of various genres and this is the first time that I come across such a situation.
Some other time, I had to search a sleeping character. I searched him and exited the activity screen. It turned out then I hadn't searched him enough so I was missing an item. I tried to search him again, but it was impossible. Again the puzzle was locked and I had to reload. I don't know if this was an actual technical glitch or if it was designed that way on purpose so as to frustrate the player, but if it was the latter, it succeeded.
On another occasion you are in Washington, visiting a woman in her apartment, and you have to take some info from her. To make her talk, you have to flirt with her in various ways, and part of the process is bring her whiskey as gift. And what do you have to do? Fly back to Manhattan, because Washington obviously has no bars, buy a bottle from the bar opposite the hero's office, then take the plane and return to Washington. Oh, and if you try to buy the whiskey beforehand (ie, before flying to Washington in the first place), you are unable to. I know it's a game and realism is not exactly necessary, but some things are just too much.
Despite all this, I did enjoy the game and liked it a lot, although I am not very much into this genre. There is enough mystery and intrigue to keep you interested, and there are a few pretty intense situations that you will surely remember for a long time.

Industry veteran Jane Jensen joins forces with Phoenix Online to deliver a new adventure. The result?
Contrived writing and formulaic characters (not exactly surprising if you've read that Jensen interview on Gamasutra...), mostly vapid ideas, some daft puzzles, but clearly the most eminent problem lies with the Holmes deduction process analogue mechanic: it probably sounded a great idea on paper, in practice the solution is either a) blatantly obvious, akin to compiling a simple form b) total guesswork: "what did they have in mind when putting together this trope-y character?"
The execution looks budget, with the usual issues stemming from the use of 3D characters; it's not intolerable, more like excusable, what with the KS campaign having raised slightly more than 400 grand, but definitely noticeable. At some point the game was updated to Unity 5, and it appears the job was likely done hurriedly, leaving behind very obvious bugs. There's also some blurry textures here and there.
Noteworthy: while the game is under most respects almost exactly what you would expect from a modern adventure in terms of general experience, it does bring back some old fashioned design decisions nobody really missed in the first place; in one instance, it combines them like inventory items to unleash maximum mayhem on the unsuspecting player: the Rubber Tree lesson went out of the window here in favor of a throwback to the heyday of Sierra, and there's no manner of autosaving or checkpointing, so it's definitely possible to be forced into replaying a whole chapter (or two). If you hated Resonance for not saving close enough to the ending, this one may elicit long strings of insults.
Nevertheless, I couldn't muster a real dislike for the game; it shares elements with Cognition, and indeed many Phoenix people have worked on this one as well; but past the opening and on to the second episode, that one already seemed a better game than Moebius.
I would only recommend this game to specific types of players: the indie adventure game renaissance train may have made a short stop at this station, however, it has also long left the platform.

Moebius: Empire Rising is a (relatively) new adventure game by Jane Jensen. If you've played Jensen's previous games (e.g. Gabriel Knight, Gray Matter), then you might have certain (high) expectations.
If you are a Jane Jensen fan, you probably won't be (too) disappointed. Her signature strengths are mostly here. The game has many flaws, but they will likely be tolerated by most.
Additionally, if you are a Sherlock Holmes fan, you are even more likely to appreciate this, as there are numerous similarities (e.g. likable antisocial lead with high intelligence and observational prowess, awkward bromance with sidekick).
If you are unfamiliar with Jane Jensen but like adventure games, then (assuming you even exist) this might not be the best place to start unless you can get it cheap. Also, you should be aware that this, like other Jensen stories, are, uh, somewhat "metaphysical" in nature. If you need a game to be squarely constrained by generally accepted physical laws of reality, then you might want to pass on this.
GOOD
* Good writing
* Clever blend of real and fake history and current events
* Great voice acting
* Good music (though seems a bit inappropriate at times to me)
* Great concept
* Good story
* (mostly) Good art (somewhat inconsistent)
* Interesting 'analysis' puzzle concepts (but, can be frustrating sometimes)
NEUTRAL
* Old school point system
* Mostly easy and straightforward, but some rough points
* Mostly unoriginal puzzles
* Hotkey to reveal interactive objects in scenes (except
) with intuitive radial interface
* Hint system exists, but I haven't tried it
* Low budget CG cutscenes, 3D models
* Many "missable" achievements
BAD
* Weak, inconsistent writing in places
* Some terrible animations (e.g. Malachi's walking)
* Needlessly frustrating
puzzle at the end
* Glitchy scripting, including some game breaking bugs (save often!)
* Some interface glitches
* Aforementioned bugs have gone unresolved for over a year, new bugs were added with post-release updates
* At least one broken achievement
Parting thought - I can't help feel that this could have been a much better game. But, I enjoyed it. There is also hope for the future as this seems quite open for additional titles in a series (though this title is quite self-contained).
Disclosure: I received a copy of this game as a gift from a friend (thanks!)

This is the latest game(2014)  from Jane Jensen, creator of the Gabriel Knight series, a classic sierra's adventure game made in the 90s. She made very interesting puzzles at the time, and some terrible ones, but the end result always won.
Now, she comes back with a kickstarter project that begun in 2012 and came up in 2014, this time working independent, with little money of course, and a new small team of game devs called Phoenix online.
The truth be told, when i first tried the game, the first impression was pretty shocking, and not in a good way... Of course this is a small team working, with a tiny budget, but still there are some things that can't be justified just because having little money. What i mean is, the first impression was bad, and yes, i am talking about the graphics first, because that's one of the first things that you take from a game, but its not the only thing, also the game was bad (aparently) meaning the puzzles, and even the main character was bad, alltough this could be atributed to his akward way of walking (little joke there).
The thing is, the game starts to make some sense some time around the end of the third chapter (almost half of the whole game). The story starts to come around, there's this theory of moebius, of the pattern and these special persons (no spoilers here) and then the main character starts to develop, he becomes more interesting, he's having weird dreams and visions and it somehow relates to what is hapenning in the main story. The great music of Robert Holmes (creator of the gabriel knight soundtrack) comes in full force here, like in old times having some great moments, specially during the revelation moments. The puzzles, about analizing patterns and people starts to emerge  and it's something interesting to try and adds to the game. The graphics, still ugly, get somehow much more better, in terms of finishing and polish. It's like the game almost changes around the second half, and then you arrive at the last part of the game and all that diminishes somehow and you encounter the same problems, and the samethings from the first half.
And that's the problem, right there, a double problem. First, you have no consistency. Because , i liked this game (in parts) , meaning at first i didn't like it, then yes, and then no. So, it's like i've been playing two different games in one. So you have great elements, interesting story, great music, some interesting puzzles, but not at first, and not at the end, so when the game starts you don't really want to play it that much, then if you have patience you reach the good part, and then...in the end, you are left with a bad impression, again.
The second problem with this game is that, ive played it because i like (and knew) about past jane jensen's adventures, and i know what she is able to do in a game, and that's why i even continued playing this one after the start (and i did get my reward, i like this game) but if i didn't knew jane jensen was behind it i've probably wouldn't have tried it, and i don't see how people who are new to her would get interested in an adventure like this.
It's a shame because i love adventure games, and i want to see the genre succeed (and it is coming back in these last years) but not with games like this. The genre has to move forward, have great production values have great game mechanics, be modern, be fun to everybody, played by everybody, not only hardcore adventure gamers (without stop being and adventure game), like for example the Sherlock Holmes games by frogwares.
I liked Moebius, but i don't think it will appeal to people outside those who played old adventures games  (you can try fellow newcomer, but , you are warned)
It's a shame also, because to be honest, this game's story has great potential, and i see why jane jensen would like to continue it. In fact, her previous adventure game from 2010, Gray matter, didn't have as good a story as this , and funnily enough, that game had better graphics than this one. But Moebius has in fact a greater a story, one that it has certain moments that are more close in spirit to the 90s era with gabriel knight. Even the music is more close to the Gabriel knight series.
I have to say, in the end i liked moebius better than Gray matter. Moebius is a better game because it has heart in it, and it is more a jane jensen game than gray matter will ever be.
I can't recommend this game to everybody, but i like it, and that's why the positive thumbs up calification.
I would say that, from 2014, this was possibly the best story for and adventure game. but not the best game by far.

This game is rather fun and filled with a great amount of thrill! Project Zomboid is a game where you create your very own player with his or her own traits and job which will end up changing how you may end up playing the game. If you are near-sighted then you may not see zombies so well far away and may need to play it more safe or if your deaf then you may need to be more aware of your surrondings while your job gives you some perks from shooting a gun to stitching up a wound. At the start of the game there will be water and power as well as a few zombies, yet as you progress the water and power will be turned off as more zombies appear in hordes (you can set the game to any stage so that you may just toss yourself in the most difficult situation). You as the player will need to loot nearby houses for supplies so that you may build up protection for your home base. Now the issue with the game is that once you have looted the houses and built a strong enough base you will end up finding yourself bored! This boredom occurs often in the game for you can easily make any house a strong fort as long as you go through the grind and loot some nearby buildings or kill a few zombies, but when you do confront a problem it can easily become your demise and make you thrilled and excited. A zombie horde can easily find you and attack your fort, yet each zombie is a great threat for one bite from them pratically writes your fate in big letters. House alarms and random noise events can allure zombies to your location or away to your location depending on where the noise had occured, and it is these moments that leave you shivering as you see hordes of zombies walking by to the on going house alarm down the street. You can easily add more to the game with the Steam Workshop for it has plenty of mods that add new maps and new items to the game which will cure that boredom for you if it dare occurs. I reccomend this game to any player that is okay with periods of bordeom and a bit of grinding, yet are also ready to face serious obstacles and battle against giant threats. I give Project Zomboid 8/10 Zombie Heads
