The review to solve whether to buy this or not.
First off, most of the negative reviews are from people with low time spent in this game. Ignore them. Please.
I was a super fan boy for the concept, but I have mixed feelings about the game. I also played in ESL with Epex for a while so I'll give a fairly honest review and this should be enough to decide whether to buy this. Here we go. First the good.
1) This game is fun with friends. Like dead serious fun.
2) This game has a learning curve. It is very intricate and each match comes out different. Yeah yeah its go find monster, fight, run go find monster, blah blah. 99% of shooters are hey put metal bits into one another. You still play those.
3) The DLC scandal is phony. Day one DLC was simply cosmetic. Anyone who doesn't understand that is just stupid.
4) I got bored of this game a bit because of the balance changes that were happening. They released Arena mode and I believe its fun again for people that don't want to raise their skill level to enjoy the game.
5) You WILL be bored if you refuse to learn the roles in this game. You WILL feel like its a running simulator if you dont understand the monster is FASTER than you and you need to cut it off. You WILL be bored, essentially, if you're gonna play like an idiot. You will be VERY entertained if you learn to play this game. Its not your normal shoot shoot reload.
6) I feel as though you need 5 hours into the game (About 20 matches) to understand a single hunter. I believe you need 20 Hours into the game to understand each class.  I believe you need 40 Hours to start playing at a intermediate to advanced skill level with a few characters. 10 hours/40 matches to understand a monster, 50 to play at an intermediate to advanced level. The numbers sound big but the matches go very quickly
7) The hunters are all quite unique and are creative. Theyre fun to use. Who doesn't like launching missiles from space onto a 2 story tall killing machine? Or use a chemical flamethrower? A lightning gun? Thats not even covering the ability to be some very very fearsome monsters. Summon and control lightning, breath fire and teleport around?  Create a huge rock barrier from the ground? This game is a monster movie you can be in.
8) The visuals are stunning. The level of detail in the world, wildlife, hunters, monsters, etc is astounding.
Now for the bad.
1) When this game launched, it was a pathetic mess. So many issues. SO many bugs. It was terrible. I only played because I loved the game and spent $100 on the Monster Race Bundle. Worth it. It was playable but felt way worse than the Beta.
2) The balance in this game sometimes is pathetic. They either don't have good QA testers or idk. They released an Assault with damage numbers insanely high. They then nerfed the new medic's damage and he is easy to kill once you find his counter play, at least before his damage made up for his squishyness. Its frustrating to deal with some of the balancing decisions. It doesn't usually affect normal public matches. The only major balance failure was the aforementioned assault character. People complaining about certain monsters being "OP" just didn't know how to play against them and refused to think.
3) The timeliness of updates is also bad. This is due to the number of issues the game launched with. Alot of effort was put into fixing issues rather than being proactive. As of this review they have mostly caught up, so we will see how well updates work from now on.
4) Very often, updates would cause problems to match the number it fixed. This is frustrating and feels like issues are being replaced rather than resolved.
5) When you have a stupid teammate in "Hunt" mode, you're usually screwed. There needs to be a kick feature. The new Arena mode doesn't rely as much on teamwork and is a great new point about the game.
6) The other game modes are fun for a while. However, no one usually stays for an entire round of Evacuation. Its fun with a full party, not in public matches.
7) Some maps are just stupidly favored. The new maps are really awesome looking but for playing the game are kind of...annoying to put it nicely. Opinion shared by much of the pro community.
8) Terrible marketing and promotion of the game. Absolutely ZERO official statements or effort to correct the terrible, unfair youtube reviews.
9) Anyone who thinks the AI in this game is good...they must be REALLY terrible at this game. Its okay to start off against, but you should quickly surpass it.
General thoughts:
I was entertained consistently for 350 hours before it started to wear on me a bit. It seriously was that replayable.
Playing with friends is FUN.
Learn to use the jetpack better. It shouldn't be increased, its perfect as is. Trust me.
Is it worth full price? Only if you like the concept and have friends to play with. If youre the only one, wait for a sale.
BEFORE you consider buying this game, wait for the Sunday ESL Cups. Watch Black_Aegis or aSeeds on Twitch as they cast the pro league games. WATCH a PROFESSIONAL LEVEL game, and see if that kept you interested. If so, buy it.
You should buy this if you like monster movies, awesome weapons, unique and cool hunter characters, falling out of a dropship into a cool world, a cool new gaming twist, or being an unbelievably awesome bone crushing monster. I truly believe this game has the potential to be really, really big in the coming years.
I would not have recommended it for the longest time, but with the new Arena mode I feel this game is WORTH IT for the average player with even mild interest. If you can stick to it for a decent amount of time, you will be rewarded.

I was skeptical at first, and I didn't plan on getting this game. I was heavily invested into EVE Online and decided to try this game out during the free "Big Alpha" test or whatever it was called. My computer had a really hard time handling the graphics, but besides that, I enjoyed my time playing the game.
Fast forwards to Evolve's release. I'm still happily invested into EVE Online and I see a lot of mixed reviews. About 70% of the reviews were positive, and about 30% were negative. I watched "Angry Joe" youtube review of the game, and I think he was too harsh on the game, but in general, I just didn't want to spend $70 to play this.
After awhile I saw that someone I follow on youtube was playing a lot of Evolve and uploading videos. The game looked fun, based on what I saw in his videos. Then I decided to give it a try. I do not regret buying this game. It's well worth the price tag, as the developers have put a lot of effort into this game, and you can tell.
The monster designs are awesome, the terrain, wildlife, graphics, rain, snow, sound effects, visual effects, the commentary between the characters, the background story, it all creates a fun environment to hunt monsters in... or BE the monster in.
This game is like the most intense version of hide and seek that you can play.
One of the biggest reasons why I got into this game, is because I used to play a fair bit of League of Legends years ago. I loved the competitive aspect of the game, but I hated getting teamed up with bad players. I would lose my temper, and not have fun. So I stopped playing because I was just getting too angry. Now when I play Evolve, I have the option of either teaming up with other players to hunt down the big bad monster, or I get to SOLO PLAY as the big bad monster.
The choice is yours... do you want to have a social gaming session, where you get to celebrate in your victories or lament in your losses with 3 other players... or go in like a lone wolf to tear up the hunter team?
Negatives:
-There are some balance issues, but the developers seem to be working actively on this and introduce frequent "micro-patches" to tweak the game towards the best balance that they can achieve.
-You need at least an Nvidia GTX 560 to play this game. The game looks beautiful on max settings though :)

Cuphead is a fun thrilling third-person shooter with the majority being boss battles and some platformer levels. The difficulty isn't easy, even in Simple Mode; the difficulty doesn't change and bosses are only shorter, so this game isn't for you if you can't keep up with the game's pace. (Actually, the game doesn't even let you progress if you play the bosses in Simple Mode.) However, the controls are fluent and gameplay is great. All the levels require memorizing how to dodge/counter a boss's attacks or safely get through a platforming level. In the Regular Mode for boss levels there are usually three main stages, and they always have different attack patterns. All the bosses stages are very creative and I applaud the developers for this. Every boss comes off as original even if based on something else, such as the cat that resembles Tom from Tom and Jerry. (Is that technically a spoiler?) For both the boss and platformer levels, there's no checkpoints, making you get it in just one try. The platformer levels are literally run and gun, so run, shoot, jump, and dash your way to the goal! You could also play as a Pacifist in the platformer levels by not killing any enemies. Every time I lose a level I have the urge to play it again and again until I succeed, which makes this game super addictive and a great time-consumer. The artstyle is exactly like "rubber hose animation" used in cartoons from the 1930's. All the traditional hand drawn cel animations and watercolor backgrounds in this game were done by the creators and their animation crew, so this game took a lot of time, effort, and dedication to make. Then there's the music! Cuphead's OST (Original Soundtrack) was composed by big band recording sessions, creating the original jazz recordings and other themes of music the game's description mentions. All the music works great with all the levels! Like the visuals, Cuphead's soundtrack is just like the times it captures so well. This game's price is currently $21.99 CAD and let me tell you, this price is a bargain considering this game's visuals looks so beautiful and is just super fun to play (with the vibe of feeling like I'm immersed into a cartoon). Yes, the game may be short, but beating any level can take a very long time. You can have multiple playthroughs because this game isn't one that gets old after one playthrough, so you can play this again in the more challenging Expert Mode after completing it normally if you think you're good enough! Or try co-op mode! I do recommend using a controller (I use a PS4 controller but whatever works for you) because it feels better than with the keyboard. This game has full controller support. And for local co-op, all you have to do for that is open the game, open your game file, and then connect your controller, simple.
Difficult, but not impossible. A controller is highly recommended.

I've been a gamer since I was around 5 years old, and over the course of time I got better at games and learned what I like and don't like in them. At the same time, I've absolutally loved older cartoons like Tom and Jerry for the silly animation and concepts that made no sense but you accepted them anyway because it's a cartoon; it's still my favorite type of animation to this day.
Cuphead is a game I never thought would exist. The whole idea of a game that so perfectly fits my ideals just seemed impossible to me. Cuphead was excecuted perfectly. The blend of hand-drawn animation and platformer gameplay is so well done here, all finished off with a static filter over the entire course of the game. The bosses transforming themselves into verious objects and doing things you'd never expect them to do truly made it feel like I was playing an actual cartoon, cause no matter what they did, you still feel like it's totally acceptable in Cuphead's universe. Not to mention the soundtrack fits perfectly.
Cuphead has everything I've ever wanted in a platformer, most notably in its boss battles. I like boss battles more than normal levels in general, so having more boss fights in a game like this put a big smile on my face. Adding on to it, the boss fights are extremely fun and well designed, havinig multiple unique phases and attacks that force the player to move in some way. And the difficulty remains consistant as well, cause each boss doesn't do the same thing as the last. The aeroplane battles were also unique to the game, giving a touch of my other favorite type of gameplay, bullet hell. I never had a single moment of boredom during gameplay.
Aside from all my praise and love for this game, do consider your level of skill before buying. If you are not good at games like this, I highly recommend you build some experience with platformers and side scrolling shooters. Keyboard controls are also difficult to learn on the Steam version, so if you have a PS4 or Xbox controller it's best you try using one.
I absolutally love this game, and I hope it leaves a huge mark in video game evolution.

Jane Jensen is a master not just with intelligent plotlines (which sadly is rare in adventure games) but is also the master of storytelling and editing.  Giving succinct but a lot of valuable information in various ways as to never be boring and, if you are like me, learn a lot while having a heap of fun at the same time.
The storyline background was art history and the unfolding plot was about Moebius Theory (there are the same patterns throughout history, everything repeats itself)
Your character is an antiques dealer who becomes involved with an organisation that wants his insight into a few people.  You investigate each character which have information points, once you collect all the points you solve a puzzle by comparing these character's facts with historical figures.  Along the way, we see how the Moebius Theory unfolds through him personally and the people he is investigating.
Each chapter is usually in a different country, but with only about 2-3 places to visit in each country, you don't get lost and it is very easy to go back and forth via a map if you miss something, thus minimising or eliminating the need for hints (which this game does have) or a walkthrough.  There are a few puzzles but even with the
there are logical clues.
Glitches in the achievements have been fixed, they all now work.
Now to the not so great:
-  Artwork - sometimes is in the just OK range
- The multi-step inventory, I could have done without the 'envelope' icon and just use the interactive icon when I wanted to use an item.
- Main character is plain 'I want to bonk him in the head' annoying.
He does improve a bit as gameplay progresses but not quickly enough to care about what happens to him till near the end, where there is a redeemable characteristic.  In Gabriel Knight the main character was a sexist pig at times but he also was a lovable rogue.  Sherlock Holmes was very loyal and really nice to people he found interesting.  House M.D over time, was very loyal and cared in his own way to people in his life.  This game isn't long enough to develop a "House" type character.
Overall I loved it, preferring the storyline and plot over GK and Grey Matter.  Maybe if Jensen had more unlimited funding it would have been a longer more involved game in every way than GK and even Contradiction.   But, it's still a really good game, good puzzles, great plot, dialogue and well worth playing.  I really recommend it.

I am always on the lookout for the latest point and click adventure, so after reading the description I jumped at the chance to play this game.
The plot is inspired by the Moebius theory in which time forms a loop with events repeating however in this game it is not events that repeat it is a person's biography, his/her life pattern. (Not to be confused with reincarnation where it is the actual person that is born again not just his/her story). Example: Mozart's bio goes something like this; wrote his first piece before the age of ten, marries at age twenty, has two children, lives the life of a pauper, and dies in his mid thirties unexpectedly of an acute infection. Now in the present time Malachi Rector (the main character) will attempt through his extensive knowledge of history and observation skills to find the one person that could fit that profile. He is hired by a top secret organization to do just that.( It isn't Mozart but the bios are of people you as the player would recognize).
Some of the characters might not be likable but all are interesting especially Malachi. I am reminded of a certain late nineteenth century character a flawed but brilliant private detective. It is David his bodyguard that gives Malachi a touch of humanity or should I say a bit of compassion for David is everything Malachi is not,
There were times when I got frustrated because some of the solutions  to the puzzles didn't follow a logical and  intuitive conclusion. In fact there was one solution I felt was down right ridiculus.
Definitely thought and care were invested in the graphics department.
I give this game a rating of 7/10 it isn't the best point and click I have experienced, but certainly not the worst. I bought this game while it was on sale so I feel I got what I paid for.

What a truly wonderful experience. Genuinely absorbing storytelling, hugely creepy atmosphere, scary and interesting enemies, great weapons, Bioshock is just one of those games where everything came together perfectly. My top ten gaming list was for a long time home to games solely made in the 90s and early 00s (Thief, Deus Ex, Baldur's Gate 2, Half Life, System Shock 2, Morrowind, Planescape etc.), but Bioshock really does sit comfortably alongside those classics. If you enjoy first person shooters with strong stories, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

A truly unique experience with fun combat and great narrative. The game's opening sequence is one of the most memorable and immerses you into the world right from the start. The narrative is mainly driven by audio diaries that the player picks up, so there is a lot of exploration involved if you want to learn story of Rapture. Collecting these is optional, but I would definitely recommend taking the time to explore the environment and collecting these audio diaries for a more satisfying story experience.
The combat in the game has good variety because of the many different plasmids (essentially superpowers) you unlock throughout the game. The variety in the combat can also be attributed to the diversity in weapons and the different Gene Tonics (powerups) that the player can equip. (The weapons  can be accessed by the number keys/scroll wheel or by the weapon/plasmid menu, so there isn't any swapping/equipping weapons in and out.)
My only gripes with the game are the hacking, which can get extremely frustrating towards the end of the game due to RNG, and the gameplay involving the research camera. The research camera felt like unecessary work and was just overall annoying.
I would definitely recommend this game if you want a unique FPS with a great story and have the desire/patience to explore the levels of the game. I would not recommend this game if you do not have the patience to explore or if you want a fast-paced FPS.
P.S. Play this version instead of the Remastered. Just finished a playthrough of the Remastered and it definitely is not worth it due to the bugs and the ridiculous amount of random crashes. (I am running an i5-6600K and a GTX 1060)

Five years later, Darius Mason, grandson of Martian Revolution heroes Alec Mason and Samanya, runs a lucrative business from Bastion, underground hub of Colonist activity. Mining, scavenging, mercenary work--if the job is dangerous, Darius is your man. Few sane people now venture to the ravaged surface, aside from contractors like Darius and the smugglers who run goods between the settlements.
When Darius is tricked into reopening a mysterious shaft in an old Marauder temple, he releases a long-dormant evil and unleashes Armageddon on Mars. As Colonist and Marauder settlements are torn asunder, only Darius and the Red Faction can save mankind. The battle will take them across the storm-blasted planet--and below it, to the very heart of the unspeakable threat.

Beyond Good and Evil is a relic from a time when Ubisoft didn't fill their games to the brim with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it was a much simpler time where they still cared for the things they created and one can see the care that went into this game.
Created by the same guys behind some of the better Rayman games, BGE plays like a Zelda game mixed with Pokémon Snap. You control Jade, which for me was an interesting enough main character. Most of the characters in this game are well written in my opinion, Jade, Pey'j and Double H being the best examples. Each character has his own quirks and oddities but they don't become caricatures because of this. The story is filled to the brim with genuine emotions, I cracked a smile more than once while playing but when it gets serious, you really feel it.

Some minor problems: I played this with keyboard and mouse, the camera could act kinda wonky at times and there is a certain part where the controls get reversed (this is for story reasons and will make sense once you get there) which was kinda annoying.
Now if only Ubisoft would stop ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out♥♥♥♥♥Creed games every fifteen minutes we could maybe get a sequel to this masterpiece. It definitely suffers from the Half-Life syndrome, it's way too good to not deserve a sequel.

Red Faction: Armageddon gets flak for being short and not living up to the acclaim of the previous title in the franchise, Guerilla. But it's still a good game.
You play as Darius Mason, the grandson of Alec Mason from Guerilla. Set fifty years after Guerilla, the premise is that the Cultists and their leader, Adam Hale take control of the terraformer, the machine which supplies Mars with its sustainable atmosphere. Darius, working with Red Faction forces, try to assault the terraformer and take back control. Ultimately, the Cultists end up destroying the terraformer and some time later, Darius is a contractor taking on drilling jobs in the underground. Things go awry when, on a certain drilling job he takes on, he awakens an infestation. Turns out he was set up and now he has to save the planet and bring order back to civilization. Along with some help.
The unique mechanic in this game is the nano energy and SAM. SAM is like Cortana, but not as emotional. She helps you decrypt things, unlock doors, give you power ups, etc. The nano energy is cool, like the repair mechanism so that you can rebuild bridges you need to cross over canyons or lava flows.
The enemies include both the Cultists and the infestation of bugs. The bugs were a dormant species living on Mars that Adam Hale had tricked Mason into waking. They're kind of what you'd expect, and more. They vary in size from flying little things that annoy you, to walking fiends that fire lasers at you. And giant behemoths that charge and shoot green gases at you. And tentacles that pummel you. Basically, there are plenty of enemies and you'll never be bored fighting them.
Most of the game takes place in the underground, and I think the devs really nailed Mars' undreground. Mars seems like the place where the underground would be vast and large with flowing lava in various places. But also gloomy and dreadful because life on Mars means being in constant fear of death from seperate factions or unknown species. Especially underground where there are unexplored territories and systems that may have been abandoned long ago. It's really interesting to think about, honestly. You don't see much topside beside the opening mission and maybe two or three more bits, but over 90% of the game is underground.
Everything else is nice too, graphics, sound design/mixing. Rarely any bugs. Music is a bit overkill with the guitars. I would have liked something more electronic to fit the mood of sci-fi action. Or at least more orchestral. But the guitars and drums didn't do it for me.
Anyway. The game's plot started iffy for me, but I grew into it and ended up really liking it. Also, start a new game plus after you beat it for the possibly the greatest weapon out there, Mr. Toots: a mini-unicorn you carry that shoots rainbow plasma from its booty.

If one were to fall in a hole there, one would then be on earth again. One can find all kinds of vodka in all of the stages.

It has some strange controls that have a learning curve, and you'll need to redo some of the key bindings like the basic WASD and others but let's go to the pros and cons list:
Pros:
- Beautiful art, well pixelated textures.
- Great Music.
- Unique Quest Giver.
- Unique biomes and mobs with rarity and different traits.
- Physics are good, Trees falls to the right and the logs separated into rows. Unlike Terraria, which logs fall from above.
- It is a little Hardcore.
- Many promising upcoming features.
- Awesome combat system.
- Excellent color managment.
- RPG elements (I like the Souls system that they put in the game, it remembers Dark Souls and I'm a huge fan of Souls franchise).
- Unique weapons with rarity and buffs.
- Each monster has it's own move animation, makes the game's combat system better and looks beautiful.
- Pretty nice building system.
- Good game's mechanic.
- Can create a living village with villagers.
- Most of monsters can be captured (Gotta catch 'em all!)
- Magic creation system.
- Devs are very cool and attentive to the players.
- Adorable chickens.
Cons:
- Multiplayer not avaliable yet (is coming very soon).
- Rocks grow like grass, which is something that is just too unrealistic, even for a game (for me).
- Gameplay is pretty much empty right now (as I said, there's a lot of content incoming).
- On this stage of development the game life time is limited, you can beat the game with a few hours.
- There's no story right now, you just fell with your spacecraft, pick up the quests and survive.
- Strange controls on the beggining.
- Unfinished translation (In my language, Brazilian Portuguese).
And thats it! This game has quite a journey ahead of it to get to the glory the Devs have promised. But it's very enjoyable and if you like games such as Terraria, Starbound or even if you've never played any game similar to this, I highly recommend this game.

Currently the game is in alpha and story mode is being released on August 1st. However, I've got quite a few hours into the sandbox and it never fails to feel fresh and exciting. There are updates frequently that improve game mechanics, content, and even expanding the game world.
Today there was a bit of drama surrounding the trailer for chapter one of story mode. A lot of people were angry and decided to rate the game negatively or change their existing rating. It's really a shame.
If you are here reading reviews because you are interested in purchasing this game please keep in mind that those recent negative ratings are based on people's expectations and assumptions and not the game itself. If you are a fan of serious survival games that strive to be as real as possible than please give The Long Dark a try. I honestly believe you will not be disappointed.

As wonderful as the blue sky is, as wonderful is THE LONG DARK.
Hinterland Studio created with The Long Dark a game, that should never be forgotten. A game which shows how brutal, harrowing and desolate, but at the same time beautiful and quaint the nature can be.
The Developers showed the rest of the studio's creating survival games, that you don't need to invent a new type of hostile or neither force a hostile into a survival game, when there is already a true unfeigned enemy: NATURE.
In THE LONG DARK you have nothing but yourself to take care of. The goal? Surviving.
As soon as you jump into the game you will need to figure out the keys of surviving.
Finding resources, food and medicine which people left behind, escaping the cold and the snowstorms, finding shelter and get yourself comfortably warm, keeping yourself alive and adjust to the circumstances you are in. You might ask, what is so difficult about finding food? Well the answer to this is: you are not the only one who is hungry. Better be ready, when a hungry wolf or bear picked up your scent and is coming for you.
Hinterland Studio created something, which is not only a game, which is not only a quick idea that is made to create volume; it is more than that. It is a tribute to ourself, a tribute to the world we live in. It is art.
This game portrays the apex of the survial genre.
My personal wish for this game and the Studio is, that those guys never stop creating such beautiful content and never stop perfecting this masterpiece.
And to all this people being impatient and respectless: you don't need a story mode, when you are the protagonist which can create his own story.
Thank you, Hinterland Studio!

If you are interested in this game, please read. I will explain the current wave of negative reviews.
TL;DR: Devs made silly mistake, game is still awesome and devs are not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. If you like survival games, this is leading the way into the future as an extremely robust and enjoyable experience.
Don't take the recent negative reviews as something that should skew your view of the game.
I bought this game a long time ago, $17, back before Pleasant Valley and when it looked rough.
I view the updates more as free DLC, more content has been added to this game without extra cost than most mainstream games add for a price.

Hey, don't let the negative reviews lately dissuade you from buying this game. It truly is an INCREDIBLE game. It's one of only 2 survival games I can bat an eye towards (the other being NEO Scavenger). It's immersive and beautiful. The sound design, map design, music, art style, all of it is just really high quality for a studio as small as Hinterland. They've put so much love and work into this game. It's changed so much since I've first been following it -- which has been about a year and a half now, I think? I'm so proud of this game. I
don't find myself immersed a lot but I do in this game. I find myself anxiously looking behind me while walking on a lonesome road at night, ears pricking at the slightest noise outside the usual. Was that footstep mine or a bear? Are those wolf yips and howls nearby or am I safe? I find myself shivering along with my character as we trudge along together through blizzards at 8% condition anxiously looking for shelter through the thick snow. I find myself getting lost on my way home from scavenging when the fog rolls in and I can barely see just inches ahead of me. I find myself counting calories and scraping by, rummaging through every drawer, looking behind every crevice, praying I find that one extra bullet I might've missed, that one can of soup tucked under a bed that will keep me going an extra day. It's a game that emphasizes survival of self. Nothing is a bigger threat to you in this game than yourself. Not the weather, not the wildlife, not disease. Your willpower, strength, dilligence and taking of risks are what make you or break you. Are you willing to risk your life through the blizzard to get the supplies you desperately need, or will you huddle at home starving gnawing on cattail stalks? Is it worth following this path just a little bit more to make it where I need to be before health runs out, or should I abandon the path and look elsewhere, risking getting lost or being mauled? Can I make it to the lodge just up ahead or will I let the Long Dark take me?
The Countdown everyone is mentioning WAS a stupid mistake, but overall, I think, an innocent one. They fired off the wrong signals and left the fanbase wanting more. The dev's need to work a little harder on PR and communications really. But the devs know their mistake. They don't need us to punish them. Spamming poor reviews sabotages the game further and pushes story mode further away. Please. Buy this game while it's still in Early Access, before it's full price. I would personally buy it full price myself if I didn't already own the game, but this is a good opportunity to get it while it's cheap. If you don't like the game, refund it. Whatever. But PLEASE don't let these stupid babies whining that they got their hopes up dissuade you.

i'm not typically a serious fan of city/army builder games like this, but Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes is one of those games that is just what I was looking for at the time. If you're a fan of Sid Meier's Civilization series, this game MIGHT be up your alley. In my opinion, it is way better in many ways. A lot of people say differently... So here's a rundown of why I recommend this game:
1) You get to have a 'main character', which you either pick from, or make your own through customization options. You can also make your own faction up, so to speak and pick your perks etc.
2) There is an EXTREME PLETHORA of troop choices due to customization options to create the exact troop type you are looking for, You can even customize how they look, including gender. Seriously, this is an amazing thing that I haven't seen in too many other games of this type.
3) The battle system is like a hybrid of regular turn-based strategy games of this nature, and something like a less-intricate version of games  like Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, and Agarest (tactical battle games). See your unique leader and troops battle across actual landscapes, with terrain that affects movement and line of sight in a much more  detailed way than typical builder games. Strategize your positions. Feel like you're actually battling!!
There's really only one big problem I have with this game, and that would be the lack of multiplayer... I hear it crashes a lot, but I haven't really had much issue with this. Other than that however, I don't really see a whole lot wrong with it. I saw someone saying it's not a 'completed game' but I felt pretty content with it. I mean, I wouldn't go paying 40 dollars for it but I wouldn't pay that for almost any game, simply because that's a lot of money to me... I don't make that much...
Should you buy this game...? It really depends on what you want in a game. If you're a high-fantasy fan who loves customization and city building, maybe. If you're a fan of grid-based tactical combat games, it just might be up your alley. If you like all of that stuff, you'll probably like this game. Should you spend 40 dollars on it? Ehhhh..... I wouldn't but if you have tons of money to blow, why not? I would honestly wait for a sale, or do some more research beyond my review... I hope i helped you out somehow in your decision however.

Moebius: Empire Rising is the newest game from Jane Jenson, creator of the classic adventure game series, Gabriel Knight – one of my favourites. As I backed this game on Kickstarter, I obviously really wanted to like it. Sadly… I didn’t.
In Moebius, you play Malachi Rector, a brilliant antiques appraiser whose social skills are lacking. Malachi is hired by a mysterious organization to do a mysterious job which takes him all over the world. As you get deeper into the story (minor spoilers alert) you find out what you’re actually doing. The group Malachi is working for believes in a “Moebius pattern” where the lives of people in history are being repeated in the present. They hire Malachi to find key historical figures who could bring about an era of stability and prosperity. Basically. Summarizing the plot to this game in a coherent manner was harder than expected.
The game does have some good things going for it. I did find the game occasionally enjoyable, especially at the beginning. The dialogue was decent, as was most of the voice acting. The background images were pretty and the music was good – very evocative of Gabriel Knight. There were also some unique kinds of puzzles. As your main objective in the game was to relate people to historical figures, one of the main puzzle types was matching up their characteristics. This was both interesting and educational, though once I had done it a couple of times, I figured out that just guessing was often quicker than reading though all the information.
My favourite feature of the game was a button that highlights all objects on the screen that could be interacted with. While using this could be considered easy-mode, I found it incredibly useful. Pixel-hunting for objects is not something I’m interested in doing, and this was totally prevented.
There were a few things that started out as positives, but turned into negatives. Adventure games are often far out there in terms of reality and physics. Adventurers often walk around with shovels, coffee tables and iron statues in their overcoats. Where do they put them? In this game, the protagonist often refused to pick things up until he saw a need for them. At first, I applauded that. Why would you walk around with a can of motor oil? But after a while, it got very frustrating. For example, at one point I needed to get into the VIP tent at a political rally. In order to lift a pass off someone I needed to go back to my apartment to pick up an mp3 player I hadn’t been able to pick up earlier. Once I used that to bribe someone to be a distraction I needed to go back to the apartment again to pick up some scissors. When I successfully stole the pass and had to go back to my office to get some superglue that I also was unable to pick up before. Then back to the rally to get into the tent. That’s a lot of back and forth that could have been avoided. Not picking up every single item in sight makes sense, but as it turns out, that kind of realism in video games is not a great idea. “How irritating” Malachi remarks. Tell me about it.
Items and inventory use wasn’t all bad though. I enjoyed that you were never overloaded with items and there weren’t any nonsensical item combination puzzles. No cat fur mustaches in this game.
Some of the puzzles fell flat. Malachi was able to analyze people to learn more about them, similar to the recent Sherlock Holmes games. Sounds like a neat idea, but in practice it mostly involved guesswork and the process of eliminating the most ridiculous options.
The most unforgivable part of the game was an excruciating 50+ screen underground maze at the end. There’s only something to do/interact with on maybe 5 of the screens. The rest is just running through dark tunnels. Considering how the rest of the locations in the game (like France, Egypt, New York) have only a handful of screens, dedicating so many to this awful, dismal, repetitive place is almost insulting. Who could have possibly thought this was a good idea?
Moebius runs about 8 hours long. Though there were parts of the game I enjoyed and I’m glad I finished it (other than that awful maze), it was disappointing overall.
Rating: 4/10 – The story was so-so, the characters were a bit flat and some of the animation work was downright bad. The game lacked the charm and historical detail of Gabriel Knight and really did nothing to advance the point-and-click adventure genre, or even replicate it at its height.
Quite an unusual but fun concept. Definately go and pick up a copy if you are looking for an unusual title.
Worth it for the music alone.

Although the puzzles were all rather easy, the story was intriguing enough to play to the end. It’s not as bad as many of the reviewers make it sound.
I want to address a few point I’ve seen in some reviews:
-This is not as good as Gabriel Knight.
Yes, we all love the GK series, but let’s not forget you had to put tape on a fence to get cat hairs to make into a moustache. Moebius is not GK, it’s different. Both have good and bad points, but it’s unfair to compare a current game with your memory of how good another game was.
-Malachi is not likeable.
He’s human. If you stopped to consider his character and what he has been through and seen, it’s easy to see how he became “not likeable.” I didn’t find this a hindrance to the game at all. More importantly, his character evolves over the course of the game, which is lacking in many games.
-Animations/graphics/character models suck.
They aren’t Final Fantasy graphics, but they serve their purpose. They’re obviously much better than GK3 graphics, and everyone loved that game. Yes, smoother graphics would’ve been nice, but it’s not game-breaking.
-The game is buggy.
There were some bugs. They recently released a patch which was supposed to fix many of them. The bugs I encountered weren’t game breaking; just skipped animations. But personally, I feel that bugs in an adventure game are less forgiving than other genres. You don’t want to feel like “maybe I can’t solve this puzzle because there’s a bug.” So minus points on this lack of polish.
Now on to the positives:
+ The story was interesting, and I liked how you had to make connections with historical people. The game (like all of Jensen’s) was well researched and I felt that I came out of the game with new ideas or thoughts, which is more than can be said of many games.
+ The puzzles were a bit on the easy side, and some were illogical (or just time wasters) but for the most part, they made sense.
I know I spent more time addressing negatives than adding positives, but overall, I thought the game was good. Not superb, but not half as bad as a lot of the reviews made it sound. There was nothing really ground-breaking with the game, but the story was strong enough to make it worth playing.

Good story and varied locations, add in some decent puzzles that arent mind blowing difficult, add in a socially ackward main character who has some internal problems of his own and then to top it off he learns hes a player from the past in a large web of intrigue and you get Moebius. Its a good game that takes off after the first chapter.

Project Zomboid is a refreshing gem in the survival game genre.
When I bought this game in 2011, long before steam greenlight, I stumbled upon this game on YouTube.
It was far from what you have seen before, the closest thing to it at the time was minecraft.
The developers humble about their little project.
Back then the map was tiny, weapons did not exist in the quantity they do now, the food system we have now did not exist, multiplayer was a massive requested feature but was thought to never happen, there was no progression system the graphics were odd, you get the idea it was not a big game.
Now, after 5 years a lot has changed, it has become quite a survival game.
Since the steam review section consists mainly out of overused memes, people complaining about their PC not being able to handle the games and people ranting with 1000 hours that the game sucks I will post more of an introduction than a review. I will of course say what is good and what is missing but I will focus on it more in detail than a short review would.
At the bottom I will sum everything up with a TL;DR
You
. Your character feels like he is hitting bodies made out of bone and flesh, not bodies made out of papiermâché or not rocks like in other games.
If enemies get too close (hugging close) an axe won't do much damage a knife however will. A blunt weapon is efficient as long as the enemy is in reach however, it won't do as much damage as a close ranged knife or an axe.
Guns do good amount of damage if the enemy is at the right distance. If the enemy gets in melee range it won't be nearly as accurate as if he is a few meters away.
Axes have a sweet spot where the blade contacts with the enemy where they will be the most efficient. If you swing too much your character won't hit as hard.
Your character of course does not stroll through the zombie apocalypse like it's nothing, under all those pixels he also had emotions and needs which this game wants to deliver to you.
Your character can feel pain, sadness, nausea, panic, sadness, boredom, hunger and thirst, exhaustion, tiredness and temperature.
pain and panic for example can reduce your accuracy with weapons, if you are in great pain you won't be able to sleep.
Hunger and thirst obviously will kill you if they get to great.
Boredom and Sadness don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥but change the appearance of the world (it becomes darker), in the future however they will play a bigger role.
Nausea makes you recover less if injured or if you get really sick by eating that month old lasagne then you may die.
Exhaustion makes you a slow weakling.
Tiredness reduces your awareness and ultimately makes you collapse on the street if it gets too bad.
here are some examples.
If you are in great pain you can take pain killers.
If you are bored you can go outside,
or get drunk
. He can also read or something.
If you are tired you can drink a coffee, you can also use the ancient chinese trading secret method of
.
If you are thirsty you can drink out of the toilet bowel, and so on.
he is less prone to panic the longer he is around zombies and is not so emotionally impacted after seeing corpses all day.
While creating your character, you can chose his pre-apocalypse profession and his traits, the higher the benefits of these professions the less points you can spend on other traits.
There are many traits and professions so I will only give one example.
You want your character to be able to build objects that can actually stand? Then you can pick carpender, this gives your character more experience in carpentry allowing him to build more complex objects right off the bat.
If your character does something often, he will gain more experience and gain level, this can improve how efficient your character with the knife on the field, or in the kitchen and much more.
If you don't want to starve then you need to plant food, if you don't want to get killed by a horde then you need to be able to build sturdy houses and if you want tools you need to scavenge for rocks to build tools.
There are many differnt crops that you get to plant, you need to plow the soil, water them regularly and make sure no one steps on them.
For building there are many different structures to chose from, the things you build become more sturdy the more expereience you have. This can been seen not just by their hitpoints but also visually.
Project Zomboid is a game that is challenging for new players but once you get the hang of it, it gets pretty easy.
After a month of playing the electricity and water supply will turn off because the power plant will get over run. This forces the player to find a well in the middle of nowhere to obtain more water or to drink out of every toilet bowel in the city. Since there is no power you can not refrigerate anymore, meaning you will have plant food yourself.
There is no greater goal to accomplish but not dying which truly makes this game a survival game, this can get boring over time.
A much requested feature are NPC, they once were in the game (around 2012) however the developers found that they simply were not smart enough, so they removed them. Since then they have been working on them and other projects so they won't blow♥♥♥♥♥once they are in the game, people simply have to be patient.
Other things like generators a nutricion system is coming too, so don't you dare think that the developers have become lazy. The fact that these guys are still dedicated to this game after such a long time (this being their first project) is very comforting to know. They are also remaking the visuals and combat system for the third time to make it even better, you can check
for some footage of that. They always have new ideas and mods can also improve on the experience. (
is my favorit one as an example)
There are things I can not mention because of the character limit on steam, like the map editor for example.

There are enough amount of players and rooms but mostly they are private and they don't play Race or Deathmatch but Adventure mode; i don't know why. Hotseat (local) play is always available.
Cooperative adventure mode is a little bit chaotic. You accidentally (or purposedly?) bump and kill your partner and/or prevent them to reach their goal or they do the same to you. Let us, for a moment, forget all the negativity that swallowed this game, making it "cancerous".
The fanbase became swooped over by a wave of cringiness. You know, the type of cringiness that includes OCs, sexualization, and just in general bad fan creations.
Let's forget all that. Go back to the beginning. A few days subsequent to its release. This is my review.
The game has a dark atmosphere. The atmosphere you'd get from a run-down, low budget chuck-e-cheese.
The animatronic design is poor(lore-wise), albeit rich in creepiness. The ambience that plays and the random mascot tune obscured in the blanket of echoey darkness is spinechilling. It sounds closer when you click on the right camera, yet sounds so far when you lower the tablet.
The lore, although covered in mystery, is a type of story-telling not done before, and I feel as if the sequels following this title were neccessary. With this game alone, no one would have known of the killer or even Fredbear. That is what allowed Scott to follow this story-telling; he leaves a paper trail and when we think we're close, he hits us with more clues that make us cover our tracks and rewrite everything we thought we knew.
I never thought I'd ever be afraid of animatronics, let alone haunted ones.
The fan creations and fan actions may have tainted the franchise, but I will still love the FNaF universe even if my friends are disappointed in me. I'll take that risk, dammit!
All in all, a great point-and-click atmospheric strategy horror game, that took the internet by storm and was the first of 5 other games to create the FNaF universe.

This game tries so hard to be too many different things. It starts off seeming like it's pretty great, but then the more times you play it, the more you realize in its efforts to be a little of everything, it's not good at any one thing particularly. There's too much resource management for this to feel like a true rogue-like, so you're constantly monitoring the amount of resources you have and lots of different modules. The tower defense elements are not really that well implemented, you must rely on the heroes to do much of the work - but if you try and stick heavy with leveling and outfitting your heroes, you'll get creamed later on in the game when the waves get much larger and more vicious. Even well equipped heroes with many bonuses have a hard time against some of these creatures, but unlike most tower defense where you can give yourself a lot of time to chip away at them, you really can't.
In this game, you use dust to power rooms, without power the rooms can spawn creatures and you can't put any modules in that room. You can't light all the rooms, so at best you can just make it so they only approach from a few vectors. This chokepoint idea seems like it would be fun in theory, but in practice it works poorly. You have to place modules down to increase the resource gains per door opened (turn) but you'll almost have to place these along the route to the exit for each floor for them to be protected and useful. So you have to place your valuable modules in the direct path of where bad guys will be walking along, and they'll smash the modules quickly. To make matters worse, you must research every module besides a few very basic ones. This research does not carry over between matches, so you restart this process each new game. Each module takes 3 turns to research, but if you start research on one and there are only 2 doors left on the floor - you're SOL for the research you just spent on that. Again, in a game that was more balanced this would be an acceptable risk, but losing out on things like this will screw you over so fast you might as well just give up.
So unfortunately, this game causes lots of frustration after you spend quite a long time on a run and then lose it because the game decides to throw too many creatures for you to handle. Whereas losing a run of Binding of Isaac or FTL is irritating but gives you another chance to learn without feeling to punishing, Dungeon of the Endless takes a lot of your time to get through a run and messing up after spending so much time on a match feels awful and sharply decreases your desire to make multiple runs. This game is much more of a sit down and make a run, and if you lose, just quit and come back another day (To compare, I found myself playing many runs of FTL and Binding of Isaac as both felt way more receptive to quick runs and not these long drawn out things). To make note - the creatures don't always spawn every turn, sometimes none spawn. Even with well prepared defenses, heroes set up in good positions, you will still get absolutely smashed. You'll be pausing to heal your hero, unpausing, then a second or two later pausing again to heal, until you either have nearly no food left or they just die.
While all rogue-like games have that element of RNG and unpredictablility, Dungeon of the Endless piles that on top of a mediocre tower defense and dungeon crawler. FTL is frustrating for those same reasons (RNG), but you can tactically plan much better than you can in Dungeon of the Endless. This game is just too lackluster in too many areas to be worth it. Yes, the art style looks pretty nice and the music is pretty good - I wanted so much to like this game, but I just can't. The game has too much going on for its own good and brings down the overall experience completely.

I don't get why the overall score on Steam for this game are so high. I'm not one to bash a game, but this game is not that great. It has a great concept, but it's pretty boring overall. It took me 7 hours to beat, and for probably 3-4 of those hours there was almost literally nothing happening. I was just wandering around looking for the items needed to progress and not finding them while completely avoiding enemy patrols (there's no reason to go anywhere near them and they are very easy to avoid). When you are forced into a confrontation, such as needing to deal with guards around an object you need, you simply distract them with an alarm clock or a wind up toy, then walk up and grab what you need. Or later, if you find weapons, you can just kill them with no problem at all. You can also escape from enemy patrols by simply running away. Once I figured this out, I would just run constantly; it didn't even matter anymore if I was seen.
The objects you need to find to complete the scenario are really hard to find... until you realize there are a few ways to see where they are, and then you don't have to do any exploring at all, you just walk straight over to them. Several of the islands I explored took me 90 mins. to 2 hours to complete, but once I realized a good way to find the objects you need, I completed the last two islands in like 15 mins. each, which was very anticlimatic. I didn't explore those islands at all...
There are a few good moments here and there, like a chuckle from the writing, encountering new and creepy enemies, and a few tense standoffs with enemies, but the sheer amount of hours where nothing at all is happening really drag things down, as do the anti-climatic encounters with easily killed, tricked, or out ran guards. I heard that the devs worked hard on the sound design, and that does show in the sound effects. Pretty unsatisifying overall, which is a shame, as a game with this exact concept and set-up could be really cool if done right.

Score: 8.5 / 10
Price/Value: -$20
Time: 11 Hours (Including A+ time)
Difficulty: Completed Regular, working through Expert
Actual Difficulty: Minor / Moderate
Input Used: Keyboard & Controller
Cuphead is a wonderful delight in it's animation and nostaIgic melodies; a somewhat challenging colourful action platformer in the guise of a 1930's children's cartoon.
As mentioned above, Cuphead is an action platformer focused around two types of stages: Run n' Gun & multi-form boss fights. Many gamers of experience will immediately compare Cuphead's gameplay to that of Contra, Metal Slug & Mega Man; as the controls are incredibly tight - both on controller AND keyboard. I will comment that the game does become something of a cakewalk when a controller is used, making keyboard controls another layer of challenge. Recommend the standard W,A,S,D configuration.
Difficulty, let's address it and the hype. Is this game as brutal and punishing as many claim it to be? No, not in the slightest. I have certainly played far more challenging titles of a similar nature in my life and the keys to success in Cuphead are the following: PATIENCE & PATTERN RECOGNITION. This game is beatable and can be a delight in the process; I'm looking forward to completing Expert - which seems incredibly simlar to Regular, just with a slight speed increase and weapon power decrease.
Upgrades come in the form of: Super Abilities, Shot Types and Off-hand Charms.
Super Abilities are just that, SUPER abilites! These are ready for use when your super meter at the bottom left of the screen is full charged. Being three in total - a horizontal attack, temporary invincibility and a form of mega cuphead tornado - I found myself sticking to the first.
Shot Types are classics from NES/SNES games of old: Spread, lobber, hookshot, homing, etc. You purchase these from the shop and equip them as you please - two at a time - before entering a stage. A little trial and error will help you figure out the best combination for each stage.
Off-hand Charms are many, but I used only one 'Smoke Bomb'. This allows you to dodge with an invincibility effect through enemies; incredibly handy.
A delight from start to finish; decades old gamers will find a gem here that will remind them of games from their own childhood in the skin of our cartoons. Highly recommended.

I never write reviews for games because I feel everything I could possibly say has already been said.
That being said, I feel compelled to write this, especially in light of recent events.
Let me just start off by saying that I absolutely adore this game. It's challenging, it's relaxing, it's engaging, and it's stressful. No matter how many times I move on to another game, I always find myself coming back to this one.
I bought TLD shortly before the update that Coastal Highway, so I have seen firsthand the incredible evolution it has made.
I've played my fair share of EA titles, got burned a couple times (looking at you, Starforge). But never once have I felt misled by Hinterland. It's true, they have pushed back the release date of Story Mode at least two or three times.
Unfortunately, the game fell victim to its own success. Hinterland, not wanting to disappoint its growing fanbase, expanded the scope of the game, began adding ideas suggested by what I considered to be a positive and constructive community, and lengthened story mode.
Now this whole countdown timer thing is threatening to tear apart the community and give the devs a bad name.
I think the whole point of having it countdown to simply announcing the exact release date would be a relief to the community. Now we have a definitive date, no more "Late 2016" or "Third Quarter 2017". A day. A time. A big sandbox update within the next month or so. A teaser trailer that's gotten me pretty excited.
How ever anybody decides to feel about the countdown timer, there's no denying that Hinterland means it this time.
I will be marking my calendar and requesting the week off from work.

Regarding the countdown backlash: the countdown marketing was terrible, there is no other way around it.
It could have been handled much better, BUT Hinterland apologized and recognized the mistake they have done, and for me, thats the most important thing, becouse they are showing transparency and humility, unlike many major companies out there.
Not recommending the game just for that marketing disaster is just silly.
Anyway, my tiny review:
Bought this game some days ago while it was on sale and played the hell out of it. Despite its Early Access status, the game feels polished enough to be considered done (at least the sandbox mode).
Atmosphere: Top notch. The feeling of being lost in a land with hostile wildlife,  nothing to eat and freezing to death, only to find shelter at the brink of death is really addicting. Most times I felt like living an experience rather than playing a game.
Graphics and art style: I personally love the "cartoony" style they choose, while its not super detailed,  it's expressive and conveys the artist's vision (if you want 4k texture on everything so you can see each molecule of every object, probably this is not the graphic style you are looking for).
Sound and music: Every tiny sound you hear has a purpose and can help you judge the next move. Do you hear wind in the distance? Maybe a blizzard is coming. Flapping sound? Could be a flag or a cloth material, maybe a manmade shelter is near. Everything is a clue to survive.

I received Moebius: Empire Rising for backing the Pinkerton Road Kickstarter and just finally got around to finishing it. It wasn't a terrible way to spend my time, but I wouldn't describe it as a good game and I wouldn't recommend it unless you really have nothing else you'd like to be playing. The feel of the game overall was very unpolished, and while I could forgive the aesthetics not being perfect, things like the animations were not only stiff and unrealistic, but they were very slow and you'd have to just sit watching the characters slowly and awkwardly move around while waiting for them to do what you told them too. In the instances when it was unclear exactly what you were supposed to be doing and I was having to repeat certain actions multiple times trying to get things right it got very frustrating.
They did try to do some interesting things with the point-and-click genre, for example, you couldn't just pick up everything you'd eventually need right when you first encountered it if there was no reason for you to be carrying that thing around, so you'd often have to remember where you saw something useful and go back for it, and it seemed to work out pretty well most of the time. There was also the analyzing of people to learn more about them, which mimicked the BBC TV show, Sherlock. That was clever at first, but it mostly ended up with things either being obvious or else needing to guess randomly. They also relied a lot on stereotypes, and it got kind of insulting at times, especially towards women as it seemed like half the women were vain and out to get a man, often the protagonist, Malachi Rector. Malachi thinks pretty lowly of most people, but his generally insulting attitude combined with the use of negative stereotypes about beautiful women, various tropes like women getting fridged or damseled, and the women in the game almost all being puzzles or tools to use to solve a puzzle, including sometimes in a sexualized manner, was pretty disappointing. Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers wasn't exactly great in its treatment of women, but there were more interesting and diverse female characters around, even if Gabriel himself was a bit of a womanizer, and I had hoped that Jane Jenson was capable of writing protagonists who didn't objectify women so much and that this game would have been able to show better gender representation than a game from the 90s. And while I'm on representation, Malachi and David's relationship borders dangerously on queer baiting.
Overall, there were some good moments in this game, and I didn't hate it, but mostly I felt that it fell short and that there were elements that could use quite a bit of improvement in every aspect of the game. If a sequel were made I definitely wouldn't get it right away, but I would see what people have to say about it and find out if they've made enough improvements to make it worthwhile.

Moebius: Empire Rising is a point and click adventure game by Jane Jensen and published by Phoenix Online Studios. If you aren’t familiar with the name Jane Jensen, she is one of the big names in adventure games from back when adventure games were the showcase genre of the PC who are still working primarily in that  genre.  I don’t want to go all auteur theory, but Jensen’s is important because Moebius is recognizably the kind of game she’s been making for the last couple decades. There’s a pulpy, melodramatic concept and story. There are some continually repeated minigames that are too simplistic but seem like they could be great with a little more work. There’s an annoying maze area that should have been cut entirely from the game. Basically, fans of Gray Matter will probably like this. For those who haven’t played Gray Matter, some more explanation is probably needed.
Moebius is traditional in design, to the point of being predictable.  You pick up objects, and use them on other objects in a, hopefully, logical way to advance the plot. The only change to the standard gameplay is that Moebius only lets you pick things up when the puzzle requiring them has been reached. So you can’t just pick up a boat pole and carry it around for no reason, unlike the kleptomaniacs who starred in the adventure games of old. Occasionally you need to guess passwords, but this is usually done by selecting the password from a drop-down menu, there is one that you enter manually, so the passwords aren’t fundamentally different from finding and using items. The passwords also provided the best example of how the game is too eager to keep thing moving for the puzzles to be really engaging, Late in the game there is a password that involves using cryptography to decode the password hint. You’re provided with various keys and three methods of encryption and decryption to figure out the password.  It could have been an interesting exercise in figuring out how to use the different methods. Instead you’re brought to an interface that applies the encryption for you. All that the player is left to do is apply the cipher and copying down the decrypted message. A shorter way to put it, this is one of maybe three that I’ve managed to complete without a walkthrough.
The game isn’t all item puzzles and passwords, though. There are two minigames intended to emulate the classic “Sherlock scan” and the comparison of modern and historical people respectively. In the Sherlock Holmes minigame you’re given different qualities of a person, like “shifty eyes,” and then select one of three options for what it tells you about that person. This isn’t inherently a bad idea, but these options always break down the same way. One is an obvious joke option, one is relevant but doesn’t actually relate to a character trait, and one just flat-out tells you some character trait of the person you’re analyzing. Comparing people to historical figures is probably the biggest disappointment of the game. You are given a list of traits and next to each of these traits are the historical figures who had those traits, then you need to figure out which of the historical figures shares the most traits. So if someone has seven traits in common with Eli Whitney and one in common with Chuang Zi, you need to sigh deeply and imagine what could have been. It really should have been an exercise in comparing and contrasting information is instead a test of whether you can count.
The story is very much in line with the goofy-but-sincere gothic melodrama that Jane Jensen usually does. Malachi Rector (keep in mind that Jensen’s Gray Matter featured a character who wore a literal Phantom of the Opera mask without a trace of irony) is asked by a mysterious quasi-governmental organization named FITA (which was sadly changed from the far more appropriate FIST) to determine if the life of a recently murdered woman resembles any historical figures. After carrying out his mission, he is attacked by ninjas, who photograph his passport, and finds out that he is the center of various conspiracies and so it goes. I don’t want to expand on the plot too much, because people hate spoilers. I will say that if you’re a fan of Jorge Louis-Borges, you might be disappointed, as it’s nothing as clever as that. It is a very entertaining pulp sci-fi story that has a lot of genuinely well done moments, and runs with its central conceit fairly well. I really thought the story was a strong point of the game, except for one problem.
The problem with the story is Malachi Rector. He is a whiny, entitled, self-righteous, narcissistic, judgmental prick. They were obviously trying to emulate the BBC Sherlock, with Malachi as the insufferable genius who everyone needs despite his grating personality. They even tried to emulate the look of the BBC Sherlock in many of the cutscenes, with floating text to represent Malachi’s analysis of the situation. The BBC Sherlock has a couple of advantages, however. First, that has Watson around to look at the camera and sympathize with the viewer, and, second, Sherlock is not the viewpoint character and you get an occasional break from him. The Watson in Moebius is so bland I’ve entirely forgotten his name and Malachi is the viewpoint character for most of the game, which means almost everything the game tells you is passed along by him; this is a problem when most people will want to punch Malachi in the face every time he speaks. I don’t think it kills the story completely. If you keep in mind that he’s supposed to be unlikeable, it’s actually hilarious what a ♥♥♥♥♥ he is.
Graphically, it’s exactly what you see on the screenshots and video above. It’s got a nice stylized design intended to conceal the low quality of the models, the animation is a little off at times. Overall, I think it works well, when it works. The engine for Moebius, like Cognition, the previous game from this Phoenix Online, has a tendency to suddenly pitch a fit every so often and the character models starts flopping around, an absent character remains a hot spot in the level, or the game just locks up. I don’t want to exaggerate this too much, I had four or five noticeable issues in the nine hours I spent playing the game. Three were cosmetic and only one, when the game locked up, required me to restart the game from an earlier save. I’d advise you to save often, though, in case the game does suddenly freeze on you.

To sum up, I may have accentuated the negative a little too much here. Moebius is a nicely traditional, if overly easy, point and click adventure game with an interesting plot that is partly kneecapped by unlikeable characters, oversimplified puzzles, and the occasional bugs. That sounds bad when you put them all together like that, but I really do recommend it if you like the genre. If you’re not a fan of point and click adventure games, this probably isn’t the best place to start. Maybe try the Blackwell games or Gemini Rue or something first.

I consider myself a big fan of Jane Jensen's and classical adventure games in general (as you can probably tell by my choice of the Steam avatar), but I cannot in good conscience recommend this game. It rehashes all the  adventure game tropes and clichés (not in a good way) and much of the puzzle design is flawed or illogical. Most crucially, though,I found myself getting bored with the plot and couldn't care enough to keep playing. I never got to finish the game as much as I wanted to because it felt like a waste of time. It simply wasn't fun or engaging enough. In a genre of games that specializes in storytelling, I'd say that's a big minus. The characters (especially the main character Malachi Rector) are unlikeable, the dialogues are uninspired, and the animation is stilted. For the longest time, I seriously wondered to myself if the main character was supposed to be a hunchback by design because of his very unnatrual-looking posture. It turned out it was just bad character modeling. You'd think they would invest some time and effort in designing him to at least NOT look like a disabled person. He's only the protagonist of the game. That you have to stare at for the ENTIRE duration of the game.
In the meantime, I will be eagerly awaiting the arrival of GK 20th Anniversary Edition.

This game is underrated...
The single biggest complaint from other people is that it's "not enough like the older games because of the aliens. Why'd they add aliens?" Really, that complaint just shows that the people criticizing it for that haven't actually played anything but Red Faction Guerrilla (which itself was a great game, btw). Red Faction 1 had aliens, and in fact many of the aliens in RFA look like modernized versions of the RF1 aliens. Additionally, RF1 was linear, just like this game. Like it or hate it, RFA is more like the older games in the series, not less, and it's not some sort of betrayal or unfounded design design.
On another note, the game is well optimized, good looking (I find the screenshots actually undersell it in most places), and has responsive gameplay. The series' signature destruction is also intact, so the switch back to linear gameplay hasn't changed much in that regard.
It does get tedious after a while, and may not hold up to a second playthrough (keep that in mind when you're deciding how much you're willing to pay), but it's worth the current price of $20 to people who've played other Red Faction Games.

Running Though Russia is yet another endless rumner in the slew of mobile/non-mobile entries to the style on Steam. Take control of a Russian man on a quest for vodka as you run through the country. The differences in terrain come from certain colored bottles. A white (can't tell if that or very light blue) ushers in winter, or green ones to venture to what appears to be Hell, all the while avoinding bears and the deep purple bottles that are instant death when consumed.
Between poorly hand-drawn graphics and the game's music, Running Through Russia really doesn't offer anything for even the most seasoned of casual gaming veterans, especially if you gotta pay. This is something best left as a free download on mobile stores, or your favorite mini flash game website. Really, the only humorous bit is not the cartoonish racism, but bottles randomly falling over or through holes when transporting to the different terrains, as well as the bears that often stand stuck between ledges.
Unless you're an achievement hunter, it's best to avoid this boring title, but even then over thirty of the achievements cannot be unlocked at this time. The content required for them will be included in a later update. It's a tactic I'm seeing appear more and more, and hopefully the developer will follow through with this statement in the discussion page.

Reviewing only Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad  - i did not own Rising Storm.
RO2 is the dream of any hardcore WW2 fan. The game features battles from World War 2 between germans and the russians in Stalingrad. But why is it so great?
That's simple: Because of the way they created it. You will fight in small troups as either normal soldier (only equipped with a Rifle and a Grenade) or as a special class, equipped with extra equipement. Mg's, Sniper, Tank destroyers, elite soldiers [..] There are various classes to choose from. But all of them are limtied, just like it was back then. The majority of players will always end up in the Rifleman Class. And that's good!
This is none of you usual run and gun games. It's a hardcore, challenging and very realistic team shooter. One shot to your chest? Likely dead. A shot to your arm? Well, yo can bandage that. A sniper bullet in your bottom? R.i.p.
Gunplay is incredibly well made, reloading single bullets or clips is totally sufficient! The lack of an HUD just adds to the experience.
The graphics are good! Not the best compared to today standards, but fitting to this kind of game. Dark atmosphere, dirty snow, dirty houses [...] Stalingrad lives again...
The sound is one of the best i have ever experienced in an online shooter. While the normal shots are just your average sounds, its the overall package that makes it so great. Beeing shot at by an mg, jumping into cover, just to hear the player next to your dying slowly because he was hit by the bullets - you feel sad, angry and frightend. You don't want to peak out of cover when there is a sharpshooter ahead. You don't want to run through mg fire. You are afraid for your life. You are happy when you can get to the next trenches - it means there won't be anyoone able to snipe your head off.
You will start to really feel like you are there, not just playing a game.
The community is mostly very good! Roleplaying is not uncommon, neither is having great team leaders and commanders. Communication is proceeding smoothly, making it not only an fps, but also a strategical game.
I could go on like this for hours, but let's just say: If you want a highly realistc, challenging world war 2 shooter, and don'tmind the high initial learning curve, this is for you! Buy it!
One of the few game where you get a real sense of how it would have been in the war

Evolve Gameplay And Performance Review: A Humans Vs. Monsters Hunt
It was being hunted... The monster had been avoiding a team of four hunters ever since it saw them jump out of the spaceship. But by the time the hunters’ feet had touched the ground, the monster was already distancing itself, jumping over large boulders and running through trees in order to get away from the human threat. Along the way, it would slay any of the indigenous wildlife in its path, to devour, in order to evolve and become stronger.
Time passed, as the monster played a dangerous game of cat and mouse with the four hunters, while continuing to feed. Now, it felt strong enough to take on its pursuers. But before it could take the fight to them, a blue dome came down around it, trapping it in a small area while four hunters stepped into the monster's field of view.
With a roar of defiance, the monster charges into a hail of bullets, determined to wipe out the group of hunters. But who is really trapped in that shimmering blue dome?
That is how you are going to feel when playing Evolve, a 4v1 multiplayer game developed by Turtle Rock Studios and published by 2K Games. It pits a player-controlled monster against four other players that assume the role of hunters tasked with tracking the monster down and killing it -- preferably before the monster becomes too strong and kills all of the hunters or destroys a power relay station.
The game has taken its developer about four years to finish and, during that time, it has been able to remain in the public’s consciousness. But not always for positive reasons. Turtle Rock was acquired by 2K Games in an auction when THQ went bankrupt and, before any images or footage of the game were released, its DLC was being promoted. In fact, it has been the massive amount of day one DLC available that has caused some backlash against the game leading up to its release.
But glossing over that particular issue, has Evolve been worth the wait? That is what we are here to find out. Suit-up, this could get messy.
