Fallen Enchantress Legendary Heroes (FELH) is a rock solid game that is filled with a lot of great content (when adding in DLC) and ideas. The problem is much of the cotnent are set pieces in the game and new things don't happen often enough to make the world feel dynamic or lived in.  That is a problem.  You either steamroll eveything by midgame or complete the huge quests late when it doesn't really add much.
Combat at the strategic level is usually fairly easy.  The CPU soes not really seem to know how to use its armies and will invariably park all of them in cities, unless it can be roused to enter a fight.  Unfortunately these armies are eithe rnot well contructed, updated or used effectively.  Like I said even in all out war the AI parks them.  So you conquer everything else and then go for the killing blow.  On a tactical level combat can become quite challenging and the AI seems to handle this aspect of combat better.
The DLC is a mixed bag.  There is some good stuff like the undead, but the items and maps packs feel more like a donation to Stardock than great additions.  I did but them all, mostly when on sale (2.50 is a better price point).  What is missing is a workshop.  This is what makes GalCiv3 so awesome, user created content.  Even the ability to make magic items was something Master of Magic had... 25 years ago.
The ability to customize your own race/wizard is really cool and for the most part superior to Master of Magic.... save for one thing, this is humans and undead only.  As in everything, save for a few monstrous units from spells.  You want elves, dwarved, halflings, gnomes?  Best of luck, chump.  Units can be cusomized and upgraded too, which is cool and while there ar eoptimal paths there are also lots of options that can differentiate units.  Sadly there are no fun mercinary units to hire like Master of Magic either.  Getting back to races a cool thing about MoM was that you could conquer cities and those cities made different units (big difference between a dark eld city and a human one...).
As you progress in FELH you will pick up heroes and they can be customized to some degree (earlier ones more so than later ones).  They can get gear and expand thier skills/abilities.  Here there are a few more racial options, but for the most part its a humans club.  The great balance here is that while heroes are awsome and powerful you really need an army to bloster them especially early but even later units of heavy cav and wizards do wonders to help them.
Anyways this is a fun game and while I iwsh it were more of a challange, had a workshop and more variety in almost everything it has to offer from quests to races... FELH still is a great game and a worthy inheritor to the bar set by Master of Magic for a 4x game.  While it does bring that old game forward with the basics, what is missing is not only noticeable, but glaring.  Which is a shame.

Do you like good games? Then this game is not for you. Do you like demented puzzles and being annoyed out of your pants? Then this game IS for you. Ironically, though, I have no doubt whether to recommend it or not - I enjoyed it, a lot. Guess it's a question of what you're looking for.
If you're looking for Cesar Bittar, by jove you've found him. It is obviously a game developed solely by him without any involvement of that pesky Jane Jensen whatsoever. Or at least by Phoenix Online, and not by Pinkerton Road at all. Pay attention.
If you're looking for, say, cool characters, then you should marry it - Malachi and David are amazing, and everything that concerns them is done brilliantly. From the beginning of their friendship through all the shunning of Gretchen to the pointed indifference to Amble it's downright adorable, sincere and applauds-inducing. And man, I love these straight to the point dialogues where characters are saying the most logical things that suit the situation. I can't say enough just how perfectly it is done. It was  a pure enjoyment and a crate of marbles in a world of pervasive bureaucracy and Leisure Suit Larry remakes.
Unlike everything else in the game.
The story? Have you heard of the world's silliness contest of '72? Where Helen Slapps was standing on one leg on a frozen turkey with a thrashing fish in her mouth and an open urn of ashes on her head, and playing a triangle? It was waaay less silly than the plot of Moebius.
The puzzles? Oh, don't even start about the puzzles. When I was flying back to Chicago from New Orleans because I forgot to pack my toothbrush, that was painful. And this game made me relieve the experience. Honestly, the only good thing about them is that they're easier than the ones in The Walking Dead.
The graphics? You know you have issues when you visit New York, Venice and Zurich, and the only pretty place is still a bar in New York.
The music? Well, there were some niceish pieces, but nothing comparable to Gray Matter.
The technical issues? I thought it's good pairing when characters are walking through one another on a regular basis.
I must say, it IS a Jane Jensen's game, mainly meaning that it's amazingly written and tries to tackle metaphysical issues with a healthy dose of excitement and a pinch of old fashioned naivety. It is worth your playthrough. It's good like that. It's just you'll have to put up with its♥♥♥♥♥♥ and there're surprisingly big amounts for a game you can complete in ten hours.
So there. Scratch what I said, don't marry it. It will ruin your life.

After playing the demo and catching up through reviews I decided to wait until the price of the game dropped and it just did that a few days ago.
Everything you can read about the game in negative reviews is true, but unless you have a very limited and narrowminded view, it will likely not be as true for you. The 'strained' relationship between the two main characters can easily be explained with a bit of human insight.
This game really starts off on the wrong foot. Everything, but the characters, looks nice and it takes quite awhile to get used to the poor lip syncing, wandering eyes, animations and pauses, but once you are past that it's quite entertaining and chuckle worthy on occassion. The puzzles are generally pretty straightforward and even though you can't pick up anything before you actually need it, which is a really bad design choice imo, it isn't really that interruptive to gameplay, which can also be alleviated by using the location travel from the toolbar and movement in areas by the double-clicking teleportation.
I had to turn off music (volume down) after 10 minutes, because it was giving me a headache. I recommend using space a lot to highlight points of interest - I didn't do that in the beginning and I missed an item and was stuck for an hour. The hint system is pretty useless, completely unlike the spectacularly userfriendly one from Broken Sword: The Serpents Curse. I only got one analysis wrong (Caroline Aflfonse) and had to check online for mismatches, because I was dead sure about some mismatches, which wasn't shared by game logic.
I spend around 25 hours on this game due to some mistakes, that "interrupted the pattern" followed by clicking on the wrong button (I clicked on Load and realized that the game had made no autosaves, no progress saves and that I generally had forgotten to save any games beyond the intermissions) and the game also crashed on me once. "Retry" is the key to use and saving in general is a good idea, unless you like repetitious gaming.
I would rate this game 7/10, because of bad design choices, poor lip syncing, wandering eyes, weird movements, annoying pauses, jittery animations and a general lack of polish. Had those things been fixed I would have rated it about 8.5/10, because despite the glaring faults it's actually a pretty good game with some interesting new points of Adventure and story-telling.
As annoying as the sluggish character movements are, I really enjoyed the story :) Let's hope they continue the story in a few more games!!

This game will be a must-buy when full release hits. In it's current state it already has a lot going for it, and is especially fun to play with a friend or two.
While I recommend this game, I do not recommend it for those looking at it's planned features. If you are to buy the game, buy it for what it currently is. Development is slow, but very deliberate. Everything implimented so far has been well thought out, and aside from a couple of things (sheet ropes make the game a bit too easy IMO), well balanced.
Pros:
- open world where no buildings are purely cosmetic. They can all be explored and used     strategically.
- a LOT of settings to create the perfect sandbox for your play-throughs
- in depth crafting system with countless recipes, without making crafting a requirement
- massive hordes - even as slow stumbling blunderers, the sheer numbers can force you to leave an area you once thought safe
- choices matter. Zombies don't kill you, bad decisions do.
- simple, but pleasant graphics (though understandably not to everyone's taste)
Cons:
- I would be lying if I said the development speed was fast
- late game is a bit too easy to get to once you know what you are doing
- dedicated servers can be a bit fiddly to get working properly.
- single player, in the game's current state can feel a bit too lonely.
TL;DR - Play the demo, see if you like it. If you do, buy it - if not, check it out in a year or so.

This is the best FPS game I've ever played.
If you're into world war II and have the patience and the will to study the maps and the hardcore mechanics of the game, a complete joy and satisfaction is guaranteed.
Especially for history lovers, there's nothing more exciting epic and terrifying than opening up on a cinematic wave of enemies who are attempting to cross a bridge on the snowy outskirts of Stalingrad, as your comrades are being shot around you and break your heart as they cry for help, while an epic music is being played in the background. It feels just like this game has been directed by a genius director.
Here are some of my favourite points about the game:
-It gives you the needed freedom to wander around the map and be a lone wolf, but still forces you to stick to the objective and help your team in one way or another.
-It has a great atmospheric soundtrack that makes you feel like you are in an extremly emotional and honest war film.
-The combat is very realistic yet simple, the game gives you the ultimate world war II experience but still makes sure that everything is simple and accsible.
-Although it is a game about war, it feels as if this game was created in order to show you that war's no game. Let me explain: even during the multiplayer battles, you can hear your comrades and even yourself begging for mercy, crying when injured and craving for home, and if that's not terrifying enough, sometimes when you're on a satisfying kill streak you can hear the enemies you eliminated squirm, cry and shout. The whole "system" creates a heartbreaking scenario that drags you into it and leaves you with combined emotiones.
Final thoughts?
This game is nothing but a masterpiece.

Evolve Gameplay And Performance Review: A Humans Vs. Monsters Hunt
It was being hunted... The monster had been avoiding a team of four hunters ever since it saw them jump out of the spaceship. But by the time the hunters’ feet had touched the ground, the monster was already distancing itself, jumping over large boulders and running through trees in order to get away from the human threat. Along the way, it would slay any of the indigenous wildlife in its path, to devour, in order to evolve and become stronger.
Time passed, as the monster played a dangerous game of cat and mouse with the four hunters, while continuing to feed. Now, it felt strong enough to take on its pursuers. But before it could take the fight to them, a blue dome came down around it, trapping it in a small area while four hunters stepped into the monster's field of view.
With a roar of defiance, the monster charges into a hail of bullets, determined to wipe out the group of hunters. But who is really trapped in that shimmering blue dome?
That is how you are going to feel when playing Evolve, a 4v1 multiplayer game developed by Turtle Rock Studios and published by 2K Games. It pits a player-controlled monster against four other players that assume the role of hunters tasked with tracking the monster down and killing it -- preferably before the monster becomes too strong and kills all of the hunters or destroys a power relay station.
The game has taken its developer about four years to finish and, during that time, it has been able to remain in the public’s consciousness. But not always for positive reasons. Turtle Rock was acquired by 2K Games in an auction when THQ went bankrupt and, before any images or footage of the game were released, its DLC was being promoted. In fact, it has been the massive amount of day one DLC available that has caused some backlash against the game leading up to its release.
But glossing over that particular issue, has Evolve been worth the wait? That is what we are here to find out. Suit-up, this could get messy.

short review: it's red faction gurilla warfare LIGHT.
long review: you play as a relative of the hero of the last game. it is set a long time after the last game, so everybody from that game is dead. and the creatorsof this game have apparently thought something along the lines of "DAMN! our last game was really good and ground breaking! let's see if we can still get good reviews AND a lot of money, if we make another game, but cut all the things that made it good, in half!" as you now CAN'T destroy everything, and it's NOT an open world anymore, (in fact, if you try to go to far, you get a warning and a timer going from 10 seconds and down. i never let it reach zero so idk what happends if it does, but i guess you die, or fail the mission, and have to start again.) i mean, why do you wanna REDUCE or REMOVE things that made the previous game popular??  you got a AI on your arm, who can't take a joke, example: the hero says "this guy is starting to become a real pain in my a$$!" and then the AI says "i cannot detect any damange to your lower abdomen" so, the humor seems to be aimed at people too young to be playing this game. but don't worry! the steriotypical black guy is here to save the day, BRO!! if you have ever seen or heard a black stereotype, you already know how this guy acts, so i don't need to write it. but personaly: i really like that guy! but i can understand if some people don't. they also removed the mines, as you won't need them much anymore. but now for some GOOD stuff! they give you a bunch of really cool weapons. like the nanite rilfe, nanite shooter, nanite bomb, and a bunch of other nanite stuff. (nanite is what destroys everything. and builds everything!) and a gun that shots black holes! (although the radius of the black hole is REALLY short! like 1 meter or so) and when it's done it EXPLODES! (which has a radius of about two meters.) but if it actually hits an enemy or sucks it in, it's certain death for all but the big guys! they give you guns that shot trough matter, and a shotgun. just a normal shotgun, like we have in our time. which was, for me at least, refreshing. so... a bunch of guns, and a bunch of upgrades. and ALL the upgrades, even the FIRST one's cost 1.000 salvage, and the last ones cost 1.500. and salvage! you know the things you got from everything you destroyed, in the last game? well, those are now small containers, which gives you 60 each, and you sometimes have to search for them. the only time i can remember to have gotten salvage besides those containers, was when i shot a big explosive tank, which didn't give me much. BUT! you can buy an upgrade that gives you salvage from killing enemies! i didn't SEE the salvage, but i'm guessing i got it. you can download 3 cool skins, that does nothing besides look cool. but they don't show up on the videos in game. the previously mentioned AI is very helpful to the hero, as it says when there are enemies incoming, and where to go. mostly in the videos, but it shows you where to go when you play, so that's good.
so.. do i recommend buying this game? if you HAVEN'T played the last game, red faction: gurilla warfare, then you will probably think this game is AWESOME, as you can destroy nearly everything!  if you HAVE, on the other hand, played the last game, then this will feel like a bleak comparison, a hurried project, a fan made game, who didn't have the time/resources or the permission to program the game to let you destroy everything. so.. final judgment: buy it if you DON'T have the first one, THEN buy the last one! and if you HAVE played the last one, DON'T buy this, unless you HAVE to have EVERY red faction game! good game, half a$$ed compared to the last one.

This game is about as generic a shooter one can get. While it's unique features are the ability to destroy and recreate some parts of the environment, much of it cannot be destroyed and this mechanic holds only some relevance. The writers seem to have lost sight of what the Red Faction series is about because this whole game is about fighting aliens while occasionally fighting cultists with no explanation of their irrationality, instead of fighting an oppressive force using what little you have.. The sub plot love story is very generic, cheesy, and obvious from the start. All of the characters are very forgettable, including the protaganist himself. Most of the jokes are midly amusing at their best, and evoke no reaction often times. The hardest difficulty is not hard at all and provides little challenge throughout.
If you want a mindlessly easy generic shooter game with a plot one will not care about, this is the game for you.

So project zomboid is a game I, and many other friends have enjoyed a lot. I owned the game DRM-free for about a year before buying it on steam to join the multiplayer hype. A short lived adventure indeed.
Now the game itself is quite enjoyable. However, many flaws too. As well as a seemingly lifeless development team, pumping out the occasional new feature to quench a lasting thirst - nothing too substantial unfortunately. With a lot of members of the community wanting the same feature (NPCs) and a lack of responce from the development team, the numbers have started to dwindle. I, for one, have lost interest.
The gameplay has a lot of potential, and the features included provide a great experience. The slow gain of skills make for careful character planing in order to specialise in a few skills such as first aid, foraging and cooking, opposed to being a jack of all trades. This play style can help develop specific characters, creating a character who will forage for food and avoid combat in order to survive, moving house to house in order to keep off the radar can be a total different playstyle to somebody who creates a fortress of solitude and charges head on to defeat the horde single handed.

This game.... is not for the faint of heart, which may be strange, a zombie game that focuses on realism in the zombie apocalypse, being a bit rough for some. In this game its fun, yes, can be a bit repetative when you find yourself repeating cycles of actions,  but otherwise its very good. I playyed it at a friends when it was very early in development, back when katie and bald spots story was sometimes in the game for some updates, sometimes not... and i remember the processes well from then. "Run, find food, stuff food away, run home, store the food, repeat. Find hoard closing on home, run home, grab gun, run a bit in the opposite direction of home, make noise, fire gun at approaching hoard, run to secondary home and live on chips for 2 days, then run to main home. Get bored, go adventuring, get caught in a bad spot, regret. regret. regret. Some how make it home, badly beaten but alive... then realize what it cost." The injurys are so severe that theres not much you can do until they heal... and the food stock was already getting low before you left... now its worse. And the thoughts go through your head again and again.... positives? still here.... negatives.... and you realize that, in your fort, in the safe part of town, nigh inpenatreble, it was your own stupidity, the need to feel danger, that rush, that has you not dead, but locked in your safe house, with two fractured legs, and a low food supply, your trusty axe nearly broken, as you had to use it to fight off a intruding zombie on the stairs, and to knock down a door to use the pieces as a splint, before crawling down the street chopping at anything that got too close, somehow making it into your safe houses wall, getting actual medical attention, and realizing the cost of a little "adventure" and "fun". No this game is not for the faint of heart, funnily enough. in this game, your main purpose has to be survival, making every thought and action calculated to where you already know the outcomes, and always have the creeping knowledge that at any time... it can and will come tumbling down... its not a question of IF you make a mistake, its when, and when you do, how far will you fall? All in all, solid game, 8 or 9/ 10, would reccomend.

I went into this game as a big fan of Starbound and Terraria. Games much like this one. I expected it to be pretty copy/paste, but not in a bad way. And while I was right there, it does plenty to differentiate itself from those two aforementioned games. In those games, as much as I love them, they're relatively shallow compared to Planet Centauri. A lot to do, but not too many ways to really optimize how you go about it. A few potions and an arena in those games and you're all set.
This game is quite the opposite. Not too much to do, but so many ways to go about it! The customizable magic is intimidating at first, but it is really worthwhile, the monster capturing and animal morphing work well, taking the best from games like Pokemon and such to make it feel like something that can only benefit you.
Don't let the trailer fool you about it's current state. I'm 99% sure the trailers show off a future version of the game. Possibly an unstable build. Most of the things you see there are not present in the actual game at this time.
I said there wasn't much to do, and I meant it. Very few skills, the worlds are small, the "customizable" magic has several options that are visible to the player but not implemented yet... or there's something about it I don't understand. And weapon types are few and far between. The skills you can aquire are few in number as well, and not too effective.  the Transformations I spoke of are, while useful, very limited in number. In terms of the magic, that's been shown to be fixed very soon from some of the trailers.
All those issues are likely to vanish with time. I made this review less than a week after the game's release, so I have no doubt that the issues involving lack of contect will be fixed in time.
A few issues I have that might not be adressed with time are that a) it doesn't seem to stray too far from typical fantasy material. Giant talking crystal, check. Zombies, check. Worms, check. Skeletons, Check. Slimes, check blah blah blah. Not easy to do, but it needs to find it's own style late into the game.
Incredibly basic progression. Copper/Tin to Bronze to Iron to Steel to silver to gold. No variation on that. That's... all there is to say.
The inventory system and hotbar are VERY unintuitive going into it. I couldn't figure out how it worked for two hours before I started being able to use the left mouse button.
Building, even worse. I won't even start. There's room to make something amazing with it, but it's so time comsuming to even make something acceptable to the human eye.
There's one window you can open by hitting the U key by default, that doesn't seem to do anything. I think it's meant to be there to upgrade weaponry, but again, It's never explained and I have no idea.
Last and biggest problem for me is that the difficulty it reaches doesn't line up to the power you can attain. Or maybe I just suck, but it really does feel unfair with equipment I currently have. Especially that purple dungeon.
The difficulty isn't something fun and engaging, a fun challenge to work around like in Dark souls, but it comes from poor design decisions. Mostly the SP system. Another game, Starbound, has an extremely low SP cap, but that's balanced by insane regeneration. Terraria has a good balance of SP/Mana cap and it's regeneration. This game, doesn't have enough in your pool at any given time, and it regenerates painfully slowly. And not just that's it's too slow for in-combat regeneration. If you run out, you have to sit in your base, and it'll take about 10 minutes to regenerate. Not fun.
There is an insane amount of potions, a few dozen, each with about 6? (I think) levels of strength. You have combinations of herbs that determine what type of potion, the "catalyst" you use will determine the strength.
Sounds great, but those catalysts are horribly planned out. You need a lvl 1 catalyst to make a lvl 2, so on and so forth. Each one takes a rare material added to it to upgrade it. Those materials are way to rare for something you need so much of. and the catalysts ARE consumed.
One solution to this issue, is related to chickens. You can create coops, that you can stock with feed to attract chickens to get eggs. The ability to make similar structures for the scorpions, (their tails are required to create the lvl 1 catalyst) would solve this problem. And the ability to create gardens for specific herbs would also be a welcome addition.
I will sing it's praises though. It's incredibly well polished in it's animations and it has a great visual style. It is only sprites, but they're FANTASTIC sprites. Enemy variations keep things fresh and challenging, everything has a nice feel to it but the double jump.
In short, it's nothing special now, but good GOD there is SO much potential here. Click follow on this game to keep up to date because I'm willing to bet money that these'll be patch notes you NEED to read. This game is going to be fantastic, but for now, I feel like it was released a bit early. Maybe two patches into the future it'll be in a state where release would have been better saved for. Don't buy it now, it's nothing special for now, but keep your eye on it, wait a few months or a year, and it's gonna be one hell of a good time.

This game is amazing.  It is very effective in making the over used WW2 setting enjoyable again, while still staying as realistic as possible.  You are able to choose from many classes, each with it's own weaknesses and strengths.  Each map is incredibaly detailed and very pleasing to the eye.  The game has a few different modes such as countdown, which is basically a timed match where one side must defeat or destroy the other, cross fight, which is basically a battle, and territory, which has you and many others trying to capture all objectives and keeping sure you have enough reinforcements to survive.  In RO2 the reinforcements mechanic makes me care more about my squad and each casualty, more than games like Battlefield 1942 and Day of Defeat.  The tanks are amazing in many ways making you have to work together with your team to control the tank.  Each side has many different types of weapons that differ greatly from each other.  There is never a class that everyone would always play as, nor a class that no one will play as.  Being able to pick up fallen comrades weapons is a nice touch, being that some classes such as the anti-tank or machine gunner have main weapons that cannot be used unless put on a tripod.  There are also different modes for the game, such as action, for those who are used to playing games like COD, realism, which is for players who like nitty gritty realistic games like Verdun, and original which is in between.  One of the biggest complaints I hear are the bot AI.  First of all, games like RO2 are usually meant to be played with other people, so AI is usually not the biggest project for the devs of a multiplayer game.  Second, I have had no trouble with the AI.  The AI are a good touch for offline players and people who want to increase their skill.  The steam workshop mode is awesome because you can pick any map, any gamemode and up to 64 bots in a slaughter.  The steam community also has a lot of custom maps for you to try out if you get bored and have played on all of the maps.  Anyone who dislikes the game is just probally just doing what they think is cool like many did with No man's sky.  They think the game is going to be much different than what they thought it turns out to be and the say the game is bad.  Thanks for reading my review and please consider purchising red orchestra 2.

Dungeon of the Endless expands on the basic formula of a roguelike game without losing the heart of the roguelike.
Roguelike games are always about doomed choices. You an either go forward or not, but every step increases your peril and it's up to you to get out of it however you can. Random chance can kill you, but if you're good it will kill you in spectacular and story-worthy ways.
Dungeon of the Endless takes this core play tenet and adds in a party aspect and a tower-defense aspect that somehow fit perfectly with the beating heart. You are always seeking to balance your limited resources, keep your party alive, and find the way out of the current level of the dungeon, and it's always possible that the next door you open will be the one that kills your party off.
Each resource is perfectly balanced against the others, so you can't (say) ignore food in favor of science, or you'll have hugely technological idiots who die easily. If you focus on industry then you might be safe on your current level, but the moment you move to the next level it all starts over. The only way forward is to balance everything all the time. Good luck!
Time is a resource in this game as well. You can do tons of things all the time, move your units around, build stuff, etc. but you only get new resources when you open a new door in the dungeon, giving it a quasi-turn-based feel. It's another impressive balancing act the devs have pulled off flawlessly.
Add to this not just one, but several stories that weave through the game and connect it to the other games that Amplitude makes and you've got an amazing package.

This is a simple and elegant game that I consider a classic of the steam library, It's a puzzle game with all the elements carefully crafted.
The colour pallet in the game is very relaxing and customizable, the music further ads to the chill atmosphere and beneath that lies a progressively difficult puzzle game, starting from extremely simple and slowly progressing to devilishly challenging.
The achievements in the game also happen to give some very useful icons (this was a massive bonus before the advent of all the achievement trash games on steam). There is a sort of campaign to go through in the game consisting of sets of puzzles for each letter of the English Alphabet, as well as some challenge games that change periodically for those who ran out of campaign challenges.
Lyne is simple in the way it looks and plays, but clearly had quite a bit of work put into it by the creators to make it so. It is a product worth supporting in this landfill we call Steam today.

This game is bad. The "vanilla" experience is incredibly shallow and bare bones. With five years of development time, I'd expect more from a retro-isometric game. The base game's only saving grace is it's multiplayer, which has been where I've put most of my hours into. Playing this single player, without friends, is incredibly boring.
The game -can- be made much better by installing some mods, ala The Elder Scrolls (which is another game series that relies upon it's modding community to make the game enjoyable). Mods such as Hydrocraft, ORGM, Cremation mod, Pump Power, Quick Bags/Swag, ect.
The only downside to this, is that trying to get mods working together is a pain in the butt. You always get one htat doesn't want to work right with the others, and there hasn't been anyone gracious enough to dedicate their time to creating a modpack (as far as I can tell).
Apparently they will be adding vehicles and npcs at some unspecified time in the (probably far) future.
During an apocolypse I'd expect things like animals running all over, people looting, pillaging, and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ There isn't any of that. From what I can tell, your character doesn't even care about corpses piling up around them, or rotting in the sun.
Speaking of which, you can't and don't need to wash your hands or take a bath. Personal hygiene is one of the most important parts of staying healthy! No matter how much you eat or drink, you don't need to urinate or defecate.
No matter how much blood and gore you've splashed around in, your clothes never need to be change. Even if you did want to change them, you wouldn't even be able to really see what you are wearing because everything uses the same models on your character. Similarly, you can't roll around in zombie gunk to trick them into thinking you are one of them.
The map is ALWAYS the same. Speaking of which, look to the community made maps to play on- they are much better than the ones the devs have made. This game would be a lot better if the devs werent stuck on the idea of using some real world place in Kentucky that isn't even a very good representation of it.
The inability to rotate the camera around is pretty annoying when you are trying to build stuff.
I can't chop a limb off to prevent zombification and find a prosthetic to use.
Weapons are very limited. I probably have more weapons in my house then the police department has in game, without mods. With mods you can find different armor and stuff, but I can't even tell if they work, because you can't tell if you are wearing something or not.
Everything breaks so fricken fast it is annoying.
This game is just very limited in scope. I know it is an early access game, but it's been in development for five years, and in said early access for what? Going on three?
Imma go back to playing now. . . Just don't get it unless you want to end up frustrated and questioning why you got it, and why you and your friends can't stop playing. It's bad. Wait till it gets better, or at least until you and some buddies can dedicate some time to playing it together- preferably in teamspeak/vent/ect.
Fun in my tum. Could use some work on the multiplayer side though, unable to get working even after the update to supposedly make it easy.

Just to get it out of the way, I knew about the things that were not implemented, I knew that the trailer showed stuff that wasn't in the game, I actually read some of the EA notes.
I think this could become the next Terraria (until Otherworld is released) because it does seem like a whole lot of fun, what with the transformation and monster capturings.
The graphics are nice, I like them, I am also grateful that there is a zoom in button, as I feel nausea when things are too small on my screen.
I do not like the Tutorial crystal though, it doesn't feel right to recieve better gear by simply making a furnace and whatnot, Terraria didn't have that, which made getting better loot satisfying. The tutorial should be an optional thing for those who have never played, and also be its own button in the menu.
The thing that ruins the game for me, is the clunky building and inventory controls. Terraria made it nice and easy to do stuff, you select the block with a number, and plonked it down, then you hammered it to get a different shape.
In this you have to select the block, the CHANGE whether you want to put it as a wall, or a back wall. Then choose the shape you want to place down, THEN pick UP the building material and THEN place it down. That is a lot more things to do, and honestly it made me cringe.
I love building stuff in games like this, I usually did that in Terraria while my friends went adventuring, I don't even know what adventuring is like in this game, because it just made me angry playing it.
I can say with honesty, that I hated playing this game, only because of the way it controlled. I will repurchase it with my friends, once the multiplayer comes out with a few more patches.
I don't know how to make the gameplay better, all I can say is that Terraria did it better. But that is an unfair comparison, as Terraria continued to improve well beyond its EA stage. So to say it nicer, take some hints from Terraria, even try to take contact with the guys who made it, maybe they could give some pointers, cause I would hate for this game to not succeed.

It is finally time for another Jane Jenson authored game, and this one is called Moebius Empire Rising. You are going to take on, primarily, the role of Malachi Rector, an expert of antiquities. You will soon find out that your abilities are far more specialized with a secret organization calls on you to find someone, but here's the twist, it is the reincarnation of a famous historical figure. Will you be able to take on the challenges presented in front of you, how deep does the conspiracy that you have unearth go, and will you be able to trust anyone who crosses your path?
Graphically this game looked decent, there were definitely some animation issues which made a character appear to be limping around the screen, and there were also issues of colision with the background which was really just a picture and not geometry. I did like the different character models, they definitely gave life to the characters, but the facial movements left much to be desired. There were several times where characters were talking through their teeth, and there were times where the movements looked over dramatic to try to add additional effect.
I did really like the music that went with the game, there was always a slightly different flavor when you went to different places, as well as a main theme that you could find either in the main menu or between chapters.
The controls are pretty straightforward you are going to be point and clicking with your mouse. Now I highly recommend that you familiarize yourself with the arrow and target icon that can be found in the menu system that you can pull up from the top left of the screen, clicking on this icon will allow you to see all possible objects you can interact with. Oddly though there are a couple of places where when you are just trying to find the exit, and there's nothing else to interact with you can't find the exit.
So you are playing a Malachi a pill popping, overly dramatic, character who is a brainiac. One could say that he is a Sherlock Holmes type of character that does not give a lick about crime, and what is going on in the world as long as it does not interfere with his day. There was definitely a little bit of a soap opera feel to some of the parts, and there were some stereotypical characters that were thrusted into the story. You are going to go on many different adventures, but at the end of the day this game is STRICTLY an origins story. You don't really get your feet wet with what this franchise can do, which is unfortunate because I felt that the story had finally picked up to where I not only needed to play the next chapter, but had to. The thing that basically puts a nail in this game's coffin is the fact that the title never makes sense by the end of the game.
So at the end of the day, this game falls a little bit flat with a couple of faults sprinkled throughout the game. If you like a good mystery point and click adventure, this would be a good starting point but it will not satisfy the hunger you are looking to feed. I will say this though, I CANNOT wait to see the next chapter of this game, and I hope it comes sooner than later. This game gets a 6.7 out of 10.

I really enjoyed Moebius: Empire Rising and it's certainly one of the best adventures I've recently played. It's got a very interesting story with two sympathetic protagonists. This game is not without its issues - primarily technical, which have been covered at length in other reviews. Yes, the animation leaves a lot to be desired, there are noticeably long pauses waiting for an action sometimes, and the lip syncing makes the characters look somewhat scary at times...
However, despite all that, I don't just recommend this game for adventure fans, I wholeheartedly recommend it!
It's strange to me that so many reviews on here have panned the story and the puzzles in this game. The puzzles weren't overly difficult, but I didn't feel they were bland either. They matched the tone of the game, never felt forced or shoehorned in, and were quite fun.
Perhaps, as a fan of the fantastic, I have less problems with the primary conceit of the story (the Moebius idea), and as a history buff I found the idea far more intriguing than a lot of people might. What I can say is that it's the first adventure game in a long time that has held me glued to the screen until I finished the entire thing.
The mystery is intriguing, the main character is surpringly likeable given his personality, and he comes across very much like a modern day sherlock holmes. In fact, the little analysis puzzles that pop up through the game attached to people or objects give the game the best "sherlockian" feel of any game i've played - including the sherlock holmes games themselves.
Overall, highly recommended.

Moebius has a gripping story that takes you all over the world searching for the perfect match for someone in the past. This someone is important to the future of the global economy and different factions are trying to get their hands on her. And only one man, Malachi Rector, can decipher the clues as to her identity. In true Jane Jensen fashion (famous for the Gabriel Knight series and Gray Matter), this is a game that holds true to her style. Intrigue, danger, a mystery that spans centuries, and even the occasional bit of lighthearted humour make themselves known throughout this seven chapter epic. There are even some romantic undertones for the observant to pick up. The music and voice acting are top notch, the backgrounds are beautiful, and the story and dialogue gripping. The only real negative point that I can make here is that the animations could use a bit of touch-up. But this is just a minor gripe that is far overshadowed by the positive aspects of the masterful tale woven by Jensen.

Dungeon of the Endless rocks.  This is one of the few truly unique and fun games I have played recently, and that is saying something given the endless flood of indie and "early access" games these days, particularly in the roguelike genre.
Which brings up the question, what genre is DotE?  Well... it's a little of everything.  RPG, strategy, puzzle, etc.  Mostly, though, it's a tower defense and turn based strategy game.
Like towere defense games, you place different towers in rooms you have unlocked so that when mobs inevitably spawn, you are able to defend your "crystal".  How many rooms you are able to build in is dependent on how much "Dust" you have.  Dust is more or less like electricity in that it determines how many rooms you can power, and figuring out where to utilize this limited resource can be a tough choice. There are 3 resource types, Food, Industry, and Science, which you must manage to be successful.  You also have 1-4 heroes who are able to fight, increase the output of your resources, and perform special abilities.  The ultimate goal of each floor is not just to survive, but to eventually find the exit, then go pick up the crystal, and carry it safely to the exit, along with getting your other heroes there.
If it sounds like a lot, it sort of is, and your first few attempts will likely be disastrous.  But DotE is the sort of game that makes even dying fun, and every run it is easy to walk away with something new, whether it be a character unlock or a better understanding of what works and what doesn't.
Pros:
Gameplay- first and foremost this game is FUN.  The combination of building up your heroes, resources, and equipment, along with mounting tension as the waves of monsters become increasingly untenable, really works.  The game is compulsive enough that even though you probably will die a lot, its just so fun that you keep playing.  I don't complete too many roguelikes, and that isn't saying that DotE is easy.  It's just that enjoyable.  It's all the more amazing that it's as fun as it is given how many disparate gameplay elements the developers threw together.
Graphics- the pixel art style is really effective here, and you can tell a great deal of work went into making the character concepts distinguishable and interesting.  Little details like how Rakya is constantly chain smoking and Josh runs like a shut-in intellectual really give character to the game.
Sound- the sound is well done, with the music providing atmosphere without being too distracting from the action.  Certain special enemies make distinctive noises, while the memorable noise of one of your heroes kicking the bucket is hard to forget.
Story- the game doesn't have a "story" in the conventional sense, but there is a lot of subtext to character interactions.  As you unlock new heroes who have conversations with other heroes, new journal entries show up in the main menu of the game which tell more about the different heroes and the story overall.  For a 2D pixelart game where very little dialogue takes place, I will admit that it is easy to grow to care about the heroes just because of how interesting they are.  Don't get me wrong, this isn't a sweeping narrative epic, but the story helps the game and doesn't get in the way of the action.
Cons (its hard to find things wrong with this game):
Random- while I think the game has an appropriate level of difficulty for being a roguelike, there are times when you will just get a floor layout or monster composition that feels impossible.  In most cases, you can use your heroes to compensate for these sorts of situations, but it can still be frustrating.  For players of FTL, this is sort of the same issue.  You can do everything right and still lose.  This can be a turn off for some people.
Variety- I'm really sort of being picky here because the game is THAT good, but a little more variety in terms of equipment types and monsters would be a help.  It's not that its repetitive, but there are only 4 weapon types, and it might be interesting if the game had more options there.  Also the number of different enemies, while plenty challenging, might could use a bit more spice.
In summary, get this game.  At the price-point its hard to find a better value if you are a fan of roguelikes and tower defense games.  It's unique and challenging without losing playability.  The developers have continually supported the game and added content, and deserve the praise they've gotten for this game.

When I first purchased Elemental way back years ago, I had every hope it would make for a great table top RPG platform as well as the regular strategy game it was designed to be. When I got my copy I was able to see what could be, but it was still an “alpha” game… So I let it go,  kept checking the progress and changes overtime, but nothing got my attention. Then along came 1.7 update and much of what I read I liked so I purchase Legendary Heroes.
A BIG WOW!
I am so happy the developers never gave up. This is very much what they had promised back when they were making the first Elemental. There is still room for improvement (lots of potential for growth and expansion), but the main concept is all there!
So, soon as  they let us make scenarios using the “workshop”,  a custom monster toolset (like the spell toolset) and add a hot seat feature to the game it will appeal to many D&D table top players like myself.
I love the way the mechanics and AI  have developed and evolved/improved, I love the customization aspect so, so, so, very much. Changing gear is actually visible in game play, love the way cities can level as well as almost everything else, we just need equipment to level as well (hopes).
The artwork is splendid. I have loved the art from day one! So perfect for this kind of game, the way the story is presented through text and that unique artwork makes me feel like I am actually reading a D&D campaign and I can get my fiends involved (rolling dice to make decisions, character customization, etc.) we played all night as if we were playing table top, and we never once looked at the time, it was great fun, different, but not so different that it did not work. It is thanks to the freedom to customize just about everything that makes this game so rewarding and usable as a tool for a good old fashion table top game. If you have an imagination and fun friends to play with give this a try. ( mind you we are doing this without hot seat or multiplayer, image if we had that!)
In short I am very happy that my bias for DLC’s went away almost instantly, “sell me as many DLC's for this game as you want!" if they are useful and enhances the game like the current DLC’s.  If you love fantasy strategy games give this version of the game a try, you will love it more and more every turn you take, there is something different and new for your imagination to create in good fun! Recommend!

Nothing is really clear, other than that the stonehenge can weaken the barriers to other worlds -don’t say it's magic-. I don't think it is very fitting, however.
The Graphics
People complain about the graphics in this, and they are not very realistic. I think they are nice and stylised and reminded me much of “undying”. There is fog, and it’s all not very colourful, but I think the graphics well suit the game. There was graphical errors, but these had little effect and I think it is because it is randomly generated. the robots and houses and such look appealing, the ground and the rocks could use some work. There is fog, and I can see some people being bothered by that, however you can still make out things in the distance clearly.
The Gameplay
There are a few weapons(pistol, shotgun, rifle, blunderbuss, axe) which is a good thing, as inventory management is a big thing, and there is little space for many weapons and an effective load of ammo. Each has a defined purpose, and there is nothing else fitting that could be added and not feel unnecessary. It took me awhile to get used to combat, as the sensitivity was strange at all levels. New items don’t spawn in, which mean you can’t play around in one place too long. Some enemies are unkillable, and over all it feels like you are meant to avoid all enemies. Despite being open world and randomly generated, it has low replayability. I blame this on the fact it has only one mode, a scavenger hunt .
The game starts you off the center island, with an equal in size island to the north, east, south and west of you which you can go to at anytime by finding a dock in the direction of the island you want to go to. The goal is to find 20 or something gems, which you need to put into the stonehenge to win. These gems are scattered around the islands. There are number of enemy types that randomly patrol the islands, the more gems you return, the more enemies will spawn. There are towns and other building with loot scattered around the islands. Depending on the class you can start with almost nothing, but with luck you can have a ton of good loot fast. You can store found loot in the buildings without fear of them despawning. It took me only a hour or so to realise you can also stash gems in buildings, so the game does not spawn in more enemies. You can find maps, which you can use to mark 3 spots. 3 spots is more than enough, as it allows you to mark 2 towns where you stashed goodies and a final one for the dock. Your position appears on the map, so navigation with one is real easy. The gems produce smoke which can be seen from far away, but even then there was some frustrating times where I could not find the final gem on an island. Once a robot patrol finds a gem, 2 of them, and a robot dog guard it. Only the first and most basic robot hunters guard gems, and so it is not hard to just shoot them and take the gem. Gems are normally far off the beaten path, so robot patrols will to too long to arrive if you move fast. Alternatively you can throw a clock or bottle as a distraction, but this is far harder to pull off and more risky in my mind than violence. The fact only basic robots guard means you only have to encounter these basic robots, as you can just hide from the other, perhaps cooler types. It was easy for me in the final hours of this game, to make a safe point and stash near the dock of an island, and then find and retrieve the gems with ammo to spare.
Mechanics
-Stealth
Not like most games, there is no sneaking up behind people and stabbing them in the neck or what not (there is no one hit melee). Rather you are more like a powerless convict running from police. Areas are randomly patrolled, and there are a few options of distracting enemies. This is hard to do, and sometimes it feels just easier to kill them. The game does not pause when you loot, so distractions are even worse. There is bunch of guarded items you need to collect, I think only 2 of which I used a distraction. Some other reviewer said this game was more like guerrilla warfare, you hide, shoot a few shots, pick something up then run away.
-Combat
Once you get used to it, it feels good. The health system is very forgiving, but once you run out of rags(which do not respawn) to bandage, you are dead. Eating food frequently will allow to regain health. The guns are powerful, but lack range, even for the sniper. Ammo and guns are rare, yet almost necessary. There is an ADS function that greatly improves damage and accuracy. Going in guns blazing never really works even on small groups later in the game, and if you chose a real class, you will only have a gun by then. If there is something you really want, you can try to sneak up to it, distract the guards or pick one off, hide, pick another one off, hide…. It is repetitive, but also fun.
-Inventory
You can keep thing in homes without them despawning, so you are encouraged to keep caches of food and ammo in easy to reach spots. Nothing knew spawns in, yet you can discard things, so watch out. There are 3 types of loot: junk, dubious and useable. Junk does nothing, dubious hurts your hunger when used, and useable is what you want. I at first wondered why there was useless items, but I figure it is to keep you looting and exposed longer. People complain about not being able to go in homes, yet being able to enter them would ruin the game. It is never worth it to kill every one guarding lootables, so you need to sneak up on them, and loot what you can quickly before you are seen, to be able to enter the homes would break this. Judging whether it is worth the risk is one of the biggest aspects about this game.
Horror
The game was unconventionally scary just like its stealth. It is “you hide behind a stone wall as a clunky robot flies past, wondering to yourself if it will see you” kind of scary, no jump scares or anything. The point of the game is to avoid enemies, you never really encounter these scary enemies up close, limiting the thrill of the game. I think more horror would have improved this game.
Other Notes
Over all it is a beautiful game, I just love to see a line of hunters march in a line through the long grass. However it is kind of niche, and the novelty of it wears off once you finish your first play thru. There is just not enough game for it to be worth 20$. I encountered no bugs, and it felt finished.  It took me 4 hours to beat it, and I was not rushing. The Devs claim the game has replayability do to its randomness, however when the game is so straightforward do to its one goal and limited supplies, that replayability is questionable. The is no other modes. There is starting classes, and that's all to make each game different, other than the map not being the same. This game is dying for more modes. It's a great game that will take up an afternoon, but for 20 bucks? At its current state, which it will most likely have forever, it is worth 5 dollars, there is just not enough content to justify such a price.

Star Wars: Empire at War Gold Pack is a Star Wars RTS. You have Empire at war and Forces of corruption both! Both games were developed by Petroglyph and released in 2006.
The story for Star Wars Empire at war follows along the story leading up to Star Wars A New Hope, and ends roughly after it. There's no reference to Rogue One, of course, because this was before the days of Disney wiping Kyle Katarn from the existence of the galaxy.
I personally found the Forces of Corruption story much more engaging and interesting... but that might because of the large collection of Expanded Universe knowledge. ...Guys guys guys, Admiral Thrawn is in this game, you don't even know!
The gameplay for Star Wars Empire at war as a whole is very much an "RTS", you have your galactic view where you build ships, space stations, troops, buildings, fortifications, defenses, factories, and more.
You need to build certain structures to develop troops. There's also a science system.... The Empire develops their own technology, while the rebels steal technology.
The importance of technology should be pretty clear right away. You start out with Z95 headhunters, which are then quickly replaced with X-Wings. For those that don't know, the Z95 is basically a garbage ship when unmodified
, I would blow them up in X-Wing alliance for sport. A flight of Z95's vs a YT 2000, HA! Child's play.
there's a lot of cool features in the game, and the RTS is really fun... ...but only for about 3 or 4 hours in. That's when I lost interest in leading each of my battles because in that time I had fought probably 4 space battles and 4 land battles.
If you plan to lead each battle and try to avoid taking excessive causalities, you're going to have long slow fights. And I'm not gifted with RTS anyway.
Unfortunately I don't really think Star Wars Empire at war is really that great as an RTS. I definitely recommend giving it a try, but caution against how long the fights are and how pointless they feel very quickly.
To sandwich that in on something cool though, fighting on each planet is really cool, because the developers clearly did their research on the type of planet you're fighting on. On Geonosis you see the natives and the familiar landscape you see in Star Wars 2. on Tatooine you see the Desert and various local inhabitants. Some planets sympathize with one faction over the other, and aid them in defending or conquest.
There are some changes in the Forces of Corruption DLC, you're "supposed" to use a new feature which corrupts planets to spread Tyber Zann's Influence. But I said "screw that noise", and instead just built up a big army and conquered the galaxy the normal way: skipping battles and auto-calculation. You can't fight your way out of 100 guys vs 1 guy, even if he fights like Chuck Norris... I'll just come back with a bigger army.
This review has kind of derailed a few times, what you should take away from it is this: I enjoyed it as a star wars fan. I don't think it stands up so great as an RTS. It lacks in modern optimization and resolution values (It doesn't have 1920x1080, there are tricks to cheat the game if you feel like modding).
As a whole I enjoyed Star Wars: Empire at War, I enjoyed Forces of Corruption more. I suggest you give this a shot, Star Wars works with any game Genre.

Very fun zombie survivor game. You will die.
Surprisingly varied amount of items to be found lying around, most of which are not that useful but this is realistic. Some of the things you find will more than likely become useful as time goes on and development continues. Mods can also help to greatly alleviate this situation.
You are punished quite severely for firing weapons. It draws a great deal more zombies than you could ever hope to deal with. Your melee choices for effectiveness are quite limited. It leaves you with bats or axes most of the time. It can make combat very repetitive.
You can alter zombie behavior to combat this a little bit with sandbox mode, but it's still a prevailing part of the game. Most other games will naturally draw zombies with gun fire as that is a standard for the genre, but it really is severely punished in this game particularly. Some people may enjoy that. I can't say I really do given the lack of other options for countering large groups of zombies (of which there are plenty - there is no effective option for dealing with them at this time).
I'd just like to actually be able to go on the offensive a little bit from time to time. I simply don't have that option in this game from my experience.
It's a great game none the less and development still seems fairly active.
Plenty of great mods as well.

Be fancy gunner girl on modded multiplayer server.
Run around carrying your expertly crafted BB Gun with a side mounted scope and bayonet for the dankest of memes.

Tactically try to approach the area. Enter from the door on the side, seems least dangerous.
Open the door and instantly pull out your combat knife as you pierce it through the zombies skull.
Hear the scream of the dead zombie attract two more.
Without effort, begin to charge forth as if you were some edgy guy with a troubled past named Kirito.
Slice. Dash. Hack. Cut. Stab. Skull penetrate.
After Zeds are gone, go to loot the area.
Realize you're hungry.
Find a well crafted salad on the zombie and some sick gear.
Take it all.
After a while, realize that you HAVE to eat this sald.
Eat the salad.
Suddenly panic as your character becomes super depressed.
Realize that no zombie has that kind of good gear on them.
Realize that the salad was poisoned with bleach.
Panic wildly as you contemplate crafting a suicide note to prevent yourself from turning.
Quickly try to run back to base as you slowly turn towards the withering world of the undead.
Give up after a random zombie falls from the roof and gets up and bites your groin hard.
Kill it with gun and just keep shooting, hoping that your friends will hear you.
Run out of ammo, only one bullet left.
Reload the clip.
One bullet. One suicide note. One chance.
Fire the bullet.
Miss somehow.
Cry as your body will slowly be violated and turned into FemZombie.
Eventually die moments later.
Learn the moral of the story: Never trust salads. Salads are bad.

This game is very well made. Everyone else loves the 1930's theme to the design, and I cannot disagree with them. The hand-drawn elements are very well-done and were worth the extra time waiting for this game. For the price, it is also definitely worth it. Just 20 dollars with a very high abundance of quality makes this game quite a steal for the price. However, the key elements to the game are these, in my personal opinion:
1. The difficulty in this game does not have to do with the bosses themselves. It has to do with the pattern, rhythm, and pace at which they fight. Once you understand and adapt to their movements and speed, it becomes very easy to counteract their attacks and to beat them very easily.
2. The graphics are in fact another huge element into further accentuating the game's uniqueness. It is pretty much unheard of there being a game that is themed in the style of a 1930's cartoon. In general, all of the graphics were in-fact hand drawn and inked in. This made the process of making the game take a lot longer than expected. However, the payoff was very much worth it. In just 34 frames/34 drawings, the smooth, crisp, and very fine movements of the characters in the game are very well done. Kudos to the artists for taking so much time to make it as authentic as possible.
3. The music is insanely good. Being a massive music nerd myself, I am entirely in love with the jazz in this game. And for the time period, it is very accurate. The big band and the big jazz band used in these pieces are supremely talented and the composer of the music is an incredibly talented gentleman who has definitely worked hard to make these pieces sound as fine and authentic as humanly possible. I give my full respect to those who participated in the making of the music in this game, they have done a stellar job at working on it and it paid off tremendously. Each piece was so fitting for the area. Railroad Wrath was incredibly accurate, High Seas Hi-Jinx was very well-written, and the use of the Baritone Saxophone as a key soloist in a few of these pieces and the lead trumpet also being a key feature was definitely a very valuable asset to all of these pieces. The piano pieces were very unique and the style at which they were played was very well done. In conclusion, the jazz in this game is amazing. Everything about them is perfect in every aspect possible and it definitely encourages me to become more involved with jazz.
In summary: Cuphead is a very well-made game. The music is fantastic and authentic, the graphics are uniquely made especially for a video game, and the gameplay is more related to coordination than difficulty. However, these are all just my opinions. I will not judge you if you disagree with my opinions because I'm not one to say that my opinions are factual and that if you objectify them then your opinion is wrong. I completely understand and will respect your choice.
Many thanks for those of you who took the time to read this. And for people who are wanting to buy the game, please do so. For the price, I would say it is more than worth it.

Apparently resources are used for building, healing and leveling your character. Wait there is more then 1 tab which I can build from?
You continue to find more monsters and some loot to equip for your characters and find the exit.
You are like: "How do I continue?" and after a while you find out that you can pick-up the crystal from the start and go to the exit to the next floor. But as you try to do that and forgot to lit up some rooms with your dust you get swarmed by all monsters that spawn from the "Exit event" and die.

Is Moebius bad? Short anwser: Yes, and I wouldn't recommend it. Long answer, see below.
There will be spoilers below.
The game starts out fine, if a bit odd that Malachi would go investigate a murder victim when his specialty by all accounts is evaluating artifacts and antiques, but I'll go with it. The puzzles are fine for the most part (if we ignore the end of the game, more on that below), the only real gripe being a safe code that is the date a newspaper article was written about a character's parents' divorce. Let's assume it makes sense to have some attachment to the day your parents announced publicly they were getting divorced, why would you then use the date from a newspaper story about the announcemen, which was presumably written at least a day later? Did the character get really attached to the newspaper article?
But that's relatively minor in the grand scheme of things. The real problem with this game is the story and characters. The story has the potential to be interesting, but is executed terribly. Character motivations are never really apparent, because you don't really know anything about them. No real attempt is made to make anyone likable, even Malachi. Some might say this was intentional with Malachi, but that's just silly. If you can't like the character you're supposed to be, then you have no real emotional stake in what he or she is trying to do. Even anti-heroes are made to be likeable or at least developed to invoke some amount of empathy. Not here.
The point when I went from finding this game mediocre to bad came fairly late in chapter 6, though. At one point you are required to seduce and then hold a knife to a woman's throat to get information from her. That was just vile. If the point was to make me loathe Malachi and Moebius, it was succesful. This is all followed up by a fairly simple but boring, boring, boring maze. The maze is broken up by an even more boring puzzle where you click on pictures that might be related to the location you are in. Then you are "treated" to a rather anti-climactic cutscene that ends on somewhat of a cliffhanger.
The character models and animations are bad, but that's not something that really concerned me. If there was a good game underneath I would easily look past that. Sadly, there isn't.
I don't really think I'll be paying Moebius 2 and I would recommend you don't bother with Moebius 1.

TL;DR the story has potential, but suffers from mediocre dialog, and flat characters. The animations and character graphics are bad. The puzzles are varied with some interesting mechanics, but not necessarily hard. It has a solid length.

Well backed the game on kickstarter, played through it.. The graphics are rather bad (or the characters are), and the animations are awful.
That would be ok if the story was solid, but it really isn't. The idea is good, the premise is ok, but the execution and dialog is medicore. Well the dialog is at times really bad, corny and too predictable.
The characters are awkward but not in a good way, and they are rather two dimensional and uninteresting. I'm reminded of the scientist Joshua from the Runaway series, though perhaps not that irritating (really felt that it hurt runaway 2 that he had a more prominent role).
The protagonist Malachi is not very likable, but that is intentional. He suffer from bland/poorly executed character development. It is a bit like the classic windows progress bar, it comes in weird chunks and it is not entirely sure how far it has to go.
The interaction between characters are bland and lack depth. There is a weird chemistry between the main characters, which "left unexplained" but with rather heavy suggestions. I would have prefered if the story either had aimed at Watson/Holmes buddies relation,  or a more serious approach with deeper meaning.
The FITA and the baddie seems like they have been slapped together in a hurry, as they do not offer much other than trying to frame the story.
The story is rather predictable once the scene is set, with a few twists here and there. The last chapter feels both rushed and drawn out, especially the last puzzle since the highlight feature is turned off and it suffers from the slow transitions between scenes.
I found the puzzles in general to be quite nice, with good variations. I did get stuck a couple of times which is nice enough, but for the most part they were pretty straight forward. Some of the puzzles does suffer a bit from "no that is not the right order" syndrome. Such as why do I need to climb an object in order to get to the object i'm interested in, especially as Malachi says "I need to climb box first", please just do it. It is however just minor inconveniences.
I really like the compare/analyze historical people mechanic, that is the guess who this person is puzzles, not the overly negative, shallow and nonsensical "look at that tramp" analysis of the characters in order to get the obvious clue for conversations.
The historical comparison is a nice mechanic, and there are a lot of interesting historical facts in them , well also some mythical "facts".  It worked for me all the way up until the last part of the game, where the historical characters began to be too modern, and not enough "space" to support the idea behind the moebius pattern.
Some reviews on the net talks about game breaking glitches, I did not run into any, but the slow and glitchy animations were a nuisance at times.
The music is quite good and provide a nice ambiance.
All in all Moebius has a lot of interesting ideas and mechanics, but suffer from poor execution, shallow characters and not enough polish. As a point and click adventure game there are two areas you should focus on, the story, the characters and the puzzles, and both characters and story feel rough.
I do not regret having backed the game, but do hope that Pinkerton Road will listen to the critique and do better with their next game(s) because the potential is there.  I know it was created on a tight budget, and for that I can forgive a lot of things and i would probably score it at 5/10 leaning at 6/10 due to the analysis puzzles.

The kitschy 2D art is sort of acceptable if you close one eye; the poor 3D models and inexplicably terrible animations, however, are not. Either the artists are aliens who never saw a real human being, or they are simply people stuck doing a job they have absolutely no talent for. The ugliness permeating the game is unbearable.
But okay, looks aren't everything; let's be mature and look past that. How does it play? Well, badly. Everything is stilted, unresponsive and seems to be plodding through a thick layer of mud; even the simplest actions take half an eternity punctuated by random pauses. And speaking of actions, let's discuss puzzles. By and large, they are oversimplified to a point that's almost insulting, and yet still manage to make little to no sense:
1. There is an object lying in the corner of a dark alley. Malachi will happily come right next to it, but won't pick it up, because it's too dark, and you need to fix a streetlamp first. It's a brick.
2. A cut lanyard is fixed with superglue. Lanyard. Superglue. Seriously.
A bizarre addition to the traditional formula is that Malachi won’t pick up objects until he knows where he’d like to use them, with precisely one result: backtracking guaranteed, which really doesn’t play nice with the lumbering pace of it all. And dear lord, the whole thing ends with an honest to goodness
. In an adventure game. I thought the nineties taught us never to do that again, but apparently I was mistaken. So. Dull.
But alright, alright, who cares about puzzles. Characters and story, that's what adventure games are all about! – Well, that is the worst thing. When I first learned what the overreaching plot was, I burst out laughing. Not because it is particularly funny, but because it is absolutely ludicrous. Sure,
and
got sort of silly towards the end, but
gets to that point about one third in and never stops going until it dissolves in a raging torrent of crazy (and painfully sexist to boot). And as far as characters are concerned, while I sort of want to appreciate the romance angle that’s going on in here, everyone in the game is so very wooden, whether it’s talking about the models, voice acting or writing, that it’s like watching two robots trying to learn what this “emotions” thing was all about. And failing, just like everything else in
is wont to do.
Oh, well. I backed this on Kickstarter; clearly, nobody's perfect.

Moebius: Empire Rising is kind of a mixed bag, and it's easy to pick out the negative elements and highlight them. The writing is sometimes a bit cheesy, and every character is unlikeable, with far too little done to bring you around by the end. Some of the puzzle solutions are laughably ridiculous, and both recurring puzzle mechanics are irritating at best, semi-random at worst. The tech really needs a lot of polishing: Character animation is almost universally terrible, the interface is buggy, inconsistent, or simply non-intuitively designed, and character models don't even begin to look human, much less realistic or evocative. (Seriously, have you ever met anybody with fingers that long? There's not a single person in this entire game whose fingers are less than eight inches long.) Also, it's shortish (around 10-15 hours) with a lot of loose plot ends at the end, which makes it feel more like an "episode" (or a few episodes) of a seasonal game than like a full game.
However, the game mostly succeeds despite itself, and I played it pretty much exclusively through from beginning to end. The puzzles for the most part are followable with very little "just try everything together" (with the exception of the observing-a-person puzzle mechanic, which often does devolve into just trying every combination). The story is interesting, and as much as the characters may not necessarily be likeable, you do get caught up in wanting to know what happens to them, to at least some degree.
I think I hoped for a lot more when I backed and when I bought this game, but what I got was still enjoyable, and I think that if you're interested in this type of game (point and click graphical adventures), it's definitely worth playing. Jensen is also clearly setting this up as the first in a series, so it would behoove you to get in on the ground floor.
One last note is that if anything one of the largest disappointments came, oddly, during the end credits, where you get to see artists' mock-ups of the various characters. They universally fit the characters much better than the clunky mess that the implemented character models wound up being. It made me long to have played *that* game, with those characters.
I feel like Pinkerton Road's standards did bring this game up above the standard Phoenix Online fare, but I really think that if the two continue to partner together and work together, they have to strive for better.

Minimum hud, mostly single shot guns, no 3d spotting, very few vehicles, bullets that actually hurt, limited snipers, good autobalance and excellent team work. One of the best shooters by far, especially if you find it hard to enjoy arcade shooters like the Battlefield series.

Pacing is something lacking from realism themed games simply because some time compression is needed for entertainment value. One of the subtleties lost in modern shooters is the balance of time taken recognizing targets, acquiring them, aiming and aiming while firing which makes engaging with large squads and volumes of fire interesting and fun.
RO2 not only models the timing of this affair well in a ww2 setting but has a very nice progression as your solder's skills and skills with certain weapons increases:
I recall running around on the left flank of Gumrak outside the first objectives as defender with a level 50 SVT, fending off wave after wave of diving germans who have been unable to take the first caps for about 10 minutes. Our position was keeping the germans at bay, who were exposed on the flank and lacking smoke. The experience of making 25 kills per life against a well armed enemy in a game where a single bullet kills is unparalleled, but possible because the high level weapon and soldier has definite advantages gained through hard experience. Veteran players play like vets, and they don't have special powerups or perks that identify their status. This ends up making the game fun for all level players but you will definitely be wanting to level up more and more...
The game requires you to make careful judgements and employ a variety of tactics if you don't want to be one of the fodder.
It has some issues of course, such as occasionally erratic animations and some quirky deployment ssystems (both weapon and spawn) but has aged into a mature and accessible shooter with a tense atmosphere and entertaining community.
