The stealth system sucks: PLEASE READ BELOW before immediately dismissing my argument:
Being clever at hiding is not a viable option:
- I've played dozens of games of man-hunt, hide and go seek, created successful ambushes. I'm an excellent seeker, I think both in and outside the box. As a runner/hider In real life: I've hidden right under people's noses as long as I remembered to:
a) be aware of my surroundings
b) be deceptive
c) remain quiet, and well-hidden,
d) think both inside AND outside the both (i.e don't hide under the car, stand still feet hidden behind the tires, be robust and silently maneuver. Also, don't go for the Tall car shrouded in darkness, Go for a small car in a BRIGHTLY lit area. Find a ladder? Climb up and either take up with you, or place it opposite side of the house of your location. Many a times I've been asked: "How the hell did you get up there!?
- In reality: I've won almost every hide and go seek type games using methods mentioned above.
Don't believe me? Fine I bet you're the dumbass that traps yourself in the darkest room with no escape route. Hides "Behind the velvet curtains" and my personal favorite: "under a pile of clothes"/"Buried under leaves." Very obvious.
Here are a few examples using a,b, c, and d.
1) simply hide behind any door, DO NOT CLOSE IT!!!, instead: squish yourself behind the middle of the door as open and inviting as possible so your pal won't slam you in the face by openng the door): the seeker walks in, checks the closet, the chest, under the bed, piles of clothes, the entire bathroom then leaves.
2) flattened myself as close as possible to the front of the couch., seeker walked straight past me to "check behind the TV set, when he got there, I volted over the couch and touched base.
3) hid behind a small car right across from the seeker, feet tucked in behind the car tires. Fool thought I'd hide behind the TALLER cars because they had more cover. While he was checking under the wrong cars, I won.
4) Hid on the opposite side of a wall like a ninja, sitting comfortably on a slab of concrete. The gaem had no base so I just chilled there for 30 minutes listening to the footsteps off my budies being chased, running back and forth, on the other side. Finally the seeker caled it quits (Ironically right behind me!) and gave him a good scare.
So you see, that is why the stealth system is unimmersive and crap. Another Argument of mine is thus: The AI CLEARLY do not have Heat Sensors, as you can still sneak up on them and whack the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them with a bat. They magically gain the sixth sense. but ONLY if you trigger them first!
The only alternative to survive when out gunned in this game is to run, far, far, away. That shows laziness on the creators' part for the AI
And Yes, I know this is just a game, but I play stealth games because I enjoy using wit, deception, and innovation. This game surely was innovative, but the broken stealth, and the bi-polar AI ruined it.

9/10: A tight puzzle-platformer with a dark atmosphere. Make your way from left to right while weathering challenges such as giant enemy spiders, mind-controlling glow worms, and a decaying environment just waiting to crush you.
Limbo seems pretty simple. Walk left or right, jump, climb up ropes, push and pull some things, and make your way towards the ending by solving problems before they kill you. Yet combined with the art style and no dialogue, the game feels uniquely surreal and desolate... in a good way.
There's not a "story" to speak of, and whatever questions you have won't be answered. All you have is the shadowy child you control and the certainty that there's something coming up designed to end you. Are you really in Limbo? No idea. Who are you and how did you get here? Does it matter?
Yet as the environment change, the puzzles grow more intricate and use a refreshing variety of mechanics. Where at the start it keeps things constrained to familiarizing the player with timing their jumps and interactions, soon enough it'll come to electrified platforms, buzzsaws, utter darkness, rising water, and even gravity reversal. Even so, it presents each challenge in a sequence without becoming overwhleming, opting to keep the pace of the game cautious rather than hectic.
Overall, Limbo is a thoughtful, well styled and designed puzzle platformer. Closer to Braid than Super Meat Boy in pace, it's focus on a dark style and juicy, well-paced puzzles make for a great time.

I find myself obsessed with making even the slightest progress when I play alone, even if you can’t really call it progress. I fist punch the air when I come across a decent enough weapon, or a working generator knowing that it will increase my rate of survival somewhat, only to become outraged that whilst I was looting a fridge a zombie bit my neck because I couldn’t see it coming behind me. You can take all of the precautions you like whether you last 1 day or 100, surviving another day is quite a thrill and although these sorts of games are not short in supply, most often miss the mark by some distance, where as this game, that is lucky to even exist; is truly remarkable and will no doubt ,be an indie game worth mentioning in years to come. Long live GOOD Survival zombie games.

Welcome to Project Zomboid, a Post-Apocalyptic 4th person view zombie survival game done right. This game instead of going towards the current meta of FPS Zombie Games or First Person Zombie Survival Games such as Dying Light/Dead Island, opts to instead revolve the gameplay around completely on just surviving to the next day.
Whether it is stocking up on water and non-perishable food for when the plumbing and electricity go out by any means necessary, or bulking up your house to better prevent the undead from entering it to rip you apart, the game has nailed the survival aspects right on the head. Even with the 4th person view and the pixel-like graphics (Which I love both by the way, they were excellent design choices) this game is an all encompassing immersive experience, and for the most part extremely realistic. This game has not even been completely finished yet either, and has a large modding community along with multiplayer! The Developer teams is constantly updating it, patching bugs, tweaking gameplay to be more enjoyable or realistic, and adding new content. I personally applaud the developers from The Indie Stone, bravo!
Anyhow, let's get right into the basics of this game. First and foremost, the game only has a few select maps so far that you can travel between in the world using the same character. While the entire maps are not randomly generated, everything else in the game IS along with things such as zombie placements, what items spawn in what containers, whether or not a zombie will drop anything besides clothing, whether or not the scratch from a zombie hitting you will turn you into a zombie or not, and the amount of time before the water and electricity shut off. The latter of this you can set in a custom game and through difficulty increase/decrease it depending on whether you want it to be easier or harder. This is a very important part of the game, as it gives you a certain amount of time to prepare before this and set yourself up so you don't just die right off the bat. This is because certain foods that require a fridge to be kept fresh (Perishable Foods), will no longer be able to keep you fed for very long after this. They will rot, and you may die from eating them from the ensuing infection (Depending on RNG, you may get sick and die even with medicene, so choose wisely! This is rare, but it still can happen). Water, will not go bad from what I can tell so far although this may be added much later as a feature in the game to prevent you from just water hoarding 90 Gallons of water then never having an issue. Also, there is Permadeath in this game! If your character dies, they die. You can make a new character to then continue in the world you made, which makes it harder and harder as it goes on due to the previous ones ransacking it along with the world slowly becoming more hostile as zombie spawns ramp up with most easy food sources disappearing. There is also a feature where as just like in The Last of Us, due to much of the worlds population dying, the Wild will begin to retake urban areas and once inhabitated human settlements. This means that you cannot just stay inside one house forever, as eventually holes may start to appear in your house as it is slowly torn apart by nature and decays in Time. This does take a long time, but it is a very interesting feature. This will cause you to begin to either start repairing the house frantically, or just build your own which too will wither away without your constant vigiliance on the state of the home. There are also seasons in the game, so you must adapt for each season accordingly (Heavy Clothing in Winter, Light Clothing in Summer, etc.) as you progress.
In combination, you have one of the most realistic Indie Open-World Zombie Games called Project Zomboid! I highly recommend that you check it out for yourself! At the end though, it still does not score a perfect ten as it does not appeal to all players due to the extreme difficulty and large learning curve. It can sometimes be irritating to continue trying to get good at it, if you aren't a very serious player. Along with this, it is missing some key components from the last time I played recently, including NPC Humans, Vehicles, Pets, etc. When it is finished into public release and all of these are met, it will score an easy perfect score.

I have played Dungeon of the Endless since it was released in Early Access. The game started simple and fun but through its development the creators really grew the game into something great.
At it's core the game plays somewhat like a tower defense game meets roguelike. You control 1-4 heroes... err prisoners that crash landed on [a dungeon] and must carry your escape pod's power core through each level in order to power rooms and elevators. You must do your best managing your resources (food, industry, science, dust - typical resources in the endless games) while you set out to find the elevator in each level of the dungeon. There is a huge risk-vs-reward system, as each room you explore must either be given power or left unpowered (allowing hostile monsters to spawn). And it almost goes without mentioning that, being somewhat of a roguelike, that there is permadeath; If you lose your heroes, or your ships crystal, you will have to start a new game.
Each hero, building and item really feels like it has worth. You will really feel it when you lose a hero or building (module) to an agressive wave of mosnters, though you will meet other prisoners and natives throughout the dungeon that you can hire by sharing food. Each of the 16 heroes has a very unique feel with different skills, narritive and stats. Each item ranges from humrous to epic as you upgrade from using your salvaged starter weapons to the more advanced technology spread throughout the dungeon.
The finished game has a very well done progression-to-unlock system that gives you every reason to keep playing the game after you have finially made it to the end. New heroes are exciting and new starter ships change the way the game plays, plus there is a ton of unlockable art and such. I haven't had any experience with the multiplayer but it seems like it could be tense and a lot of fun. I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes roguelikes or tower defense games!

This time around, we are playing as Darius Mason, son of Jake Mason (from the film Red Faction: Origins), and grandson of Alec Mason (Red Faction: Guerrilla). The terraformer has been destroyed, driving all of Mars' human residents underground. But even deeper inside the Mars crust lies an alien threat. If that sounds Red Faction: Armageddon has ventured into B-movie / game territory, you'd be right. It's a linear shooter, with some fantastic weapons (magnet gun! though the Napalm Laser is another favorite) and decent atmosphere and graphics. While I suppose much of Armageddon has been done before, it's done well here. So well that I was disappointed when the game ended that there wasn't more to it.
If you're looking for more to do after finishing the single-player campaign but don't want to play through the campaign again, there are two additional modes available. Ruin mode (destroy the environment) is a lot of fun: destroy the environment as fast as possible. You'll be able to use whatever weapons you've unlocked in the main campaign. But there are not enough maps and only two varieties: Free Play and Challenge. Multi-player cooperative horde mode (up to four players on a team), fighting waves of enemies, in either Survive (what it says) or Defend (repair / defend something while waves of enemies attack). There are eight multiplayer maps, each in two varieties for 16 maps in all. There is some fun to be had here, but with so few people playing the game, matchmaking is a problem. You won't be able to get 100% of the game's achievements without getting some folks to help you out.
The "Path to War" DLC, now included for free, is a series of four missions that tie into the main campaign. There doesn't seem to be any reason for them to exist. Maybe the missions were rejected from the main campaign but the dev team were perhaps proud of the level design and released them anyway. The missions are fun, but it is a short, disjointed experience.
I'd like to think that the dev team, knowing THQ was facing troubled times (they went bankrupt shortly after the game's release), said something like, "However big or small our budget is, that's how big /small our game will be. Whatever. Let's make it the best game that we can." And they succeeded, it's a tremendously fun game. If you enjoy playing it as much as I did, at the end you'll be wanting more. But there is no more to be had...

What where the developers thinking when they were creating this? For those of you who didnt played Red Faction Guerrilla wont see much to complain about this game. However for those of us who have it you will soon understand why this game was a fail if compared to Guerrilla. First it looks like a downgraded version of Guerrilla not a sequel since in this one you dont have the same free roam GTA style sandbox game. In this one you play as one of the Grandsons of Alec Mason RFG(Main Character), blasting off endless corredors with aliens trying to kill you. Differing from RFG Guerrilla where you had an open world in which you could destroy and do anything at anytime you wished. However this one is more like a corridor shooter where your only option is to go to door A to Door B then next level. Its not that this one is a bad game it just that when they decided to remove the open world feature it made this sequel look like an inferior product if compared to its predecessor Red Faction Guerrila. Now talking about the improvements this game improves from Guerrilla by allowing you to buy upgrades directly through the game menu, instead of having to go to your safehouse weapon store, like in guerrilla. Another main improvement was giving you the reconstructor gun in the beginning of the game instead of it being locked until you beat the game or inserted a mod, like in guerrila. Other minor improvements where a better GEO-MOD more optimized and causing less framerate drops and a small improvements in the graphics engine.

Long story short, a fun and interesting game. (MAY HAVE SPOILERS)
the good:
- fun gameplay
- nice art
- detailed settings and characters
- nice dialogue
- decent gameplay pacing
- fun story to unravel
- user-friendly
- parts of the gameplay can be pretty comical, like how obviously stupid the NPC's can be :P
- original "analysis" game mechanic is pretty cool
the bad:
- buggy at times (maybe they'll do some patches?)
- the 3D animation and meshes are a bit wonky
- to me, this game doesn't top Jane Jensen's best older games
- I don't know about the Chekhov's Gun game mechanic -- to me that just means more time taken wandering around just to get items you could have taken earlier
Here's my "essay" version of my review.
I really enjoyed playing through this game. It's hard enough for me to want to look at an online walkthrough here and there, but easy enough for me to figure out how to move further into the game without a walkthrough, most of the time. I really like the analysis mechanic. It's a different way of learning about people, objects and the story.
I have some complaints though. Game design-wise, I wouldn't readily praise the "Chekhov's Gun" take on collecting items. In the end, it just means "oh there's an item I need, but I can't take it now but I will later and take a jumbo jet to come back for it..." it seems arbitrary to me. Is this to save space in your inventory? *shrug*
Story-telling-wise, this game was alright. I really liked the mystery. I never gave a second thought to the meaning of the title for the past two years, long after I'd helped fund the kickstarter for it. But I'm glad I didn't give it a second thought, because it helped in creating a positive gameplay experience. The text appearing as a way of telling us Malachi's thought processes? I've seen very few other pieces of entertainment that use this method of telling us what the character's thinking... and the only other place I've seen it is in the TV series Sherlock. I get pretty bothered when a creative piece is being this blatantly obvoius about borrowing, if in fact this is what happened.
There isn't nearly as much shock and twists in this story as I would have liked. There's way more intensity in Gabriel Knight, for example... and wasn't that how Jane Jensen was advertising Moebius? So that we'd have another game that's like Gabriel Knight? (I'm thinking of Sins of the Fathers).
As for the art, the 2D art is pretty nice. But there's a lot of inconsistency and distracting wonkiness to the way the 3D models react to their animations, as well as the animations themselves. The first time I saw Malachi's walk cycle from the front, for example, I complained about it out loud.
I'm not asking for every creative piece to have "top notch" graphics, whatever that means. Someone decided to have this game use 3D characters and objects... so it's going to bother me if Gretchen's upper arm bends completely the wrong way as she's drinking her martini, unless it was completely intentional. My only expectation is *consistency,* no matter what style of graphics is chosen. This is one of the reasons why I sorely miss the old game graphics from Jane Jensen games... like that of Gabriel Knight or King's Quest VI.

The introduction to this game is an unforgettable experience, even more so if you go in blind as I did without having a clue what the game is about. The way the city of Rapture is presented to you is awe inspiring, and I remember feeling something along the lines of "What the hell happened here?" with a mixture of "Oh crap I gotta get out of this place" while playing. As you explore the game you find hints and clues about the events that transpired in the city before your arrival, and how those events culminated into the hell you find yourself in, keeping you in its immersive grip for as long as you allow.
The gameplay leaves little to be desired for a game of its time. Moebius: Empire Rising is a new Adventure game created by Jane Jensen (Gabriel Knight series and Gray Matter) and Phoenix Online Studios, best known for Cognition: An Erica Reed Thriller and a never-finished fan-made game entitled The Silver Lining, which was based on the King's Quest series.
So it's a decent pedigree (at least as far as the writing is concerned), but is it actually a good game?
In my not-so-humble opinion, no, it's not. I wish it was, but unfortunately, the game barely qualifies as bargain bin fodder. I'm not someone who hates Adventure games, either. I grew with up Sierra Online and LucasArts games, so I've played a bunch, both good and bad. It's a shame, but this title is within the "bad" camp.
What's bad, you ask? Basically everything except the story. Phoenix Online Studios took on a lot more than they could handle. It's too bad the game suffered for it.
My reasons for the "thumbs down" review are below:
Character Models: The characters look gangly, with unusually thin arms and legs. They have high armpits and long, thin fingers. They also move awkwardly and their faces contort in odd ways when speaking. One character in particular looks like she's snarling when she speaks.
Animation: The characters move like stiff dolls at best. While I didn't expect motion capturing or super high budget work, I'd have liked to see animation beyond what would be normal in the early 2000s.
Textures: I know some AAA games have poor textures at times, but virtually every texture in this game is sub-par. Honestly, it looks like a game made in 2005 (and even that's being generous). Skin looks flat, hair doesn't move, clothing is blotchy, and cars look like plastic toys. In addition, background characters look like low-res VGA placeholders.
Environments: At first glance the environments don't look too bad. They're 2.5D and quite decent. When you look closer, however, you see the low-res work, jagged contours of objects, poorly placed light sourcing, and ridiculously inept shadows.
Seriously, the shadows under Malachi and Gretchen in the antique shop make them look like they're floating. Plus, the shadows are blocky and tend to shimmer. It's like looking at a PS2 launch title.
Audio: The music is quite good (I actually left it on, whereas I usually turn music off in games) and the general sound effects used work fine. It's when the characters speak that it all falls apart. The voice actors deliver their lines in a flat, awkward fashion, as if the voices were created by a synthesizer. The only voice actor who was good at all was Malachi's, which is good I suppose considering he's the main character.
Options: Not much to speak of, but it's a Point-and-Click Adventure game. It's not like FOV or SSAO would really matter much. That said, there is an option to choose up to 8x antialiasing, but it doesn't work. Jaggies are ever-present in the game.
When you start the game, a launcher appears and you can set the resolution and graphics quality (although your options only range from "fantastic" to "fastest"). You can also decide if you want to play the game in a window or full screen.
One thing that's odd is there's a tab for input on the launcher, only it's meaningless. It doesn't affect a damn thing in the game and gives the impression that a gamepad could be used. It can't, and I have an Xbox 360 controller hooked up, so it's not like I need Xpadder or any other piece of software to "trick the game."
Interface: It's all mouse-driven, with the exception of a few hotkeys. You can also press F5 and F7 to bring up the save/load menus. Like classic PC games, these are real manual saves (not quicksaves or autosaves or checkpoint saves!) and you can even name them.
Story: It's a Jane Jensen game, so it'll have an interesting storyline. I haven't finished the game, but if I had, I wouldn't go into detail here. Doing so might accidentally post a spoiler.
I will, however, say that the characters aren't that likable, especially Malachi, the protagonist. He's a jerk and not a charasmatic jerk like Gabriel Knight.
End Thoughts: If you play this game, do it for the story. Try to ignore the mess that makes up the rest of the game. I'd also strongly urge anyone interested to wait for a sale, preferablly one that's at least 75% off the normal price.

Firstly, I'll begin by stating that I am an avid Jane Jensen fan and was a backer for Moebius ER.
As for my review, I'll begin from the positives:
* The story is great. It’s mature and somewhat relevant to real global events and pulls you right in the mood for a grand mystery.
* Malachi is a TERRIFIC main character! He’s well-written, multi-dimensional and evolving through the story… (I was hunting for all the hotspots just to hear what he had to say about them!)
* Another thing about Malachi… His VA (Owen Thomas) hit the role out of the ballpark! His was the best performance in the game by far. He MADE the character, not unlike Tim Curry made Gabriel Knight.
* David is also a great sidekick to Kye, and there’s a great chemistry between the two.
* Robert Holmes, again, paired the game seamlessly with a terrific Soundtrack, ranging from mysterious ambient themes to action-packed thrilling rock pieces.
* The multiple locals are diverse and beautifully rendered and colorful on most chapters.
* The game is pretty long and will take an average player from 9 to 12 hours to complete, depending on how long you’ll get stuck.
Now to the cons:
* Some characters’ body proportions and / or postures are way off, too bad one of those characters is the main one.
* Animations are ranging from mediocre to bad.
* They are also unbearably slow, esp. when there are multiple animations performed in a row.
* The music is sometimes too loud and you have to rely on the subtitles. (The prison scene and some movies towards the end come to mind).
* The subtitles going up from the bottom of the screen and flying out again is annoying and straining on the eyes, especially during short sentences.
* Some puzzles felt too simple and the game “held your hand” while solving them. (Sometimes getting stuck is a good thing in an adventure game!)
A trully wonderful game. Get it on sale right now! :D

Fallen Enchantress is an awesome 4X turn-based strategy/sorta-RPG game. One thing that I enjoy about the game is that it’s VERY different from other fantasy 4X games in a number of key ways.
First, it takes place many years after the world was devastated by a war of magic – it’s essentially a post-apocalyptic fantasy world. Virtually everything concerning magic and technology had been lost (technology in this case being the standard medieval-level of weaponry and military tactics). You’re leading a rag-tag group of survivors to build your faction’s first city and begin to rebuild. Of course, you were chosen as leader because you are one of the only people remaining who can wield magic.
Secondly, there’s none of the standard Orcs, Goblins, Elves, Dwarves, blah blah blah that have become standard fare for fantasy games. The races are all (with the exception of Men) completely original, as are most of the bestiary that pose a constant threat outside of the safety of your cities. However, the game makes all of the new races and creatures easy to understand with a very thorough and easy-to-access online guide that seamlessly integrates lore and story with game mechanics. Want to know what the Trogs can do before you play as them? Just hover over the attribute marker reading TROG BLOOD in the character roster and see their benefits and disadvantages. Got an army of Brood Hunters headed for a city? Just click on the army on the map and click their profile to read all about them and see their stats.
Also, virtually everything is customizable. Make new leaders, new factions, new units. Just researched Warg Riding and want to make some cavalry? Just pop into the unit design screen and design them, what armor they wear and what weapons they carry, etc. Just make sure you have a source of Wargs handy – depending on what weaponry and armor you give your units, you may need a variety of resources (metal, horses/Wargs, magic crystal, etc) to create them. These can be found on the map and brought under control of your cities by building on them.
All-in-all, it’s a great game that slipped under the radar to a certain extent.

Downside is the core game comes with very few maps to play in (especially if you want to play a long game so you get a chance to explore all of your city and unit options). You can fully customise your sovereign hero (essentially your in game representation) as well as the race you choose to play if you want to create your own, to make some pretty amazing and fun combinations. No game is the same I find, although Life Magic seems to be the single most important school of magic to have access to.
Unfortunately the game seems to crash *way* too much, but as long as you remember to save often (don't trust the autosave) it's still a great deal of fun entertainment for the kind of gamer who prefers patient resource management over the old zerg rush.
Definitely recommend, but can't imagine it being a game for everyone.

Limbo is probably one of the most well-known indie titles, constantly praised for the work of one man. However this is not the title I would recommend to someone that would like to get into the indie scene.
Let's get down to it.
I wish steam had a neutral review system, because it's definitely not a bad game, it's just not one I'd recommend getting for the full price even if you're a fan of indie titles.

The first time I saw Limbo, I was immediately taken away by its graphic design. With just the two most basic colors, the developer was able to make one of the most atmospheric game I have ever seen. The black represents the overwhelming darkness while the white plays the role of the soft, weak light. The minimalistic sounds also helps set deadly, isolated atmosphere. The sounds of the steps or the water feel very real. However, black-and-white has its limited. The world they create doesn’t change throughout the game so if you spend your time looking at it too much you may find it boring after an hour.
Talk about the gameplay, you spend most of the times encountering and solving the puzzles. There are sometimes it’s more about jumping and running. But puzzles are the core of gameplay. I’d say the quality of puzzles is decent. With just some old mechanics from other platformer games like the boxes, the elevators or the reversed gravity, they create some very clever puzzles. It does not feel really satisfying to control the character. The mistakes are easy to made when you have to timing, jump on small platform. And the fact is that it’s really easy to die in this game, you can be killed by a fallen box or if you fall from a bit too high place. Therefore, it’s kind of frustrating when you have already knew how to get through but you still have to retry several times to ultimately get to the next one.
The game is pretty short and it’s better this way, it does its best to offer an enjoyable gameplay in one of the most unique worlds in video games.
Very happy with this little brain teaser

This is like those games and not like those games. It's like them in that it's super innovative. It's not like them in almost (I say again almost) every other respect.

For Amplitude: I am sold. Really, just keep up quality like this and I will tell you to shut up and take my money every time. You guys are amazing and I really hope everything goes well for you for this and any other project you guys work on.

A timeless classic with amazing gameplay and storytelling.

A breddy gud WWII shooter with a lot of good ideas but it's held back by some major flaws.
Red Orchestra is as authentic as a multiplayer WWII shooter can get, if you can ignore the constant nazi-bolshievek arguments that keep appearing in the chatbox. In any server with more than 20 people you're going to pick up the rifleman role or any of the lesser roles, gamechanging roles like marksman, commander and machine gunner are few in numbers and the entire game can hinge on how well those players can make use of their roles. Everyone else is just cannon fodder, you go out, try pick off as many as you can but you're going to end up getting shot from someone you can't see. It sounds infuriating but it's really fun. The large numbers of soldiers, the wide open maps, the look of the game, the way it plays all lend to the immersion. When you're hold up on the second floor of a bombed-out building with artillery dropping around you while you put a few rounds into the gut of a German who entered downstairs and you hear him scream for a full 15 seconds that's when you know you're having fun.
This game has some really obvious problems and they do ruin the fun. The main one being that this game just isn't fluid at all, movement is clunky and often unreliable, simple inputs like switching weapons often requires multiple attempts if you're doing anything else at the same time, it's so easy to interrupt reloads unintentionally without even realising. It doesn't feel fair if I die because I ran out of ammo and switching to my secondary took me a full ten seconds to do because moving slightly to the left is apparently too much for the game to handle. Some maps have some serious balancing issues too, although I know it was probably difficult to find a good spot between realistic and fair but it's frustrating when the 10 servers with more than 10 players are all playing the same 3 maps with those issues. The game also doesn't explain a lot, I still have no clue what value there is in levelling up weapons, I still don't know why I'm given the option to bandage an injury only to find out I've wasted 15 seconds because it was pointless and I had to watch my screen just slowly fade to black, I still don't know how to complete certain objectives and I still don't understand certain leader functions. It's one thing for a game to not hold your hand, it's another for a game to just not explain basic things.
Either way it's pretty fun and is usually cheap.

(+)First of all let's talk about wut's good about this game.
1) Some mechanics in the game are quite fresh, like finding matches between modern and historical figures and "judge him/her by the look".
2) I enjoyed some dry humors in the game, and i'm rofl to some of the sexual innuendos. (David's joke? Ha-Ha-Not-So-Much)
3) The BGM is definitely a good part of the game. The music for opening credits was stunning.
(-)And wut's lacking in this game.
1) Character Modelling. Can it be more obvious? The way ppl walk and stand is ultra stiffy and awkward.
2) Item Interactions. The problem is that when u find something that might come in handy, Malachi will tell u he doesn't need it right now, and u have to perform certain moves to set off the "flag" then take the item to solve a miny puzzle, this way is quite absurd, since Malachi can take plenty of things with him, y can't he just take it when he sees it? (And don't get me started on he actually put a LANTERN into his suit's pocket...
(?)And in-between, let's talk about some controversial parts.
1) The Concept. To me, the concept is unique, and not unique at all. Sure, the Moebius Theory is quite intriguing, but the execution lacks novelty, just find someone with historical importance and create a modern doppleganger, wut's creative about that?
2) The characters. I like the two starring roles, I can literally cut the tension between Malachi and David, sometimes i'm even yelling to the screen "Just get over your UST you two".
Still many ppl thinks the characters are too shallow, I think the issue is that the characters are not meant for us to immerse to. Moebius is not as bad some of the reviews say but it’s not that good either, it’s a bog-standard adventure game that does very little to make itself memorable. It’s a real disappointment considering this is Jane Jensen’s newest game. Jensen’s previous games, the Gabriel Knight series and the more recent Gray Matter, were quality written games with likable characters that got you immersed in the games and their stories and are some of the best adventure games around. Moebius is not this, while the basic plot is interesting enough at first the main characters are really bland and the side characters are all horrible people but not in an interesting way. The puzzles are alright for the most part, but the last section of the game is a terrible slog of padding and occasional trial and error puzzles. The graphics aren’t good, but they were on a budget so I can easily forgive it. I didn’t run into any glitches so it’s solidly designed in that regard.
Ultimately I don’t really regret buying it, but I wouldn’t recommend it. There are more than enough  recent adventure games that are far better that you could play instead. (Broken Age, the Blackwell Series, Kentucky Route Zero, Gone Home, Walking Dead, and Wolf Among Us just to name a few) Not to mention that you’re also better off playing the Gabriel Knights and Gray Matter, the former you can buy on GOG, the latter on both GOG and Steam. You can do a lot worse when it comes to adventure games so I would only suggest getting this game if you’re really hurting for adventure games and it’s on sale for cheap. Overall though Moebius is just really mediocre and easily forgettable; for the average person I’d say skip it.

Not too bad, but slightly annoying. The other bug was on a few levels where the spawn was located on top of the door to the previous level, we would constantly enter that door upon death.
Overall this is a fun party game that includes a few other multiplayer modes alongside adventure, giving it some decent replayability. Worth a couple bucks.

Moebius is an entertaining and decently good point n' click game that lacks a lot of polish. Jane Jensen's story is bit silly but interesting. Robert Holme's music is fantastic but bit repeatitive. The gameplay is little bit disappointing because of the narrow amount of choises you can make. Moebius feels like a simplified and slightly modernized version of those 90s point n' click adventure games that we all grew up with. The length of the game is around 10 to 15 hours for an average player.
I liked the characters in the game and I liked the story. Althought I do have to write that Jane Jensen in past has written better material than this. There're issues with the narrative that feel stupid after you've played the game though. And even during the game you occasionally wonder why certain things had to be done in a particular way.
Moebius is a fairly basic point n' click game that doesn't do anything particularly well or bad. It's like it was made following a googled tutorial on how to make a point n' click adventure game. It doesn't add anything new or even try to challenge the existing concepts.
Most of the puzzles in Moebius are fairly easy to figure out. There's usually only one route to take to a puzzle and only one solution for that puzzle exists. Sometimes the solution is rather unrealistic. To avoid making Moebius a "hidden object" game and to add some realism into it the game doesn't allow you to pick up items or go to some places until the need to do so arises. That leads to an issue where you need to remember place of certain items you previously couldn't pick up. Occasionally there are more challenging puzzles that are well written. The main character also has infinite pockets to stuff things to which I thought was amusing.
Towards the ending of the Moebius started to fell apart. For example (without spoiling anything) the player needs to fly from Washington to New York to pick alcohol from a bar the main character has contantly refused to enter into any given point of time during the game. There's nothing indicating you need to do so. I don't even understand why there couldn't be alcohol store at Washington player could enter. This is done so because main character thought that the antique item in his shop he saw earlier would still be there and that he needed to pick that up for a certain character. This is done based upon observation of that character's tastes. And so upon exiting antique store main character thought that he would also need to bring alcohol seeing the bar on other side of the street. That is some truly horrible game writing and game design in my opinion.
Graphics in Moebius are decent and I like the art style. But this is probably a good point to start talking about the bugs. Moebius has lots of bugs. None of those bugs break the game and they're mostly just visual annoyances. Such as main character is able to stand on certain places he isn't supposed to be able to stand. Or certain water effects are places on surfaces where they shouldn't be. Occasionally the animations have timing problems. Sometimes there are texture related issues such as really low resolution textures. None of the visual issues are dramatically bad. It's just a sign of a lack of polish in Moebius.
Music and audio is good and there are lots of nice music. However sometimes the main theme just repeats itself so much that it's the only thing you'll remember after you've played the game. This is due the fact that the main theme is also present in various tracks in a suttle ways. So even if I do like the main theme quite a bit, it became an annoyance to hear so often during the game. Sometimes there were audio tracks where the mixing had failed. Voice acting in this game is decently played out.
User Interface of the Moebius is weird but it works. There are no "verbs" which makes the game easier to play since the game always offers only the actions you can do with various points of interest. Moebius is designed towards people who have little or no experience with point n' click adventure games. The way UI has been designed and the strong hint system in this game reflects that. I also thought it was weird that the game didn't have end results screen despite counting points in a similar manner to the classic Sierra adventure games all which have the end results screen.
Technically the game works fine most of the time. But being based on top of Unity Engine has all the good things and all the issues that come with the Unity Engine. For example the game has freezing issues on certain hardware. But those can be corrected with a launch parameter. And sometimes the rendering quality is pretty bad.
To sum things up, Moebius is entertaining game which is fun to play. The story is interesting but sometimes badly written. I liked the main characters and would like to see more of their adventures in the future. Moebius as a game also severely lacks polish and fine tuning. It's worth the cost but it's not outstanding game like Gabriel Knight or Gray Matter.

Today, Phoenix Online Publishing has released their highly-anticipated mystery adventure game Moebius: Empire Rising for both the PC and Mac.  The mind behind this title is Jane Jensen who launched a very successful Kickstarter campaign to back this project and deliver a very entertaining title to her fans.  Jane is a veteran of the gaming industry and mastermind behind amazing adventure-based plots.  Her company, Pinkerton Road, teamed up with the indie team at Phoenix Online Studios on this project.  Moebius: Empire Rising is available through their online store for purchase or via Steam.  Later this year, the game will release for Android, iOS and Linux platforms as well.  The game is also available for Demo if you just want to check it out before buying it.  For an “official” description, here is part of the press release from Phoenix Online Publishing:
Ok, now that all of the official stuff is out of the way…you want to know what I thought of the game, right?  I was generously granted a review copy of the game, via Steam, and spent in excess of 15 hours playing it.  It’s a single-player title that supports both Steam Achievements and Steam Trading Cards.  I was able to work my way through the entire game during that time and really only found myself “stuck” in a couple areas.  My first impressions of the game were that the cut scenes were very well done and while they can be skipped, I would recommend sitting through them to really get a feel for the story.  If you’ve read the prologue comic (if not, go read the damn prologue comic) it will also help set the table a little for the game.  One thing I enjoyed about the cut scenes along with the story line is it made the game feel very much like an interactive comic book.  That is not to say it’s graphically set that way, it isn’t.  The story line however was very well done and engaging.  The other major thing that I noticed straight off was the soundtrack.  I am serious when I say, it may be one of the better soundtracks that I have experienced in any game I have ever played.  The music was spot on with the story and really added to the overall feel.  It was clear from the beginning that there was a lot of thought put into this.  I found myself feeling like I was not only playing some sort of interactive comic book but rather watching a novel develop before my eyes.
You play the majority of the game as Malachi, who will come off as a brash and pompous pretty boy for the most part.  Malachi possesses several talents, some of which I will not spoil for you but the main talent being that he has an amazing ability to analyze situations and details.  This serves him well as part of the antique business that he owns and where he makes his money.  I will admit, this is typically not my genre of gaming.  I am normally an FPS or RPG type guy, but I also enjoy games involving puzzles.  This is what intrigued me so much about this title, solving puzzles.  I found that throughout the course of this game, up until the ending cut scenes, I was really learning to shape the way I was thinking in-game.  Once I started looking for those minor details that would eventually get me past an area, I was hooked.  It’s a game where attention to detail is key and decision making is crucial.
As Malachi makes his way through the story, I found myself liking him more than I did when the game began.  I am sure this was by design.  The other main character is David Walker, a former Special Forces operator who Malachi eventually teams up with.  The two character’s couldn’t be more dissimilar and I thought David was a great addition to the story and game.  As a matter of fact, once David was introduced to the game, I found myself laughing a lot more throughout the story and conversations they would have.  I won’t spoil anything, but do yourself a favor and listen to David’s corny jokes.  By solving puzzles, analyzing people with detailed dossiers and web searches as well as choosing the right topics and questions to present to other characters you progress through the game and often affect certain paths.  That is not to say it’s a “choose your own adventure” style game (my God I just dated myself) but there are situations that can go one way or another based on actions/dialogue.  Some of the puzzles may seem a little mundane but I will say that some really made me think, and a couple of them had me simply stumped.  The game also offers the ability to turn hints on or off, and there is an achievement for completing the game without them on at all.
Overall, I started the game admittedly skeptical because it just wasn’t my typical genre.  What I was left with was a very great appreciation for the time put into the game and just how engaging it ended up being.  For someone that likes a solid story combined with thought-provoking puzzles and situations, this game is fantastic.  Add in extremely well put together cut scenes and an incredible soundtrack and I would say that for $29.99, you’d have a winner on your hands.  Honestly, aside from some moderately corny dialogue and wonky walking animations, I couldn’t find any significant flaws with the game.  There is no current DLC plan for Moebius: Empire Rising but I will be surely keeping an eye out for some or any new titles from this publisher and studio.
In the end, I would give Moebius: Empire Rising 4.5 out of 5 Pink Cows.

username: The Man Who Bought The World
text:
A game of vigilance and planning.
This game will make you twitch, shiver, and worry. And the wildlife will keep you on your toes because this game succeeds in invoking that primal fear we all have for our survival.
You will learn to identify each sounds you hear and be wary of them. You will learn to squint in the midst of a blizzard to find shelter. You will plan carefully and have it go awry in the worst possible way from time to time.
The artwork is gorgeous, even though it's not necessarily realistic. Together with the ambience sounds, you will be immersed in this in no time. I live in a tropical region and haven't much experience with blizzards, but I do know how it feels when your face feels numb due to cold winds, so I especially appreciate the immersion, the roleplay, that this game has brought me.
There are roleplaying elements such as survival skills and inventory management, but what truly makes this a roleplaying experience for me is the cold desolation, the white hell.
Easily 9 out of 10 from me with rooms for improvement in graphics and gameplay elements.
Here's hoping for a greater game at full release with Story Mode.

When I first saw this game on Steam it looked like a copy of Starbound and/or Terraria. But unlike some people, I'm okay with a game using elements from other games I like. Instead of waiting for Starbound 1.0 or Terraria 2, I get to play a new game with a different team of devlopers taking it to it's own direction.
Out of the Early Access games I have (see my profile)  this is one of the most polished ones in terms of bugs. It isn't perfect but it's very much playable with very little interuption.
Combat is pretty straight forward and basic until you get transformations and tamed creatures. The transformations work like you'd expect, you gain the traints of that creature (including flying) and taming creatures is very similar to Pokemon in that you need higher tier capture items to capture certain ones (well pokemon is more RNG but it follows a similar concept on creature power vs. capture power. Oh, and there are custom spells. I'd love to see more 'types' added to how the elements work but the spells are indeed custom where you craft them with different stats like "Speed, size, direction, damage, etc..." all of which change the level of the spell and thus require higher gems you must find and craft in order to create the spell.
Content is still pretty lacking (when compared to Terraria and Starbound which have been worked on for years) but it's still enough to dig a solid few hours in and have an idea of where this game wants to go.
I'm really looking forward to see where this game goes as it feels like Terraria with Starbound's fancy elements. Both of which are things I like and want to see more of.

I have been following this game's development for a while now and I have to say a couple things (TL;DR on the end) :
Pros :
- The art is awesome. I didn't see much games with as smooth animations as Planet Centauri. Overall, there is an unique atompshere in Planet Centauri and you won't find it in Terraria or Starbound. Every biome feels different especially thanks to the excellent color managment.
- The engine has a LOT of potential. It can run on toasters and it's not even optimized yet. As a hobbyist developer, even in an early state, it is pretty usable and well designed. Come back in a couple months (/years more probably), and you'll probably get pretty neat modding. Something more evolved than the minimal/nearly useless Starbound modding at least. If it is as nearly moddable as King Arthur's Gold, I'm spending the rest of my life modding this game. Well, probably not my entire life (hopefully).
- The music isn't in a chiptune style, so the game doesn't really fall in the "retro" games box and that's good as it is IMO. The ambiance really matches up what the biomes should give. They're not so much matching my music tastes, but I really like some of the pieces - Shadow Forest is my favourite.
- The developers are really dedicated. I think the lead coder forgot any definition of "holidays" or "week-ends". Don't bother them with such really strange words. Just give a look at the count of their answers (onilink's and Planet Centauri's). There's also an IRC channel on
#centauri if you want to talk out to the lead coder or to some other players (the channel is nearly unpopulated as it is now, come!)
- Planned features. Just look at them by yourself. Even the electronics part, if done well, could be a whole game by itself.
- Multiplayer is coming very soon.
Cons:
- Gameplay is pretty much empty right now. It's being improved over releases, but the game relies more on being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ against enemies (i.e. when locking yourself up somewhere you can attack enemies but so they can't attack you). Some weapons get also overpowered at some point so there will be basically no fun at least until the 2nd underground layer. Pretty sure improving it is one of the devs' focus right now.
- The game lifetime is limited. You can reach up the "end" of the game (i.e. get the dragon scale armor right now, pretty much) in only a few hours. This will improve over releases, of course. But right now, there's nothing interesting apart of building good-looking stuff and making hugefreakingfarms after you've reached a certain level in the game.
There's no story right now and when there will be, it won't be the biggest interest of the game. If you're only playing sandbox games to get feels, look for another game.
TL;DR : The game has lots of potential. It looks beautiful. It has an unique ambiance, and is very coherent overall. Don't play it if you want advanced combat gameplay, or a story, in the state as it is when I'm writing this message. If this review is a few months ago, please verify the facts I'm stating - They're maybe not true now.

Dungeon Of The Endless is one of those games that tries to blend too many genres and fails. I purchased it for myself and my wife since it seemed to be an RPG of sorts, with a blend of tower defense. From all the videos we could see, you actually controlled one character.
In reality, you don't really control characters so much as you direct them into "rooms", an action that not only is not super fun, but also feels incredibly clumsy and unrewarding. There is very little in terms of "micro" strategy in the game, as your position in combat barely seems like it matters. Building things is also not exactly fun.
In general, there's just something missing for us in this game. It is overall just not a very satisfying experience to play. I did my best to get my wife to give it a chance, as she usually loves these types of games. Sadly, this game was the first time I've seen her quit out of a game in less than an hour. She *really* hated it and was dissapointed that it was not as it seemed.
So I guess, maybe check this out if you're interested in the weird gameplay experiment they attempted. It really just didn't strike a chord with me or my wife. I suggest watching a ton of youtube let's play videos before you purchase this, it is definitely not for everyone.

(TL;DR) [Read the comments for a good discussion on the topic]
+ Great Community (Just watch how many will downvote this review in defense)
+ Devs keep you up to date regularly through updates and news
+ Offers a Unique and realistic approach to the genre
- Another prime example of how early access can go wrong
- Updates are little more than “polishing” and offer little to no gameplay changes or improvements
- Many promised and crucial features that have yet to be released or even given a timeframe (NPCs/Vehicles)
I will start out by saying I love this game, not in the way that you love a good game, but rather in the way that you love something you have invested both time and energy into supporting and following. However, it has been nearly three years and the features that were “in development” at launch are looking more and more like a pipe dream. Originally, the end goal of this game was to have a “Walking Dead” gameplay type where you could create a group of survivors (either NPC or Player) and attempt to survive the zombie apocalypse in the most realistic way possible. With its simplistic graphics and top-down gameplay you would think that adding in core features would be just around the corner. However, at the time that I am writing this, the devs are busy polishing the 3D models and animations rather than improving the core gameplay. If you enjoy dark souls, roguelikes, or any other difficulty-based game you will feel right at home with the current build status. There are no NPCs, no Vehicles, and no word on when either will be available. While it might seem like I am nit-picking, these are the two features that have been left out of plenty of survival games (who promised them) and thus caused the games to fail. Look at Dayz as an example. Dayz (the standalone version) could have added vehicles much sooner instead of polishing, yet they wasted their time and now they are the target for plenty of jokes involving poor development. This is the problem with kickstarter/early access games as the devs already have their money and therefore have no motivation to introduce new features that might attract a new audience (or appease those who are waiting for new core features). This is not to say that the devs are not dedicated, but they are more interested in making their game as “pretty” as possible now that they have no reason to produce further deliverables. In normal software development, this path gets a project cancelled very quickly (keeping the stakeholders waiting in the dark while you polish the features and “feel” of the software). This is not what early access is about, as the features should have been released in their initial and “buggy” state from the start in order to let the community know that the features existed and to let them play. As of now, the devs talk very little about any new features which does not bode well for the future of this game.

A breddy gud WWII shooter with a lot of good ideas but it's held back by some major flaws.
Red Orchestra is as authentic as a multiplayer WWII shooter can get, if you can ignore the constant nazi-bolshievek arguments that keep appearing in the chatbox. In any server with more than 20 people you're going to pick up the rifleman role or any of the lesser roles, gamechanging roles like marksman, commander and machine gunner are few in numbers and the entire game can hinge on how well those players can make use of their roles. Everyone else is just cannon fodder, you go out, try pick off as many as you can but you're going to end up getting shot from someone you can't see. It sounds infuriating but it's really fun. The large numbers of soldiers, the wide open maps, the look of the game, the way it plays all lend to the immersion. When you're hold up on the second floor of a bombed-out building with artillery dropping around you while you put a few rounds into the gut of a German who entered downstairs and you hear him scream for a full 15 seconds that's when you know you're having fun.
This game has some really obvious problems and they do ruin the fun. The main one being that this game just isn't fluid at all, movement is clunky and often unreliable, simple inputs like switching weapons often requires multiple attempts if you're doing anything else at the same time, it's so easy to interrupt reloads unintentionally without even realising. It doesn't feel fair if I die because I ran out of ammo and switching to my secondary took me a full ten seconds to do because moving slightly to the left is apparently too much for the game to handle. Some maps have some serious balancing issues too, although I know it was probably difficult to find a good spot between realistic and fair but it's frustrating when the 10 servers with more than 10 players are all playing the same 3 maps with those issues. The game also doesn't explain a lot, I still have no clue what value there is in levelling up weapons, I still don't know why I'm given the option to bandage an injury only to find out I've wasted 15 seconds because it was pointless and I had to watch my screen just slowly fade to black, I still don't know how to complete certain objectives and I still don't understand certain leader functions. Great Doujin Bullet Hell

An updated version of the now outdated game, Gundemonium Recollection strives to improve on the basic formula that the original Gundemonium has set.
Recollection is a side scrolling bullet hell. By default you can either play as Eryth, our main protagonist, or one of the many Earl Support units, who are much more configurable. If you go through the game doing certain things, you can also unlock Elixirel, who is just as ridiculous as she is in the other Gundemonium games. Difficulty is, of course, fairly high, and the game will do everything in it's power to make you cringe at all those close calls you'll be having. The hitboxing is good, and nothing in the game feels "unfair," though you'll definitely be squeezing through some really tight bullet walls for most of the game. It's important to know where your hitbox is, something that's a bit difficult because the game doesn't give you an indication of where your hitbox is, except during non-combat sections (for some reason?...). Your characters do have indicators on their sprites to show where the hitbox is (for example, Earl units have a small bell to serve as their hitbox indicator) but an actual marker would be nice.
The game is beautifully sprited, with everything being vibrant, contrasting, and colorful. Also, anime tiddies as per the norm these days. There's even a censored version if you're put off by the nudity. Not sure why they added the nudity in but I'd assume it's a Gundemonium Original thing.
Absolutely worth it for the price that is offered, especially if it's on sale. Hell, just get the entire Collection. It's worth it, all three games are excellent for anyone who enjoys bullet hell games. Whether you want to expertly play the game, or enjoy it as a time waster, Gundemonium Recollection is pretty damn neato.

LYNE developed by Thomas Bowker and released onto the PC on Mar 17, 2014.
As of this writing, On Metacritic
it has an average user score of 7.7
A game with the concept of connecting objects with lines. How hard can that be?
For me, LYNE (L in short) is the Dark Souls of puzzle games. It is truly challenging. Unforgiving. You have been warned. Gear up your +int and +vit gears. We are headed for a torturous journey.
What is LYNE about:
L is a single player puzzle game. It basically requires players to connect the respective objects together. As of this writing, L offer players with 2 game modes:

All in all, that's a whopping
levels of puzzles.
Visuals, Audio, Controls:
L adopts a clean, simple, minimalistic UI & the color scheme is lightly toned bright colors. Mostly green. The Audio are soothing and for every object that you click, there's a feedback sound. L only utilize the mouse. Click to draw the lines. Nothing fancy.
L allows players to change game resolution, a window mode, audio muting, a level system - for progression purposes. All of which I had highlighted in my last review for another puzzle game. Because of this, credit must be given to the developer for thinking though for the product as a whole and implementing these options for our ease of use. +1 Thank you!
Game Mechanics:
L has 2 groups of objects.

The game requires you to connect all main objects together while filling up the connector blocks. That's where the challenge lies.
The most important aspect/the most critical function for L is the ability to redraw/draw the lines. In L, there is a auto "snap-on" feel, the ability to reverse the lines/undo clicking function at a particular object. This function on the lines work flawlessly and its because of this, users get to draw the lines/retract back the lines
to make the game replay-able. This is the highlight, the core function that makes L to work so damn good. Kudos, great work on the line connectivity function. +1
If you don't appreciate this function, try imagining when you draw your lines & they don't work properly or you can't reverse/undo your moves. Instead you are forced to restart the entire level *Gasp!*
My personal thoughts:
Firstly, let me say that, I don't play a lot of puzzle games because of my horrible gaming experience with them. This is my second writing for a puzzle game so I have something to benchmark on but let me say this: LYNE is a clever product. Not just in terms of game design but also in terms of branding/positioning itself in STEAM community.
Why do I say this? I don't know whether this was a intentional or unintentionally design choice but regardless, LYNE has benefited from this. It has placed LYNE as one of the highly desired product on STEAM because of the letter achievements. These letter achievements allows steam users to place words/personalize their steam page profile. A smart move to place itself above the rest of the games on steam.
For me, there is no question that the puzzles are challenging. They do gradually get harder as you advance further into the levels - or - when you advance further in the letters. The last 4 levels were stupendous. 25 sets of 4 x 7, 4 x 8 puzzles. Nothing can prepare us to face such difficulty. It reminds me of Dark Souls. Not in a positive way.
Because of this, it feels as if L was made specifically for a niche group. Either for Hardcore, highly intelligent people or both. The product was not designed for the mass market. Not just speaking in terms of age but on a common personality wise. Look, How many players would go through 700+ over levels? Out of those who completed 700+ over levels, how many cheated? Out of all those people who did not cheat, how many percentage of people actually
playing it? Was LYNE designed to be enjoyable or punishing? The line is starting to grey out when I touch on the game difficulty.
The last game that made me play 100+ over levels repeatedly - MEANINGLESSLY, I gave it a hulk-mode review. That's not a nice thing to do. The same question I am going to pass to the developer. Why 25 levels per letter? What is the justification? Why do you put players through 700+ over maps when it seems its just a set of 4*8 with different combination over the levels? My next question is why not 30? or 40? why not just 10? WHY? Can the developers justify why the heck 25 levels per letter - does it give me a better gaming experience? Does it teach me something new? show me, enlighten me, does this keeps me engaged more? WHAT? WHY? TELL ME WHY>!
*flips the chair* *skin is turning green* o_o oh..no..its happening.

My Summary:
Honestly? All my rage while writing has turned into a massive dump of disappointment for LYNE. As much I would like to say ME SAD. ME WANT TO SMASH LYNE! I no longer have the desire to do so. I don't review often, but this game deserves every positive review it gets.
To compare this game to other Star Wars strategy games is like comparing a tie fighter to a star destroyer. Other SW games pack a punch, but Empire at War blows them away.
But here we go: Star Wars Battlegrounds but in 3D with space battles, command posts like from classic Star Wars Battlefront games, more units, more heroes/villains, a huge galactic conquest spanning across multiple planets BUT less upgrades and less factions.
The expansions in this edition are welcome. They do provide a new faction, new units and new types of missions and mechanics that are quite fun to experience! But personally, I didn't find them all that interesting. I was quite happy with the Empire vs Rebels. I wish the expansion was an official clone wars dlc, but don't worry, the mods have you covered, whether you like the clone wars from the movies or the clone wars from the series! Some mods also expand/improve/overhaul the game too, acting like expansions themselves.
There are plenty of skirmish maps here to play too, both in space and on land, which is quite nice if you prefer not to get into massive campaigns.
Speaking of campaigns the game comes with one for each faction! I haven't had a chance to finish them, but from a game as old as this, you can expect that you'll get some dated, but true feeling lines and appearances from all the main characters. I reccommend checking out the outtakes for the Forces of Corruption voice acting too. They can be entertaining.
Overall, great game.

Concept: Civilization Style Fantasy Game
Pros: Very Technical, High Functionality, Tons of Features, Very Cool World
Cons: Tired Graphics, Wanted Bigger Maps
Every Single time I see a "Civ clone" I'm intrigued and have to try it out. But make no mistake this game is no Civ clone. It has the formula that Civilization has, but manages to completely make a new, fresh, and original game. Also, this game is definitely NOT Warlock, which(I love) IS a Civ clone. Anyways, to rewind a bit, Fallen Enchantress has been out on Steam for over a year at this point. I've been waiting for some sort of commentary on it and nothing. I has a Metascore of 80, which isn't bad, but I'm not investing $40 in a wild card. Well I knicked it in the Steam Summer Sale for $7.49 and after several hours am proud to say its worth the full price. This is a game that I will be playing for years to come until a sequel is released.
Right off the bat I found myself comparing it to the hallmark in this style of gaming. And for the life of me I was finding loads of features in this game THAT SHOULD BE STANDARD. For example, when you research new technologies and unlock new equipment you can either use the default units that are created or... you can MAKE YOU OWN UNITS. This is one of the coolest features I've ever seen. You can customize virtually everything. Sure there are the cosmetic customizations, but you will spend so much time making the perfect hero, unit, army, and city. Oh, this is cool, you can specialize your city as you level up. Do you want it to be a military city? How about a research enclave? Or how about just a standard town?
the game has eliminated worker units so everything that they would do, now you the player can do by hand. This is such a relief. I hated having a dozen workers take forever to build a road from city A to city B. In Civ it can take ten to fifteen seconds to load each turn because there are so many units on the board that the game has to move, in a game with thousands of turns you can spend hours just waiting. That problem is gone with Fallen Enchantress as there are far less units on the map.
The game does a great deal more. You have quests, and monsters, magic, and more. The part of the game that gets a bit tired might be the combat. When you get into combat with an enemy it takes you down to the field and you play out the battle. I like this. However, I died so much. And if you get dragged into a battle that is clearly over your head you have to play out losing unless you have the flee 'skill'. In this respect it will start to feel like Fire Emblem. If I lose one of my heroes, I'll quit the game and restart from a previous save point. Sound familiar?
Second Look: For those of you that don't really play this genre I don't really see too many picking this up. It may interest you if you like a good fantasy game, but it's complexities would turn away most people new to this genre. Where one person might see a game full of ways to control the flow of the game, another person might see a game bogged down with too many mechanics that get in the way of the core game.

Project Zomboid is interesting, and I recommend it, but I'm not sure I can recommend it to everyone.
The basic idea of the game is that it's a simulator that tries to accurately simulate surviving the zombie apocalypse. In this regard it is uncomprimising, going as far as prioritizing realistic(As realistic as you can be with a zombie apocalypse scenario, anyway) and immersive mechanics over stuff that is actually, y'know, strictly about making the game fun to play. This results in a lot of features that are pretty cool in concept, but can end up being frustrating in the context of the game itself, with its sort of clunky strategic top-down gameplay. Here are some examples of this:
-Enemy variety, currently there's just human zombies. No special zombies, no animal zombies, just human zombies with varying degrees of speed and strength. This can get dull and, coupled with the next feature mentioned in this list, makes guns kind of not worth using since melee weapons deal with everything pretty well.
-Anything that makes loud noise attracts zombies, as does any kind of noise in general. No using the gun you spent ages looking for, it's more dangerous than useful.
-The game has a large featureset for building but building also means hauling around heavy objects that put you at max encumbrance, meaning a lot of trips to and from the trees you're harvesting for wood.
-Skills level slowly, progression can take what could be called a "Realistic" amount of simulated time with it being possible to survive for months and years worth of ingame time.
-Zombie infection. This is the big one, being infected slowly but surely kills you and can result from one bite.
Now, all this isn't to say that the game isn't fun to play - it is, but it's the sort of game that appeals more to people who like slow, strategic survival gameplay and anyone who wants a zombie apocalypse sim that prioritizes attention to detail over all else and features possibly the most comprehensive persistent open world used in a zombie or survival game to date. Anyone expecting an actiony/arcadey zombie survival game will end up disappointed.
The only thing I can objectively count as a negative is that melee targeting on corpses will occasionally not work, and I've had a lot of characters ended by having a zombie I'm trying to stomp on stand up inside them and instantly deliver a bite that has something like a 90% infection rate. Be wary of that!
I rate this game 3.5 out of 5 in its current state.

Difficulty: Completed Regular, working through Expert
Actual Difficulty: Minor / Moderate
Input Used: Keyboard & Controller
Cuphead is a wonderful delight in it's animation and nostaIgic melodies; a somewhat challenging colourful action platformer in the guise of a 1930's children's cartoon.
As mentioned above, Cuphead is an action platformer focused around two types of stages: Run n' Gun & multi-form boss fights. Many gamers of experience will immediately compare Cuphead's gameplay to that of Contra, Metal Slug & Mega Man; as the controls are incredibly tight - both on controller AND keyboard. I will comment that the game does become something of a cakewalk when a controller is used, making keyboard controls another layer of challenge. Recommend the standard W,A,S,D configuration.
Difficulty, let's address it and the hype. Is this game as brutal and punishing as many claim it to be? No, not in the slightest. I have certainly played far more challenging titles of a similar nature in my life and the keys to success in Cuphead are the following: PATIENCE & PATTERN RECOGNITION. This game is beatable and can be a delight in the process; I'm looking forward to completing Expert - which seems incredibly simlar to Regular, just with a slight speed increase and weapon power decrease.
Upgrades come in the form of: Super Abilities, Shot Types and Off-hand Charms.
Super Abilities are just that, SUPER abilites! These are ready for use when your super meter at the bottom left of the screen is full charged. Being three in total - a horizontal attack, temporary invincibility and a form of mega cuphead tornado - I found myself sticking to the first.
Shot Types are classics from NES/SNES games of old: Spread, lobber, hookshot, homing, etc. You purchase these from the shop and equip them as you please - two at a time - before entering a stage. A little trial and error will help you figure out the best combination for each stage.
Off-hand Charms are many, but I used only one 'Smoke Bomb'. This allows you to dodge with an invincibility effect through enemies; incredibly handy.
A delight from start to finish; decades old gamers will find a gem here that will remind them of games from their own childhood in the skin of our cartoons. Highly recommended.

Gundemonium is a normal shmup in a lot of ways, but with a couple of unique twists. You've got your normal shmup fare, attack, special attack, bomb... there's also a neat rapid fire attack that will overheat a certain character's guns if you use and on another it's worthless. The most unique thing in this game is the phase level mechanic. Depending on what difficulty you start on, your phase level will change, with demonic locked in at 11. The higher your phase level, the harder the game is. You can lower your phase level by getting hit or using a bomb, or raise it by beating a boss or using a bomb just as you get hit, also known as counter bombing.
Your hitbox is very small in comparison to your large sprite, which allows bullets to cover most of your body without you getting hit. Personally, I would prefer a larger hitbox or a smaller sprite, but it isn't a big deal. Espcially considering this game's difficulty. It's a pretty difficult game. Do not buy this if you are not prepared to die often. That's really the only reason to stay away, or if you just don't like bullet hell games. I love this game, and I highly reccomend it.

While the trailer and screenshots should give you a faint idea on how the game works, allow me to convey how it feels to play the title.
The game play of Lyne, in short, is fairly similar to running a presidential campaign. Each stage is like an abstract representation of a sensitive social topic, which you, the candidate had to satisfy and solve. By navigating the treacherous waters of political intricacy, you have to meet the demands of various interest groups, whether they are reasonable or not, while avoiding to contradict yourself in logic.
Once you have completed the first leg of your tour, fulfilling the easy ball questions, you will advance gradually to the national theatre. Now, not only are there more interest groups per subject, but their demands ever more outrageous than the last. You will have to employ every deceitful tactic to advance, double talking to your audience, introducing false equivalency into every debate to confuse the masses, making sure your support base are all too occupied with double think to see your wacky logic. All eyes on you as the media broadcast your every road trip and every “achievement”.
When you have sneaked and snided your way to presidency, gaining the support of 26 states (chapters) and obtaing the votes of 650 territorial delegates (stages), you will have the pleasure of tackling the day to day operation of the country, taxing your mind evermore with the daily happenings of the world (daily puzzles).
Such a campaign by the political veterans should take around 10 hours to complete, though if you are willing to cheat like a real politician, it can take as little as 2 hours. As for the uninitiated, without the help from aids (guides), it can take around 30.
