text:
A game of vigilance and planning.
This game will make you twitch, shiver, and worry. And the wildlife will keep you on your toes because this game succeeds in invoking that primal fear we all have for our survival.
You will learn to identify each sounds you hear and be wary of them. You will learn to squint in the midst of a blizzard to find shelter. You will plan carefully and have it go awry in the worst possible way from time to time.
The artwork is gorgeous, even though it's not necessarily realistic. Together with the ambience sounds, you will be immersed in this in no time. I live in a tropical region and haven't much experience with blizzards, but I do know how it feels when your face feels numb due to cold winds, so I especially appreciate the immersion, the roleplay, that this game has brought me.
There are roleplaying elements such as survival skills and inventory management, but what truly makes this a roleplaying experience for me is the cold desolation, the white hell.
Easily 9 out of 10 from me with rooms for improvement in graphics and gameplay elements.
Here's hoping for a greater game at full release with Story Mode.

Bit of backstory:
I picked up Project Zomboid way back in October 2011, some time after it first became available on Desura, and there was no telling when (or even
) it would appear on Steam.
Back then, the graphics were quite a bit simpler, the map was smaller, zombies all looked the same, and dying from fire was common; I had been reading the Zombie Survival Guide right around that time, and liked the idea of PZ going in a direction that would allow you to use some knowledge gained from that book.
Looking at it now, a lot has happened in five years, and what's been added so far has me confident it will fulfill its potential, as the lovechild of the Zombie Survival Guide and The Sims*.
From the back of the ZSG, there is a list of the top ten lessons for surviving a zombie attack, and quite impressively, 8 of them apply to Project Zomboid even at this fairly early stage; cars and bikes are not in yet, meaning #7 is out, but you can definitely break staircases to keep zombies from following you up.
And although #5 (concerning the ideal protection being tight clothes and short hair) is also not currently that useful, layered clothing is, at the time of writing, being worked on, along with greater weapon variety, more realistic backpacks, bloodied characters, and further zombie variety, with more to come.
If you like relatively realistic isometric survival games and zombies, this might just be interesting to you too.

I understand that the game is still in-development, and I just hope that this small review gives the developers more input, and more opinions to those of you looking to buy the game itself.
"This is how you died." Very straight-forward in the very opening of the game when loading, though it might be from boredom. There's not that much going on for now, and it feels very much like The Sims: Zombie Hoards. You manage a single character in a world with nothing but zombies, a sometimes perplexing crafting system, and an unavoidable death.
The boredom is more that there isn't much to keep action going if you get to a certain point because you can live comfortably in your safehouse until the game throws several waves of zombies at you at once, which feels kind of cheap to me, but, once again "how you DIED" not "SURVIVED".
If you don't master the crafting system pretty quick, or how to equip bandages, you're pretty well dead from the start, which is enough to discourage people from picking up the game again out of frustration. More direct crafting/equip/health menus would be very much appreciated, at least from my point of view, as it's rather awkward in the current version.

Though disappointed initially by the lack of Nietzsche,
delivers a good action-adventure game that delves into some surprisingly dark themes and mature content. The beautiful visuals really have helped with how finely the game has aged over the years, with lighting in particular creating some stunning vistas and stellar views of the various landscapes and colourful underground.
A gritty approach to science fiction,
follows the young photojournalist Jade, a caretaker of sorts for a bunch of ragtag kids and orphans on the planet of Hyllis, along with her long-time friend and mentor Pey’J. Futuristic but with noticeable fantasy and steampunk influences, the on-going war between the supposedly benevolent Alpha Sections regime and the “DomZ” – a seemingly endless alien force – in the backdrop to an otherwise peaceful, everyday setting gradually begins to appear as more than it seems. Pulled into a momentous conspiracy cover-up, you’re tasked to reveal the truth and ignite a revolution.
Gameplay is broken down into a mixture of free-roaming, puzzles and stealth sections. There’s a decent enough amount of content for you to try outside of missions, but most of it generally comes down to forgettable mini-games and pearl hunting. The stealth system is very simplistic but works well for what it sets out to do, even if you’ll find yourself asking how on earth you managed to sneak past that guard without being detected.
In terms of puzzles, they’re generally straightforward to do and rely on grasping the layout of the level’s environment, though may appear bewildering in design at times. Any more than this I can’t really comment on, considering my own legendary impatience and lack of skill in solving video game puzzles.
Be ready to add a bit more on to the average completion time if you’re in a similar position.
The art style is great, with a nice vibrancy and cartoonish aesthetic to it, and character models equally so. The sound design is fantastic, with the score in particular really creating a moody, sci-fi ambiance. Some of it’s almost reminiscent of Kelly Bailey’s work for
and suits the game perfectly.

However,
does suffer from the typical trappings of the genre’s design. The fixed camera positions can be a nightmare at times, especially in vehicle sections, and this has a rather significant effect on not only basic navigation but the otherwise smooth and relatively satisfying gameplay. Jade has some great moves in combat, (think of a more dexterous equivalent to Monkey’s style in
), but the camera and constantly changing direction of movement controls can be immensely frustrating to wrestle with. Also, facial animations and lip-syncing doesn’t occur for in-game/contextual dialogue… another odd drawback. Some other more minor issues generally come down to noticeable clipping and some A.I. quirks but overall the technical aspects are quite good.
The biggest failing of
is in the constant grind that is required to progress throughout the main story. Being an older adventure game and thus featuring the obligatory unlock currency system,
requires you to upgrade the central hovercraft vehicle with the collectible pearls that are scattered throughout the map and various levels. While most of these you’ll come by incidentally, completing tasks or through purchases, you will eventually be required to painfully grind to receive the next unlock, most likely at the end of the game, where this shouldn’t be happening at the most. (♥♥♥♥ing hell, that final boss fight was brutal.)
While I can understand this age-old trope of game design, it really detracts from an otherwise enjoyable game when the story itself is locked off to you. There is no cheat code or other way to bypass these mind-numbing sections outside of a custom editor, so the grind is unfortunately inevitable. You might argue that this was done to encourage exploration, but the game was already worth delving into and shouldn't have to be forced upon players either. The best way to avoid it would be to just carefully scour the levels early on and try and complete miscellaneous tasks wherever possible.
In all honesty, I don’t usually go for these kinds of games but found
to be really enjoyable. If you’re a fan of the likes of
,
,
or
, you’ll be right at home here with a good experience all-round on offer, totalling around 10 or so hours of play.
You can also remind yourself of what Ubisoft used to be.
It may be in development hell, but whenever the second game comes, it’ll be worth it. Thumbs up.

I purchased this game to enjoy co-op with a friend, and multiplayer appears to have been shoved in as a half-baked implementation.
Problems with multiplayer:
- If you only have 1 hero, you will break your Operate bonus if you go to interact with any level features, like shops, new heroes, research crystals, etc.
- You can't trade or give picked up items to other players, except by selling / buying to a merchant, which ends up costing your friend the full price of the item
- If a player loses their only hero, you can't transfer control of an extra one to them, so the run is over
- Finally, and most glaring... you are unable to save in multiplayer. This means any runs you do have to be done in one full run, which could take hours.
On a different note, a lot of the abilities and skill descriptions are worded in the most confusing possible way, which will leave you wondering what they mean. They read like a cut and paste from Google translate.
Items in shops often grant a specific passive bonus, but don't explain what the passive bonus actually does, which is frustrating when you are new, since you'll have to look it up in a wiki or something.
Finally, some of the rules are not easy to understand. In our latest run, we opened a door and enemies spawned like normal, then suddenly all of the doors on the level opened, and more enemies spawned. It was as if we had picked up the crystal, but we had not, we had only opened a door. Why did that happen? No idea, the game provided no indication.
It is fun in the few hours I've played. The core game offers a lot of strategic and resource management decisions that must be made. I mainly wish that the co-op was properly implemented. It is deceiving to say that co-op is in when it has gamebreaking deficiences like being unable to save progress and continue later.

TL;DR || The game is a fun mix of dungeon crawling RPG and tower defense. Perma-death, random dungeon layouts, and a good selection of characters add to the replay value. Multiple heroes to unlock. Level 'em up. Gear 'em up. Meet new heroes while in the dungeon and have them join your party. Find ancient treasure. Research new tech. Die, lose it all, and happily start over again. The devs are a pretty swell bunch too!!!
I think the art style is fantastic, and the same can be said for the sound design and soundtrack.
The gameplay is quite fluid with a nice interface and can also be quite challenging with a good bit a strategy mixed in. Clear the dungeon room by room using your heroes, while setting up defenses to protect your ship's power core. Once you find the floor's exit, defend one of your heroes as he slowly carries the core to the elevator. You can power up rooms to prevent enemies from spawning in them and use that power to set up turrets and resource nodes; this helps you create a defensible path to the elevator, because once you touch that core, they don't stop coming.
The developers are worth mentioning too. AMPLITUDE is hands down one of my favorite studios. They put out quality products and continue to provide support for their games beyond their initial release.

Alright, if you're here, then you probably know what the "bullet hell" subgenre is, or at least its parent genre, shoot 'em ups (from now on referred to as "shmups"), but if not, I'll briefly explain:
Shmups are generally defined as any top-down or side-scrolling shooter, such as Galaga, Space Invaders, and many others. Bullet hell games, on the other hand, take this to the EXTREME; some of the screenshots for this game should show you just how many bullets you'll have to deal with. To compensate for this, your character's hit box is extremely small, really only a couple of pixels big, so that this is at all possible.
With that out of the way, the actual review!
The presentation:
Generally pretty good quality sprite work; I wouldn't say it's anything outstanding, but certainly nothing to scoff at. The menus are a tad bland, but function well, and aren't boring; just simple.
The story:
It's a little hard for me to comment on this one, honestly; the story isn't really well told throughout the game. To give an example of how important the story is, there's an option to disable the pre-level "cutscenes", which are only one screen with text and some pictures anyway. I believe it has something to do with humanity doing something dumb, and that causes some evil person to attack (again? I'm not sure; I haven't played the first game), and you, being part of some millitary group, have to go and face her. Not terrible, but not super deep either. But that's probably not why you're here, is it? You're looking for...
The gameplay:
Is fantastic. Before you start the game, you have the choice between two characters, Eryth and Earl, and another once you beat the true final boss (which, I should mention, I have not done). Now, there are two conflicting sources on the amount of characters; one (this very Steam page) says that there are two starting characters, with the unlockable third, while the games official webpage states that there are FIVE characters, along with an unlockable sixth. Neither of these are completely correct. The second character, Earl, is actually a customizable character; you can use one of four presets, or you can mix and match her three selectable abilities. These abilities, of which Eryth has as well (however, Eryth is stuck with one skillset), include your normal shots, "bombs" (which almost never actually includes using a bomb), and "Mana Action", which requires your Mana bar to be filled up; this can be done by killing enemies. The game isn't too long, probably about an hour or less if your good; but that's a pretty tall order. The first time I played through this game (playing as Eryth, Revised (normal) difficulty), it took about two hours of multiple retries to get past these five stages. Despite the difficulty (which is pretty normal for these kinds of games), I had a blast, and felt extremely satisfied once I finally conquered it. Thanks in no small part to...
The music:
Now, personally, I loved the music. It's probably one of my favorite game soundtracks, and I'm not exaggerating; I rank this up there with Cave Story, Mega Man X, BlazBlue (the collective series), all of those amazing soundtracks. And the soundtrack actually comes including in the Steam folder for the game once it's installed, so that's a huge plus. However, looking at another review, it said that the musical wasn't all that great. So who knows, I might be in the minority on this one.
Overall:
Hopefully this review didn't end up being too long-winded; I don't exactly have a lot of experience with reviewing. However, I found myself having to hold back on how much I said, because I quite bluntly love this game. It's one of my favorites, and I'm pretty sure the next few days will be spent on getting the achievements. I hope you decide to pick this game up, because it's definitely worth it; I plan on buying the other games in the series at some point soon as well.

So, you want to play a Shoot Em Up, do you? Well this game is definitely a good one to start with.
The game has four controls, plus 8-way movement. It's a side scroller, like the Gradius games, but it has no powerups. You use what the character you select has, as well as one of four alternate costumes which change their way of playing.
Music in this game is what you'd expect from a game from overseas; really good. It's not overbearing, and you can hear everything in the game without the music blocking anything. Plenty of different songs in each level, too.
Level design goes from Easy to moderate to a bit tough to really tough to "If you are not godlike, quit now" tough. Difficulty ramps up REALLY fast towards the third level, which is only 10~ minutes in. The fifth level is just incredibly brutal, and this isn't even a hard game. Consider it an entry to Bullet Hells, because this is only the tip.
A great game for beginners to learn the fear of Bullet Hell games. I'd like to think of myself as a fan of shooters, and I own a few on consoles, but Bullet Hells continue to make me realize that I haven't even begun playing hard games. Get this if you want an introductory to a challenging genre of games that actually takes some skill.

I have to say this game is incredibly beautiful (not the most advanced graphics but in time who knows) the picturesque landscape is actually incredibly beautiful. Gameplay is varied from life to life(including loot or even structures or resources), so no playthrough is exactly the same. This is truely a survival game because of the harsh canadian climate and the realisation that resources dwindle quickly, health concerns from paracites, food poisioning, hypothermia,and so on, also becuase of the aggressive anial behavior. Think of the basis of DayZ standalone Loot system that is non respawning(yes, everything is limited) which makes every choice important. There are several maps in the game which is awesome and they are all linked together to stitch together one massive world. With limited resources you can only surive in spots for a limited amount of time before you need to move onto the next area, although you can extend your stay in each area via fishing, setting snares and hunting wildlife. Wildlife can conist of fish from ice fishing holes, rabbits that you can set snarfes for or Deer, wolves and bears which can be taken down by the bow or the rifle.
All Wildlife behave differently rabbits and deer will run from you if they see you or smell you either from wind or smelly items. Wolf and bear hunting is a little bit more tricky. Wolves are very very smart. once they know your in the erea they will howl and all near by wolves will be alerted to your presence. They can smell you if the wind is going their way regardless of what is in your inventory or even more so if you carry meat. Wolves are pretty nasty when you play stalker or higher difficulty. They will physically hunt you down and attack you on stalker or higher difficulty. and if they catch you well your in a fist fight for your life at that point. You can use some tools to help you defend your self if you are lucky enough to have them. Bears on the other hand are an entirely different beast. They can sense and smell you like a wollf can... but instead of some minor to medium wounds from fighting single of multiple wolves at once a single bear attack will leave you barely consious and bleeding out near death on the ground if you are at a high enough condition to start out with. however one bear can feed you for a week, a wolf or deer for about a day, or several fish or rabbits a day. so make you choices wisely or end up one of the corpses you may have looted.
Eating hunted food whiloe savign your packages food is always a smart move because as you move from map to map you need to be able to feed your self during the journey staying away from smelly food because of the attention is attracts. There area really only a few genres of food int he game. packaged or canned or hunted food. hunted food goes bad canned goods do not, and for another layer of frosting eddating meat harvested from carnivores has a chance of giving you paracites which will take you 10 days too cure assuming you have the medication. as the predator meat gets to be worse and worse quality after it is cooked the chance goes up dramatically. so it is my opinion that if your hunting try and bring home two types or meat. Passive meat being the deer, rabbit and fish wont give you these paracites but you don't get as much meat from passive animals compared to a bear for example. Bears are like food jackpots but are very very risky to kill.

Why am I giving it a negative review? Well, it's the same old story.
I was at one time invited by the devs to offer constructive criticism of the game onto their forums. I did so, and the devs promptly threw a hissy fit and tried to start an argument with me. I was then promptly banned both from the forums and from commenting on their Steam page - over nothing. These people will label constructive reviews as "Abusive" for being negative even if the review praises the game and offers constructive criticism. They'll ban anyone for speaking their honest opinions about this game in a respective way.
Seen in the light of the development time and quality of updates, this does not reflect well on them. This is the negative aspect of indie gaming. The least you can expect from a gaming company is to be mature and respectful. Not so with many indie devs, including this team. (There's probably a quite a few people who work on this game and have no relation to such poor and unprofessional behavior.)
They need a PR person.
Here were my suggestions.
- Special zombies and more challenges
Challenges are actually really fun, but it seems like there no update on them and there's hardly any mods that add to them. (More on mods later.) Special and more challenging zombies will go a long way to make the game more enganging. A story will too, which is another issue about the game.
The apocalypse happened, but there is no signs of people anywhere. It's just an empty map... The Drayton mod has much in the way of an envriomental story. (I highy reccomend that mod.)  In the Drayton map, there's blood and signs of death. Dead bodies left behind, some of people who decided to off themselves. There's spray paintings on the wall bemoaning the military and a cure. There's signs of struggle, of life, of a story... that map doesn't feel as empty even when you're the only one.
Bad behaviored devs aside who don't know how to act maturely or take criticism, this game is very complex and well done. There's an intricate crafting system. The farming system is really well-done. The enviroments are huge and intriquate and fun to explore. The zombies have very interesting behavior and it really feels like you're trying to survive the apocalypse.
But then we get back to the fact that the world is so empty.
Here's how a typical playthrough will go.
-Spend 30 mins creating a character
-Get a weapon from the kitchen
-Loot houses for supplies (This is the fun part)
-Skip town because now the zombies are swarming you like there's no tommorrow
-Head for a farm somewhere where there's a well (infitnite water)
-Farm, farm, farm
-Now you have infinite water and food. What now?
Eventually you get bored and just kill yourself somehow, put the game down and then picked it up again a few months later. This game is best enjoyed in short bursts.
There is really no longterm goal. The most fun I have is roleplaying different scenarios and acting how I really would if this happened in real life. It's funner to set yourself up for failure by boarding yourself up in your apartment and stay in the city or mall.
Once you "learn" the game and the zombies aren't much of a challenge anymore, there's another problem that I mentioned before. Once you start exploring, the whole game feels so empty. There's no cars anywhere. Just empty roads. No signs of a civilization past. Just empty houses. Empty streets. Empty diners. Does that sound depressing? Well, it is. (In addition, the devs said that they'll be adding cars in the game FOREVER, and a modder already made a mod that adds working cars and abandoned cars in the game for free, on their own spare time.... go figure.)
Zombie survival games are a dime a dozen now, and this game has been in development for more than half a decade. Think about that. What updates we get aren't anything to sing home about. The enviromental degration system and immersive sounds we're both made by a (great) modder. That's the only two updates that really added value to the game... in the meantime, they updated backpacks and now the TV's will spout nonsense repeatedly, the same 15 lines a million times over.
People have devoted a large part of their life to this game, waiting for them to complete it and still there is no hint of the Big One. Npcs. A feature that will complete the game, and made it significantly more fun in addition with a long term goal of some story.
I owe you a warning. The vision the devs have for this game probably isn't what you had in mind. As I said, I had some interaction with them before. They went of some pretentious rant about how 'humans are the REAL monsters' and explaining the artistic merit of Dawn of the Dead. Their vision for this game is more along the lines of The Walking Dead than a true zombie survival HORROR game.
I'm sorry to Walking Dead fans. I sort of liked the show too, but WE GET IT. HUMANS ARE THE REAL MONSTERS. We get it everyone! Humans are bad. Violence is bad. Our basest of nature is bad. We are a bad and violent people.
The reason why the Walking Dead is so hated is because of all of the dumb melodrama, and how the zombies stop being scary and become just background noise to whatever relationship problems some whiny brat has. (Who explicity has salon styled hair and high-end make up...) I said this before and I'll say it again. In the zombie world, zombies are the main character. We want to see horrors. We want to be scared. The ultimate nature of humanity isn't scary. It isn't horrifying. Sorry. Once zombies stop being the main character, then it stops being scary and we wake up from the nightmare.
So I'm looking forward to the NPCs, but I'm not interested in the direction they are taking this. Fair warning. Dying Light is a good example of what I mean. The original story sucked and detracted from the quality of the game. However, The Following; the story was quite good and added a lot of depth to the game and zombie lore. The difference is that in the latter, the monsters were the main character in the plot. This is how horror succeeds where other genre's fail.
But, by the time they finish NPCs the lifespan of this game will be long over. No Man's Sky is coming out soon. It's indie. The devs are actually friendly. It's complex and awesome, and suprise, surprise! It's actually finished within 10 years. Why waste time with drama and an empty, unfinished world when I can just play another game? Please tell me.
This game has value, but be aware - before buying, it's just ANOTHER zombie survival game that's in EA that will probably never be finished within our lifespans.
Oh, and to add insult to injury... they focused on multiplayer for $$$ instead of the NPCs.
One last note: None of the mods for this game are that exciting. Wow, I get purple hair and now I can eat bugs. There's nothing really big in the mods section. The most popular mods are female nude mods and a Deadpool skin... enough said. Nothing to add challenge. No big overhaul, unlike the wild and creative mods you can get with games like Civilization. There is this one modder who said that they wanted to make a mod that turned this game into The Mist. Where did you go? Because that is a great idea. How about a mod that turns this game into The Thing?
Here's an idea - wouldn't it be great if we could start playing while the infection is JUST beginning rather than AFTER the apocalypse already has started?
Imagine it. You wake up, living your normal day like in real life. Then someone gets infected. It's slow at first, until people (NPCs) panic. More and more succumb to the infection. You are living the begining the the World War Z diaries. That would be great.

Red Faction Armageddon is the fourth installment in the Red Faction series. Armageddon takes place 45 years after Red Faction Guerilla and 25 years after the events of Red Faction Origins in which a group of Cultists release the dormant armageddon plague once sealed within a temple by Axel Capek. The protagonist Darius Mason equipped with his Nano forge, traverses through hordes of horrifc creatures, eradicates the queen, and reactivates the Bakhuysen Terraformer before the plague overwhelms the entire martian population. Red Faction Armageddon is a very linear, close quaters title, opposed to its counterparts offering a vast open world of sectors like Guerilla, and the explorative Ultor mines of Red Faction. Similar to Guerilla, Armageddon boasts GeoMod 2.0, an engine that focuses on destructable building based geometry instead of environmental geography, however also encourages players to use the Nano forge to rebuild terrain and structures to progress, probably one of the most entertaining aspects of the game would as a matter of fact, have to be recreating the environments using the Nano forge. The weapons available within game are another satisfying addition to the game, encompasing various tools to play around with, whether it be enemies or the environments you use them on. Its flaws occur solemnly corresponding to its poor plot contrivance decisions, forced, generic, and uninteresting characters, and mediocre gameplay consisting of shooting colorful aliens and martians by either smashing or shooting them. Its multiplayer suffers from a lack of intent and goal, causing players to be burnt out quicker, opposed to the sprawling, unique matches of prior games. Red Faction Armageddon is a lackadaisical title that forced Volition to drop the franchise entirely, and is not a title I would recommend to new players to the franchise. It's not as bad as Red Faction II, but it does fail to recognize the faults of the prior games of the franchise. I would recommend newcomers to get a feel for the prior games before playing this one.

Exactly what you want in a Roguelike -- Lots of depth.  Lots of variety.  Lots of strategy.  Very rewarding to play and master.
9 out of 10 (with the potential for 10/10 with further development which is in the pipeline)
Starts off very hard, but you always know why you died/failed.  As you learn how the game and characters work, the game gets much easier and starts to really shine.  If you're on the fence, get the basic 'Pixel Pack' - you don't get much with the upgrade to Crystal (one hero, one game mode).  I play on Linux under WINE with no major problems, although it's not supported.
Pros:
+ Great characterizations, diverse skills which dramatically change the game
+ Monsters which force you to change tactics floor-to-floor
+ Game modes, while a little thin, do offer a good dose of variety
+ Music/Sound is excellent.  even at 100+ hours in, the music is still a welcome addition.
+ Tactics and strategy matter - a lot!
+ Lots of replayability and more in the future thanks to continued development
+ Even if you're an expert, there's still a lot of challenge
Cons:
- Tower defense aspect is really a second fiddle to the heroes, especially in lower levels, mostly due to one enemy type (Zoners) destroying minor modules
- Multiplayer is still rough (but being improved patch by patch)
- The music in the first video is not in the game
- Interface could use a little work (health is hard to see, 'restore skill' is hidden, can't pin heroes to rooms)
- Characters sometimes don't attack/repair immediately (minor quibble, really)
- Crystal running is usually trivial
About the difficulty: it's hard, yes (and I like hard), but you get to the point where the balance flips and losing becomes a rarity.  It's still difficult and rewarding, but the heal mechanic means you can just overproduce food and heal all the time, so it's actually hard to lose outright.  Many of my first few losses were simply being to skimpy on healing; lesson learned...always top heroes off if you want them to live.
Other tips:
* take 30 minutes and read a guide or two; it'll save you a few failed runs.
* start on 'very easy'
* PAUSE. all the time. assess how the battle's going.  is one hero in trouble?  are enemies going a path you didn't anticipate?
* don't heavily invest in offense modules; your heroes should be doing most of the fighting
* change your strategy if you see Zoners (triangle guys which attack minor modules), Dozers (big rock guys which attack major modules), or Riders (can open doors). monsters are set per floor.  if you see one of the above, the level is going to be much, much harder
* Max is very, very good thanks to his ability to generate dust on door opens.  makes floors 8+ much easier.
* Controlling aggro is essential, although there are many ways to do it.  the easiest is with Skroig, the necrophage character, and his Red Plume skill - reset (on the character sheet) when necessary; it's cheaper than healing/rebuilding.
* Floors start at about 11 doors for level 1 and go to about 32 doors. generally, keep building resource generators until 2/3rds through. shoot for two operators at all times. make use of mechanical pals, when you'll be sure they pay off.
* when dust gets short, have one 'exploration' wing where only one room is lit for defenses (with a combat hero that can control aggro), and one 'production' wing where all rooms are lit.  only open more rooms on the 'production' wing when you have enough dust to light the room you're going to open.
* neurostun, tear gas, and biotransferrance are some of the best support modules
* research 'Shop's and put an Operator on any merchants you find post floor 7-8

This is one of those rare games where you really feel like you're in a world, not unlike what you'd experience in an Elder Scrolls game. A combination of the first-person perspective, the AI-driven enemy behavior, the atmospheric art and soundscape, the stealth mechanics, and the fact that almost everything in the world has some kind of purpose really made me feel like I was on that terrible little set of islands running from robots. It's immersive and tense, and most of the time playing on default settings I felt like there was just enough give for me to scrabble my way through the game to victory.
It's not a perfect game - I'm not sure what the purpose of junk items is (to scare you off the Take All button when looting, I assume?), the highly restrictive savepoints can be frustrating, some of the controls could be explained a bit more clearly (like secondary functions and inventory shortcuts), but overall Sir, You Are Being Hunted really delivers on what it needs to, and the plethora of setup options means that everyone should be able to tailor the experience to their level fairly easily.

LYNE was an impulse purchase for me at a time when I was looking for simple puzzle games to fill spare hours with. It fulfilled that promise with a little more than I was expecting.
Each level in LYNE is full of squares, triangles, and/or diamonds. The goal is to connect all the similar shapes together with one unbroken line. Octogon pieces act as intersections. These intersections will allow two, three, or four different lines to cross through them. How many is indicated on each octogon via small, see-through diamonds. One an octogon is full, the see-through diamonds are filled and the shape is outlined.
Pros:
- The controls are simple: you're clicking and dragging the mouse.
- The game gradually gets harder as you play it.
- There are plenty of levels and there are daily challenges.
- As you complete puzzles, you unlock new color schemes.
- The experience can be really relaxing, especially in the beginning.
- If you're perfecting games on Steam, the achievements are challenging but not impossible.
Cons:
- There is no "hint" option if you get stuck. You can get stuck on a puzzle for hours.
- Some of the color schemes are really hard on the eyes.
If you're looking for a cheap, fun challenge that you can return to, LYNE is going to be a good game to add to your collection.

I've been playing this game on and off for a few years now. It's really come a long way and is definitely something I've got to recommend to others.
The gameplay typically consists or finding/securing your safe house, scavenging for items/food, and exploring the map. Finding/securing your safe house is actually pretty fun because the maps are huge and you have a ton of options from which house or location to pick. You can board up windows, build additional walls, and do other really neat fortification options. You need certain materials to fortify your house properly as well as defend yourself, and this is where the scavenging comes in to play.
Looking for materials throughout the world is one of the biggest parts of the game, and luckily, it's one of the most exciting. There's a fog of war system in the game so if you're frantically trying to pry open an unknown building's window, you may suddenly turn around and find a horde of zombies waiting to ambush you. The world feels truly scary and unsafe at every turn. Because of this feeling of insecurity, I never felt bored or annoyed that I had to go search for items again. The only area for improvement I feel for this aspect of the game is to improve the UI while managing your inventory. It's not necessarily bad in my opinion, but carrying the appropriate number of items and not bringing too much with you is sometimes an issue. An improved UI with more options when right clicking might be a beneficial update. What is great though, is the tremendous number of items and crafting options you have as a result. There is a very expansive crafting menu with categories such as cooking, health, survival, and more. Finding new options for weapons and survival is always exciting, and the amount of crafting options you have ensures that the game will stay exciting and fresh for a significant amount of time.
Exploring the maps is my favorite portion of the game. Things are constantly changing each time you play a different map. Once my friend and I (stupidly) wanted to use a bunch of guns we had. So we went to a seemingly remote area and started taking out some zombies with rifles and shotguns. What resulted was us frantically sprinting through woods and neighborhoods desparately trying to return to our safe house while hordes of zombies swarmed our location. It's the crazy, exciting moments like this that make this game unique. You truly do feel the inevitable demise of you and your friends around every corner.
This game has been in development for a wicked long time now. But it sincerely gets better with each update. And as of right now, I'm enjoying the game as if it's in its final state. I honestly love the graphics because it reminds of older games I used to play when I was younger. The sound is really nice too, and the tension that results from unknown gunshots being fired in the distance never gets old!
This is my all time favorite Early Access game. It does not faze me at all that it is not technically "complete" because I enjoy it more than most of my final release games anyway!

This is a good survival game in many ways, but ultimately, it lacks consistency and useful player feedback. For instance, after surviving 30+ days, equipping myself with wolfskin coat, deerskin pants/boots, double fisherman sweaters, etc, etc - I was at the point when I basically did not become cold during daytime. I could also sleep outdoors, which was good because I wanted to work towards the very-difficult-to-achieve feat of getting a permanent bonus to 'feels like' temperature.
Anyway, I had just finished killing a bear, setting up all the gut/hide to cure, and I went to sleep outside, with a fire burning for 2 hrs, in a wind-sheltered area. I died. Instantly. Apparently I froze to death, but there was only a flash of "Affliction: Hypothermia", and then it vanished, and I was "Faded into the long dark." Why? 100% health, bedroll, tons of clothing, and 2 hrs of + temperature, but, I'm dead. In the past, my character at least woke up in poor condition if the temperature dropped too low. I'd add, those were much more poorly equipped characters - and yet, it seemed there was the opportunity to escape immediate harm, unless it was something like a bear attack, which I would understand. I don't mind if my character dies in a bad situation, but this was totally inconsistent with my previous time playing this game.
Ultimately I can't recommend the game. I spent a lot of time getting to 30+ days playing off and on during early access, and came back hoping to prepare for the story mode. This is hugely discouraging and suggests all that time was a huge waste of time, not an investment in future time spent with this game. Disappointing.

The Long Dark is a very unique game, despite the recent release of many new survival-mode game titles. This game is the closest game that I could find to ever match realistic survival in a realistic scenario. Just the AI of the animals, alone, is enough to impress anyone who understands that most games (and I mean at least 80%) spend almost no time into creating such accurate AI, and to think that these people (Hinterland Studios) are still developing and improving their AI!
I am truly amazed at Hinterland Studio's work on The Long Dark. It's as if their passion is driven by their Canadian spirit and their experience with AAA games. I feel as if they will never truly stop developing this game - no matter how many sales that they make or how much people hate them. I honestly can't believe that a game in this early stage can have this much potential. This is more than a video game, this is a simulation of real-life.
I want you to go into the game with some questions in mind:
1. Is this how long I'd survive in this situation?
2. Can I survive in an area that I know nothing about, have no GPS to help me navigate, and have no one to ask for help?
3. Can I do this, by myself, without referencing from a Wiki (which there is an Official one) or asking other players for help?
I'd recommend taking this game as a test/challenge to yourself. See how you compare. See whether your logic and approach to survival will save you or get you killed. See what you can do to better yourself, make better choices, and how long you can keep fighting despite being at 1% life. Go farther. Go deeper. Be better.

Bolstering lovable characters, an interesting story, a believable world immersed in conflict, and an interesting array of dungeons and world building, BG&E is a very fun action adventure title that's well worth its price. It's not a perfect game, nor is it "incredible", but it's in no way just average. Some minor quips are that the controls and camera can act pretty awful, and it sometimes becomes pretty easy to get lost.
Personally, I feel that the game is at its strongest in the first of its four dungeons, as it is most evocative of Zelda during this time. Following the first dungeon, the game begins to stress its stealth elements, something rarely seen in Zelda, but not unwelcomed in BG&E. I feel that the game's dungeons tend to take a small dive, but it recovers for the end and wraps up in a satisfying conclusion. (That is, unless you watch after the credits)

Aesthetics and music are top notch. The story is so-so.
However, I must say that the core gameplay is either mediocre or downright annoying. Most of it is thanks to the camera. What happens is that, in some sections (combat & stealth), the camera is fixed at an angle, but you can still move it inside its axis. This creates a few undesirable situations, where you're fighting multiple enemies and the camera keeps snapping forward, or the camera angle doesn't actually show what's ahead (in stealth sections). The main problem is that your controls change when the camera changes, so an abrupt change can make the camera keep snapping forward and backwards, making you run up to enemies you don't want to fight.
The stealth gameplay in this is very simple. Enemy saw you? Run to another room. Got into a fight with patrols? Pray the camera doesn't keep getting in your way.
The story starts pretty good, but after mid-point, I realized everything was being rushed towards the ending. I didn't really like it.
The "open world" aspects are almost nil, and the game is rather short. It has 2 "big" areas where you'll spend most of your playtime in, then a very small stealth section, and finally the last stage, which is awfully paced (a few empty corridors and easy puzzles), probably because of the rushed ending.
All in all, the game is rather entertaining, but beware of its cons.

Bloody Trapland is both fun and cooperatively challenging. Being a fan of platformer games, this somewhat reminds me of the classic NES "Super Mario Brothers". At first glance I thought the game would be similar to the Rage Game "Cat Mario" but this just proves the saying "Don't judge a book by it's cover". Bloody trapland has the uniqueness of a game that no one has created before. The puzzles do in fact get more and more challenging as you progress through eash level, but they're not impossible to complete. I would recommend playing this with 1 to 2 more people, but be warned it can get a little messy if you accidentally jump on a friends head.

Although Bloody Trapland originally looks promising, it quickly loses its appeal. The game is no more difficult than any typical platformer, with its "difficulty" originating from unclever traps (blocks you cannot see crushing you). Instead of the skill game you would expect from a "difficult platformer," the game feels more like a memorization game - memorize the location of the traps and develop a muscle memory to work through them. Also, multiplayer is mediocre at best - it's far too easy to accidentally kill your teammates in adventure. For those of you seeking the deathmatch option, it really doesn't work with less than four players. In my experience, two players just led to a spawn camper (with correct timing you'll instantly die upon spawning) and with three two players can easily team up and ruin the fun for another player. Finally, the ambience of the game is lacking a great deal of work. The tiles, music, and characters feel childish. No particular theme is accomplished, as many games which choose a more "retro" look. I would avoid Bloody Trapland - It's not worth the cash. Maybe pick it up if it ever goes on a super sale.

This game is very well made. Everyone else loves the 1930's theme to the design, and I cannot disagree with them. The hand-drawn elements are very well-done and were worth the extra time waiting for this game. For the price, it is also definitely worth it. Just 20 dollars with a very high abundance of quality makes this game quite a steal for the price. However, the key elements to the game are these, in my personal opinion:
1. The difficulty in this game does not have to do with the bosses themselves. It has to do with the pattern, rhythm, and pace at which they fight. Once you understand and adapt to their movements and speed, it becomes very easy to counteract their attacks and to beat them very easily.
2. The graphics are in fact another huge element into further accentuating the game's uniqueness. It is pretty much unheard of there being a game that is themed in the style of a 1930's cartoon. In general, all of the graphics were in-fact hand drawn and inked in. This made the process of making the game take a lot longer than expected. However, the payoff was very much worth it. In just 34 frames/34 drawings, the smooth, crisp, and very fine movements of the characters in the game are very well done. Kudos to the artists for taking so much time to make it as authentic as possible.
3. The music is insanely good. Being a massive music nerd myself, I am entirely in love with the jazz in this game. And for the time period, it is very accurate. The big band and the big jazz band used in these pieces are supremely talented and the composer of the music is an incredibly talented gentleman who has definitely worked hard to make these pieces sound as fine and authentic as humanly possible. I give my full respect to those who participated in the making of the music in this game, they have done a stellar job at working on it and it paid off tremendously. Each piece was so fitting for the area. Railroad Wrath was incredibly accurate, High Seas Hi-Jinx was very well-written, and the use of the Baritone Saxophone as a key soloist in a few of these pieces and the lead trumpet also being a key feature was definitely a very valuable asset to all of these pieces. The piano pieces were very unique and the style at which they were played was very well done. In conclusion, the jazz in this game is amazing. Everything about them is perfect in every aspect possible and it definitely encourages me to become more involved with jazz.
In summary: Cuphead is a very well-made game. The music is fantastic and authentic, the graphics are uniquely made especially for a video game, and the gameplay is more related to coordination than difficulty. However, these are all just my opinions. I will not judge you if you disagree with my opinions because I'm not one to say that my opinions are factual and that if you objectify them then your opinion is wrong. I completely understand and will respect your choice.
Many thanks for those of you who took the time to read this. And for people who are wanting to buy the game, please do so. For the price, I would say it is more than worth it.

I first played this game in Early Access, and discarded it pretty quickly. The balance was off, it felt too restrictive, and didn't really offer me anything fun. I ditched it fast.
But I've just installed the release version, and now I'm suitably impressed.
The game operates on the idea that each door you open represents a "turn", a turn where heroes are healed, resources gained, technology researched, and cooldowns ticked. During that turn you might fight monsters, open chests, find merchants, stuff like that. Your main ways of influencing the game aren't to physically control the characters while they fight, it's to position the characters in rooms such that they do the most damage. Or pop their abilities at the right time, swap their equipment, or change which rooms have electricity going to them (and consequently, have light/defenses/resource collection).
Unlike normal RPGs - there is no gold and no experience points. There are four resources; food, industry, science, and dust. You level your heroes up with food, build turrets/resource gatherers with industry, research new technology with science, and power rooms with dust. Each of these resources is crucial in it's own way, and the management of those resources defines if you win or not.
Because there's no gold or XP, this game really feels different. The incentive structure is completely unique; you don't want to fight enemies, you need to open doors. But opening doors might get too dangerous once you get near the end of a floor, and it might be better to skip it and run. You might spend food on levelling up, or healing your people. There's no global currency, merchants accept a random resource as currency in trade, and each resource gets used every floor, so you never hoard anything.
The coop is fun, but it also really needs fixes. You cannot save coop games, so you have to be prepared to stick it out for the 2+ hours required to play a round - or abandon the game. Players cannot share items between them (but they can share resources), they need to sell items at the merchant and have the other player buy it - at a loss. Random crashes and freezes during level load completely take down a lobby (which means you need to start an entirely new game, see the "no saving" above). And there is no character sharing. So if your friend's only character dies, and you're left alone with two characters, you can't share it with him. You might as well start over, or wait until a new character appears in a floor. Characters that aren't controlled by you don't get unlocked in your game. So if your friend took a character you haven't unlocked, and plays the game until that character is unlocked for him, you won't get the unlock. *You* have to play the character (probably in singleplayer) to unlock them.
Overall the bugs aren't too noticeable. And it's a neat game that took all the usual formulaic elements of a game and twisted them slightly to make a totally new sort of game, without getting too abstract or weird about it.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

A boy enters LIMBO...
In LIMBO, you play as a boy looking for his lost sister. The game begins with no explanation, and indeed the entire experience has absolutely no dialogue or exposition whatsoever - everything is left open to the player's interpretation. A side-scrolling 2D "platformer", LIMBO will have you overcoming obstacles and puzzles in pursuit of your lost sibling, and is sure to elicit some shock value due to some of the content (why are there dead kids?).
LIMBO is also proof that you do not need a big budget or fancy graphics to create a fantastic and immersive game - this is perhaps the definition of "atmospheric", thanks to wonderful use of a black and white world to draw you further into the gloom and confusion, and some of the best sound design I have ever heard in any game. There are so many tiny details added in which increases the illusion - the soft puffs of dust as the boy runs, the tiny patter of raindrops falling, etc.
This is not far off being an artform... highly recommended to anyone looking for an experience, rather than a distraction.

Project Zomboid is a survival game first, and a zombie game second. Surviving requires resource management and good decision making. Food and water are both important, and within the first month the water supply is cut off and power is gone. One day is an hour of play on default settings for reference. Water sources such as sinks will still hold a bit of water after the water supply is gone, but for the most part it's up to the player to provide for themselves at this point. Most food expires, and this requires planning of when to eat what. There are many interesting mechanics that make surviving fun, such as the ability to freeze foods so they last longer, or growing crops and canning them in summer so they can be used in winter.
Yet, there is still plenty of fun to be had in this game by rushing hordes of zombies while trying to loot a warehouse with powerful weapons and rare construction materials early on. There is a perk system in place that requires players to give themselves negative traits in order to obtain positive ones. This allows for a variety of playstyles. You can create a loud character that has poor senses and is more likely to be seen by zombies, but is incredibly strong and can tackle large amounts of them at once, or create a weaker character that can sneak around easily and survive in the shadows. The immense character options are coupled with the fact that there is a sandbox mode with a healthy amount of options.
Want more zombies? Set the population to very high and watch as they overwhelm you even on the outskirts of town. Don't like how zombies tend to spawn within urban centers? Make them spawn uniformly and you'll find random ones lurking in the woods. The settings also include whether or not to begin with basic supplies, how long it has been since the outbreak began, and how long it will take for the power and water to shut off. There are many more and I encourage anyone who enjoys survival games to pick this one up for themselves and take a look.
All of that being said, it is important to note that Project Zomboid is still in early access. There are some bugs around, and in my opinion the interface is still relatively clunky to use. The game takes some getting used to, but has a big payoff in the long run. The developers have improved the interface in recent builds, and have weekly "Mondoids" where they keep the community up to date on what's what. Development on the game can feel pretty slow at times, we've been periodically promised NPCs that are fellow survivors for several years but they are still not implemented, for example. If you can handle all of this, then by all means I recommend picking up this game, it's worth the price and more.

This is a good survival game in many ways, but ultimately, it lacks consistency and useful player feedback. For instance, after surviving 30+ days, equipping myself with wolfskin coat, deerskin pants/boots, double fisherman sweaters, etc, etc - I was at the point when I basically did not become cold during daytime. I could also sleep outdoors, which was good because I wanted to work towards the very-difficult-to-achieve feat of getting a permanent bonus to 'feels like' temperature.
Anyway, I had just finished killing a bear, setting up all the gut/hide to cure, and I went to sleep outside, with a fire burning for 2 hrs, in a wind-sheltered area. I died. Instantly. Apparently I froze to death, but there was only a flash of "Affliction: Hypothermia", and then it vanished, and I was "Faded into the long dark." Why? 100% health, bedroll, tons of clothing, and 2 hrs of + temperature, but, I'm dead. In the past, my character at least woke up in poor condition if the temperature dropped too low. I'd add, those were much more poorly equipped characters - and yet, it seemed there was the opportunity to escape immediate harm, unless it was something like a bear attack, which I would understand. I don't mind if my character dies in a bad situation, but this was totally inconsistent with my previous time playing this game.
Ultimately I can't recommend the game. I spent a lot of time getting to 30+ days playing off and on during early access, and came back hoping to prepare for the story mode. This is hugely discouraging and suggests all that time was a huge waste of time, not an investment in future time spent with this game. Disappointing.

The Long Dark is a very unique game, despite the recent release of many new survival-mode game titles. This game is the closest game that I could find to ever match realistic survival in a realistic scenario. Just the AI of the animals, alone, is enough to impress anyone who understands that most games (and I mean at least 80%) spend almost no time into creating such accurate AI, and to think that these people (Hinterland Studios) are still developing and improving their AI!
I am truly amazed at Hinterland Studio's work on The Long Dark. It's as if their passion is driven by their Canadian spirit and their experience with AAA games. I feel as if they will never truly stop developing this game - no matter how many sales that they make or how much people hate them. I honestly can't believe that a game in this early stage can have this much potential. This is more than a video game, this is a simulation of real-life.
I want you to go into the game with some questions in mind:
1. Is this how long I'd survive in this situation?
2. Can I survive in an area that I know nothing about, have no GPS to help me navigate, and have no one to ask for help?
3. Can I do this, by myself, without referencing from a Wiki (which there is an Official one) or asking other players for help?
I'd recommend taking this game as a test/challenge to yourself. See how you compare. See whether your logic and approach to survival will save you or get you killed. See what you can do to better yourself, make better choices, and how long you can keep fighting despite being at 1% life. Go farther. Go deeper. Be better.

Generally speaking, Evolve is a great game. It's refreshing to see a 1v4 game that's as well balanced and unique as this is. Gameplay is great, presentation (aside from some awkward dialog) is amazing, competitive and tactically deep strategy. There's not a lot of negative to be said about the game itself.
While they did right by the DLC in that it in no way divides the community whether you own any of it or not, they pushed way to aggressively with it. Preorder pushing everywhere far in advance, multiple deluxe editions, season pass and a shop with skins and bundles galore as soon as the game dropped. That said, aside from selling addition characters, it's all cosmetic and so doesn't affect the balance. They also seemed to oddly try to force it to be an esports game before there seemed to be any real interest in players for it to be one.
The playerbase for this game is dwindling fast, and while there are some resurges while they've been putting on free skin community challenges during the weekends, you can see that the peaks are less each time. It's a nice gesture by Turtle Rock, but unfortunately I don't see it fixing anything in the long run. According to Steamcharts, the average number of players has fallen by 90% since February. It's a shame, because this is a legitimately fun game.

There have been a lot of games recently trying more and more desperately to mash together as many genres and styles as possible in some sort of misguided attempt at resulting in something fresh and original. Amplitude is one company that has achieved this, either by design or by luck they have combined elements of rogue-lites, tower-defence, RTS-style resource management and so on, and rather than ending with some terrible chimera monstrosity that drowns you in confusing mechanics and other complexities they have something more graceful and inviting.
But easy-to-pick-up definitely does not mean easy, its gruelingly hard and I've only managed to beat "too eay" mode twice, and playing on "easy" is basically taunting death itself.
But that challenge merely  highlights something special about the game.
You don't play Dungeon of the Endless for a trivial pat-on-the-back with the instant gratification of easily acchieved quests and levelling. No you play Dungeon of the Endless because the fun in it is geuine, not a trick of marketing and impulse rewards. You have to earn your successes and you enjoy the sense of winning all the more for having worked for it.
That's my opinion anyway

Dungeon of the Endless is a very clever cross between a rogue-like adventure game, and a Tower Defense game.
Each time you start a new game, you choose two starting heroes (up to two more can be recruited during each game), and then set off to beat, consecutively, all of the levels of the dungeon.  On each level, you start in a room with several doors; every time you open a door, there is a chance of monsters spawning, and in each new room there is a chance of discovering valuable resources or treasure.  Those resources are necessary to level your hero, research new defenses, and to build defenses, while the treasure takes the form of weapons, armor, and special items that improve your heroes.  Resources roll over from one level to the next, encouraging you to use them as little as possible--and to search out as many rooms on each level as you can.  Once you've found the exit to each floor, you can leave--but only after running a gauntlet as monsters spawn and attack you from every direction.
All-in-all it's a great little tactical game.  It's challenging, but not so much that you feel you can't make progress.  And there are enough challenges and unlocks to keep you interested for a good while.  The graphics are retro, 8-bit style; it's certainly not pretty, but it gets the job done.  And some of the loading screen dialogue between the characters is even pretty amusing (although it does get repetitive after awhile).
So if you like challenging, tactical gameplay, especially if you are into off-beat tower defense games, I strongly recomend this one.

Recommended for fans of TBS strategy and 4x games.  It plays similar to a cross between Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic.  It is imperfect but may be the best fantasy 4x game out within the last few years.  Pros and cons listed in DETAIL below if you find them helpful.
Pros:
-Fun gameplay.  It delivers a quality 4x experience.
-Intuitive mechanics.  If you have played 4x games, you will grasp this game's concepts quickly.
-Good tactical combat.  You can make a difference if you take command versus just autoresolve everything.  Tactical combat is not as strong as Heroes of Might and Magic or Age of Wonders 3, but it is a fun and useful part of the game.
-"Tame the land mechanic".  There are plenty of neutral monsters and quests to make expansion more than an uninteresting early-game land grab.
-Satisfying empire building.  Your cities level just like your heroes, and there are a variety of customizations options for each city.  This is a great mechanic!  Yet city management is streamlined enought that you don't get too bogged down late game with many cities.
-Custom units.  You can make your own custom military units with their own characteristics once you've gotten the appropriate research and resoruces.  While more customization options would be nice, it is a very cool and welcome mechanic.
-Minimal waiting in between turns (in contrast to the long waits in Civilization 5).  The AI is thinking about its turn when you are taking yours, so the time it takes to execute their turn is minimal.  This is a big plus.
Cons:
-Graphics are ugly.  I suppose on the spectrum of 4x graphics, it is somewhere in the middle (with Dominions being ugliest and Civilization/Heroes of Might and Magic/ Age of Wonders 3 being pretty).
-Spells are bland and there are not enough of them.  I was never excited to get access to a new spell.  Spell research is also somewhat confusing - you get spells through a confusing combination of leveling your heroes and through research.  Master of Magic got spells exactly right and I wish more modern games would simply copy and improve on their model.  In MoM, you could make your own towns a paradise (all with nice little spell effects), you could summon awesome units, you could blight an enemy town with pestilence, chaos rifts, etc (all visualized nicely), you could plunge the world into eternal night, and you simply researched each spell individually and intuitively.  FE has fewer and less exciting options.
-Hero advancement is similarly bland.  Although there was an extensive list of traits to acquire, I was never excited to gain a new level with my hero because none of the traits were that interesting.  Contrast this to the excellent system in the Heroes of Might and Magic series.  In that series, getting Grandmaster Fire Mage or even Basic Logistics was always exciting because the skills were useful and interesting.  This is not so in FE sadly.
-Not enough fantasy creatures on your side.  You may get about 3 uninteresting summoning spells (only 1 of which is good) that are limited to 1 summoned creature per spell per hero.  So you will not lead a shambling horde of zombies and skeletons or demons like you could in Master of Magic or Dominions.  A few races also have access to 1 fantasy creature that they can recruit directly from towns (and you can even customize, which is cool but really limited).  If you capture the right location on the map or complete a long questline, you may get a dragon (one) as well.  Humanoid troops are nice fodder and need to be there, but they should be 60-70% of your army, not 98% of it.  The reason people want to play this type of game instead of Civilization is specifically FOR the fantasy creatures and the spells!
-Races are bland.  For some reason, Stardock departed from fantasy conventions of men, elves, orcs, dwarves, etc.  Instead, they have races that are elf-like and dwarf-like and orc-like, but they are  more humanoid and less interesting.  Except for a few structures and traits, they all play similarly.  Again I must compare to Master of Magic where each race had its own unique units and tech tree.  Also compare to HoMM 3 or 5 - each race felt unique and played differently.
-Weak, uninteresting quest items.  In spite of a lot of questing, I seemed to only get bland, weak, and uninteresting reward items.  I would always replace them from the shop whenever I researched the right tech.
-Furthermore, there is no mechanic to make your own powerful items.  Master of Magic, Dominions, and to a lesser extent Age of Wonders all got this right.  I should be able to expend considerable magic resources to make a great artifact for my heroes to use.  Whether that's a sword that raises  slain foes as zombie minions, armor that makes the wearer ethereal, a horn that empowers the troops, or a staff that disintegrates the enemy, this mechanic is sorely missing in FE.
-There is little penalty for heroes defeated in combat.  They simply get a tiny permanent debuff (typically of little to no consequence) and respawn the next turn at low health in your nearest town.  While there should be some mechanism to retrieve your fallen sovereign or save your heroes with extraordinary magic, I personally prefer both my heroes and my enemy's heroes to die and stay dead under most circumstances.  Heck, in Dominions not only did dead characters stay dead (albiet with the possibility of resurrection or magical unlife), they could get significant battle wounds even if they survived victorious combat.  In Heroes of Might and Magic, the defeated hero would abandon your cause entirely.
-Poor optimization.  The game chugged on my old computer to the point of unplayability mid-game.  It still gets a little chunky on my new Alienware hotrod.  For a game with such primitive 3D graphics, that should not happen!
Conclusion:  Recommended to fans of the genre
This game is a good, fun empire builder.  As an empire builder, it is better than Age of Wonders III but not quite as good as Civilization 5.  Unfortunately the fantasy elements (spells, hero advancement, fantasy creatures, and races) are quite inferior to games like Master of Magic, Heroes of Might and Magic, Age of Wonders III, and Dominions.  However, the game is greater than the sum of its parts and a good empire builder with (albiet bland) fantasy elements is still a worthy part of a strategy fan's library.  Though I've listed a lot of cons, I really did have a good time with the game.  Its shortcomings didn't bother me until well after I had gotten my money's worth of entertainment.

Is it possible to take the best parts of Red Faction: Guerilla's sandbox world and fit them into a linear third person shooter, and still make them just as fun? The answer, it would seem, is yes.
Those coming from Guerilla and considering giving this one a shot, here are the important points:
- Destructible environments abound. Fortunately Volition knew they had a great thing going with that in Guerilla and decided to keep it for this one.
- The list of foes has been expanded to inlude both humans and vicious aliens of the Dead Space-ish variety. Gives a bit of a horror element, and a definite change of pace from the ol' EDF army.
- The arsenal covers the essentials and then some. The sledgehammer and mining charges are back (the latter are fired from a gun now but work essentially the same), but are eclipsed by two things that are even better: the magnet gun and the ability to repair structures after destoying them. You don't just tear down buildings in this game, YOU USE THEM AS A WEAPON. AND CAN DO SO AGAIN AND AGAIN. The other guns you get are focused on either killing baddies or breaking stuff, sometimes both.
- Like Guerilla, there's salvage to collect and weapon upgrades to purchase. Capitalism, ho!
- Environments seem to have switched to lots of underground tunnels, with the only direction though levels being straight forward. Some folks will be fine with that, others will miss the open world of Guerilla. There is enough variety in the level design to keep it from getting stale, however.
- The story, unfortunately, has gone from "simple but serviceable" to "needed a bit more proofreading." Those who twitch when they see story-breaking plot holes are advised to proceed with caution.
So yes, a mixed bag, and the genre shift will attract some people and repel others.
