This is my first Early access + Survival game purchase. I have only clocked 5.1Hrs of gameplay when making this review, and can honestly say i have already got my moneys worth (purchased on sale £7.50). I have yet to see any bugs, this is a very polished game. Currently no story mode, but the regular sandbox survival mode is impressive enough. This games all about surviving nature, and does well to show this.

The game is pretty fun, theres a lot to figure out and do.
Animals are incredibly strong as they should be. But its annoying when you fight off a wolf have it ravage your clothing, create enough damage that requires 2 hours of bandaging and it chases you back if you don't immediately gtfo.
The game requires thinking, a bit of planning and it definitely is one of the more fun survival games I have played.
However there are some realism issues that really bothered me. You cook a can of tomato soup and you actually get dehydrated from eating it. Same goes for every food source. Most humans nowadays actually drink less because we get most of our moisture from the food we eat. So its a♥♥♥♥♥♥off that you must consume pure water at all times. Even a 3% boost to dehydration would be a bit more realistic.
**Haven't played too long but if you want the survival experience dive right into the hard mode and you will learn from failure.
GRAPHICS: Artwork is kind of nice but a little too simple and lacking detail for my tastes, but its good enough for what the game is and doesn't detract from the gameplay.
ATMOSPHERE: You feel like you are in the game as well, progress bars slightly take away from the immersion (nitpicking here) it would be cool to do things with keybinds/mouse to speed up actions, just to get the player more involved. However the dire requirement in a survival situation still makes them tolerable and makes me feel as if I am counting on that fire myself.
SOUND: A bit minimalistic here, there are quite a few actions that lack any sounds to them, but they are clear (when they are present) and do contribute to the depth of the game. Wind howl, player character sounds add more immersion as well.
GAMEPLAY: Not too bad, movement and navigation is quite easy to pick up, you can find many "alternate" paths by walking up the slopes of hills and the like.
So far 2 hours in and I'd give this game a buy. I can see myself playing the survival mode on and off occassionally.

The concept behind Evolve really is a unique one. Four human players have to hunt down a monster before he manages to Evolve and and become enough of a force to openly challenge the hunters. The 4v1 idea is indeed an interesting one, and one which developer Turtle Rock Studios has skilfully executed. However despite its unique concept, Turtle Rocks fails to expand and build upon its original premise. Mind you this isn’t a bad game… in fact its good, sometimes great even, however unfortunately despite everything Turtle Rock gets right, its newest shooter fails to Evolve into something truly special.
Evolve is set on Shear, a human colony that has been settled due to its rich mineral deposits; however the local fauna isn’t exactly happy to see us there, particularly a bunch of ferocious and intelligent monsters. After the colonists realise they’ve bit off more than they could chew, an evacuation is announced, and a team of hunters is dispatched to eliminate the beasts while the rest of humanity packs up and leaves. And… thats just about all the story you get in Evolve, which basically serves as a means to dispatch you on exotic, and extremely dangerous hunting trips. Now while you shouldn't expect much on the narrative side of things, the games characters are are well voiced, memorable and bursting with personality. The world of Shear has received similar attention to detail. All the maps are extremely well designed, and filled with lush vegetation and hostile wildlife, and are graphically stunning due to the power of Cry Engine 4. So it comes as a great shame that most of those maps look exactly the same. Towering cliffs, dense jungle and industrial facilities make up most of the scenery in Evolve’s numerous settings, and while it helps to establish the world of Shear, it means that none of the maps particularly stand out, as often you simply wouldn’t be able to tell the damn difference.
Evolve consists of four game modes, however just like the locations you are sent to, none of those modes manage to stand out on their own. The fundamental mode on offer here is Hunt, in which the hunters must track down and kill the monster before it manages to Evolve to the point where it is likely to make said hunters its midnight snack. Now one immediate thing to note is the large amount of downtime, as you will spend most of your time not fighting the monster, but instead looking for it, a burden mostly put on whoever decides to play the tracker. This is where Evolves great emphasis on teamwork comes in, something which is often both a blessing and a curse for the game. You see, your enjoyment with Evolve is often dependant on the people you play with. If your tracker is incompetent, than good luck ever catching up to the monster. If your medic is screwing around, than no-one is there to heal the team. On the flip side if the monster doesn’t know what he’s doing, than the game might be over far too quickly. Unfortunately Evolve is only excellent sometimes, and when everything clicks, when your team is working together, and the monster is putting up a good fight, than you are guaranteed to have a good time. When you finally defeat your enemy as a result of great teamwork, or manage to outwit the hunters, you will feel a sense of satisfaction rarely present shooters these days; however that is a lot of variables all have to fall it place for that to happen. This is why I highly recommend playing Evolve with friends, the same way I wouldn’t recommend playing with a bunch of randoms in Left 4 Dead. Because when a game is so focused on teamwork and coordination, than you better make sure you play with the right people.
Now the other modes are only slight variations on the original formula. For example the hunters might have to destroy a bunch of eggs, or protect civilians. However sooner of later it all comes down to the same 4v1 battles, and while the objectives might be different, the scenarios that you end up with are practically the same. Sure, modes like defend might eliminate a lot of the downtime by immediately upgrading the monster to stage 3 and ordering him to destroy a series of objectives, but essentially the end result is the same confrontation between the hunters and their adversary. Turtle Rock has created a great foundation, but has then failed to build upon it. Playing as the monster however is a lot of fun, and it is always entertaining to go from vulnerable to near unstoppable in a matter of minutes, and you are presented with a wide range of abilities with which to crush your opponents. From fire breath and rock throw on the goliath, to lighting strike on the kraken to teleportation and cloaking on the wraith. Currently there are three playable monsters, with a fourth sold as  DLC… oh yea… DLC.
As you might have heard Evolve got was under fire recently due to its approach to downloadable content, most of which isn’t even included in the season pass. Now granted a lot of that content are skins and cosmetic items, but also includes an extra monster and hunters. While this isn't as big of an issue as some people made it out to be, when a AAA game launches with 100 dollars of DLC, it just stinks of the publisher attempting to milk the player of evey last dime. I also took issue with Evolve’s progression system, which felt unnecessarily convoluted. It works on two separate levels. Your player progression improves your overall player rank, unlocks new perks, and is generally increased by simply playing the game. Your character progression is specific to the class you play. For example by playing the medic you will level up that particular class. Makes sense right? Well… not really. New gear unlocks with new characters, and in order to obtain the next character in said class you will have to completely master the previous one. This means it takes ages to unlock new characters and gear, which is a real great shame considering how just much that later equipment can increase your enjoyment with the game. It really should be pointed out that all the weapons and equipment here are unique, feel great to use and all serve a specific purpose. Which is why it sucks so bad that a lot of it is locked away until much later, where many players simply wouldn’t be bothered to grind for it.
At the end of the day, Evolve is not a bad a game. I think this should be made blatantly clear. In fact it is a very unique monster hunting game which occasionally shines of greatness. It is a very polished game, and when everything clicks the hunt can prove to be exhilarating, however it seems that while Turtle Rock came up with an excellent idea on which to base their game, they have rather ironically failed Evolve it into something a lot more worthwhile. Meaning this is a game built around one gimmick, and once those 4v1 battles get boring than so does the entire game. In conclusion I would recommend Evolve to those deeply interested in the concept, just bring some friends if you can.

Really enjoyed the game for what it was.  Now, it's hard to get a decent team together because of the low pop, but I still recommend the game (if you can find 3 other friends to play with).  The 4v1 model has all the action that L4D2 tried to incorporate into it, only it's done so much better by not trying to cling to the horror genre (because, really it was just an action game).
Addressing all the DLC hate: sure, this game released with a bunch of DLC... but have you looked at it?  It's just goofy weapon skins for the majority that No. One. Buys.  It really has no impact at all on the outcome of a game, and you're not punished for not buying it.  You still get all the features of the game.  However, the Season Pass is the only true DLC (imo) that has been released for this game.  It's 4 more hunters (1 for each class) and a new monster.  Also, not mandatory.  If you're in a party with one of the new hunters and it looks like fun, spend a couple bucks.  But please for the love of all don't think this game's DLC is anywhere near as bad as something like Destiny; that's what most of the reviews ♥♥♥♥♥ about in the first place.
So, TLDR: great game if you're teamed up with 4 other friends, or fun if you're just looking to professionally monster.  But PUG'ing in this game is the dumps due to the low pop.  Also, DLC not mandatory and really can be ignored -- top tier hunters are a mix between release and DLC hunters (favoring the hunters at release).

Evolve is some of the most fun I've had in a PVP game. The biggest and most common criticism I have heard is that the game is repetitive, and I strongly disagree. The game is only the repetitive if you play every game the same, which is how you lose games. There is a lot of thought and strategy needed to be effective at this game, especially as you get better at it. If you are hunters and you play against a good monster and you do nothing but follow daisy and shoot the monster when you see it and trap it when you manage to get close, you will lose. If you are playing against a team of skilled hunters and you just run across the map whenever they see you, you will lose. This game has some of the best strategic choicemaking I've seen, and one good or bad decision could be all it takes for the monster to shake the hunters off its trail just long enough to evolve to stage 2 or for the hunters to catch a weak monster in a dome with no terrain to hide behind.

Since there's so much hype about this game, one may aproach it for the first time with certain expectations, or maybe just wanting to know what it's all about. That's why I'll start this review with what NOT no expect.
1) Game mechanics are OK.
Don't get me wrong, they're really good, just not anything remarkable inside the genre. Platformers traditionally make mechanics their main appeal, but this is not what makes LIMBO stand out.
2) You may not like the puzzles.
Nothing gets explained and the player must rely on trial and error, where errors tipically mean you die and start over. Sometimes you can get stuck on something that will later seem trivial, only too obscure. A lot of parts are really finicky, requiring a specific sequence ef moves executed perfectly with perfect timing.
Some people find this frustrating. That being said, I don't think it compromised inmersion, nor would I say it's a difficult game to beat.
3) There's no plot.
Of course, the internet is filled with theories and speculation, but all of it requires abstracting a bit too much from what's being presented in the game itself, and ending up quite distant from it. Go check that out if you're into that. Personally, I couldn't care less. The point is: you won't find any of those stories in the actual game.
So, why do I recommend it, then?
Well, for me it's all about the atmosphere. When you play LIMBO, you navigate through a feeling. As you advance in the game, that feeling morphs and eventually turns into something else. In the beginning, you wake up in the forest, intranquil, maybe even scared, but you're drawn to explore. There's no background music, a great use of silence that amplifies the unsettling sound effects. You soon find out how hostile this enviroment is, but think you have an objective (the girl) and feel motivated to venture on. However, this will fade; things will make less and less sense and with every step the end will seem farther away. You stop believing you'll reach your goal. As you feel progressively more numb, eerie, sustained notes displace silence. Deaths are unnavoidable, but they are part of the experience. They remind you how weak you are and how little your surroundings care about you. The'll become almost rutinary. You are trapped.
This is what makes LIMBO unforgettable. Don't think about the reviews or the interpretations. Just relax and let the game engulf you.

Warning, this review may contain spoilers. I wasn't paying close enough attention to the story to tell you if any of the events were foreshadowed or not. Read at your own risk, since I'm not recommending the game, I don't think you're missing much by seeing some of the minor plot points.
It's hard to write an in depth review about this game because it does so little that is new or unique. This is essentially a by the numbers over the shoulder shooter and will fail to keep the attention of those who don't find the "story" interesting or capturing, but few are going to be really captivated by it.
The games gimmick is that you can destroy areas of the world and rebuild them again using some magical nano builder gizmo that apparently only you possess. I wasn't paying close enough attention to the story to figure out if they ever explained why you're the only one with one of these tools. While it sounds interesting on the surface, the destruction tends to feel unsatisfying after the first few times. Most of the time when you are actually noticing the destruction physics going on around you, it is because an enemy with an explosive ability has destroyed the area you were standing on and then you get to rebuild it later once you've defeated them.
Enemy variety is fairly limited, and the environments while pretty, are fairly boring to look at and consist mostly of being in tight corridors or in an enclosed outdoor space. Very rarely is there ever any wide open areas. You get your basic trash enemies that you spam the melee key to get rid of, the typical flies around and is annoying but not really dangerous enemies, and then the takes a bunch of ammo to kill enemies that have more powerful attacks. It doesn't get any more complex than that. Some of the enemy designs blend in quite nicely with the environment, and while they tried to add special effects to make them stand out, they were sometimes unsuccessful to make them visually distinct from what they are attached to.
Mason has to be one of the dumbest and unluckiest protagonists I've seen in a video game. He's repeatedly tricked, knocked out, and captured, and he repeatedly runs into situations without a plan, without backup, and without thinking things through, often cutting off the recommendations of his personal assistant computer which is trying to give him good advice. It's hard to feel sorry for him and hard to feel connected with him or his plight, which seems to be mostly self inflicted. If anyone on the entire planet of Mars had a few brain cells they could have probably resolved the entire story of the game within 3 days of the introduction.
The primary mission objectives are to destroy something, fix something, run around in mazes killing enemies, kill all the enemies, and escort vehicles through heavily scripted events. Most of it is in the guise of him being a good guy and helping out, but a lot of it just feels tedious and forced, just padding out gameplay length. The whole game can be rushed through in about 6 hours if you feel like it, and it isn't terribly hard even on some of the higher difficulty levels. Difficulty curve is fairly flat other than an occasional spike and a hard upwards curve at the end of the game where they throw everything they have at you.
Most of the weapons feel unrewarding to use and enemies act like bullet sponges until you begin upgrading. The weapon variety is decent, offering you some fun toys to play with, but you'll likely pick the weapons you like in the first half of the game and never venture out into the newer heavy weapons that the game gives you. Ammo for the heavy weapons tends to feel as though they are giving you very little of it, or way too much of it, depending on the situation. You'll need to keep some of the standbys with you anyways because while the game lets you choose any four weapons, you don't want four heavy weapons. The fire rate is too low and the ammo too limited.
There are some fun mech segments in the game, and the unlimited ammo gets put to good use, but it makes you part with the suits too quickly for that high powered, bullets actually kill things feeling to last. Generally you're walking around at a modest pace, and going from place to place takes time, often more than I'd have liked, giving the game a plodding feeling to it. There is a sprint mechanic, but it doesn't last very long and has a moderate recharge time before it can be used again, leading me to believe it is more for panic events than travel. The dodge mechanic feels slightly clunky as it is tied to the jump key, and while useful in some situations, I didn't find myself using it very much.
You are given a GPS which always shows you where you need to go, and the pathfinding for it is top notch, working around broken obstacles, or pointing out the path even in there is something broken that is required to advance. You'll make good use of it should you choose to play the game.
If you're looking for an over the shoulder shooter that lets you shoot things, has some pretty physics and decent graphics and audio, but not much else, this is right up your alley. If you're looking for something that a plot you can, and want to follow, and something that isn't going to get boring after a few hours, then you should look elsewhere. If this game suffers from anything, it's being too average and mundane.

Beyond Good & Evil mixes many gameplay elements to create a fun, adventurous, yet surprisingly serious storyline about the struggles of a reporter who slowly uncovers the sinister plot against her home planet. Although it gained some recognition in the past five years, this game is still one of the most underappreciated sparkling gems of this century.
Beyond Good & Evil was praised by both the press and players alike, yet it is still a perpetual resident on any list that collects the best rarely known games from the past 10-15 years or so.
At first glance, these ratings are difficult to justify – after all, the game is a strange hodgepodge of various genres: puzzle, platformer, stealth, 3D brawler, treasure hunt, with some driving and racing on top.
While these mixed-genre games rarely work, somehow the designers managed to keep all of these elements together in a tight knot. After getting used to the controls (a controller helps), we find a game with great mechanics, astonishing levels of large variety, and a small world that constantly offers some activity between the platforming stages, but not in a distracting manner.
The final selling point is the story: we follow the adventures of Jade, a reporter and caretaker of some recently orphaned children. She gradually gets entangled in the war between her home planet and the invading aliens, only to discover the sinister truth behind the attacks, the recent kidnappings, and her own past.
Despite the serious nature of the story, both the aesthetics and the writing tries to be light-hearted and fun, giving a great sense of adventure even when you are discussing battle plans in the back room of a bar. The cast does a wonderful job of delivering some memorable lines, elevating Beyond Good & Evil into a classic status, recommended for anyone who never had the pleasure of playing it.

Ok, so this is my first review so please don't judge! :)
This game...
It's unreal, one of only 2 games (the other being terraria) that has ever given me back that feeling I had as a child, where I'd wait for pokemon games or fifa games. That feeling of happiness and joy that seems to be disappearing with all the games we play today. This game is incredible. But now to the game.
You're a survivor in one of two towns (more coming and plenty available in the workshop) trying to fight his or her way through a zombie apocalypse. With crafting aplenty and incredible survival mechanics, this game will put you in incredibly tight situations, where pressure and decision making are vital! (example: I was in a room with 4 zombies pounding on the door, with my limited nails and hammer I boarded up the door to buy myself more time to think. This was a fatal error, as I no longer had the nails required to attach my sheetrope to escape through the window. Rather than face the encroaching zombies with my damaged baseball bat, I decided to attempt the jump from the second floor. Bad choice. I broke my leg on impact, but managed to slink away slowly to my home. Here I tried to survive for several days, before getting caught out by a small horde as I chopped wood.)
The choices you make are vital. Most importantly you have to remember death is permanent, however you can respawn into the same world as a different survivor, if you want to return to your base.
With meta sounds throughout ensuring that the zombies are constantly moving, the challenge is always there. You might go to sleep and awake to zombies breaking into your house, because a horde to the south heard a gunshot to the North. And if you hear the chopper.... Well in this case, don't listen to Arnie and don't get to the choppa!
There are also plenty of sandbox modes where you can alter zombie respawn rates and whatnot if you find the game too challenging.
Lastly multiplayer. They recently implemented a simple to use server hosting system, allowing people to make small co-op servers to play with their friends. Alternatively go for the full PVP or roleplaying experience with permanent servers that are easily available to find.
Lastly the price of this game. For the amount of enjoyment you can experience from this game, the money paid is totally worth it. On sale, it'll never go below halfprice, but honestly this game is worth it at full price.

I used to dream about a zombie survival game that was based on the rules of the world we live and breath in. A game where ransacking houses felt real and natural, where locating fresh water was as important as bashing zombie heads, where finding an axe was cause for celebration, and where facing zombies was something that was scary, and never stopped being scary. A game that trusted you to be smart enough to stockpile food to avoid starving to death, and that had the balls to make getting bitten by a zombie something that actually followed well known zombie lore. (IE; you're going to turn into a zombie. No, there is not some magical cure, you're going to die. May I suggest avoid getting bitten by zombies in the first place. What's that you say? That makes the game tense and unpredicatble, because dying means you lose all your character XP? Indeed. Now you're getting it. Surviving a zombie apocolypse in the real world would be tense and unpredictable....)
I always knew this imaginary zombie survival game of my dreams would be independently produced. Why? Because AAA game developers are so terrified the average modern gamer will get distracted by something shiny, their version of the game would grant you a "fish from heaven" magical spell, simply to balance out the requirment of finding food and having to satisfy a hunger stat. Or they would simply make the hunger stat regenrate if you sat in a corner for a few seconds, making one wonder why its there in the first place...
For those not keeping up, (I'm looking at you mainstream console gamer for whom the regenrating hunger stat was created), Project Zomboid is that zombie survival game of my dreams. At least as close as one can possibly get. I absolutely love the fact that the game more or less simulates how well I think I would do in a real zombie apocolypse. That is to say, I one hudnred percent believe I'd die backed into a corner, flailing about with a hammer in a mad panic, and eventually getting too fatigued to fend off the hordes and landing up a zombie snack. (No, you would not chainsaw them into bits and flick-flack out the window into the arms of a hottie with enormous breasts, mainstream console gamer, and no, I don't care how much you try and convince me otherwise. Get a job.)
In conclusion; yes I recommend Project Zomboid. And as a final thought; you have not known desperation until you've tried to stab a zombie to death with a spoon, simply for complete lack of other options. Another reason I love this game. I commend the developers, and deeply hope this game sees much success. I'm eager to see how it progresses.

This is my first Early access + Survival game purchase. I have only clocked 5.1Hrs of gameplay when making this review, and can honestly say i have already got my moneys worth (purchased on sale £7.50). I have yet to see any bugs, this is a very polished game. Currently no story mode, but the regular sandbox survival mode is impressive enough. This games all about surviving nature, and does well to show this.

The game is pretty fun, theres a lot to figure out and do.
Animals are incredibly strong as they should be. But its annoying when you fight off a wolf have it ravage your clothing, create enough damage that requires 2 hours of bandaging and it chases you back if you don't immediately gtfo.
The game requires thinking, a bit of planning and it definitely is one of the more fun survival games I have played.
However there are some realism issues that really bothered me. You cook a can of tomato soup and you actually get dehydrated from eating it. Same goes for every food source. Most humans nowadays actually drink less because we get most of our moisture from the food we eat. So its a♥♥♥♥♥♥off that you must consume pure water at all times. Even a 3% boost to dehydration would be a bit more realistic.
**Haven't played too long but if you want the survival experience dive right into the hard mode and you will learn from failure.
GRAPHICS: Artwork is kind of nice but a little too simple and lacking detail for my tastes, but its good enough for what the game is and doesn't detract from the gameplay.
ATMOSPHERE: You feel like you are in the game as well, progress bars slightly take away from the immersion (nitpicking here) it would be cool to do things with keybinds/mouse to speed up actions, just to get the player more involved. However the dire requirement in a survival situation still makes them tolerable and makes me feel as if I am counting on that fire myself.
SOUND: A bit minimalistic here, there are quite a few actions that lack any sounds to them, but they are clear (when they are present) and do contribute to the depth of the game. Wind howl, player character sounds add more immersion as well.
GAMEPLAY: Not too bad, movement and navigation is quite easy to pick up, you can find many "alternate" paths by walking up the slopes of hills and the like.
So far 2 hours in and I'd give this game a buy. I can see myself playing the survival mode on and off occassionally.

Cuphead's a lovely little game that features handdrawn animation styled to look like 1930's cartoons. That's what it is on the surface. On the inside it's a tough as nails platformer that'll take some real effort, determination, and a dash of luck to beat completely. The game even penalizes you for playing on simple mode, by not letting you beat the game completely. Some people think this is a load of garbage, but I say good for them for doubling down on the difficulty. So let's sum this up real quick.
Gameplay: Typical run and gun, but the customization is nice options, providing things for several types of players, and some options which work a lot better with certain bosses. Little extra secrets you wouldn't think to look for but are nice touches, and some amazing boss fights. Beating this made me feel real accomplished.
Art: Oh good lordy the art. You'd have to be a monster to think the art in this game is bad. It takes so much effort to do stuff like this, and they went the whole nine yards to make it handdrawn and give it that incredible style that feels you with joy and nostalgia. Until you're distracted by now nice it looks and die for the 200nd time.
Music: The music is all perfectly suiting of its locations. It has a way of not taking up too much attention, but you can't also help humming along to it after your 30th time doing a boss because you now have every note memorized somehow.
Final words: Looks great and sounds great. You'll only FEEL great if you actually beat that boss, otherwise it's gonna haunt you while you sleep.

Edit: Now that Evolve Stage 2 is out in beta with a Free-to-Play model, I'm going to revise my review soon.
Original Review: Evolve is one of those games that is gonna always have a devisive, spirited base of opinions.
*On one hand, there's the the hate on the DLC model. Here's my short opinion on that, but it's not the basis of my review:
- absolutely don't care that they charge for skins. If you want them, buy them. If you're a collector, they're there, not that expensive individually, and some are rather nice. If you don't want them, don't buy them and don't compain. They don't give anyone an unfair advantage.
- I kinda wish the skins were body skins and not just weapon skins, but I don't really care that much.
- So far, the first round of new maps have been free and it seems like that is going to be the model for the future.
- Character and monster DLCs are paid, though, and I don't mind it. I do, however, think they're a little on the expensive side. 7 bucks each individually is a little excessive considering the base game was AAA full price. That's a con.
- There's a challenge every week that rewards people who play online with special free skins. I particularlly like the voodoo skins for monsters.
*Moving on:
another thing people complain about is how the base game is lacking. I don't see that at all. With 16 hunters, 3 monsters, and >10 maps in the base game, there's a lot of different combinations you can find and I gaurentee them you will be able to have fun without spending an extra dime. As of writing this review, I haven't bought the new tier of hunters/monsters, and I probably won't for a while, because I'm still having fun with the base characters trying to reach elite level with my favorites.
*Turtle Rock Studios is a team that really cares about the community. They're regular on the forums and in game. TRS streams weekly to report on news, debut a new challenge, or interact with the community. 2K streams weekly also, and regularly plays game within the 2K crew or with the community.
A rather large problem with the game right now is bugs and balancing. The balancing has been getting better, and its something TRS is dedicated to. There was a patch recently with some tweaks. It isn't perfect yet, but it's better and perfectly playable.
There's still some lingering bugs. Behemoth's rock wall was all but pointless for a long time. Just today I played a game where I went to revive a teammate and a crowbill sloth hit me (even though I was cloaked and he shouldn't see me) and knocked me under the map. Fun.
Pro: graphics. My laptop forces me to play on "low" graphics settings and lower-than-720 resolution, and I still think Evolve is a fine looking game. The artists at TRS did a phenomenal job, with the character models, the monsters, the maps, environments, wildlife, everything.
Even considering all that, Evolve is a game I'm gonna be playing for a while. She's far from perfect, but she's fun and the potential for improvement is there, and there's a dedicated team striving to get there. 3.5 stars out of 5 for now, and I'll come back to edit that rating as i think the game improves.

I cannot say enough how enjoyable this game is. I love the art style, the game music is magnificent, the gameplay is simple and intuitive but still challenging and so enjoyable. While it is a rogue-like game in that once your character(s) die you finish that play session there are different modes which modify the gameplay dramatically from a super hard mode where you get way less resources and start off with the only characters you'll get to a mode where you get a super strong hero that can be brought back to life using the food resource.
Another reason I am so infatuated with this universe and game is that the game makers (Amplitude) incorporate a currency called Dust into all of their games; Dungeon of the Endless, Endless Legend, Endless Space - as well as the obvious naming conventions used in all of their titles. There is continuity between the games suggesting a similar universe. You can even, with purchase of special items, get species or character types in one of their games from another which I just think is the cat's pajamas.
In addition to having nearly endless replay value the multiplayer with friends adds so much more that you can do in this game. While you can completely play singularly multiplayer adds a new dynamic which, again, adds to the replay value.

Mmmm, a little on the fence with this one.  If I would give it a number on 10, I would give it a 6.  Although I like it, this game could have been awesome if the bugs had been fixed and it had been optimized.  Here is a description:
Bugs: Through my 14 hour playthrough, I had two crash to desktops.  Also had a game breaking bug that I had to work around during a battle.  An enemy warlock would try to summon a creature that would never appear.  Reloading the game 3 times did not resolve it.  The game would just sit there, with nothing happening for 3min before I closed it through windows.  The only way I could fix this was to try to kill the warlock before he tried to summon his creature.  Worked fine after but that's not normal.
Performance:  This was the most nagging aspect of the game and what I believe soured my experience.  On a normal map, the scrolling would not be fluid and clicks felt laggy.  It doesn't make sense that my computer would struggle with this game.  See, I have an 3ghz i7 processor with 6gigs of ram and a GTX670.  Civilization 5 works perfectly fine and runs a millions times better than this game.  Civ5 is a much more beautiful, bigger and CPU/GPU intensive game than Fallen Enchantress.
Gameplay: So is the game fun?  Yes, it is.  It reminds me of an old Magic game by Microprose back in the old dos days of computers.  It is a mix of Civilisation where you create cities, build and manage them while you conquer the world in a way that best fits your style.  And then battle enemies with your armies of heroes and units that gain experience and level on a grid battlefield a little like Might and Magic: Heroes, but better since good unit placement is actually important.
Graphics: They are subpar at best by this day and age.  I thought the textures looked dull and certain equipment items for your heroes were blurry and I sometimes could barely make out what they were just by looking.
Audio:  I thought that the audio was good, nothing stood out here.  The music was fine, not excellent.
Can I recommend it?  Yes.  Although I can't help but think what this game could have been.  A classic if the studio would have spent a little more time polishing it.
Would I have played longer than 14 hours if the experience was better?  Completely!

This game is really good. Basically it's one of, if not, the most realistic FPS I have ever played. The maps are huge and it tries to make sure each team is balance. It's not like most FPS where everyone can pick the same gun and dominate the game, then have that gun be nerfed, then people making another gun op, no. There are 64 people in a game, and there are multiple classes in it, which each class provides a limit to how many people are allowed to pick a class. For instance, some games only 3 people are allowed to be snipers, sometimes only 2 are allowed. This isn't a game where you can go Rambo, accuracy is important to this game, there are no crosshairs, so shooting from the hip is quite difficult unless you're really close range. For many rifles, missing just once is the difference between life or death. You have to take cover and aim if you want to rack up on kills. Also, you will accidentally kill your teammates, and that's because names won't appear above anyones head until you get close to them, but remember it's trying to be realistic, so it makes sense that you'll struggle to identify enemies from friendies, just like in actual war. I really recommend this game for any FPS fans that are willing to try something that's not Call of Duty, and I hope you enjoyed this review.

First I have to say that I've played this game twice, and it was such a good overall experience I eventually plan to play it again.
Red Faction : Armageddon separates itself from the previous Red Faction titles by moving from a first person shooter perspective to a third person shooter one. Otherwise, the game stays true to legacy of destructable environment that somewhat defined the franchise.
The game includes nice additions, like the hammer and the power gauntlet, that allows you to feel like a techno-barbarian along with the cosy and warming feeling of being a futuristic soldier. It's really nice to mix close range battles with enemies you can shock, and your regular shotgun-rifle-sniper-rocket launcher cycle.
The levels are varied and crafted enougth to deliver a good-to-great experience.
Your character has some kind of a skill / buff tree in shape of several rings, so you can fine tune him to fit your play style. Anyhow, you'll end up with every one of them, so don't fear to make a mistake or forgot something crucial.
The storyline is decent, and credible enougth to justify that level of rampage.
Even if Red Faction : Armageddon will not blow your mind, it's a very good game that gives you a licence to blow every piece of man-made environment to the ground, and rebuild it with your nanobots if you feel it's the right thing to do.

And nothing changed. No major updates in wildlife. No story mode (up until now) that has literally been teased so long that I no longer care whether or not there is one. The difficulty settings are absolutely absurd. On stalker, essentially "hard" mode, once you have crafted the correct gear, the game literally becomes a fishing simulator. And a bad one at that. I've been ice fishing many times my dudes. No one catches 200 salmon a day. For all the concentration on "realism", this game really ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed. So you shot a deer anywhere except in the head? No problem! you can just track its blood trail...Oh wait, no you can't. It ran 47 miles over a mountain never to be seen again. Holy crap! That's a goddamn BEAR. I guess i'll shoot it and run into this flimsy shack until it bleeds out. Nevermind that a bear that is bigger than the shack could PLOW THRU IT LIKE A FRIEGHT TRAIN. I have mixed feelings about this game. On one hand its got the sense of isolation down pretty well, the setting is well done and the world feels very threatening. I really want to like this game but it has some pretty serious issues that just choke the life out of the game for me.
The problem with survival games where simply being outside can kill you is it actively discourages exploration. This game only allows you one autosave file for a playthrough. Meaning it's always in hardcore mode and one death is all it takes to end hundreds of days worth of progress.
The real problem I have with this game is the fact that the developers have an idea of how they want you to play it, and there are numerous examples of playstyles they do not like being attacked with questionable game mechanics.
They thought wolves were too passive, so they patched it so they are more numerous and more aggressive. No big deal, you can use fire to keep them at bay. Patch later the flares, torches, and brands don't scare them away reliably anymore and more than half the time they just run up and eat you anyway.
All the extra predators forces you to figure out of to deal with them, easiest way is to bait them with meat and shoot them up close. All the dead wolves leaves you with a ton of food, making it so you don't have to go outside for days on end.
Then the devs added cabin fever and intestinal parasites. The parasites are caused by eating predator meat, meaning you can't consume much of it anymore, so the wovles that used to be a risk/reward type deal are now just in your way and killing them is nearly always a waste of your time.
The cabin fever mechanic strikes if you spend more than about 1/2 of your time inside on any given day. It stops you from passing time or sleeping inside if you catch it. The problem is nearly all of the work benches you need for crafting are inside. All the warmest beds that heal you are inside. So if you want to avoid this mechanic you are literally forced outdoors for no real reason.
I had a bed, a barn, and a screened in porch and because of the stupid mechanic my guy is sleeping in a damn snow fort in the yard. How does that make sense? Even if you go outside every day you can't avoid it, sooner or later a blizzard will strike and they strike very often and being outside means your clothing will be torn up and you'll freeze to death so you go inside. You sleep inside because going outside at night is a terrible idea it's too cold and the wolves are more aggressive at night, boom cabin fever.
The dev's claim they are trying to stop people from hibernating inside with this mechanic, but the game actively discourages you from going outside with wolves, blizzards, and freezing temperatures. This mechanic basically forces me to take risks I don't need to take, and for what? It's a single player game who cares how I play it? The whole point of survival is minimal risk for maximum reward why would I go outside if I don't have too?
The real problem is that it's too easy to amass a ton of food and just sit forever. Because you can boil water anywhere you never run out, and  single deer or a series of sling traps can feed you for days, so going outside isn't really something you have to do. Instead of rehauling the food and water mechanics, which is what SHOULD be the thing making me go outside, they just add in some completely mental mechanics that force me to sleep in my yard every few days.
I stress that this is a single player game, and the only person you are cheating if you decide to just hibernate for weeks is you. Why do the devs care how I play a single player game? I could understand this if it was on the hardest mode, leaderboards and all, but this is on normal mode, not very hard, not hard, normal. Who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the leaderboards for freaking normal mode?
For its price its a cool wee single player. Looks like its about to go full release soon and get new DLC too. Awesome for $12NZD.

This review is based off of Version 34.28 of Project Zomboid.
Project Zomboid is my favorite zombie survival game of all time. No other game combines the tense struggle for survival with immersive zombie mechanics the way Project Zomboid does!
Strengths
* Crafting is intuitive and useful.
* Character creation is extremely deep and flexible, follows a Whitewolf perk/weakness system. Many skills and abilities allow for a great deal of replayability.
* Zombies just don’t spawn on top of you like most zombie games. They move around based off of what they hear, see, smell, and they group up in an immersive way that no other game does.
* Zombification - Losing is fun! Every time you step outside your safehouse, there is a chance you will die. Making every moment of the game extremely tense and enjoyable.
Weaknesses
* The inventory and crafting interface can be a bit clunky at times, especially when cooking larger meals.
I've been playing Project Zomboid for years now, and it is a game I always come back to. Every additional content patch keeps making this game better and better!

But as I've reviewed previously (in six month intervals) it's really dragging on becoming a...you know...game. There are a lot of things being 'added' that frankly could be updates to a completed game, just as most games patch in new content as they go along to keep growing the game brand. Things like cars or NPCs that a number of players have been waiting forever for appear to keep getting pushed aside for things like - as the recent updates note - slightly different sized trees. It's exhausting, and with the game pushing two years behind the initial announcement for release (Early months of 2015, in an interview with PC Games) it's difficult to not feel like this... a weird show of priorities? The developers seem like decent guys, and they have an update every monday - so certainly, applaud them for that, but at the end of the day it still doesn't seem any closer to done so much as it just seems different. And so, I'm very torn, because I like this game, but I would like a game that seems to progress towards a finish line instead of a game that seems to move in different directions and get bigger without actually going anywhere in the direction of that finish line.
So get it, certainly, but get it with the understanding that this is an Early Access game running on it's third year, over a year and a half past their 'expected release timeframe' with no real end to that in site, as that hinges on cars and npcs (developer notes on what needs to happen for release) but they get pulled in some different directions and cars and npcs - and ultimately the final product - keep taking a backseat.

Edit: Now that Evolve Stage 2 is out in beta with a Free-to-Play model, I'm going to revise my review soon.
Original Review: Evolve is one of those games that is gonna always have a devisive, spirited base of opinions.
*On one hand, there's the the hate on the DLC model. Here's my short opinion on that, but it's not the basis of my review:
- absolutely don't care that they charge for skins. If you want them, buy them. If you're a collector, they're there, not that expensive individually, and some are rather nice. If you don't want them, don't buy them and don't compain. They don't give anyone an unfair advantage.
- I kinda wish the skins were body skins and not just weapon skins, but I don't really care that much.
- So far, the first round of new maps have been free and it seems like that is going to be the model for the future.
- Character and monster DLCs are paid, though, and I don't mind it. I do, however, think they're a little on the expensive side. 7 bucks each individually is a little excessive considering the base game was AAA full price. That's a con.
- There's a challenge every week that rewards people who play online with special free skins. I particularlly like the voodoo skins for monsters.
*Moving on:
another thing people complain about is how the base game is lacking. I don't see that at all. With 16 hunters, 3 monsters, and >10 maps in the base game, there's a lot of different combinations you can find and I gaurentee them you will be able to have fun without spending an extra dime. As of writing this review, I haven't bought the new tier of hunters/monsters, and I probably won't for a while, because I'm still having fun with the base characters trying to reach elite level with my favorites.
*Turtle Rock Studios is a team that really cares about the community. They're regular on the forums and in game. TRS streams weekly to report on news, debut a new challenge, or interact with the community. 2K streams weekly also, and regularly plays game within the 2K crew or with the community.
A rather large problem with the game right now is bugs and balancing. The balancing has been getting better, and its something TRS is dedicated to. There was a patch recently with some tweaks. It isn't perfect yet, but it's better and perfectly playable.
There's still some lingering bugs. Behemoth's rock wall was all but pointless for a long time. Just today I played a game where I went to revive a teammate and a crowbill sloth hit me (even though I was cloaked and he shouldn't see me) and knocked me under the map. Fun.
Pro: graphics. My laptop forces me to play on "low" graphics settings and lower-than-720 resolution, and I still think Evolve is a fine looking game. The artists at TRS did a phenomenal job, with the character models, the monsters, the maps, environments, wildlife, everything.
Even considering all that, Evolve is a game I'm gonna be playing for a while. She's far from perfect, but she's fun and the potential for improvement is there, and there's a dedicated team striving to get there. 3.5 stars out of 5 for now, and I'll come back to edit that rating as i think the game improves.

There are two conflicting aspects of any game, chaos and order.
Order governs logical progression of the game. A well-ordered game will be predictable but also reliable. If you learn to play a well-ordered game properly, your actions will always be rewarded with advantages. At its logical extreme, a fully ordered game can be "Solved" and thus a concrete method can be devised to guarntee success.
A chaotic game is unpredictable. Consiquences don't always follow logically from actions and the game is never the same twice. At its logical extreme, the actions of the player have 0 impact on your success or failure as that is fully determined by the random number generator.
Dungeon of the Endless mixes these two forces and achieves a solid mixture. The game does reward good gameplay decisions, but also throws curveballs at you. A really raw run of bad luck can still end a game by a skilled player, but there is always room for improvement. Learning to account for risk and the built-in randomness is part of the learning curve and maintaining control even when events turn against you is part of where development of skill comes into play.
I have yet to complete a full run. The game repeatedly kicks my butt... but I do not feel frustrated. I learn from each failure and every time I do a litlte bit better. I highly reccomend this game. I missed the 50% off steam winter sale...but having bought it at full price, I feel I have gotten very good value for my gaming dollars already, and I'm just starting to scratch the surface.

Video version:
Story/Premise:
Dungeon of the Endless (DotE), like many other rogue likes, is rather sparse in the story department. The setup follows the tried and true Sci fi conventions of a crashed escape pod after a catastrophic space battle. The roster of available characters ranges from gun toting killing machines to skin-tight space suit wearing femme fatales and everywhere in between with a pastiche of genre tropes. Each character comes with only a paragraph of backstory of who they were before crash landing on the unforgiving world of Auriga; be they prison guard, inmate, or displaced native. Outside of the character page there is little else by way of story. You either live to tell the tale by finding the exit or die like so many others. Characters are given a chance to shed some light on their personalities when doing mundane tasks like repairing turrets or opening doors and spouting off some quip here and there. It isn’t until you start to unlocking album art and completing floors that you start to open the characters up. Since each character was on the ill-fated penal transport, some of the characters will have prior history with one another. These connections, if any, will pop up in the elevator sections in between floors. It is here that old alliances, curious attractions, and blood feuds in some cases, are played out with most ending with character upgrades. Others characters may not be so lucky.

Gameplay:
DotE is a combination dungeon crawler, survival, and tower defense game with plenty of rpg elements thrown in for good measure. The moment to moment gameplay comes in the form of moving some or all of your squad room by room exploring the remains of a dead civilization. Every new room has a chance to hold new loot, a new ally to recruit, horrifying monsters, or any number of other effects. Like many other rogue likes the game can randomly reward you or punish you on a whim and it falls on the player to adapt to each new room that opens up. But before the survivors journey too far into the belly of the beast they must protect the crystal from the monsters that march ceaselessly towards it.
The crystal is the lifeblood of the escape effort. Powered by a substance called Dust it provides a constant amount of power which is used to power individual rooms by way of a daisy chain effect. The power source can be upgraded by randomly finding large amounts of dust in new rooms or small amounts off defeated enemies. Powering a room serves a double purpose of allowing you to build upgrades and defenses and eliminating the chance of monsters spawning inside it. As each floor of the dungeon begins to sprawl out from the crystal elevator, dust quickly becomes scarce and the journey ever more treacherous making it the most important resource.
Apart from dust there are three other resources, each serving a multiple purposes, which must be carefully managed throughout your run: Industry, which allows you to build new upgrades and defenses or activate random machines; Science, which is spent on enhancing your array of upgrades and defenses or resetting your characters ability cooldowns; and Food, which is used to either level up your characters, heal them during encounters, and recruit new heroes. Unlike precious dust, each of these resources is carried over to each successive floor. Every turn (opening of a new door) the player is given an allowance of these three resources which is increased by building modules of the appropriate type. In addition to their primary functions each resource, including dust, can be randomly selected as a currency at assorted shop keepers.
As you explore the dungeon floor it’s imperative that your squad be ready to fight the hordes of enemies that are sure to pop up. Depending on what escape pod you chose at the start of the game you can begin the run with up to four characters with most runs beginning with two. Each hero has a selection of equipment slots to gear up with the proper loot type and multiple passive abilities that complement their two active, cool down based, abilities. Using food, each character can reach a maximum level of 15 gaining additional abilities and stat boosts. While many characters wind up gaining the same abilities as other survivors each of them feels unique enough without being too game breaking. You’ll need to balance each of your heroes’ strengths and weaknesses if you hope to succeed. Some characters are nimble and are good at exploring new rooms and escaping enemies while others are slower and are better suited defending choke points and operating modules to increase their output. It wouldn’t be a rogue-like without plenty of permadeath, so it’s in your best interest to keep them healthy during battles. Lucky for you after each wave of enemies you’re fully healed and ready to fight again.
Every floor is broken up into many rooms with the main goal of every level of finding the exit. Many of the decisions throughout a play-through have to do with where to explore and how much. Squad members can be used to prevent a darkened room from spawning monsters, but after a while even they won’t be enough to cover every nook and cranny. To protect your weak spots and the crystal you will need to utilize each resource to research and build modules that function as towers like in standard tower defense games. It’s a constant struggle to either risk pushing on through the level to gather more supplies, or move on to the next floor with what you have. Whether you have explored the whole floor or just want to leave sooner, to proceed you must escort the power crystal to the exit room which has to be physically carried by one of your party members while the others fight off any of the endless stream of bad guys that might be in the way. The crystal bearer is slowed to a crawl, so woe to you if you if you are unlucky enough to only have one character. Successfully completing a crystal run will demolish all enemies and reset your dust counter to an ever decreasing standard.

Presentation:
Let it never be said that Dungeon of the Endless looks bland. The games oozes, sometimes literally, with assorted colors. Everything from the characters’ outfits, rooms, and enemies vibrantly pop with impressive pixelated graphics. Every new asset introduced adds to the games surprising visual diversity. Being set in a futuristic space ruins affords the designers a lot of room to show off sci fi interiors and more clandestine spaces typically found in sword and sorcery settings. The game’s decidedly retro aesthetic ensures a smooth experience throughout with no framerate hitching while staying crisp and readable. Despite the limitations of pixel based graphics each character and monster show off a surprising amount detail and personality, but while most playable characters stand out some of the spear wielders bear a passing resemblance to one another. Other than that most of the game remains fresh and unique making exploring the dungeons and characters that much more enjoyable.
Despite the scarcity of it the writing on display does a fairly good job and breathing life into the characters although during the elevator transitions each character tends to recycle the same lines of dialogue. Even though the games deals with fairly serious subject matter the game maintains a light tone with weird weapons and armor descriptions. Found an extra magazine? Don’t slide in your gun. You should read it, get dumber, and raise your attack power. That ancient king’s armor also looks like it belongs more in a rave than a raid. The overall tone of the game is more Firefly than Blade Runner and it suits it better to be more lighthearted in the face of perpetual crushing defeat. You will die constantly and the games relishes in the occasion by taunting you mercilessly when it happens.

I picked this up in a pack along with Endless Legend and Space because I wanted to get into a new 4x game. This game wasn't on my radar before and I didn't really expect anything from it. However what I found was a surprisingly addictive roguelike that borrowed elements from a dozen other genres put together into a deceptively complex whole. I've only beaten the game once on "easy" (actually the game's hard difficulty) but doing that took nearly a dozen attempts worth of familiarizing myself with the mechanics and each time felt unique and "worth" it.
The game's art and music style are very nice and the heroes are interesting, if not in terms of personality at least what they bring to the table in terms of options available to you each run. I feel like they'd work well in a more fully fleshed out RPG setting with expanded mechanics.
It would be nice if there was some kind of persistence between tries outside of which heroes you have unlocked to start with as I do feel that is a barrier to replayability currently. However even with that said I feel like this game is more than worth the admission price. One of the most surprisingly enjoyable games I've played recently.

This game is one of those games that would sit in my library, untouched, for a long time. I was too lazy to play it at first, but once I actually played it, I got so into the game that I finished it in 1 sitting. The gameplay is fairly short, but I can say that I've enjoyed every second of playing the game. Sure, there might be times when I got frustrated because some puzzles are just frustratingly hard and it seemed impossible at first (at least to me), but after figuring it out, I was amazed by how clever the solutions are. This is one of those games where the story isn't explicitly told, there is little to no text about the story but that is what makes this game artistically wonderful. Drawn in simple black and white world, the characters and the environments might not seem too interesting at first glance. The story is told simply by the actions the characters took, while the environment and the music changes at certain points to support the emotion of the story. Absolutely fantastic how the artists could draw something so simple, yet holds so much meaning behind it. I truly enjoyed playing this game and I would recommend it to people who loves playing a game with a deep and open-ended story, where you will have to figure out what happens and draw theories from it by yourself.
P.S. about achievements, don't even get me started on the secret level. That is the most frustrating gameplay ever and I must say I have yet to complete it til now.

LYNE is a minimalist puzzle game where you connect alike colored shapes in one continuous line. There are also octogons that allow a line (or multiple lines) to pass through it mulitple times (as many diamonds are shown in the shape). With this game there are 25 puzzles in each section of A - Z, so there are at least 650 puzzles to enjoy and challenge. There are also two or three daily sections generated every day giving you even more to work with, even though they are definitely not as difficult as the last few sections in the main part of the game.
As you progress through the sections they introduce more space that you have to fill and more colored shapes that you have to make a line for, which is designed to make the game gradually more challenging. I found the difficulty to vary throughout the whole game though - there were times that I would be stuck for a long time before figuring out the proper positioning for the lines and then the very next puzzle I would finish in less than a minute. This didn't make the game any less enjoyable, however, because I feel like the easier ones were I nice mental break before the more challenging puzzles that would follow.
Overall, I found the game to be challenging (and to a point a bit repetitive because there is only so many new things that can be introduced), but my desire to complete the puzzles was never diminished to the point where I didn't want to play the game anymore. The instructions and goals are straightforward, the interface was simple to understand, and the audio was pleasant but not distracting. Of course, if you are playing for hours and hours at a time, it can become a bit stale to listen to so I just listened to my own music past that point.
I got 100% achievments in about 30 hours, but it seems like there is still more to do with the dailies to get the max number of triangle "points" if you are a completionist like I am. Regardless of whether you are a completionist or not it is a great amount of game for the cost you pay, so I definitely recommend for the puzzle lovers out there.

Excellent puzzle game, one of the best on Steam at this price level. The puzzles never get very difficult, but (at least at the higher difficulties) the solutions aren't completely trivial. It's a lot like sudoku in that respect - relaxing and interesting despite the simplicity.
I don't understand reviews making it out to be something you have to brute force. The initial puzzles are the sort of thing you can solve immediately with no prior exposure. You quickly develop an intuition for what the solution will probably look like and can solve many of the puzzles on the first attempt or with minor corrections (even for the more complicated ones, since each puzzle set tends to have its own "theme"), which is a large part of the draw of the game. Failing that, there are some simple common sense rules/"tricks" to quickly exclude certain possibilities, much like what's used in crossword puzzles, sudoku, or pretty much any other puzzle. You of course can brute force it if you want, but that sucks the joy out of nearly anything.
Finding an inital (approximate) solution and learning from it is a bit different from other puzzles that just use a logic hammer until you're finished, but more enjoyable in the end. Proceeding through sudoku-type rules is an option, but unnecessarily cumbersome and time-consuming in most instances, but you may prefer solving the puzzles that way. You'll likely love the game as long as you're not brute forcing the puzzles.

If you liked the original Red Faction titles because of their open worlds, faction system, and replayability; skip this at all costs!!
RF:Armageddon is merely an on-rails console port that has nothing in common with the original games in the franchise except detailed destruction, a few of the original weapons, and the Red Faction name.
The story is very uninteresting, and the dialog is just horrid. Everything smells of console trash; from the magic floating arrows over anything of interest, to the designated checkpoints, to the on-rails approach of each mission (i.e. cunscene after cutscene).
There are NO factions - 99% of the game is fighting aliens, not the EDF or any other factions. There is no free-roam; with very small corridors and caves that have the all too familliar checkpoint system that makes you reload over and over and over until you finish it.
In the spirit of the earlier RF titles, I can't recommend this game at all, unless you just want another mediocre console shoot-em-up.

While the ability to wreck the scenery is reasonably entertaining for a while, the missions are very, very linear and the weaponry appears to differ only by visual effect. None of the guns seem to do a lot relative to hurling chunks of scenery around with the magnet gun (lifted from Half Life) so they're rarely used. The combination of repetitive gameplay (walk round a corner, horde of bugs spawn from empty space, slaughter them) and uninspiring, underpowered enemies makes the act of thinning their apparently limitless numbers a bit of a dull distraction from the scenery-chewing. A bit unfortunate in a shooter. It's quite pretty and knocking buildings over is fun for half an hour, but after that I wouldn't bother.

I say I would recommend this game with a hint of reluctance. It's a good game, storyline is good (but not great). The only thing that pisses me off is the combat system. I prefer an FPS in which everything dies more quickly, like Call of Juarez: Gunslinger (now THAT's a great game). I don't mean make the game easier, as I always like playing games on hardest mode. What I mean is, shooting the same god damn thing for ages waiting for it to dies gets boring after a while. Headshots don't seem to make much difference either. They could have made it so that enemies take much fewer hits to kill, and the protagonist is much easier to kill too (less health). Granted, you do get the sniper rifle which (when upgraded) gives you one shot kills, which is great. BUT you don't get the sniper until quite late on in the game. Also, because each enemy takes so many shots to kill, you often find yourself running out of ammo. Sure, there are ammo crates all over the place, but you can't hold that much ammo so I find myself running out of ammo whenever I'm faced with a big enemy that takes a lot of shots to kill.
All in all, the fact that enemies take a lot of shots to kill, and that they usually quite fast and move around a lot, make the combat system a little bit annoying. Otherwise, not a bad game at all. I have tons of other FPS games to recommend instead of this one though.

But, are bakenekos that scary…?
Losing his parents to a traffic accident, a boy lived his daily life in solitude until he began to take care of the stray kitten “Nuri”!
However, this kitten possessed strange powers similar to that of the bakeneko.
If that weren’t enough, he met “Yura,” who manages the existence of souls, and “Sora” from out of the blue. With a strange twist of fate, the boy will begin raising two children…

While the story may be light and fluffy with slice of life aspects. What I do not get is, Yura bad endings like how is getting locked up in a room with her and losing your virginity is a bad ending? Visual Elements – For the visual aspects I think it is generally well done and the art style is unique well for me at the very least, since I am used to moege art style. As for the backgrounds they blended in with the whole visual novel. There is not much I could really say for the visual aspects of this game.
Audio elements – There is nothing really noteworthy for to talk about here other than the fact that the CV of Sora and Yura. Sora is voiced by Sakura Ayane and Yura is voiced by Maaya Uchida. So what so special about it? Well as a person who loves idols and seiyuu related stuffs, these are kind of important to me. Sakura Ayane has voiced characters like Cocoa Hato in Is the Order a Rabbit? and Nao Tomori in Charlotte while Maaya Uchida has voiced characters like Ranko Kanzaki from The Idolmaster Cinderella Girls and Sharo Kirima from Is the Order a Rabbit? just to name a few. Well having these 2 is a plus for me for sure.
Would I recommend  My Little Kitties? I would say yes if you want a short heartwarming story that is cute and fluffy that has kittens though do note that some of the bad endings makes totally no sense at all and it feels extremely forced. Like I said at the top how is getting locked up in a room with Yura and losing your virginity is a bad ending? I really cannot grasp the logic behind this. Well just the bad endings only for most of the part of course you can choose to avoid them but then that would not be a full completion of the game. With that said I end my review here.

Beyond good and evil is an action adventure mix without any outstanding design decisions, but everything that is in the game, is very well implemented, while still being kinda basic. There is a simple combat system, which doesn't reach the levels of a spectacle fighter - reminiscent of Starfox Adventures. There is a stealth system, but it isn't as deep as the likes of Metal Gear, Splinter Cell or Thief. There is some sense of Open-World-Exploration, but please don't expect GTA or Skyrim. There is photography, but (sadly) no Prof. Oak to evaluate your skills regarding capturing Snorlax' butt on polaroid. And there are racing-sequences, which...well they are rather tight actually - I lik'em.
This game gives you a bit of everything in bitesized chunks and delivers a quite well presented story on the side. It is vast, but not intimidating. You can actually complete it 100% without doing a lot of unnecessary walking and searching - yet it feels rewarding. IMHO this is a game that you need to play to experience its appeal firsthand. Don't read about it, don't watch a Let's play - play it. It is really well polished, casts some memorable characters and, apart from the overall length of the game, does not leave much to be desired.

So, I finally got round to playing a fairly new release AAA game, and I went with Evolve. I was rather sceptical with purchasing it at full price on launch, however I was able to get a key fairly cheap from another site so decided it was worth a try.
I'll start off with the graphics; this is one of the best looking games I've ever seen. Played on full settings and the environments just look stunning. The lighting looks spectacular as well.
The games main aim revolves around a group of four hunters chasing after a monster. There are four different classes available, assault, trapper, support and medic. Each of these classes are well balanced and gives you all sorts of different weapons and abilities. My personal favourite is the support class.
Audio in Evolve is very important, at times you have to rely on it a lot to try and listen out for the monster when you are trying to find it. Every single sound effect is done to perfection.
There are two different game modes that I have found, regular skirmishes and Evacuations. I have been putting a lot of time in Evacuations which is essentially five different games; each having different objectives, but each game is different depending on how you have done in the rest of the maps. For instance, if the monster manages to destroy a power plant in on map, the next will have toxic gas floating around. Apparently there are around 800,000 different combinations of scenarios available through this mechanic, which can only be a good thing if you ask me.
The difficulty of Evolve can vary. My first match I was playing as the humans, and obviously the monster was a more experience player with a lot of skill as it completely wiped the floor of our team, but sometimes you can get matched up with a lesser skilled monster and it be the complete opposite.  The game entirely depends on how good the monster player is to be honest.
I have been playing for about seven hours now and I don't see myself giving up any time soon, I still feel as if I have barely scratched the surface in terms of content to see and experience. I have been playing with a friend the past few hours which has also added to the fun, I think it would be perfect if you had a full team of people you know on voice chat.
From what I have seen so far, there doesn't seem to be an underlying story, just each game offers you a little story in its own right.
I only encountered one technical issue, and it wasn't exactly game breaking, just more of an annoyance, my mouse cursor was showing on screen as well as the cross-hair of my gun, not a major issue, one that was fixed by quickly restarting the client.
Do I recommend Evolve? Sure - I am having an absolute blast playing it. The only complaints I see in reviews are from people who say it has no replay ability, but they have poured 50+ hours into it already....to me that sounds like you have had plenty of replay ability out of it. Another complaint people seem to have is that there isn't anyone playing... well at the time of writing this, there is ~1200 people playing. That's a pretty large number considering you only need 4 other people to get a game going. Evolve is certainly one of my favourite games of the year so far, and one that I will be continuing to dip into to play with friends, I'd seriously recommend this, maybe wait for the sales to start if you were sceptical like me, but it is worth it.
