Evolve isn't as great as I thought it would be, but for trying to do something new, it's a pretty decent game. Below I'll go through the pros and cons, but ultimately I will upvote Evolve simply because it is something new and isn't all that bad in the final result. Will update review as I find/remember other things to review.
- MAP SELECTION: There are a lot of different maps and many of them have different effects/buffs/debuffs that you can select for it (such as inclement weather, hostile wildlife, poisonous plants and so on; there are many)... If you really toy around with this, you can get a pretty fresh experience out of the same map. Additionally, All of the maps are actually different and aren't copy-paste jobs with minor changes. One of the most annoying things in multi-player games these days is a lack of different maps that cater to certain game modes, Evolve does not lack in this category at all, and will expand even more as additional content is released.
- GAME MODES: For this idea, they implemented a satisfactory amount of game modes such as Hunt, Nest, Evacuation, Rescue, and Defend... Ultimately, the decisive way to win either of these game modes is to either kill the monster, or the monster kill all players. Once this is done, it doesn't matter how well you've been winning a specific game mode.... since you're dead... Other than this obvious likeness between all the game modes, they are all pretty different if you try to play the mode instead of just hunt-and-kill. I will go over the game modes farther down...
- GRAPHICS: The graphics for this game are phenomenal and there are no noticeable glitches to me. The only issue I see is that the V-Sync is next to worthless and pretty much non-existent. I have a $2500 system (almost two years old value when purchased) that I take extremely good care of and keep optimized (IT professional here). My graphics card is an EVGA SC 980 and my processor is an Intel i7-4775k 3.5GHz w/ smart cache... See my profile if you want more specifics. Even with V-Sync turned on, while having a more than fantastic CPU and GPU, tears in the screen are frequent and very obvious. I can tell no difference with V-Sync turned off or on.... This needs to be fixed because I know it's not on my end. There are other games I play that are more graphically demanding (even having higher hardware recommendations) where the V-Sync works and I have no tears. So it's for sure the game.
- WEAPONS: The weapons are freaking awesome IMO, and each hunter has his/her own unique weapons and abilities which helps keep it fresh just as long as you switch it up frequently.
- HUNTERS: You have 16 different hunters, again I'll say all of them come with their own unique weapons, abilities and personalities. There is definitely no lack of variation here. Only issue is that it may take forever to unlock certain hunters and monsters, which can create grinding. And lets be honest, nobody honestly like grinding...
- MONSTERS: The same goes for the monsters, only I can't help but wonder why we only have 4 different monsters, while all minions are always Goliath babies, when there are 16 different hunters... We can definitely tell that the priorities were 75/25 here... They need to put more monsters in here and make the minions/babies the same kind of monsters as the main monster in the specific game being played at the time is. Other than this, no complaints.
GAME MODES:
- In HUNT, you've got the basic one-and-only objective: The monster must kill all Hunters, and/or evolve to stage 3 and destroy the generator before being killed. If you're the hunters, then you just do the opposite: stay alive and kill the monster before it evolves to stage 3 and destroys the generator. This game mode is great as is, though the generator part is a little random in my opinion.
- In RESCUE, there are a certain number of survivors throughout the map that you must find, and protect/escort to an evacuation point. You have to rescue a certain amount of survivors to win, and if you're the monster then you have to kill a certain amount to win... This amount is 5.... There are also multiple groups of survivors each round. This makes it to where it's really a game of chance, which is annoying. The other annoying part is that even though there are aboutr 20 survivors throughout the whole game, you only have to rescue or kill 5 in order to win.... This game mode idea is a great idea, but it really needs to be revamped to make it worthwhile. If they set it to where there is only one group of survivors per round, and make it to where you have to rescue a majority of the total of 20 in order to win (unless you kill the monster, or vise versa), then this game mode will be a lot better, it will make a lot more sense, and it'll be much more skill/tactics oriented. I've won this game mode by aimlessly wondering around and sometimes never even encountering the monster... In practicality, it will be a lame game mode until the revamp it AT LEAST in the ways I mentioned.
In NEST, the monster has infested the specific map and there are 8 eggs throughout that are ready for hatching. The monster must protect and/or hatch all eggs while keeping the babies alive in order to win. Or must obviously kill all the hunters. It's pretty obvious what the hunters have to do. This game mode is cool and may be my favorite to play as Hunters in. The downside is that the monster can only hatch one egg at a time and the baby will roam around aimlessly which can make it easy bantha fodder; while the hunters have no limitations in regards to the eggs. The other downside is that all minions/monster babies are Goliaths..... even though you may be playing this game mode with the Kraken or another monster.... I didn't think the Kraken produced Goliath offspring... This is the same case no matter what monster... the minions are ALWAYS Goliaths, which to me is annoying and lazy on the development part..... If the egg limitations are removed for the monster, and if the minions actually reflect that of their parent species, then this game mode will be better and will also make more sense.
In DEFEND, The hunters are defending a ship that's refueling to leave with refugees from a monster invasion. The monster is attacking with multiple minions per wave and the Hunters have to hold them off long enough for the ship to finish refueling and leave; or they obviously have to kill the big daddy monster. It's obvious what the monsters have to do. I don't really see much wrong with this game mode other than the previously mentioned minion annoyance, and you should have more customizable defense options...
In EVACUATION, it is a prolongued mini-campaign mode that consists of all game modes played back to back. The winner is the best 3 out of 5.
- DLC: The whole DLC thing for this game is utterly awful, terrible, and straight up pointless!!! The whole DLC shop, other than the season pass, is nothing but SKINS.... Yes, so you can the color of your monster or guns, and each pack is about 5 whopping dollars.... Really??? You think I want to spend another $5 dollars to just to change colors of♥♥♥♥♥♥? Uuummmm no.... that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I will spend $5 on real content that actually effects the game, not these lame♥♥♥♥♥skin packs that the developers are spending way too much time on and milking customers with, when they could be making real money and time worthy content.

Investigative reporters/journalists don't always have it even moderately easy. They are the soldiers for truth on the battlefront of deceit and cover-ups, and are occasionally sent on excursions nothing can quite prepare one for.
Players step up to the role as Miles Upshur, a very ambitious self-employed investigative journalist who follows a lead from an anonymous source to the  Mount Massive Asylum, where an apparently dubious operation is being conducted by the unscrupulous Murkoff Corporation.
With the front entrance locked down and no security personnel to be found anywhere despite the presence of an unusual number of different law enforcement vehicles stationed in the front courtyard, it becomes quickly apparent that something is very askew. Still determined, Miles eventually makes his way into the building, only to stumble upon a horrific scene of mutilated and slaughtered members of one of Murkoff's own elite security teams.
And so the freefall into a hellish gore fest with a nightmarish origin commences...
An illegal experiment headed by the Murkoff Corporation, dubbed 'Project Walrider', has been carried out on almost all patients at the Asylum, further damaging their mental state and making them physically stronger. As a result, many have degenerated even further into sickeningly sadistic and monstrously cruel Variants, byproducts of a malevolent entity at the heart of the project that would break even the darkest recesses of the primal mind. Some of them also have a great love for full nudity and the dark desires that accompany it.
Outlast is first-person survival horror game which makes use of the
series'  mechanic of providing the player with only a limited set of equipment and pickups to survive with, foregoing any form of fighting and instead focusing on a feeling of helplessness. Undoubtedly, despite many games in this day and age making use of similar mechanics with clear inspirations from some titles, some people would still draw a single line of comparison.
progresses with a very different premise, setting, and the utilization of some present day equipment. There is no health bar or health consumables, either. Miles can only take a set amount of hits which depends on the difficulty setting and the frequency of the attacks dealt to him. If one gets hit and evades the enemy for a brief time, the hit will be recovered from and the amount is reset. It also noticeably lacks a mental state mechanic no matter how long one spends in dark or light environments.
Along the way, details about patients and events come to light through collectible documents in set locations, as well as recordings from Miles' main equipment that one will use almost exclusively, a video camera with a night vision mode. Every time the video camera is used, it consumes battery power, and night vision even more so. Additional batteries can be found in many locations, though less spawn on the higher difficulty levels, and less can be kept on hand at a time.
A strong emphasis is placed on a foreboding and eerie atmosphere which is often underlined with heavy breathing and fearful swallowing from the player's character. Occasionally, it's cranked up in intensity by means of jump scares and/or nerve-racking chase scenes with one of the many deranged patients of the Asylum or one of the particularly pronounced inmates such as the hulking Billy Walker, a recurring boss enemy that stalks the player up until the end of the game.
The visuals are pretty plain and simple, with an overall settings range from irregular lighting and flat textures to finer details on security badges and bodily scars on patients and the player character.
Along with the atmosphere and plot progression, the game's strength lies in its audio, with suitable sound effects like rain and thunder, and superb voice acting through boss characters like Dr Richard Trager.
Besides the main campaign, the
DLC includes a side story featuring a different player character - who so happens to be the employee that sent the email tip off to Miles - and takes place in different parts of the colossal Mount Massive Asylum in the same time frame as the main campaign. The DLC story might be shorter than the main one, but it is no less impactful and contains some disturbing scenes that dwarves even some that are present in the main game.
Lastly, to add a bit of a challenge to the survival horror element, the game features an Insane mode for both the main campaign and DLC. Players can only take two hits from patients and one from any boss before they die, forcing them to restart the entire run from the very beginning.
is a grotesquely beautiful horror title with very few, if any, cons to it. It's a fresh entry in sometimes oversaturated category that provides a unique sense of dread and disturbances in a deviously well-construed way.

Instead of creating spaceships, you create train and/or breed different miliary units, train distinctive heroes, etc.  The basic premise of exploration + research + conquest remains the same, however.
The game has some baggage that comes with it from an earlier buugy release.  I missed out on all of that, picking it up after the bugs had been resolved.  My experience was solid and bug-free... though the winning solution did seem more apparent than with either of the GalCiv games.

Early game is great, tons of quests, neutral mob, decent hero leveling.... But then it starts to fall short. The mid to late game kinda feels like they dropped the ball. The kingdom vs kingdom warfare is basically a match up of the two leveled up armies which 9/10 decides who wins the war. The in game art style and sound asset are also very weak. With only a handful of maps and a poor end game FE is an OK game. I would say only buy it if your desperate or it's on sale.

If you had me describe my "dream game" it would likely involve grand empire management Civ style and battles would be turn based "tactics" style. While no game has really encompassed the rest of the details of this dream, this game does get a lot of it right. I've enjoyed playing this game and seeing it evolve even since Elemental. I do not think it's a perfect game by any means, but it's a lot better than what it started from. The problems that it suffers from aren't anything major. It's just a lot of little stuff here and there that tends to add up to an experience that feels slightly flawed but not in the context of a flawed gem. It's rather difficult at times, and given my experience with the game I can't always say it's been my fault either. There is a strong "rogue-like" vibe with some of the monsters that roam the map and I'm certainly not complaining about this. You have to pick and choose your fights, but often this is a bit deceptive in that I'm sure I THINK I could beat this whole nest of spiders because they are close to my army's power. It doesn't mean however said spiders won't shoot webs all over the tactical map so my melee units can't even move, then pick everything off with poison. Then other times you just romp over them like sewer rats. I'm not 100% sure I love random in my strategy games, but I do love it in my RPG games. That's kinda where this game stands too. It's half strategy and half RPG. I don't feel like it does either amazingly well, but there's just not many games that put these things together and have it cohesive. There's times where I'm not even sure if I'm playing the game right and I still have no idea what I should be doing. The point is though: It's fun to try.
Any fan of Civilization that doesn't mind trying to defend their nation from literally being eaten by dragons should check it out. If you want a relaxed city-building experience, then look elsewhere as the game isn't catered towards pacifists and fighting is largely the entire point of the game with the empire building not quite in the background, but most certainly second stage.
Another note: the developer has added a ton of content and balancing to the game on a regular timeframe. A larger "2.0" update is incoming as I write this as well as another expansion of sorts. I'd much rather see a company funded that has the idea that they will refine their game until they can justify paid content, over one that just sidecars new DLC every 3 months because they can. The DLC for this game is 100% not needed for a great experience and there's some rather large MODS that completly change the game's dimensions if you are into that kinda thing. This is a true PC gaming , strategy experience in my eyes with depth, customization, external support and so forth.

This game is pretty straight forward as a FPS in its controls and intuitive interface.  Not much overly revolutionary from that aspect...  But the play is Very fun.  I have found myself absorbed it its Quirky little world.  I always know its a good game when I find myself talking to the game as I play it (as opposed to cursing it).  Despite the lack of Blood and big guns, I have enjoyed this game more than anything since the orginal Borderlands. If I have any suggestions/complaints, there are two.  ONE: Stratagy hints flash up between load screens (typical), but they flash so quickly, and often contain a lot of info, its difficult to take in the suggestions.  Id rather have the guide avalible as a "help" option.  TWO: Finding the 15 Pieces of the mysterious artifact you need to assemble inorder to complete the game, can be frustrating. You more or less need to stumble upon each part, rather than Hunt the parts down. The one tell as to the location is extremely subtle and difficult to spot unless you are right on top of the part.  The majority of my frustration with the game is spending far too long randomly looking for the 15 parts.

Erfwerms Honest Review
Graphics 10/10
- Easily one of the best aspects of the game. Its a physics game, so objects, including yourself, react in the world as they would in the normal world. Dirt specs fall, dust settles, light refracts, things like this make the game visually appealing and on top of all of that.. they add a grainy film (edgar allan poe-ish) visual to the whole thing which just makes you feel like your in that enviroment. Really cool concept.
Gameplay 10/10
- The game is a platformer and it plays beautifully. No glitches or bugs that I saw, and everything was nice and smooth. Animations are fluid. The puzzles themselves are generally straight forward, but will still give you a challange. A few of the puzzles definitely made me stop and think (or die a bunch of times), and there was only 1 puzzle where i had to look up the answer (and after i found it, i was mad that I had missed it).
Story ?/10
- There is no story. The game description says something about how you are looking for your sister I believe, and the game starts with you waking up in a field. Throughout the game, you see other "kids" that seemingly are trying to stop you from achieving your goal or advancing, but they dont explain who they are. At the end SPOILER -----> (you find your sister, and they still dont explain where you guys are, or what happened, or even if thats your sister). A game like this leaves it open to your imagination, and because of that, i could see how someone would love the lack of story. I know I'll be thinking of the "kids" and the ending for a few days, trying to figure out my own conclusion of what really happened, and thats exciting for me.
Overall 10/10
- I picked up this game on steam for less than 3 bucks. It downloaded and installed in about 3 minutes. This was my first real platformer on pc since my old console days (Earthworm Jim anyone), and because I enjoyed it so much I'm now looking at some other titles on steam that cost a bit more but look awesome. I really enjoyed the dark concept of this game. If your on the fence about it, pick it up. I used a game controller to play and I would highly recommend the same if you have one. Buy this, grab a comfy chair, turn the volume up (because the ambient noises are awesome), and get lost in the game for a bit.
Thanks for reading, hope this helps someone.
Edit - As a side note, my gameplay says about 17 hours. I tend to leave my PC on when i walk away or go to bed, so its not a full 17 hours to complete. I'd say it took me about 3 or 4 hours in total to play. I took my time and didnt rush through it.

Well, what are you waiting for? Here it is, Cuphead, one of the major breakthroughs in indie gaming in recent memory, having garnered an austere fanbase in less than a month of its release and having attained an astounding feat of reaching over millions in sales in just the span of a week or so. This game, having completed it, is definitely a good deal--especially when you consider it's relatively affordable.
Things to consider, though:
The difficulty is, indeed, a bane to casuals. If you intend to breeze through this game without even a modicum of challenge, then I can assure you that this is not your cup of tea (pun not intended); in fact, this game will take that cup of tea and scald your face with it. However, there's no need to be harrowed by all the talk of this game being only for "elitists". Anyone can beat this game. It's just that you need to actually put in effort into it, unlike the vast swarm of hand-holding titles we've got these days.
The art style and music are, as already many have acclaimed it to be, beyond exceptional. This game is a testament to humanity's passion and drive, with each--AND EACH--of the landscapes and characters you see here in this game, from their idle animations to their attacks, are ALL handpainted. Brush by brush, stroke by stroke; this game was painstakingly made frame by frame on paper and then scanned into a digital medium. Something that many of today's corporate-minded game developers would never even consider.
Mind you, this game began development that spanned almost a decade, with 2013 being the earliest date of a prototype build. Even then, during the 2013 build, much of the art assets and music compositions were already done. It took them years of refinement to release the game as it is. Looking at the game now, how there is little-to-none in terms of bugs and glitches and how everything flows together so seamlessly as if it was an actual moving picture show from the 1930's, it shows how much dedication was pumped into this project of theirs. This makes an embarassment out of all those shoddy, poorly-cobbled-together "Triple-A" titles of recent memory.
Now, as for how the game plays out, it's quite smoothe, actually. The controls are responsive, and the actual levels and boss fights are well-structured. It clearly is very optimized, with it being not so intensive on PC specs. As for the storytelling... well, it's almost nonexistent, but that's not the game's main selling point, anyways.
Also. Yeah. This is totally Dark Souls. /sarcasm

TL;DR; If you want a game to keep you occupied for an hour or 2 or wish to see crowd simulation at work, then at the discount price it is worth a bash. Otherwise, I wouldn't recommend paying the full price. But please, read the rest before you judge.
This is a relatively simple (and as the developer pointed out - unique) game.  I suspect this game is more an exercise in optimisation (whether it be code, compiler or underlying maths/algorithms) and crowd simulation technology rather than an attempt to make a successful money-earning game.  However, the graphics are simple and well done and the game feels and looks finished though it is limited in scope.
The aim of the game is to build a pyramid and to do that you need to build fields, bakeries and huts (and extra tax houses if you want to spread out a bit - but the starting one serves) and then employ workers to transport water -> field, field -> bakery, bakery -> hut/tax and bricks -> pyramid.
There is probably some ratio of fields -> bakeries -> houses -> total workers/distance but I found that I didn't need to work out what that was in order to optimise as it was simple enough just to mass produce food and thus mass produce silver to employ as many workers as I needed/could.
Although this game is quirky I don't think there is much replay-ability in it - good for spending an hour or 2 and maybe for trying to speed run it but that is about it as there are no random events etc.
Something that could be improved upon is that when you select a building to build, the map could highlight all of the possible places to place chosen building, instead of you having to scroll around trying to find a spot, (which is not always easy because the workers get in the way and the placement "bounces" around them).
If the dev were to extend the options in game, (eg. add a quarry and require you to balance builders/stonemasons/miners) or add some random events (eg. plague, draught) then I would consider changing this review from a negative one to a positive.

'Dungeon of the Endles' is really something special and it's hard to describe, what it really is. Throw the following genres: tower defense, strategy, RPG, economy management, dungeon crawler and a tiny breeze of gambling into a mixer and have a delicious juice. I'm not sure how to describe the result, so just let us stick to the name 'Dungeon of the Endless.' The game acts in the 'Endless Universe' like 'Endless Space' and 'Endless Legend'. Unlike the other 2 games is 'Dungeon of the Endless'no 4X game, but if you have already played an Endless title, then you will notice, that the game shares the same background story (most notably races) and the typical ressources like Dust, Food, Industry and Science, which is pretty great. The Endless universe is awesome and it's really adorable to see, how AMPLITUDE Studios is handling it and how different AND successful games of the same universe can be.
Before you can start your journey you have to choose a capsule and your starting hero(es). Why a capsule? Because your spaceship will blow up and you're forced to make an emergency landing (story at store page)! There are several unlockable capsules to choose from and each provides a different challenge. Your objective is to defend your energy crystal, to find an exit in form of an elevator and to finally carry your crystal to the exit (which will summon endless hordes of monsters), stage after stage (most capsules have 12 random generated stages) until you have reached the surface...alive. You don't navigate your characters directly, instead you can send them from room to room and they automatically engage in combat, once they've reached the target area. Skills, levelups, healing, research, building and vendor actions are completely under your control.
To find the exit you'll have to open A LOT of doors. One newly opened door = one turn. You will gain ressources (Industry - needed for modules, Science - needed for research, Food - needed for healing + lvlup, Dust - needed to light up dark rooms) according to your production rate. You never know, what's hiding behind a closed door. It can be a group of monsters, recruitable people, monsters, a vendor, monsters, resources, monsters, research stations, monsters, the exit or nothing. More monsters can only spawn in dark rooms after every turn. They don't have to, but they can. You can switch the light on for 10 dust per room, but you're only able to light up a room, which is next to an already powered room and the power supply always has to be connected all the way to your crystal. Usually you're not able to light up the whole stage and this is the point, where the real fun begins. You have to spread your power and make decisions, where and how you want to put up your defenses and how to move on with your exploration. There are very different types of enemies. Some will hunt your people, others are magically attracted by your crystal, some prefer to simply destroy all your modules and others...oh god how I hate them...want to open even more doors, which can lead to a total apocalypse. Luckily you can research and upgrade loads of different modules to increase your production and defense, but usually you will have a hard time, which will force you to grind and open more doors. It will become an addiction, even if you don't really need more at the moment, but more is always better, right? Right. And then the moment will come: stage 10, 11 or 12, everything is fine, just one more door and boooom, hell on Auriga, 2 hours wasted, AGAIN. So keep in mind: one single door can lead to a massive escalation. Don't become to greedy, especially if you've already found the exit!
The game has triggered a door addiction for me. I could wander all day long through my home and open doors, close them and open them again...so satisfying, aw yeah. On a more serious note: the game is pretty great, addicting and the blend of different game genres works surprisingly well, which turns the game into something purely unique. My experience in single- and multiplayer was very good. However, the multiplayer has still some flaws like connection problems and no save/load function, which can ruin the fun sometimes, but the devs are aware of it and are working on it. If you're merely looking for a great multiplayer experience, then you should definitely wait for the update and keep your money in your pocket, BUT don't forget about this gem of game. If you prefer to play alone or don't have any friends (please insert 'forever alone meme'), then I can really recommend it to you. There are some things, which could be improved in my opinion and along with the multiplayer flaws I have to give 'Dungeon of the Endless' a 7/10 for now. The game deserves a 8/10, once the multiplayer is really finished. It's still a great game!

I'm not a fan of horror games, purley because I personally am a major wimp who will alt+f4 out of a game if a frog croaks behind me. So basically take what I say about this game as the opinion of  someone easily scared, if you're a veteran horror gamer, you might view things differently.
Five Nights at Freddy's strengths come from the atmosphere it is able to build. The game's ability to work as a horror game relies heavily on being able to build tension through it's sound design, game mechanics, and the design of the locations within the game. For me, it works. The mechanics are simple, but cause the player to focus on multiple things at once, it can become overwhelming for a new player, and coupled with the creepy atmosphere and sound design, causes a great horror tension throughout.
However, once you've gotten the hang of the game, it does lose a bit of its edge. Once you have a good understanding of the mechanics, the level of panic decreases, which makes the game, by its very nature, less scary. The atmosphere is great because it builds to the jumpscares, which makes it better than a game that relies only on jumpscares, but like any game with jumpscares, they can also get a bit old, which also makes the game less scary.
This doesn't really matter if you're looking to get more replayability out of the game, as the custom night allows you to get a lot of mileage out of the game just from challenging your skills, which can still be fun even if the game has become less scary to you.
Personally, I recommend playing it for the atmosphere alone, it's a wonderful little game that's good for a few days of fun, well worth the price, and (as you're probably aware) has spawned an insane amount of fanfare and a huge community.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

When this game first came out, everyone was telling me how "scary" it was. I didn't pick it up immediately though because I was worried it was just another jump scare simulator like FnaF. After five years of putting it off I finally picked it up, and I gotta say, I was pleasantly surprised. I'll just keep this review simple since I'm not a very good reviewer :p.
The atmosphere in this game is perfect. It's dark and gruesome, but it doesn't feel like they overdo the gore at all. Tension is built up around the fact that you initially can't tell which inmates are dangerous. There will be times were they seem harmless, but when you turn your back on them they'll attacking you.

The story is mainly told through two different types of collectibles, recordings or documents. It's still possible to piece together the main idea with collecting anything, but don't expect to fully understand story without them.
The gameplay is very simple, which mainly consists of running or hiding from enemies (either option works at almost anytime). The only resource that you'll have to manage is batteries, which power the nightvision for your camera. Unless your playing on one of the higher difficulties though, managing your batteries won't be that big of an issue. This is honestly my only issue with the game, it gets kind of repetative after awhile due to the lack of gameplay variety. The game however is only around 6-8 hours for your first playthrough, so by the time you get tired of it, you'll likely already be at the end. If your someone who doesn't like managing several different resources, and complex crafting systems then this is the perfect horror game for you.
The graphics and voice acting are also incredible, ecspecially for an indie game (I honestly thought this was a AAA title at first). Outlast is a horror game that's defiantly worth it's full price, and the whistle blower DLC is also a great addition as well. So what are you waiting for? just buy it already instead of reading this trash review >_>.

I will forever love the little bits of comedy that came around during cinematics/gameplay.
It's those little chuckles that get you through it all.
However...
- First off, this feels nothing like a Red Faction game. You fought the Ultor Corporation in the first one, Sopot's military in the second, and finally the EDF (military/corporation) in the third. This one just suddenly jumps to aliens. What the hell?
There were no hints that I recall in the previous 3 games that even remotely stated aliens were here. They just suddenly exist. I suppose you could say those
you fought in RF 1 were a hint, but even then...They were mutants. Animals/humans Kapek experimented on with his nano-tech.
Not even (some of) the  journals which tell of events prior/during/post RF 1 still felt right. They seemed out of place, what with their recordings being about aliens and Kapek, rather than something more believable (like Kapek and experimentation on humans/animals they brought (see/play RF 1 for animal/animutant encouters)).
__
What more can be said? This engine knows how to supply the demand for endless carnage.
Whether you use a Magnet, a Hammer or a Rocket, just about everything can and will be blown to bits.

My only gripe is..
Long story short, you will be constantly repairing the entire level you just destroyed. If you don't, you're likely to blow up the bridge you needed to cross to get through the campaign. There's as much repairing as there is destruction, which can get annoying.

That aside, it is a decent playthrough, though not as good as it could have been.

At first I was only interested for the story mode to come, but then friends kept bugging me about how amazing the sandbox was, I wasn't biting it, it's just a survival mode in which you know you WILL die, looks like a fancy score based game to me, compare inches of ♥♥♥♥ by how long you can survive, but then articles kept coming, people still kept bugging me about how great the game was. Well, I decided to give it a chance before the final release to know what the fuss was all about. Man, it blew my mind.
First of all, it's not a simple game of survival, watch meters and number dwindle down as you starve, get tired or dehydrated, although, there is plenty of that too. What's incredible is how contemplative it is, you're always on the look for something yes, you need to keep moving, keep exploring, the world isn't safe, it's dying and it wants you to join it, it feels sometimes the only true warmth you'll ever find is the embrace of death. Outside time leaps, everything you do takes precious time and sunlight, harvesting wood, exploring, getting from point A to B, you're always freezing or going hungry, but then you find shelter, and you like the character can rest.
You still have to do something to be alive in a shelter, light a fire, cook food, boil water, but at least you can think, you can prepare your spirit for the terror outside. You have to survive, not because you want to prove something to anyone else, but out of spite, in a land that wants you dead, you want to rebel, you refuse to give up. But it's still respite, at a shelter you can think, plan your next day.
In a way it reminds me of Hemingway's old man and the sea, it's about an internal struggle, even if nature gets the final say, you'll wont rest easy, you'll kick and scream and in that defiance you can have your final laugh.
There is so much that can be said about this, even the play though that cemented my appreciation of this game could be a tale in itself, but for now it's enough, I wrote too much already.

This is a great game for me.
This is really 2 games in one, one game is being a hunter and the other is being the monster.
As hunter, teamwork is very important.  You are nearly useless alone.  There are 4 hunter roles (support, assault, trapper, medic, and all of those roles are rather self-explanatory)  and you need all of them in order to beat the monster.  Hunting down the monster makes you feel like an actual hunter, such as watching the landscape from a mountain top in search of a shaking tree or running animal, indicating a monster nearby, or following the footprints left by the monster and always keeping him on the run.
Being a hunter is really all about the hunt, and I haven't played a game that makes you feel like an actual hunter until Evolve.
The other side to the game is being a monster.  As a monster, you start off as level 1 (relatively weak, can easily be killed by 4 hunters) and you have to run away and kill wild animals and eat them to evolve.  Being a monster is all about stealth, trickery, and tactics.  You have to run away and get a good enough head start to kill animals in safety, knowing that every time you hit a tree or scare birds or leave footprints you will give your location.  You can sneak around to not leave footprints, or lead footprints to a bunch of wild animals to distract the hunters, or you can run in crazy circles making your footprints impossible to follow. "Dungeon Of The Endless" has a nostalgic art style that does, indeed, carry a certain appeal.
Unfortunately, the actual game fails to be really fun.

This wouldn't be so bad if the game was a blast to play, but it isn't. It's mostly an exercise in trying to make essentially the same, cautious, resource-management choices again and again. Yes, the game is randomized, but that doesn't make the gameplay strikingly varied or engaging. It mostly just means that you can't get the equipment you want, and the rooms look a little different while being connected in a different way.
This title seems to appeal to a good number of folks, but for me it was a strange combination of unenjoyable tension, repetition, and exasperation. After finding a bit of a groove, and then losing everything because of a mistake, I just didn't care enough to try again. I thought about having to do everything over again, and realized that the doing over of everything didn't appeal to me at all.
I wasn't having fun, and that's what games are for.

Five Nights at Freddy's is the hit new Indie jumpscare simulator game developed by Wisdom Tree for the Sega CD using click and play. In this game, you take control of some loser whose only job he can even get is being security guard at a children's baby play place. Now because this is a spooky Halloween scary game, it's got all the things you expect to make you wet your diaper if you're a big little baby idiot.
It's got all the creepy music, and sometimes you see someone looking at you over there, and... Oh look out suddenly he jumped out in front of your face you weren't even gonna think you would've saw that right then! But you did, and now you're probably scared.
What really ties together Freaky Friday is its innovative revolutionary gameplay system. It really maximizes the horror that  those blender Chuck-E-Cheese mascots have to offer.
To play Five Freddy's, you click cameras and sometimes maybe close a door. You do this for convenient 10 minute bursts, designed with the big name Let's-Players in mind. Now some of you might be asking "But ROCKCOCK64, is that all there is to Five Nights at Freddy's?" And to you I would say... Yes. Yeah, that's it.
Now it may sound really easy, but there's actually a lot of depth and strategy behind the gameplay. Sometimes you have to close both of the doors!
Graphically, this game is perfect. Now, while in most other games, this look, this ♥♥♥♥♥♥, ugly, pre-rendered garbage wouldn't really work. This game however is a horror game, so you get to be totally creeped out by the one pre-rendered room you're stuck in that has this weird pixelated cylinder filter applied to it. You get to be totally creeped out by that and then pay like, a dollar or two on the app store to put a little plushie on your desk.
The scares are also REALLY effective. Especially when you run out of power or one of your doors is broken, so you already know the loud scream scary spook is coming. Jumpscares work best when I know about them ahead of time. Then I get to plan out my funny facecam reaction. Some people say that jumpscares are a cheap and effortless tactic to try and instill horror. And that's just insulting and dismissive of how brilliant of a game Five Night Freddy is. Cheap and effortless are the LAST two words I'd use to describe this game.
Would a cheap and effortless game have a sequel almost entirely finished two months after the original release? No!
Would a cheap and effortless game take advantage of free ad space on gross websites to extend its audience? No!
Would a cheap and effortless game try to milk microtransactions off of cheats and cosmetics through a mobile version that was hastily slapped together? No.
Overall gamers, Weekend at Bernie's has earned its spot as one of the most legendary horror games ever. A game about being scared as the guy dressed as Chuck-E-Cheese giving you a pizza belongs in the same league as a game about the scariest thing the Internet could think of: A very tall, well-dressed, white man.
Any dumb idiot can play it, and it makes a loud scary noise here and there, what more could you even ask for?
FINAL SCORE:
3/10 GAMEPLAYS
2/10 GRAPHICS
2/10 SOUNDS
10/10 HARDCORES
4.25/10 OVERALLS (BEST SCARY GAME OF ALL TIME!!)

This is not a great game.  Sure, the art direction is unbelievibly great and yes, it has some homages to classic games.  But the gameplay is not fair.  I've beaten my share of difficult games and I can struggle through most of this one.
The controls aren't quite accurate enough for a game this punishingly hard.  The hitboxes are not consistent for either the bosses or their attacks.  Some levels obscure the screen during bullet hell sequences.  The game often ignores a parry, jump, or dodge and instead takes my life.  I get some huge framerate drops and stuttering play at odd times.  If the game was a bit more forgiving I wouldn't need perfect controls.
The parry system is poorly implemented here.  I'm used to parrying in Street Fighter III or Just Defending in several other fighting games.  First of all, hardly anything in the game can be parried.  The parry range is super small and the punishment for being off by a pixel is one third of your life.  The reward? A tiny bit of super meter that's barely helpful.  The ghost train level parry mechanic to move your cart is beyond infuriating.  The thing you have to parry is so close to the ground that it's very difficult to hit, plus after it moves it's untargetable for about 2 seconds.  It's easier and far safer to play the game pretending that the parry doesn't exist, as you only need it in a couple of boss fights to open a vulnerable spot.
I love the animation, the art, the style, and the soundtrack.  The world 3 stage theme song in particular is fantastic.  Some of the bosses are very creative.  I was looking forward to this game for several years after a couple of seconds in the MS E3 presentation got me hooked.  Ori was tough but fair.  Oniken was tough but fair.  NES era Mega Man was tough but fair.  This game is exceedingly difficult with randomized elements to prevent you from commiting boss fights to pure muscle memory.
The simple game mode prevents you from seeing the last part of every boss fight, which is a shame because those are usually the best parts of the game.  It also prevents you from even viewing the Casino endgame.  Having an easier difficulty setting in no way diminishes the enjoyment of those who want to play on higher settings, and it allows more people to enjoy the wonderful creativity and art of this game.
I'm forcing myself to continue to play through and finish this as I'm not going to let this thing beat me.  Doing so hasn't brought me elation at beating each boss and moving forward.  Rather, it's just a soul crushing slog that I dread playing.  I only find relief that I never have to waste my life on each stupidly hard boss ever again.  It's work.  I'd rather go to my day job or do chores than play this game.  I'm close to the end, so I'm going to push on through.  It's just disappointing since Cuphead has just about everything I look for in a game.

It pains me to say this, but I don't like it... There is a number of core fundamental things wrong with it that I just cant get past.
First off, the game is EASY. I am good at shooters, I'll say that right off the bat. So to compensate that I started it on hard difficulty. And not once have I ever felt like I was in danger, or in trouble, or that I wasn't able to handle what the game is throwing at me even when I am not really putting effort into it at all. And the game relys a lot on atmosphere to make the game, but I feel like I am invinvible. I have only died twice so far. The first was a what "What am I supposed to DO?!?" situation. And the other was where I went balls to the wall charge headfirst into something because I thought it would be more fun. And it wasn't really.
Then there is the atmosphere. The game is dead space 2. Just going to say it, the game is 100% comprised of the pard in DS2 where you were in the mines. I can't stress this enough! Like seriously, that is exactly what the game feels like, looks like, plays like, sounds like, and what the enemies look like. Which I will say is not nessasarily a bad thing. But they did it all wrong. The atmosphere is (supposed) to be creepy, theres scary ambiant noises, coupled with moments of dead silence that is supposed to build the "What the ♥♥♥♥ is going to happen to me next" mindset. But as a player playing through the game, you gave me weapons that make me feel invincible. So I don't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ about those scary noises! Which makes me feel more like "Bring it on! I can take all you mutherfukers!" and less like "I really really... /really/ don't want to open this door". Which every other part of the setting and atmosphere is begging you to feel like.
Weapons, they are all ineffective and almost useless when compared to the standard assult rifle. BAD WEAPON DESIGN! Also the only weapon that can be used to hit targets at long range is the nanorifle. Which is cool, but its primary purpose is to surgically destroy buildings. Not kill stuff. Also the sledgehammer sucks.... :/
Then there is the destruction, which is both the only good thing and a big setback. As far as destroying buildings goes, its cool! I liked destroying buildings with the enemies inside of them! That was fun! ... I just wish that when the building collapsed it killed them... The problems with it though are that they aren't that many buildings.. and you can destroy only some of them, and not others. And thats ok! Level design and all that stuff. But there are more times than not where I want to destroy something, but it won't let me. If it was a diffrent material or something, that wouyld be cool. But it looks exactly the same as the one next to it which I can blow up... so? Huh? Ther are also some parts of the game where you have to fight inside a destructable building. But all of your weapons (aside from the assult rifle) Destroy objects. So every time you shoot you destroy apart of the floor, which makes you stop and repair it so you can continue. and do it again, and again, and again. Not fun. Though you do have the nano forge which lets you literally magically rebuild objects that you blew up. which is cool. But you use it more for fixing things that you didn't mean to break than for anything else.
I wanted to love it so badly! Red Faction: Guerrilla was the first game I ever played on my gaming rig, so it holds a special place in my heart. But this whole game was about as big of a letdown as the ending of Mass Effect 3. At least everything else in Mass Effect 3 leading up to the end was fun...

Okay so here goes.  I am a State Level Emergency Manager, and I saw this game when I was recovering after a hospital stay.  What they say they deliver not only is it a great game one of the only truly open ended games I have ever seen.   It also follows pretty much what would happen theoretically during a wide scale Emergency Event.
The Vanilla game is good, drop some Mods onto it and the entire game gets a depth that I have not seen in other franchises.  I have well over 2000 hours played on this game, but it needs to be said if you like a thought provoking game, where you will pay dearly for complaceny then this is the game for you.  If you want a mindless game set in the zombie world then this is not the game for you.
I have to say this game will be one I play for years and with the mods and multi aspect of it it can be immersive as you want it.  I played it with my kids (there is an option to lift the zombies out) and tought them some fundamental survival skills though a game normal survival concepts work and pay off.
I have also found the team at Indie Stone to be highly responsive to their gaming community and their pride in product shows.  I recently showed this product to several state level emergency managers and they were impressed at the implications and concepts that could be taught, ala the Oregon Traill game in the early 90s.
I have not lived that long with any of my characters:   top one year - however I understood how I died and in this game you learn from your mistakes, dont make them again and you live longer.
In closing thank you Indie Stone and thank you to all the Mod Developers and people that make this game so good and give it a depth that is almost never reached

is an odd game to me. Personally, I don't like turn-based games because I don't have the patience to wait for my next turn. But, somehow, I still bought this game because I like the RPG-element in it. Against my expectations I really liked the game because the world looks pretty awesome with the magic and monsters (especially the dragons.. I love dragons). I have spent a lot of time creating new factions and sovereigns because you want to try everything out when you see something new.
The point of the game is to build a kingdom/empire, research and defeat or work together with the enemy AI's, kill monsters (there are dragons, giant spiders and some really epic monsters I  haven't encountered yet) and there can be an event going on like the plague, the shroud (can't remember what it was). All in all, you must make a lot of choices; Shall I attack these monsters and leave my base undefended or shall I make a new squad to defend my base while I'm attacking the enemy? Shall I research better armor or do I need to research better economics?
Doing quests around the map gives you items (sometimes unique ones) which your sovereign or hero can equip. Doing quests also increases your fame, fame will get you heroes, heroes will make your army stronger.
I had a bit of problem getting the hang of this game. The tutorial wasn't really helpful which is a shame. By restarting the game a few times you will learn the game step by step. So don't expect to get the hang of it right away.
+ Lots of choices between factions and heroes.
+ Nice graphics (world, kingdoms/empires) when zoomed out.
+ Lots of enemies.
+ Challenging.
+ Customizing your own faction and Sovereign.
- Most of the battles you will be selecting auto-result (skip the fighting stuff and know the result right away)
- Bad graphics (npc's and some monsters) when zoomed in.
- Hard to get the hang of this game (I suggest watching some youtube video's first).
- When heroes fall they will have permanently decreased stats.
- Unpredictable AI. Sometimes out of nowhere they start a war or are angry.
If I had to give this game a score I would give it a 7.5.

LIMBO is an indie game released in 2010 by Playdead. It's a single-player platformer which features a young boy (the player) wandering around in a forest. The game quickly transforms from a peaceful walk in a woods to a dreamy experience through various deadly 2D-enviroments. The whole game is in black and white, but that just builds up the weirdly haunting atmosphere.
LIMBO is not a horror game, even tough the player will die in horrible, horrible ways countless times during the first playthrough. And even though the music and the game itself will sometimes make you...
. LIMBO is more of a puzzle game ranging from logical puzzles to timing puzzles with varying difficulty.
The gaming mechanics are simple and all you need are six buttons: four to move, one for grabbing objects and one for pausing the game. There is not much to say without spoiling the wonderful experience. Turn off the lights, plug in your headphones, relax and dive in to the Limbo. Literally
figuratively speaking.

Dungeon of the Endless is a rogue like of epic proportions. It's endlessly addicting, rewarding, and brutal. It's endlessly endless because you will be spending hours trying to even achieve one victory.
Dungeon of the Endless is an extremely unique mixture of genres. It's very hard to describe, but let me explain it like this: Tower defense meets tactical RPG meets dungeon crawler! TDTRPGDC, if you will.
The summary of the positives (+) and negatives (-) of this game:
+ Creative and innovative. The mixture of genres makes this game a standout gem.
+ Beautiful and striking pixel art aesthetics, with some actual physics simulation and dynamic shadows going on.
+ Unrelenting difficulty, even on "EASY" mode.
+ Rogue-lite elements provide replay value.
+ Huge selection of unique characters, with their strengths and weaknesses.
- Poor performance in large battles and when a lot is happening on screen. Your mileage may vary.
- No permanent item unlockables or passive buffs to enhance your odds of winning in future runs.
- Very likely "too difficult". This is my biggest gripe with the game. It takes a long time to achieve even one victory. Sometimes, it feels like pure luck when you survive. Due to this, the game punishes you for exploration in later levels, forcing strange bits of dominant strategy such as using nothing but "Prisoner Prods" and leveling up one character just to get the "Operate" ability. The fact that "Easy" mode is still too difficult makes it feel like the game is mocking you, and turning it down to "Too Easy" feels embarassing. Changing the difficult level names to "Normal" for "Too Easy" and "Hard" for "Easy" will make it feel less like the game is making fun of you.

It has been a little bit since I last played this game (busy doing other things) so certain details may be a bit unspecific.
Gameplay: 7/10
The gameplay in this game is pretty standard for a third person shooter, however it adds an extra layer with a single feature. Near the beginning of the game, you are given a weapon that fires a magnet to one thing, then you can attach another magnet to something else and bring them together. This "Magnet Gun" is where the game shines the most (and lags the most depending on your computer). In Red Faction: Armageddon, the environments are almost completely destructible. There are some things you can't destroy, but it's amazing fun finding out what you can destory. Attach a magnet to a building and launch it towards a wall, squishing enemies along the way. Launch an enemy towards a wall and watch them go splat! The amount of destruction you can cause is amazing and satisfying. There are several guns you can pick up throughout the game, but I rarely used anything but magnets. Enemy around the corner? Magnet something in their direction and let physics take care of it. Enemy standing comedically close to a fall? Just thinking about those poor saps gives me vertigo. The best part about this destruction though is that so long as the destruction is not story required, you can use a machine to reverse time to build it again! Did I mention that the Magnet Gun has infinite ammo? Because it does! Unfortunately, as the Magnet Gun is possibly the best thing in the game, it's also why I have to dock a few point off of gameplay because of how all the other guns pale in comparison (especially the non-explosive ones). The game can be completed without picking up a single gun outside of the Magnet Gun and anything story-required.
Story- 5/10
I can't say too much about the story. As mentioned above "Gameplay", there are many details I do not remember as it's a been a while since I last played it. However, I feel I am somewhat good at remembering characters so long as I find them interesting. I found nearly nothing interesting about any of the characters. Your main character (whose name I can't even remember!) is very one-dimensional. He's the typical "I screwed up, life sucks for me, I screw up AGAIN and now I can redeem myself". There are nearly no plot twists I did not see coming and none of the moment I assume were meant to be sad really made me the least bit sad. I'm going to give a quick run down of how things set in motion, but if you feel like you want everything to be a surprise, consider this a "Spoiler Warning". Your character is part of the military on Mars I think (not sure) and are going to stop a bad dude who wants to ruin the civilizations that humans have built there. You learn about the game and move in to stop the bad guy. You find a wounded soldier who tells you where the bad guy went, where you then run into your commanding officer or whatever, but surprise! You and officer bro were the only ones in there! The wounded soldier WAS the bad guy and your character is an idiot. Bad guy wins and life goes downhill for people on Mars. Your character is now working in excavation for some reason and there's some chick (who I don't remember being mentioned beforehand) that knows your character and there is obvious lovey dovey stuff. Your character gets a job that pays well and all he has to do is break something! Sounds simple enough, right? Well it was! Destroy some stuff and go explore where this new hole in the floor you made goes, but surprise! The bad guy was sealed under the thing that anyone could've destroyed and now aliens are everywhere and your character is an idiot. I think he's even tried to redeem himself to his assumed girlfriend by saying "it payed well". Did it protagonist? I don't think they paid you a cent and I think your actually paying for this in guilt and ammunition. Unless you use the MAGNET GUN and it's INFINITE AMMO!
Graphics-7/10
I won't spend too much time here as I don't spend much time thinking about graphics (I'm more a Gameplay watcher) but from what I remember, the Graphics aren't too shabby. However, most of the game is dark which is very annoying in segments where you have to kill all the enemies in the area but it's too dark to see them. You have a radar that gives you a general location, but it isn't as helpful as you may think. In this game you fight against aliens, but the aliens, for the most part, are very agile and hard to hit as they jump around. Your radar could say you're right on top of them, but in reality, it is they who are on top of you. The darkness in this game makes for some frustrating moments when you want to find that one enemy you need to kill, but they're in the shadows above you and decide that if they shot you, you'd know where they are, which would give you a chance of winning.
Enemies-5/10
The enemies are very unoriginal and bland. None of enemies even talk save the bad guy from the beginning. You fight so many of the same enemies over and over again you start to figure out how far away the magnets would have to be to one-hit kill them. I played on Easy, but even so, the enemies were all easy to predict. Enemies only really ever got a hit on me when I was lagging from a building I launched at them. You have all the typical enemy types as well. You have the big bruisers that never flinch, the small bug things that are really only there to feel satisfying when you squish them under a rock you threw with you magnets, the fast and annoying ones, the ones that mess up your vision, the ones that spawn enemies and so on. Even the bad guy is very unoriginal and I can't even remember why. I think it had something to do with his people but I wasn't really interested in anything he said. At first, seeing new enemy types is exciting and you get to try out new tactics, but in the end, it loses the "Wow!" factor rather quickly and it seems more like a chore. The AI isn't much better either. As mentioned in Graphics, the AI and darkness make for a terrible combination because it's difficult to see enemies and they refuse to shoot you for reasons unknown. Have they had a change of heart? Are they planning on catching you off guard as you slowly go insane trying to find them? Did they run out of ammunition and are now to scared to come at you because they know they'll die? CAN they run out of ammo? No matter the reason, this usually boils down to using the magnets to launch anything and everything until they realize you've gone insane trying to find them, then go for the kill, only to be squished in your onlsauaght of rocks. The ragdoll physics are pretty hilarious though!
Sense of Progression-6/10
This game doesn't really feel like it gives you much in the way of feeling like you are actually doing something. There aren't very many guns in the game, character reveals don't really feel amazing, the plot twists couldn't even wring a towel and even the upgrade system is lacking! I don't remember how to upgrade, but I never even used it! I think there are items you collect like in Dead Space that you can use, but they are very generic upgrades that aren't even all that necessary! You have some kind of Force Push move that you can upgrade to make stun enemies, but the enemies are so stupid, they don't need to be stunned! They'll just stand still on their own! The game feels like it repeats itself and rarely mixes things up! You have very basic mission types that never actually add a twist and when you finally face something that isn't one of those bugs, you've already lost all sense of worry because of the AI!
Overall-7/10
The way I described the game may seem like it deserves less than a '7', but I still enjoyed the game quite a bit! I'm not one to ever hate a game and I find something appealing about the destructible environments. I can't say this is a game for everybody, but if you like Mass Effect, you may enjoy this game.

I only recommend playing this a bit, to get a feel of the game. But I wouldn't recommend trying to beat it, not without a walkthrough and strategy guide. The difficulty is unforgiving and escalates with each found objective. You, on the other hand, don't get any upgrades and have to fully rely on random loot. I managed to find 8 pieces and then was unable to make further progress. I never found any weapons, and only a few bullets.
Objectives:
There are 15(?) pickups to find across 5 large islands, and the difficulty escalates with each one. They are not shown on the compass or map (you don't even have a map until you find one). At night(?), glowing will-o'-the-wisps can slowly guide you to them. Or just wander around until you see smoke surrounded by enemies - because the objectives are always surrounded by enemies. You are always forced to sneak up close, then dash in, grab the quest item and start fleeing. The objective items vary in size and can take up up to 1/3 of your inventory space, so you have to leave enough room just in case, to avoid getting screwed as you try to grab the item.
Resources:

So here's this game I played several times on the PS2, and it is SO FUN. PC is no exception.
People may have seen the camera on the box art back in the day and said to themselves "Ew! Camera in the gameplay, no way!" Sure the camera is sometimes a necessary part of the game, but combat and stealth are major gameplay elements that shouldn't be overlooked.
The story centres on Jade and Pey'j, in a strange world where half-animal people walk around on two legs and talk. For example Pey'j has a definite boar-like appearance. The world is under siege from the Domz armada, and the Alpha Sections are there to stop them. During an attack Jade discovers she's out of credits and her lighthouse shield power is cut off. In an effort to make some credits she takes on a photography job for the local science centre, and through a turn of events ends up working for a secret underground movement called the Iris Network.
The plot is fairly straightforward - you go on missions looking for evidence, once you find the evidence you take photos of it, and then you get the hell outta there. The missions are few and large, and the best way to approach it is to go sneaky stealth mode on everything. It is possible to attack your enemies too, but you will have a hard time.
Gameplay combat is all 3rd-person, but not all of it is melee. There are battles on the water inside your 'tugboat', and towards the end of the game there is even a spaceship battle, which I thoroughly enjoyed. Enemies hit hard in melee combat though, so it pays to grab all the health upgrades you can find. These can be manually distributed to your companion too if you think they need it. As already mentioned, subterfuge is your friend - you will have more fun with sneak attacks and trickery than trying to face-tank your way though the game.
Other gameplay elements include speed-races to get your stolen credits back, minigames (that game in the Akuda Bar is badass hard), finding all the species to photograph for more credits, finding all the pearls for more vehicle upgrades. There are a couple of foot-chases too, to add whipped cream to an already delicious cake of a game.
So how delicious is it? Well the music is a blast for starters. It has a wonderful style to it, melodious and alien. Well-suited to the game. The graphics are a little bland but good - with a main character like Jade it makes sense there's a bit of a green theme to it. Voice-actors have been cast well, there is a lot of great voice-acting in the game and it helps to suspend disbelief, helping immersion and reinforcing our empathy towards the characters.
Highly recommended to anyone that loves stealth, a great story, or just wants to try something new. The hours I've played it on PC are not representative of my total hours (PC and PS2). Worth it just for the soundtrack!

The story ties back into the previous games and playing them first would be benifical.
Weapons are inventive and forceful and are fun to use, especially the mechs and tanks and their respective missions.
Visuals have gotten better from the last game and there is still destruction of buildings but this time you can bring anything back with the new Nano rebuilder to recreate destroyed stair ways etc so you are not stuck trying to climb the geometry to make progress after a fire fight which was a problem in guerilla.
The only problem is the Aliens are used a lot and are thrown against you overwhelmingly at some points so it can get a little repetative fighting them again and again.
Overall if you're coming back here for more of Guerilla you will be dissapointed but if you enjoyed the first game's structure or like linear shooters in general theres fun to be had here.

So Petroglyph did the unexpected and revived the multiplayer and added workshop for a decade old game; which in fact it's more than a decade old now, a surprise to behold.
I've been wanting to write a small summary/review for this game for a while now and now that the game's been updated with a pretty major patch I think now is a good time as ever. I don't write reviews ever so this might come out as "shoddily written summary/review" but hopefully you might consider taking a read.
---
STAR WARS™ Empire at War is an RTS that has held up exceptionally well for being a game from 2006 and it's probably my favorite RTS of all time even. Though it may be a casual RTS it can definitely be challenging when going up against other people, and if PVP isn't your thing; with the use of mods the AI can be incredibly challenging. Plus with a pretty active modding community you can easily get a lot of new content from the workshop or Mod DB. You can get more engaging gameplay with said mods and make your game look like it was made in 2017. Mods can also be used in multiplayer aswell. A great thing about this specific RTS is that it can be both equally casual and challenging, it's an entry level RTS. If you're looking to get into RTS games, this is a pretty good game to start with. (Might I also recommend Halo Wars?)
A really big part of the game comes from the sound design, the use of the soundtracks are superb, the voice acting is really good, the authentic sound effects from the movies for each unit are great, it all comes together excellently. Just the feeling when you and your enemy's armies collide and the comms from your units start going off like crazy with the music changing from ambience to action is something to behold.
There is also a singleplayer campaign in which you can play as the Empire or Rebellion, in the Forces of Corruption DLC you play as the Consortium, I can't really say anything about the single player as I haven't much played it.
The only bug I've come across with the game is "synchronization error" which is a somewhat common problem when you play the game using mods (it occurs dramatically less without mods), or if there are a lot of players in a lobby.
All in all Empire at War is an excellent RTS that caters both to veteran and new players with basic gameplay mechanics that can be both casual and challenging. Plus with a very active modding community and the recently added workshop support and revived multiplayer, this game is a must have for both RTS and Star Wars fans.
That's probably all I have to write down as of now, if you read the entire thing, thanks.
