I got this game on disc when I was about 9 or 10 "back in the day" and played it for years. Then my best friend got it on steam and we had to do some manual patching wizardry and use third party software to play together. It was still one of the best games we've ever played, despite the headaches getting it working. Now they've updated it out of nowhere with multiplayer and workshop support. SO, allow me to share my experience and a few tips for some of you who may just now be discovering this old RTS masterpiece.
First, a quick overview. You've got the Rebel scum, the Super Pirate scum in the expansion, (admittedly they have some very fun toys such as the OP Driv-I mean Mass Drivers -- we'll get to that...) and everyone's favorite the glorius Galactic Empire. You battle in space and on land with fairly standard base-building RTS mechanics. In space you expand your space station and on the ground you build your structures in predetermined locations. You also capture neutral buildings with various functions in both modes. It's very straightforward. There's a Campaign, [a typical scripted RTS campaign from what I gathered from playing not that much of it] Skirmish, and Galactic Conquest, where you build all your buildings ahead of time from the galaxy screen and then once a battle takes place, you have to work with whatever you built up as your defense and garrison or whatever forces you brought as the attacker. Think Total War games. But still with the neutral buildings and turret emplacements to capture, and production buildings like the barracks will occasionally produce extra units for the defender. (if they built one, of course.)
...That wasn't so quick, but let's move on nonetheless. Here are some tips and general fun stuff about the three factions. This is (almost) all about space combat because I don't care much for the ground combat and avoid it whenever possible. Also some of it only applies to the Forces of Corruption version. It's better. Just play that one. :P
The Rebels have a wide variety of units available bla bla bla here's what you need to know: They have better small stuff. Their fighters and bombers tend to outperform Imperial counterparts. (especially if you micromanage X-Wings -- they can be told to fold and unfold their s-foils for speed or firepower. time it right to crush those Ties.) Their most outstanding unit IMO is the B-Wing. It is INCREDIBLY powerful against fighters and capital ships alike. They use rapid fire lasers and more proton torpedos per run than the actual bombers. They too can lock their s-foils and I suggest you keep them closed because they are very, very fast that way, and their firepower only goes down from *Ridiculous* to *Really Quite Good*.
TEH MIGHTY EMPIRE has STAR DESTROYERS. ...They also have Tie Defenders which are fantastic but are just a bit overshadowed by the B(roken)-Wings. But mainly they have the Victory class and Imperial class late game ships which are just beautiful. ALSO almost every Imperial capital ship (basically just not the interdictor cruisers) comes with a fighter compliment which replenishes throughout combat so long as its hangar bay survives. (did I mantion you can target subsystems of capital ships? You can target subsystems of capital ships.) They get AT-ATs too, which can just♥♥♥♥♥♥out Stormtroopers and wreck every other vehicle on the ground. (Yes the Rebels get snowspeeders. Yes they have tow cables.) BUT the BEST PART about the Empire is their Galactic Conquest endgame. At final tech level you can build the Executor (the giant ♥♥♥♥-off star destroyer from ep.5 and ep.6 that crashed into the death star if you're not a nerd) which can spawn INFINITE RANDOM TIE FIGHTERS (one at a time on a cooldown; it's not THAT broken) and THE DEATH STAR 2 WHICH CAN TARGET SHIPS, STATIONS, AND PLANETS. Tired of those pesky ground battles? Did the Rebels sneak in and re-capture the planet you rightfully conquered and oppressed? BLOW IT UP. WIPE OUT THEIR FLEET AND BLOW IT THE ♥♥♥♥ UP. Ten year old me was very happy when I discovered this feature. Can you tell?
The Zann Consortium (the badass pirates who are so badass they kill all the other pirates and think they can rule the galaxy) get all the (really) interesting units and features. Corrupt enemy planets and profit off of them in Galactic Conquest, revive Destroyer Droid production and steamroll enemy infantry, use cloaking technology to sneak into the middle of the enemy fleet and then self destruct them to death, or MASS DRIVERS Here comes the bit on MASS DRIVERS Do you have time to talk about our lord and saviour MASS DRIVERS??? Ahem. The Mass Driver is a weapon type just like Turbolasers and Proton Torpedos. Actually it's both. See, Turbolasers are the big conventional guns that go BANG BANG BANG BANG BANG et-cetera at some speed and pound enemies into dust. Proton Torpedos are big and slow and aren't fired very often, but they IGNORE shields and do ALL THE DAMAGE. Mass drivers are both. Seriously. They don't compromise; they aren't a hybrid. They are the best of both. They go BANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANGBANG STRAIGHT THROUGH SHIELDS AND OBLITERATE EVERYTHING ON THE OTHER SIDE. The guns are equipped in space on the Vengeance class Frigate, their super-capital, (basically their star destroyer or mon calamari cruiser equivalent) and their upgraded space station. On land they are THE BEST DEFENSIVE TURRETS AGAINST EVERYTHING and also are on a tank that also has shields which is the best tank in the game IMO. The DOWNSIDE is... well the Vengeance class doesn't have shields, and all their units are expensive. If you're a turtle player like me, this won't even phase you, but good luck rushing with them.

Excellent strategy/rogue game, probably one of the better of that sort I've come across. Instead of sharing all its pros and cons, I'll give you a few tips on how to complete your first 12 floors (because even "too easy" will seem difficult without a few pointers.
Tip #1 - Operate. This is a passive skill in several characters which can give you major bonuses towards your modules (especially useful in the early floors when the enemies are weak). Use Max and Deena to start, they can both operate a room after you level them up to level 3. You'll notice they're operating a room when a cog appears above their head. All you need to do is leave them in a room with a module and reep the rewards.
Tip #2 - And this is what continually got me killed when I first started playing...Ready? MONSTERS CAN ONLY SPAWN IN ROOMS THAT ARE UNPOWERED!  Keep as many rooms powered as you can. I would wonder why I was alway overrun by floor 6 or 7 because I was trying to save my dust for rooms with major modules. Don't make this same mistake.  After I learned this fact I easily survived 12 floors.
Tip #3 - Explore in one direction. Limit the directions you can be attacked by. Once you reach a deadend, have every room powered from your crystal to that deadend so won't have to worry about that area.
Tip #4 - Worry the least about your Science supply.  There's times I never even build a science module but have multiple Industry and Food ones.  It doesn't cost much to upgrade your modules, however it starts to get very pricy in food when you need to level up your characters (which is far more important).
Tip #5 - Pay attention to what resource the merchant sells his goods for because it changes everytime. Any resource could be suspect. NEVER purchase items with Dust. Dust becomes too scarce in the end rounds and no item is worth losing Dust over. If you can sell your old items for Dust, however, that can give you a huge advantage for that floor.
Well I hope this helps you get started. Have fun.

This is an excellent combo of empire building and RPG.  I did read previous reviews and I can see the Civ 5 comparison and it is valid, there are similarities with city building & tech trees, but it has the extra dimension of having heroes to find loot, do quests, upgrade weapons, armour and skills and it works brilliantly.  It's not as easy as some reviewers claim (unless you save the game before battles and reload if you lose, which I think takes away the fun) but if you like turn based combat you will love it.  You learn to pick your battles, there are no shortage of heroes so if you lose one its not too bad, they do heal after they 'die' but in the early game it does limit what you can do and you will fall behind your rivals. I do like the fact that, unlike most turn based combat, your armies can have up to 9 units so you have a mix of defensive, ranged and attacking units.  Although set in a Fantasy style world I am avoiding magic (alright I do have a healing spell) and with my second attempt (on default settings) I am  managing to hold my own but not always in the lead. I can see many different ways to win, the maps are randomly generated each time, the difficulty setting is variable, the diplomacy is better than Civ 5 and I am looking forward to many happy hours of game play.   I would recommend a look on YouTube before you buy and if you think you might like it you definately will.  I havent seen a clip yet where they are having as much fun as I am now... 9/10

Evolve fills a niche that I never thought would get attention. From the developers of the original Left 4 Dead, they took the idea of "four survivors against a Tank" and nurtured it into an entire game centered around 4v1 monster hunts. For someone like me who always wanted a game like this, the level of polish and character just can't be found anywhere else. I don't think anyone else could have pulled it off the way Turtle Rock Studios did.
This game is not for everyone, it has a level of strategic depth that takes time to understand and is possibly frustrating for new players. However, giving it time and, better yet, learning the game with friends, Evolve can really make for one of the best experiences in competitive gaming. I think the only thing holding it back right now is the price point. I don't think this game needs to be free to play, but I would consider $40 to be a fair price point for the base game.
Overall, despite the price, poor marketing choices by the publisher and confusing preorder packages, this game provides an experience that some have been craving and can't be found anywhere else.

This is not a great game.  Sure, the art direction is unbelievibly great and yes, it has some homages to classic games.  But the gameplay is not fair.  I've beaten my share of difficult games and I can struggle through most of this one.
The controls aren't quite accurate enough for a game this punishingly hard.  The hitboxes are not consistent for either the bosses or their attacks.  Some levels obscure the screen during bullet hell sequences.  The game often ignores a parry, jump, or dodge and instead takes my life.  I get some huge framerate drops and stuttering play at odd times.  If the game was a bit more forgiving I wouldn't need perfect controls.
The parry system is poorly implemented here.  I'm used to parrying in Street Fighter III or Just Defending in several other fighting games.  First of all, hardly anything in the game can be parried.  The parry range is super small and the punishment for being off by a pixel is one third of your life.  The reward? A tiny bit of super meter that's barely helpful.  The ghost train level parry mechanic to move your cart is beyond infuriating.  The thing you have to parry is so close to the ground that it's very difficult to hit, plus after it moves it's untargetable for about 2 seconds.  It's easier and far safer to play the game pretending that the parry doesn't exist, as you only need it in a couple of boss fights to open a vulnerable spot.
I love the animation, the art, the style, and the soundtrack.  The world 3 stage theme song in particular is fantastic.  Some of the bosses are very creative.  I was looking forward to this game for several years after a couple of seconds in the MS E3 presentation got me hooked.  Ori was tough but fair.  Oniken was tough but fair.  NES era Mega Man was tough but fair.  This game is exceedingly difficult with randomized elements to prevent you from commiting boss fights to pure muscle memory.
The simple game mode prevents you from seeing the last part of every boss fight, which is a shame because those are usually the best parts of the game.  It also prevents you from even viewing the Casino endgame.  Having an easier difficulty setting in no way diminishes the enjoyment of those who want to play on higher settings, and it allows more people to enjoy the wonderful creativity and art of this game.
I'm forcing myself to continue to play through and finish this as I'm not going to let this thing beat me.  Doing so hasn't brought me elation at beating each boss and moving forward.  Rather, it's just a soul crushing slog that I dread playing.  I only find relief that I never have to waste my life on each stupidly hard boss ever again.  It's work.  I'd rather go to my day job or do chores than play this game.  I'm close to the end, so I'm going to push on through.  It's just disappointing since Cuphead has just about everything I look for in a game.

Dungeon of the Endless may just be one of the better examples on how Early Access can work.
On first glance it may seem like a cavalcade of modern indie gaming "trends" (i.e. gimmicks): 16 bit Pixel Graphics, Roguelike, Tower Defense, Hero based game where you deal with hordes of MOBs on prescripted routes while defending a  central object et cetera, et cetera.
Some of these are elements that seem like they may not mesh well, but after spending some time with the game I've found that the extended stay the game has had in Early Access has allowed the developers at Amplitude Studios enough time to iron out the vast majority of the kinks and deliver a very smooth and really addictive game. Also, one that's hard as hell. The only difference between the two initial difficulties that I've found is really *when* the game starts becoming tough. On Easy it's on floors 3-6, on Very Easy, it's floors 6-9 (out of 12 that you have to clear in a game). Past that it's just starting on hard.
So it's a potpurri of gaming ideas mixed with a strong sci-fi aesthetic, has a kicking syth soundtrack and is overall a blast to play.
The only real problem being about which package you should get, since the two different packs offer a very false choice: get reduced content or get everything. Just get the crystal pack. Not for the extras or even the "bonus" hero, but for the "bonus" ship, "The Library" - each of the ships in the game is basically an entirely new ruleset variation to how to play the standard game, and missing out on one of them once you get hooked is going to feel like a kick to the cajones.
That tomfoolery aside, a highly enjoyable and very interesting experiment on how to combine every concievable indie-game trend into a fun, demanding and enthralling experience.

Also, on the topic of graphics, why does it take forever to load in the dungeons?  I mean Minecraft generates worlds faster than this game does a single level, and that game is Java based.
Ok, I know all of that sounded a little ranty, but my point is that this is one of those games that tries too hard to be something it's not.  It is not a tower defense game, and it is certainly not a dungeon crawler.  What's left? I don't know, maybe an exhibit of why modern games are trying too hard to sell rather than make a decent and worth-while gaming experience?

A poor copy of an earlier version of Clicker Heroes, which shouldn't be a surprise, as that game is mentioned in this one's description.  There are graphical glitches (mainly concerning clicked-on animations for monsters), audio glitches (will play BGM whenever booted up before realizing you saved the settings as "Music Off" and abruptly going silent), and data management glitches (I've had to reset my computer because the application was "running" or "syncing" half an hour after closing the window).  And I highly doubt that new patches are releasing in the days to come.
There are only two reasons I've sunk in as much time as I have: mild amusement at seeing little numbers grow into bigger numbers, and a need to look busy so I don't have to give all of my attention towards an even less enjoyable task.
Sometimes, two halves are better than a whole.  This is not as visually appealing as Ragnarok Online, nor do you get the same satisfaction when progressing as in Clicker Heroes. And since both of those games are also free to start, I cannot think of any reason why you're not playing either of them instead of this underwhelming experience.

Red Faction: Armageddon is a game I have come back to again and again, and I would like to try to explain why...
Almost nothing about Red Faction: Armageddon could be described as 'spectacular'. The plot, for example, is a pretty standard sci-fi 'bug-hunt' affair that sees you battling a plauge of generic nasty aliens and a bunch of crazy religious space cultists, all whilst cracking wise with your AI companion.
Graphically Armageddon looks nice, but is nothing to write home about. The game controls well on a gamepad or a keyboard/mouse and mechanically Armageddon is a very competent game, but doesn't exactly push the games design envelope very far.
But it turns out all of that is fine, becuase the aliens blow up real good when you shoot them, the voice talent is pretty enjoyable and franky you get the impression that Red Faction: Armageddon is trying to be nothing more complex than some good old fashioned alien-blasting fun!
But there is one feature that really stands out, one feature that makes this otherwise average game demand your attention: the destruction engine. You just can't have a Red Faction title without being able to blow literally everything up with a pocket full of high explosives, and believe me when I say that in this area Armageddon really delivers!
As you would expect, almost any man-made structure can be blown apart and you have a generous arsenal of toys with which to do it, ranging from sledge hammers and rocket launchers to high powered lazers and supremely cool 'Magnet-Gun', which will see you launching segments of wall at your foes from across a level and ripping the legs off of guard towers before watching them collapse onto explosive containers and  not-so-innocent bystanders.
Each level presents you with a veritable playground of enviromental destuction. With so many  tools at your disposal you really have the opportunity to get inventive with your violence and use your enviroment against your foes in creative ways. The whole experince is hugely satisfying!
If I had to sum up Red Faction: Armageddon in one word, it would undoubtably be 'fun'. It will never win any awards, it will probably never make it onto anyone's top 10 list, but I guarantee you I'll be re-installing this game in the near future to watch things go boom.
Would I recommend? Absolutely.

-Decent gameplay
-Entertaining physics
-Okay story I guess I played it like 2 years ago and barely remember what it was about tbh
-Linear, not very buggy, and pretty solidly entertaining all the way through
Cons
-Doesn't have much going for it beyond physics
-Kinda boring gunplay
-You can literally play through like 90% of the game with the magnet gun you get in the beginning, and frankly it's more fun to do that than to use actual weapons
-Previous point kinda negates all the weapons in the game because half of them are just "Explosions caused by different sources and under different circumstances but in the end it's just explosions."
So long story short I guess it's fun if you just want a quick linear adventure, doesn't have amazing replayability because once you've seen it, you've seen it. Not worth the price, I have no idea how people pour more than like 14 hours max into a game like this. If you're one of those people who gets their rocks off from having super overpowered guns that eliminate any sort of challenge or from screwing around with physics because you have nothing better to do with your hollow life then I guess maybe 6/10.
Don't base your decision to buy it on whether or not you liked Guerilla because it's not even the same breed of game honestly.

Beyond Good and Evil is Ubisoft's under-rated-masterpiece, it was first released on the PlayStation 2 on November 11, 2003. The beautiful Music was Composed by Christophe Héral.
Beyond Good and Evil is by far the most beautiful, outstanding game I ever played on the PS2, and when I saw it was available on Steam I exploded. There are many games that we as gamers 'play and forget'. Beyond Good and Evil is one of the games I will never forget.
Beyond Good and Evil's Protagonist is a bright young woman named Jade. Jade is an avid martial artist, photographer and investigative reporter. She has been staying with her 'Uncle' Pay'j
to help take care of orphans at their lighthouse home.
Jade and Pay'j are on the mining planet “Hillys”. Hillys is under siege by an extraterrestrial group known as the “DomZ”, the DomZ are skeleton-reaper-like-aliens whom abduct and drain the life from their victims. Recently a group known as “The Alpha Sections” have taken up residence on Hillys. The Alpha Sections have sworn to defend the population of Hillys from these devastating DomZ attacks.
You play the game as Jade, in a third person camera view, the game is broken down into two modes: combat mode and stealth mode.
When in combat, Jade wields a special Bo Staff known as a “Jō”; Jade preforms strikes, flips, and power attacks while in combat mode. If you were unsuccessful in sneaking past enemies you can fight your way through many parts of the game. However there is definitely an emphasis on stealth rather than fighting.
When in stealth, Jade sneaks and rolls, there are oftentimes alternative paths to sneak around guards, other times you need to distract guards by creating a diversion to take them away from their posts, while you sneak past.
There are no achievements in the game, however there are extra things to collect while playing. You can take pictures of all the animals in the game, and collect all the pearls, and find every M-disks.
Beyond Good and Evil is priced at $9.99, my first play through I unlocked everything before beating the game
the game can easily take anywhere from 6-8 hours to complete.
When I was younger playing this game on the PS2; I remember that I almost beat this whole game in a day. My parrents left the house in the late morning and I started playing Beyond Good and Evil, when they got back that evening I was still playing. Needless to say, they were not pleased with my binge-playing-habits.
Seriously, just buy and play this game.

Beyond Good and Evil is hands down, an all-time favorite game from my childhood. What immediately grabbed my attention was the art-style and the music. Even after finishing the game multiple times, I often find myself listening to the soundtrack.
The characters in the game are wonderfully done (in my opinion), including the two companions whom join you on your mission. A bonus was that I never had to run around looking for them, only to find them stuck on an obstacle or anything like that. Even while progressing, collecting all of the pearls and playing the mini-games are fun distractions too.
I did have a few issues with glitchy textures and whatnot, but the forums quickly fixed the issue and I was able to play it within a few minutes. The only thing I'll half heartedly complain about is the semi-wonky camera. It can be a bit annoying to maintain in the Beluga, and I had it get stuck once or twice. The few times the camera got stuck on walls, I was easily able to fix it without having to restart the game or losing any progress. As for the vehicle; I doubt it'll work for everyone, but I stopped having issues with it while driving if I didn't move the camera with my mouse.
Something I'm saddened by is how little commercial success this game received. That, and the fact that apparently this was the first installment in what was supposed to be a trilogy. The sequel was originally revealed in 2008, had a video leaked in 2009, and was announced to still be in development in 2011 and 2012. Interestingly, a poster of Beyond Good and Evil 2 concept art of Jade was shown in 2013. I'm unsure if anything else has been announced, leaked, or otherwise, but I personally still have my fingers crossed for the sequel.

A satisfying Rogue-lite that is heavier on careful planning than reaction speed. Dungeon of the Endless mixes elements of RPGs with tower defense and dungeon crawlers to create a surprisingly deep strategic experience. The randomized floors and unlockable hero characters give it great replay value, and the chance to mix rules with different starting setups make this a good time sink.
The game features a resource management system that forces you to think about your choices: "should I construct more turrets to make sure I survive this next wave, or can I save some construction points for the more difficult stages later?" is something you have to ask yourself constantly. And as with almost all Rogue-lite games, the Dungeon features permadeath of characters. Mixing permadeath with healing supplies consuming the same resources as leveling up can cause some stress as you must make the choice between securing a team member's life and giving them a vital level up that'd make them stronger later on.
Overall, Dungeon of the Endless has thus far impressed me with it's versitility and highly apparent replay value. It has already been worth it's price, and I'm fairly confident I'm going to be spending even more time with this challenge of risk and reward.

Evolve fills a niche that I never thought would get attention. From the developers of the original Left 4 Dead, they took the idea of "four survivors against a Tank" and nurtured it into an entire game centered around 4v1 monster hunts. For someone like me who always wanted a game like this, the level of polish and character just can't be found anywhere else. I don't think anyone else could have pulled it off the way Turtle Rock Studios did.
This game is not for everyone, it has a level of strategic depth that takes time to understand and is possibly frustrating for new players. However, giving it time and, better yet, learning the game with friends, Evolve can really make for one of the best experiences in competitive gaming. I think the only thing holding it back right now is the price point. I don't think this game needs to be free to play, but I would consider $40 to be a fair price point for the base game.
Overall, despite the price, poor marketing choices by the publisher and confusing preorder packages, this game provides an experience that some have been craving and can't be found anywhere else.

Let me start by saying I am NOT a 4x player (infact I didn't even know what that was when I got this game), so this is coming from some one relatively new to the genre.
FE:LH is the perfect example of an intimidating game.  There's just so much going on, so much custimization, so many options, and so much thought process that seems to need to go into every single turn to be successful, to a new player the whole experience can be more then a little overwhelming.
Now that's not inherently a bad thing, obviously its not the game for you if your looking mindless fun, but if you enjoy a good strategic experience, a game having this much meat to it can be a really good thing, and can allow for a tremendous amount of depth and replay value.
What it DOES mean, however, is that its absolutely crucial that the game has a top notch tutorial to ease a new player into the complexities the game has to offer.  There are various ways this can be accomplished, though my favorites have always been games which provide multiple missions/quests which start with only a small portion of the game available, and incremently add on more and more until by the end the player has had time to at least begin to understand each aspect of the game and is not putting it all together.
Unfortunately, that is not the case with FE:LH.  The single player campaigns, while enjoyable, are not very informative or what I'd consider good learning tools.  Although there is a dedicated tutorial, its not very long, it mainly just shows you "how" to do a handful of things, then its over, providing very little information as to the why, and generaly leaving the players head spinning from the massive information dump.  It's reminsicent of some fighting games whose tutorials invovle asking you to do a bunch of a characters special moves, you do them, and then the tutorial is over.  You come away knowing these are things you can do, but not really knowing when or why you should do them, and it was all over so fast you probably won't even remember half of the moves once your in a match.
Despite the lack of new player friendliness, I'm still giving this game a recommend.  Why?  Because I'm finding that if you're willing to endure a pretty terrible introductory experience and learn the concepts of the game the hard way, the actual game itself is quite well made and actually pretty darn fun.  I honestly feel that if this game had a quality tutorial this would be one of the better PC games out there, maybe even a must own.  As it is though, it takes a very special kind of dedicated player (or some one already familar with the 4x genre) to spend the hours learning things the hard way it takes to actually get to the fun part where you know what your doing and your making meaningful choices instead of random ones, so keep this in mind before purchasing.

A mix of CIV and Heroes of Might and Magic. The maps can be enormous and will take you 20+ hours to complete. There are also smaller maps that, of course, are much less time intensive.
With a mix of empire building, research, resource management (yes, you can run out of iron to build those awesome units, but so can the ai) mixed with RPG leveling of your sovereign and champions, there is a lot you can do.
That said, the pace can be slow. You have options on the customization of creating a world, but I kind of like the slower pace as my units are not obsolete in 10 turns. Research basically allows you to upgrade armor, weapons, etc. of basic units. Not like CIV where you have spearmen, pikemen, etc. They are essentially the same, with different buffs. You can give them fire resitent cloaks, magic necklaces etc. However, it will cost you more in resources. In a strange twist, it is more expensive to buy things for your heroes!
The AI is pretty decent, but not that good at measuring army strengths and weaknesses. This can lead the AI to wasting expensive troops against their counters. Afterwords, you can mop them up as they have little armor.
Overall, it is engaging and does have that "one more turn" thing. It deserves an 8 of 10.

Ragnarok Clicker is yet another clicker game where you go through the levels, hiring heroes and comrades to aid you with DPS (Damage per second) to kill a variety of monsters in your path to progress through the levels.
One thing that sets this clicker game apart from the rest of them is the art style. I really enjoy the art; the backgrounds are really pretty to look at, and the monsters are all designed with care and consideration. That much is obvious. Even the achievement icons are reminiscent of old 8bit games and this is something I really enjoy.
However, there monsters aren't varied. There are new ones each ten levels, but we just see those all repeated. I suppose for a game as large as this that there has to be some room like this, but also, it would be nice to see different designs for the levels. After playing those 10 levels, the designs get extremely boring to see over and over again.
An aspect I really like about this game is the achievements. They're all relatively easy to get, a lot of them can be farmed in the background when you have a high enough DPS level, and a lot of them are stackable, making them easier to achieve. (For instance: boss kills also count as monster kills.)
I really enjoy playing this one, even if there isn't much variety within the actual game.

Fun game despite all of the arguments about its difficulty.
I've found that the game gets MUCH easier if you clear out areas on "simple" difficulty, collect coins, buy power ups, and then go back and try again. A couple of bosses that I thought would be impossible were much easier with different weapons or powerups.
I'm not going to be one of those people saying "LUL GIT GUD!!!!1" but... well, it's amazing how much easier things can be after a little practice, trying different loadouts, or maybe watching other people beat a level you're stuck on to see if there's a strategy you hadn't thought of.
Some people have complained about RNG being a factor, and I agree in some cases. I've died a few times on that Bee level because platforms just stopped spawning on the side of the screen I was on and there was really no way to avoid getting hit. Really no amount of skill will save you in those situations, and that's just bad design. A bit of "controlled randomness" would have probably been better in a few cases.
That said, MOST of the game seems really well designed and thought out, and this game lives up to the hype.

Beyond Good and Evil is a 2003 Stealth Action-Adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier, the studio behind the Rayman series and also responsible for original titles like From Dust. Montpellier, as a creative powerhouse, delivered Beyond Good and Evil to critical acclaim, but devastatingly poor sales have infamously seen the sequel perpetually delayed.
This is a horrible port, and you should not buy it.
Beyond Good and Evil is not a perfect game. This is the only version of it I've played, so my experience is not all encompassing. However, I felt that most, if not all, of the problem with the game stemmed from what a horrendous port this is.
It controls absolutely awful, because for a game that is designed solely for gamepads, it dictates that you use the keyboard and mouse. Trying to steer Jade while clicking away in haphazard combos isn't fun at all, along with common mishaps like sticking to walls and desperately waggling the mouse in radial-based menus like an idiot.
There is no gamepad support for this game whatsoever, outside of using a clunky 3rd-party program like Xpadder. So that means when the game restricts you camera to a 2D plane, you just have to deal with it. When it decides to wrench your camera away for you for no apparent reason, you just have to deal with it. When you're desperately wrenching the mouse while janking the hovercraft with the WASD keys to get it around corners, you just have to deal with it.
Those are just the control issues. Even after disabling a certain amount of options to get the game running at above a powerpoint rate (note: simply lowering the settings made the game perform even worse) I had constant plummets in framerate and constant graphical glitches. This port (not by Montpellier) makes Ubisoft's recent debacles look good.
It is, however, a decent game. The gameplay is shallow, and the amount of distractions in the disappointingly small hub-world one-note, but the game is carried by the amazing art style and music. The art style speaks for itself, and the music is worth tracking down if you can. While not sold on the game's cult classic status, the game is a solid casual Action Adventure that doesn't demand much in the way of attention and delivers on the premise plenty.
I'm not recommending this, not because you shouldn't play this, but because you shouldn't play this version. Play the HD version, emulate a console version, by Jove even dig out a sixth gen system and track down a physical copy if you're truly dedicated to playing this game and seeing what the hype is all about.
Playing the Steam version of Beyond Good and Evil will only sour you on an already hard to sell game.

First of all, I'd like to point out that this is my personal opinion about this game and I am NOT speaking on behalf of other players. This game continues the "Red Faction" story, but there is plenty of thing I consider awesome and some are not that much. I'll try to make it short.
Good stuff:
-Things still go boom as in previous parts of this saga and it's fun to watch.
-I liked the weapons selection in this part of the game even more than in "Guerrilla".
-Good interface and as always, so is the music.
-Nano-forces are sometimes unnecesary, but the "Repair" one really helps a lot.
-I liked the ambient of this game.
Meh stuff:
-You have to listen to your AI all the time.
-No jetpack. Where is my jetpack? It's not really essencial in game, but it wouldn't hurt to have one.
-Main story is pretty meh. This game series is about fighting for your freedom and not about killing aliens. There is "Dead Space" series to do that if you are feeling like it. And you'll spend most time of the game doing preciselly that... Killing aliens. It's getting a bit boring after some time.
-Coop is a good idea, but... It's a big meh in this game, considering it's all about blowing stuff up or killing aliens.
-Escort missions... Who wouldn't like these, right?
Sucky stuff:
-First of all and this is very important... If you are looking forward into roaming the Mars freely, blowing stuff up and doing secondary missions from time to time like in good old "Red Faction: Guerrilla", you ain't getting that in this game. Armageddon is completelly lineal, from start to the end and it's ruining the ambient badly. Yes, I know... First and second (Second is pretty bad, by the way, just ignore it's even existed) parts of "Red Faction" are lineal as well, but these games give you some space for improvising freely, at least. You still need to get from point "A" to point "B", but at least you are not held by invisible hand of the developer, pushing you constantly to the point where you should be. "Guerrilla" was a revelation for me, a masterpiece, a demolitionman wet-dream. This game failed to deliver that.
-Glitches, bugs and crashes. Not really constant but you'll identify one immediatly if you see it.
-Your guns are unmoddable. You can just use salvage to give yourself some passive skills... Yeah.
-The stupidity of main character amazes me deeply.
-Point 5, because other 2 colums had 5 points. Actually point 4 isn't needed as well, but it's a fair point.
So, in my personal opinion, the game itself is enjoyable and fun for some time... Untill you'll get tired of smashing bugs and playing as a poopoo-head of main character, blaming yourself for the stupid things he is programmed to do. So... It's a solid 7/10.
And by the way... When THQ went bancrupt, "Nordic Games" bought the rights for "Red Faction" series. I don't think they'll ever get to read the reviews on steam and less, my reviews (Even I don't care about my reviews), but guys... PLEASE... Please do the right thing and when you'll work on next "Red Faction" game, make the world free to explore. Every gamer in the world would masturbate furiously on that, I can assure you that. Thanks for your attencion and have a good life.

A mysterious cult destroys the Terraformer, thus destabilizing Mars' atmosphere and driving most inhabitants on the planet underground.  Five years after these events, protagonist Darius finds mining work anyway he can, having left the Red Faction after their failed attempt to retake the Terraformer.  He accepts a contract from a group of shady Marauders and unwittingly releases an entombed alien race.  He is eventually ousted as the the one responsible and forced on the run.  Darius encounters old allies though as he runs and eventually begins the laborius task of driving the aliens back and finding the true identity of those who tricked him.
Armageddon is played in third-person similar to Guerrilla.  The campaign is single player only, but there is also an online co-op "horde mode" for up to four players and a sandbox/score attack destruction mode for you to fool around with solo.  Environmental destruction is one of the game's attractions.  At the start of the game, you are given a special tool that allows you to rebuild destroyed structures and objects.  Whereas a broken staircase in another game would prevent you from moving forward, in Armageddon you can literally rebuild the stairs.  Enemies can also make a mess of the environment.  A hulking alien can smash through every wall you put between you and it.  Tentacles will snatch fallen debris and throw it at you.  Destroying buildings is really fun just to watch them crumble.
There is a a good variety of different weapons to use that destroy the environment in different ways.  Most of the time you will use these weapons to fight various classes of aliens.  Aliens frequently swarm you so your build tool also has some AOE attacks (such as a shield, anti-grav, and force-like push) to create some breathing room.  You will also get to pilot some pretty awesome vehicles.  The story plays out as you would expect it but what you'll be doing in each mission is highly varied.  The campaign never got dull for me and I was excited to play through it again on a harder difficulty.  Co-op is sparsely populated.  Although you can play it alone, it really is not as fun as the campaign.
The aliens in Armageddon look amazing.  Their are multiple varieties of creepy crawlies each with their own color scheme, behavior, and on-screen effects.  All of them are very well animated.  Sound and lighting are also very nice, giving you the claustrophobic dread of being trapped in the dark underground.  All of the environments look nice too, whether they be vast caves, undeground towns, or surface camps in the middle of a lightning/sand storm.  Voice acting and cutscenes are great and the cast is alright for what the game is.  Music choice is appropriate though nothings really stood out to me.
Red Faction: Armageddon is a fun game to play through on your own a couple of times.  Fun gameplay, straightforward story, quality design, and environmental destruction are the reason to get this game.  Try to get it on sale if the short campaign and lack of multiplayer options deters you.

A turn-based strategy game that borrows heavily from Civilization and that ilk, this one has some distinctions to set it apart.  Like in Civ you'll manage a growing empire of cities looking to spread across the world, and dominate it via one of several victory conditions.  Unlike with Civ the combat is turn-based tactical where clever use of your stuff will allow a weaker enemy to prevail against a stronger one.  Also the setting is a sort of high fantasy where magic is an important resource, the mastery of which is crucial to the game.
More importantly, Legendary Heroes lives up to its name by giving each side a sovereign, and several lesser champions which gain in power as if in an RPG.  These heroes can be mages, warriors, or generals, with large and varied skill trees to progress along.  It's this last bit that makes this such a fun game: at the start of the game where many of the early turns are about watching your cities grow your heroes can be mucking about, exploring and killing bandits.
A great entry in the 'just one more turn' category of games, Legendary Heroes does right a lot of things its predecessors did wrong.

NOTE- If you're going to write a review for this game, or any game, please, for everyone's sake, play the game for MORE THAN AN HOUR.
I personally feel that a lot of negative reviews towards this game are incredibly unfair. People forget that this is not Metal Gear, it's not Ghost Recon, it's not Assassin's Creed, and it CERTAINLY is not a copy/paste of other survival genre games. Allow me to rebuke some negative comments I've heard about this game.
-Yes, the game plays slow. Sometimes, it plays slow as hell. Obviously this is not a style of gameplay for everyone. This DOES NOT, however, mean the gameplay is faulty. Sir is a game about survival at it's core, and you are intentionally given few options to fight back. Sneaking is your alternative to fighting, and if staying slow and steady isn't your cup of tea, don't ruin this game's credibility by calling it broken gameplay. And for the love of mercy, yes, standing up in an open field WILL get you seen and that is NOT unfair gameplay!
-I've read complaints about guns being useless due to their noise attracting enemies... um, duh. That's what guns do. Unprofessionalism aside, I actually really enjoyed this feature. It adds a tense cost/effect relationship to defending yourself that very few survival horror games honestly have. You can't just shoot an enemy, walk two feet, hide, and not get spotted; besides, I've used guns in this game a number of times and I've NEVER been spotted but once or twice after using them. Shoot a robot to avoid being seen, loot his scrawny metal♥♥♥♥♥corpse, and run like hell before his buddies show up. Seriously, if you're having trouble because you haven't played the game before, it takes PRACTICE and TIME to learn how to survive using what you're given.
-The axe... okay you guys win, the axe needs to be fixed. It's realistic! The problem is, eh, it's too realistic, and because the enemies are as aware as they are in this game, it's damn near impossible to use the axe for its intended purpose: sneaking up and attacking enemies from behind. That being said, perhaps some tweaks could be made. Make the axe do more damage so robots can't just run away when you hit them, even if they've spotted you. Use the axe to cut lumber and build a campfire. This item really does need to be made more useful.
-The save mechanic also needs to be addressed. Because of the game's slow nature, players are unable to return to a boat or the standing stones before being surrounded by hunters. Perhaps a feature could be implemented allowing players to find books that they can "use" to save their progress on the move, but maybe like ink ribbons in Resident Evil they're a one-use item. Also, can we please get more standing stones than just the one at the central island? I can't stress enough how much longer this game honestly gets having to make trips one piece at a time between islands.
In short, there are a few flaring issues with this game, and they should be addressed. However, a lot of people who write down on this game seem to share something in common: they've barely played it for an hour or two, and they've already decided they know exactly how the game works. This is not a game you can just pick up and play; it's trial and error. Sure, it can be tedious, but that doesn't make it a bad game. If anything it makes it a dynamic game. The lesson of Sir is that survival is hard, and should not be taken lightly. Speeding through it, wantonly fighting robots, and getting impatient WILL GET YOU KILLED. So please do keep in mind, sir, that you are being hunted (nailed it).
I personally recommend this game to anyone looking for a new experience when it comes to survival horror. While Sir isn't necessarily horrifying, it's pretty damn chilling the first time you're dropped in, and it takes a lot of getting used to. SO: if you get this game, be patient. If you don't like it, oh well, it's not your thing. Now go out there and... don't die. I guess. Good luck.

Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heros is best explained as a Civilizations type genre where you build up an empire with cities and develop them while fielding troops to protect your piece of the world as the A.I. competes against you. You are given the freedom to choose from the individual races included or customize everything you want from your living avatar to the lowely footman securing your borders. In addition to maintaining your empire as it grows you use your avatar to search for new resources to conquer and complete quests to grow in wealth and power. The world also grows with you in power, monsters that litter the landscape will reposition and gain in levels if unchecked, becoming fearsome legends in time. Should you take care of them earlier on or risk everything and wait for a bigger payoff? It is a turn based game and large world games can stress lower end computers in the late game but smaller or medium worlds are stable. I would recommend having at least the higher end computer requirements if you wish to play the largest settings.

This game... I was really excited to play Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes.  I'm a big fan of tactical and turn-based strategy games and I couldn't wait to dig in. On paper, this game has pretty much everything a strategy fan could ask for. Your developing kingdom or empire has a lengthy tech tree with three distinct branches. You can engage your armies in tactical combat, controlling each troops movements a la Tactics:Ogre or just let the battle play out automatically from the overworld. You can use your sovereign to cast tactical and strategic spells, decimate enemy armies, and tame dragons to fight alongside your army. You can even customize your avatar, kingdom history, racial traits, and design all of your units.
The list of things to do in this game is just about inexhaustible... which is likely where everything went wrong.
This game is an incredibly un-polished experience, so much so that I wonder if the devs even test-played it, as this very much feels like a game that is still in late beta stages.  In my opinion, this is because there's just so much going on, that the developers were incapable of playtesting everything thoroughly. I ran into more than a few save bugs and stability issues, and late game lag is incredibly common, even on a very high-end rig. While the environment art is pretty exceptional and overa-all enjoyable, I found the character models to be among the most hideous designs I've ever seen. They are amateur at best and downright ugly at worst. While not a core component, I did feel like something was lost in the customization when no matter which outfit I picked, my sovereign still turned out to be an eyesore.
But, due to the insane levels of customization and depth of gameplay, all of these foibles could be easily overlooked if not for one glaring, inescapable issue.
The AI in this game may be the worst artificial intelligence I've ever encountered in a game of any kind. There are extremely limited diplomacy options, which basically boil down to: pay money, or be paid money for peace, neither of which are very fun or exciting. While more are unlocked later in the game, you're unlikely to ever see them before going to war. The AI seems to have one goal and one goal only: to declare war. It might declare war in the first five minutes of meeting you, or it might wait for five hours, but you can be damned sure it's going to happen.
The way that the AI decides friend from foe is a complete and utter mystery to me. More than once, the enemy AI went from being my best friend (green happy face) to being at war with me the next turn, which was completely baffling. Once at war, the AI will throw every platoon it has at you. It will send all of its troops straight to their death, over and over again, never adjusting its strategy, until it has completely exhausted all of its kingdoms resources and must surrender to you.
At the end of the day, I want to recommend this game so badly, because there is just so much going on that begs to be explored. But no matter how great the rest of the game is, there is just no way around the AI.

Half dungeon crawler, half resource management sim, Dungeon of the Endless is a simplistic "Rogue-like" set in the Endless universe. The thing that sets this apart from so many others in its genre is how you keep your party alive; major slots on dungeon floors allow you to build Major Modules (used to harvest resources), along with minor slots for offensive, defensive, and supportive modules. Three resources are harvested per door opening and modules add to their production: Food for healing, leveling, and recruiting heroes, Industry for constructing modules, and Science for researching upgrades and resetting your party's ability cooldowns. A fourth resource, Dust, is much rarer and is used to power the crystal you are escorting, which in turn powers rooms for modules.
Gameplay is both turn-based (new resources are harvested from when you open a door to a new room) and real-time (combat, movement, healing, etc.), keeping you constantly engaged despite the AI-controlled combat. The first few floors are simple enough to clear out but about halfway up you need to decide which is more important: risking your party's lives and possibly the crystal itself or running to the exit ASAP? Keeping a balanced party and wisely spending your resources will make or break your runs. Luck is always a factor but I felt that once I knew how to control the flow of spawns and properly construct defensive chokepoints that most of my losses were admittedly my own fault. This game rewards planning and strategy instead of demanding you get lucky unlike other recent Sci-fi rogue-likes (looking at you FTL & SotS: The Pit!).
Newcomers will be overwhelmed and probably give up easily because the tutorial is terrible and most of the game's systems have to be studied on the wiki, even with the extensive tooltips in-game. Although it practically plays itself at times and still could use some polishing and TLC, Dungeon of the Endless is a very unique Rogue-like and is worth checking out for fans of the genre.

So I noticed that most of the negative reviews of this game are from people who haven't play this game for more than 2 hours, so here is a review from a more experienced player. This game is a blast. It does a wonderful job of creating tension naturally. Even though I’ve played the game a couple times, my heart always still races every time I find myself creeping through a robot infested town or when I am running through the country side being chased by two hunting parties.  The grim atmosphere and constant threat of danger is always enough to keep me on edge.  The inventory management adds a very fun element to the game. It limits the amount of supplies that the player can carry, forces the player to make tough choices on what to bring and what to leave behind.  I like the inventory system because it makes me feel like I am on the run. I can only take the essentials, and if I want to keep something, I have to cache it somewhere on the map. I can't just stock pile weapons until I can go full Call of Duty on everyone. I have to conserve ammo and only use them when I am in a bind.
I do have some criticisms of the game though. When walking through the brush, the frame rate drops. I personally think the game should have permadeath. I know there are some mods that offer that but I think the game should include it. My funniest play through were the ones where I told myself that if I die, I would have to start over. I only felt like I was playing the game the way it was supposed to be played when I couldn't use the saving system as a crutch. Even with the save system though, the game can still be punishing, just not as punishing as I think it should be.
Overall, this is one of my favorite indie games, and I think it is worth a play through. It’s a game where I can play through a couple times, drop it for a month, and then pick it up again.

Pretty addictive. It's a fairly unique combination of genres - I'd call it primarly a resource management/tower defense game with roguelike elements and some RPG mixed in rather than a roguelike with TD elements, but that's just me.
+ High replayability - unlockable ships (influences how you start as well as your strategy throughout) unlockable characters, randomized maps, loot and research opportunities makes each playthrough different.
+ "One more turn/game" appeal - whether I was trying out a recent unlock or simply trying to correct the mistakes I made last game, I found myself wanting more.
+ Challenging without being unfair, tactical without being overwhelming - this game can slap you into the dirt, but when you lose it tends to be because of your own actions rather than RNG. And while there are enough mechanics in play to make the game interesting and intense, you won't find yourself lost. You die, you do better. You die, you do better.
+ Good sound/music. Not much else to say.
- Ugly. If you're used to roguelikes you'll be expecting this, and if you're like me you'll get so immersed that you'll forget it's ugly entirely. Lyne is a puzzle game inspired by the Nine-dot problem. The game introduces multiple lines  with separate sets of target dots distinguished by different colors. As anothre addition, there are vertices at which the lines are allowed to cross. While the original puzzle is a nice demonstration of insight problem-solving and out-of-box thinking, solution of Lyne puzzles does not involve either of these. Rather the solution is achieved by an exhaustive and often random exploration of the tree of all possible states. The difficulty is increased by asking the player to solve puzzles with deeper and wider trees.
The controls are lacking: It is possible to modify the line that has been drawn only at its end. If you want to modify a segment of line at where it started, you need to redraw the entire line. That's not a big deal with small puzzles but it can get annoying with more longer lines.
The game is intended for screens with portrait rotation - i.e. screens with height>width. Such choice is awkward since most displays are intended for landscape viewing and, for instance, it's not feasable to physically rotate laptop screen or a projector display.  As a consequence some slim puzzles will occupy 1/8 of the width of your screen when viewed in landscape mode and it can get really tricky to accurately draw the desired line.
It appears that the game partly gets its current overwhelming rating due to the attractivity of its achievements. Achievements aside, I don't think the game deserves such rating. I don't recommend it.

Red Faction Armageddon is a third person rail shooter, and even if i'm not a fan nor a vet of the gerne i really enjoyed it.
The narrative is actually good enough, surely the plot is not amazing in itsef, but thanks to a good mix of badass, funny (thanks S.A.M.) and dramatic (in particular THAT dramatic moment) well written lines and moments it really becomes a very pleasant experience, (the absence of secondary quests or other errands which could break the "flow" of the main story may also be a plus in this regard). Most levels also have a very good atmospheric feeling.
The gameplay is very solid, you have bunch of very different weapons at your disposal (the magnet gun, you never grow tired of that:), plus the distruction mechanics (i think is the best i've seen in a game so far) really let you solve the various challenges you have to face with different approaches, also boosting replay value. Also a nice character progression is implemeted and you may upgrade Darius' gear and abilities proceding in the game.
On the technical side graphics are very good, in particular the explosion looks gorgeous, and the performance were fine. I've not expereinced any glitch, bug or crash (but other rewiers instead did).
Once you finish the story you have a story+ option that let you replay it with all your upgrades and special weapons (ever dreamed of disintegrating your enemy with a rainbow ray coming out from a pony's♥♥♥♥♥ I didnt but whatever) unlocked from the start.
There are also a singleplayer destruction mode that can be a lot of fun and a very good multiplayer coop survival mode (even if recently might be hard to find players online).
Conclusion: I really enjoyed this game (completed the main story 2 times and i'll probably come back for more sooner or later) and i surely raccomend it to anyone which is interested in pleasant, linear, story-driven shooter experience.

This game... I was really excited to play Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes.  I'm a big fan of tactical and turn-based strategy games and I couldn't wait to dig in. On paper, this game has pretty much everything a strategy fan could ask for. Your developing kingdom or empire has a lengthy tech tree with three distinct branches. You can engage your armies in tactical combat, controlling each troops movements a la Tactics:Ogre or just let the battle play out automatically from the overworld. You can use your sovereign to cast tactical and strategic spells, decimate enemy armies, and tame dragons to fight alongside your army. You can even customize your avatar, kingdom history, racial traits, and design all of your units.
The list of things to do in this game is just about inexhaustible... which is likely where everything went wrong.
This game is an incredibly un-polished experience, so much so that I wonder if the devs even test-played it, as this very much feels like a game that is still in late beta stages.  In my opinion, this is because there's just so much going on, that the developers were incapable of playtesting everything thoroughly. I ran into more than a few save bugs and stability issues, and late game lag is incredibly common, even on a very high-end rig. While the environment art is pretty exceptional and overa-all enjoyable, I found the character models to be among the most hideous designs I've ever seen. They are amateur at best and downright ugly at worst. While not a core component, I did feel like something was lost in the customization when no matter which outfit I picked, my sovereign still turned out to be an eyesore.
But, due to the insane levels of customization and depth of gameplay, all of these foibles could be easily overlooked if not for one glaring, inescapable issue.
The AI in this game may be the worst artificial intelligence I've ever encountered in a game of any kind. There are extremely limited diplomacy options, which basically boil down to: pay money, or be paid money for peace, neither of which are very fun or exciting. While more are unlocked later in the game, you're unlikely to ever see them before going to war. The AI seems to have one goal and one goal only: to declare war. It might declare war in the first five minutes of meeting you, or it might wait for five hours, but you can be damned sure it's going to happen.
The way that the AI decides friend from foe is a complete and utter mystery to me. More than once, the enemy AI went from being my best friend (green happy face) to being at war with me the next turn, which was completely baffling. Once at war, the AI will throw every platoon it has at you. It will send all of its troops straight to their death, over and over again, never adjusting its strategy, until it has completely exhausted all of its kingdoms resources and must surrender to you.
At the end of the day, I want to recommend this game so badly, because there is just so much going on that begs to be explored. But no matter how great the rest of the game is, there is just no way around the AI.

I havent really tried out the multiplayer but I have heard that PVP is not that good, considering that shooting is purely luck based and that melee combat is who hits first wins, and I do think the combat system is pretty sound in singleplayer but definitely not meant for multiplayer.
The community. Oh my good lord the community... The modders are the best thing to ever happen to this game. Dont belive me? Go play with Hydrocraft. And again I have never been on servers so I dont know how people are, though I expect it to be similar to Rust, if you are on a public server, you will be shot or hit from behind.
As for gameplay, its amazing. Dont go into this game thinking you will be able to sprint around and slash heads as if you are playing castle crashers. Patience is key, look for areas with very little if any zombies and carve out safe roads, and if you think that it gets easier over time, just wait till you run out of power and water and the winter months set in, then tell me it gets easier.
This game is hard to master, and even the smallest mistake on youre part can kill you, building a house and accedentally fell off the roof? You need to splint that or you will die. Got bit by a zombie because you werent concentrating? You got a 9 in 10 chance of infection and zombificiation. Got cut by a shattered window? You got to carefully remove every shard of glass, stitch, then bandage the wound before you die.
9/10 Must play this game, if you like zombie survival and are patient as a dark souls player, this is definitely the game for you.

The Long Dark is the type of game you love to hate. Everything about the struggle to survive that extra day, and the challenge of learning how to adapt to the changing environments requires a tactical mindset. Even playing through on the easiest setting is still no cake walk. Your first few days, if you can even make it that far, will leave you feeling like you've overcome some major milestones. However, it's much more likely you'll take a wrong turn, get caught out in the cold, and freeze to death. Your 2nd attempt maybe you make it a little further, but ultimately you succumb yet again to the brutish unrelenting merciless world you thought you were starting to understand.
For people who enjoy that oldschool experience of gaming that presents a true challenge, this game is incrediby rewarding in that regard. You're dropped into a bad situtation that's only going to quickly get worse and you have to adapt or die. You won't get the hang of it immediately, you have to figure things out along the way, and its not at all black & white. Sure you could read some guides or watch some tutorials, but you would be denying yourself the pleasure of figuring it out on your own.
Applying yourself, relying on your own wit to overcome the struggle and harship to come out victorious feeling lilke you've accomplished the impossible. Then a wolf jumps out from behind a rock, rips up your clothes, breaks your bow, and leaves you in tatters. As you stumble back to your feet, you notice a small red dot in the snow. Then another just a ways beyond that. You realize the wolf is bleeding and track him down to watch as it slowly bleeds out, then you harvest the corpse to make a slow recovery back to that echelon of nature's champions, re-establishing yourself in your rightful place at the top of the food chain. Then you spot a bear....
The immersive enivronment will keep you looking over your shoulder, trying to plan out the shortest routes from your shelter as you branch out a litle further in search for supplies wondering wether that last match you've been saving is going to let you see the sun rise again come morning. With each passing day your ability to survive is reliant upon your ability to plan ahead for the challenges you've yet to even encounter. Laughing arrogantly in the face of mother nature as she constantly reminds you who's in charge. How long can you endure?
-----
The scenery is astouding. The gameplay leaves you with nothing to be desired. The struggle is real. If you enjoy survival games this is certainly one you won't want to pass up. For the asking price it's deffinately worth its value and then some. You'll be hard pressed to find a more rewarding experience in this genre.

The best part of this game isn't the survival mechanics, or really anything remotely concerned with gameplay. It's that it makes you think, feel, and act like you're in a survival situation, and just making it through another day and seeing the sunrise the next morning is all you need. One of my favorite games of all time, easily a 10/10 purchase.
You'll find no zombies here. No players running around with a KOS mindset. Chances are, you won't find anything except for the animal inhabitants. And the cold.
You'll never escape the cold.

Simply fantastic. Every single part of this game shows polish, attention to detail, and a passion for the project. It is a bit of a wonder that this game finally/ever came out, but I'm definitely glad it did.
Right from the get go you are greeted with a simple yet charming tune and hook to the story. But the real meat is in the gameplay obviously. It is fast, punishing, beautiful, rewarding, devilish, and just plain fun. This game really is quite a challenge, but always rewarding. To be able to beat the bosses or run and gun levels takes a lot of skill, and trial and error. The game justifies this punishing bullet hell with a reliable and responsive control scheme. In the end, however, it's always down to you to beat it, and when you finally do it's a jump for joy and sigh of relief. During the game you are also able to get different abilities. I wouldn't really call them upgrades as they all have a trad eoff as well as a boost; it's just a way to suit your play style.
The gameplay is supported by a fantastic original musical score, and of course the very unique (to gaming) yet all too familiar art style; each enemy, and level having been beautifully hand animated.
I really don't have anything negative to say about this game. It's rewarding, and fun; reliable with no glitches I've found; and gorgeous to look at. I can't even say it's too short. Given it's price tag I'd say it's more than a fair bang for your buck. Pick up this game, it's awesome.

I really enjoyed this game, and it's one of those games that just stuck with me after I've finished it. The story is not bad at all, and keeps you invested from the beginning to the end. The game is very linear and there's not many options other than whats presented to you. However I don't find that a bad thing, I actually think the game benefits from it. This is not a game that you walk around exploring your enviroment or wander off on some side quest, but rather sit back and enjoy as the story unfolds itself. It's decently long and can accomplish this without making the game feel repetitiv.
Now let's talk about the best part, the destruction. A lot of stuff in your environment will break, and I mean a lot. You can bash through a wall with your sledgehammer and tear down pillars and buildings to their core. This means that you can destroy any cover that the enemy might try and hide behind, but so can they. You can repair stuff to quickly make cover for yourself or you can grab a piece of a wall and swing it on your enemies. It never gets boring and will make a huge difference in how you play the game.
Aside from the single-player action you can team up with some friends and play coop missions. These center around fighting waves of enemies while trying to survive. I found this to be very fun and intense gameplay, but it falls short when it comes to veriety and exensivness.
If you can find this game on a sale, I would highly recommend it.

You have your 4 Resources, Food, Production (Which allows Building Defenses and Production Buildings), Science, And Dust.  Food Allows you to level up, buy items from vendors, heal in the middle of a turn, and even to hire new characters.  Science allows you to Research New Buildings and Building Upgrades, and also to occasionally buy items from vendors although it's more likely to see a vendor buying either Production or Food, And Dust allows you to power rooms for Defenses, Production, and (Most importantly) to stop Monsters from Spawning in a room. The Monsters are pretty Tough to say the least and can make you almost smash your keyboard into the wall which makes resource and power management more crucial to your sanity. To get through a Level you must find the exit and get both your Main Gem and your characters into the Exit Room. This game is Worth the Money and the developers are amazing for this game. If you have the money pick up a few copies for you and your friends

I'm not going to mince words: The stealth gameplay is quite simply sh*t, and the survival mechanics and map design (a key element of every stealth game) do nothing to make up for that fact.
You know all those tense moments in other stealth games of sneaking up on a mook oh-so cautiously, praying he doesn't turn around, to take him out, then methodically do the same to every one else in the area so you can explore unimpeded and progress? That simply doesn't happen in this game. There are very very few tactics for you to use against the robot and this means the gameplay is incredibly boring since actually interacting with the main obstacle of the game is counterproductive to the game's objective. Perhap it's unfair to expect this game to have gameplay more similar to a stealth-action game since this could be more a part of the survival horror genre than the stealth genre, but it was not able to immerse me or terrify me with it's minimalistic presentation. The robots don't seem scary, just overpowered. Now about the survival aspects of the game: they are incredibly simplistic, the game enviroments are sparse and dull from a mechanical perspective, and there are few interesting tools with which to fight or avoid the robots. Some other reviews say the game simply needs "more content", but that does not address the fact that the problems with it are mostly on the design level, in my opinion. The game does not need more stuff to throw at you, it needs a more interesting way of putting all that stuff together to make your encounters with the robots more nuanced and exciting or make exploring the map more interesting. It is a bland and wholly un-interactive experience.

I really wanted to like this game, but I just can't. I love the premise: sneaking around a bunch of run-down British islands, hiding from British robots who are trying to kill you. The atmosphere is really good too. But the gameplay is decidedly lacking.
The point of the game is to sneak around. You can get weapons, but they're not really common, and they're not great (to use an axe, for example, you have to close to melee range against a shot-gun wielding enemy, or to use a gun you have to make a ton of noise that can bring other enemies to you). That's all fine by me: I enjoy stealth games. But there's no real stealth system. If you're standing up and someone looks in your direction, they see you. If you run anywhere near an enemy, they hear you and come looking. The only way to avoid notice is to crouch around. The main problem with that? It's slow as hell.
That was my biggest problem with the game: it was incredibly tedious. You're collecting these fragments of a machine/magic device/whatever for reasons, and they're scattered around five seperate islands. You have to wander around these fairly large areas, and if there's ever an enemy around, you have to do it at this ridiculously slow speed. And to make matters worse, the only times you can save are when you're at the device at the center of the center island, or when you're at a boat on any of the islands. So if you mess up, all your work since the last major thing you did is gone, and you have to do all the tedious BS all over again.
I only played an hour, but I played that in three or four seperate sessions, because literally every single time I played, the session would end with me alt-f4ing in frustration after making one mistake and getting blown away in two shots. I don't mind my character having low health; I don't mind it being difficult; I don't mind it having few save points. What I mind is spending 15 minutes sneaking up to one of the fragments you're supposed to be collecting, distracting the guards, grabbing the fragment, then getting killed by a robot you didn't see and realizing you have to do all that sneaking and setup again.
This game could be a lot of fun if there was a better stealth system (maybe if different terrain made different amounts of noise, so you could run across soft grass, for example, and not be heard, or especially if sneaking wasn't so damn slow) and maybe a bit more to do than just creep around the island. You can loot stuff to get more items, and you have to eat to survive, but there's barely any crafting (you can cook food on a fire) and there are no interactable objects anywhere.
So Tl;dr: it was tedious and it was boring, except when getting killed and losing all my progress, and then it was frustrating. But good atmosphere and setting.
