Evolve has a really nice concept which is made extremely well. The game works and has few to no glitches/bugs and the gameplay feels smooth and nice. My only gripe with the game is the price of the core game and all the DLC. This would have been so much better and it could have achieved a bigger playerbase if the price was around 20-30€ and cheaper DLC. I mean 7€ for a Hunter and 15€ for a Monster is just ridiculous when the game itself is 50€. It feels like an overly hyped cash-in that's actually good. It could have been so much more.

After having played this game for some months now, I wanted to re-write my review. First of all, Evolve truly is my favorite game to play right now. I absolutely love it! For those of us who are big fans however, we may be a "cult following", as it were. At least it seems that way from a lot of the other user reviews. Unfortunately, because this game's life depends on perfection almost, those less patient or less forgiving of certain aspects will dismiss Evolve very quickly.
Again, I personally LOVE this game and will continue to support it, and reccommend it. But here are my main issues..
DLC - expensive and silly structure does make you feel kind of ripped off after paying premium price for the game - skins just cost too much! Considering that skins are the main "evolving content" of this game, along with new monsters and hunters (which I hope they continue to regularly release), the price point is just too high for the devs to depend on in order to keep people happy about new content. (New skins are coming out frequenly, and some of them are admittedly pretty damn sick.) Ideally, they should continue to add new challenges for players to earn these skins for free. (Currently elite skins are the only "achievable" unlocks once you reach lvl. 40. Which doesn't take that long really, to get to lvl 40.) I will say, that I am glad they are not making players pay for new maps (currently anyway. They just released two new maps for free.)
Unlocks/Goals/Achievements - Along with my point above...While there are a number of different badges you can unlock and customize, again, it does not take long to unlock most of them. And there certainly could be more. Hopefully they continue to add new visual elements to badges. Quite simply, seasoned players need more rewards for playing!! While there are weekend challenges that award players FREE skins, which is great, there needs to be more. (:
Bugs - Yes. There are bugs. Dead players seem to frequently fall through the map, making Lazurus a gamble as to whether or not you'll contribute much to your team's victory (Laz can bring dead-dead players back to life within a limited amount of time after death.) Furthermore, it's been reported that at least one of the perks does not function properly (perks are movement speed boost, reload speed boost, jet pack boost, etc.) I have also played several games where one player will start the game in midair and never land, forcing you to restart the match. Not a HUGE annoyance, but still. Wall climbing with the jetpack can stand to be tuned as well. There are a few other minor bugs that don't affect the gameplay too much as well, but they are still there.
Missing Community Content - As of this writing, you are unable to friend other players through Steam/Evolve. This is just dumb. Considering there does seem to be a limited number of people playing online, not being able to friend those that you work well with really hurts this game. I cannot even view "current game's players" or "past game's players". This needs to be fixed ASAP.
A few other things -
Personally, I think it would be nice to have a "sandbox" mode, where you can hop into different maps and just run around lol Especially for new players, it could help get a sense of the maps, hiding places, strategies, creatures on Shear, etc. for both human characters and monsters alike.
There is currently a companion app/game for iOS and Android that allows players linked to Evolve to watch past matches with the aeirial view. This is a neat feature. It would be nice if this feature were included in the main game as well, without requiring the phone app. (I'll admit, the phone game is kinda fun though, and does tie to the main game to help you level your characters. It is a freemium game though, of course...)
Also, a monster v. monster mode would be AWESOME! I can't imagine this would be *that* hard to pull off, though the monster attacks are tuned of course, towards human ememies. But if they could make it work somehow, this would be a fun addtion to toy around with. Similarly, since they've added an "observer" slot already, it would be kinda cool if there were a 6th PLAYABLE slot in the game, in which another player could take over a minion and assist his monster friend in battle...just a thought.
Additional Game Modes would also be welcome. Currently, Hunt, Nest, Defend and Rescue are the only different game modes, which can be played together in Evacuation, which is a five round match which players play through all of these modes. Perks are added to the next map depending on if the monster or the humans win - it's a pretty neat feature. However, I hope they add more modes to keep things interesting.
END NOTES:
Overall, Evolve is a brilliant game with great replayability on its own simply due to how much FUN it is. However, for many hardcore gamers the lack of extensive achievable/unlockable content may limit Evolve's shelf life. The dev's biggest issue is RETAINING players, which consequently will affect how many NEW players they get. Bascially, keep your village happy and more people will want to move into it! lol I DO reccommend this game to anyone interested. Don't let the haters scare you away, but DO be aware of the things I have mentioned above. As I said, despite of all this, Evolve is still my favorite game to play right now, and I imagine will be for quite some time.

Amazing game, which took me a bit by surprise. I was expecting a more typical rouge-lite; when in actuality it is a unique hybrid of rouge-like & tower-defense-esque strategy.
You play the game a set of prisoners crash landed from a ship, and must make your way upto the surface or something.
To do this, you need to find the elevator on each floor, and activate it by getting your entire party to it with the power crystal. If all your party dies, you lose, if your crystal takes too much damage, you lose.
You move heroes room by room, and activate their special abilities, but do not directly control them in combat. Time in level mostly progresses when you open doors. Play mostly focuses on properly positioning your heroes, selecting which rooms to activate, and wisely allocating resources to keep your heroes alive.
While it cribs mechanics from tower defense games, and lets you build various defensive turrets, the focus is much more on the heroes, providing a much different feel, so if TD games aren't your thing I would still take a look.
The game is also proudly hard. The insult train starts with the beginning modes of "Easy" & "Too Easy" :/

Lyne is one of those great "sick day" games; the kind that you spend the better part of a day playing when you're layed up in bed or hunkering down during a hurricane, just trying to pass the time and keep from getting the cabin-fever (assuming power is available during said hurricane). Don't get me wrong--Lyne is much more than a mere rainy day pixel-dream; it's a downright challenging, at times frustrating, always satisfying puzzler that keeps entertaining long after all of the main sections have been solved (Daily level sets!).
I love the beautiful sound design and the subtle animation. And the lack of a soundtrack is not a problem; I simply play my own. I highly recommend pairing Lyne with the music of Brian Eno or Autechre -- Eno if you want a stimulating yet relaxing mind-tournament--Autechre if you're up for an energizing brain-battle. You'll look up at the clock and wonder where you've been for the past two hours.

Ok seriously, check the time I have into this game. Yes, it was left open while minimized as I did other things, but I wouldn't bother opening it and leaving it there if I didn't think this game is one of the better idle games on Steam. If you like idle games, I'd suggest giving this one a try. It's not like it's gonna cost you anything.
Nice graphics, probably some of the best idle graphics I've seen(even though they were better before the update that overhauled all the sprites).
There are sounds effects for many(if not all monsters in the game). The only reason I'm not sure on this is because I keep my own personal music on instead of the sound effects and game music.
Plenty of ways to progress(although like every other clicker, it's still slow).
Multiple play styles;
-Idle: Get cards that boost some in game functions(i.e coin gain, dps) if you don't click for 60 seconds.
-Active clicking: Get multiple cards and abilities that boost pretty much everything about clicking(i.e. damage, crit chance, crit damage, and even an "exponential" damage growth for active clicking, plus a lot more)
Now because it is an idle game, going for the idle route would seem like an obvious choice right? To make this game different from ever other idle clicker, the devs added many more boosts and advantages to clicking rather than idle. I haven't tried the active clicking path yet, but I intend to so I can get the rest of the achievments.
Guild system: There is a small multiplayer aspect to this game, and it's known as guilds. You can create your own guild, or join an already created one. Joining someone else's guild is probably better unless you like being alone or have friends. Basically, guild members can leave messages in a guild chat to communicate, guild members can team up in raids to fight bosses that are too strong to take down alone to get rewards, and... okay that's about it for guilds but it does help and it will help you to join one. The way "raids" work is you click on it, it brings you to another screen where all your idle levels are disabled, and you have to click to damage the boss. Damage you do to it is saved for the next person to carry on where you left off. One boss per day, getting harder and harder.
If you're still not sure about getting this, just do it. It won't hurt you.

Download size: about 8 gigabytes if I remember correctly
Play time: about 8 hours (with the DLC)
Red Faction Armageddon (RFA) is the latest in a series of games made famous for their “destroy the environment” gameplay. Like its predecessors, in RFA you can use your sledgehammer or guns to blow apart basically anything that is “manmade” in the game. This includes walls, bridges, and entire buildings. You can’t break through “natural” obstacles like cave walls, the floor, or most rocks on the ground. A lot of people I’ve spoken to seem to think that RFA is a step down from the previous game Red Faction Guerilla, but I like RFA more. For one thing, it’s much more straightforward and action based (Guerilla was an open world sandbox game like Grand Theft Auto on Mars).
You don’t need to have played the previous games to get into Red Faction Armageddon since this game takes place a generation or two after Guerilla. Now the “Red Faction” is the legitimate military of Mars and you’re one of them (in the previous games they were rebels). In RFA you play Darius Mason, an engineer with an artificial intelligence computer companion named Sam who helps you out, like Cortana in the Halo series. Your enemy is Hale, some kind of cult leader who tricks you into unleashing an ancient alien race sealed deep underground. The rest of the game is spent trying to fix your mistake.
RFA is a third person “over the shoulder” shooter game with a variety of weapons and “super powers.” The super powers are part of the Nano Forge technology that Darius wears on his wrist and can get you out of any jam. You have Impact (a force push), Shockwave (lifts up enemies around you), Berserk (some kind of damage buff), and Shell (an area effect shield).  All of the powers share the same cooldown bar. Money in the game is “salvage” just like Red Faction Guerilla. Salvage is glowing junk that is left over when you blow stuff up and can also be found just lying around. You mostly spend the salvage upgrading your character, but you can also unlock cheats like infinite ammo or vehicle weapons (guns that are usually mounted on vehicles but you can now use when walking around).
Speaking of vehicles, there are a bunch of times when you get into an EXO suit or an assault walker and run around blowing stuff up with your heavy weapons. In the Path to War DLC for the game, you spend most of the time in vehicles. The DLC adds about 2 hours more gameplay and a few easy achievements.
I haven’t tried the multiplayer much since the game has been out long enough that nobody’s playing online anymore. You can use the “Infestation” game mode to grind for more salvage since Infestation shares the same unlocks as the single player campaign. Any upgrades you buy in Infestation (except cheats) can be used during the campaign and vice versa.  Infestation is a survivor mode where you just kill waves of aliens, which get more powerful as you progress. It can get boring fast though, since you don’t really get penalized for dying (and there’s nobody to play with).
Pros:
+Excellent graphics and story. The aliens are freaky looking and it’s always fun blowing stuff up. The game mostly takes place underground, but there are a lot of buildings that you can bring crashing down. The Nano Forge can also repair broken things, so if you accidently destroy a ladder or stairs, you can rebuild it in seconds.
+In one playthrough of the game you can unlock most of the skills, and there is a new game+ option where you can start over, keeping everything you bought. During the second playthrough you’ll get enough salvage to unlock all the upgrades you missed, plus a couple of cheats, which can be used for higher difficulty levels. The cheats do NOT disable Steam achievements.
Cons:
-Multiplayer is dead. You won’t find anyone to play with online unless you set it up beforehand.
-Like most over the shoulder games, you might get a headache the first few times you play. It varies by person though, and you’ll get used to the perspective eventually.
Overall, the game is great and you should give it a try if you haven’t already. A lot of people probably got this game from the THQ bundles back when THQ was going out of business. The main game takes maybe 7 hours to beat, so you can finish it in a weekend and rake in a few Steam achievements while you’re at it. You get about half the achievements just playing through the game one time.
Still a fun game, even if it isn't open world like Red Faction Guerilla.

The Long Dark. Frankly the title lie a bit becase its only dark half the day, except in buildings with poor natual lighting, and I die after 5 in game days. A truer title world be "rather cold and hungry" because this is a mid-winter wilderness survival game, a very good one. Now, don't get any ideas about easy crafting and building, becuase the game doesn't have buiding, this is survival in the traditonal sense; go into house to scavange food, find fire wood, stay away from that wolf, ect.
Let's briskly go over the technical stuff:
It's not a big budget game nor does it over reach. The devs don't make the graphics as realistic as possible because of design choises such as PC profomance. I for one love the graphics, they complement everything well... yes I'm ignoring the player models in this reveiw but it something i find better to "sweep under the rug". There's other things: sound and atmospheric music, voice acting to alert the player if their inevitable doom is inching slightly faster than 30 minutes ago, but its all just there to complement the other parts of the game like wolf and bear mualings. Ok, maybe the music deserves special mention so here: its good, but too short.
Nothing on gameplay I hear you say? Never threat, there's gameplay! I often found the Long Drak's gameplay true to life: harsh and unforgiving. It's as if it took the survival gonre seriously... that's because is does, unike many other survival games. The best example i can think of is my latest play of it, it lasted 15 minutes becuase of cold and wolfs, mostly the cold. So, quick survival tip for long dark: stay inside as long as possible, you are more likely to die from cold then the wolfs/bears. I could turn the dificult settings down but the three difficulties have some leaps between them, from: walking around and taking pictures like a tourist, to, death for looking at the snow's general direction.
It's fun for the time when you are alive and doing well and challenging  when everything isn't too great, which in some ways is a metaphor for life cwaling for survival tooth and nail as i take another sip of whiskey and recline in my comfy chair whilst I wait for my character to wake up from sleeping in a dead person's bed.
Quite easily the best, most immersive, and most challenging survival game I've ever played. There's nothing like it.

I bought this game because I like Stealth.  I love the Thief series.  Deus Ex.  Metal Gear.  If I can sneak and outsmart my enemies, I'm all in.
This game makes that rather difficult.  Each of my untimely demises brought about a story, and made me shout.  Each time I was able to crouch behind a bush, tree, fence, and watch the search lights of the enemy sweep past my hiding spot, I got a terrified little thrill.  There's a lot of sneaking, and searching, and standing out in the open trying to find the next waypoint, but it all leads to moments like that.
I ran into a small copse of trees to hide from several pipe-smoking robots out looking for me.  As I slipped further into the trees and into a low swampy area, I heard this sound.  It was errie, something new, and difficult to locate.  I peeped around the large tree I was hiding behind, and saw this big, round, shadowy figure slowly plodding through the swamp with the help of a cane.  I had no idea what he could do.  What his attacks were.  How well he could see.  I only knew he was taller than I was, with round, white eyes, and that huge cane.  I hid from him, not because I knew what kind of threat he posed, but because I DIDN'T know, and that was much more frightening.
That's what Sir, You are being Hunted does best.  It leaves things up to your imagination.  It is very much in the ilk of Brittish Movies like, "Cold Comfort Farm," were one of the characters constantly says, "I saw something nasty in the wood shed," but all they show you is her peering into the shed, and her screaming in terror.  Well, I saw something nasty in the water, and I'll never go for a swim there again.
I recommend this.  It's a slow, creeping, cornered by wolves sort of game, and I've greatly enjoyed playing so far.  Give it a shot!

is a bad game that could probably become a good game with just a few more weeks of tuning on the part of the developers. The open nature of the game allows for varying play styles, but any player is going to spend their time on some balance of sneaking, looting, fighting, and collecting artifacts. Most of these activities are quite badly implemented at present.
The sneaking is the selling-point of the game and thereby the most disappointing. A "visibility" meter indicates how easily enemies can see the player's avatar, but the meter flatly contradicts the apparent terrain. The avatar can be 0% visible in foot-high grass, and it can be 100% visible in a dense thicket. Aside from simply memorizing all the different plant models, there's no way to intuit a concealed way through the landscape.
The looting is not glitchy
, but it is tedious: some 90% of the loot is useless (and marked as such), and loot-areas are often clustered in identical-looking buildings, making it hard to remember which caches are picked-over and which may still hold riches. Food is so scarce that the player must spend a third to half their time in pursuit of it instead of going after the artifacts that are the ostensible focus of the game. Other essential types of loot are rare to the point of being absent. (After two hours of game-play, I've yet to find a means to light a campfire for cooking the copious amounts of raw meat I've acquired.)
The combat aspect is reasonably well developed by comparison, in that guns behave in an intuitive and non-glitchy fashion, but no matter how satisfying the gunfights are, they're necessarily a secondary aspect of the game because, even with a very agressive strategy of mowing-down most or all enemy robots early, the shuttling of artifacts requires so much time (due to a strict limits on inventory size) that food becomes an urgent requirement and the tedious process of looting cannot be avoided.
Sadly, if you're looking for a game that offers ponderous weapons, kooky loot, rotten eggs, metal men, and proceedurly generated terrain, you'll find a much more complete and satisfying experience in
.

A friend of mine did complain about how the game can't be played on multiplayer unless you're online on Steam community though.

I have my coffee, a joint teetering on my lips, and the sun hasn't broken the horizon outside. Soft notes slide off the speakers, and the holo-display in front of me is alive in neon. A facility halfway explored by three scared transients:
The door slides open. The first second is always breathless. Is this room a payoff? Another thirty seconds of tranquility in this hell-hole, or are the klaxons already sniggering in the wings, knowing that they are about to herald a spectacle that has been repeated over and over, my comrades and I fighting for our lives. Sure, we thought we were well equipped thirty minutes ago, thirty minutes ago we lost Gork. By the time they were done with him he looked like he'd turned his gun on himself and held the trigger 'til it ran dry.
Now it's just the chain smoker and the bug. I like the woman, her cigarettes remind me of hot oatmeal on cold mornings in old hotel rooms, the ones with the curtains made out of that really thick material. Yeah, you know, hotel curtains. The lady can bang soul out of any machine she touches too, let me tell ya, for profit or protection. The bug is unnerving. He moves too fast, clicking this way and that. He saved me with that spear of his though, two levels down. I guess I owe that chilling speed that. He doesn't talk too much, but I wont turn down another set of hands...claws.
It's not all bad, we've met some others down here, some wanting to come along, some just trying to turn a profit. Some of their screams are still ringing in my ears, not able to hide from the seething horde when the door slid open. Guess we'll never know.
We only have six more floors to go. I haven't told the others, but our only food generator was busted in the last push. Only two of us are making it off this floor...
*Transmission End*

Dungeon of the Endless was a game that I was avoiding. Tower Defense wasn't my "scene" and the pixelated (albeit stylized) graphics didn't grab me either. However, many of my gaming friends at "Octopus Overlords" were raving about it, so I eventually gave it a try. And I'm glad I did.
In the game, your crew of heroes must explore a floor of a spaceship to find the exit. Then, they must transport the generator/crystal to the exit to progress to the next floor, and ultimately exit and win the game. What really hooked me were the RPG elements built in to the game, where you can upgrade and customize your crew members, also outfitting them with weapons and gear. The random nature of each floor and the included encounters/events/surprises appealed to me too (but then, I'm a sucker for Rogue-like games). Lastly, as a gamer with a family, it's nice that each floor makes a satisfying, quick play session - convenient for when real life calls. (There is a "Save & Quit" option if needed mid-level).  And I haven't even gotten to the point where I've unlocked all of the ships and crewmembers to use.
Drawbacks: The tutorial is short and not entirely helpful. I had to check the wiki for clarity on some of the game basics. (i.e. - Opening doors are the "turn" mechanism; You manually choose to level characters from their inventory/stat screens;etc.).  I haven't attempted multi-player, though it seems people are reporting problems at this date. (The developers are continuing to address this with patches.) I've not encountered any technical problems, on my mid-level gaming laptop.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. It's surprised me with how much fun it has been, once I got the hang of it. To win me over to a genre that I usually avoid is high praise, in my opinion. My last thought (again, shared by an Octopus Overlord member): "Easy" level is hard. "Very easy" is normal. Don't be afraid to start there.

Ok so here it is. After about 200+ hours of gametime including Alpha, beta, and 2 months after release. Now while I give it a thumbs up, I would only purchase this game if you have a huge need to Commence in 4V1 Combat. If you don't but are looking for a game that you can sink hours into and then stop playing, I would recommend you wait for it to be on sale. If you are looking for more info, Continue reading.
Altogether, I would say this is a great game for people looking for a game to play with friends or as monster only. Monster gameplay is quite fun but eventually, you will most likely get bored of playing this game even if you play with a team. The main thing that I have had a problem with in evolve is that the new monsters and hunters are extremely slow in being released. The last update gave us four hunters and one monster and, while they got me into playing the game for another 20 hours or so, I quit again soon after they were released simply because the new characters did really add anythign new to the game. Yes, they have new abilities, yes they are well designed and yes I have a bunch of fun playing them, but they didn't really add anything to the game.
The game is simply beautiful. Unique environments, beautiful characters, great effects, altogether, just a very beautiful game. I think it is hard for anyone to dispute that. However, Between tryign to find the monster or hide from hunters, you may find it hard to enjoy the scenery. Just know that it is there and the detail is astounding.
For people looking to understand the lore of the game, you will have to play alot of game and listen to the hunters interact with each other and read lore online as there is no story mode. It doesn't look like there will ever be one which I personally find dissapointing as I want to know more about the planet Shear and how or why the monsters are there. It is really dissapointing that there is NOTHING to try to explain these events besides the chat that normally happens before a match begins.
The only thing that could possibly be called a story mode is evacuation which is a joke. You play with 4 other people with someone randomly getting the monster and then you travel around Shear and play different gamemodes such as Nest, Rescue, or hunt (everyone always picks hunt so good luck finding a different gamemode) and you either lose or win and depending on what perk is randomly chosen, the next map will either work against you or work in your favor. After 4 rounds, you come to a defend mode, which is essentually castle defense where the monster has the monions and is trying to kill your towers so it can destroy your castle and you, as the hunters, must try to delay it. if you kill the monster or ime runs out, hunter wins, if you kill the feuling station(castle) as monster, you win! !!!!!!(SPOILER)!!!!!!  Did the monster win every round? Well to bad, looks like you and all you fellow hunters get to die very painfull deaths. Were you the hunters and won every single match? COOL!, Your characters still die in the end! Honestly this evacuation mode is a joke and the game would have been better with a story mode...

"A brawl is surely brewing!" Cuphead may look like your standard old-fashioned cartoon, being most comparable to Disney's Mickey Mouse in "Steamboat Willy", however the game is by no means as simple as it first may look. In fact, the game has already been compared to the infamously difficult "Dark Souls" series. The game takes the form of what is essentially a boss rush, with the occasional platformer level sprinkled in amongst the game's threeworlds and finale. Progression in this game is relatively simple- defeat a boss, collect it's soul contract. Then, when all of the soul contracts in a specific world are collected, move onto the next world, rinse and repeat. Although three worlds may not sound like a lot of content, the game has a ton of replayability, as an in-game grade system challenges you to try to get the highest grades as possible, and doing so may even unlock a hidden reward. The mechanics are very easy to understand, parry pink objects, dodge enemy attacks, and wallop the bosses using your primary shooter, secondary shooter, EX attacks, and supermoves, yet the bosses challenge you to master each of these mechanics if you want to get by. As I mentioned earlier, there are a couple of secrets in the game- which I will not spoil here- that drives the inner completionist in me. After owning Cuphead for a couple of weeks now,  I can say that I have had a blast with the game. I've already beaten the game on it's default "Regular" difficulty, however I am looking forward to attempting the game's "Expert" mode. Some of the bosses certainly pushed me to my wit's end, but the game is supposed to be a challenge, and you must learn the enemy patterns as well as make use of your arsenal of skills and weapons to overcome it. Overall, I certainly recommend Cuphead for those who are looking for a challenge. The game is by no means easy, but that's where the fun comes from in Cuphead. "Bravo!" 10/10!

My first experience with this was short lived.
I ran outside of my front door and wielding a trusty baseball bat, attacked a group of zombies. I was 'scratched and bleeding' on the foot and I couldn't find, or figure out how to bandage myself. So I died.
From a cut on the foot.
Second character starts to freeze to death within just a couple of minutes of playing, so I get together some materials for a camp fire and make it in the safety of my bathroom. 30 seconds later my character is running around the garden being chased by zombies with his legs on fire, watching his house burn to the ground.
Third character survived for a long time. I found a warehouse and wanted to look for axes or sledgehammers but there were too many zombies around. So I lured them all to follow me, planning to trap them inside a house and then run out the back door. An excellent plan!!
I opened a house door, ran inside and the zombies started pouring in, an excellent plan I thought!! Wait, where's the back ♥♥♥♥ing door???? There is no back door. Cue Laurel and Hardy music as I sprint circles around the living room as more and more pour in the door. By the time I'd remembered that I could climb out of a window it was too late.
My first multiplayer experience with this was like an episode of The Walking Dead.
I created my character, an illiterate clumsy oaf with incredible strength and tough skin, and then spent the next 6 hours trying to get the server to work. (if you've tried everything but still can't get it to work- on the router settings make sure the device the game is connected with is your IP, not your local machine IP, or your router's IP, but your IP. Not your public IP. Damn it's complicated. For me it starts with 192.... but there are two of those, one with 256 at the end, the other with 140 at the end. The 140 one is the one I connected the game to and then it worked.)
But nevermind that.
My character's name is Rick Grimes. I ran out of my door taking a bunch of food with me and sprinted down the main road, leaving a bread crumb trail so I don't get lost. I find a huge warehouse where I scavenged a few planks and hammers, a buttload of nails and duct tape, and also somehow managed to FALL DOWN THE STAIRS, breaking my leg.
I ripped up my vest into sheets and tied a wooden plank to my leg as a makeshift splint. Sorted!
My friend at this moment managed to log in. We cheer! But then sigh as he has spawned in a house filled with zombies and the doors and windows are barricaded shut. WTF??? He screams. He sends me a voice message telling me he's already getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with the game and that he's about to log out.
Hold on!!! I tell him.... just hold on!!
I go online, load up the map of the area and tell him to take a picture of his house zoomed out. I manage to match up this quirky looking road out front of the house to where it is on the map and..... holy♥♥♥♥♥♥balls. It's miles away.
Nevermind the distance, I thought! I'm going to rescue my friend!! Hang tight, I tell him, I'll be there soon!
As soon as I start sprinting I realise that a broken leg in this game actually means something.
So 45 minutes later, I arrive at his house. To my astonishment, he's actually managed to take down the 5 zombies in his house with his bare hands and he's just been waiting there starving to death.
The feeling of seeing him stood there, through the crack in the barricades on the window, was pretty amazing. My friend called it a Golden Gaming Moment.
I looked through my inventory and♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. I don't have a hammer... I can't take down the barricades. So I start wailing on them with a golf club. Bonk. Bonk. Bonk. Nothing.... panicking that he's going to have to wait another 20 minutes for me to find a hammer, I remember my schoolbag. I open it and.... ah yeah there's my hammer.
I take the barricades down and I know for a fact if there was a BROHUG emote in the game we would be spamming the hell out of it.
We survived for a good hour and a half before we started to get cocky trying to take down small hordes of zombies around our safe house. I got scratched and cut on my leg and arm. Bandaged up no problem. But my friend got bitten on his chest and it was deep and needed rebandaging every 2 minutes or so. He was losing health.
Instead of continuing to back away from this horde, we stupidly decided to carry on trying to exterminate it one zombie at a time.
I got scratched on the foot again and decided to just back off and give up, but due to miscommunication, my friend decided to balls out try and kill them all by himself. He got swarmed!! I managed to push them all away and I went rampant as they swarmed him, managing to knock down or kill the last of them.
My friend's waddling around leaving a trail of blood.
HOLD STILL I yell to him as I frantically begin the medical check.
He has 4 injuries and is already half dead. I bind one wound- OK. Another wound- OK. I bind the third wound..♥♥♥♥♥♥! That wasn't a wound, I just took off a dirty bandage!!! At that moment, he dies. If I had bound the last wound instead of unbinding the old wound, he would have lived, but in the heat of the moment I couldn't focus and I got him killed.
There's silence. I head back to his safe house with the barricades and I take all of the best food we have scavenged so far from the fridge, with a plan to rendevous with him at his new spawn location.
His new character spawns, incredibly luckily, in MY safehouse. Barricaded windows. Two story for look outs. Sheets over everything to stop any zombies peeking inside. TONS OF FOOD IN THE FRIDGE.... oh and a bunch of turd weapons and backpacks. Sorted.
I run back to meet him and we begin our plan of scavenging the streets for food and stockpiling it all over again. But this time, his character looks like Patrick Stewart.
And my legs still broken.
Next time we play, the plan is to get a small farm going, build a wall around the house to further protect it, and head out to try and find some assault rifles or axes.
I honestly can't wait until they add cars and NPCs into the game. It's going to be incredible!!!
My friend came up with an awesome idea also, that there should be little missions that happen randomly like the power can just randomly cut off in a large area. Meaning that you have to go to a power plant or something to essentially fix it yourself. I added that without good electronics skills, you would have to just flip the switch, which would turn the power back on but it would set off a loud alarm which would make escaping and getting home difficult.
The hints that the military are going to be implemented and ideas about being able to sit in the back of pick up trucks shooting zombies while your friend drives around are the reasons why I've given up on all farming / survival games in favour of this one for the foreseeable future.
Check it out guys you won't be disappointed.

While TLD is impressively atmospheric, with a great color scheme and immersive music and sound effects, it's unfortunately equal parts frustration and joy. It is a shame, as well, because The Long Dark has a fantastic baseline to work with: it simply needs some tweaking, balancing, and those ever-elusive Early Access Updates. Seeing as this has been EA for several years, I wouldn't hold my breath.
First off, TLD is a survival purist game: no zombies, almost no building, with focus on maintaining health "Condition" via Rest, Food, Thirst, and Warmth. But then comes the problem: even in Voyager mode, (normal), you are at the mercy of RNG from spawn onward. The gear you spawn with, the weather, the daylight hours remaining upon spawn, fire starting chance, etc. etc. is at the mercy of the RNG, and you may very well find yourself FUBAR from the get-go or with only an in-game day's worth of bad rolls after several in-game weeks of smart play and success. You may be doing well, have yourself a stock pile, and so on, then the fish steal all your lines, the fire refuses to start, the wolves move in to munch on your face, and you get surprise frostbite after the wolves nom on your gloves. GG.
On top of the extremely demanding requirements to survive, like pathetic run distance, massive food needs, etc. the in-game interface and inventory is rather alien, with no real introduction as to how to use it. This can leave someone already strapped to survive confused as they have to figure out just how the game works. And just when you think you've got it all figured out, then you come to the realization that there is permanent in-game damage that can sneak up on you as the game calculates overall body temperature, while your limbs get frostbite.
Can the game be polished out? Absolutely. Will it? Doubtful. But that's really all it needs for the sandbox mode. The Story mode, which is promised, is even less likely to come.

While they are taking their sweet time with the release of story mode, I can't bring myself to give a negative review for a 20€ game that has provided me tens of hours of fun in the sandbox mode. Also, anyone calling The Long Dark abandonware or Hinterland scammers is a dirty liar and they know it. Story mode IS coming out and the sandbox mode has been actively updated with new content, bug fixes and whatnot.
Overall, The Long Dark is a great example of Early Access done right.
Shortly put: This beautiful game is fun and well designed on all levels, powerful ambiance and immersion. Well worth your time and money.

As mentioned before, it always jumps me when somebody's out the door, even when the game is near mute and I'm expecting it.
Overall, this game can be considered a jack of all trades but a master of none. You can get a chuckle out of it if you're in a less scared or panicked mindset, or this game can increase your heartrate by 50 if you let it. This is just my opinion, though. The experience could be very different for different people.

This is a very polished games, and I like polished games. Not only is it a polished game, it's a fairly fresh and original game. However, it's a tad repetitive game, and there are cases where losses largely feel like the result of bad luck (after you get the hang of the game, that is). Despite that flaw, the game still is entertaining for many hours.
The game is largely based on resource management expressed in tower defense, rogue-lite, and base-building fashions. You have to keep enough rooms lit to keep the monster spawns under control, while deciding which resource to prioritize, what to spend the resource on, which heroes to bring/keep, so on and so forth. The game gives the player a lot to think about and consider allowing for a variety of strategies. Dungeon of the Endless does something better than most rogue-lites, it actually makes you feel like you're slowly falling apart and losing control of the situation. Although there are a few examples where the map layout more or less screws you over, or you just don't get the natural resources our layout to function. Most of the time each death is the result of your own mistakes over a few floors.
However, the game can get a bit dull. There are not that many unique events or rooms you can come across, and the ones that you do find are pretty mild. Items are also pretty uninteresting. Lots of runs may seem familar. There is one almost genius remedy, however. In all but one modes of the game, you only pick half of your team of four heroes at the beginning, and you find and hire the other two as you play along. This makes it so you almost always play a different team each match, keeping each match a bit different, and keeps you waiting in anticipation to see what your team can be.
This is largely because most of the heroes are all relatively unique, although all could be filed into about four catagories (operator, tank, DPS, or speed/crystal carrier). Still, almost all are different enough to warrent experimentation, save two or three characters. That's coupled with handful of different "pods," which are basically modes. Either way, AMPLITUDE makes an effort to keep their game going a dozen hours in. Even at asking price, I would recommend this game. Not that you would. This is Steam, after all.

Evolve has a really nice concept which is made extremely well. The game works and has few to no glitches/bugs and the gameplay feels smooth and nice. My only gripe with the game is the price of the core game and all the DLC. This would have been so much better and it could have achieved a bigger playerbase if the price was around 20-30€ and cheaper DLC. I mean 7€ for a Hunter and 15€ for a Monster is just ridiculous when the game itself is 50€. It feels like an overly hyped cash-in that's actually good. It could have been so much more.

After having played this game for some months now, I wanted to re-write my review. First of all, Evolve truly is my favorite game to play right now. I absolutely love it! For those of us who are big fans however, we may be a "cult following", as it were. At least it seems that way from a lot of the other user reviews. Unfortunately, because this game's life depends on perfection almost, those less patient or less forgiving of certain aspects will dismiss Evolve very quickly.
Again, I personally LOVE this game and will continue to support it, and reccommend it. But here are my main issues..
DLC - expensive and silly structure does make you feel kind of ripped off after paying premium price for the game - skins just cost too much! Considering that skins are the main "evolving content" of this game, along with new monsters and hunters (which I hope they continue to regularly release), the price point is just too high for the devs to depend on in order to keep people happy about new content. (New skins are coming out frequenly, and some of them are admittedly pretty damn sick.) Ideally, they should continue to add new challenges for players to earn these skins for free. (Currently elite skins are the only "achievable" unlocks once you reach lvl. 40. Which doesn't take that long really, to get to lvl 40.) I will say, that I am glad they are not making players pay for new maps (currently anyway. They just released two new maps for free.)
Unlocks/Goals/Achievements - Along with my point above...While there are a number of different badges you can unlock and customize, again, it does not take long to unlock most of them. And there certainly could be more. Hopefully they continue to add new visual elements to badges. Quite simply, seasoned players need more rewards for playing!! While there are weekend challenges that award players FREE skins, which is great, there needs to be more. (:
Bugs - Yes. There are bugs. Dead players seem to frequently fall through the map, making Lazurus a gamble as to whether or not you'll contribute much to your team's victory (Laz can bring dead-dead players back to life within a limited amount of time after death.) Furthermore, it's been reported that at least one of the perks does not function properly (perks are movement speed boost, reload speed boost, jet pack boost, etc.) I have also played several games where one player will start the game in midair and never land, forcing you to restart the match. Not a HUGE annoyance, but still. Wall climbing with the jetpack can stand to be tuned as well. There are a few other minor bugs that don't affect the gameplay too much as well, but they are still there.
Missing Community Content - As of this writing, you are unable to friend other players through Steam/Evolve. This is just dumb. Considering there does seem to be a limited number of people playing online, not being able to friend those that you work well with really hurts this game. I cannot even view "current game's players" or "past game's players". This needs to be fixed ASAP.
A few other things -
Personally, I think it would be nice to have a "sandbox" mode, where you can hop into different maps and just run around lol Especially for new players, it could help get a sense of the maps, hiding places, strategies, creatures on Shear, etc. for both human characters and monsters alike.
There is currently a companion app/game for iOS and Android that allows players linked to Evolve to watch past matches with the aeirial view. This is a neat feature. It would be nice if this feature were included in the main game as well, without requiring the phone app. (I'll admit, the phone game is kinda fun though, and does tie to the main game to help you level your characters. It is a freemium game though, of course...)
Also, a monster v. monster mode would be AWESOME! I can't imagine this would be *that* hard to pull off, though the monster attacks are tuned of course, towards human ememies. But if they could make it work somehow, this would be a fun addtion to toy around with. Similarly, since they've added an "observer" slot already, it would be kinda cool if there were a 6th PLAYABLE slot in the game, in which another player could take over a minion and assist his monster friend in battle...just a thought.
Additional Game Modes would also be welcome. Currently, Hunt, Nest, Defend and Rescue are the only different game modes, which can be played together in Evacuation, which is a five round match which players play through all of these modes. Perks are added to the next map depending on if the monster or the humans win - it's a pretty neat feature. However, I hope they add more modes to keep things interesting.
END NOTES:
Overall, Evolve is a brilliant game with great replayability on its own simply due to how much FUN it is. However, for many hardcore gamers the lack of extensive achievable/unlockable content may limit Evolve's shelf life. The dev's biggest issue is RETAINING players, which consequently will affect how many NEW players they get. Bascially, keep your village happy and more people will want to move into it! lol I DO reccommend this game to anyone interested. Don't let the haters scare you away, but DO be aware of the things I have mentioned above. As I said, despite of all this, Evolve is still my favorite game to play right now, and I imagine will be for quite some time.

This game is, hands-down, the greatest zombie survival game I have ever played. Once it is finished, it will be everything I want it to be.
The Project Zomboid devs have updated this game a lot, but the playerbase seems pretty dead unless you want to be on a whitelisted server. It's still a fantastic Zombie Survival game, but it seems to be getting buried since it's in an oversaturated genre, and GRAFIKS kiddies are turned off at (seemingly) basic graphics.
Sounds: 8/10 Sound is very important in this game as a gameplay aspect, and the in-game sounds have been improved a lot since the game came out. The music is good, but I usually turn it off with the 'm' button to listen to some of my own.
Gameplay: 10/10 You're in the small home you've claimed as part of your scavenging. You used to want a larger one, but you've learned that they're harder to fortify. You've got boards nailed across the windows, using the precious few nails you nearly died to get out of a garage. Under the sink are the canned goods you managed to scavenge. It'll get you through the day, and maybe the next one. The bathtub upstairs was filled with water, along with the sink, but only half of the sink is left. You've been drinking soda you managed to pry out of a vending machine. your arm is bandaged from where you cut it climbing through a broken window when you couldn't find an easier way to get into a particularly enticing convience store. Every evening, before you collapse from exhaustion, you sneak around in your yard, making sure the thousands of undead in the city haven't noticed your home yet. The baseball bat you've been using is a major upgrade to the golf club which broke apart days ago, but even it's beginning to look shabby. You may have to use some of that duct tape and pray it holds together longer, or look for a sporting goods store. You climb into bed, the room darkened with sheets over the windows, praying that they don't find you in the night, that you can hold on for just one more day.
-Graphics 4/5 Completely servicable. Clean, crisp, and not incredibly complicated. I really don't need the highest-tier CRYENGINE. This isn't a first person game, and I appreciate that. It has a unique aesthetic. My only complaint it that, even after all of this time, some of the graphics are still placeholders while they sort things out.
-Replayability 8/10 The maps are the same, but where you start in them are random. Your character is customizable, and the loot generation is random. Even better, you can customize the zombies (speed, strangth, sense of smell, infectiousness, etc.) It does start to wear after a while, but then you can always paly on a server online, if you can find one with people.
-Cheese -0/5 No cash shop, so no cheese penalty.
Total Score 30/35 This is a fantastic game, and I give it my highest recommendations. The devs pay attention and update regularly, so it's always getting better.
Although I await the day it gets off of Early Access. I BOUGHT THIS YEARS AGO PEOPLE!

I bought this game a while ago and found it enjoyable, and left it.  Just recently, I came back to it to see if there have been any major updates to the game.  Besides a few cosmetic updates, there really is no change.  Not to mention, the skill system is garbage.  The gun system is pretty dumb too.  For example, I found two rifles on a corpse with much ammunition, each gun having two seperate boxes.  Opened the first box, and not only does each bullet weigh .1 (so thats 4.0 added when opening a box), but I used approximately 30 rounds before I killed a single zombie, while shooting into a crowd of zombies at close range.
Shortly after, my character had become tired, but I was on the path to nowhere as stated before, so I kept following hoping I'd find a house to sleep in.  Over this course of time, I had become exhausted, where the text said I was in danger of passing out.  To me, passing out would be great because I couldn't find a goddamn bed, so I fast-forwarded the time.  About a day later, my character is still in danger of passing out, but he never did.  From then on, I sprinted down this endless path because I saw no zombies around me and figured I would get to wherever quicker.  Then, the most annoying part of this game, ultimately, the reason I am angry and writing this review, is because my character got tired from running so much.  A strange voiceover of a man panting became more obvious in the background, and I figured, oh okay, it's just because I'm tired from running, I'll take a break.  The sound kept looping...no matter what I did. I fast-forwarded time another day ahead (I still didn't pass out), and the game still kept playing the tired voiceover, and I was still tired from running.
From that point on, I decided to just eat all my food and fast forward so I wouldn't die of starvation (Unless that's just another empty threat like passing out).  4 Days after I had first fast-forwarded for being exhausted, I was still suffering from high exertion and exhaustion, with the voiceover of a panting man playing in the background.
Overall, this game is annoying beyond belief to me, because of the lies that it had told me.  "You will pass out," it told me, and I had never passed out after fast-forwarding a grand total of 4 days after that notification first alerted me.  "You need to take a break to recover," the game told me for sprinting too much, so I fast-forwarded a total of about 2-3 days, and I still suffered from overexertion.  In the end, I just threw a molotov cocktail at my feet and shot my remaining rifle ammo into the air, and uninstalled.
Fin.

The Long Dark is another type of game with original ideas. Much of the emphasis in the game is placed on survivability in a climate comparable to that of rural Manitoba during the winter season.
Having lived a primarily rural life, I am biased towards stating that this game is not an accurate simulation of outdoor survival in the Canadian winters. However, the basic principles of survival are simulated to an extent that the game is playable with a level of challenge that would not be present if it were to be a more accurate survival simulation.
For example, ever since lighters were invented, the younger generations of people in rural areas have replaced the use of matches with lighters, because lighters last longer, take up a smaller space than a comparable set of matches, produce a more reliable fire-starting flame, and if they run out of fluid, the spark-creating material in them is flint and steel, so they double as an ignition source and an accelerant all in one. Why they have been excluded from the game is beyond me, but I'm assuming that they would remove some of the challenge surrounding outdoor survival and perhaps make it less interesting for the city folk to enjoy.
I'm recommending this game because it's a unique piece of art and deserves to be played, even if you are like me and you know it's not accurate.
Pros:

- 100% original content. Not copied from other games.

Evolve's multiplayer mechanics are well balanced and no individual class seems overpowered. The addition of buffs for both sides  (monster and humans) is also nice. My initial thoughts about this game have been seeing Evolve as a "Pay to win" type of game but since playing it has changed my view dramatically. I like playing as all classes and the monster. The enviornments are well balanced and the attention to detail is very impressive. I will be playing more of this game and will continue to as it feels like a spiritual successor to Left 4 Dead 2.
Theres not much i have to say about graphics. Its a very good looking game and runs great on most hardware. I myself am on a 980 and it has no issues running Evolve.
If you have a 7.1 system definately play Evolve with it enabled. The sound quality and doppler effects with 7.1 is ASTOUNDING. Its nice hearing every little leaf moving around you in the enviornment and really gets you in the mood for a survival action game.
Overall if i was to highlight some flaws it would be...
-Amount of DLC at launch (obvious)
-Some controls can feel jerky at times such as evolving and trying to look around at the same time.
-The tutorial recommended before you play multiplayer, yet puts the annoying pop ups in your real game anyways.
Give the game a try before being so critical about it based on strictly dlc. Remember, Call of Duty does the same pre launch DLC bull that Turtle Rock did.

I've been very interested in this game for a long while. It was shaping up to be the zombie survival game I've always wanted. After playing it for the first time, I fell in love. It had the right amount of depth and realism needed to really make it special. You had to deal with all the struggles of surviving in a zombie outbreak, from not getting eaten alive by the zombies themselves to depression. The game also has a good amount of difficulty, even if the game is easy to learn and master after multiple playthroughs. Surviving for a skilled player becomes trivial. That's where the NPCs come in though, to spice up the playthrough.
And that's the reason why I am not able to recommend this game, unfortunately. I understand the NPCs the devs had planned were very ambitious (probably too ambitious for a small team) and need time to get right. I also understand that the devs have went through development hell, and that's also part of the reason for NPCs not being close to finished. However, it's been about 6 years since I started following this game, and I'm beginning to give up hope of ever seeing NPCs in this game anytime in the near future.
For me, NPCs are a big component of this game, and not having them just makes the game seem hollow. Sure, you have all this depth to this survival experience, but it's really hard to have the motivation to survive if you have nothing to survive for. I feel like NPCs are what would take this game and really turn it into something special. Unfortunately, the devs have decided not to reveal anything about NPCs until they are in their final phases of development. While I understand why they are doing this, it is causing many people who follow this game (me included) to lose hope of ever seeing NPCs in the game.
However, there is multiplayer. If you are the type of player who loves multiplayer survival games, then go ahead and pick this game up. It works very well from what I've played of it. However, I personally am a singleplayer fan, and so NPCs are what makes or breaks this game for me. Unfortunately, until NPCs are added (or we get any news about it in the upcoming months) I cannot recommend this game for anyone who isn't wanting to play multiplayer. While it is fun for a bit, the singleplayer will get old rather quickly.
My biggest fear is that they will start to focus exclusively on multiplayer rather than NPCs. I really hope this is not the case, as I've always wanted a good singleplayer zombie survival experience.

If there is a game that can tell that you are nothing but meat in a war is this one.
No game has ever given me the sense of morale, chills and terror as RO2.
When you join a 64 player server and a new map starts all you can hear is all your teammates charging to the objective, when you hear that you know that match needs to be won.
You can command your own Tank/Half-track (on certain maps that allow it) with different players occupying each role inside the vehicles, Yes you heard that right, no ridiculous 1 man inside tank that does-everything-at-same-time♥♥♥♥♥♥here. Your tank driver gets shot? Too bad, you have to move yourself to the driver seat and use the vehicle with a less than adequate crew count.
Being a machine gunner in this game is really fun, specially when you can use MG's like
that shred any Yuri on its path and the pure terror of the gun firing so many rounds is incredible. The game has a very nice mechanic where your gun barrel can get extremely hot and break the gun if you fire too much, too fast, requiring you to switch out the barrels.
You don't find your usuall CSGO/COD kid here. The rambo gameplay that works on other games will never work here. That's a bonus right there.
It is a blast playing with good Team Leaders. They use their brain to strategically order heavy artillery on a fortified area via radio & relay orders to squad leaders to go attack/defend certain locations via voice chat.
The game has actual suppresion mechanics. If you fire at a sandbag cover for example where 2 enemies reside, their vision will become extremely blurry/hazed/fuzzy and gray. This allows you to cover fire your teammates just by firing enemies cover while they move up.
With all this you got an authentic WW2 simulator.
If there was a version of this game with official developed VR support, you could probably get PTSD from play this in just a couple hours.
(Also note that every dlc has been free)

A clunky, ugly, Civilization-style 4X strategy game that is overly complicated and makes little effort to explain itself. Fallen Enchantress makes a big deal about its RPG elements, even including a win condition where you can practically play it as a single player RPG to defeat the ancient evil while virtually ignoring your in-game neighbors. You can also equip your (legendary) heroes with armor, weapons, and trinkets, put points into large active & passive skill trees, and use them to enhance your cities, increase your resources, or just go out and kill big monsters. However I feel all this added complexity takes away from the strategy elements of the game and are poorly explained; there is only ONE 10 minute tutorial for the whole game, with everything else explained through tooltips, brief popups and an in-game encyclopedia. In fact, many of the new game "tutorial" popups just link to the in-game manual's page on that topic.
If you can look past the low quality, repetitive music, terrible graphics with flat, undetailed textures and poor character models (why is everything so ugly when there are so many close-ups of your heroes?), clunky UI, and tinny SFX, you might have fun with this game. Fallen Enchantress is a very mundane 4X Civilization style strategy game that tries to be something bigger but is too underdeveloped to be worth playing.

Firstly, I didn't have a chance to play this when it originally came out and I also don't have too much experience with the 3rd person action adventure genre, so this opinion is relatively nostalgia or genre prejudice free.
My issues with the game are mostly related to technical difficulties when attempting to get it up an running:
Probably something a patch or two could fix but they seem to have abandoned this one. You could also work around the controller issue by mapping the buttons using a 3rd party software such as JoyToKey, but you can't make it analogue though. I played this on keyboard and mouse due to that limitation and it's not bad, I just would've liked to play on the couch in Big Picture mode.
Apart from those technical issues I could say that everything else about the game is good. The story and the characters are likeable and well-written. I particularly liked Uncle Pey'j, who is probably now one of my favourite sidekick characters in all games. Voice acting was pretty much spot on for each character, maybe little on a campy side with different accents and all that, but as long as it fits.. Same could be said about the music.
I was a little worried that the early 2000s 3D graphics haven't aged well, but luckily my worries were in vain: Especially character movement and facial animations have stood the test of time and overall the game is still a pleasure to look at.
I wasn't really a fan of the face to face combat sequences, which occasionally just turned into mashing fests with little to no idea which enemy I was targeting. Your character, Jade, also locks into enemies which can make her a bit hard to control in combat. Stealth sections were a nice change of pace though, and I didn't have too much trouble with the camera that seems to have been an issue for others.
Solid fun for 10+ hours. I'm joining the group of people waiting for the sequel.

Red Faction: Armageddon was quite a surprise.
I got it way back in the THQ Humble Bundle on December 6th of last year, and up until now went unplayed. What a fool I was not to have tried it until now! It's a great game, and to have gotten it in a bundle? *mindblown*
Armageddon is a Third-Person Shooter that puts you in the shoes of Ex-Red Faction member Darius Mason on the surface of Mars. After a series of events spanning a few years, you are set on the path to stop a madman from destroying the planet. Along you way you will face thousands of alien lifeforms hellbent on your demise.
But do not worry! You have plenty of weapons with which to arm yourself. The most notable of which is the Nano Forge, a glove-like apparatus that can not only project a burst of force ahead of you, knocking back anything in its way, but can also repair ANYTHING in your environment. Found an Upgrade Station or Weapons Locker, but accidently blew it up in a battle against aliens? Come to a broken bridge that halts your advance? NO PROBLEM! Just use the Nano Forge's Repair ability to fix everything right up in seconds! You will definitely make use of this tool because literally about 98% of what you see on screen (terrain, buildings, etc) can be blown to bits. Other nifty weapons include the trusty Shotgun, 2 different sets of twin pistols (standard Pistols and later the significantly more powerful pair of Banshees <3 ), and even a Singularity Cannon, which fires a mini black hole which sucks in all around it, then explodes!
One of the mose useful tools, but one that some might consider the game's way of "holding your hand", is the GPS. Simply hit tab and for a few seconds a path will be lit up showing you the way to proceed. For people who like to figure things out on their own, this may seem an annoyance or a turn-off, but for others who prefer the action, shooting, and storytelling, this won't be a problem at all.
As you play you will collect Salvage, which you can use to buy upgrades, which range from more health, faster reload times, extra Nano Forge abilities, or increased damage and effectiveness with certain weapons. There was even an upgrade that awards you Salvage when defeating enemies. The game will reward you salvage for exploring your surroundings, as you will find some in dark corners of each area. Just look down every path and around every corner!
All-in-all, Red Faction: Armageddon is an exciting shooter, which you will enjoy til the very end. The only downside is that I was able to complete the campaign in just under 8 hours, so it's a tad on the short side. But there are multiple game modes (like New Game Plus) and even a multiplayer I believe, to take the game further. I cannot comment on these because I just played the main campaign though.

When I first saw this games' screenshots I thought it was another crappy zombie game with nonesense graphics. Currently there are no npcs but they are working on that.
Anyway, your goal is survive as long as possible. You have to scour the entire map for food and weapons, while dealing with sickness, fatigue, sleep etc.. You can read books to boost skills, so there is rpg elements as well. There also TONS of mods out there now, so you can modify the game so much to liking (zombie count, zombie behavior, food, items, etc.) This is pretty fun, and it takes some strategy to last as long as possible.

The zombie survival genre. A wasteland full of FPS games that all go similar ways. it all feels like some mish-mash of minecraft and a unique idea or two. Do you have to tread the streets welding a measly spoon as your weapon of choice? Rember Zomboid does NOT play around, from the start the game makes sure you know it ain't screwin around
All I want you to take out of this review is that Zomboid is an amazing survival game that really does ask the question, will you survive the zombie apocalapse?
Also these devs are f*cking awesome, I always play on the opt-in builds and I rarely notice a bug. Do note, this game is not going to be done any time soon. Though that is to be expected with a four man team.

If you are old enough to remember Master of Magic from the glory days of pc gaming, and Age of Magic, you will know what this game is.  4X in a fantasy vein with great customization ability for factions and leaders.  Stardock has been doggedly working to improve the game since it's first incarnation as Elemental, so ignore reviews of earlier iterations and check out the more relevant (and very positive) critical reviews.
If you pick up FE:LH, there is no need to buy any of the earlier games.  As for DLC, though I have everything and enjoy them, the Undead faction DLC is the only one that really adds some enjoyable toys to the mix, unless you're like me and enjoy monstrous maps, in which case the map pack is worth picking up.
Like most Stardock products, the developers seem to honestly care about their creations and their fans, constantly tinkering with their games long after release, just like Microprose back in the day.  Never been disappointed with anything in their catalog.

Five Nights at Freddy's at one time was just an Indie game with a low profile; but nowadays, the series is huge. Everyone has heard of FNaF, and it's sorta become a current age thing. However; when it comes down to it, has popularity effected the game?
Gameplay is kept very simple; you take control of the Night Guard, and sit in your office. You have the ability to turn on door lights, shut the two office doors, check a map and observe the enviroment; however the building has limited power; so you can't be constantly staring at the camera; or slam the doors down the whole time. Your objective is to maintain the power until Morning comes.
Essentially; FNaF is a survival horror game; with 4 Animatronic characters; Freddy, Chica, Bonnie and Foxy; attempting to capture you. All 4 operate on their own AI set paths (Bonnie will always attack from the Left, Chica will only attack from the Right, Freddy will follow a set path to reach you which can only be slowed by finding the room he currently resides in, and Foxy is on a timer which slowly ticks down based on how often you check on him. Check on him too much and he'll rush, but don't check on him enough and he'll rush. Foxy always comes from the Left, Freddy from the Right). If you get caught by the animatronics; you're treated to a short jumpscare and shoved back to the main menu.
FNaF features 5 Main Levels, a bonus 6th stage, and a Customizable 7th stage. The main menu features 3 unlockable stars; 2 for beating Stages 5 and 6; and a final one for clearing Night 7 with all the animatronics maxed out (a task which borderline banks on luck).
Graphics are hit and miss; while the Animatronics are all well designed, different and scary; the images used for the cameras are static images with very little motion; with the exception of when the animatronics feel like messing with you. Still; they are rather realistic, adding to the unsettling depth of the game.
Sound design is decent; there's ambient sounds to give clues on where the animatronics are; and other tidbits; but there's little audio aside from Freddy's music box and the unsettling menu music. The story is also hidden amongst the game; with the mysterious Phone Guy giving you tips about how to survive while also helping you piece together the horrific tale of what happened in FNaF.
If you're into the lore; than the games are for you; Personally, I'd recommend the third game more; but the first isn't bad. At about 6.00$, it's not a bad game; but it comes hard to recommend unless you're bored; as FNaF quickly becomes tired and boring; this is sorta a game you'll play a few times, maybe trick your friends to play; and than it'll sit on your profile gathering dust. Honestly, there are Flash Games online for free; that are of higher quality than FNaF.

I have to admit that it became a little bit boring at first when I could play it outside of the Alpha or Beta, while I was blindly running around the map, only keeping an eye open for the monster. However, this is not how it was meant to be played. If you start reading the well elaborated creatures and beautiful areas it becomes a lot of fun, trying not to run around but to think forward and trying to slip into the shoes of the one playing the monster. Yet this is what many people are not doing. It becomes even more fun when you actually talk to your fellow hunters and work on a solid plan instead of just mindlessly fighting it. If everyone works on his her own, the monster is clearly in advantage. This is not, however, a fault of the game but of the players if there's no communication between them. That's why I almost only play together with other friends, which is kinda sad, but like I said not the fault of the game.
Many people also complain about the fact that when you play together with a friend that you can't play as a monster. Yet again, excluding the monster in that case was the only logical option to prevent friends supporting each other in getting achievements and leveling up, thereby ruining the game for the others.
For those who feel ripped off by the price: It is quite a high price for this game, I admit that, and that DLC stuff is something I dislike,
it has the exact content it promised, all DLCs announced in advance. You knew what you were getting for it, and yet you still bought it. Everyone has to evaluate for him-/herself if the price is worth it or not.
The hunters and monsters are well balanced despite what many others say. All you have to do is actually learning how to play them, how to react in different situations, and how to evaluate the situation in relation to your character and the environment (and the other characters in case of the hunters). You can't just learn how to play one of them and then expect to master them all. Some character might just be not your type, and some hunters work better together than others do. But it's a lot of fun in my opinion to find that out, how the different combinations work and how to adapt your playstile. In case of the monster: How to adapt your playstyle in different stages of a game and the hunters. It gets even more thrilling since you have to choose your character before you know what the enemies picks.
That does
apply for the new monster (Behemoth) and the 4th gen hunters right now (according to my personal experiences). But I'm confident that they will soon patch them up to an equal level as the others.
Additionally mentioned: I was experiencing no bugs since the game launched, and the game did not crash. That seems not to apply for everyone, but it works fluently in my case.
If you are ready to learn how that planet Shear works, how to read your opponent's mind and how to master the adaption to the millions of situations that this game can offer on those magnificent maps, all combined with rapid action and thrilling fights, then it might be a game for you!

What it adds is civilization elements such as choosing technological paths, civic production, and unit design.  What it loses is interesting combat, reasonable game lengths, software stability, and user interface.
There are some flaws that are particularly aggravating.  The game decides on its own when a player has completed his turn and  automatically enters the AI cycle, often when the player isn't completely finished.  The spells seem to range from worthless to overpowered without managing to make the combat more interesting.  Above all, a lot of turns are just spent doing nothing while waiting for construction to complete.
I'd suggest looking to King's Bounty: Armored princess or Heroes of Might and Magic III (or 4) before this game.

LYNE is a $3 puzzle game with a simple concept: connect all similar shapes, don't cross the lines.  There are 26 sets (A-Z), and each set has 25 puzzles, totaling to 650 puzzles.  It's also $3.
As you progress further in the $3 game, you can unlock a few things, such as different colour pallets, and daily puzzles.  The dailies are randomly generated each day, giving you access to two to three sets (that's 50 to 75 puzzles) on top of the others.  All for $3.
I was able to get nearly 24 hours of playtime out of this $3 game, and with the dailies, I can always go back and get a little more play if I so desire.  If you like puzzle games, I highly recommend this game.
...seriously, it's only $3, you don't even need to wait for a sale; that's cheaper than most fast food meals, and it's less likely to give you the runs.

At first I was only interested for the story mode to come, but then friends kept bugging me about how amazing the sandbox was, I wasn't biting it, it's just a survival mode in which you know you WILL die, looks like a fancy score based game to me, compare inches of ♥♥♥♥ by how long you can survive, but then articles kept coming, people still kept bugging me about how great the game was. Well, I decided to give it a chance before the final release to know what the fuss was all about. Man, it blew my mind.
First of all, it's not a simple game of survival, watch meters and number dwindle down as you starve, get tired or dehydrated, although, there is plenty of that too. What's incredible is how contemplative it is, you're always on the look for something yes, you need to keep moving, keep exploring, the world isn't safe, it's dying and it wants you to join it, it feels sometimes the only true warmth you'll ever find is the embrace of death. Outside time leaps, everything you do takes precious time and sunlight, harvesting wood, exploring, getting from point A to B, you're always freezing or going hungry, but then you find shelter, and you like the character can rest.
You still have to do something to be alive in a shelter, light a fire, cook food, boil water, but at least you can think, you can prepare your spirit for the terror outside. You have to survive, not because you want to prove something to anyone else, but out of spite, in a land that wants you dead, you want to rebel, you refuse to give up. But it's still respite, at a shelter you can think, plan your next day.
In a way it reminds me of Hemingway's old man and the sea, it's about an internal struggle, even if nature gets the final say, you'll wont rest easy, you'll kick and scream and in that defiance you can have your final laugh.
There is so much that can be said about this, even the play though that cemented my appreciation of this game could be a tale in itself, but for now it's enough, I wrote too much already.

The Long Dark is a lot of things, but most importantly: it's not another unfinished game on Early Access. This game is going places. The Devs work really hard, and this game has been virtually reinvented in the time I've owned it (about a year). Hinterland has laid out a roadmap for where they want the game to go in the future, and those ideas are being regularly implemented in updates every three to four months or so.
What are in the updates? New features and additions to the Sandbox mode, the best part of the game at this point while we wait in anticipation for Story Mode. The Sandbox is amazing. The wildlife simulations aren't perfect, but the whole weather systems and the places you can explore (mountains, lakes, mines, dams, scenic overlooks and seemingly endless forests) and the things you can do (kill deer, wolves, bear, craft items, balance cans of soup on the corpse in the camp office of mystery lake) are what makes this game great. The sunsets are surprisingly beautiful at the end of the world.
