It's as if "The Most Dangerous Game" by Richard Connell was brought to life - but with deadly british robots! The entire time you are constantly on edge, trying to survive and make tactical choices throughout the entire game (day and night cycles are equally nerve-inducing). All the enemies, items, weapons and encounters are unique, and the game gets harder as you progress towards successfully escaping the five inter-connected islands. Stealth is key to this game. If you do not like taking your time or being stealthy, then this game WILL punish you; you will find yourself running away from enemies or dying most of the time as a result.
Despite a few personal issues I had with the lighting and game mechanics (mainly item usage like the alarm clock or bottle), I believe this game was a quick, fun, and overall entertaining way to spend an evening. I was able to finish a complete game in a single day that lasted a little over three hours. Just know that those were very worthwhile hours though. To me, there is not too much immediate replay value, but I can see myself coming back to this game some future afternoon. There is also a multiplayer option outside of the single-player gameplay, but I cannot comment on this since I have yet to have friends willing to play it with me.
Basically, I know this game won't be for everyone, but it is a solid stealth-based game. Therefore, pick it up during a steam sale when you get the chance! Also, due to its relatively short single player, if you do not like it within the first hour or so, you can always get your money back from Steam. I hope this review helps you in making your decision to buy this game or not, but if you have any questions about the game before you purchase it, feel free to add me or leave a comment here about it.

Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes is a unique game that tries to combine major elements from two of the biggest and best turn-based strategy series in history, namely Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic. Just like in Civilization, you start by founding a city, you improve it with new buildings, and then expand by founding other cities and/or conquering other factions. But taking a cue from Heroes of Might and Magic, you explore the fantasy world with your hero(es), the battles take place in a separate screen and you can do quests to earn loot for your hero.
It’s a very interesting mix of two familiar concepts carefully designed into a surprisingly unique whole. For example, between dealing with other factions (whether you’re in war or not), you can scour the gameworld seeking out and completing various quests available to you whereas in Civilization there is not much to do in these moments except building your empire. On the flipside, it makes you miss certain elements from both Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic. For example, even though you get to research civics, military improvements and magic just like you would research technology in Civilization, Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes lacks the clear sense of progression. Or to use the city battles in this example, in Fallen Enchantress they are exactly the same as they are anywhere else on the map whereas Heroes of Might and Magic provides a compelling conquer/defend mechanic in its city battles.
It is perhaps unfair to compare this game so intensely to other games, but at the same time, there is no escaping the fact that these were very important and clear influences. The similarities aside, it needs to be pointed out that Fallen Enchantress totally nails the depth, scope and addictive nature that the genre absolutely requires. However, it does seem to favor the aggressive approach over the diplomatic one.
The production values are modest. The graphics are rather outdated, but this is offset to a point thanks to the truly wonderful and distinctive art-style. Unfortunately, there are no excuses for the sound design. The soundtrack consists of a scant few derivative fantasy melodies whereas the sound effects are just poor.
Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes is a deep and addictive turn-based strategy game which doesn’t quite reach the very top the genre has to offer and as such won’t keep you playing for years to come, but it does offer a surprisingly unique mix of gameplay elements that will definitely delight any fan of the genre.

The game was a huge hit in the Indie Horror category of games, getting 3rd place in the category for the 2014 Global game awards. Over hundreds of Youtubers have critiqued this game, and with the positive reviews in all stores sold I was intrigued in giving it a try.
The animations and graphics in the game is very limited since we have only the office and the security cameras to look at, but by no means were they dull. Like any Horror game, it has its nerve-racking moments and FNAF seems to induce profuse amounts of it. Every waking moment in playing this game will leave you trembling until 6:00 AM, with the only calming remedy being the sound of the timer once it’s morning or when you hear the ‘phone guy’ speaking. FNAF is a must-play for anyone who is engrossed in all aspects of a classic and/or simple horror game.

Note to the developers: Make multiplayer more stable. First, the game likes to desync in the multiplayer lobbies. Second, multiple times runs have been ruined by crashes (with people not being able to join in via an invite for some reason, thanks devs.), and people being stuck on the loading screen.
In the design department there is one thing that bothers me and that is unlocking characters in multiplayer. I understand that in single player it is good to have a challenge, and you only start out with two characters making recruitment make sense. However in multiplayer with a party of four, having the three room requirement ON TOP of the instability makes this a big problem.
You might ask, "Why not play single player?" My answer is that multiplayer when working is a lot of fun. Talking about strategies with your pals and then excuting them is great fun and where I think the game shines, but progress for us is slow because when we are not dying due to it being a genuinely challenging but balanced game, we are being kicked out  sessions prematurely.
Overall I think the game is a good buy for people who might enjoy this single-player. However if you are like me and see the appeal mainly in multi, then I can't recommend it whole heartedly.

Ragnarok Clicker and its origin.
most who leave a bad review claim this game is a "rip off of clickerHeroes without trying to hide it", True and false. Yes indeed it's the same engine, in fact the people who made clickerHeroes gave GRAVITY the permission to use the clicker heroes engine and helped them create RagnarokClicker. So now that we got that out of the way, let's start with the review.
Ragnarok Clicker is a Ragnarok Online themed Clicker game, complete with monsters, music, maps, cards, and character classes from the original ragnarok online game. It even has the ability for you to create a guild or join a guild just like the original Ragnarok Online, but in this case it's use is very different. It plays very much like a typical clicker game but it has its quirks and charm that make it different and appealing, especially to those who find love and Nostalgia in a ragnarok online themed game.
Would i recommend this game to others? yes and no.  Yes if you're familiar with RagnarokOnline and have nostalgia for it, or just enjoy clicker games in general. No if you don't like clicker games in general, you wont like RagnarokClicker.
If you never played a clicker game but have played RagnarokOnline, try it out
Personally i stick around for the Nostalgia and achievements, It's why i tolerate it. Others who have a passion for clicker games might find this game enjoyable more than i do, so please, if you like clicker games, try it out.
As for any devs reading this and want my suggestion?  Add even more Fields/Dungeons. There's the potential for Niflheim, Glast Heim, Prontera Maze, Amatsu Dungeon, Ayothaya Dungeon, Nameless Island, Thanatos Tower, Geffenia, etc. The game can get a little stale with the same field/dungeons it currently has, and thors dungeon/GhostShip have the same music...We need more Field/Dungeons!

A casual, fun pedestrian smashing romp through Cities, an airport, a countryside village and more. Carpocalypse Now is a more fleshed out and greatly improved sequel with plenty of playtime, and even existing multiplayer for those willing to set it up. Racing is a minor part of this title and most of the fun comes from upgrading your vehicles and destroying your enemies.
Carmageddon 2 released at the height of video game censorship in the late 90s, and instead of benefiting from the widespread but controversial publicity like the first game, it suffered low sales in Germany, the UK and elsewhere where the law and market made it harder to promote. It was also mostly disliked by critics at the time who criticized early technical issues, and it took a long time before Carpocalypse Now was accepted as a great game and classic in its own right.
Following on from Carma 1 and the updated Splat Pack edition, Carmageddon 2 added a huge number of new tracks, powerups, enemy vehicles, abilities and more, all under a much better engine that, due to some intelligent designs, still runs well today despite aging graphics. For me, this was a game that never got the attention and player-base it deserved at the time, and remains a cult classic.
The development company SCi were basically a collection of 8 young programmers and developers with varying skill levels and very little experience in launching a game. They went with the principle that "if it sounds like fun, let’s try and do it", as a result, there were crazy little things added to these games, like the Prat Cam, the
, and a number of weird secrets and mission modes. These help to add depth and humour to an otherwise flatter racing game.
* An amazing soundtrack with several tracks from Sentience and Iron Miaden. The original game release contained the uncompressed tracks which meant you could play the game CD on your CD Player/CDROM and just skip the game data as a single track.
* Incredible responsive handling and controls for the time which help controlling the cars remain a fun experience of itself.
* Arguably too easy a game due to the unrestricted customization and different play styles. The single player campaign can either be too hard or too easy depending on the way you choose to play, but a cast of difficulty modes would have worked better.
* The multiplayer framework used IPX, which was outdated even at the time of release and made multiplayer all but dead for most players. To this day, you need to use a private network like hamachi to play with friends.
Priced on Steam at £5.99/7.99€/$9.99 at the time of review, and with at least 9 hours of gameplay, multiplayer (via use of a private network like Hamachi) and plenty of replay value, Carmageddon is good value for money so long as the dated graphics and gameplay aren't a problem for you.
The previous title,
is available on Steam at the same price, and may be worth picking up if you've never played the classic before.
At the time of review, Carmageddon 2: Carpocalypse Now and Carmageddon: Max Pack are available together on GOG for the same price as either title alone on Steam, and may be a better choice.
* Carmageddon was originally intended to be licensed under the Mad Max movies, but after the developers were unable to find the company who owned the rights, Carmageddon was moved to match the Death Race 2000 movie license and was actually filenamed Deathrace.exe right up until release when the first movie license deal fell appart.

It's 4/9/2015, and Evolve is one day shy of two months old.  I just finished my first couple of rounds under the fifth patch, which is a bundle of hotfixes and balance changes to the four new hunters and new monster, Behemoth.  I've played this game almost every day since launch, around 240 hours, and it's just surpassed the greatest game in my Steam library for duration played.  After playing the Alpha and Beta both, I paid for the fantastically pricey Monster Race edition with the understanding I'd be "kickstarting" some four months of content releases which have already been flowing out the door.  Do I think it was worth the cost? Yes.
This game is daring as hell.  It's a multiplayer 4v1 game where a team of dedicated specialists hunt and kill a monster as it struggles across the map, feeding and evolving.  There isn't another game out there like it, and there may never be one again.  It's not a permutation or a derivation of any kind: it has elements of MOBA's, FPS shooters, and other strong design principles, but it is by itself a new genre of game, characterized by moments of quiet where every visual detail you take in matters, bleeding into loud, cataclysmic brawls where every misstep can mean brutal death.  Whatever new monster this thing is - it is fantastic.
Evolve has the unfortunate blessing and curse of being a AAA game; it couldn't have been made any other way.  It uses its fancy graphics and lush environments as more than mere decoration - your eyes and your ears are important tools here, and hunting monsters as an experience requires the fidelity this engine puts out.  But it's also a continuous content model game - the kind of business model you'd normally see in a cheaper F2P, selling characters at $7.50 (975 RP in LoL parlance) or bundled up in four for $20.00, with monsters running for $15.  The combination can be a little heavy on the pocketbook - it's worth every penny, but if you're sticking it out for a sale, I can see your reasoning.
Content-wise, it's got a core experience that's strong enough to last, and a continuous content model that should keep it fresh for as long as its supported.  The dream is clearly a MOBA-esque menagerie of monsters and hunters released over time, creating a bevy of team comps and unique experiences as it expands out infinitely in story and scope.  Under current support the content may only grow to be about twice as big as its release - but what's out is already fairly infinite in its permutations.  You could spend a summer on this.  I've already lost the spring.
It's hard.  It's really, brutally hard.  It's got a Dark Souls level learning curve, monster bosses with slow attack animations and clear tells but hard to dodge attacks, only run by clever human beings out to kill you while you coordinate with three pubs who are crucial to your success.  The early games can feel slow - until you learn how to dome and fight the monster well, the pace of action is glacial, instead of the intended rising/falling action curve that you see at the higher levels.  The learning curve on the game is an investment, and you will lose a lot until you start winning.
When you start winning?  Oh, victory is so sweet.  Your allies are your comrades-in-arms.  Your monster is the destroyer of worlds.  Every game is a tense round of back and forth, fight after fight after fight, with both sides getting black eyes before the final punch is landed.  Rounds end with monsters scraping out power relays on the final sliver of health, with daring minute long games of cat and mouse trying to catch that last living hunter before the dropship comes.  Everything is balanced on a knife edge, every game can be twenty minutes or five.  As a monster my games end in shakes and shivers, with all the raw adrenaline of having faced down four other clever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at once and won.  As a hunter, every man on my team is a hero, and the behemoth fallen at my feet the ultimate test of skill.
As game balance goes:  It's pretty balanced, and still balancing.  Wraith had a strong run in the first month before the first real patches came online, the new hunters were similarly strong and are now quite less so.  At this point, most every character is within a 5% winrate of each other and hunters/monsters typically run 52/48 one way or the other.  Of the five patches, three shifted the balance in significant ways, and a new micropatching system should allow for weekly updates.  Even the metagame has been tuned, with silent domes and traversal tweaks adding more consistent action to each stage of the game as monsters are more frequently trapped.
Because it's AAA, it's got a moderate amount of bugs cycling in and out of existence.  Matchmaking awkwardness, occasional through-the-map glitches, crashes, strange invisible spectator drones - nothing so common or bad as to ruin the experience, but worth noting.  Matchmaking can be tricky for duo or triple queues - it runs lovely for singles and quads, but if you're flying solo you should be prepared to play monster a lot.
For a game of this expense to take these kinds of risks is a thing worth noting.  The AAA industry in its current iteration may never produce something this daring or original again.  It is something unique and beautiful in its own right.  It is a thing nobody has seen before and that most are barely beginning to understand - flawed, but living, growing, and evolving.  Most of all, it's really, exceptionally, unbelievably fun - and it's worth your time and your money if you're willing to invest them.
Oh, and if you're hunting monsters - bring friends.  You'll need them.

I've been part of the Elemental odyssey since the early days of the paid beta for War of Magic.  As we all know by now, Elementa: War of Magic arrived in a pretty bad state and never recovered from its severe design deficiencies.  Stardock, being Stardock, refused to abandon their dream of a great new 4X fantasy game and released a stand-alone expansion, Fallen Enchantress, that tried to rectify what went wrong with the first game by cutting out lots of features of the original that just didn't work, and by enhancing what was left.  When all was said and done, while Fallen Enchantress was a marked improvement over EWoM, it still struck me as a mediocre game.
When Legendary Heroes was added to my account (I was one of those who were 'comped' with two free expansions) , I was not in any rush to try it.  I mean, seeing how FE was still nothing that great, I figured LH was going to be just another incremental improvement on the base game.
I WAS WRONG!
Legendary Heroes has completely amazed me with its gameplay (especially with the recent 1.4 patch).  Finally, we have an Elemental game that lives up to the hopes and dreams we all had when Elemental was first announced!  This is now a fantastic fantasy-based 4X experience with lots of faction/hero customization options that really adds a great RPG element, as well as a smart implementation of the core 4X (explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate) gameplay dynamic.  The tactial battles, which were a bit bland before, are now fun and challenging endeavors (the tactical AI is very good!).  City building, which was also rather boring in the previous iterations of the series, has received a lot of love, amking it a quite enjoyable to watch your cities grow.  Questing has also received some nice attention, making for some interesting one-off battles.  Add in some "game changing" random events (something Stardock is known for), and you now have a very addictive, very polished experienced.
Stardock has also just begun releasing DLC for the game.  While I have only purchased the Quest DLC so far - it seems to offer the most bang for the buck at the moment - I suspect we can expect a lot more that should really enhance the game even more.
Lastly, this being a proper PC game, there are some great mods already available.
Long short: Legendary Heroes is a very good 4X fantasy game that is well worth your gaming dollar.  I don't think it is too much of a stretch to say that with some more DLC and/or an expansion, Legendary Heroes could well match the revered status of Stardock's sci-fi  magnum opus, Galactic Civilizations II.

Time for Five Nights at Freddy's from an older gamer's perspective...
If you like games that you can play in short spurts that also have that have the calming effect of a good adrenalin rush - and you find the robots at Chuck E. Cheese or your terrifying moments of youth at Showbiz Pizza Place well....terrifying, then Five Nights at Freddy's just might be up your alley.
Initially I wrote the game off seeing the banner on a web search because it sounded like some kind of sleepover mystery puzzle solving game with cartoon animals - oh boy was I wrong!  A family friend's son introduced it to me after seeing that my old Atari games looked like a particular element of the sequel (I collect Atari 2600 games, that should tell you how old I am).
So lo and behold I got introduced to a NEW game franchise finally, and the nice part is I could actually sink my teeth into it because it did not require hours upon hours of learning how to play the darned thing, and I could play it in short spurts.
The genius behind Five Nights at Freddy's is that it's a very simple game that's easy to learn, but tough to master.  On one hand, it's pretty obvious after the night 1 phone call what can be done to defend yourself, what is not obvious though is how to properly impliment the resources given to a particular strategy to survive six in game hours a night while the Animatronics hunt you down for whatever reason it is they hunt you down for.  This sort of gameplay element to me feels like it's a lost art in today's mainstream game landscape.  This is a HUGE reason this game got so popular.
The atmosphere of the game is perfectly punctuated by the graphics and sound.  It really does feel like one is sitting in a delapidated old Childrens Entertainment Pizzaria that's been around since the early 80's without a remodel (or apparently a Janitor, seems Bonnie sees the cleaners more than the cleaner guys do).  All of the animatronics carry that friendly yet somehow undertow sinister tone to them.  Fans whir, the sound of aging electrical devices buzz and fizzle, the animatronics themselves though kind of sound more like some guy in black coming to take you away than some kind of creepy cartoon robot seeking to stuff you into a suit.
What's also nice is how the violence is implied, but not overdone, keeping the series appealing to a broader audience than usual - meaning I don't have to put a password on this when my family comes around, nor do I feel really strange for playing a game full of cartoon animals.  Another nice plus is this early in the series, the lore is not the primary focus of the game, the gameplay is, so you can dive as deep into the lore as you want (or as little as you want), and still enjoy the game regardless.
An impressive bit to think though how this game generated so much attention and eventually grew to have multiple sequels, a freebie RPG spinoff (FNaF World), and now quite a lot of merch (Freddy and co were stalking me through the stores all through X-mas 2016).  And it was all done by one guy - a Christian game dev and animator working at a humble chain store at the time.  It really does show you don't need a 1000 person team and a million dollar budget to make a good game, and as a retro-gamer I'm rather tough on that part of things.  I like seeing my games in my collection as "art" rather than as some kind of major marketing effort.
Overall, I highly reccommend this title.  While it's not some bloody gorefest like some horror games, it has that magic to it that an old Disney or Looney Tunes cartoon has - a little something for everybody, without veering too far in one direction or the other.

This is the hardest game I've had to review. There are positives and negatives so great that whether you enjoy this game really isn't something you'll know until you've played it; so, let's get into it.
Positives:
+This game has mechanics that you never realised you wanted, but that you'll miss as soon as you start playing another FPS- the ability to sprint whilst crouched, or to lean whilst prone, to zero in your sights or scope- I think you can even use iron sights on a weapon with a scope.
+This game has a realistic damage model and weapon handling- generally speaking, one rifle round will kill, range notwithstanding; and recoil on fully automatics is very high.
+This game has a good class system in battles to prevent everyone from running the best weapons (though even the bolt-actions are very usable; in fact my most used weapon by far is the Mosin-Nagant M1891/30), and a respectable weapon progression system.
+There are tanks and other armoured vehicles.
+The maps are very realistic and open-ended (though this can sometimes cause problems; see below)
+There is a vault system and (I think) large jump cool-down to eliminate insane jumping.
+There is still a respectable number of players.
...but the game also has some negatives...
-The map design is in many cases atrocious- spawn killing (or nearly) is unresolved, and many objectives are basically impossible to hold, with others being insanely open and hard to defend.
-Due to the open-ended maps, expect to be killed many times by people you cannot see.
-The controls are a bit wonky, to be honest. It's sometimes impossible to get over obstacles that you should easily be able to vault.
-The game has ping issues (rubber-banding) at a lower ping than most games I've played (~200 instead of +300).
You will die a lot- even in the most outrageous and unavoidable situations. I've even gone as far as to describe it as a "die-out-of-spawn sniper simulator".
Then why do I recommend this?
Simply put, because even if it's just once per hundred insane deaths, you will get the most amazing gameplay- an eight kill flank with an PPS-42, or enough kills at 100-250 m to cause you to expend all your magazines with a DP-28, to give two of my experiences.
In the end, if you're someone who can put up with a lot of nonsense for the occasional amazing streak, you'll enjoy this game- even if at first you don't understand why; but, if you're someone who doesn't want to put up with nonsense 90% of the time, even for the occasional return, I'd recommend you stay away.

Since 4 years this is only MP game, and the most played gamemode is Territory. Two teams fight for contorl over a map, fighting for every field on the regular maps, on which one side is defending and and other attacks. Each province controlled prodives team with 5 combat power, while defending costs 25 and attacking takes 75 of it. Moreover, losing tickets during fight also decreases combat power, so phyrric victories, which are quite common here, arent the best way to go. But what about game itself?
Before anything else, you have to pick a class.  They differ by loadouts and role - one of them is not even supposed to fight. There are Assaults with SMGs, MGs with... come on, thats obvious, Snipers and the core: Riflemen. This class takes ~75% of the whole teams, so get accomodated. They are equipped with bolt-action rifles that are really lethal if you know how to use them. Last two classes are Squad leaders and Commander - their roles are tactical so as a newbs stay away from them, as they require proper mic and great game knowldege.
So as mentioned earlier, taking over the province requires winning the map. This can be done in few ways. As attacker, you can either take all the points or make enemy team lose all the tickets. As defender, you either make enemy run out of tickets or hold a point till Lockdown timer kicks in. If they fail to take point before lockdown timer runs out, they lose.
Remembering that every bullet has potential to kill, this is challenge. Team work is crucial here, and while many games say so - here you can only die alone.
Rising Storm is more of the same - only difference is that instead of Europe, we fight in Asia and sides and weapons are different. There are side-excluisve classes, though. Allies have Flamethrowers and Axis has Light mortars (baisicly Riflemen with additional6-rounds mortars). Both these classes are awesome, with Flamers being slightly OP.
I have no idea how to say everything that i love about this game. Putting a bayonett into the spine of the mot*******er who took half of the team with MG. Killing enemy Commander. Blowing up Flamer by shooting at his fuel tank. Hundreds of scenes that make you enjoy every minute in this game. There are also bad things: idiot teammates running in front of friendly MG, newbs taking tactical roles, AT class (Seriously - class with slowly firing AT-rifle, pistol and AT grenade, while tanks dont get slighlty damaged by these AT rifles. Great). And - why is there so much fog on every map?
All these cons are tiny problems, which shouldn't really take fun - that is, if you manage to get to understand the game and forget about carelessly running into the MG - because here it is a bad idea.

Beyond Good & Evil puts you in the role of Jade, a young woman who, along with her humanoid pig uncle Pey'j, runs a lighthouse on the planet Hillys. Hillys is at war with an alien force known as the DomZ, and an elite squadron known as the Alpha Sections protects Hillys from the alien threat. Or does it? An underground rebel organization known as the IRIS Network charges that the Alphas control both sides of the equation. IRIS is essentially a rogue news network, informing the people via a newsletter that strives to expose the link between Hillys' protectors and the alien menace. That's where Jade, a photographer-for-hire when not tending to the lighthouse, comes in. You quickly hook up with IRIS and spend the bulk of the game infiltrating Alpha strongholds.
But you won't go at it alone. The game gives you a companion most of the time, and many puzzles will require you to get your associate to do things. Only one contextual button is used to command your companion, so it's usually pretty easy to get him to act. The AI of your partner is usually pretty good, but we occasionally had to backtrack to get him unstuck from walls or railings.
Most of the game's interior sections have you out, on foot, and in search of photographic evidence. You're looking for specific pictures, and the areas of interest are marked on your map. The game does have combat, but it's a fairly straightforward system that suffices without excelling. The real meat of the gameplay comes from its puzzle-solving, though there's a little too much repetition in the puzzles, which can make some sections of the game feel pretty tedious. Almost every room will require you to do a little thinking. Sometimes it's as easy as using your projectile attack to push a button on the other side of a force field. Sometimes you'll have to find fuses in other parts of an installation to power elevators or other equipment. Sometimes you'll have to learn a password to proceed into a locked area. And there's a whole lot of sneaking around.
In Beyond Good & Evil, stealth is treated much like the rest of the game's puzzles. You simply want to get to the next room, but patrolling guards are in the way. So you'll either have to avoid detection by staying out of sight or incapacitate the guards by blinding them with a well-placed shot to the tank on their backs. A guard can repair another guard's faulty tank, so in rooms with multiple guards, you'll have to either be a fast shot or find a quieter way through.
The game's 10- to 15-hour quest also has you piloting a hovercraft, which is your primary mode of transport on Hillys. The Hovercraft can shoot, and you'll upgrade it over time to fire more powerful blasts, as well as give it the ability to jump. Upgrading your Hovercraft requires you to spend pearls at an upgrade shop. Pearls are fairly rare on Hillys and you'll get them in various ways ( for example  by defeating bosses or purchasing them from seedy merchants using credits, the game's main currency which you can earn by defeating enemies, find them in crates or by taking photos of the different animals in the game).
The game controls quite well with a mouse and keyboard, using fairly standard third-person action game controls that are, of course, fully configurable.
While the game behind the presentation is pretty good on its own, the entire package benefits from some pretty nice audio and video. The game is graphically impressive. The world of Hillys is beautifully rendered. It's large and atmospheric, and the outdoor segments show off some nice-looking water. The interior of the buildings you'll be infiltrating are appropriately dark and intimidating, with a hefty dose of effective lighting. The game's shadows usually look great, as well, though we noticed a couple of instances of shadows being unnaturally cast on walls and ceilings. It's a minor point, for sure, but given how amazing the rest of the game looks, little things like that tend to stick out. While the console versions of the game look outstanding in their own right (played on Nintendo Gamecube), the PC version definitely has a sharper, cleaner look to it. The water effects, well-placed blur effects, reflections, textures, and models really jump off the screen.
While the game's repetitive nature and short length take away from its overall impact, Beyond Good & Evil is a fantastic-looking game that tells its story well. It may be short enough to complete in a day or two, but fans of action adventure games will find enough to love in the game's overall design to make it worth purchasing.

now it says 0 hours for this game but i played it on console while i had PC repairs done and the only reason i have this game in my library is that it came in a humble bundle and all the other titles were decent but getting to the point ....just ...wow... to date this has to be not the worst game i have ever played but definitely the worst sequel. i mean it was never going to be an easy task living up to the standards set by the games predecessor Red Faction: Guerrilla but whoever was leading the Dev team for this game had clearly either never played the first game or was doing so blindfolded and with noise cancelling earphones on. the list of issues i have with this game makes it difficult to know where to begin.
okay so Armageddon is a linear third person shooter set in the Red Faction universe. the game follows the great grandson of Alex Mason (the Hero of the first game) named Darius Mason. Darius is a soldier in the Red Faction army who now rule mars after the events of the first game but after a monumental screw up on his part humanity is left living underground unable to survive on the surface of mars. the story to this game is many things and none of them good, its generic, poorly paced, poorly written and has a penchant for making scenes appear dramatic when you can blatantly see them coming. it even has a love interest side story to it (totally not trying to copy and paste from the first game) which gets a fittingly poor ending to it. its not the worst writing i have ever laid eyes on but its damn close to it. they say if you gave a thousand monkeys type writers and left them alone they would eventually type out the complete works of Shakespeare.. this game is what the monkeys typed out.
down to the core of this game, the mechanics .. now despite my disliking for this game the mechanics are one of the few things that this game actually got correct. gun mechanics work perfectly as expected, movement is smooth with no issues and in general the games mechanics are as solid as Armageddons (there is a god after all). this is a rare redeeming feature in a sea of disaster. the only real issues you could have with the mechanics would be during the flight mission when the ship does control a bit like you are having a seizure at the wheel but  other than this instance they are fine. the best part of this game which i very much believe they just copied over from the first game is the destruction engine (i shudder to imagine if they had redone this aspect as well) the engine is great providing seamless destruction of cover and environments. this is the best part of this game just being able to blow up or disintegrate the cover preventing you from slaying the enemy (be warned this works both ways) and i did quite enjoy this diamond among the rough feature after the hours of endless fun you get from it in the first game.
back to whats wrong with this game then. its a LINEAR sequel to a SANDBOX game ... how hard did the games developers hit each other over the head with a hammer to think this would work. look at any successful sandbox game such as Grand Theft Auto or Saints row ... imagine they had a linear sequel ... it just doesn't work .. this kind of game is meant to be played as a sandbox. this very story driven linear progression also hampers the range of missions the player has access to. in the first game the player conducted a wide range of mission in order to advance, now though the levels can be summarized by starting each mission and being told .. follow this line and kill everything in your path. there is no diversity it is just a repeated slog of go here run this way and kill this thing. there is also NOTHING but story in this game, no side missions except for collecting a few audio logs left in blatantly obvious places throughout the game. the first game had a wide variety missions and activities set aside from the main campaign. why would you develop a game and then remove all the content for the sequel? its just stupid really. the linear environments also have a negative affect on combat. no more flanking the enemy or sniping from afar no for this game you just have to slug it out in toe to toe combat 90% of the time unless that specific part of the game requires the use of a sniper or other specialist weapon. because we totally hated having the diverse arsenal of weapons available at any point in the previous game .. thanks THQ you are a real star .. NOT
and now we have the multiplayer.. what can i say for this other than DON'T!!.. the multiplayer for this game is almost as terrible as the single player with majority of the issues from the core game crossing over into the multiplayer. to simplify it you have two modes a mode for destruction where player stake it in turn to see who can cause the most destruction in a map and a kind of horde mode where the player stares down waves of aliens hoping not to become E.Ts Dinner. the destruction mode is pretty fun to begin with but there is again not much diversity to it and it gets pretty boring pretty quickly. the horde mode lasts a bit longer with more maps and a better experience if your playing with other players but again its just the same thing over and over and over .. the maps are okay but the AI for the aliens is shoddy at best. sometimes they wont even notice you when you stand in front of them or on the flip side they will spot you from a mile away and bring all their little buddies to tear your martian nads right off (funny when watching it happen.... not so funny when it happened to me :( ). its a great laugh if you are playing it every now and again or in split screen but it doesn't last. the hype for this game actually quite excited me at the time and i (regrettably) pre-ordered this game thinking it would be as awesome as the first game ... i was wrong. in short this game is a less than enjoyable experience. the linear, poorly written generic story and tedious gameplay coupled with the poor multiplayer experience and community make this a game i wouldn't be in a hurry to play again. despite the redeeming features of the amazing destruction engine and all around good mechanics for this game they are twinkling plus points in the sea of disaster that is this game. in short .. if you buy this game after reading this you probably have a power drill or some other sharp object jammed in the side of your head O_o in which case you probably loved the ending to RAGE and live on the moon..

The sequel to one of my favourite games ever. You kids will have no idea what Carmageddon is, but it was a brilliant but controversial racing game from waaay back in '98.
This improves on the original in almost every way. The mission mode adds some variety, and some of the new cars are awesome, but otherwise the core mechanics remain from the first. If it ain't broke, don't try to fix it, right?
The driving mechanics are actually quite "realistic" i.e. cars have real weight and momentum and you won't be making hairpin turns at anything over 40mph. I personally prefer realistic to arcade style driving games so I like it here.
The controversy centres around the fact that basically, pedestrians on the map are a resource. Killing them gets you money and time, and doing it in funny or novel ways will get you a bonus. If you have psycho-sociopathic tendencies, please do not play this game. If you are a normal person and realise that the actions within this game are, in context, hilarious and entertaining, I can't recommend Carmageddon 2 enough. I think it's slightly better than the original, and that's saying a lot from me :)

Confusion, curiousity, admiration, then slowly fear sets in before I straight up panic.
That is what my first 20mins into TLD was and if I'm honest the same emotions are still there with maybe less confusion.
Unlike every survival game I've played there is no point in TLD where you can feel comfortable that you've setup a base and successfully defeated the 'survival' aspect of the game...nope, never. You just buy yourself a little time.
Resources are difficult to find, the man made stuff doesn't respawn, carry weight is limited, everything wears out, animals hunt you, you have to keep moving but you can't take everything with you... which forces you to make decision that will probably kill you.
This is a game about mastery, not just of skills but of nature itself - knowing what signals the change in weather or what to do when the shtf. Good times.

Evolve was a game that I had been waiting for since its launch trailer at E3, and with all the hype I thought "I have to get evolve, it looks like the kind of game that a few of my freinds and I can compete in and have countless hours of fun gameplay." Sadly, that thought was wrong. If i could rate this game out of ten, I would give it a five. Dont get me wrong, the graphics are mind blowing, The A.I. are the best I have seen in a videogame yet, and the concept of 4 v 1 gameplay across multiple different variations of characters and maps is filled with potential, but I feel as though the negatives outweigh the positives in Evolve's case. There are multiple bugs that I found in my first five hours of gameplay, the most annoying and fun gameplay-depriving one I have seen is models dropping through the world. Bodies of teammates that I would try to use the lazarus device on to revive would fall through the bottom of the world, and I caught a screenshot (that can be seen on my profile) of me playing kraken, and falling through the world. Aside from the minor bugs, the gameplay is so-so. The two modes ever played in Evolve are hunt, and evacuation, and they get repettitive after some time. Also, it takes from ten to twenty hours max of playing multiplayer to unlock all of the characters, leaving you with nothing else to be rewarded after hours of using a weapon you necessarily dont like just to master it. Plus, A story or story-mode of any kind is non-existant, and the bits of information about each character that you hear in the dropship before deploying for battle is fragmented, and repettitve. One of the things that really makes me mad at turtle rock is the fact that buying the game standard only gets you three monsters that are easily unlocked, and after unlock, leave you scratching your head and wondering what to do next. To add any sort of fun gameplay after the 30 hours max of gameplay it takes to get all the unlockable monsters and characters, you need to spend an additional 15 to 30 dollars to get new dlc characters and a new monster. (or two, depending on how much money you are willing to throw away. In conclusion, i'd say buy evolve if you have a few freinds that are willing to spend $60 or more to play 30-40 hours of interesting gameplay, until nothing is unique anymore and the things about Evolve that once impressed you just make you yawn. I picked up this game during early access, and for some reason it didn't click with me at the time. I found it too punishing, and all that creeping around was painfully slow.
But after watching a couple of Richspeed's charming SYABH YouTube videos (check out Ep 13), it was clear I'd been playing all wrong, and far too timidly! I should have been running around and only stealthing while bots are near. Also, the hunting rifle is powerful and satisfying, so it's worth scavenging around for one.
I suspect the devs have done some tuning since my first go at it, and now the gameplay just feels right.  Plus, having the single-player option to start with a rifle (as the Officer) made a huge difference.
I've also played a few co-op multi-player sessions with friends and I'm here to report it's a ton of fun. The art direction and gameplay are both top-notch, so we found it a very satisfying experience. And the networking was solid, no issues there.
If you enjoy the stealth and combat in Skyrim, Sir You Are Being Hunted will probably appeal to you as well. I recommend this game.

Ok, so- I just deleted my review to give an updated and more detailed one. I am once again writing a positive review, but this time more in depth and updated. This review is spoiler-free for Story mode! Warning: I am no expert game reviewer. Just some guy who likes games.
Cost: For a Steam survival game? You could find cheaper. For a good game about survival? A very good price. Keep in mind, console games are TWICE as expensive, so why not get a good game? If it was ONLY avaliable on the console, (It's avaliable on PS4 and Xbox) there's a decent chance I would have bought it for normal console game price. Except for the fact I don't have an Xbox or PS4... I'm one of the people who bought it for $20 when it was still in early alpha. Unless you really want it A.S.A.P, I'd wait for the possible sales to approach since Christmas and Thanksgiving are coming.
Graphics: These are AMAZING. It's not too hard on your computer as long as you don't have a really old and crappy one, too. The wolves, items and scene of nature's beauty is all around you. At night, when the sun's about to set, the sky turns a beautiful orange that I always pause my gameplay for to view.
Gameplay: I like the gameplay, It's a game that you play for two hours, pause, and pick it up the next day. While you can play it for fifteen minutes or six hours at a time, I find this game a thing you do after school before working on your homework and eating dinner. Well... personally I homeschool, so I just play it when I finish my work. I've been playing The Long Dark on my own computer for more than a year, I can guarantee It's a good game, but not for everyone. While I haven't played it every day, or every week in fact, I LOVE playing it when I do get on it. If you hate scavenging, managing resources, and having to face the waiting game once every now and then, I would think that this game isn't going to be your best friend or anything.
Story Mode: This part of my review contains NO SPOILERS. I personally think story mode was a little buggy at first, but the TLD devs have fixed that for the most part. Other than that, I was a little dissapointed in story mode... I was expecting a bit more, considering It had been a little over two years since their promise. But hey, making a game is very hard, I understand. Also, keep in mind. The TLD devs are a VERY small team. They have their own independant studio, and It's hard to get things done as fast as a giant company would.
Survival Mode: Truly the pinnacle (pun intended) of the game. This was the original mode, of course, and had a very unique feel. The lonliness or isolation felt... different. It felt more realistic- No, that's not the right word. It gives you a certain feeling that defines a game. It might just be good nostalgic memories of playing TLD during good times, or my desire for a wilderness survival game that had realism and wouldn't make you bored in an hour, but either way, it's just a great thing that feels one of a kind. I don't have much else to say about survival mode, besides I would like to see more firearms added, or even just one. I had a .357 magnum double action in mind, like a Smith & Wesson model 27, or maybe even a .45 colt single action, like a Ruger Blackhawk, the newer models.
Challenges: A great thing to do in your spare time if you get bored of survival mode or finish story mode. Not much to say about this besides the fact that they're called challenges for a reason.
Cost: Fair.
Graphics: Very great.
Gameplay: Good.
Story mode: Doesn't meet expectations, but not bad.
Survival mode: Great.
Challenges: Fun.
Overall: A great game that I recomend you add to your collection if you're a fan of tough, realistic survival. Comes with the fun and struggles of realism.

I'm not normally one for survival games, but as someone who grew up in the middle-of-nowhere Alaska, this game really sucked me in.  Moreover, it sucked me in during early-access.
I'm more excitied about the upcoming features than I am for the current state of the game.  For instance, right now there is only winter.  You can live for a full year and it's still winter.  Within the next 6 months there should be a spring available, and within a year they're shooting for all four seasons.  Every season might end up playing like its own game, which is pretty exciting.
AND there's talk about adding NPCs and group NPC dynamics.  That, combined with the future plans for the game being moddable, means this game has HUGE potential.  Whether it will realize that potential remains to be seen, but even in its current state I think the game is worth it.
According to the devs, 2/3 of the team is working on story mode which isn't even out yet.  There are some areas in the game that are spooky as hell and I can't wait to see what's in store!

If you're into serious survivaling this is probably your game. Evolve was a game that I had been waiting for since its launch trailer at E3, and with all the hype I thought "I have to get evolve, it looks like the kind of game that a few of my freinds and I can compete in and have countless hours of fun gameplay." Sadly, that thought was wrong. If i could rate this game out of ten, I would give it a five. Dont get me wrong, the graphics are mind blowing, The A.I. are the best I have seen in a videogame yet, and the concept of 4 v 1 gameplay across multiple different variations of characters and maps is filled with potential, but I feel as though the negatives outweigh the positives in Evolve's case. There are multiple bugs that I found in my first five hours of gameplay, the most annoying and fun gameplay-depriving one I have seen is models dropping through the world. Bodies of teammates that I would try to use the lazarus device on to revive would fall through the bottom of the world, and I caught a screenshot (that can be seen on my profile) of me playing kraken, and falling through the world. Aside from the minor bugs, the gameplay is so-so. The two modes ever played in Evolve are hunt, and evacuation, and they get repettitive after some time. Also, it takes from ten to twenty hours max of playing multiplayer to unlock all of the characters, leaving you with nothing else to be rewarded after hours of using a weapon you necessarily dont like just to master it. Plus, A story or story-mode of any kind is non-existant, and the bits of information about each character that you hear in the dropship before deploying for battle is fragmented, and repettitve. One of the things that really makes me mad at turtle rock is the fact that buying the game standard only gets you three monsters that are easily unlocked, and after unlock, leave you scratching your head and wondering what to do next. To add any sort of fun gameplay after the 30 hours max of gameplay it takes to get all the unlockable monsters and characters, you need to spend an additional 15 to 30 dollars to get new dlc characters and a new monster. (or two, depending on how much money you are willing to throw away. In conclusion, i'd say buy evolve if you have a few freinds that are willing to spend $60 or more to play 30-40 hours of interesting gameplay, until nothing is unique anymore and the things about Evolve that once impressed you just make you yawn. As all old games, you have a few issues playing this on modern OSs. Mind your compatibility mode and do some googling to find advise. the game itself may run smoothly (like it did to me) but there are plenty fixes published for those who can't run it. (because hey, 99% of old games need a little something in order to run on win 7 and win xp platforms like they did on win 98s etc)
This game was obviously the awesome sequel of a major idea of a racing game where you can smash and disable your opponents instead of just winning the race first. Numerous games took after this franchise including the burnout games. The game has an awesome point awarding system where you can earn points by running over pedestrians, smashing opponents, destroying them, going through checkpoints and of course winning the race. The point system helps the player to buy the cars of fallen opponents (only when they're smashed to death) and use them onwards.
Meanwhile the variety of cars available in the game is ridiculous and pretty awesome. You get to drive vehicles from hot rods and rally cars to supercars and heavy duty trucks, all buffed up with blades and addons that make them look ready to kick♥♥♥♥♥
All cars have a pretty hilarious way to be introduced, each unique and each with a driver that is one of a kind. Another cool thing is that you don't have to keep buying new cars if you don't want to since there's an upgrading system the evolves you car's armor, force and speed abilities as you play alloying you to stick with your favorite vehicle even by playing 99% of the game with it if you want to.
The game includes some nasty missions along with the races. Kind like boss battles. Some are really stressful and some are way too fun not to make you wanna replay them.
The graphics of the game are awesome of its release. You can smash your opponents' and your own vehicle in any way imaginable. Crash on them, throw them off cliffs, push them on explosive barrels, cut them in half, fry them explode them.
Use ridiculous powerups that make you throw flames or elecrify pedestrians, fart bombs from the back of your car and on your opponents behind you, make your car bounce, jump, turboboosted, undefeated or mess you up with drugs and alcohol effects.
The game is CRAZY and totally worth having fun with if you are into the genre.
Do mind that of course its not perfect. There are physics issues like the levels of handling on some cars, the was steering works on most, the sticky feeling of some walls of you crash on their side and other little details that for me didn't take out of the fun of the game at all.
Can't wait to play the sequel :D

So, uh, Five Nights at Freddy's. My favorite game.
I've had a lot of aggression for this game in the past, but after various review edits, deletes, second thoughts and gameplay hours, I've landed on my final decision.
Five Nights at Freddy's is not a good game, but it's not
either. Now, don't get me wrong - it is bad, but it is bad in a way that is slightly more presentable.
There's not much to say about this game because it's extraordinarily lacking in content when you look at it in full, but I'll try my best to cover everything.
Here's a relatively quick rundown of the story provided. You play as a security guard who recently got hired at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a pizza establishment that runs on animatronics and the battery of an iPad. All information is given to you via phone calls provided by a more experienced worker who is "just finishing up his last week now." Of course, he says the animatronics come alive at night because they are set with a free-roaming mode that is activated after hours to prevent their servos from locking in place from lack of movement -- I mean, that actually makes, like, no sense, but whatever. The animatronics, for lack of a better player death excuse, are also programmed to recognize any humanoid roaming after hours as an endoskeleton without its costume.
This is against the rules.
So they ♥♥♥♥ing kill you.
Getting stuffed into a Freddy Fazbear robotic suit "wouldn't be so bad if the suits themselves weren't filled with crossbeams, wires, and animatronic devices, especially around the facial area. So, you could imagine how having your head forcefully pressed inside one of those could cause a bit of discomfort...and death."
There's not much story left in this game, aside from vague outside references and
That being said, what little story the game has is mediocre at best. I, personally, find it very difficult to immerse myself in a demented, twisted horror story with so little information, with the game leaving only scraps to the imagination when it comes to enjoying the game as it was "meant to be."
The "DIY theory" argument is useless when theories are so plentiful with major gaps in story not properly filled that it dilutes the value of each one to such a low standard, that "aliens" could be the generally accepted answer. Pieces taken out of the story are fine when they are done in moderation -- in the proper way. It's incredibly daunting and confusing to come up with a story when the only scraps provided to you are "The Bite of '87" and the paranormal, dead, golden Freddy Fazbear suit. Without any actual substance to the story, theories become weird, make no sense, they become sprawling and confusing, creating a much more sledgehammer delivery of a story as opposed to actually telling one, where you can take it in much easier.
Scott Cawthon could've patched more of the story much easier, even with the strange gameplay delivery he was given, so I find the little we have from this one installment only to be disappointing and awkward. And, yes, I am aware that Scott could've planned a sequel beforehand, but Jesus, if you have to make an entire sequel dedicated to patching story because you had none to begin with in the previous installment, you're doing something wrong.
Story's mediocre, disappointing, and it's generally just a cluster♥♥♥♥.
Gameplay is lacking and boring, but it's definitely better than the story.
The gameplay really isn't conventional, talking horror games, in that there's no player movement. All actions are completed through point-and-click mechanics and looking around your office. You have three tools at your disposal: the doors to the left and right sides of your office which are closed by pressing buttons -- which halts animatronics from entering your office, -- the lights, also operated by buttons just below the door buttons, used to spot animatronics, and the cameras. The cameras can be used to view various parts of the establishment, including the restrooms, halls, hall corners, dining areas, the animatronics' stage, so on and so forth.
The lights and doors are pretty self-explanatory, but are unnecessarily loud, producing a very janky feel to everything around you. You don't really interact with anything else, and the gameplay really just... consists of watching animatronics and closing doors. On later nights, you have to close doors faster, even. So, uh... yeah.
You have some animatronics, which consist of Freddy Fazbear, an anthropomorphic bear, Bonnie, an anthropomorphic purple bunny, Chica, a chicken -- also anthro, -- and Foxy, a pirate fox who looks like he had too much to drink last night.
They all act the same, excluding paths, except Foxy, who will lunge out of "Pirate Cove" sooner depending on the time you spend looking at his cove, taking your west hall and banging on your door to drain power.
They all jumpscare you if they get into the office when your camera panel is up -- again, except Foxy, who just charges right the ♥♥♥♥ in -- or when you run out of power. The jumpscares are mediocre and don't have a real scare effect to them, happening too fast to actually startle anyone, instead often leaving players confused as to what happened.
Oh, by the way, "power" is a thing, because I guess this establishment does not run, on, y'know, a city grid. It really does drain faster than an iPad.
That's basically all the gameplay. I could go into more detail, but doing so would be difficult when there's not detail to begin with.
Graphics are weird and sometimes gross. Moving your camera left and right produces a nauseating effect caused by the fact that the game is trying to be 3D but actually isn't. Animatronics have OK design, except for Foxy who was literally designed during a bumpy car ride. There's also these posters on your wall, one of which honks when you press Freddys nose.
Super.

I don't have much else to cover, there's no soundtrack or anything. The bits of the game I've covered are really all there is.
Five Nights at Freddy's may be more successful now, but how exactly it got there from this game will never click with me. I guess just because almost pubescent kids will consume any horror or relatively original RPG game they can lay their eyes on.
In any case, I don't recommend it.

I once bought this game, almost ten years ago retail. Never managed to finish it back then, cue to my computer crashing. The new one couldn't handle the disc..
But now, steam has it, and I finally got to finishing it.
Great story, great gameplay, has some stealth, racing, photographing, good dungeons, puzzle solving, amongst other things. It has some camera issues though, you might get annoyed by the fact that the camera is a bit hard to handle sometimes.
Overall, I've had a great experience. The story and characters are all great and well-made, and the gameplay is well done although you might think "photographing as a gameplay element, what?"
It is a bit shorter than many modern day games though, since back then you couldn't fit all that much onto a disc so it couldn't grow as massive as it wanted. (what I mean is, don't expect a twenty-hour long odyssey from this, I got through the whole game in just seven hours).
For those who may be wondering, this game does not have multiplayer, it is singleplayer only. Meaning no versus, co-op or other such things.
However, it is a bit poorly ported to the newer OS-versions, meaning that it will probably not be fully functional straight-off. Graphical and sound issues are the most common problems, and for some users it doesn't even start. However, ti did start for me, and the graphics bugs I fixed by turning off "HW vertex processing" in the advanced settings of the game's startup menu. The sound issue I've heard is related to multi-core, and mostly fixed by telling the game to use only one core. Still, I would recommend that you turn on subtitles, just in case. (it doesn't always work flawlessly with the voice, occasionally some pieces have been known to disappear..)
Still, though, a really great game.
To summarise, you should really consider buying this straight up, right now, if you don't mind a few problems, many which are quite easily fixed for some people.
Of course, since these bugs vary from player to player I cannot know which ones you are going to have (for me only the graphical issues, along with some occasional missing sound in dialogue or music, were present. The repeating voice bug, was not) so therefore I will not take these bugs into consideration when rating this.
If I disregard the problems that arrived when getting this to newer OS, this would get a solid 9/10 from me.

Tired of losing AT-ATs to rebel planets filled with pesky airspeeders and OP artillery? Use the Death Star to blow the planet up!
Everything has a counter but most things aren't hard counters with some exceptions:
-Artillery (on the ground) is a little OP. They one-shot infantry and have huge range and large splash damage. Their laughable health means you can use some fast vehicles to take them out but they can be very annoying to deal with.
-Infantry take forever to die, except vs artillery. This is something that mods fix but an infantry vs infantry fight lasts a silly amount of time IMO.
-Corvettes are a little too good vs bombers. If there is one in the general vicinity of your bombers they will die in like 2 seconds. The empire has a large supply of bombers but the rebellion has to pay for every squad...
I haven't played the expansion much but in the base game the two factions are very well done. As the empire you just use brute force. Units like the AT-AT and Imperial Star Destroyer have high health and damage but are rather slow. The rebels can do cammando raids and have to be carefull where they strike because they are weaker than the empire but most of their space units are much faster than comparable imperal ships.
Each battle (space or ground) is played out with time paused in the rest of the galaxy so you can really focus on your tactics or just use movie mode to watch the battle. There is no base you have to babysit and unit production is only done in galactic map view between battles. The models aren't very high-resolution but I still enjoy just watching the battle once I know I will win.
The mods out there are also great. Republic at war and Thrawn's Revenge are my favorites. (If you read the extended universe books Thrawn's revenge inclues lots of that stuff). Mods really spice things up but I would recommend playing the base game first. Thrawn's revenge fixes all of my above complaits but the AI isn't very good. Republic at War the Confederacy AI is infamously hard (it will focus fire and retreat damaged ships).
Speaking of AI, the AI in the base game is very competent most of the time, it will often rush you with corvettes to kill off your fighters which is really really annoying but a very effective strategy. It try to only attack you when it has a larger force and it builds up ground defenses on every planet.
It is possible to play multiplayer on GameRanger but I have yet to do it.
I bought the game on sale but I think it is worth full price.

Ok, so- I just deleted my review to give an updated and more detailed one. I am once again writing a positive review, but this time more in depth and updated. This review is spoiler-free for Story mode! Warning: I am no expert game reviewer. Just some guy who likes games.
Cost: For a Steam survival game? You could find cheaper. For a good game about survival? A very good price. Keep in mind, console games are TWICE as expensive, so why not get a good game? If it was ONLY avaliable on the console, (It's avaliable on PS4 and Xbox) there's a decent chance I would have bought it for normal console game price. Except for the fact I don't have an Xbox or PS4... I'm one of the people who bought it for $20 when it was still in early alpha. Unless you really want it A.S.A.P, I'd wait for the possible sales to approach since Christmas and Thanksgiving are coming.
Graphics: These are AMAZING. It's not too hard on your computer as long as you don't have a really old and crappy one, too. The wolves, items and scene of nature's beauty is all around you. At night, when the sun's about to set, the sky turns a beautiful orange that I always pause my gameplay for to view.
Gameplay: I like the gameplay, It's a game that you play for two hours, pause, and pick it up the next day. While you can play it for fifteen minutes or six hours at a time, I find this game a thing you do after school before working on your homework and eating dinner. Well... personally I homeschool, so I just play it when I finish my work. I've been playing The Long Dark on my own computer for more than a year, I can guarantee It's a good game, but not for everyone. While I haven't played it every day, or every week in fact, I LOVE playing it when I do get on it. If you hate scavenging, managing resources, and having to face the waiting game once every now and then, I would think that this game isn't going to be your best friend or anything.
Story Mode: This part of my review contains NO SPOILERS. I personally think story mode was a little buggy at first, but the TLD devs have fixed that for the most part. Other than that, I was a little dissapointed in story mode... I was expecting a bit more, considering It had been a little over two years since their promise. But hey, making a game is very hard, I understand. Also, keep in mind. The TLD devs are a VERY small team. They have their own independant studio, and It's hard to get things done as fast as a giant company would.
Survival Mode: Truly the pinnacle (pun intended) of the game. This was the original mode, of course, and had a very unique feel. The lonliness or isolation felt... different. It felt more realistic- No, that's not the right word. It gives you a certain feeling that defines a game. It might just be good nostalgic memories of playing TLD during good times, or my desire for a wilderness survival game that had realism and wouldn't make you bored in an hour, but either way, it's just a great thing that feels one of a kind. I don't have much else to say about survival mode, besides I would like to see more firearms added, or even just one. I had a .357 magnum double action in mind, like a Smith & Wesson model 27, or maybe even a .45 colt single action, like a Ruger Blackhawk, the newer models.
Challenges: A great thing to do in your spare time if you get bored of survival mode or finish story mode. Not much to say about this besides the fact that they're called challenges for a reason.
Cost: Fair.
Graphics: Very great.
Gameplay: Good.
Story mode: Doesn't meet expectations, but not bad.
Survival mode: Great.
Challenges: Fun.
Overall: A great game that I recomend you add to your collection if you're a fan of tough, realistic survival. Comes with the fun and struggles of realism.

I'm not normally one for survival games, but as someone who grew up in the middle-of-nowhere Alaska, this game really sucked me in.  Moreover, it sucked me in during early-access.
I'm more excitied about the upcoming features than I am for the current state of the game.  For instance, right now there is only winter.  You can live for a full year and it's still winter.  Within the next 6 months there should be a spring available, and within a year they're shooting for all four seasons.  Every season might end up playing like its own game, which is pretty exciting.
AND there's talk about adding NPCs and group NPC dynamics.  That, combined with the future plans for the game being moddable, means this game has HUGE potential.  Whether it will realize that potential remains to be seen, but even in its current state I think the game is worth it.
According to the devs, 2/3 of the team is working on story mode which isn't even out yet.  There are some areas in the game that are spooky as hell and I can't wait to see what's in store!

TL;DR: Zomboid is an immensely intricate, challenging, rewarding game supported by a dedicated team of indie developers, and is a must-play for anyone interested in the zombie survival genre.
Many people choose to turn to the FPS genre for their zombie apocalyptic survival games, but with Project Zomboid, I feel that the developers at The Indie Stone scratch that itch perfectly.
For starters (and I feel that this is sorely mentioned in reviews), The Indie Stone has been CONSISTENTLY developing this game since it was released on Steam. They continue to show their passion for this project with regular updates, developer blogs, videos explaining new features, and much, much more. They have provided a strong example of how Early Access is supposed to be done, and I fully anticipate that they will have a full release of this game at some point (though, as far as I'm concerned, the game in its ‘early access’ state is worth far more than the $15.00 asking price).
As for the game, mechanics can be read about here in other reviews, found online (particularly in the Zomboid Wiki), or learned as you play – they aren’t that difficult to grasp, and their simplicity makes the game that much more charming.
HOWEVER, do not be deceived by the surface simplicity – this game is incredibly challenging, and as a good game should, it rewards those who ‘get it’ with a truly unique gaming experience. Every time I start up a new character, I get further than I did on the last. Let that be a testament to the game’s consistency – you’re not going to die constantly from zombie bites if you know how to evade/fight them; you’re not going to bleed to death if you know not to climb through a broken window OR how to patch yourself up if you do.
Virtually any building can be made into a shelter. Doors and windows can be barricaded. Ropes can attach to upper story windows for security. Furniture can be moved, taken from other buildings and brought to yours, or built. And with tools like the sledgehammer, virtually anything can be destroyed. You can even build entirely new structures once your carpentry skill is high enough and you have the supplies to do so.
How do you get the supplies? Looting. This game’s inventory system is simple and repetitive at times, but it gets the job done. Backpacks and hiking bags help you deal with the large amounts of weight you’re going to be carrying. Looting houses, diners, warehouses, and even banks requires thought and skill to decide what you need and what you don’t. Supplies are finite, so there’s always the constant thought of, “well, maybe I’ll need this box of paperclips sometime! Better grab it now while I’m here!”
When looting, be careful of your surroundings. Zombies are almost always present, and while at times the game can feel like more of a general survival simulator rather than a zombie game, they’re always lurking around the next corner.
I could go on and on about the intricacies of this marvelously crafted game, but suffice it to say that, if you’re looking for a zombie game that surpasses the norm and want to support fantastic indie developers, look no further than Project Zomboid.

Based on: two full and multiple partial playthroughs
(+) a purposely understated, open-ended story of a lone boy who wakes up in a dark forest, told without any dialogue through gameplay alone, with only a brief non-interactive sequences at the beginning and the end
(+) simple and clean, but creepy and nightmarish greyscale visuals coupled with film grain filter, high contrast, and a strategic use of focus and light sources let your imagination run wild every step of the way
(+) minimalist, often distorted ambient sounds with no music to break the eerie, haunting, almost palpable atmosphere of oppression and loneliness
(+) simple controls with a wide variety of clever environmental, mechanical and physics-based puzzles with hardly any repetition, each scenario presenting a different challenge or a twist on the tried and tested platforming mechanics
(+) frequent checkpoints and wickedly gruesome death animations make the constant trial-and-error less frustrating and gratifying in its own twisted way, each failure serving as a learning experience
(+) perfectly playable with just a keyboard, but even better with an analogue controller (it’s an Xbox 360 port after all)
(+) a very impressive little gem that takes less than 100 MB of space and doesn't require a high-end rig to run
:
(−) can be considered too short for the asking price
(−) the ending may be considered anti-climactic and leave some players unfulfilled

An enjoyable RTS / Tower Defense / RPG hybrid with roguelike elements that will sink in your head for days. The gameplay is original, yet extremely challenging even on the lowest difficulty, the art-style is gorgeous and minimalistic, and there is tons of content just thrown at you at every turn. It's also story-lite so there's no walls of text thrown at you constantly.
The game has a steep enough learning curve, only giving you a short tutorial on the basics, requiring you to figure out things for yourself.
You start with two heroes, but eventually you will unlock up to two more hero slots as you find them in the dungeon, with a total of 16 different heroes available to choose from. Resource managing is key in Dungeon of the Endless.
If you want strong characters, you'll need to build food modules,
if you want tons of laser cannons to stop wave upon wave of enemies, you will need machinary resources.
And if you want access to additional modules ranging from decoys, lasers, bombs, then you'll need to gather science resources.
(Here is the part where I explain how to play this game, making it even more confusing.)
The game has a unique "turn" system, designated by a door, i.e. when you open a door, a turn will pass, giving you resources based on modules you have built. Anything can happen during these turns. A wave of monsters can surprise you, power can go out, you may uncover a buff crystal or a research post, or a shop where you can spend a specific randomly chosen resource on some neat stuff.
The objective of the game is to find the exit in the dungeon, allocate a hero to carry the crystal at the start of the level, and escort them to the exit, while of course, being bombarded by enemy waves.
Rooms can be lit up using "Dust", the primary resource in the game. It's collected from enemies and certain rooms when opened. Dust is also the crystal's health, so if attacked, you will lose dust, thus losing power in rooms.
Lighting up the rooms stops enemies from spawning during turns and the "final" phase, but also allows you to place modules on the dungeon floor at the cost of machinery resource.
The game is perma-death, so if your crystal is destroyed, if your heroes die, or if the hero carrying the crystal dies, then it's game over, and back to level 1 again. There is a number of different "pods" you can choose from, all with various difficulties and requirements, so there is plenty to mess around with here.
There is so much more to this game, including levelling up your heroes, learning new skills, abilities, picking up or buying/selling items, weapons, armour and accessories, triggering random events and most importantly, taking a whole bunch of risks.
It's one of the most perplexing and gripping games I've played in a long time and you should buy it when you can.

I can safely say that Outlast made me jump out of my chair more often in its four-hour descent into Hell than any other game ever has. It's a tense, brutal trek that strips you of any power to defend yourself as you try to avoid the deranged mental patients that roam the halls of this horrifyingly gorgeous world.You'll run, hide, and just generally be terrified as you discover the horrors that reside within Mount Massive Asylum. But in between the wealth of scares and beautiful environments, Outlast has a tendency to bog down via uninspired mission objectives and a few disappointing design choices.
From the get-go, Outlast is one of the best-looking and sounding survival horror games to date. Everything from the dynamic lighting to a fantastic soundscape work together to keep you on edge every second of the experience. On both PC and PS4, I dreaded entering any new areas or opening any closed doors for fear of what lurked in the dark unknown. Little details that are often forgotten in games, like leaving a trail of bloody footprints after stepping through a pool of blood, really help sell the illusion that Mount Massive is an actual place.
