Linear as is most liearly-possible. I'll try not to compare, as Armageddon is a game in its own right of course, but it is, however, part of the Red Faction franchise... so I'm going to compare anyway.
To start: why? I'm utterly amazed by design decisions that went into this game. RF Guerrilla is an open world, near sand box-destruction, action-shooter. Completing RF Guerrilla, I thought "Wow. Great game. The next'll be even better! It'll be in a dense, grimy, overpopulated martian city! Yeah! I'm going to be able to bring entire sky-scrapers to the ground!". Nope.
GEOMOD 2.0
Of course, the destruction engine is fantastic. Any better than Guerrilla? Collapsing structures have an effect on camera, and deal varying degrees of damage to enemies and you, according to their size/weight. This aspect I feel has improved from RFG as there feels like a real weight hangs behind each structure and destroying one is both a satisfying and almost awesome experience. Why almost? Well, I've seen it. Done it in RFG; this game makes no attempt to scale up from its predecessor, and if you havn't played RFG, then destroying small structures that are verticaly impared, (Of course they're going to be; The game's set underground), will get pretty old, very quickly. That's another thing; the game's setting just doesn't allow for the exploitation of this franchise's destruction engine! I mean, what good is blowing up stuff if you can't see more than 3 meters ahead of you!! The game doesn't even allow you to manually activate your flashlight! Overall, this destruction engine is just wasted, and it's easily the best feature of the game.
NARRATIVE
Bah I havn't even completed it. Honestly, I got bored. That might speak volumes to you, about the game, or about me in fact, eitherway, I washed my hands of the story instantly. It's good in short bursts; I've been on and off the game, but I'm in no way hooked. It's the destruction engine that keeps me playing the game.
GAMEPLAY
Your standard 3rd-person perspective; the camera is of good distance from the character and worked well without any issues.
Good god- Agile bullet-bags! All of them! Small arms weapons, such as your pistols, assault rifle, shotgun, are all just a bit...meh. There's no stopping power behind them, and that's hugely unsattisfying. Enemies dart around, in and out of sight, usualy never bieng able to hit you or, for that matter, doing any real damage. They feel merely time consuming and tedious, for the most part, thanks to frantic AI and pea-shooters for weapons. This isn't the case for all weapons however..."AND ON THE EIGHTH DAY, GOD CREATED THE MAGNET GUN". Truly, there has never been a more fantastic, utterly enjoyable, gun in gaming history. Got a big fella getting all up in your grill? That's ok; Bring down the very building that he stands in, on top of him! Attatching a...err...clamping node first to whatever you desire, you may then fire off an attractive node somewhere adjacent to the clamping node; the clamping node, and the wall/enemy/debris to which it was attached, will be violently accelerated accross the map towards the attractive node. Chaos, death, destruction, follows. Wonderful!
As I've said before, the game features primarily underground sections-this makes the game a bit dull, in terms of locations and scenery, and does not aid the linear gameplay at all, as I found myself quickly bored by the overall atmosphere of the game. The game has Exo suits that you can hop into. They're barely worth a mention; yes you're unstoppable, and a badass, but that gets boring when you're an unkillable, unstoppable, badass. Bieng unkillable, actually, I consider, is the opposite of bieng badass; What's the point of it all?! I played on normal, the reccomended setting, and this game has yet to challenge me. Enemies just feel like a tedious filler, much like all the scenic walks through the game's martian underground.
Have I mentioned that the game is increadibly linear? Oh. Yes. Ah.
Perhaps they were going for a more...atmospheric and cholsterphobic Red Faction game...If that is the case, they do not focus on the darker elements of the game enough; the main protagonist wipes out any trace of grit about the plot immidiately, enemies are not to be taken seriously- they are mere insects to you, only to be crushed completely and utterly with ease. With this game's setting, it could have been a horror; the enemies look terryfying enough and there's plenty of corpses strewn about. The lighting is dark and moody, and yet, these features were never focused upon; the game does nothing in the way of building any tension. Yes, this isn't the Red Faction I wanted, but this concept... It's not done well, in many of the aspects the game claims to be about.
To round up, (Well done for reading this far), I'd like to say that this game is a setback for the Red Faction franchise; the design decisions that are present baffle me, in comparison to Red Faction: Guerrilla, and in some cases just downright backwards. The game's predecessor aside, Armageddon itself is just boring, samey, and needlessly restricted in many aspects. The engine's destruction is good, fantastic, in fact, but that's all I've really got out of this game. Without Geomod 2.0, the following rating would have been far worse.
5/10. Worth a 90% off, for the somewhat restricted spectical of the Geomod 2.0 engine, but otherwise, buy Red Faction: Guerrilla.

Well... personally I homeschool, so I just play it when I finish my work. I've been playing The Long Dark on my own computer for more than a year, I can guarantee It's a good game, but not for everyone. While I haven't played it every day, or every week in fact, I LOVE playing it when I do get on it. If you hate scavenging, managing resources, and having to face the waiting game once every now and then, I would think that this game isn't going to be your best friend or anything.
Story Mode: This part of my review contains NO SPOILERS. I personally think story mode was a little buggy at first, but the TLD devs have fixed that for the most part. Other than that, I was a little dissapointed in story mode... I was expecting a bit more, considering It had been a little over two years since their promise. But hey, making a game is very hard, I understand. Also, keep in mind. The TLD devs are a VERY small team. They have their own independant studio, and It's hard to get things done as fast as a giant company would.
Survival Mode: Truly the pinnacle (pun intended) of the game. This was the original mode, of course, and had a very unique feel. The lonliness or isolation felt... different. It felt more realistic- No, that's not the right word. It gives you a certain feeling that defines a game. It might just be good nostalgic memories of playing TLD during good times, or my desire for a wilderness survival game that had realism and wouldn't make you bored in an hour, but either way, it's just a great thing that feels one of a kind. I don't have much else to say about survival mode, besides I would like to see more firearms added, or even just one. I had a .357 magnum double action in mind, like a Smith & Wesson model 27, or maybe even a .45 colt single action, like a Ruger Blackhawk, the newer models.
Challenges: A great thing to do in your spare time if you get bored of survival mode or finish story mode. Not much to say about this besides the fact that they're called challenges for a reason.
Cost: Fair.
Graphics: Very great.
Gameplay: Good.
Story mode: Doesn't meet expectations, but not bad.
Survival mode: Great.
Challenges: Fun.
Overall: A great game that I recomend you add to your collection if you're a fan of tough, realistic survival. Comes with the fun and struggles of realism.

Well, after wrecking my way through the original Carma and the Splat Pack, I fired up Carma 2.  And wow is there a world of difference.
Carma 2 follows on from the success of the previous game and keeps on going and going strong.
But unlike Carma 1, this game has made some changes to keep it fresh and challenging.  There are now Groups of races as opposed to the ranking system of old.  Complete the races in the group to unlock the mission that you need to complete to advance on to the next group.  Missions range from a Time Trial against the clock, Destroying certain objects in a set amount of time and Destroying opponents.
The upgrade system has changed also.  No longer are you able to just upgrade before a race, you upgrade DURING it.  Its an odd system, however it promotes exploration of your environment to find Bonus Slot pick ups to increase the available slots to your various upgrades and also finding free increases as opposed to buying them, which can be expensive.
Also, no longer are certain cars available for you "steal" like Carma 1.  In this, any car wrecked is fair game to be purchased after the race providing you got the cash to get it.
Power-up also had a bit of an overhaul with now, manually activated ones.  My fave being the Repulsificators ( seriously, they are awesome xP )
Opponents this time get a status bar, showing you their health, what they are doing ( Checkpoint Chasing, Sulking ect ) and a mini map marker so you know where they are, which is real handy if you want to hunt them down.
Graphically, the game is real good looking, cannot fault it and some music, which I didn't know until recently, supplied by Iron Maiden....thats cool as hell!!!
This is a worth successor to the original and carries the torch still.  TDR 2000 was good n'all, but nah, Carma 2 is still the king of this franchise...for the moment.  Just got to see how Reincarnation fairs, because its got some pretty big shoes to fill, left by Carma 1 and Carma 2.

I do not recommend this game because of the technical issues that I've had to deal with. I will make it clear that I think the game is fun and enjoyable, but only when it isn't giving me errors and/or crashing. I have had to spend too many hours trying to troubleshoot the root of some crashes, and updates are released for this game so infrequently that if you do encounter a technical error, it is most likely you will have to fix it yourself. I've personally had enough of that. I still to this day get random crashes while playing the game, and they happen at inconsistent rates. Some days I won't have a crash, others it will crash every time I try to play. I've even gotten crashes by just using the main menu (the Steam Workshop and Options menus are the worst offenders in my experience).
Like I said: I think the game is fun despite it having a high learning curve. I've had an enjoyable experience - I just wish the game worked more consistently for me because I'm too tired of troubleshooting it myself. I've spent way too many hours (10 at least) trying to fix it myself.
Do note, if you buy this game, you are only buying it for the multiplayer. The AI is one of the most braindead things I have ever seen in my life. It is also extremely inconsistent on any difficulty. I've had moments where it had godlike accuracy, and I've had other moments where it couldn't hit the front side of a barn to save its life. In addition. the campaign missions are shallow versions of the "Territory" mode in multiplayer, and it is not worth a look. Even if you wanted practice to learn the maps, there are plenty of servers that usually aren't too populated with people, just bots.
A true World War 2 experience.

The game, as others have mentioned, is a mix of genres that appears a bit too complex at first, Roguelike, tower defense, RPG, 4X might seem to much to handle at once, but if you play the game for ten minutes it will make sense and feel natural.
The game mechanics depend a fair amount on luck, but luck is at the core of roguelike games: you might find the exit right away, or might end up exploring the entirety of the floor before being able to move on. Getting dust, the resource required to power rooms and weapons in your dungeon, is scarce and rare, but that adds a lot of intrigue and uncertainty to the gameplay: if you found the exit, do you keep exploring to get more resources knowing that you might end up with too many unpowered rooms--and hence monsters--or do you move on immediately to a higher floor with maybe not enough resources saved up for future levels? Making hard decisions in an environment out of your control is a part of the experience. You crashed into a hostile dungeon, after all. You have to make do.
The visual style and music are, as others have mentioned, gorgeous, and deserve much praise. The game is a joy to eyes and ears, which contributes positively to the couple of hours required to finish each run.

Fun dungeon crawler/survival game with a maximum of 4 players.
Each member has thier own set of skills and its up to the player or players to use them effectively to manage resources, set up defenses and explore dangerous floors to find an exit in the darkness.
Resources include the following
-Industry for building items
-Science to perform research and gain access to better equipment to build (ex. turrents,  hp generators, stronger resource modules, traps, etc)
-Food for not only healing your wounds but also for recruiting survivors along the way or level up your characters.
-Dust, your main power source to keep the lights on in areas of your choosing because with out it, mosnters will spawn from the darkness... literally. No lights then the next door you open could spawn waves of monsters in those dark rooms...
In multiplayer you must communitcate with your associates if you expect to leave alive. You don't share resources amongst yourselves initally but you can give each other resources if ya want. Once you and your team is ready to leave, someone picks up the crystal and heads for the exit. In this phase, the crystal-holder (as i call them) wil have thier speed reduced and cannon defend themselves so its up to thier team-mates to make sure they get to the elevator. Hopefully everyone is on the elevator because if not... well consider them left for dead and you'll have to find a replacement.
Will you survive the constant nightmares from the darkness and escape to the world above after your horrifying crash or will you an your team die a gruesome death? If its the latter, I hope you go out like a badass. If its the formor, I hope you can do better next time around on the other modes.
Good luck!

I'm in love with this game, and would absolutely recomend it. Some pros of it are that it looks gorgeous, it's challenging (at least for the first 8-ish hours of gameplay), it's fun, it's realistic for a survival/exploration game, and it's pretty immersive.  I won't lie, though. It does have flaws. After getting into the game and playing it for around 15 hours like I did, it stopped getting as challenging. Granted, I'm only on medium difficulty, but for a survival game, challenging gameplay throughout the game is nice to have. Another thing is that it isn't a finished game, and you can only play sandbox mode (this isn't really a bad thing, but if you're iffy on buying it, then you should probably wait for the finished product). The most frustrating part is that you can't jump. All in all, I'd still say it's worth the price, but like I said earlier in my review, if you're iffy on buying it, it may be best to wait to buy it, unless it goes on sale for a better price.

Like most who have purchased The Long Dark before it came out of early access, I was pleasantly surprised to see that the long awaited 'story mode' was finally released after two years of its announcement. Dusting the game off after playing all it could offer months ago, I loaded the game and began the story. However, after beating the first episode, I felt somewhat unsatisfied.
The "tutorial" of the game is at the beginning of the story; you survive after a plane crash and are forced to find shelter, make a fire, find food and water, etc... The standard 'Long Dark' procedure.The first thing I noticed was how the game had absolutely no prompts or guides; not even a "press spacebar to open the crafting wheel", which was somewhat annoying to me, since it took me a good bit of exploring through the game's keybinds to figure out what button to press. The game advertises itself as a "non-hand holding experience", but instead it assumes that the player has already played a solid bit of sandbox, which was again, frustrating to me. The constant "figure out how to do this and that" was frustrating but tolerable throughout the tutorial until I reached the point where I was told to make tea to help my sprained ankle. The game simply told me to "make tea" at the campfire with a certain berry that I was told when I interacted with it before that "I don't need that right now". So, I gathered the berries and went to the fire... but I couldn't find the crafting option for the tea. After thinking I didn't have enough berries, or perhaps the fire wasn't hot enough, I tried both options, but still nothing. I ended up restarting my game
times thinking it was bugged. At the point where I found the option to make the tea in some obscure crafting menu I didn't know I had, I was pretty much done with the game. But, I continued and finished the tutorial.
Throughout the rest of the chapter, the same feeling I felt during the tutorial as described above prevented me from being completely immersed in the game, as I always felt frustrated at
in the game's "non-handholding" atmosphere. Some other issues I noticed were;
The wolf AI is odd, when you approach them with a torch, they stand there and their growling sound file repeats every tenth of a second, instead of running away.
There are two crafting menus, one accessed through 'c' and 'spacebar'. I'm not sure why it's not just one.
Voice acting is sporadic, sometimes there are voice lines for characters, and other times it's just a line of text to read at the bottom. To me, it was breaking immersion.
(Neutral) The cutscene flashback animation is... odd, perhaps others will like it but I saw it as jagged and unpolished.
Overall the main issue with the story is that it simply feels... unpolished. Not incomplete or unplayable, but perhaps rushed or pushed out to release. I would give the game much more credit if the story mode wasn't teased and pushed back for two years, however I expected a more polished game after all the hype.

A fun game with a lot of depth. The game is constantly being worked on, and after taking a year long break I came back to a revamped HUD and an in-game experience with even greater range of options. It's a survival game through and through with a variety of different modes to keep you interested. You need to eat, sleep, and drink to stay a live and therein lies the challenge. Navigating zombie hordes, raiding homes, gathering supplies, and learning skills to stay alive longer.
Sometimes you'll live a few weeks into many months, other times you'll be lucky to make it out of the first day.
The end-game leaves something to be desired, but early and mid-game are enjoyable. And while it can be a grind to get your stats up, but in the end once you've leveled up a few of the important skills you're free to set your own goals and attempt to achieve them. Build a base, become a cook, wreak havoc on unsuspecting zombie populations, go fishing, learn to farm, set traps, burn hordes, burn your house down, burn your neighbor's house down, get infected, don't get infected, shoot a gun, stab a zombie with a fork. The choice is yours, and in this sandbox zombie survival you are presented with a lot of them.
Just a heads up, there is a bit of a learning curve, but it's worth it in the end.
Cannot recommend this game enough. Best zombie survival game released by anyone to date, hands down.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a game that takes place in an alternate reality in Britain where British robots hunt humans for sport. There are a variety of robots, such as robots on robot horses, robots with rifles, robots with blunderbusses, scarecrows that warn other robots, robot hunting dogs, and a giant hot air balloon that will attract robots to your location if you are spotted. With only having a rag to stop bleeding and a bottle of alcohol for vitality, stealth becomes a vital role in the game until you find enough guns and ammo and other weapons, traps, and distraction items to combat the robots, and even then is a huge role in staying alive. Even though sneaking through the map from town to town getting loot, avoiding robots, running from robots, and occasionaly attacking a robot for its loot is fun for a while, this game does lose its fun rather quickly. Because you cannot punch or kick in this game, having a weapon is crucial to defending yourself from the ever-present threat of being attacked by a robot. Typically a game goes like this:
1. Spawn, get to the nearest town, and loot it, possibly finding a weapon or two
2. Go looking for a piece of the teleporter (you win the game by returning all the pieces of a teleporter to a place called the stones) and possibly grab it if it is unguarded
3. Return one or two pieces of the teleporter and then get killed by robots
4. Repeat this process a couple of times. No problem, right? theres always some loot to be found, right? WRONG!
5. Get to the point where all the loot that will actually help you is gone, except the occasional food or bottle that can be found in some place that you somehow skipped when you looted a town
6. At this point, there will probably be a lot of robots, as more spawn as you return more pieces of the teleporter.

Limbo is a fun game, albeit one that is very short. I'm not gonna penalize it for being short too heavily though, and I'm gonna base this quick review on final product vs what I think the developers set out to do.
On my first playthrough, it took me between 2 and 3 hours to beat. I was determined to not use the internet to solve the puzzles and I still wound up having to cheat on a couple of them.  Part of this is because the puzzles were tough, and part of it was just my own laziness and wanting to keep things moving.
The puzzles themselves were fantastic.  You can tell a lot of thought and effort went into the design of them.  Most of them were extremely fair and solvable while still being difficult  enough to challenge players.  There were only maybe 1 or 2 in the entire game that I felt were a little too not-solvable, but that's ok, I would rather them error on that side than on the too-easy side.  And that could also just be my own lack of skill and puzzle ability.
The game's checkpoint system is more than fair.  They don't wanna waste your time by having you redo things over and over.  The way respawning works keeps things moving along and keeps the emphasis on puzzle solving over tedium, which imo was a great design choice.  There were only a couple little spots in the game that I felt you had to know what was coming to avoid problems.  Most of the game though is intuitive and if you're good and quick enough, you can avoid trouble without having to replay the section.
The graphics and art style are of course awesome. The game has a very creepy, eerie feel to it and it worked well.  The backgrounds are so detailed and intricate, so much attention to detail was put into this game.  This is a talented developer and one that I will continue to support as long as the quality of thier games remains high.
My second playthrough was done in about an hour.  I would have liked to have seen the game be a bit longer, but all-in-all I'm not that upset about it.  I'm about to go play Inside, so here's hoping it's maybe a bit longer.
My 2 biggest complaints in the game are the lack of widescreen support, and the lack of control customization.  I had to use the arrow keys for movement in this game, something I've never had to do before. It was awkward because I like to use my left hand but the arrows are on the right side of the keyboard.  Letting players choose which keys they want to use is highly reccomended.  This is really inexcusable and makes me wanna dock a point.  Also, lack of 21:9 support is getting old.  This game came out in 2011 so I'm gonna overlook it, but I bet my life that when I fire up Inside here in a minute this is still unresolved.  1.5 points deducted for these issues.
Overall, Limbo is a fantastic game that while short, is engaging and offers puzzle platforming of a very high quality. I reccomend this game even at the 10 dollar price. It's def worth playing and experiencing. If you see it on sale absolutely buy it.
Final Score: 7/10

(A review of the first 3 games.  Game 1 is the only one worth paying for, so I am leaving my thoughts here.)
Five Nights at Freddy's 1: you're a security guard of a kid's pizza restaurant, and the animatronic performers on stage start moving around at night.  If they make it into your office, you're dead.
Why do the doors require power to stay CLOSED?  Why does the security system run on a battery?!  What are you guarding???
Illogical as the setup is, it's entertaining and creepy.  The gameplay is intuitive, and it's a fun challenge to find the rhythm needed to survive the final nights.  Understanding how each creature behaves is crucial to managing your resources, and as limited as the graphics and gameplay are, they are well-executed.
Five Nights at Freddy's is an experience as memorable as it is creative.  It creates a real sense of dread, helplessness, and panic, all from still images in poorly lit rooms.
*
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 isn't as good as the first.  You're a security guard again at a new and bigger restaurant location.  No doors to close this time.  Now the creatures can get into your office, and you can't stop them.
We're expecting the jump scares, so it isn't a surprise this time, and now you have a flashlight, so getting such a good look at the animatronics kills their scare value.
In game 1, all the creatures move about in observable ways, and you can and must track them on camera, and you know when to close the doors and when it's safe to open them.
Not so with 2; creatures sometimes just appear in your office for no reason, and you only have a fraction of a second to put on the mask or the game is over.  Closing doors to keep the creatures out is intuitive in game 1.  Game 2 has fuzzy rules.
Looking at the cameras is pointless because it affects nothing, unlike game 1, in which it is the only way to keep a couple monsters from moving.  The monsters don't always have consistent paths through the building, so keeping track of them wastes too much time.  Winding the damn music box is the only reason to open the cameras now, and it means your eyes are permanently glued to camera 11, and the player doesn't get to see the building or observe the creatures at all.
Checking up on Freddy's and Foxy's locations in the first game makes the cameras part of the game because doing so prevents them from moving.  In game 2, the cameras don't serve a purpose at all.  Being able to shine light in the dark rooms affects nothing, and it takes away from the subtlety.
In FNAF1, the animatronics move in subtle ways, and because you can't see them clearly until they are right in front of you, at first you wonder if they are moving at all.  FNAF2 lets you see them clearly at all times, and yes, now they are obviously moving.
The sound effects are subtle and creepy in the first game.  Some could be mistaken for ambient noise.  In the second game, they're pretty blatant and loud.  Foxy even has a theme song that plays when he's nearby.  Doesn't add to the creep-factor.
This game feels like the cartoonish knock-off an imitator would make, not a sequel.
*
As for Five Nights at Freddy's 3...  The pizza restaurant is closed, and now you're a security guard for a haunted house based on Freddy Fazbear's restaurant.  I beat the game in less than 90 minutes, and I don't know how or why.  The rules are so unclear the game is more confusing than frightening.  I couldn't find the damn creature on camera!  Despite clicking on every view a dozen times per night, I never saw it apart from a couple sightings in the vents, so how was I supposed to play?!
If there is a place where you're told to use audio to lure it away from the office, I didn't hear it.  I read that's what you're supposed to do in a community guide.  I figured since I had made it to night 4 without taking any action, I should find out what I'm actually supposed to do.  So I hit the audio in random places throughout each night, and eventually I beat nights 4 and 5.  Did it have any effect?  It must have, but I didn't see a result, and that's the big problem with this game.  Game 1: close door, prevent death.  Game two: put on mask, prevent death.  In game 3, there is no connection between an action and preventing your demise.
I've read you must complete the minigames in cryptic, unintuitive ways to get the true ending.  I will not bother.
*

Beyond Good and Evil is a fabulous work of art that originally was released for the PS2, GC, Xbox, and those early 2000's pcs.  The game's story is amazing backed up by emotional moments, compeiling characters, and the need to find out just who is really orchestrating the DomZ attacks and who is kidnapping the citizens of Hillys.  Furthermore is the graphics, I don't tend to focus on graphics much, but, Beyond Good and Evil deserves for its graphics to be praised for a world that draws you into it beauty and to this day has aged quite well.  And the music fits every mood rather it be a tough boss battle or sad cutscene.  Gameplay is also solid--Jade's movements in battle always feel smooth and well executed.  Perhaps the most interesting thing I thought about the gameplay was how it combined not just the action adventure of a Zelda game, but the stealth you would find in such as Metal Gear.  Now there are some issues with this game I should address but shouldn't stop you from playing the game.  One, is that the game has not been optimized for modern day pcs, in fact as soon as you start the game you are given an error that your 'Graphics Card' has not been updated to the latest version, but at least you can still play it.  Then theres problems with sometimes flickering graphics and such, and one of the worst that ruined a very important scene in the game near the end was at the middle of the cutscene the sound absolutely stopped (I had to reload an earlier save, turn on subtitles and go through it again just to hear them).  In other words this game is a straight out port of the pc version that has not been optimized for modern day pcs.  But even though it has issues with modern day pcs I found that it was still enjoyable as it was back when it was released.  I suggest Ubisoft releases a patch so that Beyond Good and Evil can run on modern day pcs better, much better.  If you can deal with the issues then you will certainly have a blast playing this overlooked great game.  However if you don't want to deal with the issues then I suggest you buy the HD version on Xbox 360 or PS3.

Decisions, decisions. Every one of which could put you in a slightly better position, dramatically worse position, or end your game completely.
DotE is a very unique experience that combines RPG-roguelike, tower defense, and resource management elementals into a single game - and somehow it manages to do so quite well. Every turn you have to weigh your options: Should you spend food to level up a team member? Should you hold on to it in case you need it for healing? Should you spend precious materials on defenses before you open the next door? Should you even open the next door at all? Maybe it's better to head for exit while things are relatively safe.. Research new defenses?.. Research better resource production? Maybe you should just hold on to those research points in case you happen to run across a merchant who uses them as currency.. Maybe you should head north.. maybe east.. Maybe you should cut the power to one room and risk monsters spawning there next turn in order to power another room and make that section safer.
This game is a constant struggle with choices.. and more often than not you don't know in advance which is the better option in the remote or even immediate future. But you'll have fun learning as you go and slowly ascending further and further up the levels with each game (Except for the ones where things just go horrible wrong - Which will probably be most of them)

Super fun, and very frustrating.
Normally I'm not one to like dungeon-crawler games, but DotE (as I am shorthanding it) is really enjoyable to someone who kinda sucks like me; and challenging enough for experienced players to butt their head against a wall.
A wealth of replayability with the characters, their individual and/or linked stories, numerous items, randomly generated floors, and different ships to unlock (and there's the multiplayer as well!). Different strategies can be adopted, by going the super-turtle route and getting a TON of modules, or relying on brute strength of your Heroes by levelling them up a lot; there's a lot you can do.
DotE's art style is really nice, the pixel-theme is something you see in these kinds of games but its got its own style and is different enough to distinguish it from the rest.
I would highly recommend Amplitude's other Endless games (Endless Legend and Endless Space) as the story and lore from those two games link into this very nicely (they all take place in the same universe).
All in all, a very fun and challenging game, I just wish there were more people to play with on multiplayer!

This game brings back my best memories of the 'Aliens' board game, and then builds on that.
It is a very well designed game: the random combat element is played down, compared to most alien/maze/turn-based type games released rencently: XCom, SpaceHulk, SOTS:The Pit, FTL (or indeed board games) - you are almost completely responsible for the events here.
Though I was initially worried that the strategic toolset, or level brevity, would feel limiting, given DofE is compared to a tower defence, you will actually (want to) take 200% extra time to think about placing everything than e.g. in any RTS I've played.
All this is wrapped in a beautiful graphic format which is not afraid to break the rules, and cut the corners of realism slighlty, creating easily enough artistic value to make up for it. What I mean by this is, I would happily have DofE screenshots framed and put on the wall to be able to contemplate them longer. Also, I'd quite like the person who drew this to design my OS!

I previously reviewed this game positively and recommended it.  I am updating my review in light of today's 'countdown scandal'.
I respectfully disagree with the reviewers who who have spent hundreds of hours enjoying the EA sandox who now no longer recommend the game as they feel let down because they didn't get an update today.  Sure, it's been a long, long wait but during that time I - and perhaps you too - have had a wonderful time playing this fantastic game.  Yes, the countdown turns out to have been poor PR - and Hinterland have admitted as much - but we now know more about story mode (5 episodes), they have confirmed new game features (stone throwing etc.), and we know there will be a test branch release this month.
Believe me, it's not that I'm one of those ever cheerful optimists happy to go with the flow - I'm really not! - it's just that I recognise that The Long Dark is, for me, a very special game, a very special experience, and I am grateful for what I have had so far.  I feel I have had a ridiculous amount of gaming satisfaction from the game for the low price I originally paid for it.  I agree that more content would be good, and I too look forward to story mode but given the quality of my experience playing this game so far...I am prepared to wait a little longer.
I hope the Hinterland Team don't get discouraged by all the criticism, which is why I am writing this, to balance things.  I also hope that they fulfil their promise to us in August.  In the meantime I will continue to enjoy The Long Dark, and hope you do too.

I have been looking for a zombie survival game for years- a good one. Something I could play for awhile, something that wouldn't leave me feeling like there could be 'more'a. I remeber the first time I heard of H1Z1, and DayZ- they both sounded
. Looking at screenshots, how could I not be impressed?
How naive. If you really look around for any zombie apocalypse games, those two names are bound to come up, and with them, their history of major,
disappointment.
A couple days ago, I was looking through my Steam Queue, and Project Zomboid happened to pop up. Watching the video, I was intrigued. Yeah, the graphics weren't photorealistic, but then again, when did they ever have to be? When I looked towards the reviews and comments, I was estatic, and could only hope it measured up.
It totally did.
I've only played a few hours as of this review, but I'm absolutely hooked. In its current state, it is completely playable, and worth its $14.99 price tag.
-
Death comes swift and quick for those who don't pay enough attention. From basic survival needs like food and water, the game goes beyond and even throws in challenges in other forms. Staying out in the rain might get you sick, and if you don't take care of that, you might be visiting the Grim Reaper pretty soon. You can be cold, scratched, bitten, and you can bleed, and feel nausea and so much more. Honestly, you get screwed over pretty quick
-
Not much to say. It's got clean menus, and useful graphics.
-
Do you love zombie games? Do you still suck at killing them? No worries. This game has quite a few different play styles, each one taking place at a different time in the apocalypse. The Initial Infection (a non-canon play for those of us who suck at the games we love), The First Week (where things start to pick up, and those zombies really start to pay closer attention to you), Six Months Later (the name says it all, but you better know how to get water for yourself...), and the last mode, Survival, where you see how long it takes you to die.
The first three modes even have more difficulty options within them, so you really get to pick what type of game you want to play.
-
This game feels full, alive (or, uh, undead?), and pretty complet minus some bugs here or there. The fact that this game will only get better is really exciting!
-
By no means rendering the game unplayable, but melee is always the way I go. This could just be my game, but I occasionally have issues with fighting zombies. I'll be aimed right on them, but whatever weapon I'm beating them with will move right through them. Moving around a bit usually helps this, but it can be an ocasional annoyance.
-
Not something that is super problematic, but still worth mentioning. Some players have found cooking to be a hit and miss problem without the help of the wikia or other guides. Recipes, unless you know them, can leave you confused on what you can and can't cook. Yeah, you can make soup. But, no, you can't make bowls of cereal and milk (which I know from my own tragic expirience).
The problems in Project Zomboid are very minimal, and are not enough to turn a player away from the game. What you get with this a really fun game that you can play for hours on end. Whether you want to build a fort, or leech off existing houses, live in a Zombie-filled city, or a blank country side, you're in charge of your own tragic and inevitable death.

It's weird. I enjoyed my time with
. Yet I was bored at the same time. Why is that? And could I really recommend the game after that?
is a really basic tower defense. There is a single lane, and monsters charge towards a penthouse that looks like there might be a Halloween party in there.
(Actually there's no story at all, but I liked to imagine that reason.)
There's a diverse set of towers: single-shot, double-shot, heavy-shot, fast heavy-shot, super-fast heavy-shot... Actually they looked more diverse on the screen. There's over ten towers with increasing prices. Each one can be upgraded for increased fire rate, damage and range. No buff- nor debuff-towers exist.
One thing that stroke funny was that there's no gradual unlocking of towers as the campaign progresses. Everything is there from the beginning.
If you can afford it, that is.
, because early mobs don't give enough cash for that. So, the progression is kind of emergent as later you get more cash.
I was expecting air units at some point, because there is an anti-air cannon. But they never appeared, so I never built one. I think that cannon had a confusing name.
Instead, once in the later levels (like halfway through the game's 10 levels) I could buy my first plasma turret.
Plasma turret simply mows through everything. Nothing could get past it; not weak mobs, not heavily armoured giants - not even the fast slithering alligator things, because it simply shoots so fast.
Plasma turret is OP as hell. Every level would be won after you got the funds to build one. Then it became boring waiting until the level ended. Unfortunately, it basically ruined the game for me.
Afterwards, I feel that because of the overpowered cannons, the game was just too easy, as well as short. Its ten levels lasted a mere hour.
What could have saved it? Maybe additional challenges, e.g. through interesting achievements. The current achievements are basically earned by completing levels. Perhaps adding something like "Beat the level X without building plasma turrets" or "Beat the level Y without turret upgrades" could have helped it.
Btw, it does not have Trading cards, despite Store page claiming so, at least not yet.
It's a fine game for its price for an achievement hunter/completionist. It just isn't much anything else.

Carmageddon 2 is the first race… cargame I ever played, and I have never had this much fun with a racer since.
Since this game is so old, I'll mostly mention the gameplay elements.
Race, Kill, Destroy
That's basically it, you do those 3 things, all the time, for fun, because you can.
Back then there already were soft-body physics, and though unrealistic and totally goofy, they are still fun, satisfying to see. Not only this, but they actively, and severely influence the gameplay itself, making you actually aim for certain ways to collide at times, just to cripple your opponent.
Though crashing into your opponents, racing across the creative maps, and killing all the peds you see is great fun by itself, this is even made better with the addition of tons of crazy and goofy powerups. Nowhere else can you send a car flying across the whole map using a coil spring, but here. (and maybe soon in the new Carmageddon too)
FIND ALL THE SECRETS!
Yes these maps were all designed to be explored, making them not only great and interesting battlegrounds, but also filled with tons and tons of secrets, powerups, and curiosities. Not only this, but most maps also have challenges ready for you, to unlock those secrets; ever tried a jumping puzzle with a car? (or 10ft truck?)
The Fun, The Crasy and the Annoying.
Now a lot of fun is ready for you as you already read, but there are also some warnings I’ll have to give, especially regarding the physics engine.
Carmageddon has a great physics engine, but it doesn’t feel or play like one of a racegame; often you will feel like you’re actually floating on water, or flying through the air like you’re on the moon. (even without the lunar-gravity powerup) This by itself means… DON’T EXPECT FLUIENT RACING. Jumping puzzles are made easier because of this, but making tight corners, or any corners at all at high speeds, are impossible.
Be certain that you want a crazy, goofy, arcady game if you plan on buying it. This is not a real actual racegame, even if it is definitely a car game.
The glue that keeps the mess together.
The game has a simple GUI and should offer no problems at all. There are many quirky things to keep in mind like stats and cars to own and buy during and around the actual ‘races’, and the GUI certainly makes it easy to keep an eye on everything. The big flaws here lie with the controls settings, and the ‘map’.
The controls are by default mapped to the NUMPAD KEYS… I know, a total WTF, and to make things worse, you can’t rebind them to any key you want… meaning that you won’t be able to use arrow keys or WASD.  Trust me though, even if you could rebind them, you wouldn’t be instantly comfortable either due to the physics, so please forgive the game for this and give it a shot anyway. It won’t be long before you get used to it. I do however recommend that you try to rebind the other keys (repair, handbrake, use power, etc) to keys convenient to you. I know the game used to work with a steering wheel, but I am uncertain how it responds to the more modern ones. I do recommend using a steering wheel if you get the chance.
In regards to the map, this bugger is probably the only annoyance you’ll have with the GUI. There is a minimap you can put on your screen, but initially it’ll be in the center of the screen. You can fix that using Shift+arrow keys though, to move the lil bugger around. However, due to the low resolution of the game, it’s too small to be able to actually effectively use it as a minimap the way you’re probably used to. Apart from this there is a big map, which is a big overlay displaying the whole map at once. You can still drive though using a little portrait sized window… a bit the opposite concept of the minimap.
The GUI has a little trick that helps with the map issues though, which basically locks on to targets and the next checkpoint. The minimap displays a line in that direction then, so you will at least be able to find the checkpoints and chase enemies, after looking at the big map on how to get there.
Sounds And Visuals
Now it’s 2014 so be gentle on this old-timer. Regardless I can already tell you that, although low quality, the sound is generally satisfying and applicable within the context. Scraping, bending and crashing metal sound very much as you’d want it to, as well as a very pleasant sound for breaking glass. Apart from this, Carmageddon offers you 4 tracks of heavy metal from Iron Maiden and 3 songs from Sentience… which… I don’t even know, but it sounds alright I guess, considering the game it is. So you’ll probably want to play your own music the 2nd time you run the game, since you’ll be hearing the same song over and over again otherwise.
Visually Carmageddon is very simplistic, and very dated. This however isn’t any problem within the context of the game, and in fact can be amusing at times. If you don’t mind the old graphics style, then you’ll still find that artistically, the game is unique, entertaining and satestfying.
Personal Opinion
This game I have been playing since childhood, and has never let me down in entertaining me with some good old fun, even if it’s old.
Everybody has some game which is like a child to them, often old and forgotten by most of the population, and this is mine.

Have a Wacom tablet? I have, and with this game it’s been a pain in my buttocks. Often windows would suddenly start thinking my tablet is my main cursor input, causing many annoying bugs with my mouse. SOLLUTION: turn off the Wacom driver, either before or after, depending on how skilled  and knowledgeable you are with your keyboard.

This game scared the heck out of me. I just beat the game, watched all the credits, and I'm still jittery. So let's do some pros and cons, hm?
Pros:
- Nice graphics, while not as good as something like Battlefield 1, they still hold up pretty well for a 4 year old game.
- It's scary. This game will absolutely terrify you. Which might be a con, if you don't like scary stuff, but if so you probably wouldn't be considering buying this game anyway.
- Decent story. It's not really thought provoking or compelling in any way, but it has a cool concept and executes it pretty well.
- Good mechanics. It has a lot of cool mechanics that make it interesting, like the night vision camera, and the batteries.
- Good amount of playtime. I've heard some games take like 40+ hours to play, so compared to that, it's pretty short, but it took me about 10 hours to beat the game, and I'd call that a fair amount of playtime.
Cons:
- It's close to demonic. If you aren't religious, that probably wouldn't be a problem, but as a theist it kinda freaked me out. Like that part where
Yeah, wasn't really into that. I almost closed the game and refunded it right then, but I had played it for more than two hours (which means you aren't allowed to refund it) and I was getting close to the ending anyway.
- It's kind of a rage game at times. Multiple times while I was playing, I'd get to a certain part that was really hard to pass, and the first one or two times it was scary, but after that it was just annoying until I finally beat that section. I think I had to browse the internet 2 or 3 times when I wasn't able to get past a certain part.
Things that could be a pro or con:
- Its strategy based. Many times in the game, there are parts where you have to think of a plan (or copy someone else's) to get past certain areas.
Final word: It's a spooky game that'll give you the spooks, and while its cool and fun to play, I'm sort of torn over how many demonic themes there are. So in some ways it's really a question who you are and what sort of stuff you're into. But aside from that, I'd say its a great game that you should play if you like the horror/suspense genre.

Hardly impressed by this product. Only thing SYABH has going for it is British countryside aesthetics and the game hardly uses it to  its potential: environment is very dull and there is barely any atmosphere or lingo in flavor text, all you see is typical north England housing and robots wearing top hats(yet speaking in very broad accent using common terms).
Another completely misused asset in this game is procedural generation: supposedly it creates parts of the world from a seed, but the only difference it ever has is in occasional building, that you can only push button on to receive loot, looks different, but even with that 90% of the world is the identical tall grass and copypasted trees.

UI is functional but that is all that can be said for it, no flavor, no stylistic impression, just a grid with objects on it.

Another good point this game is capable of striking is the weaponry feel, shotguns have a nice punch to them, but even that gets spoiled when you realize every single firearm has the same sound and hitting an enemy with it results in metal clinking anyway.
Not exactly a horrid unplayable mess, but for the life of me I can't recommend it even to people whose eyes light up every time they hear Yorkshire accent.

My first Red Faction game was 2, followed by Guerilla - I really, really enjoyed both.
There have been a lot of negative reviews for this one, but most of those compare Armageddon far too strongly (and unfairly) to Guerilla. Notice that this game is called Red Faction: Armageddon, NOT Red: Faction Guerilla 2.
That being said, if you are a fan of the series, like third-person action shooters, and environment destructibility, then you will really, really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are great, with absolutely fantastic environmental destruction depending on what weapon you use. The music and sounds are good. The story is decent, plot and gameplay progression is considerably more linear than Guerilla's open-world freedom, however, you should not be coming in to this game expecting it to be Guerilla 2.
The controls are easy to familiarize yourself with and the learning curve is minimal to moderate.
There is a horde mode that can be played local co-op or online multiplayer (or even solo) that is extremely fun. You unlock the levels you beat and can start at whatever wave you have unlocked. Solo playthrough is fairly challenging but doable if you keep practicing.
There is also a destruction mode that is insanely fun. You can choose whichever weapon loadout to use (you can swap weapons by going back to the equipment console) and just destroy everything in the environment. The magnet gun is amazing - shoot two (applicable) areas and the lighter object will fly toward the heavier one. Most of the weapons available will easily cut through most buildings and materials. You can play without a time limit or try the challenges - clearing the level within a time limit.
If you like third-person shooters with a lot of action and colossal amounts of destruction, give this game a try.
Highly recommend!

Italian:

Ad ogni modo, se vi piace fare esplodere le cose e ridurre a brandelli alieni, senza disdegnare meccaniche meno ignoranti della media, Armageddon è il titolo che fa per voi.

I would like to point out first before I write the review that Red Orchestra and Rising Storm are more complicated games, requiring a person to be familiar with tactics and is fairly complex, making it harder to learn how to play. It also contains a weapon unlock system and a weapon upgrade system that goes is given when you reach a certain level, so if you do not like any of these things that I have mentioned, then this game is not for you. If you are still interested, continue reading this review.
Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm is a very fun game, with great game play and graphics. It is harder to start off playing so I would suggest playing on servers with only bots. This game has some pretty cool features, such as a commander can call in artillery strikes and have a recon aircraft flying around showing you where the enemies are at on the map. This game for AT soldiers does not give them rocket launchers such as the Panzerfaust, but instead Anti Tank Rifles. The weapons are true to life, such as the accuracy of a firearm, the ballistics and the model of the gun. The only vehicles that can be used in game are tanks for RO2, so the game is mostly infantry fighting. When using tanks, a person might want to take a bit to look at how well it is modeled on the inside and the realism that comes with tanks. It contains a great feature, that certain classes can have a set number of players in it and that the game is set out to have several squads per team. Rising Storm is similar to RO2, however it has the ability for the Japanese to use mortars, the United States can use flamethrower troops, and there are no playable vehicles.
So in summary the game is very realistic, such as being able to take cover behind objects, and being able to fire around objects while not exposing you to the enemy. It has great game play, graphics, classes, vehicles and weapons. The only problem that I find with this game is that you can’t destroy any of the scenery, buildings, or other static objects, which makes it agitating when you crash a tank into a tree or light, and then have to back up and
move around it.

Overall, if you like shooter games with some exploration and a good story thrown in, get this! Seriously, it's phenomenal.

Where to start?
This game is incredible, and probably what the survival genre need. The graphics are one of a kind, and kinda minimalist which is something I'm always fond in videos games (but some people might find it weird or odd, specially when a wolf is trying to eat you). The sound design work is incredible, if you have good heaphone I swear you think you are in a real blizzard. The voice acting is great for what we can see of it, but it's just sandbox so it feels random and out of place sometimes.
Yeah, by the way, you will pay quite a lot for just sandbox and a bunch of challenge that can be done the eyes closed. Because the game is trying to be realistic in its survival part (which is great), it's really easy to understand how all of this work and what you need to do to survive. In 16h I "finished" the game and felt like I had played whatever could be played of it. But it wasn't scary back then to have this feel, the story mode was supposed to be published later this year. But it didn't. And Hinterland made a point to be either rude or complete dimwit in their PR.
At first I really believe they just wanted to publish a game that was exactly like they wanted. But soon the update for the sandbox mode got bigger and bigger. "it's great! Don't complain!" Oh, yes, I didn't complain at first even if my eyebrow rised a little. Because apparently they are just a bunch of programmers. It's the perfect argument for the late release. But it doesn't make sense, if you are so outnumbered, to work massively on your sandbox when it has been two years people wait for a story mode.
They make enough money with it, and the sandbox being not so bad, people don't complain. I'm not saying they don't work on story mode (even if three years later I'm starting to think yes), but they obliviously neglect it. And when confronted to the facts, they just evade the question.
So, yes, I have given up on the game and regret deeply to have bought it. Not so much for the late release, but more for the way Hinterland handle it. This studios doesn't take their customers seriously nor their engagement.And they doesn't accept critic of it.
Sure, there was going to be delay, it's an indie game after all. But not three years. Three years with pathetics excuses is just another Day Z or War Z.
I'm a big kickstarter fan, and backed a lot of game. There were almost always delay, it's even logical to have them, but they always at least tell you were they are in the developpment, and don't make any more money until it is released, pushing them to actually publish it and not just wash their hands with the money of a sandbox. And they keep you updated on it.
Look at Prey for the Gods. They are even less than Hinterlands and yet they do incredible work in taking their fans seriously and respecting them at least by keeping them updated on the progress (for Christ's Sake they even did a update to explain why there wasn't one in two weeks).
So believe me, if you want this game even though Hinterlands are a bunch of ****, wait for the story mode being released, because you will get bored real soon in the sandbox if you are not completely stupid and can comprehend gameplay mechanics. It will probably have a rise in the price, yes, but simply don't buy it on Steam and it will be even less pricy than it is now without the official release.
TL;DR: Game is awesome but just sandbox so you "finish" it really quick if you are not an idiot, studio is a bunch of as**** who seems to not care anymore for story mode since sandbox is making enough money and good reviews. Waiting to buy it for the release will force them to work on it more (if at all).

Civ fanatics look here. This is Civ on crack. This is one of my favorite games of all time that I can just fall back on an enjoy endless hours of game play. You can take your hero, recruit more heroes and go on epic quests or just take over the world militarily. You can win by crafting the the most epic spell, win by diplomacy, win by kicking the♥♥♥♥♥♥our of everyone or win by achieving the hardest end quest.
I think one of the coolest parts of this game is the ability to create and customize your own army. You can pick what kind of armor and weapons it has, the gender, size. Just a whole lot of options.

Do you like Civilization? Do you like RPG's? This is basically Civ where you can level up your leader like an RPG character, give them gear and talents, and let them go forth and do your bidding. Also there's questing, recruiting magical creatures or other heroes.
You control various cities with an area of influence around them, and deal with managing cities by building structures, focusing on what the city produces, and doing research, as well as controlling natural resources on the map. There are wandering monsters (Think Barbarians in Civ) that pop up from time to time and they may attack a city if they are close enough.
You can build armies of general sorts of units, but even this has flavor because you're not just designing them and naming them, you pick the equipment and gear they use, and you do have the ability to auto-upgrade existing units to whatever the newest armor/weapons that your research has unlocked, provided you have the resources.
The real fun comes from heroes, who either are recruited during certain quests or random events, or seek you out to join you when you have accomplished enough to gain enough fame. Your Sovreign (your faction's leader) is a hero with talent trees with plenty of choices, spells, and gear just like any good RPG. They can be skilled up to be good at managing a city, good at leading an army, or good fighters in and of themselves (or anything in between really). The same goes for other heroes you come across.
There is diplomacy with other empires but for the most part you're flying solo and trying to win on your own. There are numerous victory options, and most mirror the ones you'd find in Civ.
The random events and quests are varied and interesting, and the randomly generated maps lead to a lot of replayability.
The weakest aspects of the game are the city building (which, while it has depth, is nowhere near what you'd find in a dedicated city building game), the RPG aspects (while there's a lot to do and the random events are good, eventually you'll get some repeats after you've played a bunch of games). They are both pretty well done but not great - it is better than average at both but exceptional at neither. Additionally, there's not really ANY story or campaign mode. You have scenarios, but this is largely a sandbox with a randomly generated map and any story is going to be what you personally make of it via the random events that happen.
HOWEVER: This game supports mod tools and user-created races, maps, items, quests, etc. Any variety the game lacks out of the box goes away if you poke around the official forums for a bit and find something that changes things you dislike (or make your own).
In sum, this game is quite enjoyable and I find myself equally drawn in by both the empire building and RPG aspects of it. Neither aspect is 100% perfect, but the games can be long (especially if you play on enormous maps with lots of AI as I tend to), and if I get bored with the RPG aspect for a bit, I'll spend time focusing on just my cities for a bit. The game lets me play it however I want and never forces me to do anything, and there's enough to do that I consistently go back to it.
It's been out for awhile now and you can probably pick it up at a decent price. The DLC is fine - it's not must-have and it's not a waste of money. It's mostly small things - new heroes, new quests, new items, which all randomly pop up in your game. The game is fun with them, but nothing stands out as  absolute must-haves. Get the DLC if you get the game and enjoy it and want more of it, or if you get the game bundled with it at a decent price.

Empire at War is an RTS game that is very different from other RTS games. It takes time to learn how it works, but after words, it is a very fun and unique experience.
Unlike other RTS games that focus on resource management, base building, research, and slowly crushing your enemy, this game shifts into something different. Planet side combat has you taking the role of the attacker or defender. As the attacker you are limited to the amount of units you brought to the planet and you can only have at most ten squads on the field at a time. You also have to take reinforcement points across the map in order to place more units on the field. As for the defenders, you have a limited number of slots that can be used on a plant to build unit buildings, defensive buildings, and other types of structures. These buildings are preplaced on the map and you then have to use your men and credits to drive off or destroy the attackers.
Space combat is similar, but it’s center around the defensive space station giving both the attacker and defender a more pure role.
As for story, this game is based in the original trilogy timeline allowing you to choose between the rebellion and the empire.
This game has a very unique twist on the RTS genre that is very well executed and exciting. If you are a lover of RTS games this one is well worth a shot.

So, when I was a kid, I owned this big red tricycle. Well, it was big to me, because I was around three feet tall and couldn't balance myself on a bike yet. I liked riding this big red tricycle up and down the street my grandmother lived on because there really wasn't much else to do in the house aside from watch game shows on this crappy little eight-inch black-and-white TV she had in the kitchen. That, and eat lots of Cream of Wheat.
One day, I rode my tricycle down the block, and there was this big pothole in the road that I never saw before. It was surrounded by yellow traffic cones so cars wouldn't accidentally drive through it.

Looks good, sounds good, for the most part is actually really good. Except that every turn you roll a dice to see whether the game decides it's time for you to die and start over.
It does not matter how well you're doing or how careful you are. There are random events that you have no possible way of overcoming unless you are very, very lucky. So lucky these events don't trigger at all for example.
But you won't be that lucky.

Where to start?
This game is incredible, and probably what the survival genre need. The graphics are one of a kind, and kinda minimalist which is something I'm always fond in videos games (but some people might find it weird or odd, specially when a wolf is trying to eat you). The sound design work is incredible, if you have good heaphone I swear you think you are in a real blizzard. The voice acting is great for what we can see of it, but it's just sandbox so it feels random and out of place sometimes.
Yeah, by the way, you will pay quite a lot for just sandbox and a bunch of challenge that can be done the eyes closed. Because the game is trying to be realistic in its survival part (which is great), it's really easy to understand how all of this work and what you need to do to survive. In 16h I "finished" the game and felt like I had played whatever could be played of it. But it wasn't scary back then to have this feel, the story mode was supposed to be published later this year. But it didn't. And Hinterland made a point to be either rude or complete dimwit in their PR.
At first I really believe they just wanted to publish a game that was exactly like they wanted. But soon the update for the sandbox mode got bigger and bigger. "it's great! Don't complain!" Oh, yes, I didn't complain at first even if my eyebrow rised a little. Because apparently they are just a bunch of programmers. It's the perfect argument for the late release. But it doesn't make sense, if you are so outnumbered, to work massively on your sandbox when it has been two years people wait for a story mode.
They make enough money with it, and the sandbox being not so bad, people don't complain. I'm not saying they don't work on story mode (even if three years later I'm starting to think yes), but they obliviously neglect it. And when confronted to the facts, they just evade the question.
So, yes, I have given up on the game and regret deeply to have bought it. Not so much for the late release, but more for the way Hinterland handle it. This studios doesn't take their customers seriously nor their engagement.And they doesn't accept critic of it.
Sure, there was going to be delay, it's an indie game after all. But not three years. Three years with pathetics excuses is just another Day Z or War Z.
I'm a big kickstarter fan, and backed a lot of game. There were almost always delay, it's even logical to have them, but they always at least tell you were they are in the developpment, and don't make any more money until it is released, pushing them to actually publish it and not just wash their hands with the money of a sandbox. And they keep you updated on it.
Look at Prey for the Gods. They are even less than Hinterlands and yet they do incredible work in taking their fans seriously and respecting them at least by keeping them updated on the progress (for Christ's Sake they even did a update to explain why there wasn't one in two weeks).
So believe me, if you want this game even though Hinterlands are a bunch of ****, wait for the story mode being released, because you will get bored real soon in the sandbox if you are not completely stupid and can comprehend gameplay mechanics. This article is one wall of♥♥♥♥♥kissing text, be prepared. Dungeon of the Endless and why I consider it one of the best games ever made. It’s addicting and fun, but why? What is the underlying structure that makes it such a masterpiece? Some of my favourites in terms of game design are Braid, To the Moon, Spelunky, Starseed Pilgrim and Portal.
The main three things Dungeon of the Endless gets right:
-	Pacing
-	Risk versus Reward
-	Emergent complexity
Let’s talk about pacing in games and why it is important. The human mind craves variety and has limited concentration. This is why action movies do not consist of 93 minutes of car chases and shooting. Every action sequence is followed by a buildup of tension until it explodes into action again. Games can do this in different ways. RPG’s typically have dungeons interspersed with towns in which you catch your breath and prepare for the next travel. Shooters (Call of Duty excluded), have that satisfying sound of silence to signify the end of battle after which you explore until the next shootout.
Dungeon of the Endless is a three course meal consisting of the planning phase, the defense phase and the crystal phase. In the planning phase there is time to breathe. We can spend minutes theory crafting about which door to open, where to position your hero’s and which modules to build. This contrasts with the defense phase, which starts after we open a door and waves of enemies begin to spawn. It is possible to pause and think, but every action has to be perfectly timed and combined with the others. We move around our heroes to make sure all survive while defending our modules and crystal. The crystal phase is a third phase, the run for your money when you decide that every next door opened will cost you more than you gain. These three phases work because of the reasons mentioned earlier: variety, time to relax and dramatic buildup.
The next group of things Dungeon does right is the risk-versus-reward mechanics. These are evident in multiple choices: exploring versus diving, operating versus moving and saving versus spending. Exploring more rooms will grant you more resources, but at every door we have to ask ourselves a question. Will holding of waves of enemies cost us too much food to heal our heroes, science to reset their cooldowns and industry to replace our modules? If this is true, it is surely better to go deeper. Operators pose a second risk-versus-reward mechanic. Keeping them stationary gains you more resources, but moving them around might provide better defensive capabilities. The third dilemma is spending your resources versus saving them for the next levels. All invested industry is, like dust, effectively lost when you move to the next level. Thus we must consider… Do we hold out more rounds and thus gain more resources if we build more modules? Or do we save and start on the next floor with a head start? This mechanic is ingrained in the game on so many levels. Building more expensive versus basic modules, building resource gathering versus defensive mains. The generator adds another layer of depth here.
The third aspect Dungeon of the Endless excels in is emergent complexity. There is so much depth to this game, it’s unbelievable. What module to research? What hero to hire? What hero to level? Which resources to expend? Do we rather lose modules, heal our heroes or invest science to reset cooldowns? Do we fight with Joleri, losing dust in the process? Do we buy these items or do we save? Furthermore, did you know the following were legit strategies: changing items on heroes mid fight to change their stats; buying all items from the dust merchant while another hero is carrying the crystal because power is not of importance anymore; juggling heroes in and out of a room to make the monsters walk around aimlessly? Okay, so the possibilities are… Endless. Why is it emergent though? Because we have to wrap your own mind around the game to come up with new solutions. Heck, it is not even necessary to delve deep into these decisions and learn advanced strategies to have fun in this game. Settings and pod choice influence difficulty so much that you can easily be effective while thinking about nothing of the above.
All in all, it is exquisite that a game nails all these points in game design. I do not know how to write a conclusion so this just ends he…
Endless fun!

TL;DR - I'm giving a negative overall review to TLD mainly because the development of the game has not moved forward consistently towards a v1.0, and I feel like the developers are not up to the task of producing a finished version anytime soon. [As context, I backed TLD through Kickstarter on October 2013.]
-----
Let me start by saying that I really love the game! The devs have created a rather different, yet encompassing, atmospheric experience I've come to enjoy, and that I think deserves it's current followship.
On this review, I'm not going to delve into realistic vs. arbitrary game mechanics, real-life vs. artistic graphics, or any other of the gameplay issues mentioned both positively and negatively on these threads. I will focus exclusively on the implicit contract between gamers and developers that inexorably arises when supporting Early Access (EA) games.
I've played TLD on and off for the past three years, starting when there was only one map (Mystery Lake) and rather limited and unbalanced game mechanics. Reviewing my logs, I backed TLD through Kickstarter on October 14, 2013!
Back then, the state of the game was beyond my wildest dreams, especially for an EA game. There was only one map, but it was large, and gorgeous, and functional. Gameplay was still green, but you could see why and how the developers were going to benefit from the community's input. It really felt like I was given the chance to get in early, help the development of the game, and brag that I've known and played the game from the very beginning.
And I was not alone. The game and team earned some positive accolades around this time, like ranking #9 on Gameranx's list of The Best PC Games of 2014 among other similar mentions, and allegedly raised over $260k from nearly 7,000 backers on both Kickstarter and Paypal. (Source: Project Update #30, October 16, 2013.)
Everything seemed on track, from the constant game updates, to the energy and demeanor of the communications from the dev team, all the way to the enthusiasm of the community...
But 2014 came and went, and then 2015, and just recently 2016, and there is still no finished game available. New content has been added in the last three years to the sandbox, but it has been only 5 new maps and very few gameplay additions.
Moreover, the developers have announced that v1.0, or storymode, will be released by episodes as part of "Season One", on yet a future undisclosed date. The game currently available guarantees access only to this Season One. The first release, consisting of two episodes, apparently will account for only 6 gameplay hours. After the initial batch of the five episodes that will amount to Season One (and honestly, only adding insult to injury), devs are already planning the next installment as a new game that will be marketed separately. (Source: Story Mode Progress — December Community Update, December 19, 2016.)
I feel like after 3 years from funding the game, plus any development done prior to that date, all the feedback and help provided by the community, and the additional funding the company has gotten from selling the game on Steam and other similar platforms (all this in addition to the initial funding mentioned above), should have been more than enough to produce a working v1.0. And it hasn't.
Sad as it may be, I've decided to stop buying EA games...
