First of all: This is a mildly negative review.
My first impression when playing The Long Dark was overwhelmingly positive. The first few hours of playing the game are amazing and if you are the kind of person who is satisfied with getting about 10 hours of entertainment out of a game, it might be the perfect purchase for you.
But the more time you spent, the more you familiarise yourself with the mechanics of the game and the longer you survive, the more the games inherent, irreparable flaws become visible. What flaws you mean? I will provide a short list of the most glaring issues below, but let just preface this with a quick disclaimer about the way I approach survival games:
To me, survival is all about realism. "It's a game, not a simulation!", you might interject, but no, I disagree. A survival game is always a simulation, otherwise, lacking the link to real-life survival, there would be no basis for immersion and identification with the survival situation. When you are confronted with a situation in a survival game and out the real-life solutions to this problem only a tiny fraction is available in-game, it just ends up being frustrating and disappointing. And here's how The Long Dark disappointed me in this regard.
- you cannot sleep without a bed or bedroll; not on the floor, not on a couch, not using "old bedrolls" - you just can't
- you can barely interact with your environment; you can't reclaim wood from buildings, piers and most furniture (e.g. containers), only from designated recyclable objects that then serve no other purpose. You can't even combine several beds to make one warmer bed.
- you cannot move objects before interacting with them; you have to butcher deer where they died, even if that is just a couple of feet away from your warm and cozy home, you have to break up branches and limbs where they are, you cannot move chairs, crates, etc. to store them for disassembly later, all you can move is what you can pick up and carry like inventory items, but you should be able to drag larger objects around.
- there is a severe lack of crafting recipes that are far more reasonable than the ones the game does offer; curtains, towels, even upholstry could all be turned into makeshift clothes, almost everything could be turned into a makeshift melee weapon, a whetstone and any bit of scrap metal could make a makeshift knife, etc.
- with wildlife being as aggressive as it is in the games, there would be innumerable ways of luring them into traps
- the game creates artificial scarcity in a number of ways:
..- you need more food than would be realistic
..- hunted animals yield hardly any meat/calories
..- tools wear down at ludicrous rates
..- several items are unnecessarily scarce (materials for bows/arrows, cloth)
..- you cannot freeze food (!!!) to keep it fresh or conserve it any other way [Edit: apparently leaving food outdoors makes it more durable, but potentially exposes it to wildlife]
..- fires are incredibly short lived and hard to maintain
..- time passes way too fast in relation to how fast you can move / act in the game (and don't argue with map scale! stepping outside of the house to take is leak shouldn't take half an hour and going down to the lake from a lakeside cabin shouldn't take up all morning)
- you cannot jump, which makes you take silly detours all the time because of less than 1 foot high obstacles
- you get injured very easily when walking (!) downhill
- animals respawn randomly rather than existing and reproducing in a realistic way
- you cannot do more than one thing at a time (seriously, who needs to watch water boil for two hours straight?) This is probably the worst flaw, when you have to spend hours frying one steak at a time using massive amounts of firewood.
Most of these, or at least the more important ones like interacting with the environment, moving objects, time management seem to be hard-wired into the game without any hope of them being addressed or changed as development progresses.
Therefore, unfortunately, I cannot really enjoy this game as much as I would like to.

Improved version, with added glide wrapper, meaning you can play games designed for 3dfx Glide API without the need of having a 3dfx graphics card. The 90s :)
If you go to your Steam Library and look for "Carmageddon 2: Carpocalypse Now" then right click on it you will only find "Play Game..." and "View Player Manual" There is no option to configure the glide wrapper aka "nGlide" You have to do it manually go to your SteamApps/Common folders and inside "Carmageddon2" you fill find the "nglide_config.exe" so you can configure correctly the wrapper.
Also when the game was released (Late 90s) it came with ipx support so for this release (Prolly the GOG version have it too) they added an ipx wrapper, that wraps IPX packets into UDP, so modern OS can run this legacy games with multiplayer support.
About the music, The amazing soundtrack is still here, this time is compressed using Vorbis (Lossy compression) The original release of Carma2 came in a CD, it was an Enhanced CD (Yellow Book CD-ROM + Red Book CD-DA) where the 1st track was the Data (The video Game) and the rest of tracks were the music, meaning your were allowed to put your Game CD in your CD Player and listen to the music, of course if you played the 1st track the one that contains the game data you will only hear random noise. While writing this review I was listening to the songs and found out that track Number 8 "The Trooper" by Iron Maiden at the 3:04 there is an error in the song prolly the CD was damaged/scrached, and you guys ripped it anyway, Lazy Stainless :P

I'm the kind of player who pays attention to reviews. The well informing ones are the best, whether good or bad. I read this is a brilliant and realistic game and this was no lie! There is no tutorial. I'm not saying that's a bad thing at all. The idea that the player needs to learn what to do as they go also gives a sense of accomplishment when something is figured out.Speaking of a sense of accomplishment, just discovering something new is a treat in itself.  The attention to detail is amazing. The signs. Crows flying around meaning something dead is near. The creaking of a building while inside indicates a blizzard or high winds outside. Everything has consequences. Try to overdo yourself, you die. Don't take care of the basic needs, you die. Figure you can take on a bear with nothing more than a bow and arrow, you will definitely die. Eat uncooked rancid meat, ugh! Even things such as a weight limit. I like that one. It forces you to make decisions about what to take and what to leave. It would take away from the game if I could carry infinite number of everything. I've avoided most of the wildlife so far. I think the trailer videos creeped me out not to test those waters yet.
All in all, this game is absolutely spectacular. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the survival games and appreciates one with realism.
I would really like a co-op mode, but I don't have any other complaints.

This is a tricky one to review and I have just started to scratch the surface of it, but here it goes.
First of all, the story: you are forced to flee on an escape pod before your starship gets destroyed, and after you crash-land on planet Auriga you find yourself in a depths of a multi-level dungeon, from which you have to escape with the very few resources you have at your disposal and whatever you can find in the ruins, fighting monsters in the process.
Don't let yourself be fooled by the pixel-art graphics (which are beautiful if you are into this kind of thing) and think that this is a simple game. It's not easy at all (despite the fact that the initial difficulty levels are labelled
and
) and
. The music also has a chiptuny, retro-style which fits well with the graphics assets.
The game style is a very nice blend of RPG, tower defense strategy and roguelike games. There is a constant feeling of uncertainty and fear, since stuff happens whenever you open a door: you might find new loot or something/someone else, you might trigger a mighty horde of monsters coming for you, your resource nodes, defences and/or your energy crystal (which, if it breaks, leads you to a game over). Resources are scarce so you will have to think well how to spend them; moreover, the fact that the dungeons are procedurally generated means that such a strategy will have to change whenever you restart the game.
During the game you can research for new weapons (both static defenses and items for your heroes) and for new, better resource nodes.
To me, it feels like a board game (a feeling that is enhanced even more in multi player) that changes every time you play; the board game closest to Dungeon of the Endless I can think of is Munchkin: whenever you open a door, you don't know what you will get. Riches? Monsters? Even worse? Nobody knows, but -- unlike in Munchkin -- at least your companions won't turn against you. :)
If you like roguelike or tactical games with strategic elements and you're a fan of sci-fi settings in general, I highly recommend you Dungeon of the Endless.

So the wacky french devs who made Endless Space (a brilliant space 4X) decided to make a dungeon crawler, but they can't be normal if they tried. So what you get is this weird and wonderful mix of tower-defense, squad RPG,  retro styled rogue-lite. Yeah it's different, but Dungeon of the Endless is also very good.
One of the most fun and gorgeous games out there. A real challenge.

I never predicted the fact that Roguelike and Tower Defense genres could go so well together. DotE is extremely addictive and fun for fans of those genres, it takes some of the best elements of both along with a really visually appealing take on retro pixel art. The only glaring flaws are the inability to save your game during multiplayer, and numerous current bugs involving loading and desynch in multiplayer. If they fix these issues then it'd be a contender for my personal game of the year.
A little complicated at first, but once you get to know it the game will become completely addictive!

A little tricky to figure out, but loads of fun. Beautiful, albeit redundant, visuals and an immersive soundtrack combine to produce the wonderfully tedious roguelike Dungeon of the Endless.  7/10, do recommend playing! If nothing else, and it certainly is more, its quite an experience.

In other words, if you parry *exactly* when you whould have taken damage, the parry doesn't count. First of all: This is a mildly negative review.
My first impression when playing The Long Dark was overwhelmingly positive. The first few hours of playing the game are amazing and if you are the kind of person who is satisfied with getting about 10 hours of entertainment out of a game, it might be the perfect purchase for you.
But the more time you spent, the more you familiarise yourself with the mechanics of the game and the longer you survive, the more the games inherent, irreparable flaws become visible. What flaws you mean? I will provide a short list of the most glaring issues below, but let just preface this with a quick disclaimer about the way I approach survival games:
To me, survival is all about realism. "It's a game, not a simulation!", you might interject, but no, I disagree. A survival game is always a simulation, otherwise, lacking the link to real-life survival, there would be no basis for immersion and identification with the survival situation. When you are confronted with a situation in a survival game and out the real-life solutions to this problem only a tiny fraction is available in-game, it just ends up being frustrating and disappointing. And here's how The Long Dark disappointed me in this regard.
- you cannot sleep without a bed or bedroll; not on the floor, not on a couch, not using "old bedrolls" - you just can't
- you can barely interact with your environment; you can't reclaim wood from buildings, piers and most furniture (e.g. containers), only from designated recyclable objects that then serve no other purpose. You can't even combine several beds to make one warmer bed.
- you cannot move objects before interacting with them; you have to butcher deer where they died, even if that is just a couple of feet away from your warm and cozy home, you have to break up branches and limbs where they are, you cannot move chairs, crates, etc. to store them for disassembly later, all you can move is what you can pick up and carry like inventory items, but you should be able to drag larger objects around.
- there is a severe lack of crafting recipes that are far more reasonable than the ones the game does offer; curtains, towels, even upholstry could all be turned into makeshift clothes, almost everything could be turned into a makeshift melee weapon, a whetstone and any bit of scrap metal could make a makeshift knife, etc.
- with wildlife being as aggressive as it is in the games, there would be innumerable ways of luring them into traps
- the game creates artificial scarcity in a number of ways:
..- you need more food than would be realistic
..- hunted animals yield hardly any meat/calories
..- tools wear down at ludicrous rates
..- several items are unnecessarily scarce (materials for bows/arrows, cloth)
..- you cannot freeze food (!!!) to keep it fresh or conserve it any other way [Edit: apparently leaving food outdoors makes it more durable, but potentially exposes it to wildlife]
..- fires are incredibly short lived and hard to maintain
..- time passes way too fast in relation to how fast you can move / act in the game (and don't argue with map scale! stepping outside of the house to take is leak shouldn't take half an hour and going down to the lake from a lakeside cabin shouldn't take up all morning)
- you cannot jump, which makes you take silly detours all the time because of less than 1 foot high obstacles
- you get injured very easily when walking (!) downhill
- animals respawn randomly rather than existing and reproducing in a realistic way
- you cannot do more than one thing at a time (seriously, who needs to watch water boil for two hours straight?) This is probably the worst flaw, when you have to spend hours frying one steak at a time using massive amounts of firewood.
Most of these, or at least the more important ones like interacting with the environment, moving objects, time management seem to be hard-wired into the game without any hope of them being addressed or changed as development progresses.
Therefore, unfortunately, I cannot really enjoy this game as much as I would like to.

Roguelike veteran here. First of all, this game is much less roguelike and much more tower defense.
WHAT IS ROGUELIKE ABOUT THIS GAME?
The only thing roguelike about the game is that the levels have random layouts and items are randomly found or bought from a randomly appearing item vendor. Also, when party members die they are dead for good, but more can be randomly found.
WHAT IS NOT ROGUELIKE ABOUT THIS GAME?
Very little character customization and development. As you level your characters with food that you generate yourself, skills are automatically assigned to one of the several unique characters. Also, the game does not offer the grand sense of scale of a good roguelike, either. There are 12 individual levels, and each can be beaten in about 10 minutes.
SO IT'S NOT VERY ROGUELIKE. IS IT ANY GOOD?
Definitely. I really enjoy it and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good tower defense with some randomness and a great visual style. The game is low-poly but high polish. A great pick-up-and-play that you'll be coming back to again and again.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted (SYABH) is conceptually and thematically interesting: a first-person sneaker with randomly generated levels filled with killer robots who look the part of british gentlemen. (except for being robots and the homicidal intent part).
The core gameplay loop is pretty solid, though not entirely perfect.  Stealth games rely on controlling the tension between the calm and chaos, and there are some rough edges in the loop.  As with many stealth games, audio cues and enemy animations play a significant role in determining the state of the enemy AI.  As such, some audio cues and animations were somewhat ambiguous, or seemed ambiguous.  For instance, robots in a heightened awareness who are facing away from you will nevertheless spot you immediately if your visibiility was above some unknown threshold.  Such behavior limits some strategies that were seemingly designed by the developers (i.e. throw a bottle, walk behind them); or perhaps the developers coded these behaviors so that these strategies would not be too effective?  While such AI behavior does detract from the immersiveness, it does artificially add to the tension, which feels cheap.
Also, sometimes robots would get into firefights among themselves; it's unclear what causes this, which is a shame.  One of the greatest feelings in any game, stealth or otherwise, is using the game systems to cause your enemies to wipe each other out.  Since the game makes these conditions opaque, you have no way of causing such firefights.
Another complaint I had with the game was the UI.  It could have been streamlined a lot more.  For instance, while rooting a building, there's no option to take all useful items or discard all useless items, only the option to take everything.  Or on a map, I can only place three markers.
SYABH is also certainly nice on the eyes.  During the moments when I wasn't chased by these robots, I found myself admiring the idyllic countryside.  Although this game doesn't have the bells and whistles in graphics as the latest AAAA titles, I was nevertheless impressed by the beautiful environments (which only required low system requirements!)  The character models were likewise exceptional, evoking charm and characteristics of british archtypes.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game if you like stealth games, like killing homicidal robots, and/or are an anglophile.

LIMBO is carried entirely by its atmosphere. Without it, it would offer very little that other games of the same genre do. While its platforming isn't bad by any means, and the puzzles are fairly satisfying, there's nothing present in the gameplay that hasn't been done before (and possibly better) in other games.
What makes this game unique is the artstyle, ambient sound effects, and general atmosphere. The story is barebones at best, with only general hints of what might be going on and the rest left open to interpretation. I can appreciate a vague, open-ended story, but in this case I would've liked a stronger narrative in leiu of other distinguishing features.
As such, it's still worth a play if you enjoy puzzle platformers with an emphasis on atmosphere. For some people, the atmosphere can pull them in and keep them entirely enraptured. Personally, I enjoyed the game, short as it was, but I did find myself disappointed that the intriguing atmosphere didn't pay off into unique gameplay or a captivating story.
This is a slow burner of a game, and definitely worth a playthrough if you are a fan of the genre and the atmosphere appeals to you.
Keep in mind it's a rather short game (~3 hours), and offers little replayability unless you're the type of person to go for 100%.

I hate these types of games.  It's beautiful and all, but don't ask me what it's about because there's nothing to indicate anything - no story, nothing.  You drown in tiny pools, anything can kill you - OR NOT, whatevs - random things will just kill you without warning, so you have to restart from the checkpoint and make sure you remember that thing that just falls out of the sky everytime at that one point so you have to slow down a tiny bit or die.  SO ANNOYING.
I find game mechanics like this to be cheap and incredibly frustrating.  Go, die, repeat, go, die, repeat.  It's just a bunch of random things that will kill you, causing you to start back at the checkpoint, that you easily overcome once you're aware that it's going to happen, then the next surprise thing kills you and you repeat it all over again.
You just walk along and BAM, that log collapses and you fall into a pool of water.  Dead, restart from checkpoint.  Walk along, log collapses but you've jumped to the cliff edge.  Then a tire drops on your head.  Dead, restart from checkpoint.  Log collapse, jump to cliff, tire, run back, hide under other log - but there's a spider.  Dead, restart from checkpoint.  Log, cliff, tire, run, hide, jump over spider leg to rope but rope drops you into pit.  Dead, restart from checkpoint.
It's really just a repeating thing, over and over again, with slight variations every time, SO ANNOYING.  Something kills you, restart, rinse, repeat. Dead, restart from checkpoint. You just walk along and BAM.  I find game mechanics like this to be incredibly cheap and so frustrating. You drown in tiny pools, anything can kill you - or not.  Go, die, repeat, go, die, repeat. REPEAT. REPEAT. REPEAT.

I first found Beyond Good & Evil as a used PS2 game in a Blockbuster and thought it looked interesting. The cover art was intriguing, and the basic description caught my attention. However, the first few times I tried to play the game, I could not get through it because I did not have the patience to solve some of the challenges. Then one day in college, I picked it up over a weekend, deciding to play for the heck of it and to finish it once and for all.
Am I glad I did.
The game immerses you in the story from the get-go, forgoing the typical long, drawn-out backstory. The characters are warm and engaging, and all of them, major and minor, are full of depth and life. This is the only game that can honestly make me say I was sad to leave the world when I completed it, and it is the only game I can pick up once every few months and play again, even though I already know the answers to all of the puzzles and where to find all of the hidden items. So imagine my heartbreak when my PS2 copy started to glitch each time I started a new file, and my joy finding that it is available on Steam for only ten dollars!
This game was well-thought out and developed, and I can say without a doubt that it is my favorite game. I am proud to own both the original PS2 copy and now to own it on Steam.

This game is one of the best zombie survival games out there. It's not a DayZ clone, it's full-out survival, a thing this genre needed done right. REAL survival. Not a Free-For-All PVP Walking Simulator.
Getting into a fight with even a single zombie can be dangerous, as a bite nearly guarantees that you will be infected. Scratches can also infect you, but it's not as likely as being bitten will. Always travel with a weapon ready, but be careful with what you use. A gun can bring in a MASSIVE amount of zombies from EVERY direction.
On top of that, weather and temperatures will affect your health as well. Out in the rain too long and got sick? Stay in your shelter and take it easy for a few in-game days. Too hot out? You'd better have something to drink.
If you survive all of the above, your life will get much, much harder. Eventually, water and electricity shut off for good, so you'll need to farm your own food and drink from wells or rain collecting barrels which you can build.
There's a lot more to the game, but I don't want to make this review too long. I'm going to have to give Project Zomboid an 8/10. It already feels like a finished game, and they keep coming out with updates that make the game bigger and better.

Hello boys and girls Joker here, this review/guide is primarily made for those that have experienced issues getting this amesome game to run under Windows 7, 8 & 10.. I'm currently using Windows 10 (Windows 7 up intil 4 months ago) but i know it would probably work just the same.
So, let's begin shall we..
Let me just say that installing the game caused my system to give me some kind of error message stating that the game installation could not get the required update due to it being locked after not receiving full access etc? (Err,
Anyway, i figured it out by following a few simple steps!
Step 1) Remove the contents from your library by first canceling the installation process and afterwards clearing the games cache (the game must be greyed out so to speak).
Step 2) Go over to your Windows Steam folder (Program Files x86, Steam, SteamApps, Common,..) followed by selecting the corresponding Star Wars EAW Gold file and deleting it accordingly.
Step 3) Restart your computer.
Step 4) Start Steam and install the game again, which should now work correctly..
Step 5) Start the game normally.
Step 6) This next step is a bit tricky and will most likely cause your system to hang/freeze but you can easily fix that by restarting the system once more.. (No worries, just use crtl + alt + del and in case you can't fully use the task manager, simply 'force' the PC to quick restart without actually rebooting it.)
*So, let me discuss (Step 6) a bit further now. You would like to change settings to your personal choosing, so just set the game according to your optimal/automated settings.
*Do not set the monitor settings to maximum just yet or it will be guarateed to crash (you can do that afterwards).
*Get into the game once more and you'll notice that your settings are now adjusted/adjustable..
In case your system would still crash, just repeat the previous steps and all will be working fine afterwards.
Step 7) Enjoy Star Wars EAW Gold!!! When done correctly give me a thumbs up guys, that's all i'm asking. :)
Now for my short review:
I still have the original disc copies at home and i must have played both original copies for many, many years..
That's why i decided to buy them on Steam hoping i could still be playing and enjoying them here while using Windows 10. (and This version works perfectly even without the patches i needed "in the good old days" to be able to run the expansion, which i can honestly say is quite awesome)
I must say that i'm really pleased that for me at least it remains the same just the way it was all those years ago.
Therefore i can only recommed it with my own personal thumbs up and an additional score of 8.5/10 in my book!
It's still a great game, so why should i need to say more right?
For those that might still have some doubts, buy it when it's on 75% off sales, it's really worth it and if you think not, just refund it!

First off, I highly recommend this game for anyone that is looking to kill some time. It's definitely worth the money. I bought this during early access, and am usually hesitant of buying unfinished titles, due to some scoundrel developers taking the money and running with it, leaving gamers with a half-finished product. But Amplitude has a very good track record of not only finishing what they started, but also continuing with support well after the title has been released. This game is no exception. Just when I thought the game was finished, I stopped playing for a bit. I came back to this a week ago, only to find they added a bunch more characters, and new options when starting a new game. So a big kudos to them for being a developer that really puts the work into their games.
Now on to the game.
It's simple, yet complex. Keep your guys alive, get out of the dungeon in one piece. But you can't just rush every level, or else you will skip out on collecting a lot of much needed resources and research opportunities. Opportunities you will desperately need later on. Open too many doors at once, or have a lot of unpowered rooms, and a swarm of enemies will come your way and end your game quick. It's a fine balance between greed and fear. Try to open one more door, to try and get just a bit more resources before going to the next level, you could be hammered with 5 waves of hell. But if you skip out on it, it might hurt you in the long run.
Since dungeons are randomly generated, and so are things like weapons/armor/item/artifact locations, there is an element of luck to it. But once you get the hang of it, you can make it through most playthroughs even with some bad luck.
There is quite a bit of lighthearted humour from the characters in-game, which is right up my alley. From a woman who thinks she's a spider, to an overcompensating midget with a huge sword. They all have their quirks. It's not so much a band of heroes, as it is a group of unlikely misfits. You might even recognize characters from other games, such as Samus Aran..... errrr... I mean Sara Namus...
The game plays a lot like a turn-based tower defense. First you decide how to set up your defenses and production, then you begin the action phase by opening a door.  That's when it goes from "Okay, everything seems to be coming along fine, all hallways seem to be covered" to "CRAP! DON'T ATTACK THERE! THAT WAS MY FREAKING GENERATOR YOU JUST TRASHED YOU♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!!!"
All in all, as far as bang for your buck goes, I'd rate this title a 10/10. If you like cheesy humour and tower defense, don't hesitate to buy this game. You won't regret it.
edit: Don't feel ashamed if you cried after losing on easy mode..... We all have....

I beat this game a very long time ago, but I just never got around to writing a review for it. Limbo was a game I had gotten from the Playstation Store once it first came out on the PS3. And yes, I did beat it on the console a few days after buying it. I understand many people wouldn't play it more than one time (let alone repurchase it on Steam) considering the game is linear and very short (about 3 hours of total gameplay), but for me Limbo stuck out as a masterpiece in terms of unique visuals and creative puzzles and gameplay. I got Limbo again here on Steam when the Inside+Limbo bundle was on sale, and I never played Inside (I played and beat Inside before going through this game again. You can find my review on it on my profile). Limbo was just a dollar more at the time, so I figured I'd get it again anyway, since it's been years since I originally played through it and didn't remember much of how it played out. I must say, it was well worth another play. Limbo is considerably more difficult than Inside was (Inside was made by the same developers 6 years(?) after Limbo, in case you didn't know), and the visuals and music aren't as mezmorizing as Inside (my personal opinion), but this does not mean it still isn't completely mesmorzing. Like Inside, there isn't much of a solid story. Limbo encourages you to make up your own theory on what the game is about. There, also like Inside, is no spoken dialogue. There is nothing that sticks out as a signifacent plot point. It's just one big concept. The controls are very simple: arrow keys to move, right Ctrl to pull; and even then, the puzzles range from obviously simple to infuriatingly challenging. Unlike when I played Inside, there were a few times in Limbo where I was just completely enraged out of frustration. But that's not a bad thing; in fact, I wish Inside could have been as difficult. In the end, I fell in love with this game for a second time, and will continue to play through for the achievments, and for the sake of playing what is literally, for me, interactive art.
Although it was dark and fatal, but I enjoyed every moment. What a fantastic journey with you. Thank you, Limbo.

Sir you are being hunted is a pretty unique game. You play in a randomly generated world that consists of 5 islands. The objective is simply to obtain all the "artifact fragments" on each island. There are about 9 on the main (Middle) island and 3-4 on each small island. In doing so, you have to avoid robot hunters, their robot dogs, and other enemies, as well as eat.
The game focuses mainly on exploration and stealth. It is very unique and works - for the most part.
PROS:
- Randomly generated levels where you can set the parameters. So lots of replay value.
- Stealth works well. Even if you are spotted, it is very possible to run away and recover.
- Lots of items and loot.  Use what suits your fancy.
Cons:
- While there IS a map (you have to find it) and the game DOES tell you how many artifacts are left on each island, it doesnt do a great job at documenting what you have searched. I wish it had some sort of map painting feature where i could color the map to mark off things.
- The fragments are in random locations (which is fine) and marked by (white) smoke and (usually) 2 robots. Still, most of your time is spent literally wandering in circles looking for them. This brings me back to the map suggestion. This isnt necessarily bad thing, but some people might find it offputting.

Do you have what it takes to be an expendable cog in the Allied/Axis war machines? Do you want to die over and over in the Dark Souls equivalent of an FPS? Do you have the balls to hide facedown in a trench while artillary and grenades rain down around you. Do you panic easily?

Not to give anything away, but the light and colorful starting world goes far beyond itself, showing how everything truly is. As philosophical as the title book was (Nietzche, don't get much more philosophical!), this story hits pretty close.

The camera support is very nice, the combat is fairly set up (but simple), but the majority of the game relies on caring about the world and the story, so if you like a good tale? Play this game. Help make them WANT to make the sequel we all need.

Short version: this game is fantastic.
Long version: this game is a survival extreme game that takes the term "survival of the fittest" and replaces it with "survival of the fanciest". This game could be compared to DayZ or a game of the sort, but I believe it was done better. The game follows a simple yet complex survival algoritham. All items you obtain can be used in one way or another, and sometimes that use is not stated, and experimentation becomes more and more important as the game throws more and more variables at you. The game starts off simple enough: don't die, do a thing with some rocks. But as you get deeper and deeper in and the longer you take, the more complex the game becomes, forcing you to be creative, skillful, strategic, and quick-minded as you take on the growing complexity of the opponent, be it the environment or the other players in the multi-player. Really that in itself is good enough to make an amazing survival game, but it does not stop there! It gets even more amazing as you realize that the developers put enough time and work into the game to make sure there are no cheap wins or losses. The game is well balanced, and this is done by disabling water escape, punishing you for running from opponents, punishing you for assaulting opponents in the open (as opposed to assassinating them or ambushing them), and forcing you to reset... over... over... and over. The difficulty is sufficient to keep you on your toes but not harsh enough to make you give up completely. And because of the aforementioned lack of cheap deaths, you can learn something from every play through, and get a little better each time. Overall, a terrific game, and I'd even go so far as to say it should be the standard for all survival multi-players. Great game.

This game isn't easy, at least not to me (I find it pretty nerve-wracking), so I'd recommend it mainly if you're looking for a challenge and/or you thrive under pressure. You're basically forced to keep moving all the time, because your vitality goes down constantly like you're a ticking bomb, and once your vitality hits zero your health is sapped away right then and there. In other words, you can and will drop dead just by standing and doing nothing. There are a lot of useless items to be found, and I made the mistake of eating a rat, thinking that it would restore a tiny amount of vitality, but I suffered for it. Aside from the robots on foot, there are also hot air balloons, hunting dogs... To top it all off, you can only save at the standing stones or the boat, and only if you're not bleeding or starving. All in all, it's not what I imagined the game might be like from watching the trailer. But I could easily see it being very fun and engaging for people who like games where they feel pressured, so I wouldn't not recommend it, because as far as I'm concerned it does successfully create a good atmosphere where you do feel like you're being hunted. Still, I wouldn't really recommend it for the more anxious people out there. (And I haven't tried out the multiplayer, so I can't comment on that.)

This game is a classic. It's one of the many games that I discovered while going back through games that I was too young to play when they first came out.
The world created here is remarkable and compelling. The gameplay is thrilling and horrifying. Rapture is the most terrifying place I've encountered in a video game. That's not saying a lot, though, since I don't play many horror games. This game has its glitches, and its age shows in the outdated graphics (even in the "Remastered" version), but it's a game I can come back too and rediscover all the secrets of Rapture. The stories of Rapture are numerous and complex. The audio tapes are a very interesting story telling mechanic, and it's done well. It explains the world without giving it all away at once. You get bits and pieces of how Rapture ending up the way it did.
Even if you think you know everything about Rapture, there might be an audio tape you missed that has a missing piece.
Going back to the actual gameplay, BioShock has mastered the art of suspense and horror. You hear the splicers, but you don't always see them until they're attacking you or about to attack you. You never know where they are. Sometimes you'll hear the groaning and heavy steps of a Big Daddy, and you know to either high-tail it out of there or try to rescue or harvest the Little Sister after taking down her guardian.
The choice of harvesting or rescuing the Little Sisters is a nice touch. You have the freedom to choose whether or not the Little Sisters are worth saving. Of course, you feel sympathetic towards them: they're children; but do you value the reward of instant ADAM or do you trust that Ten♥♥♥♥♥ will pay you back? And do you even think that they are worth rescuing? Granted, this is a video game and moral quandries with them are interesting, but not necessarily meaningful outside of one.
Long story short: if you like survival horror shooters and exploring complex worlds and stories, get this.

I highly recommend starting out by playing as a Rifleman class. Don't choose a class from its weapons alone.
One of the best, if not the best, WW2 shooters around.
Why buy Red Orchestra 2?
It's realistic and inmersive unlike any other game of its kind.
You feel like you're in the frontline with your comrades, nakama, tovarich or kameraden fighting the filthy enemy for the glory of Father/Motherland. It's grim, it's dirty, it's ruthless, it does not forgive. A single well-aimed bullet can kill you, a not so well aimed bullet will make you plop your head down and bandage yourself before being able to continue with your soldier. Something in the middle will leave your character slowly dying while offering his last prayers to whatever he believes in.
Soldiers in the heat of battle curse, scream, give orders... they wonder if they did hit the enemy with that one bullet, and praise themselves when they see the bullet hit. Overall, the voiceacting and sound design is a big thing in this game, you can feel there is a battle raging in both your side of the map and the other side. Gunshots from rifles and MGs in the distance, the sound of a tank firing a round at some unlucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, it's all there.
Morale is a thing now, not only shakey screen from a grenade exploding nearby, your soldier panics for fear of his life when under fire, screen goes grey, his hands shake, your screen shakes, welcome to hell on earth, now run to cover and keep your head down.
So how do you win if not by glorious CoD antics?
Winning a round is all about teamwork. When your team works together and communicates, both victory and fun are assured. I only use public servers and I can guarantee that 2 out of 3 times you'll read/hear someone trying to communicate and coordinate the team, help them and you will reap the rewards.
Okay so I have to work with the team, does that mean that what my personal actions are unrewarding?
Nope, your soldier is as weak as the enemy soldier, no unfairness of perks or trash like that here. If you run up to a guy and put a bullet in his head, he'll be as dead as you if it happens to you. Often times you'll be sneaking around behind a wall or some bushes, popping your gun out a little bit, seeing an enemy running around and that's when you feel the rush, you fire and it hits and it feels damn great to down an enemy.
There are no minutes long duels here, everything is decided by a single breath and by how smart about it you were beforehand. Did you put yourself behind cover? Are the enemies unaware of your presence? Do you know where the enemy is going to come from? Is this bush good enough to camouflage you? There are no absolute answers, but the closer you take the answers to these questions to "Yes" the more likely you are to win the 1-2 second duel you're about to have with an enemy. It plays a lot like cat and mouse, just that you're the cat as much as you are the mouse.
That's my feelings towards the game. But I'll also talk in a more mechanical perspective:
In this game you do level up, levelling up unlocks weapons, and trivially upgrades your stats as far as I know. A bullet is still gonna kill you so don't think that those lvl 99 guys are demigods in the battlefield, they'll be putting their heads down and fearing for their lives as much as you are.
The graphics might feel old to some, but to me they hold up very nicely considering how old this game is. Unless you are an absolute graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ and can not handle a game that doesn't look like Crysis 2 on max, you're fine.
I've been asked by people if the gameplay is janky. It's not, at least to me it isn't. It's not the smoothest thing on the planet but it isn't clunky jank hell either. It's in an inbetween that approaches smoothness much more than clunkiness.
Multiplayer-wise the game holds up at a steady 1,5k players online during US-EU playtimes. It's very much alive and since everyone comes back to the same big 5-6 servers that are always at the top of the list, you might even get into a routine of playing with the same people half the time. It really builds a sense of camaraderie that no other games do with its multiplayer.
Should you buy this game? A big fat yes if you like WW2 and want to feel the dreary realistic part of it. If you feel like seeing how war isn't pretty, this is the game for you.

The Expendabros was released in order to promote Broforce (a game by the same developers) and The Expendables 3, which is the movie that inspired the characters found in The Expendabros.
This is mostly a one hour long demo of the more intricate Broforce. With that said, I had fun playing what was there and I am now more interested in Broforce and at least curious about The Expendables movies. Graphically speaking, the pixel art is great. There is much attention to detail given to the backgrounds, to the explosions and to all characters (both friendly and enemy). The controls are tight and responsive while the sound design matches the artwork's polished quality. The overall presentation and feel of the game are its shining points despite being promotional software. To be fair, this game may be deserving of a small price tag even though it's only one hour in length.
Each of the playable characters are well thought out and play completely different from each other in regards to the weapons used and their special attacks. Concerning these playable characters, an interesting design choice has been made, as the player is not allowed to choose which character to use. As you rescue prisoners scattered throughout the levels and as you die, the game randomly selects a playable character for you. This means that even if you may have a go-to character for maximum damage or if you prefer playing with this or that character, the game forces the player to become familiar with all available characters. It's also important to mention that the game froze on the second to last level once and the controller bindings menu was totally glitched visually. In the end, this is a high quality, short promotional game that is worth the hour it offers of fun.

I love the zombie genre in books, games and movies. And having gone through a fair bit of different zombie material I am not easily pleased. A lot of games are far too action oriented (Dead Rising) for me and doesn't paint a believeable picture of a post apocalyptic world. Then we have Project Zomboid. Wow. Not only does the game feature hordes of the undead, but they play almost a second part to the great struggle for survival that plays out in the Zomboid world. At first you will struggle to stay out of the mawes of the undead. But when you have mastered that bit and can do supply runs without dying every time the real struggle begins.
You have to deal with finding enough food, and setting up a farming operation (or fishing and hunting) to feed your hunger. Your body might fail you and stupid mistakes will force you to deal with lacerations, burns and even broken bones! Eventually the electricity and water will go out and then its back to basics. And if that wasn't enough there are seasons too and eventually you will be hit by winter.
Another awesome feature is erosion, as the days goes by nature takes over. Trees start growing in the fields, windows gets overgrown with vines and the roads are slowly eaten up by mother nature. It makes your struggle seem small and insignificant. It makes the dead human civilisation seem like just a blink of an eye in the lifespan of our planet. And when you are all nostalgic and philoshopical its all of a sudden shotgun time as a small horde is banging on your door.
Are there any setbacks to this zombie apocalyps? Yeah, it stops short of being a Walking Dead simulation by the fact that there are no other survivors (unless you play online). I would love to rescue people and put them to good use in my homebase. We have been told for quite some time that survivors are an incoming feature. I am holding on to that thought and the fact that I have great faith in the team that have so far delivered perhaps the best Zombie Apocalyps vision to our lives, well maybe atleast tied with Red Dead Redemption.

Bizarre Earthquake is a good casual adventure game.
It has an original storyline compared with those in the "game industry" as a whole, including the adventure genre. No horror, no blood, no zombies, no vampires, no trashy things : nothing that will hurt your feelings. It's almost family-friendly BUT not in a way that you'll feel like you're playing a children game, far from it. At least it's not violent nor gore.
Admittedly it's not realisitic all the way (especially in the end), but it's a game, it's not meant to be a hundred percent plausible and the main idea remains interesting, even though certain aspects of the plot lack some depth. But given the price it's okay and it doesn't take the fun away.
Nice graphics, although sometimes animation is a bit awkward. It's still totally playable and enjoyable.
The music is fine and appropriate. Pay attention to it, sometimes it changes a bit to signify you did what you were supposed to.
It's a well-balanced adventure game : not too easy and not too difficult. Puzzles are solvable but the solution isn't given.
There are not too many back and forth in the different areas. Sure you'll have to visit some places twice or more but not in a way that makes you crazy.
You can play the whole story as the male or as the female character, or you can switch between them along the way. That gives replayability to the game. The characters don't have the same puzzles to solve in order to make progress in the inquiry.  That way you can "skip" something you're stuck in.
If you like "side quest", not that there is properly one, there are hidden objects to find in the game. Those are not necessary to complete the game but you will need to find (most of) them if you're going for the 100% Achievement.
Last but not least. Maybe since it's not a big production , the dev might answer nicely to your relevant observation/question.
Given the price and the size of the team I'd give a mark of 8/10. (Don't mind the amount of hours I spent on it, I've done many playthroughs with both characters to write a guide).
It's not expensive so give it a try. If you hesitate then wait until it's on sale. Go for it !

First of all, I personally don’t recommend this game due to many flaws I had to go through; however, I will give this game a blue thumbs up for putting a lot of effort in the game.  There are still some redeemable qualities to the game.
Here are a few flaws that needs pointing out:
The “how to play” menu should be available to view if you have an option screen.  I remember my first playthrough (after restarting five minutes in) that I accidentally skipped the “how to play” box.  When I tried to look for it in the settings or the main menu, it is nowhere to be found.  I realize I couldn’t figure out what each cursor meant especially when the pictures are so small to understand.  I had to restart to learn it again.
Another issue the dialogue “cut-scenes”.  I believe it is best that we can pause and click after each dialogue.  I feel that the dialogue moves too fast at times and I don’t have enough time to process what they are saying.
Another problem is the cursor, specifically the “walking arrow”.  I believe the developer should remove the default arrow.  There are a couple of areas where you only need the default arrow but that should be enabled on the other cursors.  Any item or person that can be clicked, the avatar will walk towards them anyways.  I understand the changing cursors for different dialogue or action purposes but the default cursor should be removed.  If not that, maybe change the setup in your engine.  Sometimes when I forgot to change the cursor, the avatar just walks to the object or person. Sadly, the avatar is now blocking the object or person and starts talking about himself/herself.  At first, it was funny, now it’s annoying.
There is a small bug I experience after I leave to the community hub.  After I leave the hub, dialogues tend to go extremely fast out of nowhere.  I’m not sure what causes it.
Here are some positives of this game:
The game is still pretty cheap and there is a good length before finishing it.
The story is bordering passable.  You can feel bored with the whole story or actually feel interested.  The story is different than other games I’ve played so that’s a plus.  I personally thought it was alright but slowly got bored over time.
The engine’s graphics won’t blow anyone away but it does feel different than your typical engine such as Unity, Cry Engine, Unreal Engine 4, and RPG Makers.
You can play between two different characters and have two different experiences.  I believe this is the developers own unique touch to the game.
At the end of it, I believe the developer(s) tries hard to put as much effort in the game to make it quality.  There are several hit and misses that really needs a makeover such as the cursor.  Again, thumbs up for a hard effort but not as recommended; however, if the consumers are curious, they can still try the game out.  The price isn’t expensive.

I had memories of playing this on my Dad's old computer, that he'd hooked up to the TV, so when I got a Steam account and saw that this game was available, I just had to play it. After only a few hours, I was hooked again, remembering all the good times I'd had playing LAN games with my brother across the house.
The game is a little rough around the edges, which is to be expected considering this was Petroglyph's first game. That being said, the space combat is a must-play for any casual or hardcore Star Wars fan, with the, albeit, less exciting ground battles taking the back seat in this instance. The game feels like it doesn't need to have a dedicated ground combat mode, but you can get some enjoyment out of it. I personally either 'Auto Resolve' or skip ground battles entirely, if and when I can.
The controlls are simple and a Star Wars fan who's never played an RTS should find it a pretty easy experience. The game is easy to learn, but difficult to master. If you can find a couple friends who want to play, that is where this game is most enjoyable.
My personal favorite gamemode is the Galactic Conquest, which put you in command of once of the three factions in the game.
Overall, I would have to reccommend this to any true Star Wars fan, and any casual gamer that wants a simple and fun RTS. Great game, that deserves a spot within your Steam Library.

First impressions, after not too much playtime:
The game is really fun so far, and I could definitely see getting addicted to it. It's also really hard, but so far I am enjoying that as well. The developers deserve a lot of credit for forging a unique gameplay experience from the combination of different genres. This kind of creativity and experimentation should be praised and encouraged, especially when the resulting game actually plays so well!
There were two things I found a little disappointing that might not be super-obvious to those considering a purchase:
First, you don't directly control your heroes in combat; you simply tell them which room to enter and they fight whatever is in there. I understand why this ability would make an already complex game even more complex, but sometimes I still wish I could pick a hero and go arcade-style on some aliens.
Secondly, and I could be wrong about this, but it appears that most of the visual differences between rooms are purely cosmetic. There's a lot of intriguing scenery that appears to have no in-game effects. The different spatial arrangements of module sockets in a room also don't seem to affect combat in a big way, although the number of sockets is important. I wish the different room shapes, contents, and specific locations of sockets made more of a tactical difference in combat.
I mention these only because the game's originality can make it especially hard to tell what features it might or might not have, and I think people will have more fun with the game if they're not expecting something else. Overall, I definitely recommend the game! In a world of copycats, this one really is different.

This game really surprised me - it's quite a little tactical wonder with lots of elements from different types of games thrown in.
But, at its core it's a roguelike because of the random, procedural dungeon levels. Oh, and there's also some tower defense elements  which are not just randomly thrown in, it's a more than just slightly important game mechanic and plays a key role in how you'll escape with your crystal in each level once you find that elevator. And you can't discount the RPG aspect, because how and who you equip with what and which skills are absolutely crucial. And tactical strategy because you have to count placement of heroes in which rooms or you'll definitely fail. Then there's the loot aspect which can make one almost obsessively compulsive about gearing up the heroes from the previously mentioned ever-important RPG portion of the game.
So yeah, that about describes it.
At its core.
In the end, though, this game is more than just merely the sum of its parts - it's all tied together very well, and ties well into the lore of amplitude studio's other games, Endless Space and Endless Legend if you're looking for those kinds of things.
And the music is pretty great.

Sinister City... it's not easy to decide whether to recommend this game or not. Is it cheesy? Yes it is. But it sort of has an explanation for that. Is voice acting sub-par? Yes it is, but again... it sort of makes sense. Is it a point-and-click adventure? Not really. It's a mix between a hidden object game and a point-and-click adventure. I suppose that if you are a fan of the latter, you won't be satisfied (even though there are also puzzles here and there, all extremely easy to solve), and if you are a fan of the former this could probably make you curious about (better) point-and-click adventures, which doesn't do any harm.
So... all in all, I would recommend Sinister City. It's short, it's cheap, and you get what you pay for, but there are some smart ideas behind it.

Pros
- multiplayer, can spend plenty of hours playing but you may experience the rage monster here and there
- good visuals and audio, the cryengine makes this game feel great
- the people that gave us Left 4 Dead
- fun combat, similar to the tank battles in L4D but more entertaining and challenging.
Cons..
- Needs more game modes
- We need more content
- 3K players average online
- Bugs, typical with AAA titles.
- The game feels like a console game when you look at the UI controls and the lack of certain basic fundamental pc graphical settings and functions.
- If you add someone to your friends list, don't expect to ever play against them as a monster and vice versa unless you both randomly join the same game.
- Evolve claims to be a multiplayer game while at the same time restricting basic multiplayer functions, prefering the console route.
- The cutscenes depict a more exciting and fun experience than what we get when we play.
-Purchasable Skins feel last minute and pointless except for as the monster.
- New Monsters and Hunters cannot be unlocked, they must be purchased meaning there are less things to do overall in place of the lack of game modes.
- Using in game chat while playing as the monster could be a fun thing to do, if they let you. You are only able to talk to the other players when you are in the character selection screen and right after the match ends, otherwise its basically a solo experience for the monster in a game specifically multiplayer.
-  Matchmaking is awful, you are limited to randomly being thrown in games MAYBE as the character you want to play and you aren't given much support for a muliplayer game.
Evolve is all in all a game that instead of just making a fun game for all platforms, went the way of most AAA developers and went for the cash grab. I look forward to Evolve 2.0 if 2K doesn't go out of business before then.

I used to play Ragnarok Online in the ye olde days, it was actually my very first MMO before I got hooked on World of Warcraft. In Ragnarok Online you can choose to play different classes and become stronger as you level. Eventually you could "transcent" and become a stronger version of that class you initially choose.
Ragnarok Clicker is made by the same folks that made Clicker Hero and in cooperation with Gravity Co. which is the company who owns the original game (not the private servers ;) ). Like other reviews have stated, the game is pretty much a clone of Clicker Hero, with the exception that the game contains assets from RO. You can't really avoid that a clicker game look alike, though.
As an old time RO player, this gives me nostalgia because of the horrible encounters I've had in the past with many of the monsters that appear in Ragnarok Clicker, as well as the horrible struggle to level up a character without knowing where the frick to go. Thanks to external guides and everyone else than the game developers themselves, leveling was somewhat possible through grinding and farming money till you could afford the gear that was needed to not get two shotted by a monster. You can say that Ragnarok Clicker does well with showing that nothing has changed much even if it is a clicker game, but luckily you don't have to play the game actively to actually get money and eventually level your characters. Achievements grants extra DPS and every now and then you can be lucky and get a gearpiece or battle manuals so you can buy cards to improve certain things in your game. When you transcent, you'll keep the DPS from your achievements, gear and cards, but you will start ove with the leveling and the money. It goes faster by each time you do this, but it'll take longer to get to defeat the special bosses that you can eventually meet.
My biggest con to the game is actually how the game looks like. While I appreciate that they have made the game look exactly like RO, with the interface and the assets taken directly from the game, I'd say the UI is probably the game's biggest weakness. It didn't look good in RO and it doesn't look good inthis game either. Some of the menues doesn't even work properly (guild) and it looks like it was rushed and not properly tweaked to look good. Some of the information about how to obtain this or that isn't clear even when you unlock it.
With that said, even if you don't know what the frick Ragnarok Online is, then I still think you'd enjoy this game if you also like clicker games. It is butt ugly, but looking beyond that, this is a good game to play while you got nothing else to do.

This game is already really great and still in its alpha. But as all other games do, it does have its flaws.
Here are my main problems with the game: the first one being that there is no jump mechanic. I was surprised to figure out there was no way to jump, especially when it can be hard to try to walk on giant rocks scattered through the wilderness – especially in Mystery Lake region. So I would really like to see that put into the game.
Another issue: I have, multiple times, been walking on the top of a hill and randomly get a sprained ankle. Just from walking. It can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and I’d like to see it be fixed. In addition to this, I feel that while walking down a steep hill, literally just walking down it, it is WAY too easy to get a sprained ankle. It’s a bit dramatic.
Another really big issue, probably my main problem, is that when it is snowing, especially during darker hours of the morning / night, there will be giant lines of color and texture that clip through the world and block my vision.
Now for the good bits – this game is incredibly difficult to get bored of. If you’re playing on the normal difficulty, Voyageur, you will constantly need to be on your feet and working on different things, regardless of your playstyle and approach to this game. Nomadic or sedentary, you’ll constantly have new things to go out looking for and new things to find and do – and the world is HUGE. Exploration comes with rewards in many forms – not just the obvious fact that you’ll find more loot which will obviously increase the likelihood of your survival but there’s an interesting mechanic to this game that not many other open world survival games have – or at least I don’t think. There are certain milestones that you can compete that can improve your ability of certain things in the game. For example, when you’ve sprinted a certain amount of miles in the game ( it keeps a record of this, obviously ) then the rate at which your sprint bar recharges will increase by 20% which is really neat and helpful.
In addition, if you’re bored of the sandbox mode, you have challenges to complete! You can play a scenario where you’re being hunted by a bear and the only way to survive is to get to a certain landmark and acquire the appropriate weapon to kill it before the bear kills you. Then there’s a challenge called Whiteout where you have thirty days to collect enough supplies to last through a monstrous blizzard – and the more challenges you successfully complete, the more you unlock.
And with all of this, there will also be a story mode eventually – something I am looking forward to VERY much. If you know the game Firewatch or you’ve played it, you will love this game. There are different difficulties so if you want a challenge for survival in sandbox then you’ve got one – or if you’re looking for laid back gameplay centered around exploration of the various regions and huge maps then you can go for that too. It’s very versatile.
I do have some suggestions as well. I would like for there to be a greater diversity in wildlife. Currently there are crows, deer, rabbits, wolves, and bears – so really not a whole lot. Given the fact that this game is set in the Northern Canadian wilderness, I would like to see some extra stuff put in. Some suggestions are perhaps hawks and / or eagles or other raptors, bobcats, skunks or weasels or porcupines, mice maybe, maybe beavers, foxes, coyotes, geese, cougars, and badgers. Obviously not all of these; it’s just a big pool of suggestions that I think would make the game a lot more interesting if we had more wildlife. And if we’re really getting creative, maybe a rare thing we could have is the occasional hibernating beehives up in a tree that can be shot down with a bow / arrow or a rifle, or perhaps a similar mechanic with bird nests.
All in all, if you’re looking for an interesting new game, you’ve got it right here. Worth the money it costs and some – highly recommend this game.

Lyne manages to be both soothing and demanding, a rarity in my games library and among games in general. The interface is minimal, using intuitive design features whose purpose is instantly recognizable without the need to add tags and prompts. The puzzles are deceptively simple and become progressively more difficult, until you have to sit and think before attempting to connect any of the puzzle nodes. The tones/sound are similarly simple and pleasant, and able to be muted. The game itself is easy to open/close, and very little interaction is required with the menus in order to get straight to solving puzzles.
Lyne is a surprisingly meditative experience, the sort of game you might play to destress, or when struck by late-night restlessness. The elegance of design certainly aids this, but the fact that the game relies on intellect rather than on bright flashing lights or reflex events is central to the game's meditative quality. Rather than bombarding you with stimulation, the game lets the part of your brain which governs logic and geometric reasoning come to the fore in a quiet, restful environment that is easy to enter and leave, but stays with you in the form of some of the more challenging puzzles.
I recommend this game for people who like puzzle games, but also for people who need something to help them wind down after a long day. The game is serene without being boring, and challenging without being infuriating.
I hope the developers continue to produce games. This was well worth what I paid for it.

Dunegon of the Endless is a fine example of what can be accomplished by minimizing graphics in favor of overall flavor. The  time I've spent getting to know this game is a great deal more than it takes to master it's mechanics, but after discovering the interconnected stories told by different characters during the elevator scenes I was compelled to complete the roster and play through as many permutations as possible in order to learn which characters shared histories or banter could be seen.
The game itself takes place in a series of 12 levels, (or an endless mode, which becomes insanely difficult past a certain point) through which you move one to four "Hero" characters, trying to find the elevator. Once the elevator room has been discovered, you then have to make sure you can make the run to that room without being overwhlemed by the monsters which will begin swarming from any unpowered room and attempt to kill the character carrying the power crystal. Even the fastest character is significantly slowed by the weight of the crystal, and they are unable to fight or use skills while they are encumbered.
This is where the tower defence and tactical elements of the game come to the fore. Where at the beginning of the level you're focused on powering rooms, building production units and aquiring tech upgrades, once the last door has been opened or you're ready to make the run to the elevator (which will open all the remaining doors anyways, creating even more unpowered rooms to spawn monsters) you have to carefully depower and repower rooms to ensure you have as clear a path as possible to the elevator, and put as many defence modules in them as you can to stem the tide of creeps.
There are a few minor moments where you'll get frustrated, like finding a merchant who's selling an awesome item, only to realize that he's bartering Dust and that you would have to sacrifice powering a few rooms in order to aquire it, or splitting your party in order to have one or two characters operating production modules in order to maximize your gains for a few turns, only to have the character or characters on point get absolutely swarmed and either waste a ton of food healing them or have one of them killed by high DPS monsters before you can hammer the "Heal" button, but overall the fun I've had with this game far far outstrips the minor annoyances.
I would recommend this game for anyone who likes tower defence games, enjoys being tantalized by snippets of stories which obviously spool into something much larger, or people who get a kick out of tactical resource management. Or all three.
Cheers.

Rock-solid rogue-like dungeon crawler with tower-defense element!  I think a brief description of the game might be the best way to help you decide if it is for you:
In Dungeon of the Endless, your goal is to ultimately lead a band of unique characters out of a dungeon.    To do so, you must open new doors in each floor to find the elevator that takes you to the next level.  As a part of the game mechanic, the opening of each door counts as a turn.  Similar to the beacon jumping in FTL, everything happens within the turn is executed in real-time.
The dungeon is dangerous and unforgiving place!  Research and build towers to help you survive.  Don't let the name fool you!!  The dungeon itself is not endless; it only takes 3-4 hours to finish a successful run.  However, finishing your first successful run can be a different story!!  It took me more than 30 hour to get there, and I wish you better luck :-)

Packed full of twists and turns and even a talking man-pig, Ubisoft has crafted yet another big adventure series.

TL/DR: I rate Evolve 4.5 out of 5 stars
Evolve is a top-tier game worthy of an A grade. I've logged over 300 hours playing Evolve, have unlocked all 16 of the original characters, have the original 12 Hunters Elite and have unlocked 44 of the 49 acheivements so I feel pretty entitled to my opinion. I've paid my dues as both a Hunter and a Monster and the recent release of the Tier 4 Hunters and Monster as breathed a breath a fresh air into a game that was very far away from being stale. For a game this early in its shelf life and with has few patches that have been released it is remarkably stable. The 4 vs. 1 lobby/party system works as well if not better than it's contemporaries but the 2-party matchmaking needs some improvement. The thing I like most about this game is the way it forces the Hunters to work together to defeat the Monster. Teamwork and communications are crucial to the team's success. My biggest peev about playing Evolve is having to party up with Hunters who don't have a mic. If you don't have a mic then don't play this game should be an unwritten rule. This game is worth every penny I spent on it and then some. Playing as both the Hunter and as the Monster as improved the way I play both. It's crucial to understand the strengths and limitations of each character whether you're playing with or against them. Don't be afraid to network with other Evolve players. 4 or 5 people parties are best and have the best ambience. I highly recommend spending your hard-earned money on this game.

Lyne manages to be both soothing and demanding, a rarity in my games library and among games in general. The interface is minimal, using intuitive design features whose purpose is instantly recognizable without the need to add tags and prompts. The puzzles are deceptively simple and become progressively more difficult, until you have to sit and think before attempting to connect any of the puzzle nodes. The tones/sound are similarly simple and pleasant, and able to be muted. The game itself is easy to open/close, and very little interaction is required with the menus in order to get straight to solving puzzles.
Lyne is a surprisingly meditative experience, the sort of game you might play to destress, or when struck by late-night restlessness. The elegance of design certainly aids this, but the fact that the game relies on intellect rather than on bright flashing lights or reflex events is central to the game's meditative quality. Rather than bombarding you with stimulation, the game lets the part of your brain which governs logic and geometric reasoning come to the fore in a quiet, restful environment that is easy to enter and leave, but stays with you in the form of some of the more challenging puzzles.
I recommend this game for people who like puzzle games, but also for people who need something to help them wind down after a long day. The game is serene without being boring, and challenging without being infuriating.
I hope the developers continue to produce games. This was well worth what I paid for it.

Dungeon of the Endless is not a game that I would normally play.  In fact, I have never even liked the Rogue-like genre.  When people told me to buy FTL, I did.  Hated it.  So, it was with some trepidation that I bought Dungeons of the Endless.  I am glad that I did, however, because it is one very unique game.
Dungeon of the Endless starts you out with two heroes that you choose at the start of the game.  These heroes survived the destruction of their ship, and the crashing of their escape pod.  You then take these heroes throughout each floor, opening each door, building defenses, upgrades, and also leveling up your heroes to combat the creatures that infest the Dungeon.  Each wave of monsters that comes at you can only spawn from dark rooms.  Rooms are lit by using Dust, which powers your Crystal that you start off with in your escape pod.
It's a very unique game.  It has been described as a party-based Rogue-like, and tower defense hybrid.  That's pretty much what it is, but it's really so much more.  The soundtrack is nice and moody, but the pixel art (which has been overdone lately) is very well done.  Nice uses of color, and lighting, make it a beautiful game to look at.
But, the game is hard.  I haven't even beat it on easy.  There are two modes, Too Easy, and Easy.  It's brutal, trust me.  I have made it to the 11th Floor, and that was it.  But, I keep trying, because the game is really interesting, addictive, polished, beautiful, and just plain fun.
Buy it, but prepare to die.  Often.
Update:
After trying time and again to conquer the "Easy" mode, I've been playing on Too Easy.  Learning the game is much better this way, especially if you are new to Rogue-likes, like me.  This is also a fun way to unlock the different characters, escape pods, and the Album which contains some backstory to the characters, written by the mysterious person behind the planned trip to Auriga in the first place.  Finding out the different character interactions, is also fun to see.  They interact with each other, if paired up, and discuss some of their backstory on the elevator ride to the next floor of the Dungeon.

The game is really interesting. It is a mix of turn-based strategy with real-time combat. You start out with 2 heroes, and go through the game trying to explore.
Each room you open counts as a turn and allows you to find new items, artifacts, merchants, and heroes to recruit. In addition, to counter these opportunities, the game adds the element of risk via unpowered rooms giving you the chance to spawn monsters that get stronger with each dungeon level you go through. Floor 1 monsters will be really easy, while floor 10 monsters can easily kill some heroes.
The objective is to try to make it through the map and find the exit. When you do, you have the opportunity to carry your base crystal through to the exit. The bad part is that you also trigger endless waves of monsters when you pick up the crystal, so its a rush to make it to the exit room before you die.

This game is the prime example of the modern roguelike done right.
Before playing Dungeon of the Endless, I've played a HUGE host of roguelikes from Angband to Tales of Maj'Eyal to Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead. As diverse as the settings and gimmicks are, roguelikes have some things in common - as you get more and more powerful and you explore the world, the game tries to match your power with more powerful foes or new mechanics, and throughout the way the game tries to kill you when you make a wrong decision, get in a wrong area, or do a wrong step. This is not necessarily a bad thing - it gives a sense of challenge and a thrill that gives roguelikes its addictive charm.
Most roguelikes also feature a huge number of mechanics and statistics that can be very daunting - for example, Tales of Maj'Eyal has at least six unique resources (health, mana, stamina, rage, hate, equilibrium), seven stats, at least 26 different types of damage, saving throws for physical, spell, and mind damage, resistances, resistance penetration, five types of speed (global, movement, spell, attack, mental)...you get it. The more unorthodox Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead has a complex crafting system, twenty-nine skills ranging from computer knowledge to tailoring expertise, and at least 102 feats for your character. All of this can be incredibly daunting to face for newbies and is a staple of the genre.
Dungeon of the Endless, however, breaks from that mold. The concepts and challenges are simple: find the exit, bring the Crystal to the exit, defend the crystal carrier against waves of enemies. There are only eight statistics all in all, with each character possessing a set of passive and active skills that will be seen as the character levels up. The skills and statistics are simple to understand and make use of.
Compared to most roguelikes, Dungeon of the Endless is relatively gimmick-free: there is one non-random gimmick about characters killing one another due to their relationship, which is incredibly frustrating but is easily avoided in your next playthrough (unlike unbeatable scenarios in FTL or some "trap" areas in Tales of Maj'Eyal). If you lose, it's not the fault of the game as it usually is in roguelikes - it's all yours. Maybe you didn't think about watching your carrier's back; maybe you neglected defending a certain chokepoint, leading to your party getting flanked and killed.
Since you know it's your mistake, you can determine what you did wrong and how you can prevent it next time. Not only is it a new game every single time, but you learn and refine your strategy, and you buckle down and see if you can make it to a deeper floor with your experience this time.
Dungeon of the Endless represents what a modern roguelike should aspire to be: a highly replayable game that provides a genuine, fair challenge that you can climb through and improve your skill in every playthrough.
(I still like Tales of Maj'Eyal better. :3)
