I arrived at the ruins of what appeared to be an old farmhouse. White in color, but with tinges of green with mold, and also black from fires. My heart was pounding. My stomach was growling. A thousand thoughts racing through my mind as I saw a fire pit. My stomach told me to cook some food over it, but my mind told me not to draw attention to myself with smoke. I walked around the property, slowly checking around corners to see if a mustachioed robot gentleman would be there waiting for me. But alas, none were spotted. I carefully tiptoed back to the fire pit to cook food to appease my rumbling stomach. I took the matches and lit the fire.
"*VRRP* WHAT'S THAT? *CLANK*"
A robot was indeed near me. I quickly threw a rock over his head hoping he would be distracted, but he was not. His sights were aimed at me, and his only concern was that I was still breathing. I drew my revolver and fired off two shots. I still don't know if either hit their target because immediately afterward, I turned around and began running through the gap in the charred walls.
I spotted a tree and immediately ran behind it. I could hear two robots now. Their clanging joints sounded like the bells ringing to mark the time of my death. I stepped from behind the tree and fired three bullets into the iron torso of one. I then felt a hot, stinging pain in my side. I'd been shot. The other robot was rushing toward me to avenge his fallen comrade. I knew i only had one bullet left. I darted from behind the tree and pulled the trigger.
The bullet rang true! The hot lead surged through the metallic skull cavity of the machine that was hunting me. I was safe!
Or was I?
I was surrounded by the sounds of beeps and whirs and clanks and I soon saw that four new robotic foes were upon me. I put my revolver in its holster and began running. Hot lead flew past me and all around me as i sprinted away from my pursuers. I came to another set of houses, but this was no time to stop and loot. Those robots meant business. Their bullets still whizzing past me, I ran through the houses into the rocky hills by the ocean. After many deep breathes to restore the oxygen to my lungs, i was left with four words that filled up my mind.
"Holy poop. I'm alive."
10/10 would wet my pants again

Hands down, The Long Dark is my favorite survival game out there, even if it's only an alpha sandbox at the time of this writing.
Why? Unlike other survival games, the only threat to the character is Mother Nature herself. No zombies, no dinosaurs, no super crafting, no nonsense. Just you, and the Canadian north. People often take their creature comforts very much for granted, and this game drives home just how much we frail humans are at the mercy of Mother Nature. With details like weak ice collapsing beneath your feet; intestinal parasites; tripping and spraining a wrist or ankle when walking down steep inclines; losing condition permanently to frostbite on various extremities; the struggle to repeatedly build a fire only to watch it sputter out and die; predatory animals smelling your fresh food and stalking you; or calculating blizzard strength, wind speed, wind chill factor, wind direction, and even wind breaks in the terrain you can shelter behind, all in order to determine just how cold you really are, The Long Dark involves a lot of complex variables that make it immersive and challenging. You'll spend a great deal of time starving, freezing to death, or getting eaten by bears. Or all three at once. You never know when you'll get stuck out in the middle of a blizzard, stumble upon a bear cave and meet your doom.
In addition to being a challenging survival experience, it is also a thoughtful exploration game. A good chunk of the game is devoted to nomadically wandering in search of resources, which rewards the player with a plethora of of man-made and natural locations to discover, each with their own story to tell: abandoned cars, derailed trains, empty houses, and wide open spaces where very few creatures, especially humans, dwell at all. One nuance I especially appreciate is how The Long Dark encourages the player to look for clues to read their environment, such as subtle changes in the lay of the land that might indicate shelter or resources, or watching the direction that birds travel to find animal carcasses to harvest, or even determine if a storm is coming. Despite the age of the engine, it's still a very visually stunning game and the player is provided with several expansive, interconnecting maps to explore. The game also has randomized loot and resource distribution amongst a pool of possible sites, so each game provides a somewhat unique experience.
Since it's still in development, I expect even greater things to come, however slowly. To those folks complaining that it "hasn't changed in years," they should look again-- many changes have been made, but until the developers refine the actual mechanics and environment, the story would be poorly implemented. Though it could definitely use some tweaking as far as performance goes-- It's not the most refined in that regard and can be sluggish even on perfectly capable machines. Frame rate suffers whether the graphics are cranked or low.
I'd recommend it to any of my friends, but it's not for the easily frustrated.

Any explanation I could give for the plot of Cuphead does not do it justice, or at least does it less than the dulcet tones of a barbershop quartet that greets you every time you hop onto the title screen. Shoutouts to Shoptimus Prime, who did a few songs like that in this game. Those guys are actually awesome; you should definitely check them out sometime. In fact, when it comes to the production side of things in this game, everything is awesome. The music was made using a real big band and a real ragtime orchestra. Every sprite, every background, and every UI element is hand drawn and painstakingly animated the old-fashioned way. Even the audio is filtered so that it makes the Steamboat Willie artstyle more than just a gimmick. From the film grain to the audio filters, the silliness of the plot and the wacky scenarios you'll find yourself in, these guys committed to their bit, and it pays off in spades. Not even Stick of Truth can hold a candle to this game's levels of making you feel like you're playing an interactive cartoon. As for the gameplay though, that's a whole 'nother beast unto itself.
On the surface, Cuphead is Contra, but only the bosses. You can find platforming stages that reward skillful play with coins that then allow you buy powerups, but it always comes back to these big battles, as beating them is the only way to actually progress. As a matter of fact, it is completely viable (if not more difficult) to completely skip the run 'n gun stages if you don't care about the additional weapons and just want to go it with the standard peashooter. But, if you feel like actually experiencing all of the game you paid for, you'll quickly find some serious strategy opening up to you in terms of what loadout you run. This is where the shmup comparisons come from: do you focus on the better damage of the peashooter, or do you stick with the realiability of the homing shot? If you go with the latter, you probably do so because using the normal weapon in a fight is too difficult or awkward. But you also do so knowing that the bosses will live longer than if you had figured out some way to fight them with the peashooter instead, potentially making the battle harder than it would have been otherwise by virtue of them being able to throw more attacks at you before going down. These are the kinds of decisions Cuphead forces you to consider, and you're encouraged to figure them out quickly because GOOD LORD, these bosses are unforgiving.
Another reason the difficulty doesn't really bother me is that 95% of the time, damage or death is your fault. Cuphead was kinda infamous for getting delayed a lot, but considering how polished it is (likely thanks to those numerous delays), I completely forgive it now. Praticing these bosses leads to a reliable strategy, and when this game is at its best, using the same strategies produces consistent results. That's the mark of good mechanical design, which Cuphead desperately needed to get away with being as hard as it is.
The reason I say damage is only 95% your fault is due to design more than mechanics. Sadly, there is more than one boss that takes advantage of inconsistent elements. There are bosses that make their home in scrolling stages where the platforms you have to stand on are randomly placed, meaning you'll never have a consistent setup and will just have to react as you go. There are bosses with helper enemies that show up wherever they feel like, even when it leads to a situation where it's all but impossible to avoid taking a hit. This is especially egregious in one fight where the boss can freeze you in place and essentially force damage on you if the minions are currently firing projectiles. And any time I'm fighting Baroness Von Bon Bon and get the waffle enemy right out of the gate, I just hit restart because the way I play, that thing just takes way too long to kill without a super.
Where this really starts to become noticable is when you're playing the game on a higher level, like if you're going for all A ranks or tackling the previously mentioned Expert Mode. The scoring system in Cuphead grades you on the following criteria: winning under a certain time limit, avoiding damage, parrying 3 enemy projectiles, using at least 6 bars worth of special moves, and playing the stage on at least regular difficulty. To earn an "A" rank, you can only make two mistakes total in any of these areas. The stage only counts as being "beaten" when you clear it on Regular, so that's a give-in. If you've played these fights enough, time won't be an issue. And you're constantly using super moves as-is, so that just leaves damage and parries as the sticking points. Essentially, you can take two hits but have to land all 3 parries, or you can ignore all but one parry but have to avoid any damage. For all the reasons I already mentioned, this is a lot harder than it needs to be.
There is often no way to know where your parry opportunities are going to come from. You can't learn which randomly generated enemies are going to decide they want to shoot a pink bullet instead of a black one, and that's if you don't accidentally pop them first. It leads to these awkward situations where you're not shooting down the mook enemies in hopes that they'll toss you a parry-able projectile, or you're holding back on the boss for a second or two for fear of killing them too quickly, and...that's just completely counterproductive to what the game is all about. It sucks, because I'm at that point. I'm into the post-game where I'm trying to 100% everything, and it's just not happening in some of these fights. Past World 1 (and even including one fight in it), if I get an A rank, it typically feels like I'm just getting lucky; which is the complete opposite from the feeling that led me to want to do this in the first place. Oh, and did I mention how all the super moves are worthless? The beam locks you in place and doesn't give you any invincibility afterwards, meaning before you get used to the timing, you're going to take a few hits just trying to use what should be your most powerful tool. The plane super fixes that problem, by the way, so what happened here? The dedicated invincibility powerup barely lasts any time at all, and the super ghost is unusable because it's one more thing to keep track of in a game that already has too many things going on at any given time for most normal people. That's the real kicker in this game: regardless of how mechanically sound everything is, some things just don't feel right design-wise. How could they? It's the studio's first game; they were bound to get a few things wrong. It's disappointing, but it affects you far less if you're not a completionist; if you're willing to take advantage of that room for error and just want to "play the game", as it were. So, take from that what you will.
Do I recommend you play Cuphead? Oh, absolutely. But not all of it. Take it from someone who's been there: if you want to enjoy yourself, don't go for A ranks, and especially don't go for S ranks in Expert Mode. Don't try to do pacifist runs of the platformer stages. And don't rip your hair out going for all the coins. Just play the game at its best, at a level of execution where everything has the room to feel just right. That is worth the effort. That is what's going to justify the price tag. And that is what makes this game something really special.

Bioshock won the Game of the year prize for 2007 and in my opinion it deserves it. This game has one of the best and most iconic video game settings of all time. Rapture, the city at the bottom of the sea, is full of stunning artwork and architecture, it makes you feel like your in a utopia gone wrong.
Rapture is a world full of wonderful characters such as the mad Sander Cohen and the mysterious Atlas, who make for a brilliant game. When released it revolutionised the FPS genre and it has stood well against the test of time.
The plasmid mechanic makes for good gameplay which is fun and there is an okay range of enemies to face. Ultimately the big daddies feel like mini boss battles that are exciting but by the end of the game they become easy.
The game is very philosopical, taking a lot of ideas from philosophers such as Ayn Rand. Consequently the game has a lot of depth and greater meaning for those who want to explore the lore further.
The only negatives in my opinion is the final boss battle, it is boring and doesnt really fit in with the rest of the game. The choices presented throughout the game also dont really impact the final ending and could have been incorporated better.
Lastly the soundtrack for the game is brilliant, with An Ocean on his Shoulders been one of the best video game themes.
Overall this game is a masterpiece, with a great setting, plot and soundtrack.

This game is the prime example of the modern roguelike done right.
Before playing Dungeon of the Endless, I've played a HUGE host of roguelikes from Angband to Tales of Maj'Eyal to Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead. As diverse as the settings and gimmicks are, roguelikes have some things in common - as you get more and more powerful and you explore the world, the game tries to match your power with more powerful foes or new mechanics, and throughout the way the game tries to kill you when you make a wrong decision, get in a wrong area, or do a wrong step. This is not necessarily a bad thing - it gives a sense of challenge and a thrill that gives roguelikes its addictive charm.
Most roguelikes also feature a huge number of mechanics and statistics that can be very daunting - for example, Tales of Maj'Eyal has at least six unique resources (health, mana, stamina, rage, hate, equilibrium), seven stats, at least 26 different types of damage, saving throws for physical, spell, and mind damage, resistances, resistance penetration, five types of speed (global, movement, spell, attack, mental)...you get it. The more unorthodox Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead has a complex crafting system, twenty-nine skills ranging from computer knowledge to tailoring expertise, and at least 102 feats for your character. All of this can be incredibly daunting to face for newbies and is a staple of the genre.
Dungeon of the Endless, however, breaks from that mold. The concepts and challenges are simple: find the exit, bring the Crystal to the exit, defend the crystal carrier against waves of enemies. There are only eight statistics all in all, with each character possessing a set of passive and active skills that will be seen as the character levels up. The skills and statistics are simple to understand and make use of.
Compared to most roguelikes, Dungeon of the Endless is relatively gimmick-free: there is one non-random gimmick about characters killing one another due to their relationship, which is incredibly frustrating but is easily avoided in your next playthrough (unlike unbeatable scenarios in FTL or some "trap" areas in Tales of Maj'Eyal). If you lose, it's not the fault of the game as it usually is in roguelikes - it's all yours. Maybe you didn't think about watching your carrier's back; maybe you neglected defending a certain chokepoint, leading to your party getting flanked and killed.
Since you know it's your mistake, you can determine what you did wrong and how you can prevent it next time. Not only is it a new game every single time, but you learn and refine your strategy, and you buckle down and see if you can make it to a deeper floor with your experience this time.
Dungeon of the Endless represents what a modern roguelike should aspire to be: a highly replayable game that provides a genuine, fair challenge that you can climb through and improve your skill in every playthrough.
(I still like Tales of Maj'Eyal better. :3)

I tried very hard to enjoy this
I bought it because it looked great and I got a FTL-y vibe and was interested in playing a more fleshed out tower defense game. However it has not grown on me after many hours.
-there is virtually no reward for defeating monsters, only a small chance to gain 1 dust which is not kept between floors. even the large special enemies in the last floors yield nothing at all. you have to spend science and/or food in combat and you risk damage to your structures/heroes, so combat quickly feels like an undesirable chore and even a risk that discourages exhaustive exploration later on.
-my first experience with the character story interactions was that the quick blue girl outright kills my fat rambo tank dude. This crippled my team in combat and the only thing I got from it was like +10% attack and -5% defense on the blue girl. I haven't seen any other interactions that are that bad, but the rewards are always something with almost no impact at all, which brings me to the next problem:
-everything is a drop in the bucket. leveling and equipping your team, improving structures and farming resources - all these things progress painfully slowly, the best you can hope for is to very slightly improve your crew on each floor and still break even on resources. only rarely do you get something satisfying like a new weapon or ability from a levelup that affects your game right away. everything else is just about very slowly accumulating tiny bonuses. they do add up eventually, but it takes hours to reach that point. Winning is slow, but losing is slower. when you lose something important like a character or resource structures, the game slows to a crawl. you'll have to spend more resources for cooldowns/heals in combat, you might lose structures, you might lose dust. much like the incremental progression, your defeat in this game will be excruciatingly drawn out - the more ♥♥♥♥ed you are the more ♥♥♥♥ed you get, you will scrape by with 2-3 characters and make it to the elevator but you know exactly that you have no chance to beat the game anymore. Genuine game overs don't happen because you will just throw the game and start over instead of wasting half an hour trying to get as far as possible.
-the tower defense aspect is very weak. there's only one turret available at the start, new ones must be researched with resources and cost 200-300% more to construct than the basic one. you will notice that it is not possible to "funnel" enemies the way I know I love to do in tower defense. if you get lucky with the layout you might be able to defend several paths to your core, but never all of them - the core itself cannot house any turrets, you would have to build turrets all around it which is just too expensive and not even reliable as they are quite weak and fragile when unattended (anything you build can be destroyed by enemies). overall turrets are expensive and unflexible, they will often be useless because half the enemies will use a path they don't cover.
TL; DR
combat is a chore, progression happens extremely slowly with barely noticeable unsatisfying increments, tower defense works out poorly due to the need to fight enemies in multiple rooms, setbacks like loss of a character or dust are a huge bummer you will not recover from and will snowball to kill you very slowly, RNG is mostly frustrating
these concepts and mechanics are the only things I have a problem with. the audio is ok, characters are cool, visuals are great. if you like spending hours slightly increasing and decreasing numbers, this game might be for you.

A very simple and straight forward game. You play as a security guard, working the night-shift at a "Chuck-e-cheese" style establishment. Every night the animatrionics come alive and attempt to stuff your soft, squishy body into an animatrionic suit, but you can't let that happen. So you use the tools available to you to prevent this from happening. You have doors on either side of you, which you may close them or shine a light to reveal any unwanted guests. However you have limited power to do so. So your objective is to survive 6 hours of the night while conserving power and resisting the urge to soil yourself. Have fun.
The only downside to this game is that it feels way too over-hyped. The jumpscares are not really all that terrifying, more annoying than anything else. For what it's worth, the only real thing these games have going for them is the lore behind them. You get a deeper experience from learning about it through blogs and videos. Check out the games if you're bored, or if you want to find all the hidden secrets. Good luck.

Alpha review:
I'm not an enthusiast, I have only played 64 hours of this game... before any of the story was implemented.
The alpha was essentially a huge sandbox. You were dumped in the world and had to figure out how to survive. Traversing the eerie and engrossing landscapes; finding food, water and warmth and desperately dealing with dangerous wildlife quickly draws you in and holds you captive. There are few games that make you forget that it's a game, but this is one of them.
I won't spoil much, but your many hours invested into exploring the world will be well spent and fondly remembered. Furthermore, once you think you have lost the will to explore at random, there are several challenges, some of which are rather difficult. And when you think you've mastered the game, try Interloper difficulty ;)
All in all, I've played a greater number of hours of this Alpha and definitely enjoyed it more than most triple A titles form the last years. I can't wait for the story mode to come out, but even if it's the worst campaign of all time, it's worth a purchase for the sandbox alone. Yet, the developers have shown that they are deeply committed and in touch with the community, which gives me great confidence in saying that the campaign will probably be great as well.

Games can be bad in a lot of ways. They can be too hard, they can be too dumb (it's true), they can be too rough, and so on. I've played plenty of games that were perfectly good at what they wanted to be, and what they wanted to be was bad. Sinister City is the opposite, in a way. It wants to be dumb and goofy in a charming way, and it would be, if not for being genuinely bad on the technical side.
You play John, a regular joe who looks a little like Tom Cruise with a painted on short-sleeve button-up and tie. His girl Nina gets whisked away by a vampire to Sinister City, an actual ♥♥♥♥ing place full of vampires that everyone is totally okay with for some reason. After getting his bearings and some vampire hunting tips from the melon-headed veteran, John makes his way into the auspicious burg to wrest his fiancee from the clutches of the undead.
It's nowhere near this epic, mind you, and that's a good thing for once. Whatever you're expecting of Sinister City is going to get upended because the story is acutely aware of its absurdities and tries to top itself constantly. Within minutes of starting the game (spoiler alert I guess?) the kindly hotel manager assembles a mystical hypnosis machine that sends you to the astral plane. To defeat the villainous vampire you'll need the help of his real estate agent wife and his therapist. There's a vampire Teletubby. And all of this is spilled on you not with a wink and a nod, or awkward tryhard dialogue, but with some refreshingly earnest humor and a willingness to just roll with the weirdness.
The reason I'm telling you all this up front is because despite the solid kookiness, you really shouldn't play Sinister City. As wonderfully campy as the story ends up being the gameplay cannot sustain it, and the technical issues just demolish what's left. The hidden object scenes here are a combination of the genre's worst habits: You can only seek five items at a time, you have to move completely unmarked objects to get at things behind them, the scenes themselves are hard to spot and tend to be in strange places, and you have to do them multiple times until you find almost every single item. This means that scenes are incredibly easy as long as you're randomly clicking on everything, which is the only way to find the movable objects anyway.
On top of that, you need to find multiples of items across multiple scenes or areas to get inventory items to use on NPCs or puzzles. These can be hidden anywhere, including hidden object scenes for OTHER items, and you get no indication that you've found everything in a given scene. Plus, you can't even pick up obvious items until you trigger the dialogue telling you to get them! On top of all this, some scenes are misaligned graphically which make it super hard to click the right things, and some objects blend far too well into the muddy backgrounds.
The amateur-hour graphics don't do Sinister City any favors either, with inconsistent 3D models and some incredibly blurry backgrounds. I must admit, though, the sound design is decent and features some nice, campy voice acting and appropriate music. But it is clear this was a mobile title first, with a lack of options and plenty of "Tap here to X" prompts. It wouldn't take you more than 90 minutes to beat even on the harder mode, so as decent as the story is in its goofy way, you're better off staying far, far away from Sinister City.

If you think a great game is constituted by aesthetics and paintjobs to your weapons, do not get this game.
If you think that a great game is constituted by enjoyable gameplay, variety of playable characters, balanced 4 versus 1 ingenuity and multiplayer support, get this game!
Developed by the creators the Left 4 Dead series, Evolve has taken the four-player Co-op formula Turtle Rock is known for and turning it into a futuristic game of deadly hide-and-seek, where the hunters need to track down and defeat the single player/AI-controlled Monster or risk becoming the prey themselves. WIth 12 Hunters and 3 Monsters by default, Evolve gives you a good range of characters to choose from, each offering thier own approach to the game allowing players of any style to find thier niche, whether it be attacking the Monster directly, keeping the team alive with sheilds and healing or debuffing the Monster. With the newly added Monster and 4 new hunters, the variety continues to grow.  While the progression system may be annoying if all you want is to play as a third tier character, it gives you a feeling of accomplishment when your weapons get stronger as your become more proficient with your selected character. And yes, you can earn skins this way.
If you like Left 4 Dead, you will like this game. Playing alone is always an option, but playing with friends to help you get through the Monster-infested planet of Shear is always a plus.

If your checking this out and still not sold.. This is probably the most authentic, tactical, and realistic WW2 FPS available. If you put some time in, the learning curve is very rewarding.
+ Squad commands - Get on the point!
+ Recon radio - reveal enemy positions
+ Artillery - 4 types. Spot your target. Radio for mortars, howitzers, rocket barage, or a naval pounding.
+ Tanks & APC (operable alone or with crew)
+ Mounted machine guns for defense
+ Classes available: Team leader, squad leader, engineer, marksman, assault, machine gunner, tank, mortar, flamethrower, and infantry
+ Big selection of maps with authentic ww2 locations, terrain, and propaganda posters
+ Preset voice commands on quick menu interface (changeable languages)
+ Authentic ww2 weapons incl: springfield, kar98, mauser, makarov, ppsh, mp40, mosin nagant, grenades, landmines, bayonets, flamethrowers, katanas! and others.
+ Realistic recoil, sound, and bullet drop effects. Adjustable sights for elevation.
+ Trench warfare and bunkers
+ Eastern front and Pacific theatres: German, Russian, Japanese, American, & British (with mod).
+ Can be played alone on an empty server to rank up and unlock weapons and upgrade abilities, if needed.
- Some bugs. Most are overcome and certainly not deal breakers.
- AI can be frustrating but can often be corrected by squad or team leaders. Take the time to learn those classes, they are
valueable assets in your team.
- Some areas on certain maps can't be spotted for artillery by the team leader, this can often be overcome with a spot from a squad leader.
- Some graphical bugs when going prone on certain maps
- The control or use key is bound by default to too many functions which sometimes conflict
- Auto balance issues with limited players
- High video settings can crash the game on older systems, some tweaking advised.
Probably my favourite game ever, enjoy.

Without a doubt, this is by far the best survival horror game I've ever played. This game shows the brutal reality that comes not only from a zombie apocalypse, but the collapse of society as well. Project Zomboid starts you up in a random location in Knox County, Kansas with only one goal in mind: survive. How this is done is up to you. Would you board up your own house and stay quiet? Go ahead. Shall you be a nomad, looting and sleeping in each house on the street. Sure thing. Or do you simply want to end the zombie uprising yourself and smash each and every head that stands before you. Go for it (though that won't end well) But the most amazing thing about Project Zomboid is how its use of realism gradually raises the difficulty. Sooner or later the power is gonna go off and with it the refrigeration. Slowly, most of the food begins to spoil. The winter months are approaching and no power = no heat. Sure you can save on canned food, but you know it won't last forever. This is also the kind of game where you might find it more ideal to AVOID combat, as infection in this world follows world war z rules; spread by bites, possibly by scratches and is 100% lethal. And if you don't like any of the characteristics of the main game, you can customize your own infection by altering the world and zombie stats in sandbox mode. To top it all off, the developers of this game are not only awesome, but embody every trait a good developer should have. They take their time with updates, only releasing them when they are completely stable, they communicate with their players, and have no DLCs :D Honestly, I believe this game is worth the full price for what it offers. If you like survival games, then you will love Project Zomboid. Though remember, Project Zomboid isn't the story of how you lived, it's how you died.

BioShock's a pretty decent game even to this day. The game gives you multiple options to go about a scenario and it's up to you to choose the one that fits your playstyle best. There's a good selection of weapons too, and most are capable of being used in to the late game, even the starting melee weapon!

Despite that, it should be noted that the game starts out strong but regrettably feels a tad drawn out at the end. The endings themselves are a bit sappy, both good and bad, but they feel relatively satisfying regardless.
On the technical side, this game isn't really alt-tab friendly if you do fullscreen, colors start inverting and it could mess up the resolution you set for the game. The intro and ending cutscene are also played at full volume no matter what you put the volume at. I had all my sounds set to 1/10 across the board and both cutscenes were very loud.
Definitely would recommend this game if you enjoy games like System Shock, Deus Ex or Dishonored. It's got that RPG vibe despite being an FPS and it does it pretty well.

Being a huge fan of horror Outlast was always a game I've wanted to check out as I've always hard good things about it and it looked like a solid continuation of the first person horror formula that became popular with Amnesia: The Dark Descent. And overall it was a good time but also disappointing and lazy in some areas.
Outlast is overall a very solid game. The graphics are still good looking for the most part and the soundtrack and sound design in general is great. The story itself is solid for the most part although loses a lot of steam towards the end. The game continues from Amnesia's formula of having to run away from things and hide instead of being able to fight back and your character uses a camcorder to see in the dark. Although I had a fun time with Outlast for being a horror game I found it rather lacking. The biggest issue here is that the game shows the player way too much. You know those repetitive horror films nowadays that basically throw jumpscare after jumpscare at the audience with many of them being fake outs? Outlast is basically the videogame equivalent of that. Although the game has great atmosphere and sound it ruins what it builds up by throwing jumpscare after jumpscare at the player and it just becomes so repetitive despite the games short length. There's also a lot of gruesome in your face segments that seem to try to be shocking the player but they just come off as trying too hard. The game would've been far more effective if it limited all of this and relied more on the environment and the unknown using things suck as shadows or sound instead of going completely loud most of the time. Of course the main element of horror in the game is the enemies which are important to talk about. Some of the patients themselves have unique personalities and themes that go along with them and are quite well done. However all the enemies function the same and you just need to hide and run away from them to escape. Although this process can be intense the first few times it becomes quite the hassle towards the end. There's also times when you need to run from just regular patients that lack any intensity or special feeling at all and are easily among the worst parts of the game.
Although everything i've said up to this point might make you think I dislike Outlast and wouldn't recommend it the game easily has enough positives for me to still suggest it. Investigating the asylum and getting to the bottom of whats going on is a great time and thanks to the games length it's for the most part well paced and doesn't overstay its welcome. The atmosphere is great until it's ruined by obnoxious jumpscares or gore but again when it works it works. There was never a time when playing Outlast that I became uninterested or wanted to stop playing and overall had a really fun time. With all my flaws I wouldn't recommend purchasing the game at full price especially considering the short length. If you can purchase it on sale (or got it for free like I did) then it is worth your time for sure. I would also highly suggest the Whistleblower dlc as it adds a lot of story to the game and acts as a solid finale.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted delivers on all the major promises made by all those Early Access open-world surive 'em up titles, sans the massively multiplayer stuff (though multiplayer was recently patched in, I have yet to try that mode out, so if you're worried about that and that alone in regards to picking up this game you can just go ahead and bail now, 's cool, I promise).  Maybe a better comparison would be the old S.T.A.L.K.E.R. trilogy.  Inventory management is very similar, there's a lot of worthless junk in the world like Bethesda RPG's, but you'll be forced to prioritze between nourishment and weapons as you progress through the game.
What makes SYABH unique is surely the English country-side art style, with all the Victorian robots running around.  The designs are not over-designed, if that makes sense.  Their comical dialog, and gentleman's dress code really adds a sense of comedicness to the bleak, foggy marshes and hills that dot the islands you explore.  Unfortunately though, for all their charm the robots are just as freaking deadly.
The game gives you a chance to save your progress semi-regularly, but the fear of death is still very real as you can end up losing nearly an hour of progress and restarting back on a beach.  This might sound like a challenge but it really emphasives how stressful the game can become, especially as you proceed and the robots begin to spawn in bigger masses with deadlier tools in their belts.  I've sat for nearly 15 minutes in the grass just waiting for patrols to die down so I can get back to the freaking boat.
I actually had to take a break from games for a few days after completing the final island of the main story purely because of how stressful the robots become.  They shouldn't be scary, but they become terrifying.  The land owner robot rivals Slenderman in terms of terrifying stalker material.  An invcible giant that makes high pitched squeels, and will follow you relentlessly once he spots you.
I played on one of the easier starting load outs with a randomly generated set of islands, though you're free to choose your starting loadout from several presets.  You can even manually adjust what types of islands and robots you'll receive in your playthrough.  With all that in mind, I can't really think of anything this game does wrong.  You are equipped the tools to configure it to your suiting right out of the box.  There's no crafting system like other major open world titles, but the game doesn't really suffer for it.
If you enjoy sandbox experiences, especially from a first person perspective, you won't regret putting this on your wish list.

Looking for a rogue-like that will crush your heart and soul?  This is it.  There is no hand-holding and no mercy whatsoever.
Strategy game at heart, you will learn the basic controls and objective, then straight into the abysss and you will not make your way to the finish line first try, or for a while.
That said, Dungeon of the Endless is beautiful in both art and strategic design.  Similar to Risk of Rain, the pixil graphics adds to the game experience with its simplicity and clarity.  The core strategic concept is just as simple as as its graphics, but also as deep and attractive.  You will learn to manage your heroes, generate resources, control monsters, place modules, and much more which again are all under this complex system with hints only learned through brutally punishing mistakes.
I would consider this a hardcore strategy game made to strike terror into the mind of feeble individuals.  But if you have determination to push through and intelligent enough to figure out the system, then you will, well, beat the game and unlock the hard mode.
Overall a very enjoyable experience for me.  This game may not be for everyone, but it is a great game.

A strange combination of roguelike, RPG, tower defence and strategy, Dungeon of the Endless is an intriguing beast to say the least. I bought it while in early access but the difficulty delayed completion until I re-installed it recently. It's still a cripplingly difficult game and requires you to take advantage of every imbalance, every loophole, to pass more than a few floors... and that's on the simplest difficulty setting.
With each failure the slate is wiped clean, but there are new characters to unlock and if you're lucky you can put together a team with some nice synergy. The currency system in game is well designed, and every module built or researched is a decision that could make or break you. The level of polish, particularly in menus is excellent and the pixelated style is well executed even if it gets a little old and chaotic as the game goes on. Music is good at first, but the number of tracks is limited and thus it grates after a while.
It's all good stuff... I feel a sense of achievement from completing it, and I have some good stories to tell, but it somewhat lacks in gameplay and variety when stretched over many hours. Multiplayer is a nice addition, and can make your life easier, but since things are essentially turn-based you could end up feeling like a spectator in what's more like a single-player experience. I feel guilty giving it such a mediocre score, but I'm going to go with my gut on this. Perhaps if victory hadn't come after such a grind the numbers would look different.[6.2]

Limbo is probably one of the most atmospheric and beautiful little indie gems that came out before the whole indie hype started. It is the predecessor of dozens of platformers that tried to steal from its ideas and yet, until this day, it remains one of the best of them. Art design, sound and the platforming elements are just brilliantly connected to each other and while the game is completely in grey, it still is able to convey harsh graphic violence and a superbly disturbing feeling along the journey.
It's not too long, but it is worth every penny. One of the most beautiful platformers within the last couple of years.

This is a unique cross between tower defense, 4X, and rogue-like game.
You have 1 to 4 heroes that explore a random dungeon consisting of rooms separated by doors. Every time you open a door, monsters spawn in all the unlit areas of the dungeon and try to attack your heroes and reach your base. You can stop them by attacking with your heroes or building defenses.
After the wave of monsters is done, you are safe and may build or upgrade your structures. This phase plays a lot like a 4X game where you must manage food, research, and industry. Each room can a certain number of structures of various types, and some rooms contain existing structures.
Your heroes themselves level up and gain skills as they would in an RPG. Death is permanent and when all your heroes die, you must restart the game from scratch.
There is a huge amount of replayability here due to the random elements and number of ships and characters you can choose. A typical game can take 3-4 hours.
As with roguelikes this is fairly difficult game, particularly if you play it on the harder difficulty (there are two difficilties, mislabelled "easy" and "very easy"). If you enjoy difficult games, you should like this a lot.

As far as I am concerned RO2 is THE WW2 game. Not Battlefield, not Call of Duty, etc.
Why? It's Battlefield with better teamwork, airstrikes, and a commander. Squad leaders are significant and actually have a task insofar as the have to mark targets for the commander to call in an airstrike. You're even able to use vehicles, and they are decisive and make a huge difference compared with other games.
This game also has a medium pace. Since the respawn times are usually at 10 seconds or so, you want to play more carefully which results in a much more realistic experience. Indeed, of all the shooters I have played, this one seems the most realistic. I actually care about my guy and for the most part I try to avoid getting killed if I can help it.
If ur gud, then is game is REALLY fun, as being good really is all about being in the right place at the right time and shooting. It's not as much quirks like noobtubing or quick scoping--which are impossible.
Basically, this game will appeal to Battlefield fans. They're similar, in that they take place in rather large maps and encourage more strategic play than Call of Duty.

I started playing this game during its much earlier development period.
There are many survival titles out. Many, many, many titles. For me, this game was the first game that I played that that pitted you against mother nature and not zombies or other monsters. I love the idea of scavanging for food, having to craft your own tools and clothing, needing to hunt and fish to survive, and having to manage your water and caloric intake to survive.
This game is beautiful. Exploration is important and you are, most of the time, rewarded for taking a chance and visiting areas that you have not been before. That is the challenge, rolling the dice so that you have a chance at finding something that will benefit your survival or die because you weren't quite prepared for the journy.
Crafting is meticulous but rewarding. Having to work to collect components for items and clothing is challenging. The payout for your hard work is never disappointing.
Realism is a very big factor in this game. They have done a good job keeping it as realistic as possible while keeping it fun.
Hunting and fishing is another aspect thats quite a bit fun and rewarding. Setting traps, ice fishing, and the use of rifles and bows. You are able to harvest animals for valuable resources. This includes meat, skins, and guts. All are used in the crafting process.
The story is OK. I like it,  but I do not play it and did not start playing it for the story(There was not one at the time and I never believed that it needed one.) The sandbox is where it is at for me. The story is interesting, but I enjoyed the unexpected vs the scripted.

The characters follow the Fire Emblem rules in that certain characters surviving splunks together will get a bonus and develop a personal story between them but death means dead, no reviving. The Tower Defense aspect comes from your need to keep your master crystal in one piece and failure to do so is game over.
These are really cool features so how does the game fail at them?
First of all the characters don't interact until every stage is finished so most of the time they are just characterless which is unfortante because they are really well animated and when they do engage in their stories they are interesting, so why are they so mute the rest of the time?
They also die, very easily and very often and the game likes to mock you about this fact with "let the tears flow" which doesn't upset but rather what it does do is make me indifferent. Imagine if in Final Fantasy 7 when Cloud goes mental after falling into the Lifestream that the game just says 'Cloud is crazy, your heroes moved on'. Suddenly the whole impact of the gravity of the situation is gone which is what happens when I lose a hero. I don't care that I lost them because the game doesn't make me care.
Characters level up, have stories, are unique and well drawn and yet that is where the RPG element ends. The characters are for the most part interchangable. Some operate modules and others can take or deal a lot of damage but other than that the characters lack any of the things that make Fire Emblem a joy to play which is a shame.
So the other side of the coin is Tower Defense. As far as TD games go, you open doors and gain dust. Dust powers rooms which allow you to power turrets. If you lack the dust (and you will) then you will soon be fighting waves of monsters and you will wipe. To counter this you can build lots of Industry and research the ability to power rooms wih industry instead of dust, a feature which becomes almost mandatory as the game goes on. Researching however is completely random so you may get shafted and be faced with an unwinnable game, just because.
Thankfuly however the game makes the chance of this occouring, very low but know that it can happen.
As for difficulty you will hear the game is too hard but this stems from the fact that "too easy" means normal and "easy" means very hard. If you play this game, keep this in mind because you will die on easy often and when you go to the forum to complain about it, believe me they know already. Everyone does.
The TD aspect suffers from being dragged down by the RPG side and the RPG side suffers from being a hollow, empty experince for the majority of the game that never improves for example
when (or if) you finally beat the game what is your reward? See that store page picture? No I am not joking. Not even a "congratulations", you just get a stock picture and that's it. I didn't even believe I had beaten the game at first; What happened after that good opening cinematic, did the budget run out? Or did they not expect anyone to beat the game? I mentioned before how the game made me not care about the heroes and the ending just reinforces how lazy the RPG element is. The story doesn't even have a proper ending, not even a line of dialogue to let you know what our heroes did next, nothing.
The music, the sounds, the art? All fantastic! But the gameplay is not good and that is a huge letdown because you really want to enjoy the game and you want to care about the world going on and the lore but each run is about as disjointed from the characters as you can get, the TD element is pretty badly done with nothing learned from fantastic TD games like Orcs must die and it just creates a really disappointing, mediocre game that you really wish was better.
The netcode is great when it works but if you lose connection their is no re-join option and you can't pause/save a MP game so I hope you have a few hours to spare. This is also a game that suffers from making you go to a wiki to learn what things do and just add to the things that detract from what would otherwise be a fantastic game.
Maybe future patches can help the game out because it does so much
that the things it does wrong are noticable like a beautiful person with a giant metal nose. You might admire the beauty but you can't ignore the nose either.

Being a huge fan of horror Outlast was always a game I've wanted to check out as I've always hard good things about it and it looked like a solid continuation of the first person horror formula that became popular with Amnesia: The Dark Descent. And overall it was a good time but also disappointing and lazy in some areas.
Outlast is overall a very solid game. The graphics are still good looking for the most part and the soundtrack and sound design in general is great. The story itself is solid for the most part although loses a lot of steam towards the end. The game continues from Amnesia's formula of having to run away from things and hide instead of being able to fight back and your character uses a camcorder to see in the dark. Although I had a fun time with Outlast for being a horror game I found it rather lacking. The biggest issue here is that the game shows the player way too much. You know those repetitive horror films nowadays that basically throw jumpscare after jumpscare at the audience with many of them being fake outs? Outlast is basically the videogame equivalent of that. Although the game has great atmosphere and sound it ruins what it builds up by throwing jumpscare after jumpscare at the player and it just becomes so repetitive despite the games short length. There's also a lot of gruesome in your face segments that seem to try to be shocking the player but they just come off as trying too hard. The game would've been far more effective if it limited all of this and relied more on the environment and the unknown using things suck as shadows or sound instead of going completely loud most of the time. Of course the main element of horror in the game is the enemies which are important to talk about. Some of the patients themselves have unique personalities and themes that go along with them and are quite well done. However all the enemies function the same and you just need to hide and run away from them to escape. Although this process can be intense the first few times it becomes quite the hassle towards the end. There's also times when you need to run from just regular patients that lack any intensity or special feeling at all and are easily among the worst parts of the game.
Although everything i've said up to this point might make you think I dislike Outlast and wouldn't recommend it the game easily has enough positives for me to still suggest it. Investigating the asylum and getting to the bottom of whats going on is a great time and thanks to the games length it's for the most part well paced and doesn't overstay its welcome. The atmosphere is great until it's ruined by obnoxious jumpscares or gore but again when it works it works. There was never a time when playing Outlast that I became uninterested or wanted to stop playing and overall had a really fun time. With all my flaws I wouldn't recommend purchasing the game at full price especially considering the short length. If you can purchase it on sale (or got it for free like I did) then it is worth your time for sure. I would also highly suggest the Whistleblower dlc as it adds a lot of story to the game and acts as a solid finale.
If you dont have this, please get it, its an amazingly underrated game !

I've played much worse hidden objects game, which were more expensive and even sh*ttier in story and bugs.
So, that's it. Mixed reviews, so this is obviously not the best game, if you are looking for hidden objects game. It's time to take a break from AAA titles and indulge in the serenity and minimalism of this game. The music score is soothing. The game concept is based on connecting the dots except that it also features color based strokes/ paths and a single stroke is needed to fill each color. The strokes cannot overlap or cross each other. You need to find a path to connect all the boxes of each of the color codes.
This is definitely a challenging puzzle otherwise it would have been dull and boring. It's hard but worry not because the pace and learning curve builds up smoothly as you easily navigate few levels in each 'set'. There are as many sets as there are alphabets in the English language. Get those letter achievements to flaunt your showcase. The game also includes Daily sets which are randomly generated but need to be completed for the particular day.
You gain skill points as you progress through the sets. The points can be used to unlock many theme colors to suit your comfort and style.
Nothing about this game is repetitive. Sometimes there is more than one solution to a puzzle. Now if you are in it only for collecting achievements, then here's a

Bought this years ago, but finally gave it proper attention just recently.  Yeah, it took only a couple of hours across one play session to beat, but Limbo still is worth the time and money, especially if you wish to 100% the achievements.  The simple controls and black and white presentation fit the ambiguous story and the puzzles perfectly.  While some of the game is pure trial and error the first time, a lot can be figured out by scouting areas before initiating the puzzles proper.  The ending is incredibly vague, but allows for the player to think about things and draw up their own conclusions about raised questions.  When I came up with what I believed was going on and what happened throughout, I fell in love with Limbo even  more!
Collecting the 10 eggs/achievements unlocks a secret level accessed somewhere in the main game itself.  The secret level is longer than one would expect, and is a great test of things you have learned and demands attention to audio cues.  I found it to be a great final challenge.
Going for it all?  Full price is totally justified.  Just looking to play through the main campaign and move on, and find the 10 bucks a little hard to swallow for a game a couple/few hours long?  Add to the wishlist and buy on sale.  You won't regret you did!

The Long Dark is a quality game. I bought it for a normal $20 bucks, which is pretty weighty for me, and it has been worth every cent. The game allows you to experience a quiet apocalypse, in which you are the lone survivor, with nobody to save you and nobody to cooperate with. No zombies to kill, no other players to murder and loot, and no way to escape. The unforgiving nature is what gives it its appeal. Nature won't bend its rules for you, and you must learn to survive in cooperation with nature, rather than working against it. The game has a very steep learning curve, but after a few playthroughs you get the concept and start to survive. At first you simply survive, but after a few hundred days in-game, you learn how to live. There is no map, and there is no tutorial. You must memorize the map roughly in order to not get lost and wander in circles in a blizzard and die (believe me, it has happened). You must learn for yourself the rules of survival.
Story mode is supposed to be released sometime in 2017, but I can't be sure. They have delayed the story mode for about a year now, though I don't care much. The sandbox mode alone was well worth the $20, and I would have been willing to pay twice that if I had too. If you pay for the game before story mode is released, you get the first two seasons on the house. I can't wait for story mode, but if it weren't ever released, I would be happy with the purchase. They have been steady with updates, and the devs are still heavy into building this amazing game.

The Long Dark is a first person survival game with a swing at realism. Your goal is to stay alive in a new-world apocalypse and endure mother nature's wrath.
Don't let the "early access" stamp make the decision for you; this is a complete and stable game at the moment (the sandbox mode at least). More changes and content will be added in the future as well as a lot of imperfections being ironed out over time.
PROS:
+ Survival tactics and resource management are really fun to carry out
+ The world, structures and items are detailed, extensive and a pleasure to look at; great artstyle
+ The graphics can be adjusted for both low and high quality PCs
+ Very pretty mapdesign
+ The ambient and sounds are spot-on
+ Fitting environmental soundtrack
CONS:
- Boredom, monotony and repetitive tasks are part of the game but yet have a negative impact on the player's experience
- Exploiting the autosave is rather easy and is often enticing you to "cheat" by exiting and reloading the save file where you last left an area or structure if you get into trouble
- Replayability is limited because after a while you know the maps, which you might think is good since you'll find your way easier, but it kind of ruins the immersion of being a survivor of a crash in the wilderness
- [Version related] The difficulties are currently not balanced too well: Stalker, the second-hardest difficulty, is too easy while Interloper, the hardest difficulty, is a bit too hard
A very decent attempt at creating a more realistic survival game. While due the realistic approach it can be kind of boring or repetitive at times, overall it's a great game.
My rating: 8
Note: due the game being in early access, this review may be updated.

I don't think I've ever written a review for a game here, but this is a game that more than warrants one. I was born in 1975. Pac-Man was the first video game I ever played. It was a cocktail cabinet in the bar at the racquetball club my Mom attended. After her games, She would give me some quarters to play Pac-Man. It was amazing. The sounds, the graphics, everything. I was in love with the idea of video games.
A few years later my friends and I were full on gaming nuts. Talk on the playground would often be where will graphics go and how much more realistic will they get in the future. One of my predictions was that some day video game graphics will look exactly like cartoons. (That’s what I thought they were striving to be back then) I know there was Dragon’s Lair and the likes, but that’s FMV, so I don’t count that. Cuphead is the first game I’ve seen that looks full on like animation you can play. This is what I dreamed of as a kid, but Cuphead is so much more. Having been born in the mid-seventies I can’t say these graphics were representative of my generation’s nostalgia, but I did see some old Fleischer Studios cartoons on TV fairly often. (particularly Popeye) It had it’s own look and that’s what Cuphead is paying tribute to.
Gameplay wise, Cuphead is throwback to mid-eighties to early nineties platform shooters and air/space shooters. These were some of the hardest games ever made and it felt like a real accomplishment to beat one. Games today are too easy. They are longer, but you never really feel like you accomplished something special when you finish them because if you put in the time and go through the motions you will finish it with little effort. Cuphead is difficult and you will die a lot, but it’s never unfair. You have to learn the fights and try and try again making you earn it. Eventually you will get it down and it feels great every time you beat a boss. That feeling I had as a kid making progress in a game and not being able to wait to get home from school to try and progress further is something I miss and Cuphead delivers by the truck load.
Do I think this is a game everyone is going to like? Maybe not because some people didn’t grow up with games that were hard like this. I could see how this might turn some people off, but if you are around my age and you remember Contra, Lifeforce, etc. then this is a must play. It took me 423 deaths to beat the game, but the game never gets boring. The beautiful graphics and style of each boss keeps you entertained. For me I could only play the game a few hours at a time before I was fatigued and would start making stupid mistakes over and over again slowing my progress. The game requires intense focus so once you start making lots of mistakes, give it a rest and go do something else. You will only make yourself frustrated and that’s not fun.
In the end this is a game I feel everyone should try. This is the core of what having skills in gaming is all about. If Mario Odyssey doesn’t blow me away, this will be my game of the year hands down.

I started playing this game during its much earlier development period.
There are many survival titles out. Many, many, many titles. For me, this game was the first game that I played that that pitted you against mother nature and not zombies or other monsters. I love the idea of scavanging for food, having to craft your own tools and clothing, needing to hunt and fish to survive, and having to manage your water and caloric intake to survive.
This game is beautiful. Exploration is important and you are, most of the time, rewarded for taking a chance and visiting areas that you have not been before. That is the challenge, rolling the dice so that you have a chance at finding something that will benefit your survival or die because you weren't quite prepared for the journy.
Crafting is meticulous but rewarding. Having to work to collect components for items and clothing is challenging. The payout for your hard work is never disappointing.
Realism is a very big factor in this game. They have done a good job keeping it as realistic as possible while keeping it fun.
Hunting and fishing is another aspect thats quite a bit fun and rewarding. Setting traps, ice fishing, and the use of rifles and bows. You are able to harvest animals for valuable resources. This includes meat, skins, and guts. All are used in the crafting process.
The story is OK. I like it,  but I do not play it and did not start playing it for the story(There was not one at the time and I never believed that it needed one.) The sandbox is where it is at for me. The story is interesting, but I enjoyed the unexpected vs the scripted.

Moustache Mountain is a fun little $2 time-killer. The smooth and simple platforming mechanics carry right over from Amatniek's previous game, There was a Caveman: with limited controls including movement and jumping, and bouncing off walls being about the most complex these moustaches get.
As a tiny (but burly) man with a moustache, you platform your way up 15 single-screen levels with increasing difficulty and traps. Heaps of bloody spikes, player-activated arrow traps, shifting blades and narrow platforming -- your goal is simply to make it to the right side of each screen without losing three lives.
A single, successful game should only take between three and five minutes, but it'll likely take up to an hour to get there the first time. To keep things interesting, each screen is pulled randomly from a handful of options (except level 11, which always seems to be the same).
As with Nauris' other solo projects, the music is the dreariest boops and bops of anti-music, easily making it the game's weakest aspect.
Moustache Mountain doesn't come with much, but it's a fun project easily worth the measly price tag it carries. I also recommend following the developer on Twitter / Patreon (@namatnieks), where he actively creates gorgeous pixel art and tutorials. :)~

Being a huge fan of horror Outlast was always a game I've wanted to check out as I've always hard good things about it and it looked like a solid continuation of the first person horror formula that became popular with Amnesia: The Dark Descent. And overall it was a good time but also disappointing and lazy in some areas.
Outlast is overall a very solid game. The graphics are still good looking for the most part and the soundtrack and sound design in general is great. The story itself is solid for the most part although loses a lot of steam towards the end. The game continues from Amnesia's formula of having to run away from things and hide instead of being able to fight back and your character uses a camcorder to see in the dark. Although I had a fun time with Outlast for being a horror game I found it rather lacking. The biggest issue here is that the game shows the player way too much. You know those repetitive horror films nowadays that basically throw jumpscare after jumpscare at the audience with many of them being fake outs? Outlast is basically the videogame equivalent of that. Although the game has great atmosphere and sound it ruins what it builds up by throwing jumpscare after jumpscare at the player and it just becomes so repetitive despite the games short length. There's also a lot of gruesome in your face segments that seem to try to be shocking the player but they just come off as trying too hard. The game would've been far more effective if it limited all of this and relied more on the environment and the unknown using things suck as shadows or sound instead of going completely loud most of the time. Of course the main element of horror in the game is the enemies which are important to talk about. Some of the patients themselves have unique personalities and themes that go along with them and are quite well done. However all the enemies function the same and you just need to hide and run away from them to escape. Although this process can be intense the first few times it becomes quite the hassle towards the end. There's also times when you need to run from just regular patients that lack any intensity or special feeling at all and are easily among the worst parts of the game.
Although everything i've said up to this point might make you think I dislike Outlast and wouldn't recommend it the game easily has enough positives for me to still suggest it. Investigating the asylum and getting to the bottom of whats going on is a great time and thanks to the games length it's for the most part well paced and doesn't overstay its welcome. The atmosphere is great until it's ruined by obnoxious jumpscares or gore but again when it works it works. There was never a time when playing Outlast that I became uninterested or wanted to stop playing and overall had a really fun time. With all my flaws I wouldn't recommend purchasing the game at full price especially considering the short length. If you can purchase it on sale (or got it for free like I did) then it is worth your time for sure. I would also highly suggest the Whistleblower dlc as it adds a lot of story to the game and acts as a solid finale.

Bioshock is a steampunk FPS with horror elements and a classic to boot.
The plot starts off with your guy (who's called jack) on a plane flying over the sea when it suddenly crash lands into the water, most likely killing everyone except you. You swim to the only bit of land you see, a lighthouse, and from there climb into a sphere shaped sub which takes you down to the city of rapture (think capitalist atlantis made by man and gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥ . A place filled with violent psychos, political fruit cakes and body modifying slug juice. All made by one man, andrew ryan. Your goal is simple, survive. The plot really does thicken throughout the game, but i'm not spoiling the plot twists.
Gameplay is like the more classical FPS games, where in you end up carrying around a half dozen guns with you. Each one is satisfying to use and provides a good amount of stopping power, except the camera. Alongside those you have plasmids, these give you special powers and elevate the combat above the standard FPS formula. From shooting fireballs to throwing sith lightning, all of this and more is avalable at your local gene splicing pump. On top of that you can also inject yourself with other plasmids that give bonuses to various abilities or modify others, nothing particularly outstanding, but none of them are useless.
typically, you'll be running around one area of rapture, killing your way through splicers as you complete various objectives and keeping an eye out for little sisters and their companions, big daddies. Little sisters provide you with adam, which allows you to buy more plasmids, but you need to kill the big daddy to get to her, and these guys are not push overs. Once you've unloaded all of your ammo into daddy dearest you can decide to drain the girl of her fluids (wait a minute...) or extract some of them and "fix" her, restoring her to a normal 6-12 (?) year old girl. This is the games only moral system by the way, do you want to kill children or save them? kill them and you get the "evil" ending, save them and get the forrest gump tear jerking levels "happy" ending.
Visually the game isn't too unique aside from a few elements here and there. The big daddies and rapture as a whole are the most unique aspects, and easily manages to keep the atmosphere its intending to put forward up throughout the game. The soundtrack isn't noticable throughout the game, but on its own its a treat.
My issues with the game are few, but still worth noting. The morality system in the game is a bit weak, i would have liked to have seen my choices make an actual impact on the overall story aside from whether or not i care about some child filled with gooey goodness that gives me powers. On a plot level, its hard to decide whether they intended this to conflict with the philosophy that some of the characters in the game, or that its just a design choice that they simply wanted to include this mechanic. Either way its not bad, but its not great. Another issue i have with it is that the weapons aren't particularly unique, each one feels very good, but none of them do anything special.
Despite these issues, i would recommend bioshock to anyone who likes FPS. Its a true classic deserving of the title, and is well worth giving a shot or two into a daddies face....wait a second...

Who would name their town Sinister City? Vampires, of course! When John discovers his bride-to-be has been kidnapped by Sinister City's number one bloodsucker, there's only one thing to do - search for hidden objects! And kill vampires! Or at least insult them until they give your girl back.
Sinister City is a casual hidden object game in which we play as a character that goes by the name of John (quite rare among these parts) and he, for the reason unknown to man, decided to take a trip with his bride-to-be Nina, to a lovely place called Sinister City.
Now you might find yourselves thinking who decided to give this city such an...inviting name, but from what we see of the town throughout the game describes it really well, so kudos to you, unkown peasant, you did well.
So our hero in the making has to find out whatever happened to his fiancee, by doing all kinds of silly stuff for the eccentric townfolk. The game itself is very straightforward and you can't get stuck on a puzzle if you wanted to, thanks to the unlimited hints system.
The puzzles are not at all difficult and won't be a problem to anyone, while the hidden object screens will occasionally annoy you with the low res graphics, but still won't be much of a problem.
The story is not trying to be serious at all, it almost felt like a parody in a way. The bad guy is a vampire that is apparently the one responsible for your finacee's disappearance, and you will have a chance to talk with him as the time goes on. The game is quite short, took me less than 2 hours to finish.
I did encounter some bugs while playing, like sometimes the graphics of a certain objects will disappear, or while in the hidden object scene, every click of the mouse will exit the screen until you go back to the main menu and reenter the game from there.
Voice acting was ok, I've heard better, but it's tolerable. All in all, if you like hidden object games you are probably gonna like this one too. If you have never played a HO game, you probably want to try a better game to see if you'll like the genre.

I'll be honest, my review will be a little be alittle biased because I love Ragnarok. However I won't pull any punches. This game is just like any other clicker on the web. Overall I'd give this game a 4/5. Compared to other clickers I've played, this has more features besides clicking. As a guild leader I can share my experience on the guild message board which is really nice. I wouuld definitely recommend this to my friends.

Got nearly 30 hours on Evolve so far, and I can safely say I love this game. I find new things to learn about my favorite hunters all the time, and the maps continue to provide neat tricks that I missed on previous playthroughs. The characters are varied enough to fit any playstyle, and each of the hunters in my favored class (medic) have something special to bring to the table, so I play them all regularly.
I also picked up the new hunters, and I'm loving them to death - new mechanics and new personalities make the game feel like the first time I played all over again. There's a ton of replayability and playing with three friends hasn't been this fun since Left 4 Dead.
The game's a bit pricey, and I'm not a fan of that. I wish they had been a bit more competitive with the way they priced the game and the DLC, but it's also a risky venture to break away from the Call of Duty model, so I can forgive the insurance policy. I'd rather pay too much for a good game than pay too little for a game I hate. At least I'm getting something I like out of the deal.
At the end of the day, I like this game a lot. I don't play much monster because I can't get my head around the pacing and the pathing, but that doesn't stop me from playing it for hours on end.

Seriously, the game has a built in timer, so you don't have to fiddle with splits, it's right there on the screen for you. Sure, for more accurate results, you could also run livesplit, but so far the speedrun community for this game isn't very large, so there aren't any contested runs yet.
As for the game itself, its simplicity is where it shines. You can jump, and you can wall jump. That's it. No finicky other buttons to press, just directions and jump. However, the game is not without its flaws. Using a controller, my preferred platforming control method, there is a bit of a problem with the controls. Touching down on the dpad causes you to stop moving entirely. So as you go from left to right or vice versa, you might inadvertently press down as you roll over to the other side, causing you to lose momentum. This could be easily remedied by the developer by either removing that feature, or allowing the player to rebind their keys. However, I don't see that happening, since there are practically no customisation options in the game, having only sound on/off, fullscreen on/off, and vsync on/off.
A solid game that I really love, that could use some improvement.

A short and succint platforming game. Lovely pixel art and that is to be commended on. You are navigating a character that is burly + presumably has muscular legs that can propel him very far, but runs a 15 min mile. He is faster jumping/hopping than running...
Things that may aggravate you 1) having to restart from the very beginning after 3 mustaches are lost. Perhaps at say level 6, a check point, then level 12 another one? 2) Smoother/more reactive wall jumping. The concept of wall jumping is great as it offers more flexibility and variable game play into a platforming game. But when you wall jump in this game, you almost have to button mash to jump off the wall before you slide off the wall (because you slide very fast - gravity!) and into your most likely death. So it becomes less focusing on how to wall jump to a specific location, but more button mash and hope you make it after that. Although, enough gameplay, this should be remedied. 3) No way to replenish a lost mustache. I finished it with only one lost at the last level, but for the less capable gamer, having a way to replenish a lot life due to a learning mistake or mis-jump later on in the game would be nice. Granted, continuously play throughs will get you used to each map and you will be able to finish the game easily in the end.
To note, some of the traps and platforms are seriously hard to see. You really have to pay attention ahead of time or you will end up jumping to a spot and wondering where to go next or recall, "oh I hear a sound, spikes will come up". If that is the intended game difficulty, sure got me a few times in the beginning. However, if the game did not intend to have melding graphics with the background, then this would be a thing to improve upon.
Randomization - I think it is a nice touch to add this in so you aren't playing the same level over and over again as you try to reach the end. It can be debated if it is truly randomization since each level only shuffles through a selected few intended in that level. What does suck is that if you are attempting achievements (say the 3 min achievement), some stages are more time consuming than others, while others can be more difficult to navigate (if you are attempting the unstoppable achievement say). It'll take various tries and maybe some luck to get a good run in for levels that are not as time consuming or the most difficult to navigate.
Overall, a nice game to play as it is a very short game. Simple platforming game with some funny quirks that can be enjoyed by most. IE: one of the later trap is a shaver - a mustache owner's worse nightmare! 7/10.
