Moustache Mountain is an entertaining, quick game that follows the adventures of a gentleman with a sweet moustache and his quest up a mountain for glory and moustache gel while avoiding pits, arrows, spears, spikes, and knives. It's an easy game to pick up and play for just a couple of minutes and while the ride is over quickly, it's fun while it lasts.
The game itself takes place over 15 single-screen levels where the object is simply to get to the right edge of the screen and the aforementioned traps will try to kill the player. The levels ramp up slowly in difficulty and are randomly picked from a pool of 30-40 stages, so even after finishing there is replayability in seeing some of the other levels, as well as a Steam leaderboard that records the fastest times up the mountain.
The graphics are good, clean pixel art that get the job done. Most dangers are obvious, with spear traps being a bit harder to see. After a couple of playthroughs, however, the player will quickly learn where they are anyway. There are whimsical touches like the lives counter having moustaches with the current life adding a little extra wiggle. There are windowed and fullscreen modes, but the window can't be resized and is really quite small. For higher resolution monitors, fullscreen is the only way to go. A scaling window is the one feature I felt was lacking here.
The sounds get the job done without frills (it's a budget indie game after all, frills are extra). What music there is is fine, but there's only one track so be ready with your own playlist if you'll be playing for any significant length of time. The controls are solid and responsive, critical in a game where the only moves are jumping and wall-jumping.
In short, the game does what it does well and delivers a fun distraction for a few minutes without promising any more. It's challenging, it's enjoyable, it provides some replayability and doesn't overstay its welcome. Moustache Mountain is well worth the price of admission for a little casual gaming.

Cuphead is a fast paced classic arcade style game using cartoon aesthetics from the 1930’s. The main draw for this game is obviously the amazing visuals, and the large amount of passion poured into this game from the developers. So, how is the gameplay one may ask? Well the gameplay is a fast paced platforming shoot em up. There are two kinds of levels, the "run and gun" levels, and the boss stages. The "run and gun levels”, while not too unique, has some fun ideas in them, but the main focus and best part of the game are the boss stages. Each boss has their own unique attack, and pattern needed to memorize combining difficulty with fairness. The game is brutal, yet rewarding to the skilled player. This game contains very few "cheap" attacks from bosses, and most mistakes will be from the fault of the player, letting them know how to try and improve for the next retry. A nice detail with this game is that the expert mode is not just fighting the same boss again, but with more health. In expert mode, most bosses go faster, forcing the player to truly master the boss. Some bosses however do have attacks unique to their regular mode counterparts, also creating a unique experience. Even with the numerous amounts of attempts I had to go through, the game remained fun. Overall, Cuphead is an amazing game. Props to the creators for pursuing their passion. The game is definitely worth the price, I highly recommend this game 8.5/10.

Got nearly 30 hours on Evolve so far, and I can safely say I love this game. I find new things to learn about my favorite hunters all the time, and the maps continue to provide neat tricks that I missed on previous playthroughs. The characters are varied enough to fit any playstyle, and each of the hunters in my favored class (medic) have something special to bring to the table, so I play them all regularly.
I also picked up the new hunters, and I'm loving them to death - new mechanics and new personalities make the game feel like the first time I played all over again. There's a ton of replayability and playing with three friends hasn't been this fun since Left 4 Dead.
The game's a bit pricey, and I'm not a fan of that. I wish they had been a bit more competitive with the way they priced the game and the DLC, but it's also a risky venture to break away from the Call of Duty model, so I can forgive the insurance policy. I'd rather pay too much for a good game than pay too little for a game I hate. At least I'm getting something I like out of the deal.

Because it's not fun to play. The biggest reason for that is, that the gameplay is based on trial-and-error.
You go along your merry way, patiently looking at your surroundings, imagining what the little boy is running from and why he can't go back and CLACK - you're dead.
Most of the traps and and puzzles are lethal by design. A lot of times, you just don't have a chance at the first try.
And that's annoying, because it broke the immersion for me. Why not have puzzles that are hard, but less deadly? Why not have scary traps that you can spot if you're paying attention?

I'm doing a positive rating because I give the developer a lot of credit for creating a platformer that made it to Steam, not because it's unique (because there are countless platformers on Steam) but because the games mechanics are responsive and because and the controls feel right. You can pick the game up with no idea what it is and have it down to a science in minutes. I personally feel that sliding down during the wall-jumps is a little hasty and I read another review that said that as well so if that is addressed there is a better chance I'll come back and play some more.
The only REAL flaw, and again this is just my opinion- the 3 lives system is a bit dated. This was a concept created for arcades to determine when it is time for the player to pay to keep playing. These days I feel like the best of the skill based platformers give you unlimited lives. I really think that should be removed. For example, I just played levels 1-12 about 7 times in a row. Now when I go back to play again, I need to re-play those levels again. The first 7 or 8 levels are too easy to really be fun after a few plays.
Besides that, it's a lot of fun. Seems to be in the early release stages and will hopefull receive some re-design in the fast wall sliding and the level system but regardless it was very cheap and now I can play it anytime. It's a funny concept and I like that.
I'll check back and re-play at some point. I hope it's updated by then to reflect the user feedback. I'm not upset that I bought it. I beleive it will only get better.

I have no friends, and am therefore unable to review local co-op mode, but singleplayer was good.

I got this on sale for $1, and I don't regret it.

I completed every other achievement before I got the 50 New Games achievements, and MUCH before the 100 New Games achievement, so I was left to grind those out by repeatedly exiting to the Title Screen and starting a new game, which was actually pretty quick, so it was less painful than it could've been.

Overall, though, definitely worth for a $1 game.

This game is one of the most hilarious point-and-click games I've ever played. It conjures up Ed Wood at his worst (that is, best). As a send-up to to B-movies, I can't find a better game.
And the graphics couldn't be better. By better, I don't mean you'll mistake this game for Crysis. I mean, it's got all the charm of a cheap budget title -- which it is, but with a wink and a nod. All-the-more self-aware.
Regarding the voice acting, it reminds me of Castlevania Symphony of the Night at is worst moments. And so if you're a fan of all the awkward conversations in that game, you'll think this one is a hoot.
The drawbacks are that this game is short and the puzzles easy. Even when you're stuck -- which you won't be often -- the game is more than happy to give you a hint that practically solves the puzzle.
But don't buy this game for the gameplay. But it for the over-the-top plot, and the hilarious satire.

Dungeon of the Endless has a sizable roster of characters for you to unlock, & different escape pods that give you additional benefits & hinderances that could make each playthrough a walk through a gloomy subterranean park, or have you destroyed in the first couple of nightmarish levels.

"Jet Racing Extreme" is a game about you driving around a variety of different themed maps with your rocket powered car that will explode into a 1000 glorious pieces when you hit a wall at 500 KM/H, the sad part is; that's the entire game summed up.

In the game your main goal is to complete the entire course, this is done by driving through a
amount of gates to eventually reach the end. however noone has enough time to live to do this withouth bursting into a thousand pieces; i'll explain why this is in the next paragraph. Eventually you'll just be driving around seeing what happens if you smash into a lamppost, though while this is a very fleshed out feature it doesn't make a racing game great; and i think that that is it's greatest fault.

Roads have a sort of magnetic lock that make you not flail off because of your ridiclous speed. This is alright for a game which just has a straight track to follow at high speeds, the problem here is that it's not that type of game at all. The game has a lots of areas where you can just drive around freely, which makes trying to break away from this road very difficult as it pulls you back like a magnet. I have read a multitude of reviews claiming that the controls are bad, they are not it's just that with this magnet locking it's harder to have a true sense of control over this high-speed death machine. Controls are slow because when you're driving a car at 500 Kilometers an hour; you dont turn very fast.
Normally in a racing game this isn't very important, in one where you'll mostly be smashing into walls; it is. This part is fleshed out very nicely, when i hit a pillar because of the awful driving i can see every single bit of my car fly over the racetrack as my driver smashes head first into a pillar. This was obviously one of the focuses of the developers as this is very fleshed out and well implemented never feeling like things were happening that made me question gravity.
Although this function is well fleshed out, it collides with the other idea of the game which is: follow the track. Why would i follow the track when i can jump off a mountain and see my car getting ripped apart like a pane of glass. This is another casualty of the developers mindset, what is well made ends up not being used to it's full potential because of the games restrictions.
The graphics overal are very decent, when you drive over dirt dust kicks up etc. Reflections are nice and it looked realistic enough for a game about a car with 4 jet engines strapped to the back. Animations for the car were also very nice as i saw that every time i pressed a button on my keyboard the corresponding item on the car showed me why the effects it was having on my car were happening going along with very pretty animations.
Same with the physics, this has obviously received a fair amount of attention by the developer, now this isn't paradoxal do the games core idea however it's resources not spent on driving mechanics; although i do enjoy the graphics i feel as if that is something i dind't need to have fun in this game.
Jet Racing Extreme is a game with a developer putting his time in the parts that are not the most neccesary, this game could've been so much more; perhaps if the developer keeps putting his time into it it can get better which i truly hope it does. And perhaps a namce change as well.

Excellent atmosphere.  Captures the sense of being isolated and vulnerable better than any other sandbox survival games I've played. There is a constant feeling of danger, as a wild predator or sudden blizzard could strike at any moment, especially on the higher difficulties.  The multiple regions give you a variety of environments to explore, and doing so feels very rewarding. (the first time, anyway)
Unfortunately, once you've explored all the regions, the game is just a micromanagement simulator.  Cold, fatigue, water, and calories constantly needing replenished.  The game does get breathless after you've traveled the world and learned the mechanics.  Also I noticed some of the audio files have a distracting white noise in the background, minor detail but detracting nonetheless.
All in all, I got more than my money's worth.  Very solid for early access indie game.

"Whispers" contains nothing more than short murmurs of what could be great, but falls flat.
=====
Let me keep this simple, short, and to the point:
After driving your motorboat through the corn field, you end up at a house where lanterns never burn out, and the only way into a house is with an axe.
What follows is bad English (though not terrible), coupled with a fairly convincing old home, complete with unsettling atmosphere, and an intriguing groundwork for a full bodied (pun-intended) indie horror title.
What it doesn't deliver, however, is anything beyond that.
=====
Do I recommend "Whispers"?
No, sadly not.
Look up some Let's Plays and you'll see why; no point in trying to play it, you'll be inundated with crashes more common than the plague.
The devs tried, but, as I stated, they fell flat in delivering much of what I was expecting...
And now for me to go find something else to talk about~ :)

TL;DR:
is a short but challenging platformer.
In
you play as a jumpy, athletic guy who has a moustache (that sound oddly familiar?) and a simple quest: go onward and reach the top of the mountain. Graphics are indie-minimalistic but fine at that, and the funky 8-bit-like music fits the game like Super to Mario.
Gameplay is simple enough. Each level is just one screen and your job is to reach the right side of it. To do this you may run (with a constant pace as there is no boost), jump, climb and wall-jump all the while avoiding traps. Initially I thought there might be some secret areas or collectables in the hard-to-reach parts of the levels, but alas, it really boils down to reaching the other side of the level.
Controls are slick and work perfectly. You can play with either keyboard or controller (I used the latter). The only shaky thing is the wall-jumping that only seems to work when moving towards the wall at the same time as you jump, which is inconvenient when you have to try and jump to an overhanging ledge but matters little when you just want to climb. In comparison the movement mechanics are almost the same as in e.g.
or
.
While those games are admittedly more difficult (and longer), there's challenge in
. Initial levels are just simple parkour challenges but soon enough the levels become filled with deadly spikes, dart traps and cleavers. You have only three lives and once they are spent, it's game over. At least there are no generic saw blades!
That sounds pretty bad though, right? No one has time for starting over these days. But wait, actually
is really short. With only 15 levels the game can be beaten in under 3 minutes. There's even an achievement for that. And thankfully the hitboxes are quite generous so you know most your deaths will be your own fault. Isn't that conforting?
To counter the eventual repetition,
has a trick to shake things up and keep it fresh: there are more levels than it initially appears. While a single run has only 15 levels of increasing difficulty, the level roster changes between runs and effectively there are something like 50 different levels. All the levels become familiar as dying is easy in any level that you haven't played before. I think this was a neat way to expand the game.
That said, I would have liked to practice specific levels more without having to play through the whole game before randomly running into them. A sort of practice mode would have been a nice addition, although after a few tries even the more difficult levels become beatable.
It's a pity that even with the rotating levels
took me only something like 40 runs to complete (both without dying and under 3 minutes), amounting to about 1.5 hours. Interestingly I can see that the challenge could be too much for some people: the less you've played platformers, the longer effective playtime it offers. You can also compete on the leaderboards for the shortest runs.
By the way: There's a local co-op mode though I didn't try it. However it seems that some of the later levels might be more difficult in co-op because of the reactive traps. Hard to say whether that's a good or a bad thing though it might add some randomness and fun to the soup.

This is a very short horror game with tons of bugs and a nasty habit of crashing on load screens.
You are some guy who is supposed to watch some old man's home. You are given a set of tasks, but these are mostly ignored for the rest of the game, except one instance where you picked up a parcel and nothing happens. The atmosphere is pretty good at first, the lighting is consistently good for most the game and if you don't know what will happen next it can be suspenseful, but that changes about halfway into this about hour long game.
After about 30 minutes of wandering the tiny house you get a gun and everything changes after that. The threat is a bunch of pitch black models with glowy eyes, and that is the only threat. They are all the same. Using your gun you can kill them in about 2-3 shots, so this changes from a horror game to very dark shooter. Everything kinda changes once you know you can fight this mysterious evil force with a basic firearm and it stops being scary whatsoever. There are also several times that the monsters would fail to chase me and just run into a wall, severely breaking the tone. The enemies can kill you in one hit which isn't a challenge, it is just annoying. Every encounter is just seeing their eyes in the dark, firing into them, and if you are unlucky then you die. Several times I died I didn't end up back at the menu, but instead I just floated in place, unable to move, making me pause the game and load my last save manually.
Everytime you die or go through a door you have to sit through a loading screen. As everyone else has pointed out, this game crashes a lot during these loading screens. You pretty much have to hold your breath and hope it doesnt crash. With the enemies damage being so unforgiving, this can be a huge problem.
This game is very short, full of bugs, and the ending just sort of happens suddenly, with no real build-up. It isn't the worst horror game on Steam, it atleast has some original stuff to enjoy, but it still wasn't very fun or scary. This game is definitely not worth $5, if you do get it try to get it at a reduced price.

To be honest I only played
to unlock its achievements. I like the game but I couldn't shake this feeling that most of its programming was based upon tutorials by Sebastian Lague. This is quite notable with the physics, movement, and platform movement functions. Unfortunately the controls and collision systems are the more frustrating parts of this game. Jumping often has to be exact, there is little room for error, but it's quite futile with how "slippery" the controls behave. Hitboxes seem to be too tight, where a single pixel of my body would often cause instant death even though it appears I'd never made contact with the deadly object.
I found that there's a incredible difficulty curve spike once the rotating saws are introduced. I eventually checked the guides and one person mentions using a cheat code to unlock every level, so I did. I still had to play the ending level to get 100% achievements but it wasn't too much trouble, apart from the slippery controls and wonky hitbox when trying to avoid the saw blades.
There's a lot of cool ideas in
, particularly with the anti-gravity and rewinding mechanics, though I feel the full potential of these features weren't met to my satisfaction and should have been explored further. Rather there was too much focus placed on the "open walls" that security cards can fall into, forcing a level restart.
I enjoyed playing
until the difficulty spike but even then I just couldn't see past how much of this game was influenced by Sebastian Lague. If the developer didn't intend for this then it's pretty amazing just how close the game and Sebastian's tutorials are in similarity. I only say this because I've used Sebastian's tutorials to make my own prototype 2D platformer, so I'm very familiar with the movement system implemented here.

Beyond Good & Evil is one of the finest titles released by Ubisoft. Although it sold poorly at launch the game has since developed a sizeable following. Don't be fooled, the game's cartoony visuals belie a plot rife with conspiracy and social and political intrigue. The characters are surprisingly well-written. Jade, the game's protagonist, is notable as much for what she is as what she isn't. Jade is one of the few female leads that isn't overlty sexualized, often a problematic of video game writting. Rather, she is intelligent, strong, compassionate and unpretentious, a true everyman. In terms of gameplay, Beyond Good & Evil is a blend of action, adventure and stealth. What further sets it apart is its incorporation of photography into the plot and gameplay, breaking up the action and moving the plot forward throughout the experience. Certainly, fans of action-adventure games will find something to love about Beyond Good & Evil.

I've tried. Oh, how I've tried. And I've had my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me so, so many times. And yet... I love it.
Imagine FTL, mixed in with Civ 5 and tower defense games. Sound weird? Good. It's a nice blend of the three games that never fails to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off just as much as it makes me love it.
The gameplay is... interesting. It's a good interesting, though. It's a blend of turn-based
real-time strategy, just like pretty much every Endless game. You lead your heroes through a door, fight any monsters that may be in there in a realtime battle, and then they loot the room and handle everything on their own. All you do is move them, open doors with them, and use their abilities for them. Once all the enemies in a given room are dead, the clock is, for all intents and purposes, paused. Research progress and ability cooldowns are all shown in the number of doors until they're finished, and so on. Powering a room with the dust you gather from looting enemies and rooms allows you to make sure nothing spawns in it when you open other doors, and the game goes on from there as you generate science, food, and industry.
If you're looking for a game that will brutalize you without warning (I've had one enemy kill three of my four heroes instantaneously before I even knew what was going on), make you question the sanity of the developers, who named the two difficulties "Easy" and "Too Easy", despite them being anything but, and have fun while doing so, Dungeon of the Endless is definitely for you. Watch a few videos on Youtube if you're skeptical, grab it on a sale if you need to, but don't skip out on this unique and challenging game.

I recommend this game for Various reasons i try to explain below, though it may not be enough information for the average gamer.
A solid Tower Defense/Turn-based strategy mixed with sci-fi and hack-n-slash. Whether solo playing or online multiplayer, "DotE" will give most players a hard time; either by high blood pressure, rage, and/or suicidal thoughts. Theres a few easter eggs you'll catch here and there, and i'll not add any spoilers, but you'll get a chuckle or two from finding them out. Replayability is high (for me atleast). And we cant forget about that futuristic and highly advanced melodic elevator music
I've noticed a few bugs here and there, like heroes getting stuck in the animation for opening doors, which is gamebreaking more or less(if you can risk a hero taking one for the team). Or your tactical map not working, and you have to manually click and drag on the map just to see whats going on. On another note, the servers arent exactly...perfect with connectivity. This game also has its fair share of "THOSE GUYS" who immediately kick you from lobbies without giving you an excuse or even saying hello. It happens ALOT, and its a bit rude and repetitive.
On the plus side, by having Endless Legend and/or Endless space, you will start seeing a few monsters and races from the other Endless titles. Brings back some decent memories, especially the broken lord Hero, and her impressive defense.Theres different Passive and Active abilites for heroes ranging from typical damage and defense boosts, highly resourceful aggro's, and turret/module upgrades. I believe this is the first game i've witnessed take advantage of hero's gaining or losing power due to thier personality and teammates within the same room as them on the dungeon floor.
Both Endless Legend and Endless Space (great games by the way, leaning more toward Endless legend) have modding options and tools except for this installment in the Endless series. Hopefully that will change in a few months time BECUASE i'd like to see more heroes, abilities, and possibly monsters and multiple factions from the other games.
By getting Emporer and Crystal packs from the other titles, it unlocks characters, ships, and artwork, music etc for DotE.
It doesnt take a genious to figure out the uses of Food, Industry, and Science (no excuses for those of you who played the previous titles), although theres a slight exception for Dust as the tutorial deosnt exactly teach you how NOT to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked the first few playthroughs.
Any way, im out. So good luck and add me if you need a companion or opponent in any of the Endless games. I also recommend Endless Legend for those of you who who like hexagonal turn based strategies like "Michael Meyers" Beyond Earth.

I love to support indie developers, and so I pick up a lot of their games.  Moustache Mountain is an example of this, and I tried really hard to like it.  I really did.  But even at a low price, the flaws in this game far outweigh the positives.
Now, let me be fair up front and say that I'm not a big platformer guy.  I know, that spells bias right there, but I can get on board if there are some interesting mechanics.  And that's the problem here -- the mechanics are just boring.  One can argue that this is intended to be an NES-throwback, retro experience, but I more get the feel that the game is being limited by either the developer's experience level or a game builder platform used to create it.  In any case, while the levels are "randomized" (they're not randomly generated, but merely picked at random from a pre-selected set), none of them are very interesting, and you beat the game if you get past level 15.  I found a lot of the challenges to be cheaply frustrating, like having to jump around a ledge/overhang while you're trying to bounce up the wall.  Maybe my lack of platforming prowess is what was holding me back, but I usually had to try 10-12 times to complete this manuever, only to die on some spike once I got past it, and then start over from the beginning of the level again.
The graphics are fairly dull, and the sound loop gets old in a heartbeat.  Rather than practice this game to get good enough to beat it, I decided to move on to another more interesting title in my collection of 600+ (and let's face it, that means there are a lot I haven't played yet, so if a game doesn't get interesting fairly quickly, it's time to switch gears).  I do plan leave it open over night to collect the trading cards, which I can at least use for leverage for other ones I'm trying to collect.  So, kudos to the dev for at least creating achievements and trading cards.  I just wish he'd invested as much time in the graphics, sound, and gameplay of this game.
At least I got this as part of a bundle, so I don't feel like I need to return it or anything.  I'd encourage the dev to keep trying, but to spend a lot more time focusing on concepts and mechanics that will make the game interesting and differentiate it from the hundreds of others available on Steam.  In the meantime, I can't recommend this one.

Project Zomboid is that game I can't stop coming back to. I have dozens and dozens of games on steam but after a while I always start to get an itch to head back to the zombie infested worlds that I've spent hundreds of hours in already. PZ is not messing around and it will mercilessly end your existance. And again. And again. Then eventually you'll get some food, shelter, weapons, etc. and start feeling good about yourself. You might think you've "beaten" the game because there's no way you can die now. Then with no warning your power goes out, the water stops running, and all your food goes rotten. Yup. Such is life in the zombie apocolypse.
Project Zomboid is a hardcore retro-style take on the zombie survival and Minecraft-esque games that have become so popular over the last several years. While there are games that do similar things to PZ, none do them quite as well. This is a hard game and it doesn't pretend to be easy. It demands both focus and patience. You're not going to just pick up a gun and start cleaning out the streets, you're going to be sneaking house to house terrified that you'll get seen and praising the heavens when you find a can of beans.
Easily the best part of this game is the community that's built up around it. There are hundreds of mods available for the game in the workshop that add so much impressive content and whole new areas. The developers have done a great job of both adding their own content and working with the modding community to ensure that the game never gets stale. The multiplayer servers are also great. This is a game that will absolutely consume you if you give it enough of a chance. Pun intended.

watch my review at
story
Musache Mountain takes place in a world where there are flying mountains. Your character who does not appear to have a name so I will call him tommy has a mustache. Tommy has a problem a good mustache needs wax to look its best, but his mustache demands only best and storebought will not get the job done. Tommy hears rumors of an ancient mustache wearing race of monks that created mystical mustache gel. The problem they decided to hide it ontop of flying mountain filled with deadly traps for they knew that facial hair grants you ninja like reflexes and they did not want this gel falling into the hands of non mustacheoed normal people.
presentation
Mustache mountain looks like an old school platformer. The level design is well laid out and changes with each playthrough. While the worlds are not randomly generated there are a number of ones predesigned so it will be random on what levels you get.
Sound
The sound effects are simple, but fitting of the games art direction. Playing with sound on helps as it alerts you of some traps giving you the time to react.
music
The music is a simple loop that fits for the game style, but gets repetative quickly. The problem with the music is you can not turn it off without also turning off the sound and since the sound helps with reacting to traps you are forced to listen to the music. I would sugest if a future update comes out enabling turning off the music seperate from sound.
control
Tommy controls perfectly he is a mustache ninja. You are able to play with both a controller or keyboard. The most important mechanic for a platformer is solid control and the developer nailed it with this game. you move and jump fluidly. Since tommy is a mustache ninja he can wall jump to avoid the hazards.
Difficulty
As you clear levels the difficulty scales up. Expect to die at least a few times on your way to the top of the mountain. The deaths never feel cheep however if you die its because your reaction time failed to be good enough. after three deaths you must shave your mustache and it is back to the beginning of the game while this might seem harsh it is not bad since if done right you will clear the game in under 6 minutes.
ending
Tommy scales 15 random levels dodges spikes pitfalls and razor blades trying to shave off his mustache. He gets to a giant mustached statue in its mouth the prize of perfect mustache gel. Tommy's mustache assends him to the heavens and he now Lords over all..... or the game goes back to the title screen adn you may start again.
bonus content
The only extra gameplay content in mustache mountain is the option to play local co-op with a friend. I had no access to another mustacheod friend so I do not have a verdict on co-op. There are however achievments to try and collect not to mention with the random level selection this is plenty of replay fun.
Final Verdict
This game is fun if you enjoy a good solid platformer in the likes of super meat boy you will most likely enjoy this game. Yes it is insanely short the record for beeting it is just over two minutes, but at a price point of $2 that is perfectly fine. I got this game the night before I did a 10k that I had to be up at 5:30am for I stayed up 40 minutes later then I wanted just saying alright one more time. I am going to be keeping an eye on future games from Nauris AMnatiaks. Mustache mountain gets Jawfins Seal of approval.

Limbo is a great game. Frustrating at times. sure, but very satisfying in the end. Beating it the first time, then the second, and the many practice runs that are mandatory for getting all of the achievements are the best and worst part of it.
Replaying gets tedious if you can't adapt or forget how the traps or general jumps go, but with many wonderful video guides you can go through it. The story's also alright, but you can call me an unsesitive troglodyte for not understanding or being deeply touched by it. I beat it because I could, not because I wanted to, and ended up enjoying it. It being completable 100% is also a big plus, especially with the skill ceiling being decently medium/high, depending on how good your keyboard, reflexes, and memory are.
Also, seeing enemies die in this game is very satisfying for some reason. I would suspect that it's just venting frustration.
The art is gorgeous at times, repulsive at others. Perfect for a glommy forest/factory/ruin that you end up getting through as the game progresses. The soundtrack is nothing special, the game only being randomly touched at times by dramatic or helpful sound and music cues. The helpful ones appear mostly near the end when they're really mandatory for continuing. A good part of this is that you can put whatever music you want while you play it, but it may impact your platforming performance. I personally made many reckless mistakes while playing really loud/fast/hype songs.
TL;DR: Overall, I give Limbo a 7.5/10. Great mechanics and art direction, possibly good story and a bit of a lacking soundtrack, but I enjoyed it. Maybe you'll enjoy it more, dear reader. :3

is a retro platformer consisting of you (a muscular man with a sexiful beard) climbing a mountain defying the laws of gravity in search of a most magical moustache gel.
As you stare at the starting menu you will discover that your mouse is utterly useless; the arrow keys are the way to go. Once your brain adapts to this you will press play and find yourself flung straight into the world of your young moustache enthusiast. The controls are briefly displayed on the screen as you bounce your way through the first level, but it is this brief explanation that produced some of the parts I enjoyed about the game and others I didn't.
In regards to story, this brief explanation was not good, because there isn't a story. If you scroll above this review and read the description of this game you will find some very descriptive words about why good Ol' Moustache Man is climbing this mountain. You don't get any of that in-game, not even a simple cut scene just briefly explaining why you are climbing these damn floating patches of dirt.
In regards to gameplay, this brief explanation made the game more enjoyable. As you progress through the game you learn things for yourself (even though they are rather minor) which made it much more enjoyable. However, I also feel that this lack of explanation was also due to the lack of content in the game. If scroll up again you can come across the list of features in the game, two of which being:
AND
15 levels of increasing difficulty? Yes, but
Judging by the achievements it's possible to finish the game in under 3 minutes so I'm guessing those 15 don't really stand a chance after a few hours of gameplay. But what about the fact that every play through is different thanks to randomisation. Is it different? Is it really that different? Barely, it's just a collection of pre made levels that are randomly chosen each time you start a new game. You will play the same levels numerous times. This begs the question, 'is this game worth $2?' I think $2 may be stretching it. If I had to choose I would say anything ranging from free-$1. I also think that you would see more positive reviews if the game was a F2P title.
Even with these said points, I still rather enjoyed the gameplay. No, it wasn't innovative. No, it didn't have diverse gameplay, what it did have was simplicity, meaning it was simple enough for me to enjoy.
Visually the game looked terrific. The pixel graphics suited the game and were done very well. The pixelated face and body of Moustache Man was not only
provocative, but one of this game's most appealing aspects.
The developer also seems to be working on adding more content such as a co-op mode. What I would like to see apart of the game in the future would be a possible 'Daily Run', more options (e.g. Key rebinding), more game modes and more randomised levels.
✔ Gameplay that lets you learn for yourself
✔ Fun simplistic gameplay
✔ Nice graphics
✔ Developer working on more content
✘ No story
✘ Lack of content
✘ Possibly overpriced

REDACTEM REVIEW
_____________________________________________________________
Redactem has to be one of my personal favorites, Redactem is a puzzle
strategy game where you need to reverse time to figure out how to get
the key and to the exit. There are many insane levels including many
different ways to succeed, or fail. However, I would like to ask about
adding some features like character customization, different perks,
and maybe more achievements? As the game lacks some of those
in my opinion. I honestly love this game and I hope the creators
make more updates. Nice work.

This is a qualified "yes" - if you love HOGs and you're willing to put up with some bugs  and poor game design choices (fewer of those), this is worth playing to watch the story unfold.  Overall, though--most people won't want to waste the time, even though the price is low sometimes on sale.
CONS
Visuals sometimes broken - large white blocks where the background should be. (OTOH, when this happens in a hidden object zone, all you see are the hidden objects so you can select them and get on with the story.) This only happened sometimes - loading error, or something like that. Restarting fixed it.
Occasionally throws you out of an object zone after every click - this is a MAJOR bug; fortunately, restarting the game fixes it.
Annoying red X and zap sound when you click a "wrong" thing. (You get used to it.)
Objects often hidden behind other things; lots of random pointless clicking.
PROS
Story is hilarious... once you stop trying to believe it's serious.
Art is good. Music is nicely matched to the mood, including the over-the-top drama.
Ipkis is the most unique vampire character I've ever seen in a game.
For all I know, this is trying to be the "Plan 9 From Outer Space" of hidden object games, and the bugs were left in as part of the "charm." (Note to devs: They are not charming.) This game deserves an MST3K treatment.
I recommend using hints liberally to avoid frustration; focus on enjoying the story, and if you want all the achievements, go back through and play it without the hints.

A thought provoking mish mash of game genres that comes together in a surprisingly entertaining way.  When the game was described to me I must admit that it sounded contrived as hell...a rogue lite rpg semi-turn based tower defense game is not exactly easy to roll off the tongue.  That said, the game is very much worth the attention it has been getting.
Like any good rogue-like/lite game you will lose quite a bit and it's from your failures that you'll learn how to get closer towards victory.  This game rewards careful planning while demanding your ability to adapt to the continually complicating level designs and enemy types.
Unfortunately (or fortunately) the different systems at play in this game are not elegant in any way, shape, or form so you will have to forgive the game for that and try to learn it anyways.  If you are willing to either research the game mechanics before hand or figure it out as you go you will have no problem with this game.  However, if the thought of playing without complete knowledge as to how the mechanisms unfold bothers you I would suggest you look else where.

I think Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a pretty amazing game! The survival gameplay and procedural generation of the game world make this a hunt to last! In Sir, You Are Being Hunted, you play as a sir or madam who has become stranded on a mysterious island chain after a grizzly teleporter accident. You are tasked with collecting the teleporter pieces to get home. Fighting off starvation is no where near the biggest threat though,
The islands are inhabited by a race of genocidal dapper "gentlebots", as you wander the ruins of what once seemed to be a productive human civilization they will hunt you for sport. ducking through thick brush, dodging the "mantraps" of poachers, the scent hounds of the hunter bots, and the ever present eyes of the hot air balloons searching for even the smallest sign of your location, you will never be safe.
Thats just a small helping of what is to come now that you have become stranded on these strange "robo-isles", not even the ocean is safe here, being constantly patrolled by a giant robo-leviathan. Your only way home is to get all the teleporter pieces, and it sure as heck is not going to be easy!
Thats not all to Sir, You Are Being Hunted though! Now with the addition of multiplayer you can hunt with your friends, or heck, even just hunt your friends! Battle for survival with multiple players on a custom island in multiplayer! It is something I enjoy about Sir a great deal since I started playing. There is near endless variations to loot, robots and islands so there is always more content to play. This is one of the reasons I can wholly recommend Sir, You Are Being Hunted to any survival game fan.

A rugged, tooth-and-nail Top-down survival experience. In it's current build (33.12, I think...) you're pitted againt hordes of zombies - the size of the hordes are up to you, depending on difficulty and gamemode; sandbox or survival. Manage your health, hunger, thirst, sleep and sanity and scavenge for supplies and resources to overcome the savage hordes. The game puts an emphasis on TRUE survival in a zombie apocalypse, meaning that it's seldom very action-packed. In fact, seeking out zombies to fight more than often ends in a slow, painful death from mouth (or a few DOZEN mouths) of broken teeth. Eventually, the electricity and water are going to go, and when that happens, what do you do? Simple; start a farm, collect rainwater, live life by the campfire. Or, build yourself an impregnable fortress of awesome and stockpile your salvaged goods. The game also stresses that all you're doing is delaying your INEVITABLE death. Eventually, something's going to get you, be it thirst, starvation, disease, depression, insanity or the scraping, rotting hands of the dead at your doorstep.
Hope you're ready for hell on earth, because this game is NOT easy.
For a zombie game in an already over-saturated market, this one stands tall among the masses of lame, overpriced, and/or sometimes downright terrible games in the zombie genre.

I was doubtful when I acquired this game through a one-time offer for 4.99$. I'm a fan of shoot'em-ups and specially sci-fi-based ones, but the comments I could read about the game were a mix of ups and downs.
Now having reached 50% of the main campaign, I must say that technically the game's a beast. Gorgeous DX11 graphics, detailed characters and surroundings, awesome effects and explosions, impressive physics engine. The bugs are so detailed they'll scare you at times. I can't raise a single complain in this respect.
However the designers screwd it up in one point: the difficulty level. Even in the highest difficulty level it's ridiculously easy to finish most stages, which combined with the strictly linear structure of the game turn what could be an awesome experience into a routine job. Switching weapons makes no sense due to this, since any weapon will do the job. When things could get a bit tougher you always find an armored battle suit or other mechanized help around. Moving from stage to stage is then a question of time and unless things change a lot in the second part of the game I think you can easily finish it within 20h of gameplay.
This said, I think for 4.99$ it's a good buy. I really enjoy blowing away bugs and cultists at the same rate, tearing stuff apart, and of course the magnet gun. I think I might try to run through the game a second time limiting myself to flesh&bone and using just the magnet gun to make it more of a challenge.

Moustache Mountain is a platforming jump puzzler akin to titles like Super Meatboy, in that it is insanely difficult at times, but also charming and fun. There are multiple variations of every stage that are picked at random for each playthrough. For such a game that is so simple at face value there is a surprising amount to talk about here.
Before I even get into my personal opinions on the game and what lead to moments of anger and despair I have to talk about what this game did objectively correct from a level design standpoint.
Like Arin Hanson said in his Megaman X episode of Sequelitis, there was a time when video games were treated like traditional games. In the sense that you would have no idea what was going on unless someone explained the rules to you. But more importantly he said “[The game’s] biggest strength has always been to teach a player through its level design.” Moustache Mountain does that brilliantly.
Level one is set up, in all of its variations, as a way to teach the player how jumping is going to work in the game. You’re typically not going to die here unless you have absolutely never played a platforming game in your life, in which case, please do not kill me when you invade Earth you alien that is surely going to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the human race after you play this game.
Level two gets a bit more complex and shows you how wall jumping works by throwing in a couple of jumps that are too high for you to reach. Now this is good, but what else is there to learn once you know this? I mean there’s only one button in the game.
Well, in level three you discover that sometimes you’re going to have to slide down walls to jump up, in level four you will learn that death comes in the form of terrifying bloody spikes, in five you’ll learn to slow down and look before you leap and in level six you will learn that these goddamn ledges are the bane of your existence.
Now, I’m not going to go further than level 6 in explaining the more complex level elements that come up, because they are genuinely surprising when they ruin your day. What I will say is, the way the game teaches you the tools you need to advance is ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant.
Now on to some opinions.
Graphically I really enjoy the art style. It’s somewhere inbetween washed out and extremely colourful which is pleasing to the eyes. I also was a fan of the parallax effect of the background. There isn’t a tonne of movement, but there is enough that the game world has some life to it, which is nice. One hang up I do have, despite enjoying the art style, I wish that there was more variety to the game’s visuals. Everything sort of looks the same and if there was more variation I think it would improve the game tenfold.
I cannot imagine playing this game without a controller. It’s a bit of a pixel hunt at times to make certain ledge jumps and analog sticks are pretty much the only way to have a proper reaction time. I also noticed that there was an occasional input lag on the jumps which can be detrimental to time sensitive puzzles.
Overall I really enjoyed this game for its high replayability factor. If it looks like something that would interest you, I recommend you pick it up. Also, the developer is a super nice guy so I have no problem saying you should be supporting him.

Dungeon of the Endless, developed by Amplitude Studios, puts you in the shoes of a group of individuals who are on a spaceship that has decided to crash. It will take teamwork, timing, and a little bit of luck to get through this game. You will have to explore level upon, randomly generated, level, and you will have to find the exit out of each level if you are going to advance.
Graphically I have to say that after playing another one of the studio's titles, I was not all that impressed with but it kind of grew on me. It kind of ended up giving off that 80's B movie feel. Sure the graphics weren't the best, but the action was good, with the waves of enemies coming at you throughout your exploration, and even though it felt dated, it worked. Sure the characters, and items felt a bit 16-bit-ish, but I really liked the look and feel of the levels.
The music in the game also gives you that old-school feel. I feel like they found space age music from my SNES and put it in this game. Now that's not to say that there's anything wrong with it, but it definitely feels like it would be right at home on an older console.
The controls in the game are basically your mouse and a little bit of your keyboard. You are going to need to open doors, trade, add defenses or boosts, and of course you are going to want to make sure your party stays together. All of that can be accomplished with a couple keys on the keyboard, and all of the mouse.
Alright so lets get right into it, this is an interesting way of doing one of those mystery tower type games. You are going to have to go up floor after floor until you reach the top. Now of course there's always going to be obstacles, and there's always going to be enemies of increasing difficulty getting in your way as you try to go up the tower. You will be collecting resources to upgrade your characters, power up rooms, and place deployables that will help you in a couple of ways.
There's definitely a balancing act in this game, and you are definitely going to have to pay close attention to your resources, which are food, science, industry, and dust. Food is used to heal your units as well as level them up. Science is used to upgrade your deployables, which will allow you to collect resources faster, give your characters bonuses, protect the room, or cripple the enemies. Industry is the resource that is used to actually place the deployables. Dust is the magical element that will allow you to power up rooms so that you can utilize the different deployable spots in the room, if there's no power the deployables don't work. Now of course to make things REALLY interesting, depending on how traders are feeling they might require all kinds of resource types to sell their items. So you just need to make sure that you balance all the resources correctly so that you don't find yourself in a hole you can't dig yourself out of.
As you defeat the tower you're going to be able to open up new opportunities to take on, and it will also allow you to start with a larger party. Speaking of parties, always be on the look out for new characters appearing in the game, if you have less than four currently in use you can ask them to join your team for food. Now of course you can boot a character out if you want to, but its probably better to try to unlock the specials revolving around that character (a new picture for the album, a new piece to the story, and of course if you are lucky the ability to choose that character as one of the starting characters next playthrough).
You are going to have to learn a lot about this game through trial and error, and unfortunately you are going to have to basically start from scratch every new game. Research does not transfer between games, neither does levels, and items. So be careful, pray that you get a good roll on the randomness of your tower, and then pace yourself for the long game. This is definitely a game that requires a lot of rinsing and repeating, sure you could experience new stuff all the time, but at the end of the day, what your only mission is, is to find the spot for the crystal to go so that you can advance to the next level. Just be careful, once you pick up that crystal the enemies come out of the woodworks.
So with that being said I think we need to get down to a score for this game, and even though at first I was turned off by the graphics, after doing the rinsing and repeating, and a ton of trial and error to really get into what the game was all about, I found that I couldn't stop coming back to it and trying one more time to see if I could reach the top of the tower. So with that my score for this game is an 8.4 out of 10.
This game is absolutely amazing, truly an underated classic. Get this game now. NOW I SAY!

So I've been looking for a great WW2 shooter for a while, and I came across this. It's a great game in concept, but it was very poorly excuted. This is evidenced by the fact that the devs removed the singleplayer campaign because "they didn't want players making negative judgements about the game based on the singleplayer experience".
The main problems with this game are techical. The graphics are very poor, even on higher settings, for some reason I'm still getting under 30 FPS on even the lowest settings (I have a sorta-decent notebook that can run many other more powerful games at 60 FPS). There's a lot of texture glitches including popping and random major reductions in texture quality (especially on scope reticles). And the worst problem is the rubber-banding. I tried playing on 2 different servers, each with only 30-50 ms of ping, and both had constant rubber banding, making the game almost unplayable.
I wanted to like this game. It had a lot going for it in terms of gameplay, but between the rubber-banding and graphics, it's not an enjoyable experience.
Notes: I purchased this game on sale, I am now requesing a refund.

So I got this game on sale almost a year ago I think and what a game this has turned out to be ...
Red Orchestra 2 is simply put the best simulation of World War II to date. It covers every single aspect of war and its brutality about as perfectly as it possibly could.It's also one of those rare games which enables you to relive the glorious battle for Stalingrad from the perspective of a Wehrmacht soldier which makes this game even more versatile and unique in its own way.
The gameplay itself is rather smooth (though it does have some problems with bugs such as texture flickering,which can be resolved by typing "umbra culling" into the console).
BUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUT I'm not here to jabber in a sofisticated way and write this review the way it should be,so I'm gonna make this short
The game is influenced by many predecessors while also featuring some gameplay mechanics which are relatively rare for an FPS game such as taking cover behind (in)destructible objects (wow so rare) and also taking part in controling a tank and hopefully avoiding 3kg anti tank bombs and mines.
Bots are probably the second most annoying thing you're going to encounter (the most annoying being getting torn to pieces by enemy commander's bombing)
Since bots are very special in this game, they are either gonna stand 5m away from you and wait for you to headshot them OR they're gonna go full commando on you and one tap you with their bolt action rifle while you're in full sprint OR in worst-case scenario they'll sneak up on you and bash your skull with melee attack and splatter your brains out in all directions.
My advice to newcomers (I suppose I still belong to this group) is to be adamant about your goal (which is to git gud)
And oh,btw,get used to getting your head blown off from a farmhouse 250m away...snipers,man :(
You ARE gonna feel like uninstalling and refunding the game within the first few hours but give it a few more battles and you will most likely gonna get used to gameplay (which will require you to dedicate A LOT of patience to be able to lay low till your team finally gathers enough power to attack,if it even happens lol)
All in all this is a fun,exciting,action-filled,brutal depiction of some of the most horrendous battles on the eastern front which I honestly recommend to anyone who is a WW2 fanatic,doesn't have a PC powerful enough to play BF1 or just doesn't want to play futuristic CoD's (and sorry to those who turned up for the Rising Storm review,haven't played it that much,even though roasting japs with flamethrowers was hella fun I must say! :D).

I originally played this years ago on Xbox 360 before I'd been exposed to PC gaming. In those days EB Games was oblivious to how exploitable their return policy was. I'd bought Star Wars: The Force Unleashed, took it home and finished it in two hours. Returned it half hour before the store closed and made a quick uninformed decision on a random game called BioShock. I'd not really heard anything about it and judging by the back cover it seemed like somewhat a first-person horror game.
And over the next 12 eye bleeding hours that ensued, my fragile fourteen year old mind was exposed to themes of Objectivism, altruism, communism, horrific violence at the hands of little girls, superb voice acting and world building that rivals anything you've ever seen or read.
9 or 8 years later, the Remastered editions are released. They are absolute trash. They crash constantly, the audio is messed up, can't change keybindings and aesthetically they're not all that much better. Do not waste your time with the remasters.
The original still looks good. Some .ini file tinkering before making it playable again but I finished it again in two play sessions largely uninterrupted.
Everything narratively holds up. Andrew Ryan, Atlas and Tene are voice acted so brilliantly. The game has hardly any cut scenes, which I wish was a trend BioShock set. Lacking cut scenes may seem like a inconsequential point of praise but having the story build and play out directly as you play, creates an immersion factor hardly achieved by video games period. The themes posited by Ken Levine are almost still as profound as the first time I played it. Even knowing how the story plays out, I found myself evaluating every side to the conflicts and finding common ground with even the worst characters. Not that I find myself affectionate toward Ayn Rand and her philosphy but it's thematically something hardly explored in media at all, let alone a video game.
Mechanically and gameplay wise everything is still serviceable. I will say the gunplay lacks any impact and I feel like some weapons, especially the machine gun are hardly useful before acquiring upgrades. Largely many of the plasmids i found either uninteresting or not really useful. Telekiness seems to work combat wise for a scripted event but outside of that it's not worth much more than to access items outside your reach. Swarm seems completely usless as many enemies seem to continue on unaffected. And many others I found uninteresting or not at all worth swapping out the shock plasmid for.
In terms of the tonics, they seem to provide much more variety and possible ways of playing. Although why you wouldn't go every tonic that makes hacking easier is beyond me. Hacking has no right to be a god damn newspaper puzzle. I guess it's cool they made it more engaging than the typical RPG hacking or lock picking but for gods sake, it can be laborous. Thankfully acquiring auto-hack tools seems to quite easy to come by but the few hacks I had to do manually, I can't imagine doing all of them that way.
In terms of minor grips, having you edit .ini files to remedy mouse acceleration and also the fact the game crashes when some key bindings have been changed? This is surely something could be easily fixed with a patch and yet these are problems that persist into the Remasters (making them even more undesirable). The crosshairs and big gold objective marker make the UI ugly and if I'm correct I believe you can at least turn off the objective marker.
A major gripe, there's an escort section at the end of the game. An escort section on it's own is bad enough. I wish the industry would do away with them but the fact the AI I was escorting became bugged out and would not move on despite me achieving the objectives. I had to let her die and restart. I remember this happening other times played BioShock years ago, having googled the problem it seems to be a random issue that doesn't affect everyone - just my luck, I guess.
A man chooses. A slave obeys.
And when it comes down to buying and playing this game, it's not even a choice at all.
Play BioShock, right now.

I recommend this game but I will start my review with the cons and not the pros.
- InDev for at least 5 years as of writing this review.
I suspect a mayor feature creep being the problem, having read all "Mondoids" (Developer Updates) I've seen some features make it in without being mentioned before while the ones that are promised "soon" are constantly being delayed. While the explanation is always given I can't help but say that The Developer team has a policy of not promising anything with a release date that they failed to keep that on numerous occasions.
A huge pro for me as I hate DRM in all of it's forms, steamworks and having to keep steam client on included, you can play the game without steam client if you so wish. (I bought it before InDev Launched on GOG)
Another huge one for me as I'm a very single player oriented gamer. Probably the only zombie survival game in which Single Player is actually enjoyable. Why that is, later. There is multiplayer of course but I can't say much about it as I didn't play it.
The game is extremely modable with plenty of great mods that expand the game available already. A huge pro from a gamer like me who likes to mod and play with other mods.
I will say, I am not a fan of preset difficulty modes, the game allows you to customize just about all aspects of your game in it's Sandbox mode, zombie lore included (How the infection spreads, zombie intelligence and whether or not they can run is up to you)
I believe that over the past few builds the game has really became a heaven for those who enjoy survival. All of the options are valid. You can do risky loot runs and live off canned dog food, have a farm, set up traps for small animals or forage for mushrooms and berries. Believe me when I say it, no matter what you like, you'll get it, whether you're an action oriented gamer who likes to bash Z brains in like me or one who prefers to keep in the shadows. Mechanics are there and they work.
A game from an isometric perspective that mixes 2D and 3D. It looks a tad worse than Fallout Tactics to be honest (I love that game) but I have found it's style to be the perfect thing for someone like me. I admit that this is very subjective though. If you like isometric graphics games like Fallout 1,2 or Tactics, you'll like this, if you expect CryEngine type of stuff and can't live without it, consider this a BIG con as I know that not liking graphics can seriously kill the enjoyment.
PZ has recently integrated the FMOD system, the sound quality is good, you can tell where they are coming from and there is plenty of ambient sounds to make the world feel alive. The soundtrack is a masterpiece of zombie genre, I want to buy it now, the guy who composed it really knows his stuff and I believe he designed some of the best music you will hear in a zombie game. Different music will play in-game depending on what is currently happening and it works very well.
Never saw a better one to be honest and that is all I'll say.
The developers provide the community with regular updates* (*read cons) they frequently reply to criticism with well founded arguments and are, in general, very helpful to the community whenether we have any questions.
All In All. I truly recommend this game to all fans of Zombie Survival Genre. ESPECIALLY if you're sick of all the FPS/TPS zombie games. This is something fresh for you despite being older than DayZ itself. It is a game crafted by people who wanted a Zombie game before Zombie games were a thing and it shows.
Note: Everything I mentioned in this review is In the game as of Build 33. I might update it if something big changes and I will update it after release.

Cuphead is a fast paced classic arcade style game using cartoon aesthetics from the 1930’s. The main draw for this game is obviously the amazing visuals, and the large amount of passion poured into this game from the developers. So, how is the gameplay one may ask? Well the gameplay is a fast paced platforming shoot em up. There are two kinds of levels, the "run and gun" levels, and the boss stages. The "run and gun levels”, while not too unique, has some fun ideas in them, but the main focus and best part of the game are the boss stages. Each boss has their own unique attack, and pattern needed to memorize combining difficulty with fairness. The game is brutal, yet rewarding to the skilled player. This game contains very few "cheap" attacks from bosses, and most mistakes will be from the fault of the player, letting them know how to try and improve for the next retry. A nice detail with this game is that the expert mode is not just fighting the same boss again, but with more health. In expert mode, most bosses go faster, forcing the player to truly master the boss. Some bosses however do have attacks unique to their regular mode counterparts, also creating a unique experience. Even with the numerous amounts of attempts I had to go through, the game remained fun. Overall, Cuphead is an amazing game. Props to the creators for pursuing their passion. The game is definitely worth the price, I highly recommend this game 8.5/10.

This game feels like it was made by talented developers following a checklist, with no regard to how the game will be received and whether the end result will be any fun. They were told to make another entry in the Red Faction franchise, so they did, got paid and moved on. I'll skip ahead and say that this game really should not exist, and it's not fun after 3-4 hours in.
The game's campaign is roughly 10 hours long, even on the highest difficulty. Most of the game is spent fighting the same 3-4 enemy types in same-looking caves. The protagonist has a ton of health and regenerates quickly, the enemies are mostly armed with peashooters, and fighting them is about as difficult as playing a cow clicker game. Most of the environment is so generic and forgettable, I couldn't recall most of the game even immediately after I finished it.
The destruction engine the Red Faction series is known for is there, but roughly two thirds of the environment are indestructible. Regardless, wrecking the destructible parts of the environment while enemies are in/on top of it is virtually the only fun aspect in the game.
Literally every level in the game is at least twice as long as it should be, dragging on so much that I had to take breaks to do something else in order to stay awake. You would think that destroying the environment inside a walker mech armed with infinite missiles never gets old, but it does - every single vehicle scene repeats at least twice, involves no challenge and no risk of dying, and consists of mashing mouse1 for 10 or more minutes.
While you can technically have fun in the game if you play it in short bursts and don't treat it seriously, the final 3 levels are disgustingly bad and *will* make you hate it. It feels like THQ told Volition the game should be at least 10 hours long, and they struggled to add enough filler to hit the 10 hour mark.
There is a reason this game sold so poorly that THQ decided to terminate the Red Facton franchise. Good riddance.

I originally played this years ago on Xbox 360 before I'd been exposed to PC gaming. In those days EB Games was oblivious to how exploitable their return policy was. I'd bought Star Wars: The Force Unleashed, took it home and finished it in two hours. Returned it half hour before the store closed and made a quick uninformed decision on a random game called BioShock. I'd not really heard anything about it and judging by the back cover it seemed like somewhat a first-person horror game.
And over the next 12 eye bleeding hours that ensued, my fragile fourteen year old mind was exposed to themes of Objectivism, altruism, communism, horrific violence at the hands of little girls, superb voice acting and world building that rivals anything you've ever seen or read.
9 or 8 years later, the Remastered editions are released. They are absolute trash. They crash constantly, the audio is messed up, can't change keybindings and aesthetically they're not all that much better. Do not waste your time with the remasters.
The original still looks good. Some .ini file tinkering before making it playable again but I finished it again in two play sessions largely uninterrupted.
Everything narratively holds up. Andrew Ryan, Atlas and Tene are voice acted so brilliantly. The game has hardly any cut scenes, which I wish was a trend BioShock set. Lacking cut scenes may seem like a inconsequential point of praise but having the story build and play out directly as you play, creates an immersion factor hardly achieved by video games period. The themes posited by Ken Levine are almost still as profound as the first time I played it. Even knowing how the story plays out, I found myself evaluating every side to the conflicts and finding common ground with even the worst characters. Not that I find myself affectionate toward Ayn Rand and her philosphy but it's thematically something hardly explored in media at all, let alone a video game.
Mechanically and gameplay wise everything is still serviceable. I will say the gunplay lacks any impact and I feel like some weapons, especially the machine gun are hardly useful before acquiring upgrades. Largely many of the plasmids i found either uninteresting or not really useful. Telekiness seems to work combat wise for a scripted event but outside of that it's not worth much more than to access items outside your reach. Swarm seems completely usless as many enemies seem to continue on unaffected. And many others I found uninteresting or not at all worth swapping out the shock plasmid for.
In terms of the tonics, they seem to provide much more variety and possible ways of playing. Although why you wouldn't go every tonic that makes hacking easier is beyond me. Hacking has no right to be a god damn newspaper puzzle. I guess it's cool they made it more engaging than the typical RPG hacking or lock picking but for gods sake, it can be laborous. Thankfully acquiring auto-hack tools seems to quite easy to come by but the few hacks I had to do manually, I can't imagine doing all of them that way.
In terms of minor grips, having you edit .ini files to remedy mouse acceleration and also the fact the game crashes when some key bindings have been changed? This is surely something could be easily fixed with a patch and yet these are problems that persist into the Remasters (making them even more undesirable). The crosshairs and big gold objective marker make the UI ugly and if I'm correct I believe you can at least turn off the objective marker.
A major gripe, there's an escort section at the end of the game. An escort section on it's own is bad enough. I wish the industry would do away with them but the fact the AI I was escorting became bugged out and would not move on despite me achieving the objectives. I had to let her die and restart. I remember this happening other times played BioShock years ago, having googled the problem it seems to be a random issue that doesn't affect everyone - just my luck, I guess.
A man chooses. A slave obeys.
And when it comes down to buying and playing this game, it's not even a choice at all.
Play BioShock, right now.

Amongst a year of many new intellectual properties and well regarded sequels, Bioshock from 2007 whisked you away with its atmospheric gameplay and story telling. Bioshock dodges annoyances such as waiting for dialogues by allowing recordings to play while fighting. In many ways the game delivers a frustration free gameplay experience while maintaining its ability to be a compelling game.
Extra attention to level design and detail makes navigating through your surrounds an engrossing experience. On certain settings, the lack of a strategic AI combat and not restarting at the beginning of levels on death can chip away at the more hardcore mindsets of some players. Toying with your godlike powers overshadows what some might consider average gun play. The story telling allows for great retrospective of your previous gameplay making this a memorable shooter for years to come.

I continue to brag about this game to my friend, 'have you tried Rising Storm?' and often I get blank looks like 'what is that game?". Despite their stares of disbelief, this is a solid game that continues to get better with each release. Red Orchestra 2, a dependable WWII game won't blow your socks off, but it is a good proving ground, and Rising Storm the next release certainly has better graphics as one would expect, although it isn't triple A quality graphically. Still, while the settings help, it's the following that helps it stand out from all other games on par with the Battlefield series.
Why are Rising Storm and Red Orchestra series better than COD games?
First is the game mode, King's Push where your team is either defending or attacking, winning objectives that push the enemy back to new maps, therefore the battlefield is constantly changing.
Second, while you play as an individual, it is only with team work that your side succeeds, thus is is a well balanced game. Spawn on the squad, or command it, or command the entire team, the options are impressive but not overwhelming.
Third, it is easy to use but is robust in the type of things you can do, like laying down traps, claymores or whatever.
Fourth, you can man a mortar, flame thrower or do other specialty things that keep is interesting and fun.
Fifth, it gives you the feeling of fighting another team and not that swiss cheese run and gun of COD maps... you really feel like you're part of an army pushing against an entrenched enemy.

I have found a save game editor wich allows you to change just about all aspects of the game. I have opted for giving myself infinite inventory. This works much better for the exploration. Finally, a survival game that doesn't require multiplayer presence to be extremely challenging.
It took me about seven times to find a difficult setting that allowed me to survive past the first three days, the cold weather has never been presented as harshly as this in videogame history. Something simple as making a fire can be a difficult task and stumpling through a frozen landscape in a unknown territory really imposes a sense of desperation as you watch your condition go lower and lower while you hopelessly try to spot a shelter before you freeze to death, just like walking home after the bar's closing time in winter.
The variables that introduces interesting unknown challenges are well done, the shelters are randomized; what once was a cozy house in other campaign is a ruin in the next one. Items change place from campaign to campaign and the weather is unpredictable as the bouncer's criterias for entry. Wildlife presents a stable source of food and materials along with the dangers. An encounter with a wolf is a survivable risk, a bear spotted in the distance is an area-denial threat similiar to those gypsy gangs in Rajakylä. Up until you find the bolt-action rifle, that is.
There are iffy things that'll bother you however, for those familiar with Half Life 2's source engine, "surfing" on a near-vertical surface is possible, the developers have tried to rectify this exploit by enabling the fauna to scale up these surfaces up until they are blocked by a map object. The hands aren't rendered when holding the rifle. The conditions that dictate when you sprain your ankles and wrists are a mystery, but it seems to happen whenever you move around on a slope. You can't jump. The textures on the map, especially in tunnels, sometimes vary wildly, contrasting each other and standing out like a black man in a supermarket. The wildlife lacks animations for turning around and generally lack inertia, hunting animals with a bow has it's challenges when your prey does a solid 180-turn in full speed in a fraction of a second. The animals detect you automatically in certain distance and lastly, the rendering engine casts a "glow" around all objects that stands out in mist or foggy weather.
All in all, for an Alpha-stage game, these things would be forgivable even from a full game, for the gameplay itself is solid. The artstyle-, even with it's difficulties figuring out how to make assets blend in with the others, -is splendid for the harsh winter setting of the game. The only major problem this game has is a very common problem with all other survival games; No definite end goal. You survive, master your envirovement and eventually all difficulties and threats become trivial to you. You do everything there is to do until there's nothing left except boredom.
The developers have promised story modes that rectify this long-term goal, these were supposed to be released by december but unfortunaly have been delayed several times.
Little polishing here and there, a bit more content and things to do (especially that story mode), and this'll be an excellent game. For all those survival-genre players, this game is a recommended purhace even in it's alpha stage.
