It's overhyped. I'd give it a 'meh' if steam allowed. Don't get it for the full price, as it's not worth the money nowadays - there are better experiences you can get for $10.
Issues with the game:
- everything is dark, to an annoying level. Dark is the cheapest way of making atmospheric games with no atmosphere and it rarely works. While the early levels are readable enough, some choices in the later game hurt your ability to know what's going on.
- It's basically a kaizo troll level. You're not puzzling too much, mostly the devs just kill you in ways you can't expect. The genre is trial and error. There are some nice puzzles here and there, but you'll spend most of your time dying to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The balance is ok in most places to not be too frustrating.
- While not too frustrating the game just isn't that much fun. I'm sure I won't revisit it.
- The controls are wonky and annoying, yet some puzzles require really precise inputs.
- Less story than in super meatboy. Literally no story. Unless you buy into fan theories. Not a problem for me, but some people want a story.
- everything is slow, yet the devs force you to repeat sections by killing you in ways you can't predict.
There are some good things in it obviously, overall a decent effort. Nothing is seriously broken or stupid (except the secret level). Some nice ideas here and there (particularly liked the brain slug). Experienced no issues playing linux version which is always great. The length of the game (about 3 hours) is spot on, it gets tedious towards the end.
If you're a completionist you're not going to have a great time, as the final challenge is to complete the game with less than 5 deaths. I don't think the game has enough replay value to justify the amount of playtime and memorization this would require.
Overall if you feel you might like it (based on the screenshots) it's worth $2.50. If you haven't played other indie staples like braid, go spend your money there - you'll get much better value.

I have sincerely enjoyed my time playing Evolve.  After logging 60+ hours of game time, I will say this game is a blast to play if you enjoy competitive online gaming.  This is not a standard multiplayer shooter such as a Call of Duty or Halo game.  You won't spend time unlocking new guns, attachments, etc. as you play each game.  The progression system can be grindy at times and, depending on the character you play, can be a bit frustrating.  However, the reward does not come from leveling up perks and abilities, but rather your actual skill with each character you play and how you can work together with your teammates.
I will say that this game is not as enjoyable if you do not have friends to play with.  Playing games in public matches are hit or miss.  Some games will be fun, competitive, and a rush after a victory.  Other games will leave you frustrated because your team failed to communicate with one another.  This game requires communication.  Without it, you will almost always lose.  Because communication is key to a competitive game such as this, Evolve feels immersive and tense.  Occasionally, you'll come across games that last up to 20 minutes, which can feel a bit drawn out and dull, but that is the nature of a multiplayer-only game.  While you can enjoy a solo experience with bots, the game was clearly designed to be played with other people, which is fine.  Playing with bots is a great way to practice with a new character or try our a different role, which include Assault, Support, Medic, and Trapper.
Those that enjoy a single player experience should avoid this title.  It's designed to be played online.  But if you like competitive shooters and want a different experience than what other AAA titles offer, then I would highly recommend Evolve.  Try to get some friends to join you though, or you may have a frustrating time playing in public matches.

Cuphead is without a doubt a gorgeous game - the visual 1930's cartoon style is magnificient. Every frame is a painting, and every character pure eye candy. The art is worth the price alone. But looking past it's raw artistry, there is a love letter to the childhood many shared in games like Megaman, Contra, and Gradius. Both the difficulty and the attack-jump-dodge mechanics of Cuphead takes the best of those arcade games and puts a retro-modern take on them. This game is inspired.
The gameplay is mostly boss fights, with some platform sections and an overworld to navigate it all. Every boss has multiple stages, every stage has it's own patterns to learn and master, and every victory feels like an accomplishment - because for most of us will take many deaths to get it right. Completing the game took me 10 hours and 250 deaths, and getting 100% achievement took another 10 hours. Replayability has been good. Cuphead puts the fun in frustration (it's in there) and this is my current nominee for game of the year.

As a result I missed the tutorial text and as such I didn't know I could reverse gravity, which caused me 2 minutes of consternation trying to figure out what to do on the 1st freakin' level!  A well-made game would put a signpost that the player can read so the user can't miss critical instructions.
Most animations consist of two cruddy frames.  If you die from a missile your character sprite is replaced by a static explosion graphic for a second.  If you hit spinning blades there's a cut-rate sound effect and the blade turns red on the edge... no particle effects, no animation frames on the blade, no animation of your avatar dying, nothing.  Then the level resets.  I feel most games should have a little more animation, some kind of quality/custom sound effect, a "you lose" message of some kind... SOMETHING other than the level abruptly restarting like a light bulb being unplugged/re-plugged.  For a $1 game, fine.  But not at nearly $5 asking price.

of any kind - completely unacceptable at this price point.  This grievance applies to both keyboard and game-pad.
The character control is difficult and frustrating.  Running, jumping, air-control, and wall-jumping all feel completely non-intuitive and I find that I have to consciously focus on basic avatar control instead of playing the game. The controls are non-intuitive and difficult.  On keyboard, the control keys are positioned such that you'll have permanent hand/arm cramps. Beyond Good and Evil (German: Jenseits von Gut und Böse; subtitled "Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future" (German: Vorspiel einer Philosophie der Zukunft)) is a book by the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, first published in 1886.
It takes up and expands on the ideas of his previous work, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, but approached from a more critical, polemical direction.
In Beyond Good and Evil, Nietzsche accuses past philosophers of lacking critical sense and blindly accepting Judeo-Christian premises in their consideration of morality. The work moves into the realm "beyond good and evil" in the sense of leaving behind the traditional morality which Nietzsche subjects to a destructive critique in favour of what he regards as an affirmative approach that fearlessly confronts the perspectival nature of knowledge and the perilous condition of the modern individual.

This game has great aesthetic, I absolutely love the art design, and the game mechanics are unique enough to set itself apart from other tower defence games, however, I feel that the dust mechanic isn't fleshed out enough for this to be an enjoyable game. To progress to the next level of dungeons, you have to open doors, and find the exit of the floor you are on, once you find it you have to get one of your heros to move your crystal (which is at the start of the map) to the exit. Once you pick up the crystal, endless waves of enemies start coming from every unpowered, and unoccupied room. So you better be ready with towers before you pick up that crystal!
This game heavily focuses on efficient resource management. You have four different kind of resources, Industry, Science, Food, and Dust. Industry allows you to build more towers that produce different kinds of resources, and offensive towers to keep the baddies at bay. Science allows you to upgrade towers, and research new ones. Food allows you to upgrade your heros, heal them, and hire new ones. And last but not least, Dust. You need Dust to power rooms in a chain as you progress through the dungeon, it keeps your towers powered, and lights up vacant rooms so that enemies do not spawn there. Unlike the other resources, you do not receive Dust at the end of each turn, it is a rare drop given to you by enemies.   My BIGGEST gripe with this game is the amount of Dust this game gives you. If you do not have enough dust by the time you find the exit, you might as well just restart the game, and skip the long dying process.  Heres an example of what I mean : You find the exit, but you only have enough dust to power rooms to get you half way there. Enemies spawn infinitely in unpowered rooms, and you cant have functioning towers in unpowered rooms. WHAT IN THE HOLY HELL am I supposed to do once I reach the halfway point? I'll tell you what you do, rage quit and start over cause this dungeon run was failed before you even opened the first door. I've made it to the second floor once so far on easy. I'm playing it on "too easy" now, but it feels like the devs are confusing game difficulty with random chance and a not fully realized and fleshed out resource system. Failing constantly on the first stage, on the easiest difficulty setting goes from being fun, to an exercise in futility.
I'll end this review by saying that I know this is in Early Access still, so I shall be watching for updates, and I'll change my review accordingly. In it's current state, I can't recommend this game at full price, it might be worth it on a %50 discount. This game has great potential, and I look forward to seeing it progress and grow.

Online, fps, realistic, authentic shooters base around in the Second World War from the European front to the pacific theatre. Red orchestra 2 and Rising storm are some of the best example of what world war 2 feels like. I like to address this that this game is a full release, don't expect any patches in the future.
[Graphic]
Running on the Unreal engine 3, the game accomplish the look and feels of the world war 2 setting. The animation plays out very smooth, and some of the detail on destructed building, explosion , and suppression effects. The game nail it when it come to graphic, but there is a few bugs and glitches. In some cases, the player can see through walls and under the maps, character model placement on turrets and deployed MG. But these bugs can sometime be very funny, but it can break the illusion that you are going to war.
[Gameplay]
The gameplay can feels so sluggish, and the maps are so cramped in RO2 and some maps like Saipan in Rising storm. This ain't Project Reality or Forgotten hope or even Arma 3. Some maps can be very open, giving you a wide range of tactics and strategy, but most are linier and cramped up which only option of tactics and strategy is to charge to the objective. Rising Storm maps are also like that, especially Iwo Jima, sure the map is huge and very open but if you're playing as an Offensive side then you're gonna have no choice but to charge up the beach and hope that none of the snipers or MG will get to you. But it's very reasonable why it's like that though, in RO2 which took place in the battle of Stalingrad, which involve cqc and house to house combat. It's overhyped. I'd give it a 'meh' if steam allowed. Don't get it for the full price, as it's not worth the money nowadays - there are better experiences you can get for $10.
Issues with the game:
- everything is dark, to an annoying level. Dark is the cheapest way of making atmospheric games with no atmosphere and it rarely works. While the early levels are readable enough, some choices in the later game hurt your ability to know what's going on.
- It's basically a kaizo troll level. You're not puzzling too much, mostly the devs just kill you in ways you can't expect. The genre is trial and error. There are some nice puzzles here and there, but you'll spend most of your time dying to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The balance is ok in most places to not be too frustrating.
- While not too frustrating the game just isn't that much fun. I'm sure I won't revisit it.
- The controls are wonky and annoying, yet some puzzles require really precise inputs.
- Less story than in super meatboy. Literally no story. Unless you buy into fan theories. Not a problem for me, but some people want a story.
- everything is slow, yet the devs force you to repeat sections by killing you in ways you can't predict.
There are some good things in it obviously, overall a decent effort. Nothing is seriously broken or stupid (except the secret level). Some nice ideas here and there (particularly liked the brain slug). Experienced no issues playing linux version which is always great. The length of the game (about 3 hours) is spot on, it gets tedious towards the end.
If you're a completionist you're not going to have a great time, as the final challenge is to complete the game with less than 5 deaths. I don't think the game has enough replay value to justify the amount of playtime and memorization this would require.
Overall if you feel you might like it (based on the screenshots) it's worth $2.50. If you haven't played other indie staples like braid, go spend your money there - you'll get much better value.

Full disclosure: I was given a free copy by the developer for the purpose of review.
General:
Forgotten Lore definitely has potential. The actual gameplay itself is fine, with some cards actually possesing interesting mechanics to them, howeverI do think the $10 price tag is way too high, at least in its current state. It's obvious the game is still in very early access, with limited deck selection, though with the cards you DO collect, for once you can actually TRADE cards in a TRADING card game, so serious kudos for that.
Gameplay:
The actual gameplay is very similar to Hearthstone, however I admit that I very much enjoy the way summoning mana is handled in Forgotten Lore over Blizzard's take on it. Every turn you draw 1 health from your total pool and convert it to mana, and can pool it to spend on bigger creatures, seeing as it doesn't reset at the start of every new turn. Overall you won't find too many new combat mechanics. There's your Hearthstone taunt for example, or a more classic, non-MTG take on poison that instead causes creatures to take ticking damage each turn, etc.
Battling:
This is where the game will have to suffer a bit. At the moment, the playerbase is small. That's not to say there's zero players on, however. As I type right now, there's a few online during the early hours of a Tuesday morning, so that's impressive enough given the early state and price tag. Thankfully, if you can't find other players at the time, there's an AI mode you can play against. The AI, however, is not that intelligent to say the least. Definitely amusing to watch them waste half their health to board clear an empty field, but you won't be getting a challenge with it, outside of practicing the actual game.
Lore:
The game prides itself on its lore, however I can't seem to find too much actually in the game myself. Perhaps a codex is coming later, or something along the lines of that, but most cards just have a line of flavor text. It's a shame really, because there is some definite humor in the card art and a few descriptions.
Art:
Actually fairly nice. There's a bit of style variation between some cards, but overall each piece of art looks nice. At the time of writing, there is a few placeholder artworks on some cards that stand out quite jarringly, but completed cards have a charming look to them.
Final opinion:
The game's fun, but nothing special in its current state. If you can pick it up cheap, and have someone you can play with on demand, by all means give it a shot, but I wouldn't recommend it outside of those circumstances until it becomes more lively, and gains more cards. I'll be keeping an eye on it and coming back occasionally.

A very bare bones game, an interesting concept nonetheless but fundamentally broken at a gameplay level.
The biggest and most blatant issue is the core game design, it essentially plays similarly to Hearthstone except with a slower pace - that would be welcomed greatly if it wasn't somewhat damaged by its extreme lack of balance nor synergy.
The game appears to have been created with no real consideration to making an enjoyable card game - rather its a complete mish mash of random card stats almost as if the creator has never really played another tcg - many cards serve no real purpose with questionable downsides and are greatly shadowed by other cards, there is no order nor thematic flow (not to mention the pretty awful flavour), it's quite simply random design.
Many 'softer' elements also make no sense, including such as the deck cap being 64 yet you can play with far less, having 64hp as base health for seemingly no real reason, the tome system which feels like an after thought (and provides no benefit if you use the weaker version) and some of the abilities like sandstorm being broken.
Knocking that aside the rest of the game isn't much to show either, the music is simplistic and annoying stock (which doesn't stay muted and turns itself back on), the UI and graphics are nothing to write home about, the bots are awful and destroy their own cards often and the online has been buggy repeatedly on my end - granted this is early access so all of these may change.
As a positive the idea of making cards tradeable is an interesting idea - my only doubt is how feasible this really would be as to work well you would need a fairly large player base, assuming that is reached it then also opens the door to an almost pay2win scenario for the future
For now, I cannot recommend it until at the very least the basic game design is revamped

Escape this shares the similar concept of Why so Evil. You have to get from point A to B, and if fail, you restart. What’s better in this game is that we start again at the same point, instead of going back to level 1.
It is a puzzle game, and one that doesn’t give quite a thrilling experience. Everything is as you would expect, with the lack of a story or various goals. You’re a cube, and must go from Point A to B. There are options, Menu and help always accessible on the top left of the screen as you play. But I find it superfluous for there to include the highlight that the map was created by Four Winged Studio. All the levels are made by the developers, unless there is a level editor available – which in this case, there is none.
One aspect that I also find repulsing is that all the levels are unlocked and able to play. Players are not required to complete the prior level to play the next, and where they can even jump to the final level if they so please. This, ultimately, defeats the purpose of progress.
The cubism presented in this art is nice, though, and with the black background it makes it easy to the eye. The effects and animations are quite suitable to the ‘casual’ level of gameplay, meaning there is minimal to zilch. The latter goes for the audio too.
Overall, the game doesn’t establish anything unique or interesting for it to be noticed. I wouldn’t even consider this game, among the thousands of available puzzle games on steam, if it had not appeared for free on a giveaway site. It’s an easy game for steam achievements, but that’s about it. That alone, isn’t sufficient to give Escape This a thumbs up, so I would not recommend playing.

is it original? no. everything in this game is derived from other games before it. that isn't a bad thing, though; no more than the evil within and soma have remixed previous ideas. it's a stealth game. it's an adventure game. it's a first-person shooter. it's an inventory management game. it's a silly game. it's a terrifying horror game. it's a tea drinking simulator. but is it unique? is it charming? is it worth the price? yes, yes, and... it depends on how rich you are.
good sound design, good visuals, good theme... my only qualms are the sometimes-wonky procedural land generator (i once had a dock surrounded entirely by land without any connection to the ocean), the horribly unbalanced riders (how the heck do you evade them? can you even?0, and the F***** SEA MONSTER (for example, i'm trying to get in the boat and leave because i'm being chased by sixteen hunters, seventeen dogs, and the landowner, but it decides to pop up in the middle of the dock, literally in the middle of the dock, and insantly kill me). other than the sometimes-infuriating bugs and glitches (and the overly simplistic and somehow simultaneously unfair ai in some cases), i have a lot of fun playing this game.
it's not gonna be for everyone. it's brutal, punishing, unfair, and will make you wish you were dead. it will destroy you for the slightest mistake, error in judgment, or misclick causing you to accidentally destroy your food and make you starve to death. oops. i'd put this on the same level as the ensign or lord of the rings: the third age on hard or metro 2033 redux survival hardcore in terms of difficulty. or i guess dark souls. and the worst part is the procedural generation will screw you over more than the tactics of the enemy hunters (which basically consist of 'shoot each other' or 'only look in one direction' or 'not pay attention to my buddies behind me getting hacked to bits by a starving axe-wielding robophobic british man or lady'). but even with all that, it's a great game because these aren't bugs, they're features. and the difficulty is definitely worth it just for the end credits.
also they added multiplayer, but i haven't played that yet. i'd like to. infinite replayability and all that.

This is a brilliant game, and absolutely worth playing.
I like deep games that can be played casually, and this game itches that spot like it's behind a dog's left ear. It took me maybe as much as 5 minutes to gain an idea of the basics,  and I was off dungeon crawling!
*Every room is randomly generated at start of a round, so it's a different game every time you play.
*You only get '1' life - no reloads or save games here. get it right, or die trying. This may seem harsh, but what it means is that your choices really matter. once you play it, you realise that quickload/save would feel really 'cheap' here, and is more suited to the SP-FPS style of play that you find in Half-Life (actually, I think that games like that could benefit going back to the days where you had 3 lives and game-over)... it would add to the life of the game (you'd get more hours out of it), and would make it a better challenge.
*each floor in the dungeon gets harder. Make sure you are researching your defensives, and your levelling your characters, too.
Graphics:
feel they leave a bit to be desired, for the money spent on the game. also, it can be hard to see whats going on in a room if it's 'full' of monsters.
Sound:
soundtrack is excellent, moody, chillstep, possibley proceedurally generated, too.
Gameplay;
It's interesting, because it's a mix of fast paced RPG and turn based combat. You can open a door at your leisure, giving you time to think and stratagise, or go get a coffee. Once you do, you get a wave of monsters, defeating them allows you to think and plan again, level up your characters, buy/unlock stuff, turn rooms on/off, and position for the next door.
Controls;
Could all be done with the mouse, but KB makes life easier... pause is on the spacebar, for instance.
Oh, I figured out this, too - groups.
shift-click on multiple characters to select them all at once.
then press ctrl+ (5-9 + 0) to make custom groups I used it to split my team into 2x2, and 1+3 () - then pressing the number key later will automatically select all heroes in that group. ()1-4 is bound to individuals, but you can rebind that in-game, too).

If you don't feel like reading the entire things here's the summary:
As with any game, keep in mind that this may not be the right combination of elements for you. I'd say if you enjoy tower defense games, roguelike mechanics, science fiction settings, and a subtle sense of humour, there is a high probability that you will enjoy this one. If you get easily frustrated or like strategy based only on skill, without an element of luck, perhaps this is not the game for you.
Personally, I love this game. It has all the right ingredients for me, and it's quickly become a favourite. I can't praise it enough.
+Solid design and game mechanics.
+Beautiful pixel art.
+Immersive soundtrack and sound effects.
+Great characters and subtle humour.
+Endless replayability. Every game is different, and every combination of heroes and items will make you rethink your approach.
+Good time versatility: you can either pick it up for half an hour or half a day. Though a complete run will require several hours to complete, once you know the game mechanics it's relatively easy to pick up a game partway through.
+Relatively frequent updates. In a time where far too many games get abandoned in Early Access stage, finding developers that actually listen to the players and release updates seems such a rarity!
-I have not tested the multiplayer
(The general consensus seems to be that it still needs some work. Same with some crashing issues. The developers seem to be aware and working on it.)
-Difficulty spike towards the later levels. Even the easiest settings can be very, very challenging. This may make the game feel unbalanced.
-On that same note, bear in mind that you require both skill and luck to win the game.
These points are not a problem for me, I've played old school roguelikes and this one feels pretty forgiving in comparison, but it may not be everyone's cup of tea. A bad combination of items, heroes or rooms, and your late game may become nearly impossible. A good one, and you can win with much less effort (though a certain degree of skill is a must, and you will still be punished quite severely for acting foolishly or carelessly).
I do like that element of luck, and find that any frustration vanishes fairly quickly in the face of the next challenge (a rarity for me these days, as I don't have much free time and seem to have grown old and grumpy when it comes to frustrating games). I  find luck a perk, rather, something that distinguishes this game from other roguelikes, and I think the immersion really helps, in my case.
-Some extra content is unlocked separately
I'm making a note of this because I've seen some nasty comments around. There is a special edition of the game (crystal pack) that unlocks an extra character and ship, but if you want the other extra character and ship you have to buy the special edition of Endless Legend, as well. I believe that the developers plan to later unlock this content, but are giving this option now for early supporters of their games, which I think is a fair strategy. I think this is much preferable to standard DLC, in any case. Your opinion may differ, so I think it is fair to give a warning.

TL;DR: Even though people who bought the game when it cost money won't getting their cash back even though it's now F2P, I'd say that it's still worth revisiting at the very least. And if you've never tried Evolve before and you happen to be curious, go ahead and install it. You won't have to sign up for anything beyond your Steam account, so you have nothing to lose by trying it out. Also, there is currently no business model implemented, so nobody is earning any IRL money from this game, at least as far as I know.
Cons:
-This game had what many believe to be one of the worst launches in video game history, with absurdly expensive cosmetics, overpriced DLC and TWO SEASON PASSES. EVEN IF YOU PURCHASED BOTH OF THEM, YOU WOULDN'T GET ALL THE GAME'S DLC. I bring this up because the game is suddenly Free-to-Play, and I haven't been given an opportunity to refund a cent of the roughly $100 I spent on this game. Instead, I was given an extra helping of Silver Keys, which is the game's new in-game currency. Doesn't quite compensate for the residual pain I feel in my butt from being screwed so hard.
-All player progress from when Evolve was still a paid game has been completely wiped. While I don't exactly care a whole lot about this, I'm pretty darn sure there are plenty of people aggrivated by this.
-Still a lot of balancing issues, even after over a year since it initially launched.
-It is a competitive online multiplayer game with public servers. Thus, you are going to encounter horrible and mean people more often than not.
Pros:
-Game actually has a community again now that it's Free-to-Play.
-I didn't have to sign up for anything when I initially bought it, I didn't have to sign up for anything when it went Free-to-Play (much unlike most other Free-to-Play games). I think it's pretty safe to assume you won't have to either. If that's the case, feel free to try it out for a while. If you like it, keep it. If you don't like it, uninstall it. Simple.
-In the game's current state, there is literally no business plan in place (as far as I know). Nobody is making any real-world currency from this game. Definitely a step up from the absurdly bad business model it used to have. But I'm pretty sure that'll change at some point. I guess we will have to wait and see what happens.
-Simplified hunter gameplay. I'm pretty sure many people would put this on their Cons, but I'm not exactly the type of person who hates on casual gamers. The hunter team used to only be as strong as the weakest link, and this made the game completely and totally unfun for casual players. While the game still certainly has a heavy emphasis on team play when playing as the hunters, the gameplay feels more polished and wholesome as a result, at least in my humble opinion.
-A lot of fat has been trimmed from the $60 version. Like, a LOT. It used to have a bunch of different game modes and a multiplayer campaign, but the game modes felt like they were shoehorned in as a vain attempt to justify the $60 price tag, and the campaign was just... not good. It felt lazily assembled. Many people would probably fight tooth and nail with me about this. But I genuinely think it's in the game's best interest to reduce it to a single gamemode and tweak it like crazy before expanding further.

Now, unfortunately, many people mention that they had some trouble running Bioshock. I'm going to post what worked for me.
I am running a windows 7 64 bit. When I first tried to run bioshock it wouldn't work. I tried a bunch of things, tweaking its launch settings, downloading special patches—whatever, none of it worked. What did work?
First I went to the start menu
>typed in " run programs for older versions of windows" click on the option that pops up.
>when it gives you the list of programs you can run and you can't find bioshock off the bat, click the "not listed" option.
>don't try to type it in, might not show up, instead, click browse. look for bioshock
>when you find Bioshock run it, it will give you the option in which version of windows to run it, click on VIsta, and that should work.
That's what worked for me.  Good luck and enjoy the game.

Overall, I would say that I recommend this game, but absolutely not at its asking price.  For such a basic game it has very few features.  The board only comes in two basic design palattes without any way to customize or make your own colors, has no music that plays in the background (so I recommend muting all sound and playing your own), and only 3 levels of AI to challenge if you don't have another person to play with.  An aspect I noticed that's different between the real game and the video preview on an actual physical version is the size of the board.  In the video it's quite large, but in the actual game it's much smaller, and can make it feel pretty cramped.
One thing that's not included but I think should be is if you destroy all but 1 of the enemy's balls you would automatically win, since that makes them completely unable to do anything offensively.  I do realize that if you're able to do that you should be focusing on destroying the opponent's king instead, but it would be a good feature to include.  Just demonstrates attention to detail.
The reason I do recommend this game, even if it doesn't have many features, is because for those like me who have never heard of this game before, it introduces you to a very interesting game.  The basic concept is simple and straightforward, but it hides a more complex system of strategy and moves that you can work out.  It is reasonable to compare this game to chess and checkers, but one key difference is that every piece can traverse the entire board as long as there isn't something in the way and when you tilt the board the balls have to roll all the way across until they hit something.  Imagine trying to pin down someone's king in chess, but instead of only being able to move one square, they could move their king across the entire board, while your only saving grace is being able to make 3 moves per turn.  Clever folks could pull off some intricate moves and strategies in this game, and that could be fun to watch.
Without someone to play with right now and the bare-bone features I don't really have any drive to play this game further.  If in the future this game was developed further it might hold my interest longer, but seeing how it was released just about 2 years ago and still doesn't have a multiplayer feature like the title screen suggests, I don't expect it to grow more unfortunately. Puzzles, gravitational manipulation, parkour, and guess what... TIME TRAVEL! Redactem is an immensley fun 2D platformer that forces users to think hard to solve problems using a wide array of techniques.
Worlds:
The users are greeted with a very instructive tutorial world that explains to the player how to use the various abilties but don't be fooled into thinking you're ready to take on the game though because Redactem makes you think...hard. So as i stepped into 'Chromium' (the first world) it became apparent straight away how cleverly each level has been designed, not only in a way that it gets harder as you progress but also in a way that it requires more knowledge and experience of each ability and requires you often to use them in quick succession to navigate the various in-game obstacles. After Chromium is a world called 'Scalium'- my in-game nemesis, and offers challenging puzzles that I am ashamed to admit kept me thinknig for probably longer than most people but anhow that only made my victory even more sweet when I finished the game.
Controls:
The controls are very accessible to users and it shouldn't take more than a couple of minutes to get used to precision jumping, unlike some games the controls on redactem are placed closely together so no longer will you have to be quickly looking down to the keyboard to find the 'm' button to use an ability - as you can tell i generally play with controllers which leads me onto the next point - THERE IS CONTROLLER SUPPORT! Its just a nice thnig to see on all games, the statement that sets all consoles players minds at ease, and Redactem really does work great with a controller which is very important when parkour comes into the equation.
Gameplay:
As i stated earlier the worlds have been very cleverly desinged and this really allows the gameplay to become exceptional the worlds work perfectly in conjuction to the movement capabilities of the player for example when they are jumping.
Graphics:
Before I talk directly about the graphics, I must give kudos to the desinger who has done a splendid job creating an environment that is easy on the eyes and doesnt get annoying after the long play sessions i've had with the game (I die...alot). Every object texture goes very well with the world in which it has been placed and this quality only makes the game even better!
Sound:
The soundtrack for Redactem is great it offers the user the kind of tunes that keep them going death after death (many of which i had) and allowed me to continue my journey to the end of the game.
Conclusion:
Redactem is a fun, fun, did i mention fun? 2D Puzzle platformer that I would recommend to anybody who wants to manipulate gravity, solve puzzles, time travel and parkour- which lets be honest is everybody... So go... go buy it, for its incrediblly affordable price!

With 75% of my inventory occupied by bottles and empty guns, but no food or rags, I need to find a source of food. a house to loot, perhaps. I scurry into a forest after the sound of a squadron falls upon my ears; I am in no condition to fight. I wander the forest for a little bit, helplessly watching my vitality droop into the low thirties. I need food, drink, anything.
And fast.
After crawling through the forest for a few minutes, I hear humming. There is a lone robot here. I scope out the immediate area, hoping to set course away from certain doom. Upon laying eyes on the beast, however, I sit in place, carefully calculating where it was traveling.
For it was passing an unlooted shack.
I watch the shack and robot from above, for I was stationed on a hill just out of sight. My vitality is hitting the low teens. This shack was is last shot at life, for any village would be too far to not starve. This is my last chance, and I need to spend it wisely. I note the robot's steady patrol around the shack, and sprint when he rounds the corner away from the door. I do not care if I am seen; I could run after I retrieved any food in the shack, and any other course of action would leave me dead.
A meter or so away, I note that I can no longer hear the robot humming. This was either my lucky day, or my last. I got within a few decimeters of the door, so close to life once more.
Snap
That is all I hear, and all I need to hear. I am dead. The abrupt and loud snap and accompanying crunch can only mean one thing.
I quickly look down to inpect my injured shin, shattered by a perfectly placed bear trap. I quickly try to undo the traps mechanisms, to free myself and run. I am interupted by a loud click above my head, to which I stand up to identify. I am greeted by the barrel of a large gun, and then by a bright light and darkness. I can feel the ground as I land, I feel it welcome me to a long, peaceful slumber. As I fall into eternal sleep, I am greeted with a lullaby, a familiar song that I am unable to name. It was unsettling, however in the way it was sung, or rather, hummed.
And it sounded oddly robotic.

Games can teach us many things. This game, teaches us that if we’re ever marooned on an alien planet after our space-ship crash-lands there, you should definitely go open every door you can find. It might kill you, since there are obviously aliens behind the doors that want to eat you. But if you don’t open doors, you can’t progress. Deep right?
Doors of the Endless is a great game, with a very refined core concept it loops through. You use your rag-tag band of heroes (up to four) to open doors and reveal rooms. If there are bad things in the room, the heros will automatically engage and fight. You can assist by healing them or triggering their special skills, which get better as you level them up. Each time you open a door, you gain resources - making the act of opening a portcullis much like taking a turn in a strategy game. The amount of resources you gain is determined by what generators you’ve built  in the rooms that can support them. There are three: Industry lets you build turrets and more generators, Science lets you research upgrades, while Food lets you heal and level your heroes. As you reveal rooms, you also gain Power which lets you power rooms, toggling them on and off as you see fit. A room without power is dark, turrets built there won’t work, and worse of all: aliens might spawn there the next time you open a door. Once you’ve found the exit, you need to go back to your ship, pick up the power core, and escort it to the exit. Aliens will spawn non-stop until you either escape, or die. If you make it, you go up to a new randomly-generated floor, things get harder, but you might uncover new things like heroes that unlock for the next time you play.
Like Rogue Legacy, Spelunky, Binding of Isaac and other games in this style, the main draw of Dungeon of the Endless is to play the game enough until you discover little tricks and techniques that are reliable. Then using those techniques, you get further in, unlock more content, and push on until you hit your limit (or the random-generator just decides to screw you over with a no-win situation, which is always possible). There’s great fun in using a game as a game, and Dungeon of the Endless has plenty of game with which to play.

Very well made mashup of rogue-like and tower defense.
Minimalist story told mostly through character backgrounds and some between floor dialog when the right combination of characters are in the room together.
Standard difficulty (called "Easy") is fairly difficult for me, easier difficulty (called "Too Easy") is probably a little too easy.
After completing the game once, different modes will be unlocked that add replayability.  For example, an "Armory" where you start with 4 armed characters, but cannot produce any tower defense-style "turrets".  Or an "Infirmary" where you have access to additonal drug items.
Characters are unlocked through play, and while characters don't seem significantly different from others in the same class, they are still unique enough for me to get excited when I encounter a new character in the dungeon.  While no character has an offical class-type to link to other characters, I generally class them as "fighter" "operator" "scout", etc.
The game has a pause function for tactical decisions in single player.  In multiplayer, no pause is available.
Overall, I really recommend it.  It is not often that I play something that feels NEW to me, but this game really does not feel derivative or evolutionary.  It seems like something quite fresh and unique!

I recommend getting it at the sale price, or trying to find free versions of the game.  Why?  It might not be everyone's cup of tea.  I have played 3 easy games so far.  I lost the first and won the other 2.
I'm sure with enough time and study there will be strategies that immerge, but until then, it is a very alien playing field and having ANY IDEA AT ALL of what to do gives a disorienting feeling.
That said, this is certainly deeper than checkers and approaching the depth of chess.  Probably not as deep as Go (but notice, it's in the same league as these very strong games).  The biggest difficulty is that for most moves there are at least 3, maybe 6 or more balls rolling around the board!  So to get my head around that is proving more than I bargained for when I bought the game, and it's challenging to say the least.  The whole board may look very different by the time your opponent finishes his move (which is really 3 moves).
I can imagine getting good at it and getting to the point of predicting opponent's moves, but that seems like a huge stretch.  I'm happy just to find an openning for the current move - not even considering several moves ahead.
But if you're not too worried about whether you'll get hooked, I recommend the game purely for the aesthetic beauty and genius of the game mechanic.  It is a simple mechanism, and beautiful to watch it play itself out, even if it makes me feel stupid in the process.  Hats off to the inventor of the game, and I'm happy to support this sort of ingenuity.

Bottom line (ahem),
is a rare masterpiece of a game: simple, complex, complete and satisfying. If you are a fan of logic/puzzle games, I’d recommend not missing this gem.
1) Minutes to learn, long time to master: LYNE’s gameplay is incredibly simple. You connect a beginning shape to an ending shape by drawing a line through similar shapes. That’s it—that’s the entire game. And yet, once puzzles start increasing in size and complexity, there’s a lot of challenge and a lot of satisfaction to be had from meeting the challenge.
2) Colour and atmosphere: Progressing through level sets allows you to unlock different colour schemes, giving you 12 different palettes to chose from. The soundtrack is player generated: each move made in the puzzle sounds a harmonic chime, while finishing a puzzle rewards you with a sustained note that blends beautifully with the sounds of the next puzzle.
3) It never ends: With 26 level sets containing 25 puzzles each, there are 650 levels for your enjoyment/frustration. Plus there’s an infinite set of random puzzles generated daily, moving up in complexity as the week progresses, to let you get a daily fix of twisted brain (if you’re into that sort of thing).
4) Bletchley Park 2: Buried in the game is a hidden cipher (for the not-so-amateur codebreaker) which reveals parts of itself as you play, and spells out a personal message from the developer. Whether you want to try to crack it yourself, or just read through the Steam discussion thread and marvel at the dedication and cleverness of the community that solved it, it’s a neat touch that makes a great game just a little bit more personal.

Dungeon of the Endless successfully combines aspects of a variety of game genres into something awesomely unique. Its a roguelike dungeon crawler with traditional rpg elements, you control up to four heroes (with many more to choose from and discover). Each hero has its own personality and unique powers that will become more powerful as they gain experience, levels and equipment. As you explore dungeon levels you can build various modules for resource generation, as well as offensive and defensive modules. This is where RTS and Tower Defense elements are quite obvious. Be prepared to defend your modules and power source against increasing waves of monsters. Each door you open could unleash wave(s) of nasty monsters, or you might find equipment, vendors, or even additional heroes to join your party. You will have to strategize risk vs reward as you carefully consider your options. The unique graphics/artwork, awesome atmosphere, and haunting music really add to the overall experience. Be prepared for an unforgiving and difficult experience even on very easy mode, it is necessary to carefully balance resource generation, the strength of your heroes, and appropriate offensive/defensive modules to make it to the 12th floor (and beyond!).

If the video game FTL and the boardgame Descent got together and had babies?  You'd get this game.
Referring to it as a roguelike/tower defense doesn't do it justice.  As an afficionado of turn-based games, I was concerned that this would be too 'realtime' for me.  Not to worry.  The developers refer to it as 'door-based', and only when you open a door does it shift to a quasi-realtime game.  Very similar to FTL when choosing to jump to a new sector.
Also similar to FTL in the sense that you want as much of the primary currency as possible but never ever seem to have enough (scrap in FTL is roughly analagous to dust in DotE).
The player is still subject to the whims of the RNG in terms of dungeon layout, shops, item availability, etc., but never punitively so.  Clever play almost always compensates for any randomness in a given run.
Dungeon levels take about 30-45 minutes of thoughtful play, which is a bonus for those with real-life time constraints.
If you're a fan of roguelike and turn-based games in general, and enjoyed FTL - I heartily recommend this title.

I don't know whether to recommend or not recommend this game (well if I already posted this then I guess you already know, but at the time I'm making the review I haven't decided yet). The thing is that FNAF (Five Nights At Freddy's) is a game that exploded because of youtube, nothing more and nothing less. I have to confess that I WAS a FNAF fan because of the deep story, but when you put that aside and judge the game for what it is...then we have a problem.
STORY: 2CRAZY2EXPLAIN...Ok no. FNAF's lore is way too convoluted to explain, but the basic jazz is that you're a security guard in a pizzeria that has killer robots...yeah, not the best place to be in. You have to survive 5...6...or 7 nights and at the end you'll get a paycheck...or a goodbye message that means you're fired...THANK GOD.
PRESENTATION: Since this is an indie game we can't expect much from the graphics, but FNAF does a decent job in terms of looks. You're office is basically a stretched out 2D image that looks like a cylinder when viewed up close, this is not the best option when you want you're game to be frightening, however when you're playing you barely notice. The sounds are typical horror game cliches like footsteps, weird noises, ect, but we do get to hear the animatronics everyone in a while. The game does a perfect job with the atmosphere, I can say that much, however it doesn't do as good of a job when trying to maintain it, since all of the tension goes away when you find out that all the animatronics do is just scream at you and that's it, and that only happened to me once in my entire playthrough. You know you didn't do a good job in terms of horror when someone like me (who gets scared even by Minecraft) finds the game more repetitive than scary and speaking of...
GAMEPLAY: In terms of how you play...it's very lackluster. You use the mouse for all of you're actions, to look at the cameras, to shut doors, to use the lights, etc, which is not necessarily a bad thing, I mean, plenty of horror games have even less control and they still manage to be good, but FNAF exploitable AI throws that possibility out the window. There are 4 animatronics to face (5 if you counts Golden Freddy, however that's completely random), Bonnie, Chica, Foxy and Freddy. All of them do specific...explodable things that make the game very easy when you know how to use them, you wanna know how? HERE'S MY GUIDE!
Bonnie always shows up on the left, so all you have to do is turn the lights on and off and shut the door when he is there, do some flash, flash, flash until he is gone then return to the pattern.
Chica is the same as Bonnie, but she goes to the right so you'll have to do the process with that in mind.
Foxy will never leave his place if you look at him even for a split second, so all you have to do is maintain the camera on him and switch it on and off while you're also turning the lights on and off.
Freddy is the most troublesome when he leaves the stage, since he can attack you at any time...but you can avoid this by simply checking on him just as you do with Foxy and he'll never leave his place.
With this in mind, to beat the first 6 nights all you have to do is: Check the light in a pattern of Right, left, right, then check the camera and go to Foxy's, then go to Freddy's, the to Foxy's again, then pull off the camera, left right, left, camera, left right, left right, OU! There's an animatronic, shut the door, camera, left right, left right, is it still there? keep the door shut, camera, left, right, left, he's not there? open the door, left, right, left, camera. Rince and repeat and there you go you've beaten the game in only 1.1 hours like I did. The only night where this doesn't apply on is the 7th night, but I'm not gonna go over that because...holy cheese is that madness.
Though keep in mind that everything you do in the game will drain power, so you have to do this pattern very very quickly. You have a total of 100% power and depending on what you do it will go down faster or slower. Just keep that power until 6am and booya! you win...that's it.
CONCLUSION: Overall I honestly can't recommend this game. It is very easy when you know what to do and it's not very replayable. I got my copy with 50% off and honestly I believe you should too. It's not really worth it even at the price it currently is...however for Halloween this can be a fun distraction.

Man, I really want to like this game, I seriously do . . .
So this game comes from the same people that brought us "Inside", which was a brilliant, near flawless game.  Limbo, of course, came first and feels in a lot of ways like a proto-Inside.
The game mechanics are pretty much the same:  a cinematic, artistically styled, side-scrolling adventure platformer.  The visuals are completely stunning and impressive, very immersive.  The controls are tight.  So far, so good, yes?
Well, here comes the bad news:  You may as well call this "A Ton of Cheap Deaths The Game".  Don't get me wrong, you'll die alot in the game Inside, but it always feels like you just should of been a little more patient/observant.  Like there was something you could have done about it.  Limbo, however, seems to be okay with killing you on the spot without any real warning . . . over and over and over again.
Like I said before, I really want to like this game, but I keep finding myself comparing it to Inside, which is pretty much the exact same kind of game, but waaaaay more polished.  But hey, if you have time for a game that is visually stunning with pretty darn good controls, but has absolutely no reservations on kicking you in the nuts when you're not looking, pick this one up.  If you want the same kind of game, but one that feels challenging without feeling cheap, pick up Inside.  (Which means, skip this one and go pick up Inside . . . seriously, go get it.)

This isn't so much of a review as much as it is a first impression... But I'm not impressed. Sir/Madam, You Are Being Hunted promises that each playthrough is unique, but in my experience not a single playthrough has been unique. You might be looking at the screenshots and saying to yourself 'Hey those robots look pretty good!' and you're right - but nothing else does. I sure hope you like the colors brown and grey, because that's the entire color palate. There are different seeds available, but within 10 minutes you've seen every house or castle or whatever on any given island because there simply aren't enough assets. 'But hey,' you might start, 'this is supposed to be drab and dreaery just like real England!' Aside from being a lame excuse to justify a bad art direction, perhaps that's why no one else makes games set in such boring locals.
Even if you try to ignore the graphics in favor of gameplay, you get a pretty unrewarding stealth game. For starters, the visibility gauge seems arbitrary. I swear I was about 10 meters away from a robot with two pips on the visibility gauge and I got by no problem. Same exact condition 5 minutes later? Instantly spotted. This is only compounded when robots are alerted and you find out they're psychic. And did I mention the combat sucks? You don't start off with any weapons and when you get lucky enough to find one, it feels awful. 'But it's a stealth game!' some fool is going to say. True, it is, but classics like Thief and Deus Ex gave you a bunch of different options to avoid combat that all felt refined AND both games start you off with a weapon that's useful, if only occasionally. If you fire a gun in Sir/Madam, you've already lost, and if you find a hatchet you've already won. It all comes down to RNG, which oddly enough, doesn't mind giving you loads of consumables making the survival aspect a formality.
Eventually you get to experience the horrible checkpoint system. You can save whenever you return one of the stone pieces to the altar and when you go between islands. That's it. Be prepared to run upwards of five minutes just to get back where you died so you can restart again. Did I say run? I meant crawl, because running makes you visible from miles around. Realistic, but not even slightly fun. And with movement comes the weird camera bob/lean. Whenever you move with the keyboard, your character leans in that direction like he just pounded down a six pack. I've never had problems with motion sickness in video games before, but this one makes my head throb.
Multiplayer is the same thing but minus the mechanics. Everyone runs around like it's team death match in unreal tournament and eventually wins through sheer luck. And if you die? Hey no problem just respawn and you don't lose any progress!
I've been looking forward to play this game since it entered Early Access but resisted the temptation. I recently got it as part of a Humble Bundle and I still feel ripped off.

To start, I greatly enjoyed the previous game Guerilla playing it twice through.
Going into this game I expected a similiar fun experience with being able to demolish entire cities. That was my mistake. While I found this game extremely fun in itself, any fan or person thinking this is like the old ones, just hold the phone there and read what I have to say.
Red Faction: Armageddon takes place almost entirely undergound, and unlike the very first Red Faction game, you cannot destroy the tunnel walls. This dispenses an atomosphere of restriction and lack of freedom, which compared to its' predecessors this game is restrictive. There are only a couple city-like places in the begginning that you can demolish and from there, you go undergound where there are just some structures you are allowed to destroy. Any old fan will be dissapointed. On top of that, the developers brought in a whole new aspect of aliens that you are fighting to save your existence. Personally, this doesn't bother me, but others may find this a turn off.
Having said that, looking at this game as if it was its own series, it would be very fun. The destruction/rebuilding engine is still awesome in the limited amount you can use it, and it is just as fun as ever to clear your enemies using with the environment, like caving the roof of a shack in on a horde of aliens charging you. The upgrade system for your weapons and abilities was definitely one of my favorite parts. I felt the upgrades were noticable, which made me feel accomplished when I could afford them. They greatly change gamplay, making each players fighting style a bit different depending on how they go about upgrading.
To wrap this up short and sweet:
--Pros--
The game is fun, featuring a moderately decent story. The mayham and methods of killing are where this game shines, allowing you to use your environment in fun and destructive ways, then rebuilding it (with the nano forge) and starting all over for the next wave of enemies, who you are already devising cunning new ways to splatter and break
--cons --
I would not even bother comparing this to the old series, and many fans will be dissapointed if they buy this.
IMPORTANT: This game does not allow for the free-roam that guerilla did, this was where most of my dissapoinment stems from.

First impression.
This is what happens when you take something that is good and try to make it mainstream. Red Faction Guerilla was one of my favorite open world sandbox "GTA style" game, and that's saying alot, since there's only a handful of those games I find most of them boring and repetitive. Admittedly, even I was eventually bored by the RFG singleplayer over time simply because that genre does that to me. What Armageddon does is basically take all the good parts of RFG, but turn it into a bog standard, linear corridor third person shooter. Remeber destroying damn near every object to gather salvage? Don't bother with that here, as salvage is only found via pickups and exploding barrels, essentially discouraging environmental destruction because you need it for cover (and using the repair mechanic, while pretty nifty, seems a tad inefficient when it's destroyed as soon as you rebuild it) and encouraging the typical "blow up the red barrels" trope that has existed since Doom.
Some how, Red Faction: Armageddo makes environmental destruction boring. How can that be possible? The sound assets feel lifeless - you don't hear buildings creaking as much when you destroyed most of its support, guns don't have any "oomph" to their sound feedback, destruction, especially with weapons that disintegrate objects is so quick that they feel more like magical or technical teleportation spells than actual explosions and deconstruction. Despite the quality of the game assets, the game just has no character, even down to the typical  "soldier needs to save the day plot". I messed around with the Free Mode, which gave me access to what I assume is end game weaponry, and even those weapons, such as the Plasma Beam, Rocket Launcher, and SINGULARITY CANNON had barely mild entertainment value at best - the gunplay is absolutely boring and is puzzling, as it was so good in RFG that I loved playing the multiplayer for the gunplay (I actually used the guns more than the Sledgehammer or backpacks, which brings me to another point that there aren't any backpacks!). Even the assault rifle feels weak, damn near useless, and not competent with head shots (my bullets always miss the dot on the crosshair, and it still takes like 5 headshots to kill a standard grunt)
There's a multiplayer horde mode that looks ok, but practically nobody is playing this game any more and there's plenty of co-op shooters to play on PC. Thankfully, I got this through a bundle so I think I only technically paid less than $1 for this. I can't honestly recommend this, unless you played all the other good 3rd person shooters to death and just want something else to play, or you like run-of-the mill modern, third person shooters and would like to play one with a slightly interesting destruction/repait mechanic. Everybody else should not bother.

Wow. I wish I had an option somewhere between yes and no. This is fun, but ultimately it is almost entirely ruled by a random number generator. I had a good time figuring out the mechanics, but after the fifth dungeon where I was only offered terrible upgrades (a mixture of hero oriented and tower oriented upgrades which did not play well together) and received almost no dust for opening doors in a highly branched and un-linear environement (thus being unable to reduce mob spawns or place defence effectively) I got pretty frustrated. I suppose that's the nature of "rogue-likes", but even Angband would allow you to regenerate a level if you got dealt total crap (assuming you could find an up staircase). In this game, if you get dealt awful it will follow you until you die (probably somewhere around level 6 or 7). It's the biggest failling of this game. Sometimes (frequently?) you will be handed a pile of steaming crap. In other rogue type games, part of the skillset is being able to recognize this and bailing appropriately. In this game, one bad level will follow you since your resource totals persist over levels, mobs get increasingly harder as you descend, and there is no going back to earlier levels if you had to bail due to terrible RNG. If there had been some option to redo a very unlucky level, I'd give this a yes. As it stands, your only option is to go deeper and there were many, many games where I knew I was done for well before I actually died. If the developers had offered some way to mitigate this, I would give this an unhesitanting thumbs up. Unfortunately, they didn't.

TL;DR: Even though people who bought the game when it cost money won't getting their cash back even though it's now F2P, I'd say that it's still worth revisiting at the very least. And if you've never tried Evolve before and you happen to be curious, go ahead and install it. You won't have to sign up for anything beyond your Steam account, so you have nothing to lose by trying it out. Also, there is currently no business model implemented, so nobody is earning any IRL money from this game, at least as far as I know.
Cons:
-This game had what many believe to be one of the worst launches in video game history, with absurdly expensive cosmetics, overpriced DLC and TWO SEASON PASSES. EVEN IF YOU PURCHASED BOTH OF THEM, YOU WOULDN'T GET ALL THE GAME'S DLC. I bring this up because the game is suddenly Free-to-Play, and I haven't been given an opportunity to refund a cent of the roughly $100 I spent on this game. Instead, I was given an extra helping of Silver Keys, which is the game's new in-game currency. Doesn't quite compensate for the residual pain I feel in my butt from being screwed so hard.
-All player progress from when Evolve was still a paid game has been completely wiped. While I don't exactly care a whole lot about this, I'm pretty darn sure there are plenty of people aggrivated by this.
-Still a lot of balancing issues, even after over a year since it initially launched.
-It is a competitive online multiplayer game with public servers. Thus, you are going to encounter horrible and mean people more often than not.
Pros:
-Game actually has a community again now that it's Free-to-Play.
-I didn't have to sign up for anything when I initially bought it, I didn't have to sign up for anything when it went Free-to-Play (much unlike most other Free-to-Play games). I think it's pretty safe to assume you won't have to either. If that's the case, feel free to try it out for a while. If you like it, keep it. If you don't like it, uninstall it. Simple.
-In the game's current state, there is literally no business plan in place (as far as I know). Nobody is making any real-world currency from this game. Definitely a step up from the absurdly bad business model it used to have. But I'm pretty sure that'll change at some point. I guess we will have to wait and see what happens.
-Simplified hunter gameplay. I'm pretty sure many people would put this on their Cons, but I'm not exactly the type of person who hates on casual gamers. The hunter team used to only be as strong as the weakest link, and this made the game completely and totally unfun for casual players. While the game still certainly has a heavy emphasis on team play when playing as the hunters, the gameplay feels more polished and wholesome as a result, at least in my humble opinion.
-A lot of fat has been trimmed from the $60 version. Like, a LOT. It used to have a bunch of different game modes and a multiplayer campaign, but the game modes felt like they were shoehorned in as a vain attempt to justify the $60 price tag, and the campaign was just... not good. It felt lazily assembled. Many people would probably fight tooth and nail with me about this. But I genuinely think it's in the game's best interest to reduce it to a single gamemode and tweak it like crazy before expanding further.

I've played TLD ever since it was released in Pre-Alpha, and I have to say it's come a long way since then. TL;DR If you're looking for a survival game that's atmospheric and beautiful, yet simutaneously challenging and terrifying, this is the game for you.
Here's the meat:
Devs: In a word:
. The devs send out massive updates year on year, adding more flora, fauna, items, crafts, maps - the list goes on. Owning this game is essentially owning the rights to new content on a semi-regular basis. None of that DLC rubbish. Just pure and honest content. The devs make TLD a worthwhile investment.
Atmospherics: You can tell Hinterland Studio spent a great deal of effort on the quality of their sound effects. Playing TLD with dolby 5.1 surround sound headphones in the dark room is enough to convince me that I've been transported to a frozen post-apocalyptic wasteland. Aside from sound quality, environmental elements like dynamic weather effects (e.g. strong winds actually feel strong as they sway even the largest of trees) adds a layer of immersion most triple A titles often overlook. In fact, TLD hinges on its ability to deliver quality atmospherics and environments. I found myself sitting at the top of a hill just watching the waves crash against the icy coastline against the backdrop of the sunset for about 5 minutes. It was the most zen moment in video game history, I assure you.
Visuals: Don't expect mindblowing post-processing, hyper reflective, overly filtered, mind-numbing graphics from TLD. It simply just isn't that type of game. It represents its own stylised version of reality. It kind of looks like a beautiful watercolour painting, except it's interactive and you get to explore it. It may even turn out to be a master stroke (pun intended) on Hinterland's part to design the game this way - using the Unity engine - as it makes the whole visual representation of the game timeless. In other words, if you play this game in 5 years time it won't look dated in the way some triple As do when it's been a while.
Gameplay: Ah finally, the gameplay. Arguably the most important factor in any video game. I'll get to the good parts in a second, but there are couple niggles I have to contend with first. 1) movement feels a bit clunky and unrefined. And 2) the inventory management system is overly complicated and lacks visual representation. It can make it hard to locate items if you aren't sure what category it belongs in. For instance, instead of just having a list of items on a grid, how about an image of the bag with compartments that clearly designate what kind of item would be found there? It's difficult to imagine fitting a rifle the length of your leg inside a bag. You could show it slung onto a silhouette of the character's body, and when it's not there, have a silhouette of the rifle, indicating that it would be there if you had one. Just a suggestion. Another aspect that bugs me is the lack of hand animations. Given the attention to detail elsewhere in this game, it's a little strange to find that Hinterland overlooked this. For example, you become a handless person who can magically reload a bolt action rifle with your mind. Sensational, but immersion-breaking. Who knows, maybe it'll come in an update.
It's not all bad though. Rummaging though houses and buildings for resources is simple and streamlined, so it doesn't feel like a chore. There are enough props and containers to make sure you aren't opening and closing the same closets and drawers time and again, and the items available for the user to find are worthwhile. I also love the fragility of the player because it doesn't take much to kill or injure yourself. What might look like a relatively small hop down from a rock might end up breaking your ankle. It makes sense, as you're likely carrying ~30kgs on top of your own weight. Even worse, once you die, there are no reverting saves. When you're dead your savegame is automatically deleted, which makes the prospect of death all the more terrifying as you extend your run. But that's the fun of it.
However, my absolute favourite element of this game is its emphasis on exploration. The playable area is huge, with every individual map weaved together via corridors of travel. So if you decide upon say 'Mystery Lake' instead of 'Coastal Highway' as your spawn point, you can always crossover during your run. Each map also offers its own unique level of difficulty, so exploration comes at a cost. But sitting around in a cabin for 40 days will ultimately see you run out of resources in your immediate area, so being nomadic is part of the experience. That doesn't mean you can't be sedentary though - but don't expect to see past 50 days unless you're meticulously resourceful.
Conclusion: It's worth every penny. The sandbox nature of survival means that there's lots of room for replayability. The attention to detail will have you totally immersed, whilst the fragility of your character means every decision you make has to be well planned and well executed if you are to live to see the next day. You won't find another game on the market quite like TLD.

Dungeon of the Endless wears a leather jacket, has a greaser pompadour, and smokes cigarettes in the bathroom. Old Man Tower Defense catches him.
"You can't smoke in here," says Old Man Tower Defense. Dungeon of the Endless puts out his cigarette on the old man's face and steals his style.
"Get lost," says Dungeon of the Endless, and Old Man Tower Defense shuffles back to his room at the old genres' home.
4X Strategy Nerd is walking down the hall as Dungeon of the Endless walks out of the bathroom, smelling like bathroom soap and Camels. DotE shakes him down for his gameplay elements and stuffs him in a locker.
After school, DotE hangs out with his friend Ritchie "Rogue-Like" Valens.
"I wanna put a band together," says DotE.
"Yeah? Watcha thinkin?" says Ritchie.
"I got all these things I stole from people at school," says DotE.
Ritchie looks at these Tower Defense elements and these 4X strategy elements and wonders if it could work. He looks at DotE and sees that look in his face - if he could trick Principal RTS into eating fifteen cans of Spam to get people to believe in base-building and resource management again, he could do this.
"Yeah. Yeah," says Ritchie. "It'll take some thinking, but we could make this work."

You also take a butterfly, a fork, the letter 'A', a globe, a hammer, a statue of a dog, a statue of a cat, a pipe, a vase, a gun, a mask, a glove, a hat, and a cup from the cabinet (John's planning quite a party tonight).  You then find the rest of the receipts and then return to the innkeep.  He then tells you that he lost the keys to the rooms because the wind blew them away or something, and that if you want a room, you have to find all of them.
As you can tell, this game is the master of pacing.

For everyone else, look elsewhere.

Sinister City is a casual hidden object game in which we play as a character that goes by the name of John (quite rare among these parts) and he, for the reason unknown to man, decided to take a trip with his bride-to-be Nina, to a lovely place called Sinister City.
Now you might find yourselves thinking who decided to give this city such an...inviting name, but from what we see of the town throughout the game describes it really well, so kudos to you, unkown peasant, you did well.
So our hero in the making has to find out whatever happened to his fiancee, by doing all kinds of silly stuff for the eccentric townfolk. The game itself is very straightforward and you can't get stuck on a puzzle if you wanted to, thanks to the unlimited hints system.
The puzzles are not at all difficult and won't be a problem to anyone, while the hidden object screens will occasionally annoy you with the low res graphics, but still won't be much of a problem.

With it's endearing art-style and sheer brilliance in level design, Cuphead's nothing short of an amazing game - and the difficulty compliments it so well! Honestly, everything feels impossible at first, but once you knuckle down and get the flow, you'll surprise yourself a few times at how simplistic a stage can be. Each world never fails at introducing whacky boss transformations that make me feel as exuberant as I am terrified!
Despite being initially developed as a platforming, boss-battle, shoot-em-up, there's a few (more traditional) side-scrolling levels that break up the pace. Though they helped make the game feel fuller, they were less impactful and I mostly saw them as coin grabbers to bolster my arsenal. Speaking of which, switching it up helps when you get stumped - extra hearts and 'Smoke Bomb' are both very viable and definitely have their place. Plus, I didn't realise how much 'Charge' melts bosses until I finished the game...
The controls are solid, even when using the default controller layout (which I used), though there were a few instances when I needed to duck and shoot a few bosses, but instead of jumping to avoid an attack, the input registered as drop down instead. This was mostly a minor issue for the very few bosses that actually required this type of maneuvere - it was inconvenient when it did happen to say the least.
Overall, Cuphead is very satisfying to complete and a pleasure to play! PS: Bee taunts and dragons are like, the worst... *shudders*

I don't think I've ever written a review for a game here, but this is a game that more than warrants one. I was born in 1975. Pac-Man was the first video game I ever played. It was a cocktail cabinet in the bar at the racquetball club my Mom attended. After her games, She would give me some quarters to play Pac-Man. It was amazing. The sounds, the graphics, everything. I was in love with the idea of video games.
A few years later my friends and I were full on gaming nuts. Talk on the playground would often be where will graphics go and how much more realistic will they get in the future. One of my predictions was that some day video game graphics will look exactly like cartoons. (That’s what I thought they were striving to be back then) I know there was Dragon’s Lair and the likes, but that’s FMV, so I don’t count that. Cuphead is the first game I’ve seen that looks full on like animation you can play. This is what I dreamed of as a kid, but Cuphead is so much more. Having been born in the mid-seventies I can’t say these graphics were representative of my generation’s nostalgia, but I did see some old Fleischer Studios cartoons on TV fairly often. (particularly Popeye) It had it’s own look and that’s what Cuphead is paying tribute to.
Gameplay wise, Cuphead is throwback to mid-eighties to early nineties platform shooters and air/space shooters. These were some of the hardest games ever made and it felt like a real accomplishment to beat one. Games today are too easy. They are longer, but you never really feel like you accomplished something special when you finish them because if you put in the time and go through the motions you will finish it with little effort. Cuphead is difficult and you will die a lot, but it’s never unfair. You have to learn the fights and try and try again making you earn it. Eventually you will get it down and it feels great every time you beat a boss. That feeling I had as a kid making progress in a game and not being able to wait to get home from school to try and progress further is something I miss and Cuphead delivers by the truck load.
Do I think this is a game everyone is going to like? Maybe not because some people didn’t grow up with games that were hard like this. I could see how this might turn some people off, but if you are around my age and you remember Contra, Lifeforce, etc. then this is a must play. It took me 423 deaths to beat the game, but the game never gets boring. The beautiful graphics and style of each boss keeps you entertained. For me I could only play the game a few hours at a time before I was fatigued and would start making stupid mistakes over and over again slowing my progress. The game requires intense focus so once you start making lots of mistakes, give it a rest and go do something else. You will only make yourself frustrated and that’s not fun.
In the end this is a game I feel everyone should try. This is the core of what having skills in gaming is all about. If Mario Odyssey doesn’t blow me away, this will be my game of the year hands down.
