I couldn't tell for a while whether this game was meant to be hilariously bad, or whether it was just bad.  I finally figured it out about halfway through that it is meant to be hilariously bad -- but it shouldn't have taken me that long to get it.
So, ignore the voice acting and story, both of which are either bad or hilariously bad.  As a hidden object game, it's okay.  It has two modes: easy mode and advanced mode.  I wish there were a middle one.  In easy mode, if you don't find an object or a location within a few seconds, it will sparkle for you.  So you might as well just mindlessly click wherever is sparkling and you could finish the game with absolutely no brain power on your part at all.  But in advanced mode, sometimes locations were finicky to find, so I spent several minutes just clicking randomly around the screen before giving up and switching to "easy" mode just long enough to get the hint, and then switching back.
I enjoy hidden object games as a mental break.  This one took me about 2 hours to finish.  For the price I paid (a few cents, on sale), it was a fine way to spend an evening.  Recommended if you enjoy the genre and don't have high expectations

From Valve, 2k Studios, and Turtlerock Studios. Evolve is a fast paced action, and frantic first person shooter, multiplayer arena that takes place on extra terrestrial planets that hunters deploy on, searching for the lurking beast that bestows upon the inhabitants there. Will the hunters win? Or will the monster thrive and create more prey for it to evolve into something nobody wants? You've got a 4 v 1 in a PvP match, with the hunters, the trapper, highly volatile in terms of keep that monster close for your chance to kill it, the assault, your damage dealer, the medic, keeping the team alive, and of course, the support class, giving some reinforcements to your teammates and dropping that big orbital barrage on the monster, just in case things get too heavy. And of course, last but not least, the monster. With hard hitting claws grabs, and the ability to evolve, will you let the hunters succeed? Having played this game for several hours, I do not recommend this if you're just looking to play a new game to enjoy for a long time to come. It will keep some busy, but this is not a game to be played so immensely. The unlockables don't take so long, and if you're a big fan of multiplayer FPSs, then I totally suggest you checking this out.

These days, although it may be sad, the moment I see something created with the Unity engine, I can already assume it will be a basic bare bone game that will look ugly and (if you are lucky) be almost playable.
So, what is there to say about this? Well, not much, because it's another one of these games that feel like they had been done by students trying to make their first game. And while it is fine for students to do that, it's a bit sad that they would think their game would be good enough to sell on Steam.
The game consists of blocks. Really, that's all there is. Blocks. Your controllable "character" is a block, the turrets shooting at you are blocks, their bullets are blocks, the teleporters are blocks with a bit less opacity to them, the "lava" (or whatever it's supposed to be. Basically a "don't touch this or you die"-substance) is also a block, although in a clssic glowing red and the whole level is build with, you guessed it, more blocks. Wow. It's almost as if the devs were going the "artistic" route in which you are supposed to substitute all these blocks for something different with your fantasy. Except it's just lazy. The devs either didn't want to create 3D models themselves or didn't know how to do it. Either way, it's just unprofessional.
The gameplay itself is just boring, as the levels aren't challenging due to their design but more due to the awful coding.  Hit detection is a mess. There are times in which you can clearly see "hostile" blocks hitting you, yet you won't die, other times they hit you and you die a couple seconds later as if experiencing lag (in a single player game, no less). Other times you die instantly by touching just one pixel of red substance. While you would think that's okay and should be the case, you would disagree if you had played the same level I had in which the path your block had to travel was almost exactly as narrow as the block you were controlling. If you weren't aligning yourself perfectly with the path, and I mean PERFECTLY, you would die and had to replay the entire level again. That's not difficulty, that's just bad level design. Simple as that.
But is there anything positive I can say about this game, aside from it having cards for you to farm? Well, if you are into collecting 100% achievement games, this one might be one for you, as it is so ridiculously easy to get 100%, I even did it on my first try without even going for it. I remember closing the game and seeing that I actually had 100% already. Then I remembered that I had actually gotten a whole lot of achievements during the first level "by accident", simply by playing the game. When I checked the achievements, it became pretty apparent as to why that was. Most of them are on the "breathe to get an achievement"-level. So there you go, easy 100% for you to get in under even 1 minute, if that's what you are looking for, that is.
Other than that? Nothing. There is no reason to ever purchase or play this game. It does nothing well, you will miss nothing by not playing it. In fact, you might actually do yourself a favor by skipping out on this one. Ain't even worth the 0.99€ Steam wants to charge for it. Take that money, go to the nearest supermarket and buy yourself a Soda can. You will get more value out of your money than buying this one. And it's cheaper, too.

Jesus H. Hotline Miami's dorky little brother went to college and read House of Leaves. Endless mode is fun and all but this is like a parody of "indie game" : the apparently innovative mechanic is time manipulation, the presentation is "stylized violence" and the narrative content is unbelievably embarrassing meta-nonsense about [extremely Charlie Brooker voice] how much agency the player really has, yeah?
One enemy type, three ranged weapons, horribly generic level designs with little to no variation or dynamic elements. Everything is memorisation based. The original pitch was attention getting, but when you think about it, it's not something that translates to a very entertaining game (or maybe it could with variation in level design?) and it's as if the designers of SUPERHOT noticed this early on and instead of at least attempting to vary the levels or the visual presentation they decided to blow our minds instead with some super hot speculative fiction straight out form 6th formers notebook in 1995.
Even without the painful narrative elements, the problem with Superhot is that FPS games are fun when they're about quick reactions and learning level layouts, enemy movements, weapon quirks...you let the player pause the game and remove the level variation, you've effectively removed the reaction element and replaced it with a shooting gallery and we're left with little more than a memory test as far as the story (:shudder:) missions go and a corner hugger in endless mode. Maybe it's super nuanced when you start being able to clock up centuries in Endless Mode, but to be honest after five hours of this monotony I'd rather dunk ten more hours in Nuclear Throne.
And twenty quid! Twenty quid! Stone me. Endless mode is worth a fiver. The story mode owes me a drink.

Dungeon of the Endless is unlike any other game. It is a top-down real-time tactical squad-based tower defense RPG roguelike, which does not make any sense as a concept. It is also, somehow, very fun and vey hard and gives all the feelings of reward and tension and loss that a well-designed roguelike game should. On top of that, Amplitude puts an exceptional level of polish and awesome UI design into this and all their other games, more so than almost any AAA or indie titles I've ever seen.
The game plays a lot like FTL on a dungeon layout rather than inside a ship - you command your units to a certain room or door and they'll set about doing whatever task they can, but it's also topped with an equipment, level-up, and skills system that gives layer of individual investment in your heroes similar to 2000-era Infinity Engine RPGs. Within every floor of the dungeon, you're also gathering and investing resources into a sort of base-building system, using build-nodes and a power grid to either auto-generate more resources or to actively help your heroes in defending rooms. It all takes a lot of getting used to, but once you get enough of a grasp on all the systems to work towards understanding them better, they come together in a really satisfying way.
The soundtrack is very FTL as well (perhaps too FTL-like, even), noticeable but not overbearing space-y background tracks that feel fitting for whatever situation you're in. There's a large amount of flavor text across equipment, research, hero dialog, and other things like that, and everything I've seen of it has been generally informative and often surprisingly funny. The humor isn't the overt RPG-parody style of something like Dungeons of Dredmor, but more simple and under-stated in a way that's appropriate to the style and setting.
The one complaint I have so far is that there seems to be no way to move multiple heroes as a unit, at least not that I've found. I very often want 2 or more heroes to stay together or all get into one room ASAP, but my instinct to use click-and-drag style group selection does not work. It's kind of flow-breaking to instead select people one by one and then issue each of them the exact same movement command, and it makes breaching new rooms as a group or falling back to a different position more cumbersome and take a bit longer than it should. A very minor interface gripe in an experience that has otherwise been awesome. (**EDIT: Nevermind most of this paragraph - there is a way to set groups and quick-select those groups. But I still think click-and-drag selection would be the ideal.**)
Bottom-line short-form summary: This game is fun, and I have never played anything like it and maybe never will again. I'm not capable of recommending anything more highly than that.

A psychedelic trip through the vaporwave bible. This is an art project through and through - it's not a good GAME, but I really appreciate what this developer does as an outsider artist. It's a genuine punk rock attitude towards game development - this is not a man concerned with reaching anything more than his super niche audience, and that's okay. I actually enjoyed the experience from beginning to end. There's nothing quite like it - it's like Davey and Goliath if it were a space opera and in the form of a creepypasta romhacked SHMUP on the SNES. There is a great sequence at the end I am surprised isn't more infamous where the developer prays in a very reverent tone for upwards of two to three minutes, then it immediately jump cuts to a crazy-as-hell bullet hell boss battle with a space giraffe over wailing, atonal noise rock. I thought it was ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. If and only if you genuinely enjoy the obscure indie artgame scene (stuff like Crypt Worlds or Cactus Arcade, for instance) I think you'll find this experience memorable and worthwhile.

From Valve, 2k Studios, and Turtlerock Studios. Evolve is a fast paced action, and frantic first person shooter, multiplayer arena that takes place on extra terrestrial planets that hunters deploy on, searching for the lurking beast that bestows upon the inhabitants there. Will the hunters win? Or will the monster thrive and create more prey for it to evolve into something nobody wants? You've got a 4 v 1 in a PvP match, with the hunters, the trapper, highly volatile in terms of keep that monster close for your chance to kill it, the assault, your damage dealer, the medic, keeping the team alive, and of course, the support class, giving some reinforcements to your teammates and dropping that big orbital barrage on the monster, just in case things get too heavy. And of course, last but not least, the monster. With hard hitting claws grabs, and the ability to evolve, will you let the hunters succeed? Having played this game for several hours, I do not recommend this if you're just looking to play a new game to enjoy for a long time to come. It will keep some busy, but this is not a game to be played so immensely. The unlockables don't take so long, and if you're a big fan of multiplayer FPSs, then I totally suggest you checking this out.

I received this game for free and was actually pretty excited to play it, but was phenomenally disappointed.
As I was playing this game, I noticed that the vehicles were next to impossible to control and would fly off the track if you went at even the slightest of turns (you know those bottle rockets you would make as a kid out of old soda bottles that would jet off wildly into the air? It felt like trying to pilot one of those). I thought it might just be an isolated problem that just I was having because I didn't have any upgrades, but as I would upgrade my jet I noticed that it still was completely uncontrollable. I then looked to the Internet to see that it wasn't just my problem, it seems that just how the game was designed. Absolutely horrendous and makes the game near impossible to play.
If having a driving/racing game where you CAN'T EVEN STEER THE VEHICLE wasn't a deal breaker enough:
The maps are very poor, bland and look nearly identical to one another. Notice how all of the in-game screen shots are in the desert. You know why? Because seemingly all of the maps take place in the desert. Which map do you choose: racetrack in the desert 1, racetrack in the desert 2, or racetrack in the desert 3 (this time with a jump)? Boring. The developers put in basic turns and things combined with the occasional jump/bridge and such in a failed attempt to make the tracks interesting, but it doesn't matter because actually trying to use these things will make you crash.
Combine all of that with a horrible soundtrack, bad controls, bizarre interface, near-nonexistent jet customization, mediocre at best graphics and the fact that the developer has seemingly abandoned this project in its Early Access phase and you get a very lackluster experience. I would not recommend that you pick this title up, even on sale. Take it at face value: not even the developer really even seems to care about it. That's saying something.

I love this game (as if my play time isn't a clue there). The style and graphics are rather retro, which might turn some people off, which is unfortunate because once you get into the game you start to realize just how in-depth it is. The world is very customizable, which allows you to play any way you want, from fairly easy to insanely brutal, and each play through varies regardless of your skill level. Sometimes when I play I'll survive only one or two game days, or I might make it six months. Each build they release adds new layers of immersion and new exciting features, and it keeps getting better and better. You can play solo or online, and you can approach the game any way you want. You can scavenge goods in the middle of the city, going full nomad place to place, or commandeer an entire apartment building and spend your days building a fortress and farming for your food. Or you could skip the city entirely and hunker down in the woods, fishing and trapping, wandering and living in a tent, or finding a permanent spot to build a cabin. It's easily one of my absolute favorite games.

This is a difficult game to review. On its own its a "good" that's plenty of fun to play, as long as you forget about Red Faction: Guerilla. For me RFG was a defineing moment in gaming. I would pend hours destroying buildings and repairing them (with a mod). Its open world of Mars was well done and a sequel was something I wanted very badly. Sadly, it never came.
Armageddon is literally the opposite of RFG. Set in tunnels and completely linear. That isn't a bad thing in itself, but following its open world cousin, its just a constant reminder of what was. The major issue with the linear, enclosed nature of the game is that Geo Mod just didn't work as well as it did in an open world setting.
Bottomline, its a linear third-person action game and in that respect its fun. Those who prefer that to an open world game I definitly recommmend this game. If you in anyway wanted a sequel to RFG, Armageddon is still fun, but depressing at the same time. Its not a bad game, just not the game RFG fans (like myself) wanted and it goes to great lengths to remind you of that fact.
I have to be fair and recommend this game, but in truth I am on the fence with it.

[9/10] - When I bought Armageddon, I was hoping for the same open world experience I got from Guerilla. Unfortunately, what I got was a linear story progression that didn't have the same charm as its predecessor. However, that does not at all mean it's a bad game. In fact, I enjoyed the game just as much as, if not more than, the other one.
The combat in Armageddon is fluid and well played. Swinging the hammer to destroy almost every piece of the world and then bringing it back to life by repairing it in an instant allows for total control over the battlefield. There are upgrades such as shockwave which pushes your enemies away, berserk which increases damage output, and creating a defensive shell that reflects bullets. These are all unlocked through progression and can be allocated to the enhancement of your choice,  giving a noticeable and substantial edge in combat. There is also a wide choice of weapons to choose from including dual pistols, machine guns, and a rocket launcher along with its own unique array of weapons like the magnet gun and rail driver. I never felt more powerful in a game bashing enemies as a single-hero-against-all-odds than I have in Armageddon.
There is also a four player co-op mode where you fight waves of enemies or complete objectives (usually defending structures) that can be enjoyable with friends. There are 15 maps total and 30 waves each, leaving plenty of variety and content to satisfy this game mode for a while.
On the downside, the game is a bit short and doesn't offer too much in terms of difficulty, at least for me. Though time has passed, and price has dropped and I would
recommend giving this game a chance. It's a fun and exciting third person shooter that has not received the love it deserves.

Dungeon of the Endless is a hard and unforgiving game. It teaches its gameplay mechanics by making you die a thousand times over. With each run you'll find yourself in a different situation, can't find the elevator exit, not enough dust to power another set of rooms, not enough industry to create much needed modules etc. It's an addictive game. Each playthrough has twelve floors, which get much and much harder with every floor.
A few hundred condemned criminals find themselves shipped on the prison ship "Success". Only for the ship to be shot by a nearby planets defensive system. A few escape pods flew off towards the planet, and crash deep inside an old facility of the Endless. The game has an roster of nineteen heroes, which are all very unique and fun to control. You start with two heroes and you can recruit two other random heroes you find deep inside the dungeon. With the big roster of heroes, you'll easily find a favorite. Each hero is balanced by his/her/its strength, defense, speed and DPS. The heroes are all set in three different factions: Prisoner, Crew or Native. This will also affect your group, heroes can have special conversations in the elevator rides in between the floors and they can have special buffs if heroes from the same factions are present in the room with each other.
Dungeon of the Endless has rouge-lite elements like FTL and The Binding of Isaac, RPG elements with its leveling and skill system, and tower defence elements with the modules that you need to protect yourself with. It's a weird combination of genres, but it works so amazingly fine. As said before, it's an addictive game, you'll die many times because of its hard and unforgiving nature. But sometimes it feels unfair and based around luck. You could've made this floor easily if only you choose the upper path instead of the path to the left. This is what I think every time I die, but that gives it just a little bit more of that addictiveness.
Dungeon of the Endless is a true gem. A game that you see or hear little to nothing about on steam, but deserves so much more attention than that it gets. With a giant roster of great heroes, and a perfect mix of genres that you would've never suspected to even get mixed. The game can sometimes be based around luck a lot, making runs very unfair at times. That being said, Dungeon of the Endless is definitely worth your money. That is if you're up for a big challenge.

This game is one of the few MMOs set in a Chinese environment and is accessible to English players. Arrive in town, and you're greeted by a giant cake, large buildings and a lot of player stalls (oddly, mostly selling mats instead of equipment). There's something special in going outside and beating a variety of cute monsters, especially the meme-worthy Pupus that come in all flavours, in the midst of simple innocent graphics. And the shining beacon of this game, in my opinion, is its uniqueness; many things in this game, even in the short time I've played, weren't really things I've encountered in other MMOs. The design of the UI and keys were outlandish. The almost emphasis on independence when you're dropped off at Eversun City to start leveling up and doing the main quest.
But look past that and you find things that new players can't really ignore. The slowness of movement, although not excruciating and even realistic in a way, is not something regular players of other MMOs will get used to. The only way to remedy it is to learn flying, which not only is an option only for those level 15 or above, but is also stashed behind a 5-man party boss. If you don't have a high level carry you through it, or have enough other new players to beat it with, you'll have to wait until you're level 20-25 to get past that barrier.
Furthermore, skills are generally used from hotkey bars that have no attachment to the keyboard, so you have to click every skill you'd like to use. This would be something to quickly get used to, if not for the fact that the game seems to reset your hotkey bars everytime you log in.
The game's text on Steam's default install is also blurry and botched, and is remedied only when you install MingLIU on your PC and change it in Main/Config/ExecParam (which is also where you can change the resolution to aspect ratios like 16:9). DOMO can feel a bit unplayable if you don't make this manual fix.
In this mix of seemingly minor but annoying features, add the dated graphics for a game purportedly in Beta just a year or two ago, and you get a game that, though charming in both characters and scenery, is not something I'd confidently recommend to just about anybody.
This game belongs in the hands of those who take the time and effort to truly enter a game, and slowly get past all the flaws of the game, like every high-level has done. And this game belongs to those who don't need grandeur graphics, and are here for the plot and to contribute to a community that needs help staying healthy and excited.
Though I claimed myself to be that kind of person, I won't be playing this game too much. I'd rather maintain most of my time working on other MMOs.
That aside... this game does need love. If you're skeptical of my "review", then install and jump in. There's a high chance you'll prove me wrong.

I had spotted a article through Kotaku, about this game. At the time I was looking for a new Roguelike to play, but also wanted a RPG feel. Tower defense didn't even cross my mind, though I enjoyed Defender's Quest quite a bit. Regardless, I spotted the review and snagged the cheaper version of the game.
Ok yeah, I'm hooked and planning to upgrade as soon as I can to show my support:
--Game--
The game is harsh in the beginning. My friend described it having a learning curve, and I agree. There is one. My first run, I got all the way to the 11th floor some how. Even got the Pug, until I found out she was a special case. I was spending hours on the game, and even played til 1am on a work day. (Normally I crash at 11pm lol)
It's not entirely "turn based." There's enough moving parts and thought to the game that I do not feel myself being bored. I love the runs where it turns out the floor works out to my advantage. I adore the floors that work completely against me. I read a description as "The FTL ship crashing into Issac's basement." I snickered at the statement, I think it fits the concept quite well.
I tried playing on the MAC, which has some bugs in concerns of getting the hot keys to work. Like any crossplatform game, there's going to be quirks. It didn't stop me from enjoying the game. If you play on a track pad, do keep in mind to re-assign the Power button just in case.
--Story--
The story seems interesting, and has gotten me interested in the Endless series as a whole. There's a lot left to the imagination about the prisoners, the security staff, and those who were on the planet. I find myself wanting to draw fan art as well.
--Multiplayer--
This is a HUGE hit and miss. Huge hit in terms of, the multiplayer is freaking crazy fun. Just playing with one friend is amazing. There's no pausing in the game, and my friend and we would banter back and forth "Ok you got that tower researched? I'll focus on ____ since I can make it but you can't."
The HUGE drawback, are two points
1.) No save state - I could see where this could cause problems. A drop in game would not work well with a game like this, but due to the 2nd issue, it does make a save state desired. The only solution I can think of is something similiar to how Civ handles their saves and what not. But in this case, make sure it saves the stats, current room set up, heroes, players/IDs involved. I do not know how hard it would be to set this up, but I'm sure the time and money would take some time, or it'd be added in another patch/iteration.
2.) Crashing. Crashing or losing your connection. Ok, more on the lines of crashing. The game is a straight grind, where my friend and I currently spend... 3? 4? hours? (4 hours the first time, 3 or less as we got better with the game) The gist is, when the game/host crashes, when you're loading the 11th floor. It makes you groan. (Granted it was a bad night. He and I then went to XBox to play some Soul Calibur and it red ringed. I stated that my friend has the touch of death at the moment.)
--Conclusion--
Still loved the game. It's a very different game from my experience. It takes elements from many other games and makes something very neat. Hope you enjoy the game as much as I had!

Beyond Good & Evil is a fine game. The story is good, the gameplay is great. It's a free-roam adventure, where you explore a small world and persue the story at your own pace. This game is unpretentiously fun.
Your character is a reporter investigating a grand conspiracy theme. Gameplay centers around Infiltrating government and industrial sites to capture clues and unravel the mystery. There are stealth elements, too, and occasional combat. And a sort of internal achievement system that rewards you for capturing photographs along the way of rare fauna.
BG&E has the best sidekick characters since Grim Fandango, and a similar smart sense of humor.
It's a console port, but the controls are decent, despite this. I finished the game with mouse and keyboard with no difficulty. The graphics are PS2-era, but they have a distinct style of their own. Jade reminds me more than a little of HL2's Alyx.
I understand that there is a "Beyond Good & Evil 2" coming soon; catch up on the storyline first.

And of course, last but not least, the monster. With hard hitting claws grabs, and the ability to evolve, will you let the hunters succeed? Beyond Good and Evil is one of those oddities in games. From gameplay to story, style, and even reception there's something strange in all of it, and all of it is fun. By no means is this a game you won't recognize. It borrows quite nicely from both Zelda, Metroid, Pokemon Snap, stealth games (Okay, A LOT of this game is stealth-based) and even a bit of  boat racing.
Where the oddities come in is how all of it is executed. This game has more story than Zelda and Metroid combined. The style is a bit reminiscent of Half-Life 2 in a cartoon universe (Hell, Jade even looks like Alyx Vance)
The story follows Jade as she attempts to uncover a conspiracy plot unraveling around the mysterious DomZ. Gameplay properly reflects this creeping, spy theme by having you sneaking through heavily guarded fortresses in order to snap a few incriminating photos and get the truth out to the public. There are even points in the game that thrust you into a classic action scene straight out of a movie.

To get it out of the way first: YES! This game is a reskin or clone or however you want to phrase it. It's made by the devs from Clicker Heroes in conjunction with the team at (what used to be) Gravity Interactive.
That being said, the main point of this game, and really of ANY clicker game, is style. With a few minor differences between the plethora of clicker games available, the biggest  draw for any of them is how much do you like the style? The graphics, the theme, the standard interface?
Back in it's time, and still going today, Ragnarok Online carved out it's own little niche in the MMO market by offering a unique look and feel, a soundtrack that stuck in your mind, and a community that was as welcoming as it was diverse. While it's too early to say how the community will flesh out here, the sprite graphics and catchy tunes are all present.
If you've ever played and enjoyed RO, this is the perfect clicker game for you.
If you've never played it before, at least give this a shot. If you find it interesting, I'd also recommend checking out the original game of Ragnarok Online.
If you don't like sprite-based, anime style artwork and are looking for something more "modern", then move along. The nostalgia weighs heavy here.

Whenever I write a negative review for a game that has a "Very Positive" review score, I always have a moment of self-doubt (as is natural, or else I'd be a sociopath). "What if I just 'don't get it'?" "What if I'm unreasonably harsh?" "What if I'll come around to it in a couple of years from now?" Usually whenever that happens, I end up not publishing a review at all, keeping my feelings about said game to myself instead. The game gets filed under "just wasn't for me" and I simply move on, saving myself from the potential dreariness of going against a vocal majority.
LIMBO is
one of those games. LIMBO f*cking sucks and I can't wait to tell you all about it. If you liked it, I won't hesitate to declare that your opinion is
. I know that sounds arrogant, and I don't make such definitive statements very often, but that's just how strong my conviction against this game is.
Before we go on, just a quick background on me as a gamer, just so you know that my credentials for judging this particular game are in good order. I love puzzle games. I have a thing for platformers. I prefer games that are harder than the average. I appreciate a good bit of horror here and there. I'm a sucker for mystery. LIMBO is all of those things. I went into it fully expecting it to be my jam.
So why was I so utterly disappointed? For a number of reasons.
First and perhaps most important of all, the solutions to many puzzles in LIMBO are completely unintuitive. To me that's a cardinal sin in puzzle game making, and a game must score perfect grades in all other aspects for me to forgive this flaw. Let me be absolutely clear BTW: I'm not implying that I enjoy games that hold my hand as I'm playing through them; quite the contrary, they bore me to tears. But! There's a whole world between that and desperate throwing of sh!t on the wall to see what sticks. I can handle a few instances of blind trial and error but when a game developer forces me into round after round of "Try to figure THAT one out, ha!", I can only interpret that as a gigantic "F*CK YOU" from the developer team aimed at me the player - and I don't appreciate being treated that way. YMMV.
Second, and adding up to the first, the frustratingly low health of the playable character. One little box falls on his head and he dies. He walks in water up to his nose and he dies. It would be mildly amusing if it wasn't for the very obvious fact that he was designed that way in order to make LIMBO harder without its developers actually having to
harder in order to build smarter puzzles for their game. Yeah, let's just make our character die if someone so much as sneezes at him instead. Cause what else would complement those non-intuitive puzzles of ours so well, amirite?
Third, this game is pretending to have a story, but doesn't actually explain jack sh*t. Like I said already, I love mystery, but if a game ends up explaining none of it, it's just a letdown. So many frustrating unanswered questions... "Who am I?" "How did I end up here?" "Who's that girl and why is she important to me?" "How did
end up here?" "Why is
in my surroundings trying to kill me?" You might hope for some answers down the line as you're playing, but you'll get absolutely none.
Oh, did I mention the mind-controlling slugs that occasionally take control of the playable character's movement? Yeah, cause that's what this game really needed: more cheap gimmicks to make it harder than it has merit to be.
LIMBO is a game where the developer team covertly mocks you for trying to play through it (at least on your first playthrough, where you don't know what to expect and inevitably fall in all of their traps). Apparently that genre has an audience, color me surprised. If you identify as part of that audience, go right ahead. But if you don't, ask yourself if you like being treated that way before you spend your valuable time and money playing it. Cause I didn't know what I was getting into, and I sure as hell didn't enjoy it.

Can't... stop... playing.
I had spotted a article through Kotaku, about this game. At the time I was looking for a new Roguelike to play, but also wanted a RPG feel. Tower defense didn't even cross my mind, though I enjoyed Defender's Quest quite a bit. Regardless, I spotted the review and snagged the cheaper version of the game.
Ok yeah, I'm hooked and planning to upgrade as soon as I can to show my support:
--Game--
The game is harsh in the beginning. My friend described it having a learning curve, and I agree. There is one. My first run, I got all the way to the 11th floor some how. Even got the Pug, until I found out she was a special case. I was spending hours on the game, and even played til 1am on a work day. (Normally I crash at 11pm lol)
It's not entirely "turn based." There's enough moving parts and thought to the game that I do not feel myself being bored. I love the runs where it turns out the floor works out to my advantage. I adore the floors that work completely against me. I read a description as "The FTL ship crashing into Issac's basement." I snickered at the statement, I think it fits the concept quite well.
I tried playing on the MAC, which has some bugs in concerns of getting the hot keys to work. Like any crossplatform game, there's going to be quirks. It didn't stop me from enjoying the game. If you play on a track pad, do keep in mind to re-assign the Power button just in case.
--Story--
The story seems interesting, and has gotten me interested in the Endless series as a whole. There's a lot left to the imagination about the prisoners, the security staff, and those who were on the planet. I find myself wanting to draw fan art as well.
--Multiplayer--
This is a HUGE hit and miss. Huge hit in terms of, the multiplayer is freaking crazy fun. Just playing with one friend is amazing. There's no pausing in the game, and my friend and we would banter back and forth "Ok you got that tower researched? I'll focus on ____ since I can make it but you can't."
The HUGE drawback, are two points
1.) No save state - I could see where this could cause problems. A drop in game would not work well with a game like this, but due to the 2nd issue, it does make a save state desired. The only solution I can think of is something similiar to how Civ handles their saves and what not. But in this case, make sure it saves the stats, current room set up, heroes, players/IDs involved. I do not know how hard it would be to set this up, but I'm sure the time and money would take some time, or it'd be added in another patch/iteration.
2.) Crashing. Crashing or losing your connection. Ok, more on the lines of crashing. The game is a straight grind, where my friend and I currently spend... 3? 4? hours? (4 hours the first time, 3 or less as we got better with the game) The gist is, when the game/host crashes, when you're loading the 11th floor. It makes you groan. (Granted it was a bad night. He and I then went to XBox to play some Soul Calibur and it red ringed. I stated that my friend has the touch of death at the moment.)
--Conclusion--
Still loved the game. It's a very different game from my experience. It takes elements from many other games and makes something very neat. Hope you enjoy the game as much as I had!

Red Faction: Armageddon focuses on destructible environments. The player must reclaim cultist fortifications on the disaster-ravaged surface of the planet and defend colonists from hostile Martian creatures in the ancient mines and chasms beneath it and cleansing infestations from all structures.
Using the Magnet Gun, Darius, the main protagonist, fires first at one object, then at a second object, and then the first object rockets toward the second.
The Nano-Forge returns, having been passed down through two generations of the Mason family. Darius' father has incorporated the tool with a function that reverses any and all destruction dealt to man-made objects. The Nano-Forge will also feature an ability known as Impact, which discharges an incredibly powerful burst of force which can blow away structures and throw enemies off their feet.
Darius' Nano-Forge, weapons and armor are all upgradeable, improving their efficiency, unlocking new abilities, and altering their appearances.

SUPERHOT is a low poly, minimalistic first person shooter-puzzle hybrid. Having started as a proof-of-concept game pitch for a 7 Day FPS challenge in 2013, SUPERHOT has taken the media by surprise with its stylish, no-nonsense presentation and outstanding execution - which has been largely carried over in the final release on Steam.
There is plot. It's the rather cliche theme of "you're not in control, your fourth wall won't protect you" deal, though it's intriguing enough to warrant not being spoiled here.
The main menu is stylised as an old school terminal; the intermission loading sequences, "cutscenes" and supplementary menu content and minigames are done in ASCII art style; and the actual gameplay is simple, low poly black and red models, blasting spectacularly apart in plain white and grey environments. This simplicity is, in my opinion, excessive, because the premise of the game could work in its favor by allowing detailed firearm animations.
Speaking of animations, despite their Kickstarter goal of better animators, it's all fairly crude. Little variation in animation, whether you fire a gun, swing a melee weapon, or a red guy stops to shoot - sometimes they fire gangsta style and that's it.
The most music you'll get is in the credits - a rather catchy Polish rock theme. The rest of the game has a droning ambience, which only tends to get noticeable in important story sections.
crunchy and satisfying sound effects, especially for the shotgun, but not for the pistol and machine gun, which sound the same and bothers me somewhat.
What you see is what you get: time moves only when you move. Looking around, moving, jumping and attacking cause time to accelerate by varying amounts, which the enemies, flying objects, debris and bullets react to. This gameplay is the closest we'll get to a proper Matrix game. It is absolutely superb, it 100% delivers on the gameplay premise.
What it
deliver on, however, is the amount of content. In less than three hours, you finish the campaign. Go have fun in Endless mode and its 5 levels with 4 variations on scoring, and replay story levels in Challenge mode, with added twists like only using a katana, or time standing fully still when motionless but you only get one shot with each weapon.
For me, this isn't $25 worth of content, even if I admit to the gameplay being so tight I come back every once in a while. The amount of unique gameplay is a hot contention point among players, but I assure you personally: you won't regret the time you spent on this game, only that you could spend more on it.

Sir or Madam, SYaBH is a nice little stealth/survival game about an extremely British dimensional traveler stuck in a land where British hunter themed robots hunt humans for fun... that is until he can collect all the timey-wimey bits of his device and rebuild it.  Toward that end you will sneak around, loot houses (or more precisely their doors),  shoot overly pesky robot hunters, and dodge those that can't be so easily dealt with.  There are 5 islands to explore per game, all proceedurally generated from general parameters you choose, on average 3 bits per island, and several different starting loadouts (occupations?) to experiment with.  The numbers of robots and and their type escalates as you gather more pieces until they become so numerous that stealth becomes tedious and combat a little overwhelming.  Still, with hit and run tactics or distractions you can still outmaneuver the robots whose AI is *usually* not that dilligent or perceptive.  If you manage to reassumble your device you are treated to a short in-game animation followed by static credits and a decent song.  I spent a little less than 5 hours beating the game my first time.  MP seems a bit too PVP focused, and doesn't currently use Steamworks so it's currently a bit questionable.  I would have liked to see more variety of loot, additional story elements to flesh out the narrative, and slightly more rifle ammo in loot caches, but none of those held back my enjoyment of my initial playthrough.
While it's obviously not yet fully polished as of this writing and despite it's currently dubious replay value, it's already very enjoyable, and, I believe, worth full price as is.  I may still have a wishlist, but no major complaints.

I started this game thinking it would as simple as the other popular survival games.
I was horribly wrong.
This game will punish you if you don't know what your'e doing. You will fail a lot, but that is okay. That is how you learn how to suvive in this game. The game will push you really hard to continuously scavange for resources. The game is currently a sandbox game without campaign but there will be campaign mode in future. Some of the things that I like about this game are -
- The game heavily relies on scavenging resources. It's challenging to survive if you run out of food and do not roam around looking for resources. You can't stay in one place for long unless you have enough resources. But, it's pointless to stay in one place for long nonetheless.
- The game has no base building, except you can make a temporary shelter which is still vulnerable to wild animal attacks.
- If you get caught in Blizzard and do not find a shelter soon, you will either end up having hypothermia or even worse, frostbitten. You can't just make a campfire like you can do in some other survival games in the middle of a storm. Why? Because the wind won't let you. Pretty realistic.
- Maintaining a campfire while you get some water from the snow ain't easy if you don't have enough fuel.
- Inventory management is crucial. You can not just bring anything you want with you because it will slow you down. In fact, if you reach 60 kg, you will be unable to move.
- Hunting deer and rabbit is easy, wolf is..... well it's not hard, bear is challenging unless you have the rifle or gun. Ammo is hard to find and should be used wisely.
- Found a cabin with a lot of deers nearby? Thinking of spending several days in your favorite cabin? Get ready to deal with cabin fever.
- Found a fishing tackle? It broke during fishing? Thinking of crafting a new one? First, do some hunting, get animal guts from their carcass, cure the guts by leaving them indoors for several days, THEN you gonna get you materials ready.
- You got bear hides wolf hides and deer hides and now you gonna make the best clothes in the game ever so you won't have to worry about negative temperature anymore. Guess what? Crafting all these clothes will take days and you need sufficient water and food and rest so you don't fall. Got everything crafted finally? Now you would have to be careful not to get sweaty because of the warmth bonus from all the clothes. You might have to put some of these off if you are inside a house.
- Your precious weapons and clothes will decay over time if you don't repair them time to time.
The looks beautiful. It gets lonlely sometimes because of no NPCs. This game is very atmospheric. The game has no horror elements but it could feel creepy at times for no reason and the game looks really scary if you get caught in a heavy storm during night without any light source or shelter nearby. The game is really good to make you feel that you actually need something like food or water ASAP.
The only major problem with this game is performance. In certain areas, it is possible to get low fps in game. It even gets lower if you run the game for quite long and doesn't fix until you restart the game. Apart from the fps issue, I have found, so far, no other bugs or glitches.
If you want a survival game with challenges, then get this. If you are looking for something to play with your friends, then you better find another game because The Long Dark is meant to be played alone where you will know the meaning of solitude.

This clever, nicely-paced game isn't quite FTL, but it's worth mentiong in the same sentence. FTL's basic gameplay is quite repetitive, but there are interesting choices to be made at the strategic level, as you find out what modules are on offer.  DOTE's basic gameplay has a fair amount of variation, but the number of viable strategies feels a lot more limited.  There's definitely a real learning curve, and unlocking character stories is quite satisfying.  However, DOTE feels much more like a series of tactical and operational puzzles than it gives a feeling of strategy.  I may be saying that because I haven't worked out the tactical puzzles yet (and am therefore blind to strategy) but there's a strong feeling of 'starting again' with each new floor that drains my sense of satisfaction and progression.
If you like exploring mazes and unlocking things, you'll get a ton of enjoyment out of DOTE.  That's not quite my thing, but I still enjoyed it for quite a few hours.

Like watching The Breakfast Club or Ghost Busters after years of mediocre and boring movies, and this is the same for The Long Dark. Frankly, I'm sick of trashy multiplayer games that have you spend your money to have an advantage over someone else, or games that are pumped out every few years by the same studios, that only really capture the satisfaction of 12 year olds and other people that generally wouldn't know better, but this, this is something else, it's like the Sherlock Holmes of Crime Movies, its like Halloween, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, the old classic movies that DEFINED the Horror genre, and when you put up Friday the 13th and The Nightmare on Elm Street against The Blob or Paranormal Activity, it makes you realise just how special this game is.. about the game, thankyou for creating the

Gadzooks! After playing this game for an extended period and then turning it off, I had a real "coming out of the cave" moment. I felt relieved to be back in reality where I'm not the only living human, robots aren't hunting me, and the weather doesn't constantly suck.
Funny thing is, I'm really looking forward to coming back to that world in my next play session. It seriously feels like a warzone, but not the kind you'd see in Modern Warfare. It's the kind you'd see in Stanley Kubrick's "Full Metal Jacket".  Buildings are falling apart and the environment is dusky and depressing. Sometimes the silence is punctuated by a fire fight off in the distance as bots start infighting with each other. It's a dangerous environment where you rarely get a chance to relax.
And then the game gets unsettling. When you hear an unearthly....."sound" off in the distance and see a giant landowner limping about with its two guard dog bots following. Or when you get impatient and attract the attention of a squad of bots when you're low on ammo. They know you're there, and they relish in the hunt. Which is made apparant by their creepy robotic laughter as they creep ever closer to your hastily chosen and flimsy hiding spot. And after waiting with baited breath with your finger on the trigger as a bot just barely uncovers your hiding place, you hear a siren go off and the area around you bathed in red light. Turns out you weren't paying attention to the balloon sentry floating around the area, and now you have to make a split second decision. Fight for your life, or try to run and hide, hoping that any bullets that penetrate your backside don't do enough damage to end you. Because it's been an hour since you last saved at the waypoint, and it would be terrible to have to find all those hard earned items again.
I'm not kidding when I say that this very scenario happened to me. I have the sweat that was accumulating on my brow to prove it. I just barely managed to escape with just 2 points of health remaining, and my heart didn't stop pounding until well after I managed to get back to the waypoint to save. It's a kind of terror that is rooted in reality. I would've lost a ton of items if I had died. God knows what would've happened if I had decided to stand and fight.
The "brutally funny" description that the developers decided to go with puzzles me. Because at least for me, this game is one of the most tense and stressful experiences I've had in awhile. In a good way. Sir, you are being terrorized.

Have you ever wanted to lead your friends into battle against robots by sounding the charge by poorly playing your rusty trumpet?
Dont answer, I know this is everyone's dream.
Look no further! This game will take care of all of your needs. Want to hide around the corner from a squad of robot hunters while sipping lukewarm tea? Now you can! Strike fear into the hearts of your enemies by equipping everyone in your game with a trumpet and stroll through the streets, sounding off the war horn, warning all the robots of their incoming demise.
I remember it like it was yesterday, *BUUUUUUUURRRRRRRR* *BURRRRRRRRRRRRRR* *BUUUUURRRRRRR* We took down countless robots trying to gather the pieces of the teleporter all while keeping our spirits up with the lively trumpet of freedom. Living off of the food we scrounged together, mainly wisky and tea, we kept our strenght at maximum. We all had our designated weapons of choice. I was the shotgun specialist with an axe and no regard for the law. Near the end of our struggle to escape, we came across an ammo supply shortage during our biggest battle yet. Thankfully we never lost our morale due to the constant *BUUUUUUUURRRRRRRRRR* our trumpeter played, both to keep us from retreating from the robot scum and to strike fear into their hearts. We started to take casualties due to having to make the fight more upclose and personal, but we never stopped the trumpet. The trumpet is a symbol of freedom, of hope. The last one of us starts to make a break for it towards our safe zone, littered with traps and stocked full of supplies. Not once did he let up on that trumpet. At this point it was just so that the robots wouldnt lose track of him into our turf. The trumpeter makes it into the ruins of a large building surrounded by small walls, filled with bear traps. This is the last stand. We need to let the world know. He climbs to the top of the pile of rubble in the center of the ruins and... *BUUUUrrrrrRRRrRRrRRrrRRrRRrrRrrRRrrRR*. Robots stepping on traps left and right. Never once letting go of that trumpet. Never once giving up hope. Not once will we let up on the trumpet. Not once will we stop taunting them with our freedom. The last trap is sprung. A robot dog dashes up the rubble and tackles the trumpeter off of the top.
The battle is over, but we've left our mark.
10/10 would trumpet again.

Pretty solid game.  It got me about 30 minutes of enjoyment.  The platforming level was very well designed in the sense that it guides you to the location of the next tree through the layout of the level.  The bullet hell stages were also cool, since they were somewhat of a challenge to beat.
You're greeted by a video of two women talking about something.  I didn't really pay attention.  After what seems like an eternity you're thrown into the first level.
The goal of the first level is to get your faith higher than the garden's faith.  You do this by collecting bible verses from destroyed asteroids, while also managing your fuel/ammo levels.  Most of the time you'll end up running out of fuel before you can get enough faith, but if you get lucky you'll get a couple cherrubium to spawn at the start so you can get extra fuel.  Avoid the giant squid thing.  Once you collect enough faith you're rewarded with another cutscene.
Then, you're thrown into a side-scrolling bullet hell.  Your character is pretty big, but the hitbox is only the size of the small person in front.  Don't get too close to the floating platforms or the floor/ceiling or you'll die.  You also can't kill the mech things, so just avoid their shots.  The level is pretty straightforward otherwise - just shoot the enemies and don't get hit.  The boss is the same as the rest of the level, so just keep shooting and dodge the bullets.  Eventually, the music will suddenly stop and he will disappear, and you'll be thrown into another cutscene.
Then, the platforming level...  The screen spins for whatever reason, so try not to vomit.  Just follow the level and collect the 7 Jesuses and you'll be thrown into the next level after another terrible video cutscene.
Then you fight the final boss, which is a giant giraffe with bubba lips and badly maintained teeth.  It's another solid minute of just dodging bullets and holding down shoot, but this time you can only move left or right.  Once he dies you are presented with the final screen and some home-recorded christian rock music.
There's nothing after this, so just hit escape a couple times to exit.  Then uninstall this game and throw your computer into the garbage.  You have just experienced the pinnacle of human enjoyment, so your life is now over.

Bioshock is a shooter, much like other shooters. what makes it unique among games is really 3 aspects. first: Rapture, there has never been a more unique and interesting environment to play in. A city at the bottom of the sea, fraught with all of the inherent danger of a thousand meters of atlantic ocean on all sides of you, designed to be a place where men ruled themselves and called no other "master," and hailed to no code of morality at all. Second: survival horror gameplay. when i first played the game, i was never full on ammo. every shot counted. enemies could appear behind you, which was fairly unique at the time, it was a departure from enter room, kill everything, enter new room kill everything, and repeat. things changed when you turned your back. Third: Story, being a story gamer, this is really important to me. i wanted to find every audio recording and build out the narrative of andrew ryan v frank fontaigne. it is a classic exercise in psychological egoism. two men vying for power, unbound by rules of engagement, and uncaring of all of the lives they destroyed in the process. At the center of them, a man with no name and a bunch of transmogrified monsters taking the shape of little girls and unstoppable juggernauts.
There're other things that were fun, plasmids and tonics, the research camera that were interesting but less unique in the grand scheme of games. the original game still holds up well due to the art-deco style where the monsters and people aren't meant to be photorealistic.

Geologist, naturalist and wearer of a very fine beard.
Aside from his discovery of the potato this nineteenth century hipster is probably best known for his work “The Origin of the Species”.
Charlie’s theory of evolution upset a lot of creationist types back then (and still does today).
If you don’t like the idea of having evolved from “ape-like” ancestors then you’re going to hate the fact that you’ve also got plenty of DNA in common with that potato our big bearded friend unearthed!
I’ll assume that all the creationists have now stopped reading and are busy composing their hate mail in response...
(By the way, if you are a creationist and you’re planning on sending in some hate mail, take a moment to look down at that pen you’re holding, you know why you can hold that properly? Opposable thumbs, isn’t evolution great!)
If you think about it, indirectly we should also thank Charles Darwin for chips, Fries, decorating the back of the British £10 note and for Evolve, the shiny new 4 v 1 monster title from Turtle Rock Studios.
Much like Darwin’s Origin of the Species, Evolve has encountered a little controversy of its own following release.
The majority of the criticism seems to be centred around the price point for Evolves proposed DLC line up and not at the game itself.
Without wanting to jump on the band wagon of hate, the DLC (which isn’t all included in the season pass) does seem expensive, but you know what, you don’t have to buy it.
The game is perfectly playable without out throwing your money at re-skinning the cast but if you find value in the downloadable eye candy then good for you, you pay your money, you make your choice.
It’s with this “live and let live” attitude that I approach Evolve.
Let the killing begin!
The first thing that will hit you when you fire up Evolve is just how good looking it is.
From the detailed scenery to the impressive character models, the graphics here are amazing.
Trees will fall, birds will take flight and wildlife will scatter before you. The lush environment is one of the most polished and lovingly crafted I've seen.
The character interactions in the cut scenes between missions are also great fun to watch (until you've seen them all anyway). Evolve has the glossy shine of a  Hollywood sci-fi blockbuster and as such is almost as much fun to watch as it is to play... almost.
Your first decision to make when you're ready for a round of FPS goodness  in Evolve will be choosing between playing as the monster or one of the monster hunters.
The hunters are split into four very distinct classes and the character classes here actually mean something and have a huge impact on how you will (or should) play the game.
The Medic class is pretty self explanatory, As the keeper of the pain killers, you'll be patching up your team mates with a little frontline medicine  and identifying weak spots on the  rampaging goliath.
The medic deals damage from a safe distance, so don't go charging down the monster with your first aid kit bouncing around on your back or you'll end up smeared  across the pretty scenery like the antiseptic paste you keep smearing on your colleagues wounds.
The Support class is there  to assist the team, boosting shields which makes your friends invulnerable for a short time.
(very useful to help give them a few more seconds to go toe to toe with towering terror).
Fancy making your team invisible or calling in a missile strike, then the support class is the way to go.
The Trapper as you might expect, can help trap the beastie by way of throwing up an energy grid around the monster, creating an instant but brief arena, stopping the monster from fleeing if the battle isn't going its way.
The trapper is also your tracker, looking for signs of the monster, following its footprints and leading your team across the lush scenery.
With a good trapper there's nowhere to hide.
The Assault class is your tank, you'll be getting down and dirty with the bug eyed beastie,  blasting and zapping away it's armour and health.
This is the hairy backed, testosterone fuelled class of the damage dealer.
Monsters beware!
Playing as a hunter isn't only limited to one character choice. As you play you'll unlock two additional characters per class, each with their own abilities and weaponry.
This adds up to 12 different hunter characters Included with the base game (three variants for each class) which should be plenty to keep you going for a while.
You can also purchase new characters as DLC, as I said at the start of the review, the price point for this DLC isn't exactly a crowd pleaser, but everything is worth what you're willing to pay for it.
So if and when you get tired of the vanilla selection, there are  options there  to increase the longevity of the game.
With each class genuinely specialised, you're going to need a competent team when playing co-op or you're going to really notice when the weakest link lets you down.
If you play online this WILL happen to you at some point. Everyone's got to learn the ropes   before they "Evolve" into the bad♥♥♥♥♥we all want on our team.
Throughout your journey with Evolve you're going to experience this from both sides.
I've spent plenty of time being the bewildered  " What should I do now" guy, where you can feel a little inadequate, but each match is a learning curve and they've all contributed to drag me from the  awful player I was initially to the dizzying heights of mediocrity that  I'm able to achieve today!
The good news is that there is a perfectly playable single player mode where you can cut your teeth as either a monster or a hunter with the AI doing a reasonable job of filling in for the other characters in the group.
I'd recommend that you use this mode to get a grip on things before heading off into the world of online humiliation.
The aspect I was most excited about going into Evolve was the ability to play as the monster.
Again, this isn't limited to just one monster type, you'll start with the Goliath, a big bruiser of a beast but as you play you'll unlock two more, the Kraken and the Wraith, each with their own unique play styles.
When you're "being the monster" , it's all about  organic abilities as opposed  to weapons and gadgetry.
You'll chow down on the wildlife to build up your armour, feed enough and you'll be able to evolve, giving you points to spend on your abilities such as breathing fire, throwing rocks and charging down pesky hunters.
There are three evolutionary stages on the path way to full "Monsterhood."
As a stage one monster, it's mostly about running away, hiding and being sneaky whilst eating the wildlife to evolve.
Stage two will see you striking back at the hunters then retreating again to feed up before you're next assault.
By the time you evolve to stage three (assuming the pesky hunters haven't taken you down already) you should be a killing behemoth crushing everything in your path. It's the hunters turn to run now.
There are four different game modes  in Evolve.
Hunt, nest, rescue and defend, any of which can be played as a one off "quick game" for those looking for a short burst of action.

Now if only Ubisoft would finish the sequel already, but of course, you can't rush quality.

This game has nothing to offer except nostalgia. It's an example of the lowest effort you can put into a product before you can call it "a game". It's a dumb, primitive clone of other (better) clicker games that reuses the assets from the Ragnarok Online that many of us love. However, even most of those assets aren't used: you won't hear most unique location tunes, you won't see spell effects or character animations (except monsters). It's mostly a bunch of static images with the same tune playing over and over and over and over again... that's how lazy the developers were.
It's almost offensive, because Ragnarok Online was actually good and unique, and many fans still want to see a proper sequel or at least a proper tie-in to the franchise. Instead, we get this - a piece of barely-a-game that has nothing good or unique about it. A parasite on the belly of Ragnarok fandom with the only purpose to suck cash out of whatever warm feelings people still have for this franchise.
It's another shameless, lazy and completely unnecessary cash-grab, slapped together in what looks like a couple of days. Better get a Ragnarok Online soundtrack to scratch your nostalgia itch, but avoid this "game".

The class/job system is extremely well done, and is one of the most unique I've seen out of a game.  While, yes, it has quite a lot of grinding straight from the get-go, it's pretty fun to level.  The Main Quest is a little obscure in how it has you go about, and you need to grind in between just one part of a quest to the next. Despite those flaws, when I play this game I actually enjoy grinding more than I do on other games as it's not overly tedious, but not an exact breeze either (depending on if your main job has AoE's or if you've picked them up from another class)

What can I say about the Long Dark that someone else hasn't already? Well, not a lot, really. It's a beautiful and challenging (Torturous on Interloper) experience that lulls you in. Yes, it's slow-paced, even in late-game, but it helps build the atmosphere that the game is aiming for: Exploring a by-gone age by a disaster that no one expected. Yes, it can be frusting when you just start, but once you get the hang of it, it's glorious.
You have to EARN your stuff too. You don't get your gun and ammo immediately (Unless you're THAT lucky) so it makes it all the more rewarding to obtain and load, and that's if you want to find the gun instead of making a bow. The game is mainly saying "You want it? Go get it", but in a very good way. It hardly pulls punches and it's just worth it, I'd say.

I think you either like or hate TLD.
The atmosphere is thick and intense, sound is great, graphics are a bit cartoonish and it’s exactly how they are meant to be, to be honest this game is not really about undergoing a realistic experience, it’s more about trying to stay alive as much as you can while exploring beautiful winterish landscapes while using this simple mechanics: Find things, save things as much as you can, survive with those things as long as you can.
Is it repetitive? Yes, it is.
Is it frustrating? Yes, it is.
Is it rewarding? Yes, it is.
Is it entertaining? Hell yes!
In my case, playing this game is like using a time machine as you are almost always under pressure, which means that you don’t really have time to get bored.
For an alpha, it is really well made and stable, it’s worth mentioning I have not experienced a single crash or major bug and the performance are quite good.
I couldn’t care less about a story (which is currently implemented) as I build my own through the game however I understand that it’s an important aspect for other players.
Would I recommend it? Well, if you’re not afraid to lose hours of gameplay because of one single error or oversight (yes, I’m talking about you sleeping bag), definitely!

I'm not a huge tower defense person. I've played a few games on my phone but other than that I never get to enthralled with them. But this game has atmospher and anticipation. The music and environment bring a sense of comfort yet a knowing it's not long before you're fighting for your life.

I started this game thinking it would as simple as the other popular survival games.
I was horribly wrong.
This game will punish you if you don't know what your'e doing. You will fail a lot, but that is okay. That is how you learn how to suvive in this game. The game will push you really hard to continuously scavange for resources. The game is currently a sandbox game without campaign but there will be campaign mode in future. Some of the things that I like about this game are -
- The game heavily relies on scavenging resources. It's challenging to survive if you run out of food and do not roam around looking for resources. You can't stay in one place for long unless you have enough resources. But, it's pointless to stay in one place for long nonetheless.
- The game has no base building, except you can make a temporary shelter which is still vulnerable to wild animal attacks.
- If you get caught in Blizzard and do not find a shelter soon, you will either end up having hypothermia or even worse, frostbitten. You can't just make a campfire like you can do in some other survival games in the middle of a storm. Why? Because the wind won't let you. Pretty realistic.
- Maintaining a campfire while you get some water from the snow ain't easy if you don't have enough fuel.
- Inventory management is crucial. You can not just bring anything you want with you because it will slow you down. In fact, if you reach 60 kg, you will be unable to move.
- Hunting deer and rabbit is easy, wolf is..... well it's not hard, bear is challenging unless you have the rifle or gun. Ammo is hard to find and should be used wisely.
- Found a cabin with a lot of deers nearby? Thinking of spending several days in your favorite cabin? Get ready to deal with cabin fever.
- Found a fishing tackle? It broke during fishing? Thinking of crafting a new one? First, do some hunting, get animal guts from their carcass, cure the guts by leaving them indoors for several days, THEN you gonna get you materials ready.
- You got bear hides wolf hides and deer hides and now you gonna make the best clothes in the game ever so you won't have to worry about negative temperature anymore. Guess what? Crafting all these clothes will take days and you need sufficient water and food and rest so you don't fall. Got everything crafted finally? Now you would have to be careful not to get sweaty because of the warmth bonus from all the clothes. You might have to put some of these off if you are inside a house.
- Your precious weapons and clothes will decay over time if you don't repair them time to time.
The looks beautiful. It gets lonlely sometimes because of no NPCs. This game is very atmospheric. The game has no horror elements but it could feel creepy at times for no reason and the game looks really scary if you get caught in a heavy storm during night without any light source or shelter nearby. The game is really good to make you feel that you actually need something like food or water ASAP.
The only major problem with this game is performance. In certain areas, it is possible to get low fps in game. It even gets lower if you run the game for quite long and doesn't fix until you restart the game. Apart from the fps issue, I have found, so far, no other bugs or glitches.
If you want a survival game with challenges, then get this. If you are looking for something to play with your friends, then you better find another game because The Long Dark is meant to be played alone where you will know the meaning of solitude.

Like watching The Breakfast Club or Ghost Busters after years of mediocre and boring movies, and this is the same for The Long Dark. Frankly, I'm sick of trashy multiplayer games that have you spend your money to have an advantage over someone else, or games that are pumped out every few years by the same studios, that only really capture the satisfaction of 12 year olds and other people that generally wouldn't know better, but this, this is something else, it's like the Sherlock Holmes of Crime Movies, its like Halloween, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, the old classic movies that DEFINED the Horror genre, and when you put up Friday the 13th and The Nightmare on Elm Street against The Blob or Paranormal Activity, it makes you realise just how special this game is.. I give this game points for charm because I liked its outrageous story line and campy quality, though a lot of the humor was labored. My favorite line was Ms. Seward's: "Now, goodbye forever, you handsome manifestation of my childhood complexes!" I agree with her. The voice acting was fine, except for Ipkis, who was overdone. It was hard to believe he was star material.
This game should be called "Fetch Quest City"; and many of those quests were silly or illogical. A bunch of lazy characters waiting around for a needy fool to show up and do their work for them. The innkeeper was particularly inept at keeping track of stuff in his own establishment. Also, some of the HOG scenes closed after every click, requiring a lot of unnecessary work because I had to reopen those scenes and click, and reopen those scenes and click again, ad nauseum. Upon replay, I discovered that by exiting to the Main Menu and clicking on Continue, that problem was resolved.
The game has no help system to explain how the game saves. Since exiting to the Main Menu and clicking on Continue resulted in a "loading" message, I figured that it was a way to force the game to save, which was handy for working around the bugs. I saved a lot to avoid problems.
I have two issues with the game's graphics. The first problem was the screen aspect ratio. It was stretched side-to-side; so everything was wide, which was especially noticeable with circular objects like wheels and gears and the two globes on the HUD at the bottom of the screen. It looked like the game was designed for a standard monitor (4:3 ratio). I tried the only option available—Window mode—but the window was the same wide-screen ratio and everything was still distorted. And the window could not be resized to reduce the distortion. My nVidia graphics card is incredibly capable of handling aspect rations, but this game did not cooperate.
The second graphic problem involved HOG scenes and puzzles. Parts of the screen were blank. Meaning: solid white. In the case of the HOGs, I was able to able to access the Main Menu via the HUD and resolve the problem as described above. When I clicked on Continue and returned to the game, the visual problem was solved. However, there is no HUD available in the puzzle screens; so, there is no way to work around the problem, except to cancel the game via ALT+CTRL+DELETE. I was unable to solve one of the puzzles because of this problem and had to skip the puzzle; so, I didn't earn the Enigmatist achievement. Upon replay, I exited to the Main Menu prior to the puzzle and clicked Continue to fix the graphic issue and earned the achievement.
"Sinister City" was cute and fun, but clunky. I'm surprised that such a recent release has these problems.

To be honest I expected much more of this game. Its okay If I were to rate it out of 10 I would give it a 5, why? because the game is quite boring after an hour or two.
The stealth mechanic is okay not the best but good enough you will find tall grass to be your best friend. The "Distraction" system for me was fantastic and the most fun for me when playing this game, using items from simple bottles, to alarm clocks, toy trains etc...  to distract enemies was quite entertaining. The enemies themselves are funny looking and fit the theme, and you discover new enemies throughout your journey.
The objective is quite dull, you must collect Fragment pieces of the "Device Teleporter" and bring it back to the special Stone circle, the fragments themselves are scattered throughout the island, that being said the fragment pieces take up 16 inventory slots and its quite irritating having to travel back and forth to dump them at the stone to get rid of them.
The Landscape is okay but it tends to get quite repetative with structures. The looting system is a bit of a letdown for me, to obtain loot you must press "F" on a door and it has items (Occasionaly barrels etc..) there are no interiors for any building aswell which is quite stale. not to mention the textures of the building are of low detail which is dissapointing for this day n age, considering the environment looks better then the structures...
You don't sprint in this game, you jog.
*Multiplayer*: The Animations/Character model are quite lame and looks like they were put together in 10 minutes, not to mention the character customization is completely useless (You can only change hat n shirt). The Running animation in this game looks completely bonkers, just take a look at your buddies when they're sprinting around like goofs.
The game itself is okay, playable for a "few" hours before it becomes completely stale, that's pretty much all I have to say about "Sir you are being Hunted".
