From the very day that it was released, Bioshock was a classic in its own right. It came at the right time, when the over-saturated shooter genre was steadily getting more stale as time progressed. The title found overwheming acclaim due to its fresh gameplay, unique story, and immersive setting. Often called the spiritual successor to System Shock 2, Bioshock is the title that put developer/publisher 2K Games on the road to success. The only real question here is... would you kindly?
Even though Bioshock was originally released in 2007, the game has aged remarkably well. Many were surprised to hear that Remastered versions of the first two titles were underway, as the graphics have held up superbly over nearly a decade. While the console versions of the game ran flawlessly, the PC port did come with its share of issues; most notably mouse acceleration problems, but also a handful of glitches that cause one to have to reload their save files. Unfortunately, these problems were never patched out despite how easy they could've been to fix.
Welcome to Rapture. The year is 1960. You are a man named Jack, aboard an airplane flying over the Atlantic Ocean. The plane goes down, and surrounded by fire and debris you swim to a nearby lighthouse. Upon entering, you're greeted by a man named Atlas via radio, after being threatened by horrendously insane denizens of the underwater city. In a somewhat submarine type of contraption called a Bathysphere, you submerge down what is assumed to be thousands of fathoms under the sea, where you enter the rustic, dystopian, Art Deco style city of Rapture.
At first the player isn't given much information on the character that they're playing, nor much of the story for that matter. The story progresses through a series of audio interactions with Atlas, and through collection audio diaries that are scattered throughout each level. Occasionally, other characters present themselves over the communication radio, and there are only a small handful of cutscenes which are placed at very appropriate moments. Without taking the time to explore Rapture and find all of the diaries, one may feel slightly lost in terms of plot and story. If you take the time to find and listen to all 122 diaries, it's easy to say that 2K did an amazing job adding depth and vibrancy to each character.
As stated before, Bioshock has a very unique approach to gameplay. Not only do you get six upgradable weapons (shotgun, pistol, chemical thrower, crossbow, etc.), but you get 11 Plasmids to play around with; however, you can only equip 7 at any given time, but you can swap out what Plasmids and Tonics you have equipped at a Gene Swap Station. Plasmids rewrite your DNA, and infuse you with outstanding powers such as Telekinesis, Incineration, Insect Swarms, and even the ability to Hypnotize Big Daddy. In order to use Plasmids, you must have enough Eve, which can be gained through injecting yourself with Eve Hypos. It's the same basic concept as spells and mana. However, Jack's left hand changes aesthetics with each newly equipped Plasmid, and there are also upgrades to find for most of them.
Suffice it to say that the game has a lot of variety to offer, especially given its age. The enemies that you will encounter are as equally unique, and they are known as Splicers. People who have been surgically modified to the extreme, whether willingly or forced, by the insane Dr. Steinman. There are a total of five different Splicers, each with their own unique attributes. However, let us not forget the star of the show here, the Big Daddy. There are two different kinds of Big Daddies, Bouncer and Rosie. Their role is to protect the Little Sisters who are harvesting ADAM around Rapture. You must face these behemoths each time that you want to either rescue or harvest a Little Sister.
ADAM is another type of currency in Bioshock, although you also have money that you collect for buying items and ammo, and it is used to unlock new Tonics, Plasmids, new slots for each, and upgrades for both Health and Eve. The more Little Sisters you either harvest or rescue, the more ADAM you collect. I should also mention here that Tonics function as your abilities, and they can also have several findable upgrades akin to the Plasmids; there are well over 50 Tonics in total throughout the game. There's also a very limited crafting system in place, so that you can find components and make ammo, new Tonics, and even autohack devices to assist in hacking Turrets, Security Bots, Cameras, and Vending Machines.
However, despite everything that has been aforementioned, the real ingredient that makes this game stand out so vividly is its amazing art direction and thick, immersive atmosphere. One really gets hit hard with the authentic 1960's vibe, which is conveyed through the Art Deco style of the game. However, instead of it being a pristine environment, Rapture is decayed, down-trodden, flooded, and rusty. At almost every corner you're reminded that you're hundreds, if not thousands, of fathoms below the surface, and at the same time you're constantly reminded of the time period; whether it be visually or by way of music. There's not a lot of music in the game, but there are aptly placed jukeboxes from time to time that sing relevant tunes from the time period. One of the hardest hitters is looking out of any given window and seeing a neon sign lit city underwater.
If you've never taken the time to visit Rapture and delve into the universe of Bioshock, you shouldn't wait any longer. The story is absolutely remarkable, and one that you will not forget for years to come; I haven't played this title since 2007, and its story, influence, and artistic direction have never left me. There is a ton to do in Rapture, and a large amount of places to explore, looking back on it now it's pretty crazy how many mechanics and features that 2K were able to implement into the title; especially being such a smaller team a decade ago. Now, would you kindly go and play Bioshock? "With the sweat of your brow, Rapture can become your city as well." - Andrew Ryan.

Alright so I'm gonna list some pros and cons, some of them more of a personal opinion here.
Pros: It has a lot of nostalgia to it, probably because I played the game years ago when it was under Aeria. The art style makes up for what it lacks in graphics. The game is colorful, but doesn't give you a headache. The game is also unique in that you can become qualified for all classes, and switch whenever you want. The music is also rather unique, and I love it.
Cons: The text is VERY small, however, this can be fixed by downloading a font called Mingliu, which can be downloaded safely and for free from FontPalace, as I did. (Edit: The font is specifically called Mingliu Regular). The game is prone to crashing often and every time you tab out. There is no quest tracker in the UI (but you do have a journal to keep track of current quests). There is no solo auto-loot. It's easy to get caught on the terrain, especially stairs and curbs. Sometimes monsters walk through the walls, though this poses no problem in hitting them and dragging them back out. From my knowledge, you cannot buy perma-costumes from the item mall (but I'm fairly certain I've seen some perma-costumes in player shops, though I don't know how they got them). Lastly, the only way to know how an item is usually priced if you're wanting to sell it in your own shop is to either ask others or check other shops and hope they have it.
Overall I really love the game and its uniqueness, maybe just because of the nostalgia, but I really recommend it, because if you can get past the cons, the game is truly fun and lovable.

If you like a zombie survival simulator, with amazing gameplay machanics and a story created by the player, this is a game for you.
However, as you can probably tell, the game is not completed yet and has a very long way to go.
Pros:
*Well thought out game mechanics and gameplay.
*Massive open world to explore.
*Well done zombie AI.
*Freedom to do whatever you desire.
*Near Spot on Survival aspect.
Cons:
*The zombies can become very predictable.
*In game activities can become redundant once you figure out how to handle almost every situation. (Even some the surprizes)
*Maps are so large that it can take hours to get to a new area, this gets old REALLY quickly.
*Ends up becoming a game that only brings back old players with the promise of new mini-features; only for them to get bored moments later and wait for the next update. (Minecraft)
More or less, this game lacks a complex "game changer" if you want to call it that. Once you figure out how to repel the zombies completely, the game becomes a chore to play.
Personally, I am waiting for the NPC Survivors to be brought back in. I feel that will make the game interesting for me again; assuming they are programed right.
Despite this though, it is a very good game for what it is. A survival game. Right now, it is probably the best you can find on steam. That is why I can recommend it.

I think you either like or hate TLD.
The atmosphere is thick and intense, sound is great, graphics are a bit cartoonish and it’s exactly how they are meant to be, to be honest this game is not really about undergoing a realistic experience, it’s more about trying to stay alive as much as you can while exploring beautiful winterish landscapes while using this simple mechanics: Find things, save things as much as you can, survive with those things as long as you can.
Is it repetitive? Yes, it is.
Is it frustrating? Yes, it is.
Is it rewarding? Yes, it is.
Is it entertaining? Hell yes!
In my case, playing this game is like using a time machine as you are almost always under pressure, which means that you don’t really have time to get bored.
For an alpha, it is really well made and stable, it’s worth mentioning I have not experienced a single crash or major bug and the performance are quite good.
I couldn’t care less about a story (which is currently implemented) as I build my own through the game however I understand that it’s an important aspect for other players.
Would I recommend it? Well, if you’re not afraid to lose hours of gameplay because of one single error or oversight (yes, I’m talking about you sleeping bag), definitely!

With the achievements being what they are, this game was somewhat an ingenious money grab. All the steam profile enthusiasts (myself included) rushed to buy this game as a result of them.
The game presents itself as a game that focuses on the puzzle genre – a goal which it accomplishes as intended. If one were to use guides, the game would still take upwards of several hours and on a normal play-through this game can offer tens of hours of pushing your mind to the limits, just so that you can get that sweet sense of satisfaction of getting the word ‘DAB’ to show on your profile. (Dab is dead now anyway)
Steam achievements aside, as one would somewhat expect, the music and sound effects are fitting for the puzzle genre. The game's aesthetic side is flawless with the art being very abstract and the animation being smooth, especially when a puzzle is completed. Seeing the tiles rotate, fade white and slowly move away gives one a sense of satisfaction. The colours sometimes compliment and sometimes contradict each other, but, in turn, they are effective in focusing your attention on some things and not on others – something that can be useful in a puzzle game.
With such a game, the requirements to play it are obviously low and the game runs smoothly, and there are no apparent bugs that appear unless you have an issue such as broken drivers. As an abstract artistic expression, the game exceeds many other puzzle games that attempt to accomplish the same thing, and along with the amount of popularity gained from other factors, allowed this game to rise to some small form of prominence.
Overall, to me at least, one of the biggest selling points of this game is the small price. Compared to games that may give you a few hours for $60/£40, the genre of puzzle games in general far supersedes this. For less than $5/£3 the game successfully manages to deliver several hours of enjoyment to the player, and is excellent as a sort of brain-teaser.
The only things I would say this game fails in are: the lack of variety - you might expect some more puzzling elements to be introduced later on, but in general, it keeps getting harder. Additionally, there is little to no replay value, which can be a big factor to some people.
Overall, I would give this game an 8/10.

I got to a new area and finally found a pistol and a hatchet. Great. -Finally- some combat. I found some robots wandering. The combat was awful. Their AI is incredibly bad. I will say the one thing I liked was the atmosphere. They definitely got the creepiness down. I enjoyed hiding from the hot-air balloons with spotlights, but that was about it.

You control a team of inmates, guards, and crewmen that were held within the prison ship entering the orbit of a planet lost to the ages. Probably the coolest thing about the game is that every character in the game (idk about the special ones from the packs) has interactions with other characters. Survive three floors and you get to hear the whole story between the two PLUS they usually buff each other.

The game is trying to do surrealist horror, but really just fails. The cutscenes are pretentious and preachy meant to just tell us how bad the game is instead of letting the game speak for itself. No, we need the girls in-between going "oooh, this is so bad, uuugh. Why would God say that?" and it all builds to a non-climax that comes out of nowhere and goes nowhere.
The game-within-the-game is not horrifying. It just drops you straight into the surreal without any sense of contrast for the normal. There is no build to make it creepy or shocking, you're just dropped straight into the mix.
On the subject of the gameplay, I have to ask. Why is it garbage? The point in the story is that this is supposed to be built as some crappy bargain bin christian game, but it has the horrifying imagery right at the start so throw out the subtle build there.
And in the end, I have to ask: why buy this game for five dollars? For the horror? There is none. For the game? It sucks. For the artistic merit? You'd really have to define that, because if this is artistic, i can whip up something in the time it takes to play this game to rival it. For the amount of time, effort, and reason to play this game obviously took and gives, it should be free. Not on steam.
That said, there's some impressive pixel art in here. Totally think the developer could be part of a dev team working art.

Not really my thing anymore, but some might like it I suppose. I used to play it while it was published and hosted by Aeria Games.
Pros:
-Interesting Class and Job Systems
-Nice art style with low system requirements
-Fair amount features while still remaining simplistic
-In depth alchemy system for item crafting healing items and armor
-Nostalgic for older players
-Automatic looting settings for those in a party (dice roll based, but limited to only party members nearby, so the guy whose AFK on the other side of the map won't steal your materials)
-In depth guilds, with ranking system and guild base
-PvP combat via duel requests
-Reasonbly helpful customer support team
-Only a little over 1 GB of a game, quick to install and delete
Cons (inb4 "I personally enjoy it, so you're wrong!"):
-Poorly written (or at least poorly translated) main questline
-Servers for different countries are rarely used because they just join the US/Canada Server, there's a lot of people who barely even speak english (ie, just got PMed "are you want buy my saphire pet")
-Poor connection to servers, even with best connection speeds
-Character customization is limited
-Generic MehMO at it's core, with all the issues coming with it
-Pets are expensive but just as powerful as a player, usually breaking the PvP system (ie, Players summoning pets mid fight and running away)
-You spend most of the time AFK to either gather resources or selling the left overs you didn't need
-In game economy, with players choosing the prices of most items that you can't buy from NPCs (for better or worse)
-Low player base, most being either anti-social or rude, very few friendly faces until they need something from you
-Extremely few new players (people don't bother to turn on WASD movement in the settings, instead immediately quitting without even glancing in the controls)
-Slow experience gains past level 25, over level 35 and beyond and an agonizing grind-fest
-Alchemy made items have slight stat boosts compared to NPC bought versions, feeling over powered at higher level alchemy skills
-A lot of items can only be bought from players or in the cash shop for real money
-Developers are content in keeping the game the same (only bug fixed and item mall additions are ever added in updates), never anything new or game changing added
Final Score: Nostalgia/10 (I'd give it a 2.5/5 stars)

Here, there is a different time zone: our watch is an hour late.And here, suddenly, birds totally different from ours: kites with a large head and by the strong feathered legs they stand motionless on telegraph poles ; in the evening, gray owls flying over awkwardly and clumsily the road.The sun has become more cruel. Even the steppe has changed, it has disappeared lush vegetation:
It is red, parched, overgrown with wormwood and dusty weeds, dry and put Esparto who cowers against the cracked earth. Some oxen dragging carts, a camel is standing in the middle of the steppe. The Volga is approaching.
You physically feel the immensity of space invaded by the enemy, a terrible feeling of anguish grips the heart and even prevent you from breathing.
This war in the South, this war on the lower Volga, this feeling like a dagger deeply embedded in the flesh,
these camels and this flat steppe and parched, announcing the desert approaching, fill with anxiety.

I started this game thinking it would as simple as the other popular survival games.
I was horribly wrong.
This game will punish you if you don't know what your'e doing. You will fail a lot, but that is okay. That is how you learn how to suvive in this game. The game will push you really hard to continuously scavange for resources. The game is currently a sandbox game without campaign but there will be campaign mode in future. Some of the things that I like about this game are -
- The game heavily relies on scavenging resources. It's challenging to survive if you run out of food and do not roam around looking for resources. You can't stay in one place for long unless you have enough resources. But, it's pointless to stay in one place for long nonetheless.
- The game has no base building, except you can make a temporary shelter which is still vulnerable to wild animal attacks.
- If you get caught in Blizzard and do not find a shelter soon, you will either end up having hypothermia or even worse, frostbitten. You can't just make a campfire like you can do in some other survival games in the middle of a storm. Why? Because the wind won't let you. Pretty realistic.
- Maintaining a campfire while you get some water from the snow ain't easy if you don't have enough fuel.
- Inventory management is crucial. You can not just bring anything you want with you because it will slow you down. In fact, if you reach 60 kg, you will be unable to move.
- Hunting deer and rabbit is easy, wolf is..... well it's not hard, bear is challenging unless you have the rifle or gun. Ammo is hard to find and should be used wisely.
- Found a cabin with a lot of deers nearby? Thinking of spending several days in your favorite cabin? Get ready to deal with cabin fever.
- Found a fishing tackle? It broke during fishing? Thinking of crafting a new one? First, do some hunting, get animal guts from their carcass, cure the guts by leaving them indoors for several days, THEN you gonna get you materials ready.
- You got bear hides wolf hides and deer hides and now you gonna make the best clothes in the game ever so you won't have to worry about negative temperature anymore. Guess what? Crafting all these clothes will take days and you need sufficient water and food and rest so you don't fall. Got everything crafted finally? Now you would have to be careful not to get sweaty because of the warmth bonus from all the clothes. You might have to put some of these off if you are inside a house.
- Your precious weapons and clothes will decay over time if you don't repair them time to time.
The looks beautiful. It gets lonlely sometimes because of no NPCs. This game is very atmospheric. The game has no horror elements but it could feel creepy at times for no reason and the game looks really scary if you get caught in a heavy storm during night without any light source or shelter nearby. The game is really good to make you feel that you actually need something like food or water ASAP.
The only major problem with this game is performance. In certain areas, it is possible to get low fps in game. It even gets lower if you run the game for quite long and doesn't fix until you restart the game. Apart from the fps issue, I have found, so far, no other bugs or glitches.
If you want a survival game with challenges, then get this. If you are looking for something to play with your friends, then you better find another game because The Long Dark is meant to be played alone where you will know the meaning of solitude.

I'm not too sure why I keep coming back to this game, whether its the cold atmosphere that makes me feel colder (i live in Australia and don't like the temperature), or whether I'm coming back purely because being alone and not having other people ruin my experience, I'm glad that I keep coming back, because every time I do it feels better.. Like watching The Breakfast Club or Ghost Busters after years of mediocre and boring movies, and this is the same for The Long Dark. Frankly, I'm sick of trashy multiplayer games that have you spend your money to have an advantage over someone else, or games that are pumped out every few years by the same studios, that only really capture the satisfaction of 12 year olds and other people that generally wouldn't know better, but this, this is something else, it's like the Sherlock Holmes of Crime Movies, its like Halloween, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, the old classic movies that DEFINED the Horror genre, and when you put up Friday the 13th and The Nightmare on Elm Street against The Blob or Paranormal Activity, it makes you realise just how special this game is.. It makes you appreciate every detail of this game, from the brutal cold winds that blister you and wither you down, or the bloodthirsty wolves that roam endlessly outside of your base of operations until the moment you step outside, not realising you don't have flares or a rifle, and your 24 day life is ended, just because you wanted to get the Pacifist Achievement, that means nothing, but makes you feel like 24kt gold, and honestly, when you play this game, whether you're practically homeless or you're the head of multimillion dollar firm, you experience the same pain, same experiences and same menacing mechanics that want to destroy you.. and for that, I must say, Thankyou Hinterland, for creating a game that I can continously go back to and enjoy, just like the first time I played this, thankyou for creating a game thats inspired me so much, to spend my own time writing a (pretty pathetic)

This is my first review on Steam, even though I've been a member for 7 years... THAT'S why you should give this game a try. ;-)
I'm a fan of builder games and zombies, so when I saw a zombie game where I can build, I had to have it. I wasn't sure I would care as much for the gameplay, but it definitely gets addicting. I spent my first few tries in an easymode sandbox and still managed to die. The graphics actually suit me great, since I'm an old-school gamer and prefer it more simpler than newer games today have. The action is pretty much the same no matter what you do, but the way it goes down differs. You could lose your focus and walk into a bathroom without paying attention and a zombie will lunge at you from behind the door. You could turn a corner and walk right into a herd. You could be bashing a zombie in the head with a shovel and think you're winning, but a zombie out of your line of sight comes up from behind and you're now infected. I once survived for 3 months and had stocked up on everything to outlive a lifespan, and then fell from a roof I was building and died anyways. Why do I keep restarting after such heartbreak? It must be a good game!
I am excited for more updates on this game. We definitely could use more to build, more items throughout, and my most requested is different maps to explore. I'd love to not only have more maps to choose from, but maps that edge to another map.

I played a lot of zombieslasher/ survival games ( Left 4 dead, Resident Evil, 7 days to die, dying light, ...) so Project Zomboid seemed to be a good choice. It is supposed to fill the gap between crafting games and survival games but (in my opinion) fails in some important aspects.
After a fun character creation (profession, many ridicolous attributes to choose from: deaf, obese ...) and a difficulty choice you spawn in your apartment in an undead infested world. You explore a giant world with towns and forrests all the while defending yourself against zombies and the elements of nature. There is no hope of survival! (and thats the problem)
This is one of those games you think should be great but once you actually try it out, its just lackluster and a waste of time. Here is why:
You kill endless hordes of undead which all behave the same (some slower or faster but thats it) and look pretty similar after some time. This might be "classic zombie behaviour" but has to be counteracted by engaging and fun combat mechanics.
Its simply not fun to right click, then hold the attack until the zombie is in reach and release the mouse button. The zombie either stumbles and falls over or you have to walk backwards and repeat. Once its down simply stomp it to death.
This is fun  for like a hundred zombies and becomes a chore afterwards.
I dont mind killing zombie hordes after hordes in any other zombie game but somehow this game sucked the fun out of it. Even worse that the whole map is
with zombies and you have to waste many real life hours to clear an area. But then you wont meet a damn zombie there for a loong time since they only respawn when you leave area for a longer period of time.
Not even the guns can salvage the complete lack of zombie-slaying fun since they are hard to come by (good) but utterly useless since they alarm every zombie around. They are also clunky and require a high shooting skill to hit anything even in close proximity. You also have no real way of aiming with a crosshair, only general pointing and praying for a hit.
There are multiple weapons in this game: Pencils, knifes, axes, baseball bats, shotguns, pistol and lots more.
they mostly look literally the same (a lot of melee weapons look like the baseball bat) and handle pretty similar in combat.
Crafting seems exciting since you have they choice between hundreds of recipes (even generators which can power lamps or a fridge). But the amount of stuff you have to find until you can craft these things is huge and can take a long time of wandering around the map searching for random loot. The result is simply not worth the grind. The UI makes handling you inventory quite annoying and needs a serious overhaul.
The main reason i cant recommend this is the complete lack of motivation to actually survive. You gonna die anyway so why even hoard supplies or farm endlessly? L4d has saferooms and some kind of escape in the unknown. 7 days to die has huge building projects to undertake (also kind of pointless but still). Resident Evil, Dying Light and many other zombie games use a story line to keep the player engaged.
Project Zomboid has nothing but building youself a poor mans fort and play farmer till you get bored to death. Of course you can still have a lot of fun but simply imagining a story in your head but why take this from the devs shoulders? There is mainly one thing which would boost the stale gameplay: NPCs combined with some long term goal ( cure, Escape or whatever). This brings us to:
This game is in development for about 5 years and gets updates every few weeks but doesnt progress anymore. The recently addet TVs and radios dont even have sound! They just repeat the same written lines like in retro games (sounds in fallout 2 for example).
The developer essays are interesting to read at first but get annoying very soon. If there happens a major update which actually implements some kind of content apart from wandering the map, killing samey zombies and looting endless containers i will gladly update my review.
Until then i cannot recommend this game at all.

The Long Dark may be one of the most polished Early Access titles I have ever had the pleasure of playing.
Each difficulty level renders a different level of challenge for the player and gives the sensation of playing a completely different game. The easiest difficuty allows the player to wander and discover the handcrafted world at their leisure. With each increasing step up in difficulty, the game becomes less about exploring and more about desperate survival. The limited resources truly give the player a feeling of desperation and helplessness. Depending on what the player wants out of the game, the game can be as challenging as they want.
The art takes some getting used to but quickly becomes a very enjoyable viewing experience. I have spent a great deal of time simply taking screenshots every couple of minutes. Hinterland Studios has done a phenomenal job at building the world.
The sound design is top notch as well, roof tiles rattling in blizzards and snow crunching under your feet as you hike through the frozen fields. The character voices are also just present enough to remind the player of their basic needs without repeatng too often.
While it is still in early access, I would wholeheartedly recommend the game in its current state and with the quality of work so far, it can only get better from here.

Linear, boring, cliched and utterly dissapointing are the words which jump to mind. This FPS action title is the follow up to the hugely successful Red Faction: Guerilla, the open world masterpiece. Sadly, someone sitting in the finance department must have decided that the strings needed tightening and that they should pursue an on rails FPS, and everything went♥♥♥♥♥♥up from there sadly.
There should be a strong story here, which follows the Red Faction universe, but instead theres a shadow of a story and a ton of bugs. There should be a ton of destruction and some great hammer battles, but instead theres a limited field of a play to smash up and then little to no reason to whip out the hammer.
So the key question.. is this even worth purchasing? Honestly, the campaign is quite long and it's not the most awful game I've ever played, maybe. So I would suggest a purchase price of no more than £3.

This is by far the best WW2 FPS game I have ever played.
It's probably not a good idea to buy this game if you scare easily. Red Orchestra 2 is best described as a PTSD simulator - even in a victorious battle you will probably suffer at least one soul-devouring death. The only way to succeed in this game is to embrace the motto of "high risk, high reward." To embrace that motto means putting yourself in some horrible situations... every veteran RO2 player knows the adrenaline rush of being trapped behind enemy lines, completely cut off from reinforcements and fighting viciously for survival. It is something that you have to experience for yourself, it's badass.
This game can be INCREDIBLY immersive, especially when the voice-chat is used as intended (for tactical reasons, rather than by trolls mic-spamming). Unfortunately the RO2 community has an unusually high number of mic-spammers due to the integrated voice-chat, if you choose to join this community just make sure you don't join in with idle chit-chat over VOIP.
It is a beautiful thing to be part of a team that is actually functioning AS A TEAM - it's even better when the enemy team is functioning properly as well because the true potential of this game only reveals itself when you are being challenged by your foe. It is often more interesting to play for the "underdog" team against any "stacked" teams because you are really forced to play at a higher level. Red Orchestra 2 is ALL about rising to the challenges, that is what makes it great.
Overall, Red Orchestra 2 rewards the cunning and the daring. It is the type of game that you can lose an entire day playing without even realising until you notice the sky outside has gone dark. There is a steep learning curve but when you make improvements to your playstyle, you reap the rewards.

While Zomboid is a great game for anyone who likes hardcore survival games, one aspect I'd like to talk about is the multiplayer. This game has something that I've never seen before in other zombie survival games. This game encourages you to team up with others and support eachother. Sure, there are people who will kill you for your stuff, but I have never met any. I think that this is because of how realistic the game is.
Keep in mind that this is a game where broken bones and injuries take a pretty long time to heal, and you don't just bounce back. Additionally, food and weapons are not readily available in multiplayer. It gets to the point where the game is so hard that teaming up with others is an obviously wise move, compared to murdering them for the rare chance that they have a weapon or food. What I'm saying is that this game often makes you think like you're in an actual zombie apocalypse situation, where people are worth more than just what items they have.
Once I fell out of a two story building's window and ended up breaking a leg. Remember, Project Zomboid is not a game where mending broken bones and injuries just means slapping on a bandage. Broken bones are supposed to take weeks to heal in this game. And to add insult to literal injury, broken bones make you slower than a sloth. Luckily, I was with other people, but without them, I would have been easily a meal for zombies.
My point is that if you enjoy realistic and difficult zombie survival games, where the emphasis is on surviving, and not killing other survivors, then by all means, do get this game.

For quite some time I have been avoiding this franchise like the plague given that it’s fanbase seems like they’re all prepubescent and utterly annoying. Five Nights at Freddy’s is a point-and-click, survival horror game from Scott Cawthon. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
I was pleasantly surprised by the intensely creepy atmosphere in the game. Despite the main mechanic of terror being jump scares, it actually works in the game’s favor by creating a continuously increasing feeling of stress and apprehension.
The lore and setting and both pretty solid and fun to learn more about throughout the course of the game.
The guy who calls in at night to (essentially) tell you how to play the game really jacks up the anxiety factor to 11. When you first get into the game, you’ve been given no tutorial on how to play and you’re fumbling around with the mouse trying to figure things out. By night number two, when helpful former employee on the phone tells you that the cameras have blind spots that are on either side of the room your in,♥♥♥♥♥♥starts to get real, man.
The Bad
Personally, I felt like the total amount of power that you’re given to use throughout the night drains waaaaaaaay too quickly.
The Meh
I’m actually going to talk more about this section following the verdict. It will just tie in better that way, I think.
Verdict: Yea
Five Nights at Freddy’s, despite it’s hordes of squeaky-voiced fans, is a fun horror game. As I mentioned up top, the lore for the game is rather intriguing. Now, I’ve done some research and (with the exception of the latest release in the franchise) it looks like FNaF installments 2 through 4, are mostly more of the same. I’m sure that’s all fine and well for some, but, only adding a few new features here and there just doesn’t cut it in my book. By using the same medium of gameplay for every game, the developer is really doing the lore of FNaF a disservice. Here’s to hoping that Sister Location takes the franchise forward.

The game's systems are too simple and the meaningful choices you have to make are to few and far between for the sandbox to hold any long term enjoyment.  The game is either monotonously easy, or frustratingly difficult, with the difficulty coming from the restrictiveness of the mechanics and a lack of the ability to improvise, not any actual challenge.  I rarely feel like I've made good decisions because there are virtually no decisions to make.  The majority of the game boils down to- Is there anything I can use here? and-  Can I safely travel to the next place with something to use yet?
The lack of meaningful choices due to the simplistic nature of the gameplay kills any long term enjoyment because there's nothing to do or strive for in the sandbox mode.  You're either playing on a difficulty where everything falls into your lap or entire houses will have a single can of soup in them.  The problem with the higher 'difficulty' is that the simple systems don't allow for any improvisation.  You either have the item you need, or you don't.  Here's a fun example-
I'm attempting to transition to a new zone while playing on the highest difficulty because there is only the aformentioned single can of soup, single pair of mittens, or single box of matches, etc for each individual building, and I'm starving and freezing to death just sitting around an empty zone.  Traveling to the next area requires me to traverse a cave system.  My only light source is 8 matches (because that's all I could find in an entire town).  Sure, I have a bunch of twigs, a few pieces of reclaimed wood, plenty of newspaper, and some lamp oil, however, I can't IMPROVISE a torch out of any of these things.  I'm 0.02 L short of lamp oil to be allowed to craft a proper torch.  I can't just light the newsprint or any of the wood on fire for a lower quality light source.  I'm not allowed to start a fire 'indoors' in the cave.  I can't start a fire outside in the raging blizzard to pull a flaming brand from.  So I'm left using my only firestarting materials, my matches, as a terrible light source because that's all the game allows for.
My choices are needlessly restrictive despite having plenty of flammable items, but this follows through to virtually every other system in the game.  Want a knife?  Well, you better find one (which you can't on the highest difficulty, at all, they don't spawn, you must craft one) because there's only one place in the game you can even make one.  Got a hacksaw, scrap metal, some wood, a whetstone and access to a workbench with a vice?  Oh well.  There's no way to say, sacrifice some extra time and calories to make a makeshift knife.  You need the one forge in the game in order to make metal sharp.  And on top of that you need specific items that serve no other purpose to do that.
Don't have a hammer?  Well, there's no way to improvise using something else at the cost of time or effeciency.
Want a torch?  Better have the one type of allowable wood and minimum amount of oil required.
Want to open that can of soup?  A hacksaw capable of sawing through metal shelves is incapable of doing it.
Want to craft a coat?  Only if you have wolf pelts.
Want some gloves?  Only with rabbit skins.
Improvise a scarf with some house curtains or a towel?  Not happening.
Use a blanket, pillows, and sewing kit to make a bedroll?  Nope, gotta find one. (Also, it hasn't happened to me, but I'm fairly certain you can die from not being able to sleep due to not having access to a bedroll or bed, despite being satiated, warm, and indoors.  "Sleep on the floor?  Like an animal?!  I'd rather die!")
Want a prybar?  Well, you better find one, because there's no way to cut any of the metal shelfs into something resembeling a makeshift prybar (nor can anything else substitute for a prybar.  I can reduce a metal shelf to a pile of scrap with a hacksaw, but can't use it to get into a metal locker.)
There's no meaningful choices to make.  There's no improvisation to be had.  Sacrifice your extra coat so that you can use a sewing kit and some free time to make gloves you can't find?  Nope.  Risk damaging your hacksaw in order to open something that requires a prybar?  Nope.  Spend extra time and calories to improvise a knife out of scrap metal and a whetstone?  Nope.
The systems are too rigid for the entirely sandbox (at this point in time) nature of the game, especially for a survival game.  It's too frustrating to be a drop of oil and the wrong type of wood away from being able to make a source of light not to mention any of the countless other ridiculous scenarios you'll find yourself shaking your head at.
A few other gripes, there a now perks which after having ran for 10km or survived for 100 days give you stat bonuses to make the game easier.  Wut?  You'd think by the point you've done any of those things, a minor stat increase is borderline pointless.  Seems like some grindy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to attempt to keep you playing.
Tons of new clothing has been added as well, however, none of it adds to the gameplay.  Clothing is either better than what you currently have, or it isn't.  Again, there are no meaningful choices to be made.  There are stats like mobility and damage reduction, but they occur in 1-3% points and a virtually negligble.  I didn't even noticed them til looking at the wiki.  There's nothing that provides a meaningful choice like a big heavy, waterproof jacket that I would bother to carry around and change into only in certain weather.  You're just going to wear the best clothing you have available.  Nothing exists with meaningful trade-offs.  Again- THERE ARE VIRTUALLY NO MEANINGFUL CHOICES TO MAKE
Don't get me wrong, I've wrung 160 hours of gameplay out of the game, but there's either no challenge or a rigid brick wall of not having the EXACT thing you need because the item spawns on the higher 'difficulties' have been reduced to virtually nothing.
You're supposed to be an experienced bush pilot surviving in the wilderness, when in reality you play a simpleton incapable of lighting a rolled up newspaper on fire.
If you've made it this far, I'm not entirely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the game, in fact I've gifted two copies of it to friends.  The game just hasn't had any of its gameplay sastistfyingly expanded on, despite 2 years of development.  Once you've seen all the areas, there's nothing to do anymore but settle into a boring routine of surviving (or dying on the higher difficulty because there are no items).   If I can be set for life with all the best equipment on day 20, why would I continue to play for another 80 game days?
If this was a Michael Bay it would be a very good explosion.

Since its release, THQ and Volition have done everything in their power to try and bring people back to the Red Faction series with very little avail. When you make a game that is a smash success it has to be hard to replicate that success in the form of sequels, which were obviously created, but were a major bust in the eyes of people who actually followed the games since day one including myself.
Volition's fourth attempt in the series is coined Red Faction: Armageddon. Now the subtitle may be a reference to where the story intends to go within the game, but it would also be a good way to describe the game itself. The story begins on Mars in the distant future; just like all others have before it. You play as Darius Mason; a Red Faction member and the grandson of Alec Mason who was the protagonist in Red Faction: Guerrilla in the year 2120. 50 years have passed since the liberation of colonies from the Earth Defense Force. As Darius, you must face off against a new enemy who is trying to destroy stability on the planet and make it uninhabitable to humans. By using terrorist attacks on the Terraformer which provides oxygen and atmosphere to the planet, he is slowly succeeding. The man responsible for all of this is known as Adam Hale. Adam is a cultist leader for the Marauders. This group of mercenaries was converted by him into his own personal army.
After the attack on the Terraformer, you are led to believe that Adam was killed during the explosion which brought the Terraformer crumbling to the ground. Everyone with common sense or awareness of the cliches which are in nearly all movies and games can already tell exactly where this is headed within the first 10 minutes of play. Everyone has been forced underground as a result of these events, which have made the surface of the planet a wasteland. Violent storms, lack of oxygen and mega tornados are what greet people at the surface so obviously a great deal of this game will take place in a linear underground environment. While all the population of Mars is being forced under the surface, a deadly plague strikes which is killing everyone. It is your job to find out what has caused this and who is responsible.
In terms of the story, it is hardly anything riveting or interesting for that fact; and leaves you wondering why you are even playing the game at all. From the beginning, you know exactly where things are going, no suspense, no mystery, just destroy everything and kill everyone until it ends. If you have played the original Red Faction, you will find yourself again questioning this game. What does this really have to do with the first game? Why are people still on Mars if everything has been so terrible three times before? The last but not least; why is everyone trying to either destroy the planet or control it in a totalitarian fashion? Obviously it has worked out so great three previous times why not give it another shot; 4th times a charm right? This series has become a joke. They took something pure and perfect then ruined it by changing the formula until nearly every identifiable shred of the original game no longer existed.
These problems started mainly with Guerrilla, carry over into Armageddon, which added a few more to boot. For the love of god choose a camera and stick to it. The series went from First Person, to a Third Person 360° viewable camera to now a Third Person shoulder locked camera; like I said earlier, formula destroyed. Geo-Mod 2.0-2.5 are again a step in the wrong direction, in the original game you could destroy practically everything, including terrain to make your own paths or find ways around obstacles. This has been severely dialed back, and I am not even sure how it can be dignified with a version 2.0 or 2.5 branding aside from it being the engine name. The only things which can be destroyed are man-made objects, no terrain. While the destruction is impressive, it is all ruined by shooting a wall and not even a scratch showing up.
Hold onto your pants because the bad does not stop there. Where are all the vehicles you could pilot in all previous games? There are vehicles all over this game but none you can drive? Really? It's kind of a slap in the face to be honest, but this comes back to changing the formula. However, they did make a wise decision and reverted back to the roots of the game being linear. The whole Red Faction/Grand Theft Auto open world concept that Guerrilla attempted to do was just too weird and turned a lot of people off; that would explain their logic for Armageddon.
After reading all that is wrong with it let's get to some things which are good and alright. The game looks fantastic in nearly every way, crisp textures, DirectX 11 effects and amazing use of physics on the destruction, the presentation is overall great. With the nice boost in visuals you will also notice some new modes, features and an updated arsenal of weapons. There are two new modes, and they are incorporated very well. The first mode is Ruin. You have a set time to destroy the most structures possible and must obtain a certain score to achieve the next level. There is some replayability to this, but it is stunted by the lack of total levels. The second mode which has been incorporated is Infestation, it is similar to Nazi zombies in CoD and Killing Floor.
You must kill wave after wave of enemies on each level. Some are purely survival and others are defense so you must protect structures from being destroyed. Each level has up to 30 waves to survive. This works out great and is a fun way for friends to play whether it be through the Internet or Lan; there is a lot of replayability here. Conventional multiplayer is something that has been scraped completely, for how this game is I think that was a smart move. If it were still a first-person shooter it would need this to compete with the others; but as it stands it's not something necessary.
The game play is fun in its own right. Very standard Third Person Shooter combat mixed with a Gears of War type cover system. What it does, it does fairly well but the mediocrity of it makes you feel as if you have played this game before. The mix of weapons keeps things pretty interesting. You have a choice of about 10 weapons ranging from just your standard shotgun all the way up to a singularity cannon which creates black holes and engulfs nearby structures. Using the varied weapons can be fun and finding new ways to kill or destroy with them is mainly what the game is about.
Probably the biggest highlight to the entire game is the Path to War DLC. This takes place hours before the events which bring down the Terraformer. The great thing about this is it allows you to actually use the vehicles and play as both sides. It definitely gives a fresh perspective to the game. I would recommend playing this before starting the campaign. With about 45 minutes of game play this makes for an overall nice addition to the game, but I don't think it is exactly worth the money.
All in all, Red Faction: Armageddon is not a terrible game on its own. I hope that is not something I conveyed here. It is a terrible game in terms of it living up to the original which can be said about Red Faction 2 & Guerrilla also, but for what they all do, comparisons aside, they are interesting gaming experiences on their own. If you are looking for a game with deep story, gameplay which is enthralling from beginning to end or something that you will have fond memories of as you get older; this game is not for you. If you want a game which is fun to jump into and blow things up periodically for 20 to 30 minutes at a time without paying attention to what is really going on; this is absolutely for you. Consider it a destruction simulator with a cliched and somewhat boring story to go with it, and you will have the time of your life.

Let me start off by saying that I hated Guerilla. I gave it at least 3 separate tries and on each occasion I felt dumber and dumber playing it. The game had huge and bland lifeless environments similar to Far Cry 2 canyon-like map only with no vegetation. The Martian physics were also something that I just couldn't get used to; the game introduced the seemingly unnecessary destruction of everything even of civilian buildings; there was the un-tactical running and shooting gameplay even though there were some guerrilla type raids involved; ultimately most missions turned into run and shoot mess.
I had slight hopes for this game because I was hoping that the linear single player story would at least be something to enjoy.
Well, as for gameplay, this is a regular run'n'shoot BUT have-the-ability-to-destroy-everything game. There is no cover to speak of, and there's no ability to take cover and for a good reason - everything goes. That is, taking cover behind a wall will result in the wall being destroyed so you would attempt to kill the enemy before he or it kills you after blowing your cover, literally. There is no real tactical movement required - just keep on shooting and moving and you will most likely win.
As you descend deeper into the Martian caves you will encounter aliens. For the most part you are going to be battling angry insectoids, small roaches, giant roaches and some other disgusting creatures including huge mean looking worms. There's some suspense to have as you go deeper and deeper into caves and the CGI cut scenes are pretty cool however, this suspense is quickly dispensed by hordes of insects swarming you from every direction throughout the game. From that point on, the game pretty much becomes a giant insect fest comprised of killing as many bugs using different weapons as well as the environment before they get you. I think I've seen this somewhere, dare I say Lost Planet 2? Only that game had co-op.
Besides, for some reason, you will constantly encounter the ammo for your guns even in the deepest caves where no man has set foot. You will never run out of ammo because the ammo caches are spread out in almost every direction.
The portable computer system that you have, SAM, is reminiscent of the Dead Space navigation pointer, except this time, SAM has a voice and it tells you what to do constantly. You don't really have to think or wander around caves because the SAM guiding system will tell you where to go. The game practically plays by itself.
The weapons are okay. We have the usual guns as well as magnet gun that connects point A and B- this gives you the opportunity to hurl objects from point A at enemies that are located at point B. You can also destroy entire multiple story buildings and constructions with one placed shot.
The graphics are great, the DX 11 and all. The water looks okay and for the most part the environments are well detailed. The aliens are sometimes revolting to look at too.
You do have the ability to break through walls as well as re-construct virtually every man made structure via your molecular reconstructor or whatever, which is neat, but extremely unrealistic. So, in the end you end up with great looking engine that actually lets you destroy just about everything but at the same time lets you fix pretty much everything. Take that for what it's worth. There are also some weapon and skill upgrades you can buy with your easily earned credits.
I guess the biggest disappointment is the gameplay. You just want to keep running and shooting without looking back. Or you DO look back only to shoot up some chasing insectoids while keeping on running.
There are no invisible walls in the game but some battles requires you to stay within a set sector without having the ability to retreat. Thus you are given 10 seconds to get back into battle...
The game is also extremely easy, even on Hard. The health regenerates within a few seconds. The game itself runs smoothly though and the controls for your character are fluid. You will be able to move fast and avoid being hit.
All in all, buy the game at bargain.

Hats off to you sirs and madames. This game is a bloody awesome spectacle of jiggery pokery. What what, cheerio, hip hip hooray for "Sir, You are Being Hunted." Graphics are a little ole school, circa 2007-ish. But what it lacks in sleek modern graphics it more than makes up for in addictive fun. Somewhat of a typical stealth game, but unique in its presentation. The complete lack of supplies makes this the ultimate challenge. You start with a handful of items, you pretty much have to figure out how things work for yourself, and you find so much useless junk that an empty bottle or rock you can throw suddenly becomes a great treasure. OMG, when you find an axe or a gun it's like the most epic loot ever.
Basically you are a human (I think) trapped on a weird set of RANDOMLY GENERATED islands. How awesome is that for replayability. You look for these glowing meteorite-like rocks, then you have to lug them back to a certain location. So, no treasure hording, which I have to admit is very hard for an OCD dungeon sweeper like myself. You are constantly being hunted by clockwork robots with red glowing eyes, robot dogs, some weird stilt like creature, big ole robot constables, and more. You can stand and fight if you have weapons, but most of the time you have to use cunning and skill to sneak around them, distract them, or even lure them.
Quite simply one of the better stealth games I have ever played. Simple, yet challenging. I grabbed it on sale for a pittance. But I would have gladly paid the full $20 if I had known it would be this much fun. I would easily put this up there with Thief, Dishonored, or any of the bad♥♥♥♥♥♥stealth games.

BioShock is a singleplayer-only and linear FPS released in 2007 and is often praised for being a masterpiece. But does it meet one's expectations or does it feel overrated?
BioShock has a unique art style, 60s music and a special libertarian underwater setting in a city called Rapture. It's using a lot of philosophical expressions unheard of in any other game, which is great. The problem with the way the game is designed is that we never got to see Rapture before it had been destroyed. You just arrive and it's already in ruins. It's the same thing with the story. The story is the most praised aspect of the game and it has its moments, but most of the background story is told via old tapes that are about things happening we are never about to see. Everything has happened before. This game design is mind-bogging to me. What a waste of an opportunity!
My biggest gripe I have with this game are the big daddies and little sisters. Basically, it goes like this: big daddies are huge mechanical dudes in deep sea diving suits that are mostly brainless and whose job is to defend the little sisters. Little sisters are little girls that are in danger of the splicers that are basically crazy junkies and want that sweet drug called adam that is in little sister's bodies. BTW, the sisters are crazy, too. You got the idea. I played through every Bioshock game and I never could get into this concept.
The second gripe I have with this game is the combat. You are mostly fighting slicers whose character model look horrible and have nothing interesting to say. They are drug addicts, crazy, act all the same and lack of any real depth. Fighting big daddies is like little boss fights, which wasn't that bad except that I didn't like their concept. My most hated enemy might be the flying robot though. In a dark-themed game that wants to be taken seriously the robots just don't fit.
There are two major twists in the game. While one twist was highly predictable from the get go, the other one is kind of hidden. Not sure if that makes it worthwhile to play though. The combat certainly isn't.
++ Unique setting about libertarianism
+ Unique art style
+ Good songs from the 60s
+ You can upgrade your weapons and skills
+ The game is still mostly decent looking
+ Some memorable moments
+ Cohen was interesting
-- Major technical issues due to being a poor console port. In example there is no audio when the headset isn't pluged in, capped animations and physics at 30 FPS, mouse acceleration and low FOV default settings with no slider to adjust it.
- Enemy type variety isn't high enough
- gunplay is not fun
- Story is mostly told in audio logs. While I appreciate audio logs here and there, the story shouldn't be only told, but also more often SHOWN.
- Ugly faces
- While the story itself isn't bad, I didn't like the big daddies and little sisters
- You can't use your plasmids (somekind of magic) on your one hand and your gun on the other like in BioShock 2.
- hacking mini-game is horrible
- a lot of boring fetch quests
- stealth is too simplistic
The first thing you'll need to fix are the 30 FPS physics and animation cap, the fov and the mouse acceleration. Those things are horrible for a FPS and I can't believe I have to download and edit some stuff to fix this game. Don't even bother to play the game without them.
Replay value: Low (since gameplay isn't really fun and the game is linear)
Rating: 6/10. It's an average game.
Recommendation: No (except if you are digging that big daddy and little sister concept)

This is by far the best WW2 FPS game I have ever played.
It's probably not a good idea to buy this game if you scare easily. Red Orchestra 2 is best described as a PTSD simulator - even in a victorious battle you will probably suffer at least one soul-devouring death. The only way to succeed in this game is to embrace the motto of "high risk, high reward." To embrace that motto means putting yourself in some horrible situations... every veteran RO2 player knows the adrenaline rush of being trapped behind enemy lines, completely cut off from reinforcements and fighting viciously for survival. It is something that you have to experience for yourself, it's badass.
This game can be INCREDIBLY immersive, especially when the voice-chat is used as intended (for tactical reasons, rather than by trolls mic-spamming). Unfortunately the RO2 community has an unusually high number of mic-spammers due to the integrated voice-chat, if you choose to join this community just make sure you don't join in with idle chit-chat over VOIP.
It is a beautiful thing to be part of a team that is actually functioning AS A TEAM - it's even better when the enemy team is functioning properly as well because the true potential of this game only reveals itself when you are being challenged by your foe. It is often more interesting to play for the "underdog" team against any "stacked" teams because you are really forced to play at a higher level. Red Orchestra 2 is ALL about rising to the challenges, that is what makes it great.
Overall, Red Orchestra 2 rewards the cunning and the daring. It is the type of game that you can lose an entire day playing without even realising until you notice the sky outside has gone dark. There is a steep learning curve but when you make improvements to your playstyle, you reap the rewards.

The positive reviews that convinced me to give it a try claim that this game is misunderstood satire. What they don't say is that it's bad, poorly made, and glitchy as hell "satire" (let's be honest though, this is not satire, this is a parody). Even its puzzles are a laugh (to a point where one could theorize that maybe it wasn't intended as a parody of the vampire genre but of HOGs -hidden object games- in general).
Yes, it has a couple of funny moments here and there and yes, it's real cheap, but that doesn't make it a good game that's worth your time.
If you get it at it's current sale price (0,09 cents) you won't lose any money, since it has trading cards, but again, this doesn't make it a good game, just an affordable one.
If you like over-the-top, absurd comedies that feature vampires and don't mind glitches that could prevent you from finishing the game, then yes, it's worth it. You'll get a couple of chuckles and I have to admit, a funny HOG is a rare and refreshing thing. But that's about it.
I am tempted to give it a thumbs-up for it's campy glory, but it has some of the worst glitches I've ever seen in HOGs and that's one of the biggest faux-pas a game of this genre can have. I can stand bad art, bad or non existent voice acting, a flimsy plot and random fetch quests. But I have to be able to play the game, to say that it's at least mediocre, don't you think?

The Red Faction franchise has always been about the one gimmick that made the game so noteworthy; the impressive "Geomod" technology that lets you rework the levels around you. Its odd then that in the latest title of the series Volition seems so reluctant to let me play with this gimmick in any meaningful way. Oh sure, I can bash down buildings and then instantly rebuild them with my "nano-forge" but the structures I take apart are all cosmetic frippery. The core of the game revolves instead around the stock weapons and the endless horde of generic aliens it throws at you.
Bereft of the Geomod technology, Red Faction Armageddon is an below-average shooter, with the usual bevy of cliche characters and the standard nonsensical plot (the latter doubtlessly assisted by the fine writers of the SyFy channel, who underwrote this sequel). The graphics - horribly shuttered by a 45 degree FOV - were surprisingly unimpressive for a DirectX 11 game. The only time the game rose from the abyss of mediocrity were in the handful of instances when it opened up a little bit and let me truly experience the effectiveness of the Geomod tech. But these were too infrequent to save the game from its fear of its own uniqueness and by the end of the game I was overwhelmed by overwhelming ennui.

My first review, I don't do reviews but this game and its developers are just so wrong, I feel like I have to give the word out. Let me start by saying I had to pay 70 bucks when this game launched. There's a TDLR, you can skip to that at the bottom. Now let's go to the pros.
PROS:
Good graphics
That's pretty much it, the concept of the game is not new. Instead of the 4vs4 like they did in their l4d series they made it a 1v4, which inevitably introduces a lot of balancing issues. We'll go further into that in the cons.
CONS:
-Balancing
The monster will always win unless you get the rare ones that don't play monster. You'll need 4 above average-play level hunters to stand a chance. That doesn't mean 4 good hunters will win, it just means they will have a better chance to win. The devs talked about the changes they will make in the new patch to balance these issues, but they have not sent the patch out and it's probably have been close to a month, instead they introduced 4 new hunters instead and charged you 24 bucks for them.
-Population
The population as of March 23, 2015 is lower than their predecessor series, l4d. The avg population is not even close to the avg population of l4d2. Every 3 pub games I play, I can point out a player I have already played with earlier that day.
-Replayability
At the 50 hour mark, this is actually stretching it, you'll have played through this game's content and the game will get repetitive real fast. One of the reason it gets boring is because of balancing, you'll either lose as hunters with the few wins against the goliath, you stumble upon a good pub team and win some games against the kraken and wraith, or you'll just constantly win as monster. I win like 99% of my game as monster, and if I feel like an♥♥♥♥♥I can play wraith, which most players will just leave before the game starts. Unlike the left 4 dead series the replayability factor comes from competition, and evolve's 1vs4 introduces too many balancing issues that the 4vs4  l4d counterpart doesn't have. Compound it with the developers' lack of care or commitment to balancing you'll have a very monotonous one sided match every game. Which is probably one of the reasons why this game's population in such a critical state, no one likes losing especially when they can't do anything about it. I also played with premades, you'll win more games with premade. You'll have to play on a premade if you don't want to get dumpstered, especially against a wraith/kraken.
-Matchmaking
You'll have an option to rank what role you want to play the most, either as any of the 4 hunter classes or the monster before you que into the game. But that won't mean anything since the matchmaking system just fills you in on a game that has a open spot. So like 99% of the time you're just playing the part of filling roles. Most of the time you'll end up in the middle of a game where you're filling a role for a rager. The matchmaking system will not start a new lobby or will let you have the option to start a new lobby game unless you have a friend playing with you, which sometimes they will split you up as one playing monster and one playing on hunters. Coming from the devs that made l4d2 that has such a better match making system, evolve's match making feels shoddy and like it's made on the fly at best. Fast forward 2 months later, now compound that with the small population it has, the ques are much longer now unless you're playing at peak hours, but at least most of the time now, you can get the role that you actually have on your preferences.
-One game mode
There's no single player as in no campaign mode for a $70+ game. Which means all its content should be from its multiplayer. There's basically one mode where you hunt the monsters, and monster eats and evade until its level 2 or 3 then fights back. There are other modes that are just a variation of that like nest, rescue, and defence but they are all overly unbalanced favoring the monster which leads to barely anyone playing those modes. There is also ai which you can play by yourself against the ai, I guess? Let's be honest here ai isn't exactly great, we all know that, but the ai in evolve is even worst, the monster is too complex for an ai since you have to be sneaky and attack at the right time, and when you're against ai hunters, yea.... that's cake walk. Cuphead is a pretty damn good game. It's a 2D platformer shooter that attempts to emulate the style of a 1930s cartoon (and nails it), in both its art and sound. The levels are mostly boss fights, but there are some regular platforming levels, although personally, I found the platforming levels to be one of Cuphead's few downsides.
The bosses are fantastic. The art and attacks are very creative and they're not too easy or too hard (for the most part), although at points, some of the bosses feel misplaced. For example, some bosses later on in the game are more difficult than bosses earlier on in. They vary between platforming and side-scrolling shooter based fights, all with a unique essence that separates them from the other bosses, testing you with several different types of challenges, such as being able to dodge and hit an enemy at the same time, or evading hazards while an enemy pushes you towards them with wind.
A problem I've found, however, is getting a perfect run on some of the bosses on the hardest difficulty can be unfair. Not because of a high difficulty, but sometimes because of RNG that can sometimes make it impossible to hit the parry requirement, such as a certain boss from the 3rd Island. But this is all optional, and as far as just beating bosses is concerned, I'm 99.9% anyone could beat the entire game on its hardest difficulty without dying no matter how random elements play out in the boss fights.
Basically, play this game. It is really good, although I find that people have exaggerated its difficulty quite a bit. It's challenging, but considering that you have as many attempts to beat any boss or level as you want, I find them to be incredibly manageable and fair.

Pros:
*Varying enemy types are quite interesting and their introductions are well-paced throughout the game (this can be configured to the player's specifications - I speak mainly of the default settings)
*Combat is balanced well enough - meaning that you while you can pick off a group of two or three hunters, anything more is a fool's errand and will attract too much attention in any case, forcing you to be stealthy for the majority of the game
*The game's atmosphere is great for creating tense moments, especially when hiding or evading pursuit
*Limited save system is effective in making you carefully consider any risks you take
Cons:
*The game gets repetitive by the third island - you won't change your playstyle much once you've got a gun, ammo, food
*Fragment placement can be quite stupid - one of the perils of a procedurally generated game - I found that often, fragments would spawn within sight of island entry points, incredibly near each other, or in one jaw-clenching instance, in an inccessible location, forcing me to abandon my first run, and on the very last fragment to boot
*Fragment detector makes the game go way too fast - starting with one on my second run after the aforementioned doomed run made that run last under two hours
*Survival elements may as well not exist - I never had to cook meat on a bonfire and was never in any sort of danger of running out of food, even with bare minimum scrounging
*Distraction items were never useful enough to let me avoid a fight at a guarded fragment
*While the game mechanics are robust enough to pull off many sneaky tricks (allowing the Squires to fight for you, setting and baiting traps for unwary robots, setting bonfires to draw attention away from guarded areas) none of them are really more practical than finding a good hiding place, waiting until there's only two guards and/or a dog, attracting their attention, strafing to avoid their first two shots, then giving them a buckshot sandwich while they reload, grabbing the fragment, and running away
Overall? It's worth the time I put into it, just don't expect to get more than 4-5 hours out of it. Buy it on sale or in a bundle.

There are quite a few annoying technicalities such as mouse acceleration, fov limitations, and 30 fps locked physics.  Thankfully, all of these can be fixed with .ini file tweaks and mods.  I have a 144 hz monitor, and there is a free mod for Bioshock that unlocks the frame rate of the physics to whatever you want to set it to.  Also, I forced antialiasing through the NVidia control panel (every single type at max settings), and I was still able to get way above 144 fps with a GTX 1080.
I would recommend doing these tweaks yourself (just type in Bioshock PC tweaks into google) rather than playing the remastered version.  The remastered version, from what I hear, doesn't fix any of the already mentioned technical issues, and it is actually very unstable and can delete all your save files (which you can easily back up, I might add).

Outlast is a great horror game. The following review covers setting, gameplay, story, graphics as well as presentation. Warning, may contain minor spoilers!
Outlast's setting is an abandoned asylum called Mount Massive - this sounds like a too classic scenario, but Red Barrels was flawlessly able to use this as a background base for their game. The asylum is a well-designed place which has a very terrifying atmosphere, especially in the beginning.
The gameplay is often quite simple: You as Miles Upshur have to discover the secrets of the so-called Murkoff corporation which has leaded the asylum since 2009 after a tragedy. You're a journalist, simply equipped with a camcorder with a night vision mode which consumes batteries. These are the main important objects to find in the levels because you'll need the night vision to navigate through dark locations. You can also find notes which give you backstory information, but you can also record sertain events with your cam to get info.
However the main point of this game is that you're not a fighter. You cannot defend yourself! If enemies are in an area you have to sneak around them or hide under beds or other hiding spots. And sometimes if you're hunted you have to run away from several scum through quite linear areas. In general the game is really linear and at some point a bit frustrating because it is kind of a trial-and-error thing sometimes. But in general for me it was a really exciting experience.
The story itself is quite unclear especially at the beginning and you have to read several documents to get the gist. I personally love that kind of telling like for example the indie title The Forest does but I can also understand people being disappointed about the storytelling in general. An example: you as Upshur are often hunted through several levels by an old fat variant soldier called Walker who patrols an area - for no real reason - and there you have to activate a few ventils in this area he's patroling. In general, the objectives are quite simple and not that innovative.
But the story itself has also memorable characters like Chris Walker or Father Martin, a kinda-of-christian-sectian pater who is quite important for the main plot as well as Richard Trager, a doctor who ... well, you'll find out for yourself. Bur the characters will surely remain in memorial.
Outlast is a horror game with great atmosphere and especially terrifying in the beginning. However from time to time it becomes a bit less scary (personal experience). The game uses quite classic jumpscares which are well-set/-used. The game itself is quite linear and has a playtime around ~5 hours. The graphics of this game are still really good and help creating that good atmosphere this game has.
Outlast also contain gore and sexual content so have fun with that :D
However, good job, Red Barrels, great horror game.

A pure realistic survival game in Northwestern Canada. The gameplay revolves around maintaining four status meters: Temperature, Fatigue, water, and Food. Completely depleting any of the meters begins draining health at different rates--you can survive for maybe a week without food or sleep, but you will die within hours if you are freezing, and days without water. You must explore to find food, tools, and raw materials to stay alive. The game ends whenever you make a mistake serious enough to get yourself killed, such as getting lost on a frozen lake in a blizzard, and freezing to death before you can find the shore, or being attacked by a wolf and bleeding out before you can bandage and disinfect the wound. Even if you play a perfect game, After a several months, tools and clothing begin to wear out, as you begin to run out of the resourses to maintain them. Eventually, you will run out of matches, and can only start fires with a magnifying glass outdoors in good sunlight.
Gameplay is generally slow and methodical. Inventory and resourse management in a major component of the game. The game autosaves your progress, and permadeath makes every decision during exploration potentially fatal. However, the game is easy enough for a casual player to learn and enjoy, but offers challenges for more serious gamers, especially at the higher difficulties.
One concern I have is with infrequent game breaking bugs. This game is in early access and has improved in the few months I played it, but I lost a save file after 130 days in-game and had another save file become so glitchy that it was impossible to play. Most recently, I spent 5 hours grinding towards several in-game accomplishments, and after achieving them, saving, and quitting the game, they disappeared when I returned to play again.
Despite these glitches (and there have been others that the development team have addressed), I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I have spent over 100 hours playing it, and would buy it again, even knowing about the bugs. However, the effects in-game of these glitches have been catastrophic due to the permadeath feature. Consequently, I think I am done with this game for a while.
