The best survival game I've ever played. The atmosphere in this game is so thick that you could cut through it with a knife and then spread it on your toast, the frightening moments will have you sh*tting your pants (surrounded by a wolf pack and your last flare just ran out) and the rewarding moments will have you jumping out of your seat (finally found that elusive prepper cache chock full of supplies)
Isolation is really what made this game for me, it's only you vs. the wild from the start and god knows you'll do whatever it takes to win. Another thing that really makes this game for me is the very realistic inventory, you have a finite amount of weight you can carry, but you can choose to go over it. Be warned though, an overencumbered character moves slower and tires faster, not to mention they are also an easier target for aggressive wildlife.
TLD won't let you run through the forest swinging an axe to fell trees and strike down animals, every action consumes calories and time (two things that are in short supply most of your playthrough) and every action outsides adds the risk of exposure. Huge blizzards rip through the map every so often and gargantaun clouds of dense fog cloud everything, obscuring any potential hazards from your view.
In the first two hours of my playthrough, my character was already cowering in an abandoned coal mine with his clothes torn to shreds and multiple bleeding wounds. He also had food poisoning and was crying about how death would be welcome compared to the hell he was going through. Two seconds later, he died of severe dehydration and acute "wolf-bit-my-face-off" syndrome.
This game is brutal. Buy it.
Also see if you can break my record for consecutive wolf attacks (mine's seven).

Steam really needs a review system that allows for more than just "Recommend" or "Don't Recommend", because I feel like SUPERHOT is, like many other games, neither good nor bad enough to be placed into one category. That said, this is ultimately a positive review, because I did have a good experience and most of my complaints are about a lack of getting more of that experience. It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years! But that doesn't mean it's without flaws.
First off, SUPERHOT plays extremely well. There's something about the slow-motion, time only moves when you do combat that is just inherently satisfying; if you don't believe me, there's a prototype/demo online (search "superhot demo" and you should find it) that will give you a taste. There's nothing too fancy aside from that, at least at first: just different weapons (pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, baseball bat/tire iron, katana), the ability to throw them, the ability to pick weapons up after punching an enemy to stun them (or hitting them three times to kill them). Later on you gain the ability to "hostswitch" from one body to another, but you only have it for a few levels.
The level design makes the gameplay all the better. While the earlier levels are either easy to beat on your first try or have an obvious, clearly placed solution, the game very quickly moves to a point where most levels take a few tries to beat. The game feels almost like a puzzle. Since ammunition is not unlimited and you'll often run out of bullets before you run out of heads to put them in, you have to conserve it as best you can while trying to make your way to the next gun. Since every punch or bullet will kill you instantly, but bullets move slow enough for you to dodge them and you can always hit an enemy before they're in range to do the same, you have to engage in a slow dance-like movement occasionally, carefully sidestepping oncoming bullets and beating down nearby enemies before they can attack. Even looking around consumes precious time, meaning that on some occasions you can't even aim at an enemy without giving another one time to shoot. (Here's looking at you, elevator level.)
The story... see, this is where the bad parts of SUPERHOT come into play. The story is actually an interesting idea, but you don't get even close to enough of it for them to properly deliver. Which wouldn't be so bad, if the story didn't take control of the game for long periods of time, preventing you from bashing in red polygonal men's heads in favour of watching a story that starts off intentionally obscured and almost pretentious. But right as it starts to seemingly expand on that, the game... well, the game ends.
The complaint many people have about SUPERHOT is that it's too short, and I think that is an entirely reasonable complaint. The gameplay is fun, but just as they start to move out of tutorialized levels to begin to combine the tricks they've taught you into interesting challenges, it ends in a climactic fight. Enjoyable, difficult, calling back to previous things you've learned, but ultimately... well, the end.
It feels like SUPERHOT is the tutorial to a much greater game. The story gets interesting; in the final "cutscene" (they aren't really cutscenes, but they serve the same purpose). The levels become sprawling arenas and headscratching puzzles; in the final segment. I beat the game in under two hours. I'll be the first person to say that length isn't everything about a game - I have played many games that I beat in similar amounts of time, and some of them are ones I consider masterpieces - but SUPERHOT is not a movie-in-game-form, nor is the gameplay explored well enough to leave me satisfied.
I think it really comes down to whether or not you're willing to pay as much as they're asking. I paid $21 CAD when it was on sale (40% down from $35). Is that worth a little under 2 hours of enjoyment? That's up to you to decide, but consider this: of my favourite games of all time, quite a few were bought for about $20, or even less. Many more were more expensive, but also far lengthier.
Do I regret buying SUPERHOT?
No.
Do I think I would have bought it knowing what I know now?
I'm not sure.

I found this third person shooter a lot of fun. I've never played any of the other Red Factions, and am told that some of them (if not all) had a more open world feel compared to this much more linear adventure. However, I think its average metacritic score of 70 odd suffers from these sorts of comparisons, as it's a pretty enjoyable game in its own right without any previous experience with the rest of the franchise.
There are a decent range of weapons that can float different people's boats, but I settled into my favourite four pretty quickly - the magnet gun, sniper rifle, mace (for up close and personal squishing), & a heavy damage weapon (which was the plasma cannon for a long time, rocket launcher, and then finally the singularity cannon). The best thing about the game however, is how much of the environment is destructable. It can break from enemy attack, your own attack, or you can even use it to harm enemies (particularly with the magnet gun). It's honestly one of the best features of the game, and using your particle repairer, you can build up most of the destroyed environment to destroy or throw at enemies again!
Replayability may be a little sticking point however. Like I mentioned the single player is quite linear though can obviously be replayed. However, there are another two gamemodes, one of which can be multiplayer. The first is ruin which is essentially using all your best skills at destroying as much of the destructible environment in the map you're put on. There's a short time limit and points are earned on how much damage you do and at what efficiency. You essentially need to destroy X amount of points to complete the few different maps they have and can continue to try set bigger scores. However, it feels like just the addon it is rather than a completely different game mode. The second is Infestation, which is essentially defeating waves of enemies which get progressively harder (up to 20 waves per map). You can solo this or play with other people, with some similarities to that game mode in Gears of War. I'm not sure about whether or not you spawn more enemies when you play with other people compared to solo though (as I haven't played multiplayer), but I'd hope so given I was able to handle most things solo with just the magnet gun and a decent position on the map playing it smart. The better of the two additional gamemodes for sure, but only extends replayability a little bit more.
Well worth the money I paid for it in a humble bundle. The entire red faction collection (which this game is included with) is still available both from the Humble store and here on steam (I think).

My first review, I don't do reviews but this game and its developers are just so wrong, I feel like I have to give the word out. Let me start by saying I had to pay 70 bucks when this game launched. There's a TDLR, you can skip to that at the bottom. Now let's go to the pros.
PROS:
Good graphics
That's pretty much it, the concept of the game is not new. Instead of the 4vs4 like they did in their l4d series they made it a 1v4, which inevitably introduces a lot of balancing issues. We'll go further into that in the cons.
CONS:
-Balancing
The monster will always win unless you get the rare ones that don't play monster. You'll need 4 above average-play level hunters to stand a chance. That doesn't mean 4 good hunters will win, it just means they will have a better chance to win. The devs talked about the changes they will make in the new patch to balance these issues, but they have not sent the patch out and it's probably have been close to a month, instead they introduced 4 new hunters instead and charged you 24 bucks for them.
-Population
The population as of March 23, 2015 is lower than their predecessor series, l4d. The avg population is not even close to the avg population of l4d2. Every 3 pub games I play, I can point out a player I have already played with earlier that day.
-Replayability
At the 50 hour mark, this is actually stretching it, you'll have played through this game's content and the game will get repetitive real fast. One of the reason it gets boring is because of balancing, you'll either lose as hunters with the few wins against the goliath, you stumble upon a good pub team and win some games against the kraken and wraith, or you'll just constantly win as monster. I win like 99% of my game as monster, and if I feel like an♥♥♥♥♥I can play wraith, which most players will just leave before the game starts. Unlike the left 4 dead series the replayability factor comes from competition, and evolve's 1vs4 introduces too many balancing issues that the 4vs4  l4d counterpart doesn't have. Compound it with the developers' lack of care or commitment to balancing you'll have a very monotonous one sided match every game. Which is probably one of the reasons why this game's population in such a critical state, no one likes losing especially when they can't do anything about it. I also played with premades, you'll win more games with premade. You'll have to play on a premade if you don't want to get dumpstered, especially against a wraith/kraken.
-Matchmaking
You'll have an option to rank what role you want to play the most, either as any of the 4 hunter classes or the monster before you que into the game. But that won't mean anything since the matchmaking system just fills you in on a game that has a open spot. So like 99% of the time you're just playing the part of filling roles. Most of the time you'll end up in the middle of a game where you're filling a role for a rager. The matchmaking system will not start a new lobby or will let you have the option to start a new lobby game unless you have a friend playing with you, which sometimes they will split you up as one playing monster and one playing on hunters. Coming from the devs that made l4d2 that has such a better match making system, evolve's match making feels shoddy and like it's made on the fly at best. Fast forward 2 months later, now compound that with the small population it has, the ques are much longer now unless you're playing at peak hours, but at least most of the time now, you can get the role that you actually have on your preferences.
-One game mode
There's no single player as in no campaign mode for a $70+ game. Which means all its content should be from its multiplayer. There's basically one mode where you hunt the monsters, and monster eats and evade until its level 2 or 3 then fights back. There are other modes that are just a variation of that like nest, rescue, and defence but they are all overly unbalanced favoring the monster which leads to barely anyone playing those modes. There is also ai which you can play by yourself against the ai, I guess? Let's be honest here ai isn't exactly great, we all know that, but the ai in evolve is even worst, the monster is too complex for an ai since you have to be sneaky and attack at the right time, and when you're against ai hunters, yea.... that's cake walk. It's probably good if you want to practice or play with friends that just got the game. But I wouldn't consider this a "campaign mode".
-Pricing
Vanilla edition costs 70 bucks at launch, and if you want all the content that is coming through the dlc plan they made, you'll have to pay 100 bucks and upwards. I bought the 70 bucks version because I don't know much about the game or if I want to "commit" with the 100 bucks package at that time, but nevertheless I'm just fooling myself about committing when I'm already paying 70 bucks for the game. So I play for a month or so and I now get the just of what I payed for. Skins cost 5$ a pop which are just recolors of the same skin design. Like changing red to a darker red, which one of the goliath skin is basically about. Fast forward to now for people that only bought the vanilla package, you now have to pay 24 bucks for the hunting season pass to get the tier 4 hunters, another 15 bucks to get the 4th monster on top of your 70 dollar purchase of the game. If you didn't think 70 dollar is steep enough for a game with very little content, and what content is multiplayer to get smashed by a overly unbalanced monster over and over again, you now have to fork over $40 more to experience a few new characters. You think a $70 game should give you a full game but that is not the case with Turtle Rock Studios and 2k. If you did pay the 100$ package you prob saved $10, i guess if it means anything with a 100$ price tag, but that doesn't include the new hunters and monsters they going to introduce after that, in what they call DLC. Keep in mind they just announce the DLC is coming on March 31st 2015, not even 2 months after the launch of the game and before their first balancing patch.
It's basically l4d where the devs ran out of ideas, but needed money, and quickly put together a game by putting 1 player on infested side and brand it as a new game. To balance that, they made that one monster strong enough to fight 4 players on its own. But the equation doesn't work like that because you'll have to expect the 4 players to always be equally good as 1/4 of the monster all the time and work together all the time to be a whole to have a 50/50 fair game. As a result they have a shoddy game, with shoddy match making, no campaign mode, and straight up cash grabs known as Evolve, which they stated themselves "Evolve is a game solely built from the bottom up for DLCS."
TDLR
For their lack luster content where basically you repeatedly do the following: if you play as humans on a pub just to get smashed by the monster, if you're on a team with friends on hunter to get smashed by the monster a little less, or if you play monster and constantly win easy games, or play monster against a premade and constantly win games. For the price tag of $70 where you don't get the full game, and you'll have to constantly pay 40 bucks for the next tier of characters, 24 for hunters 15 for monster, I do not recommend this game. I main monster too, but it's not fun after 50 hours of winning.
If you want to try the game like me, but less stupid, should wait for a 75% off sale and treat it like a mario party game to play with 4 other friends. Otherwise stay away from this dreadful cash grab.

I don’t know since when PC gamers become this picky and that difficult to impress, but this remastered version isn’t that bad, I feel it receives overwhelming negative reviews like this is not fair.
Unlike a large number of steam users out there who have next-gen alien technology powered Titan weapons to fire, my pc is old and can’t launch most of the AAA titles games come out now days(I play AAA titles on console), I usually play some naïve pixel graphics games on my vantage skeleton PC .
After reading so many thumb down reviews, I couldn’t stop wondering, ‘is this remastered version that bad?’ So I decided to give it a try myself to see it through. Thought it would not be able to launch since my PC barely reaches the minimum requirements to play. It turned out ironically.
I got in game with no issues at all. It runs perfectly smooth on my PC, my key binding was just fine and did not encounter any functional break down. The sensation of the mouse is not at its best but far away from horrible to control. It did not mix up with my controller either. My game did not crash once. I arrived Repture safe and sound. Honestly, I’ve tried to experience any issues players here had raged, but I had met none. The only fair point so far I’ve agreed is: This version doesn’t look that much different from the original. But I wasn’t in the right place to grumble this, since if the graphics were improved to the next-gen level, I probably wouldn’t be able to launch this game by any chance.
The developers have my respect and sympathy. They’ve made products for the most of their customers (original game owners including me) for free, now they are rampaging. Their new potential customers now are wondering around because the game got mixed reviews, their decisions are uncertain.
Honestly, I’d say: If you don’t own Bioshock franchise and would like to get them, this remastered version is definitely better than the original ones. At least, they’ve added steam achievements for Bioshock 1 and pretty fun museum exhibition mode in game. Of course, if it had trading cards and badges and creepy profile background would be brilliant, but maybe they will add it later, who knows?
As someone received these 2 remastered games for free, I thank the development team’s efforts and 2K to bring them here. I am not a fangirl of Bioshock franchise, but I knew it is a masterpiece. I don’t play many FPS games, but it doesn’t mean they are not good because my personal taste isn’t there.
Scarlet’s Score: 8.0/10(I haven’t got enough time to play this game till the end, so I can’t give exact the full review of the gameplay. However, for a timeless FPS known as Bioshock, an 8 point is fair to where it’s standard lies)

Outlast is a great horror game. The following review covers setting, gameplay, story, graphics as well as presentation. Warning, may contain minor spoilers!
Outlast's setting is an abandoned asylum called Mount Massive - this sounds like a too classic scenario, but Red Barrels was flawlessly able to use this as a background base for their game. The asylum is a well-designed place which has a very terrifying atmosphere, especially in the beginning.
The gameplay is often quite simple: You as Miles Upshur have to discover the secrets of the so-called Murkoff corporation which has leaded the asylum since 2009 after a tragedy. You're a journalist, simply equipped with a camcorder with a night vision mode which consumes batteries. These are the main important objects to find in the levels because you'll need the night vision to navigate through dark locations. You can also find notes which give you backstory information, but you can also record sertain events with your cam to get info.
However the main point of this game is that you're not a fighter. You cannot defend yourself! If enemies are in an area you have to sneak around them or hide under beds or other hiding spots. And sometimes if you're hunted you have to run away from several scum through quite linear areas. In general the game is really linear and at some point a bit frustrating because it is kind of a trial-and-error thing sometimes. But in general for me it was a really exciting experience.
The story itself is quite unclear especially at the beginning and you have to read several documents to get the gist. I personally love that kind of telling like for example the indie title The Forest does but I can also understand people being disappointed about the storytelling in general. An example: you as Upshur are often hunted through several levels by an old fat variant soldier called Walker who patrols an area - for no real reason - and there you have to activate a few ventils in this area he's patroling. In general, the objectives are quite simple and not that innovative.
But the story itself has also memorable characters like Chris Walker or Father Martin, a kinda-of-christian-sectian pater who is quite important for the main plot as well as Richard Trager, a doctor who ... well, you'll find out for yourself. Bur the characters will surely remain in memorial.
Outlast is a horror game with great atmosphere and especially terrifying in the beginning. However from time to time it becomes a bit less scary (personal experience). The game uses quite classic jumpscares which are well-set/-used. The game itself is quite linear and has a playtime around ~5 hours. The graphics of this game are still really good and help creating that good atmosphere this game has.
Outlast also contain gore and sexual content so have fun with that :D
However, good job, Red Barrels, great horror game.

Xotic is a pretty fun arcade score-attack FPS that is plagued by many, many... many problems. Chief among them is the slow and cumbersome character movement and lack of any Speed power-ups that seem to be at odds with the type of game it is. To compensate for this, most levels just put collectible and destroyable objects in a straight line from start to finish to make it easier to chain combos. Level design is inconsistent though, and while some levels basically require the player to run in a straight line, others are broken up into remote islands with hidden collectibles that can be hard to find. Voice acting is atrocious but thankfully the synthesized robotic voice only appears in the intro and the end cinematics. It should have been omitted entirely. Especially since the story is the most basic concoction one can imagine.
Unlockable powers can be fully unlocked long before the game is over, making the rest of the trip feel kind of pointless and repetitive as there is no more leveling. Xotic is the dream game for score attack gamers. It came out back when Valve actually curated the Steam store, meaning the indie games that came on the platform were generally good, or at least not the pisspoor Sh**show it is now with asset flips and student's first GameGuru/Flash/GameMaker game. Xotic is an FPS score attack game that is less focused on combat and more focused on shooting targets (scabs), collecting points, and finding hidden objects. Getting the top scores would require dozens of replays of the same level, allowing near limitless gameplay for score junkies. There's alot of mechanics at play: Shooting scabs that are near each other so they increase your chain, a chain meter that drops unless you shoot more targets, various destructable objects that contribute to your score, extra point dots that pop out of the scabs, dots  that when collected in groups of five while in air, give you an aerial combo bonus, a double/triple jump that is unlock later, a deployable shield that can also be used as a platform when you don't have double jumps, "brain" objects that provide alot of points, but need to be searched out and takes many hits to destroy - there's so much here and there are still more mechanics I could list - such as how the level scores you for accuracy and scabs found, and how upgrades are unlocked with experience points.
I will say that the slower play style and the "points over combat" gameplay will turn off people looking for a great combat experience - the enemies are infrequent, and many of them don't really provide much challenge or engaging combat outside of "shoot them and don't get shot". Later levels may have boss/miniboss types, and different enemy types I haven't encountered yet. The weapons, while numerous and effective, feel and sound weak - so even older games like Doom and Goldeneye 007 have more satisfying feeling guns.
Xotic is an exotic, unique game that can't be compared to many other games. The game has a look that as one Youtube commenter described as "Turok on drugs" - it certainly has a strange, ethereal, and alien look to it. It has a kind of polish and solidity that makes it an easy recommendation from me.

Limbo was a game I was excited to play. The art style was original and interesting, it was getting rave reviews, awards, and acclaim. I was so hyped for this game and for the most part, I really enjoyed myself. What drew me to Limbo was the art and my GOD is it cool. The black and white, film noir adds to the heavy atmosphere that engulfs the entire game. The whole world that the player explores is dark, dreary, and full of danger and the art makes it very apparent that Limbo is a place where hope and safety do not exist. The atmosphere makes the player feel isolated and shrouds Limbo in an air of mystery and intrigue. I couldn't wait to explore and uncover the secrets of this gloomy and violent world. The premise of the game is that you are an unnamed boy who wakes up in Limbo with no clue as to how he wound up there and now must find his sister. Good setup except the player going in wouldn't know this without reading the game's summary on Steam. You just wake up in a forest. No cut-scene or text explains the plot, it just starts. That's fine, it's kind of like the original Super Mario Bros. with the story being in the manual, but it still rubs me the wrong way that the main emotional incentive for going on this journey is not there in the beginning. You do see visions of the boy's sister later in the game, but I was confused at first. "Who is that girl"? I asked myself, only to look it up later and felt stupid for not getting it sooner. The gameplay consists of puzzle solving and light platforming and it is REALLY GOOD. The puzzles are challenging and inventive, involving unique mechanics involving worms that burrow into the player's brain, gravity changing switches, and using bear traps to tear the legs off of a giant spider. Failure to overcome these challenges results in DEATH. Horrible, brutal, grotesque, and revolting death. The boy experiences impalement, beheading, getting mowed down by machine guns, drowning, electrocution, being crushed by pistons, hacked to bits by giant saws, his entire torso ripped from his head by a bear trap, just to name of few. Death is so prominent in this game, it's where the game gets its title. No matter how many ways you die, you're forever stuck in Limbo. It is depressing, especially when put against the melancholy drone that is the game's music and the fact that the boy is not the only child stuck in Limbo. Other children are featured dying in this game, kid corpses everywhere and the children that still live try to kill you.
It's a kill or be killed world in Limbo as Flowey would say.
To encourage exploration, the game has these little egg things hidden throughout the game and crushing them all rewards you with a secret challenge area, which is neat. The game is also not too long, which is not a bad thing as a short length is a staple for games in this genre. The game would be a 10 for me if not for one thing: THE STORY. I already gave you the premise which I think is alright, but it's what happens afterward that loses me. There is the aforementioned spider that serves as the main antagonist in the first half of the game and the other children that try to murder you, which when encountered make the player question the nature of the world they inhabit. Is this really Limbo? The place between hell and heaven? Or has something happened to the world where killer creatures roam and only children remain? You never really know for sure. Why do the children want to kill you? What happened to the boy and sister before the game starts? How were they separated? Where are the adults? The ambiguity of the game gave way for the community to create theories for the game's hidden meaning, mostly surrounding the game's ending.
SPOILERS AHEAD. SKIP TO "SPOILERS END"
The game ends with the boy completing the final puzzle to have the gravity shift and flinging him through a glass wall where he passes out. He wakes up to find himself in the forest where the game began. The boy begins to walk forward until he sees his sister at the base of a tree, with a treehouse above her. She appears to be digging or searching for something, maybe burying something. It's hard to tell. The boy approaches her while she's is digging. She senses something behind her, maybe she hears his footsteps, so she stands up, surprised, still not looking his way. Then the game ends. The title screen appears to show the same scene except the tree house appears rotted, the grass longer, and in place of the boy and his sister are masses of flies hovering above the ground where they once stood.
WTF DOES IT MEAN? Obviously, the siblings are dead which could explain their entry into to Limbo. But they died where they stood. There are many theories that involve their cause of death, how the many threats represent the boy's fears, and so on, but I don't think any of it is a satisfying conclusion to the game. Maybe I am greedy or perhaps I am searching for a deeper meaning than there actually is, but I just think that this game had more to tell but doesn't know how to tell it.
SPOILERS END.
The creator wanted the game to have a vague story, giving details so that the player can put together the pieces to see their own "Big Picture", but from what people have come up with, I just don't think it's as deep as it thinks it is.  "Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters Limbo." That's all you need. Nothing changes knowing the theories surrounding the game, my initial impressions are the same as my thoughts now. The creator himself read the theories and said that they were "scary close" to what he actually intended. That's awesome! With the little clues that he gave, people were still able to piece it together the way he intended. That's a success. So while the riddle that is Limbo's story disappoints me, it might impress you so don't let my stupid opinion get in the way of you enjoying the game. One last thing I should note is the sound design, not music, just SOUND. It is chilling, there is no game that is layered as intricately as Limbo when it comes to sound design. It works as much if not more than the art in order to create and maintain the atmosphere. As a whole Limbo is a great game and I would absolutely recommend it. I also heard Inside is a good game to check out so I'll be sure to play that one too. Be aware that the game is short and $11 might not be worth it for some, but I think it is. This game is art, no question about it and everyone should play it at least once.

A pure realistic survival game in Northwestern Canada. The gameplay revolves around maintaining four status meters: Temperature, Fatigue, water, and Food. Completely depleting any of the meters begins draining health at different rates--you can survive for maybe a week without food or sleep, but you will die within hours if you are freezing, and days without water. You must explore to find food, tools, and raw materials to stay alive. The game ends whenever you make a mistake serious enough to get yourself killed, such as getting lost on a frozen lake in a blizzard, and freezing to death before you can find the shore, or being attacked by a wolf and bleeding out before you can bandage and disinfect the wound. Even if you play a perfect game, After a several months, tools and clothing begin to wear out, as you begin to run out of the resourses to maintain them. Eventually, you will run out of matches, and can only start fires with a magnifying glass outdoors in good sunlight.
Gameplay is generally slow and methodical. Inventory and resourse management in a major component of the game. The game autosaves your progress, and permadeath makes every decision during exploration potentially fatal. However, the game is easy enough for a casual player to learn and enjoy, but offers challenges for more serious gamers, especially at the higher difficulties.
One concern I have is with infrequent game breaking bugs. This game is in early access and has improved in the few months I played it, but I lost a save file after 130 days in-game and had another save file become so glitchy that it was impossible to play. Most recently, I spent 5 hours grinding towards several in-game accomplishments, and after achieving them, saving, and quitting the game, they disappeared when I returned to play again.
Despite these glitches (and there have been others that the development team have addressed), I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I have spent over 100 hours playing it, and would buy it again, even knowing about the bugs. However, the effects in-game of these glitches have been catastrophic due to the permadeath feature. Consequently, I think I am done with this game for a while.

The best survival game I've ever played. The atmosphere in this game is so thick that you could cut through it with a knife and then spread it on your toast, the frightening moments will have you sh*tting your pants (surrounded by a wolf pack and your last flare just ran out) and the rewarding moments will have you jumping out of your seat (finally found that elusive prepper cache chock full of supplies)
Isolation is really what made this game for me, it's only you vs. the wild from the start and god knows you'll do whatever it takes to win. Another thing that really makes this game for me is the very realistic inventory, you have a finite amount of weight you can carry, but you can choose to go over it. Be warned though, an overencumbered character moves slower and tires faster, not to mention they are also an easier target for aggressive wildlife.
TLD won't let you run through the forest swinging an axe to fell trees and strike down animals, every action consumes calories and time (two things that are in short supply most of your playthrough) and every action outsides adds the risk of exposure. Huge blizzards rip through the map every so often and gargantaun clouds of dense fog cloud everything, obscuring any potential hazards from your view.

This is by no means the perfect game. There are flaws, there are bugs, I regularly get dropped by the server. There are trolls online, both intentionally trolling and unintentionally (if you don't know what offside is, read up on it
playing!) But what it does have going for it is sheer fun factor.
If you remember Sensible Soccer, WoSO is in a similar vein, from the pixel graphics to sharing more than a little in common with Sensible World of Soccer's name. But as the telling difference in the name reveals, WoSO is an online game. You control just one player, with the other players on your team controlled by other humans (yay) or the AI (boo). And it's this multiplayer element that is at the heart of WoS's fun factor. As in real life football, playing as a team is essential; good positioning is worth a lot and a team playing as a unit can still beat a team full of better players who are all playing for themselves. It can be really satisfying when your team puts together a string of neat passes culminating in a goal, or when you've spent 90 minutes defending resolutely only to nick a 1-0 victory in the dying moments on the counter.
Controls are relatively simple; movement is via mouse (run to the cursor a la diablo), gamepad or keyboard (not a good option IMO). I'm using a controller where you have 3 buttons that I'd call "shoot" "lob" and "pass". The controls are
well explained, although there is a tutorial that gives you the basics. Bascially "lob" is a high ball, "pass" is a low ball and "shoot" increases in height with power. Hold down the button to power up. You can also control the height of the ball by either moving the mouse cursor nearer or further from your player, or moving your joystick in a similar fashion. "lob" performs a slide tackle when defending. Headers are finicky at first, but basically involve either the "pass" or "shoot" buttons ("lob" will make you slide instead).
There are no fouls - strategically taking out opponents is part of the game and underlines the arcade feel of the game. Offsides are implemented, so no goal hanging allowed. Other than that there are 3 player models (small/normal/large) you can choose from if you pay for a VIP account. The small players are however vastly overpowered (they are quicker than everyone else) and I personally find it gets boring quickly if one team has several fast players and the other doesn't; you can essentially run the entire length of the pitch with the ball without being caught, which removes any element of tactics from the game. I think there needs to be a better model for financing the servers than one that makes the game less fun (IMO of course) for everyone.
Other downsides include:
The dev does respond to requests and suggestions, and there have been several changes made to the game since release - many good, some bad, and some neither here nor there. However, active development and a willingness to engage with players is always a good thing.
Seeing as WoSO is free, there's no reason not to try it our if you like football games - especially if you were a Sensi fan back in the day. This isn't a game for the people who buy FIFA or PES for the skill moves and motion capture graphics. WoSO is much more tactical - yet also more arcadey- than those 2, by virtue of its simple nature. If you do try it out, definitely play the tutorial and practice knocking the ball about a bit. Play a couple of matches on an empty server both with and without bots to practice passing and shooting. It only takes a short while to master the basic controls. It'll take you a long time to master the game though.

Worth a play if you are a fan, but not if this if your first romp on Mars.

I like puzzle games. I really do.
And this is a nice puzzle game, for the most part.
It has a soothing atmosphere. The minimalistic looks is good. The puzzles are simple, yet complex.
Really, it seems like everything is done right?
Well. Not exactly.
This game is really repetitive. It introduces a block you have to pass mutliple times in the early stages and... that's it. Some games manage to keep things interesting, even with few mechanics, but I don't think I really works here. With the great number of level, it just feels really "diluded".
Choose one color. Make short part. Fill has much has you can with other colors. Make slight ajustements. Worked for 80% stages. I'm not trying to brag, in fact, I'm a probably few cards short of a deck, but this not a challenging game. It's long and tedious, but not challenging.
But that's not my biggest problem with this game.
If you're paying attention, you'll notice that many stages look similar. In fact, some levels are exactly the same, but upside down. This is almost insulting.
Or it would be, but this is only a 3$ game. There's only so much I could expect. It might not have blown my mind. It might not be a great game. It might not deserve a "Overwhelmingly Positive". Yet, I don't exactly regret buying it.
If you're looking for simple puzzles to solve and relax a bit, I suppose you could buy worst.

I've played many hidden object games but have never bothered reviewing any of them, partly because I think everybody generally gets the idea by now and more or less knows what to expect, but also because, with a few exceptions, there's usually so little difference between the content and quality that were I to write reviews for each and every one I'd essentially end up trying to find dozens of different ways to say the exact same thing. (By the by, just about anything published by Artifex Mundi should see you right if you're looking to get into the genre) But I'm writing one for Sinister City as I feel I need to come to its defence a little and share my own take on it.
It seems like such a cop-out when people say the only reason somebody doesn't like something is because they don't understand it. It's sort of a thinly-veiled way of calling someone stupid rather than accept they might understand it perfectly but just not like it, that they simply have a different preference than you. But after reading a lot of the negative reviews, this is one occasion where I actually feel like some people kinda didn't get it. As pretentious and w*nky as it is to say, there is a difference between something being parody, pastiche and just plain bad, and this game dips its toes into all three, which is where I think a lot of confusion comes from.
Let's get it out of the way and say what needs to be said, many parts of this game are bad, unintentionally so. Graphically it's kind of somewhere between looking like a PS2 and PS3 era game and there were quite a few times in the hidden object sections when I wished everything was clearer or more distinct. In other games in the genre these sections can have a more artistic slant with their high quality renders of interesting scenes and items. Here, everything is far more workmanlike and pretty forgettable; a straight on view of some open cupboards or top down into a box with a small handful of items in it. They don't feel hugely inspired. But worst of all are the bugs and glitches that plague the game. It happened to me a few times where some strange artifacting would appear in the form of white blocks across the screen and completely obscure my view, or every time I'd click anywhere in a hidden object scene it would kick me out of it forcing me to manually enter the scene repeatedly after every object I found. In fairness, this only happened to me in the second stage of the game then never bothered me again after (exiting to the main menu then hitting Continue eventually seemed to fix this for me. In some cases I think Steam pop-ups may have triggered this to happen, but I'm not completely sure). They were the only issues I had personally, but others have complained of far worse, like losing save data every time they closed the game or buggy achievements not registering properly, or in some cases, not even being able to start the game at all. And if anyone had these issues then they'd be absolutely right to give it a bad review as their experience with the title. But, thankfully, I had a far better time with it. Well... eventually.
[View Comments for the missing 4th paragraph]
You play as a sort of Tom Cruise lookalike trying to find his kidnapped fiancé and being lead to Sinister City in the search. A kindly old hotel receptionist tells him to stay away from there, that it's a vampire city, and the guy doesn't even bat an eyelid at the mention of vampires. Nor does he when he's invited to a session of telepathic communication to try tracking her down, he just accepts the offer and follows an old man into a darkened back room. I think pretty much everyone who plays it either laughs their *ss off at these points or else says it's stupid and loses all hope for the game, I know they were certainly my reactions. But then I got to a point where it just sort of clicked with me. I realised they understood these games are dumb and their stories make no sense, so they start having a little fun and going all out ridiculous with it. The head vampire kidnaps his own daughter to arrange for her to marry a kid's TV presenter to vicariously live out his own failed ambitions of movie stardom that he's secretly harboured for centuries. Oscar Wilde, this is not. But I love that they have fun with it rather than being so serious like most of the other games and I was surprised at how much I laughed at some genuinely funny moments in it. If you have to make a crazy, nonsense story, I think it's way better to go funny with it instead of trying to be respectable with how legit you are with your craft, and I applaud them for making that move here.
Like I said, if anyone had a bad experience with this on a technical level then I can't argue with that, and to begin with I was right there with them. But by the end this game thoroughly won me over and I had a great couple of hours with it. With some funny moments, some interesting hidden object play that I eventually came around to, and at least an attempt at a new variety of mini games for the genre, I can easily say this was the best 9 cents I've ever spent.

Hard to review this game as it makes some things really well and some thing abysmally poor. The TL;DR of this is, if you are buying it for the survival experience go ahead, if however what you are looking for is an interesting story driven game you should look elsewhere. As such I will separate my review into two parts
=== 1. Story ===
1. The story itself is, so far, nothing to write home about. To make it worse it is delivered in "episodes" which I am frankly not a fan of. I understand it is good for the studio to release content in segments but I personally don't appreciate being left on cliffhangers for half a year.
2. The two first chapters of the story (all that is available as I write this review) take about 15 hours depending on how much of a completionist you are. Not impressive for the price tag.
3. The story itself may not be bad but the delivery of it sure is. Everything is linear, you meet a couple of NPCs in the world but they have as much depth as your general quest giver on a MMO circa 2000. They serve no purpose but to send you on "fetch quests" which you must complete to progress the story. At no stage of the game any meaningful choice is given to you on how to handle these characters - you just do it as if you were in a tutorial. In fact the whole of "story mode" just feels like an extremely long and boring tutorial for "survival mode"
4. The only choice you will ever make as a player (since you character does not make any) in this game is if you want to do the side quests or not. Like the main quests they basically consist of "fetch me this" or "go check that out". The rewards could be interesting but honestly not required - the game gives you more than enough loot to fulfill your goals by just performing the "on rails" experience of doing whatever the NPC tells you to do. To aggravate this, near the end of each chapter an artificial mechanic (climbing down ropes) will force you to leave most of your extra gear behind so little purpose to go out of your way to do the side quests although you probably end up doing half of them anyway while doing the main ones.
5. I thought I had my installation corrupted or something but no, apparenlty it is a feature that only 20% of the dialoges are voiced. The rest is just text while the characters do some weird animations in the background. Even the text dialogues however are very poor. Even the text implementation however is bad, if you ask something to a character that is fairly long, like his character backstory, you will only see him reply something of the sort "wow that is a long story" and then you get a wall of text in your journal. I could understand the approach if the characters were voiced but for a "text adventure" it is just piling bad on terrible.
6. The survival aspects of the game don't shine at all in story mode. Loot is plentiful (I played my game in the "recommended experience level" set by the developers). Initially there is an idea that this survival thing is going to be hard but loot is so plentiful in the form of food and warm clothers that there is little else to worry than the ocasional wolf coming at you. For the most part you can ignore the survival elements and just focus on fetching whatever the main NPC for your chapter told you to.
I obviously hope that the next chapters in the story will be better since I think they are already part of the package I paid for but in case they aren't I see no compelling reason to buy additional chapters afterwards. Like mentioned at the start if you are buying this for the story mode save your money.
=== 2. Survival Mode ===
1. This is where the game shines. No NPCs to tell you what to do so you can enjoy either a quite walk in the woods (lowest difficulty level) or a challenging survival experience (hardest difficulty level) or something in between.
2. Especially when you start a new game the first 15-20 days feel like quite a challenge to survive. You feel the choices you make count, a wrong turn can cause you a lot of pain down the road. Permadeath only serves to accentuate the consequences of your choices.
3. It is easy to get into a rut, the bigger achievements (like "survived 500 days") seem without much value as once you survived your first 50 days even on interlopper only complacency can kill you. The end game is lacking but it is not easy to do better in a survival game and still give a sense of character progression - what to do after you become a master survivor?
4. Despite the shortcomings TLD is still one of the best survival games I played and it has plenty of replayability. It is easy to clock 100 or more hours in survival mode making the price tag of the game quite attractive.  Additionally the game is still being worked on so hopefully that means it will get better (not a guarantee since the developer has been known to take step backwards too but a high probability outcome)
=== 3. Both modes ===
The art can be initially off putting, especially in the trailers. But once you get into the game I think you'll find you enjoy it more than you expected.
Maps are nice but inconsistent on their presentation. Sometimes they face north, other times south, other times west...
=== 4. Conclusion ===
If I was judging the game based solely on the "survival mode" I would easily grant it a 8/10 or maybe even a 9/10. With the story mode bundled I would say its a 6/10. If you are looking for the survival go ahead, otherwise wait for a steam sale.

This game is a perfect example of why I wish Steam had a "Meh." option, instead of just yes or no to a recommendation.
I have played several point-and-click, hidden object games at this point, and there are definitely some things that Sinister City does that I appreciate, albeit not well enough to not be a bit, frankly, dumb.
Here's the break-down for me, + signs being positives and - being negatives.
+Incorporation of 3-dimensional character models. While most games of this type simply present you with a two-dimensional scene, in this you do actually have to move the protagonist, John, around in a space.
- However, on that same note, the areas where you can move are more or less two-dimensional and not all of them seem to have been designed with a character walking around them in mind. This results in some frankly hilarious looking scenes, like John and the TV Station security guard just hovering above the ground in front of the TV station, as if they were part of the door and not actual characters.
+ Voice Acting - for a casual game of this type, it's actually really good.
- Except for John's voice. And he's the main character. So he talks all the time. (Ipkis is pretty bad too but you only have to talk to him a couple times)
- The background music isn't bad, but it is extremely repetitive.
- Game is short, even for a HOP game.
+ Price. Guys for real, it's a dollar. Even if you end up despising it, are you really gonna cry over that dollar?
+ Story...it's satirical of your typical spooky vampire motif, which is actually genuinely amusing at times. Not funny, but amusing. Worthy of a slight smirk. Also, John and Nina's lovey-dovey-ness is so over the top that it becomes a humorous exaggeration of dime-a-dozen love stories. Whether or not this was intentional is debatable, but seeing it as satire makes it more bearable.
- Story ... buuuuutttt a lot of it feels rushed and nonsensical, even for a game about a town full of vampires (who completely openly exist and no one really questions it....?). Spoiler free example: When your character finds out his fiancee is being held in a town full of vampires, he at no point stops and says, "Woah, man. Slow your roll. VAMPIRES? Vampires are real?" He's basically Anakin Skywalker in Episode 3 of Star Wars, but without the death, ("Oh my god, what have I done? Waaaahhhhhhh"  ... "So you wanna join the Dark Side?" ... "Yeah, okay.") He just immediately accepts something that you would think would be a hell of a revelation for your average human dude who just wants to get married.
- Saw the last bit of the ending coming a mile away.
+ All the characters actually have a unique design and personalities, however minimal those personalities may be.
+ Several objects in the HOPs were genuinely difficult to find, which I like.
- But all the other minigames were horrendously easy.
All in all, it really is a "meh" kind of thing for me. I didn't like it, but I didn't dislike it. Had it been fleshed out more into a bigger and longer story, and more time taken on animation, it could have been really good. The developers definitely have some skill; it's just in need of serious refinement.
I labeled it as recommended in the end because of the price. It's only a buck, and there are definitely worse things to do when you're bored, and worse games that I've played for more money--on sale.

This is the best zombie survival game I've played, and I've played a few. The devs are great, giving the community large, game-enhancing updates at regular intervals, as well as a newsletter on their progress every Monday. Every time I come back to this game after a new update, I feel as if I'm hooked on the game all over again, simply because it's more immersive than ever. Also, it's surprisingly difficult to survive, at least for long periods of time. Custom sandbox is great for toning down the number of zombies and their ferocity, giving you a chance to get to grips with the game (there is also a beginner mode for those who don't want to fiddle around with settings), and survival mode is just brutal - lots of zombies, hardly anything to scavenge, so don't expect to last long. There's nothing like being bitten and fending off a horde of bloodthirsty zeds, knowing that you're not going to survive anyway, so you might as well go out on a high.
NPC's is a feature that I'm really looking forward to that is yet to be implemented, but I hear they are working on it. They've recently added radios, TV's and walkie-talkies with Build 33 which may be an interesting development in later updates, such as being able to talk with NPC's over the ham radio; also good for multiplayer too, as bases can keep in contact with the people they send out to scavenge.
Overall an excellent game with active devs that looks as if it's going to get even better. Would totally recommend for fans of zombie and/or survival games, as well as anyone looking for a nerve-wracking experience which will have you hiding in your house, clutching a baseball bat, as the zeds come knocking on the windows! Have fun!

BioShock is one of those games that any self-proclaimed gamer needs to have in their inventory. Yes, it is dated at this point, but man is it still a fantastic game. If you can't handle the older graphics, don't fret, BioShock Remastered just came out.
- Extremely atmospheric - you will be sitting on the edge of your seat for the majority of the game
- Fantastic original story - I don't want to spoil anything for those who haven't played BioShock yet, but it is truly amazing.
- Do things YOUR way. Want to go in shooting? Fire away. Want to be stealthy? Sneak away. Want to hack things? No problemo. There are so many ways to handle each situation.
- Exploring is rewarding. More ammo, health packs, crafting items, you name it. Also find audio diaries to get diverse insights into Raputure's history.
- Difficulty is just right. Yes you will get stronger as you progress, but you will be punished if you make poor choices.
- I still want to play this although I have finished it 3 times.
- Graphically the game looks a little old
- It is a shame that you cannot equip a plasmid and weapon at the same time - either one or the other (this was fixed in BioShock 2)
- The hacking system is laborious and dull (but still worth doing)
- If you're easily frightened you will need some clean underwear on the side
There really is no reason for you not to give BioShock a try, especially now that a remastered version is out. I guarantee you will not regret playing it. Like Portal, BioShock is an extremely rewarding and fulfilling experience.

- Lord Farquaad (Shrek, 2001).
LIMBO is a platforming puzzle game at it's core, rewarding you for exploration but also punishing you for mistakes, not knowing the game mechanics or simply being new to the trap. Although this has been done many times before (Mario), LIMBO has a unique art style that easily sets it apart from other games of the genre. The noir aesthetic of the game is fresh and immersive, as the seemingly busy backgrounds of the game are calmly blended in, seamlessly changing monochrome locations and keeping the environment from becoming stale. The plot is ambiguous at best outside of a sole objective revealed later on into the game, which does mean the game may not motivate, but it was obviously done to reinforce the mystique that the aesthetic creates. It isn't a masterpiece like many quickly claimed it was, as it is simply too short and simplistic to warrant comparison to other classic games; LIMBO is however worth the play for the breath of fresh air it'll give the seemingly rare gamer that doesn't have the attention span of an 8 year old.
But don't miss out on a unique and special experience that is still one of a kind 6 years later.

Blue Reflection.... where to start...
Well, all in all BR is a good game situated on the edge of what we should call the abyss of mediocrity. In the game, you play as a high school girl thrust into the power struggle between good and evil (read as magical girls and beings bent on the destruction of the world). You are able to recruit your newly-made normie friends into supporters to help out your magical girl team. By solving the students' issues inside the school and going on quests in the other-realm, you get stronger and so on and so forth.
What I was really hoping for with this game was a Madoka-esque 3rd episode twist that plunged the rather light-hearted affair into doom and gloom but I think that was me just projecting my wants and needs on the game.
What the game does well are:
+Smooth and interesting combat system
+Shiv-ton of abilities and equipment
+Minimal and clean UI
+NAKAMA POWAARRRRR
+magical girls doing magical girl things
+Drop dead gorgeous visuals
+An OST to die for
+DLC for the old, lecherous man in all of us
+Waifus
What it does less well:
-repetitive combat (once you figure out your strategies, you are pretty much set)
-fetch this, do this style quests for the most part
-Waifus?
Overall: If you came looking for a Persona-like game...AHAHAHAHAH. Other than that, it's a good game with an awesome OST. Check it out if you have the time/money. I'll give it a 7.7.

I absolutely love this game! It is the best Star Wars RTS game of all time. I used to play the disk version on my Windows Vista computer, even though it was originally made for Windows XP and 2000, and then I played it on an XP computer, and it was usually unstable. Now, I have it from Steam on Windows 10, and it's close to perfect. Now, I get to play the expansion pack, which is super awesome.
In the game, you get to command the armies of either the Galactic Empire or the Rebel Alliance, and then the third faction in the expansion pack. Basically, the story of the game is you get to change galactic history. You could copy the events seen in the classic films and destroy the death star as the Rebellion, take over the galaxy as the Empire, etc.
Other than the campaign stories, The game includes a skirmish, which are quick matches that take place on a single planet. They last about thirty minutes and are really fun. You can choose to play on a planet's surface or have a space battle. Each have a pretty good amount of maps to play on.
There's also the galactic conquest modes. In case you haven't played a game with galactic conquest, basically, there's a galaxy with a ton of planets. In order to win, you basically need to take over the entire galaxy, and rid it of all enemy factions. These can potentially take hours, depending on how large of a conquest you choose (how many planets are present to take over).
No matter how you play, weather you prefer long galactic conquests or short skirmishes, or whether or not you play with mods, you will probably like this, especially if your a fan of RTS games, Star Wars, or the Command & Conquer franchise.

I'm giving this game a positive rating because I've had fun playing it so far, and I think it's worth the rather meager retail asking price. However, in the interest getting my main point across, I'm going to start out by detailing some of the things I don't like about the game.
- Difficulty Level: This game is most frequently compared to FTL, and the comparisons are apt. You will die a lot. However, unlike FTL, you won't necessarily be dying because of some freak rogue-like event, but rather because no matter how many resources you gather, your heroes and modules are always underpowered, even on the very easy setting. In the later stages, if you stop paying attention for even a brief moment, one of your heroes will die within literally seconds of encountering a group of enemies. It's still doable, but there were some stages I only barely managed to eke through by throwing all my food resource into healing--which, in turn, meant no food for upgrading, meaning weaker heroes for the next stage, etc, etc.
- Immersion: We don't really understand why the various aliens and monsters are attacking the power core and the players, and so aren't particularly interested in them. There's a huge variety of enemies... but they could really all be identical for all I care, since I know nothing about them. You might learn a tiny little snippet about them in the album, but it's little more than a sentence. The heroes are a little bit better on that score, since there's some dialogue every now and then between them, but by the end of the game we really don't know much about them either. There also aren't any events in the game to break up the monotony of going from level to level. Speaking of the end (*SPOILER ALERT THIS SENTENCE*), it's extremely anticlimactic, as you reach the last stage and then, PLOP, you're out of the capsule. You've won. The end. Cut to screenshot of you outside the capsule. No difference from any of the other stages. No "final boss," no change of scenery, no plotline revelations, no culmination of all you've worked toward.
- Bugs: I haven't encountered too many, but there's one really annoying and persistent bug where, after I unequip an item from a hero, I can't reequip the item to any hero unless I save, quit, and continue from the menu screen. I also bought the Founder's Pack w/ Endless Legend, and didn't receive any of the bonus heroes or ships. These are easy fixes, though, and I'm sure they'll address them in time.
Those are the things I don't like. However, I still like the game overall. I enjoyed collecting heroes, even if I thought there could be a bit more variety in the means of gaining them (they all have the same quest: survive 3 stages with them). I enjoyed the music and the overall ambiance of the scenery. I enjoyed the balance of having to manage resources, RPG hero development, and real time employment of turrets and heroes.
This developer makes very pretty games with some fairly solid gameplay; I just wish they would work a bit more on character development, story, and variety of in-game events. When they do that, I think they'll be ready for the big leagues.

THIS SOFTWARE IS USELESS CRAP THAT DOES NOT WORK, AVOID AT ALL COSTS! DOES NOT WORK ON AUTOCAD SOFTWARE OR SIMPLIFY 3D!!!!!
Ok now having given it a thrashing I am less than impressed. The mirror option the creators recommend does not work because any mirrored part does not print. This is a pre day one launch error surely.
The work area is cluttered with useless crap like a cityscape and floor that makes seeing the model more difficult. Want to look at the underside sorry floor is in the way you will have to raise the model up to do that.
Also everything is rendered in dishwater grey making it exceeingly hard to see the detail and  it clips like a mother. This is due to the models being made for gaming unity assets you can just go buy yourself! More on this below.
There is no option to slice the model up for optamised printing in the program meaning anything you do make will look quite awful due to poor print orientation and massive amount of supports needed or you will have to spend time cutting the model yourself in something like meshmixer.
My one print so far ended up with one arm as I mirrored the other arm and was so covered in supports in order to print out that any fine detail was obliterated in the clean up or fused with the supports.
The statements by the chap who mentioned lack of scale etc I agree with 100%.
Look it is a complete waste of time. You would be better served building your own mecha from scratch.
It gets worse. All the models are for purchase unity assets designed for making computer games with. Hence the low poly look to all the parts. These were originally designed for the detail to be rendered on not sculpted and built with as few polygons as possible which is what game design demands. Doesnt work for 3d printing.
Worse is the models are not watertight because they were not designed for that. In game design it is not a huge issue. In 3d printing it is a big issue. If they were watertight I would at least have basic models I could then work in 123D to get really nice looking assets to print out, sliced up nicely etc.
The other thing is the design of the parts is not conductive to 3d printing as there are undercuts etc that just dont work.
These purchased assets also explain the hard to see dishwater grey they come in as they are designed to have skins put over them.
Knowing they dont even have someone making the models but launched with literaly unmodified off the shelf gaming assets never designed for 3d printing is the nail in the coffin for this one. I now feel I essentially paid $42 for mostly unuseable models I will have to work on in my own software to get any sort of reasonable result.
In fact I would feel I got value for money if the original creator just made all models you get with this (which are not owned by this company) as watertight STL's and sold them as an asset pack for 3d printing.

This game is really hard to place. It has a great art style, and brings new ideas to the table when it comes to the roguelike genre. Here's the kicker: it's not balanced. This might require some explanation.
You start the game off with 2 heroes and they gain minor stat increases and activated abilities by leveling up. To level up it takes food. Your ability to get food is based on the number of rooms you can power using dust which drops off monsters. Now it seems pretty straightfoward that you should unpower rooms in order to accumulate more dust from monsters, but if you spawn more monsters it gets harder every time you open another room. Also, if you unpower rooms you can't accumulate income from the modules you place, and the turrets and support modules won't work in that room. So you want to be saving up industry, food and science but you can't do that if you unpower rooms.
Dungeon of the Endless actively punishes the player for doing well, making it more difficult to push their advantages. It also becomes extremely deadly when the player is behind on item upgrades, industry and dust. To me, at least, that is the polar opposite of how a roguelike game should be balanced. It's just not fun!
Each run of this game takes a TON of hours to complete. There's 12 floors in a run and if you want to succeed you really need to open nearly every door per floor. It's the only way to get resources, so you have to! The game gets repetitive really quickly in this way. I really wish they would trim down the floors per run. It would feel more roguelike increasing the enemy diversity you encounter per floor.
Another problem is the number of enemies the game spawns negates the level of effort put into art design. Have fun watching a pixelated sword flash inside a mob of 40 pixelated enemies which would like awesome if there were only a few but endless is definitely the correct term for the number of enemies spawning.
I also have found the concept of using heroes in a turret defense, but placing more weight on research and turrets quite confusing. They have spent considerable time developing these characters and putting them in the spotlight but discouraging gameplay revolved around leveling your heroes quickly.
I'll mention briefly all merchants were bugged on release, however the devs have caught on and said it's being fixed in their next patch. Unfortunately the bug made the game virtually unplayable as your items could get stuck in your inventory, and merchants are the primary source of upgrades for your heroes.
Multiplayer seems tacked on, much like Risk of Rain's multiplayer which is still quite buggy. Most community posts concerning multiplayer have been negative. Honestly I don't know why roguelikes are even including multiplayer it's really not the point!
Unless something BIG happens to change the game balance I simply can't reccomend Dungeon of the Endless. The experience has been more frustrating than fun, albeit some interesting concepts.

The game mostly plays like a traditional First Person Shooter, where the screen is your field of view, with a small proportion of it at the bottom taken up by your weapon (the symbiotic Macroterra bug), and an area at the top of the screen is your H.U.D.. You move around the maze with the usual combination of WASD (PC version) with additional actions using the Space and Tab keys... As is customary now, the game uses mouselook, and the mouse buttons fire your primary and secondary weapons... the scroll wheel is also used to change between different fire modes, and unusually, scrolling up changes the primary by looping through the available attacks, and scrolling down changes the secondary. For me, this took a little bit of getting used to, although I tended to stick with the same attacks.
Where xotic differs from other FPS games however, is the emphasis on scoring points, collecting multipliers, beating the clock and getting a High Score on each level... there are lots of ways to ramp up the points too, with bonuses for killing enemies while in mid-air... collecting Orb essence in mid-air... racking up long chains of scab plant kills.. etc. It also feels like a 3d platform game, as a lot of the time you will be jumping either between objects, or onto platforms that you create.
Another main difference is that enemies are a lot less frequent than in most FPS games, with maybe a dozen or so on each level, in varying combinations of moving humanoid enemies and static gun emplacements. There are also some nasty crawling insects that spawn from hard to spot dirt-heaps. Therefore the main focus of play is in shooting the scab plants, collecting the orb essence and killing the orb brains in the time, though all the enemies need to be killed in order to complete the level, and this can be done regardless of what proportion of the other goals you have completed.
The focus on collecting points over killing enemies makes the game feel a bit more casual for a First Person Shooter, however the time pressure and level design definitely doesn't make it an easy game.
While not the best FPS game graphics I've seen, Xotic certainly has a very distinctive and rather lush graphical style that seems to fit the game rather well... there's also an interesting contrast between the background, which is a decaying technological world, and the bright colours of the plants that you release by shooting the scabs.
The Macroterra weapon is very cool looking, and has some neat animations when you are firing, jumping etc. It does lack the variety of having different weapons that you can change between, like in other FPS games, though the variety of attack types is not lacking, with a total of 8 different primary and secondary weapons.
The sound is well done, with some really nice sounds effects for shooting, scoring points, killing enemies etc. While the background music is good, without being either particularly memorable, or too intrusive... it fits in really well with the game and adds to the atmosphere without being distracting in any way.
I completed the campaign mode in the base game, on easy difficultly, in about 5 hours, which may not sound like much, but is pretty good for the price. There are also 3 other game modes on each level, which are Scab Attack, Essence Attack and Brain Attack, where you concentrate on one type of goal.
There are 3 difficulty levels, which affects how much time you have to complete the level, and in addition to that, on each level you earn a star rating out of 5 for how well you performed, so if you are a completionist, then you can spend a lot more time trying to perfect each level. I have managed 5 stars on maybe 60%+ of the levels so far, on easy difficulty.
I can see myself dipping into this game occasionally, given the nature of the levels and the slightly casual feel to the game, I see it as a good FPS game to 'relax' with.
