This is my definitely one of my favorite games of all time, and what an amazing experience it was.
The gameplay, the graphics, the atmosphere... everything is just stuning. The story was also very good and interesting, and was so well written that it got me hooked, wich isn't very often for me.
The graphics are also really good, even now in 2017. I could play the whole game on highest quality with 60fps without any framedrops, and I only have a GeForce GTX 1050 with an Intel Core i5, so you really can tell that they worked hard on optimization.
The horror aspect of this game is amazing and there are many jumpscares that even got me after multiple playthroughs. The chasing sequences are really making your heart race and don't allow mistakes. They are also very long, wich makes them even scarier because you don't want to loose all your progress and go through the horror again.
Now, I got all the achievments and beat both main game and DLC on Insane difficulty (Nightmare difficulty without checkpoints), and it was really fun to do. One thing that really annoyed me though was that when I was 30 seconds before the end of Whistleblower on Insane difficulty, I went into the settings to turn off fullscreen, because ~75% of the time, the game freezes after the credits and I can't get out of the game so I need to restart my computer, but when I don't have the game on fullscreen, I can just easily open and overlap the window with the Task-Manager to close Outlast. However, the game already froze when I turned fullscreen off, so I couldn't just play the last 30 seconds and get the achievment, but needed to restart my computer and play the whole thing again... I did it after 3 more attempts, but still, it really annoyed me.
Sorry for so much boring text, but I just wanted to get it out of the way. So, that was actually the only Con I have about this game, and even though it seemed like much, it was really just a small thing.
In the end, this is definitely my favorite horror game and one of my favorite games overall, and will probably be for a long time. So, if you haven't bought or played it yet, do it. It really is worth it, trust me.

And I know some people may find this to be a little bit threatening, but the truth is that the game just does enough to propagate this complexity in all the right areas and then leaves simplicity in other things, take for example refilling your ammo or bandages, which help you from bleeding out once you've been hit but not killed, to do this you simply have to walk towards a checkpoint marked in your map, and that's it, no interaction, no press this button, nothing, just simply walk to it, some people might say this is irrelevant, and this type of stuff doesn't matter, but it does, in the end it can be the difference between stopping the flow of the combat to something more agile and quick, it works great, and this type of example carries through a lot of different mechanics of the game.
Now there are a couple of issues, for starters, I really don't like the feel of some of the movement in the game, I realize it's supposed to be a "realistic war simulator" but it's kind of annoying to have your camera bouncing up and down constantly, maybe there's a setting to change this, reduce it a bit, or just simply turn it off, in all honesty I haven't check, but so far it seems to be part of the game.
The other thing that some people may find annoying it's the fact that this is certainly a game that shows it's age, i'm frankly not bothered in the least by it, and I think that the game looks amazing, but some people may dislike this seeing how as I said before, a lot of military shooters now a days focus too much in delivering an attention to detail in other areas that might make the game look prettier, but don't give a particular feel of "crudeness" that something like this game gives, both in it's aesthetic, and graphical quality, as well as in it's gameplay.
Which also might be something else to say, if you're the type of person that's looking for more of a balance between "hardcore fps" and more "casual fps" then maybe this is for you, the game it's created intelligently and knows how to balance this stuff out, but if you're really looking for a "weightless, no recoil, no threat" type of game, then maybe you won't like this game.
I frankly love the game so far, and really if it wasn't for my broken back (figure of speech) then I would be playing it right now, I wanted to get my fix of something like this for a very long time, a game that's complex but not to a point of being frustrating to me (say like Insurgency) and also a game that was simple to play but not completely (say like Call of Duty) I wanted something unique and diferent, and I think this game gave me that.
I really, really hope the next entry, which apparently will be set in Vietnam, will include all of this incredible things that I loved about this game.
Please developers, no dumbing down, but not designing the game to be punishing, keep this style of gameplay and know how can this be improved even further, think of adding a campaing and also a similarly but maybe even more fleshed out offline bot mode, and do please keep that side of the game OFFLINE, respect my right of owneship as I respect your right to get paid for the hard work you've put into this game, don't make the mistake of turning this beautiful and pro-consumer experience, into something to be ashamed.
I guess i'm simply asking you to be good to your fans, just like you were this time.

In Limbo, a young boy journeys through Limbo in order to find his missing sister.
And...that's essentially it. Limbo's story is very simple and left ambiguous for the most part, like games such as Journey and a considerable number of the Metroid games. But just like them, it's not only about the journey itself rather than a narrative, but has something to make up for the lack of narrative: atmosphere.
The areas in Limbo are very ambient as the setting truly feels like it is alive, what with objects moving in the background and then later on reappearing foreground. But what makes this game feel so palpable is the grainy, black and white graphics style, which is very unique and feels like a dark, surreal world where the meager amount of light is what you little you motivation you have of achieving your goal.
Don't believe me? When you die, the only part of your of your body to have light, your eyes, close. Metaphors, man!
However, this isn't a game where you simply stop and smell the roses, as some parts can become incredibly tense and cause you to think fast...or else face an untimely demise. It is a platformer, but to progress you must solve puzzles by interacting with the environment around you.
1. Some of them are pretty smart, such as using beatraps in order to harm a giant spider, and manipulating machinery and even gravity itself. My personal favorite is when a worm-like parasite latches onto you and controls your movement, and you must find a way to get rid of it or else die alongside with it.
Oh, speaking of death, there's A LOT of ways to die in this game. Every nook and cranny in Limbo is a death trap, and yet each death actually enhances the gameplay rather than simply making the player frustrated. Since a lot of the puzzles require trial and error, dying teaches you what to do and what NOT to do. In a way, the deaths are like a gameplay mechanic itself.
The game doesn't have a traditional soundtrack, but instead relies mostly on ambient noise that makes the atmosphere even more palpable.
In the end, Limbo is a game that while with a simple premise, has a very distinct and creepy graphics style, strong and palpable atmosphere, ingenious platforming and puzzles the tests both your skills and patience, and immerses you in a world that will make its visitors not want to leave anytime soon.
I recommend it to any fans of the genre, in case you missed it back in the day when it first exploded on the internet, such as I did.

Where to begin.
I've played enough of TLD to know the ins and outs of how to survive, I've lived long enough to know that I could survive forever, I've become good with the bow, crafting, found most of the locations, and so on. I always kept this game in the back of my mind, to come back to, as it gets closer to being completed.
But at this stage, despite the devs good intentions, it feels bad. Really bad.
The problems most survival games have is balance and pacing, and becoming inevitably repetitive / nothing to do. The reason for this is largely because most games take the entire genre from the standpoint of "Naked and Afraid", give the players nothing to begin with, and have them do everything from scratch. And while this works well with certain games / settings, it's awful in TLD, even with the minimal gear they give you.
It's terrible when you cant survive day 1 because a fire simply wont light over a dozen times at 60% chance with no storm and blocked from the wind. It's worse when you cant survive day 2 because you have everything you need except matches because of day 1, so you have no way whatsoever to light a fire. 60% chance to light, my♥♥♥♥♥ And this is on VOYAGER! (normal difficulty). Good luck crawling to explore to try to find a freaking match.
Further, as you explore, if you are able to, you just find everything you could ever want lying around the indoor areas. This has always bugged me. Why even go outside once you find some nice buildings? And once you know where everything is, what then? Just go grab the best stuff, and all of a sudden the entire game is pointless. Paradoxically everything is just sitting there, so if you get to it, it's too easy, but if you can't light fires, to get there in the first couple of days, game over. So the game just becomes an excecise of restarting enough times to know where to get stuff easily by memorizing the map (which is never randomized).
That's a dumb game in a nutshell,
(completion bar for fires, sleeping, etc) for long periods of time.
unrealistic aspects of a game that's supposed to be realistically brutal, terribly handled, terrible combat, terrible everything. And yes, putting in a blurb in the intro that "We know wolves do not normally attack people in real life" doesn't make it any better.
Meanwhile, in a game like The Forest, I'm getting 60fps lock, with photorealistic graphics and amazing effects. Isn't the point of the minimal, cardboard-like graphics in TLD partly so that you dont have these fps performance issues?  Seems like they just can't code it to where it's acceptable. And if the counter-argument is "it's not optimized because early access lol" I for one do not give half a♥♥♥♥♥♥about that. It is what it is. If it sucks, it sucks.

Oh, and thanks for
by the way. Shouldn't have that been thought of by now? Talk about fatigue... to my damn wrist, that is. Do these devs ever play their own game? Surely you must know that jamming W while moving at 30% speed for minutes at a time, getting nowhere, is♥♥♥♥♥

And I've turned the corner on this and concluded that the realism does not make up for the pain of playing this 'game'. Beautiful, brutal and intriguing; That's the kind of gameplay that you'll find with this.
Like many reviews before you'll hear compairisions to XCOM, which is fairly accurate. Hero's are unable to come back after they have finally bit more off than they could chew. Be it after you opened a door with too many dark rooms, thus flooding the one stronghold you had with monsters, overwhelming your defenses and killing your team members; things spiral out of control and before you know it, rooms are going dark and you're in damage control mode.
The gameplay revolves around the simple mechanic of opening doors, as is obvious from the trailers. Opening these doors pass time as a turn based strategy. Each turn you have a allotment of Food, Industry, and Science, these are used to heal and level up hero's, build improvements on tiles and research more improvements. Another side effect of doors opening is the obtainment of a substance called Dust. Collecting these random rooms of dust (which is automatic) will increase the amount of power your crystaline generator can put out.
Your crystaline generator is where the game turns from a top down turn based strategy to a tower defense hybrid. The power levels of your generator is where you have to make hard choices and manage the best "damage limits". For example, having weak defenses on the right side, while strong on the left. If you had no industry to build turrets, you could light up the right side of the map, while leaving the left dark. The improvments on the left could be damaged, or even destroyed without hero support; or you could lose or keep both of the improvments and the hero's you send in. The power levels will also drasticly decline over time, as you progress from floor to floor. The higher the floor number, the less likely you'll have enough power to comfortably beat the level.
Levels are divided into two parts, exploration and extraction. Exploration is the part you'll spend most of your time in, as you are sweeping levels trying to find the exit, dust, treasure chests full of gear, extra heros, merchants, research pillars and improvement allotments (leftover industry, science or food from the builders or inhabitants of the dungeon.). This is where the bulk of enemies come from, and argueably the most dangerous part, as random EMP's and events slow down your progress and could potentially leave you dangerously exposed. Extraction is after you locate the exit, and where careful consideration takes place. Once you are ready to leave a level, you send a hero (or your whole team) to the very beginning where you pick up your crystaline generator. One you have a hero with the crystal, all the unlit rooms in the floor will continually produce monsters, in a unending wave. They will not stop until you have exited the level or they have killed your team. You could shut down any un-needed tiles that are out of the way, and provide no support, and light the way up as much as you can, or you can risk it all in a rush gambit.
Moving away from the gameplay, the art style and music add a amazing ambiance to the game. Each character has it's own unique design and quirks, occationally spurting out a comment upon performing a action. The pixel art looks amazing and animates fluidly, as characters move about, fight, operate machineary or upon being left alone, read a newspaper, smoke or kick the ground. There is alot of character added to the game though its music and artstyle, you'll find that you won't get bored of seeing levels, as they change as you go up, and randomly morph to different layouts. I can say with absolute certainty, that the combination of the graphics and music will never bog down the gameplay.
Overall Dungeons of the endless provides a intresting and entertaining gameplay experience, and will entertain you for hours on end. The combination of the different gameplays, humorous item and hero discriptions and addictive rougelike nature combined with the brutal tension of power and hero management tends to put this game in a light of its own, as there isn't one game you can pair it with. I would absolutely recommend this to anyone on the fence about this title, you won't be disappointed.

Compared to most of the other games I have that require me to be on guard, this one definitely stands out in my Game Library.
First off, the game itself is cheap and I got it on sale, when it was around or under just a dollar.
It's a relaxing puzzle game with a simple concept; connect all of the shapes that are the same with lines. It's where you have a few shapes on the screen at once (Or only one in some cases), and two of each kind of shape having a white center and a darkened version of its color as an outline. You start with drawing the line from one of said shapes through all other shapes of that kind and ending in the second.
Sounds easy, huh?
Well, it is, at least to start. There are 26 sets of puzzles to start, all of them representing a letter in the alphabet from A-Z, starting at A and getting harder as you go down. Each set has 25 puzzles total in it, making for a total of 650 puzzles, and even if you get done with all of those there are still the puzzles that only come around daily so you're still entertained. If you get bored of the default green background, you can unlock new pallets for the background of the game so you can stick with the one that you like the most.
The puzzles aren't just the only thing that make this game relaxing, but the music plays a large part to add onto the atmosphere that lets you feel very at ease. It's pretty quiet, but the sound that comes from you clicking something or dragging a line through it just reverberates and, again, adds very well to the atmosphere.
I'm not sure what it is about those echoing sounds, but something about them chiming gives me a feeling of...
Hmm....
Nostalgia.....
And I don't know why.

This is an amazing game, i've played 30 minutes of it today, just that mainly because my back hurts and i'm sad right now.
But the game is great, I frankly was avoiding this game like the plague for the simple reason that the game doesn't specify it has bots, meaning an offline single player game mode, see developers this is all it takes sometimes to convince some people into buying your game, plus the game in itself it's great, it doesn't have any drm nonsense besides steam, the game runs great even when you find yourself setting up games with large groups of enemies and allies, everything is just very simple while at the same time being very complex.
It's one of those war games that tries to capture an authentic feel by basically applying a lot detail and attention to the gameplay, think of something like what some modern war games try to achieve but instead of focusing on the aesthetics and the graphics, this game focuses that same type of attention into the gameplay.
And I know some people may find this to be a little bit threatening, but the truth is that the game just does enough to propagate this complexity in all the right areas and then leaves simplicity in other things, take for example refilling your ammo or bandages, which help you from bleeding out once you've been hit but not killed, to do this you simply have to walk towards a checkpoint marked in your map, and that's it, no interaction, no press this button, nothing, just simply walk to it, some people might say this is irrelevant, and this type of stuff doesn't matter, but it does, in the end it can be the difference between stopping the flow of the combat to something more agile and quick, it works great, and this type of example carries through a lot of different mechanics of the game.
Now there are a couple of issues, for starters, I really don't like the feel of some of the movement in the game, I realize it's supposed to be a "realistic war simulator" but it's kind of annoying to have your camera bouncing up and down constantly, maybe there's a setting to change this, reduce it a bit, or just simply turn it off, in all honesty I haven't check, but so far it seems to be part of the game.
The other thing that some people may find annoying it's the fact that this is certainly a game that shows it's age, i'm frankly not bothered in the least by it, and I think that the game looks amazing, but some people may dislike this seeing how as I said before, a lot of military shooters now a days focus too much in delivering an attention to detail in other areas that might make the game look prettier, but don't give a particular feel of "crudeness" that something like this game gives, both in it's aesthetic, and graphical quality, as well as in it's gameplay.
Which also might be something else to say, if you're the type of person that's looking for more of a balance between "hardcore fps" and more "casual fps" then maybe this is for you, the game it's created intelligently and knows how to balance this stuff out, but if you're really looking for a "weightless, no recoil, no threat" type of game, then maybe you won't like this game.
I frankly love the game so far, and really if it wasn't for my broken back (figure of speech) then I would be playing it right now, I wanted to get my fix of something like this for a very long time, a game that's complex but not to a point of being frustrating to me (say like Insurgency) and also a game that was simple to play but not completely (say like Call of Duty) I wanted something unique and diferent, and I think this game gave me that.
I really, really hope the next entry, which apparently will be set in Vietnam, will include all of this incredible things that I loved about this game.
Please developers, no dumbing down, but not designing the game to be punishing, keep this style of gameplay and know how can this be improved even further, think of adding a campaing and also a similarly but maybe even more fleshed out offline bot mode, and do please keep that side of the game OFFLINE, respect my right of owneship as I respect your right to get paid for the hard work you've put into this game, don't make the mistake of turning this beautiful and pro-consumer experience, into something to be ashamed.
I guess i'm simply asking you to be good to your fans, just like you were this time.

If you're
about your hidden-object gaming...
Seriously, this isn't chess!  But nonetheless, if for some reason you're
about hidden object gaming, you'd do better to avoid Sinister City.  It doesn't take itself remotely seriously, and there are some serious weaknesses in the game design.
If you're just looking for some brief, cheap, casual fun, though, Sinister City can be just the quick, entertaining, romp you need.  The puzzles are few, the HO scenes pretty easy, so there's little to distract you from running through the goofy, parodic story that plays around with the classics of vampire film.  While there's nods to
and Lugosi's classic portrayal of Dracula, Sinister City clearly draws its influence from schlockier fare like
and the low-budget Hammer Horror films.  If not laugh-out-loud funny, the story is at least far more entertaining than a typical HOG plot.
Gameplay is the weakness here.  Your next action is frequently unintuitive; you often cannot pick up an item you'll obviously need until explicitly told to collect it.  At one point, an object's graphic failed to load, leaving me to collect a white rectangle.  At another time, the game glitched so that I could not progress -- exiting and reopening the game solved the problem, though.  Finally, Sinister City relies on a mechanism where objects that are not your current targets must be clicked to move them, to discover target objects behind them.  This means you must click pretty much everything, rather than just hunting targets.  What's more, an object that was immobile in a previous visit to an HO screen might spontaneously become movable at a later time, requiring you to click everything on every visit to a screen, in order to not miss a potentially hidden target object.
At the price, especially if on special, I can't not recommend this game.  Tolerate the gameplay; enjoy the story.

I will reccomend this game with a few caveats:
1. You have to like turn based RPGs
2. You have to like the Mahou Shoujo/"Magical Girl" aesthetic (Sailor Moon, Madoka, etc.)
3. You have to like gratuitous Yuri/Lesbian overtones
The game's strengths are its clean UI, its simple but strategic battle system, and its faithful adaptation of a tonal "magical girl" story. You can think of this game as a "low budget Persona 3/4/", essentially.
Where the game falters, and prevents itself from becoming truly "great", are in how its "dungeons" are very weakly designed with few motivations for exploration and continued combat, its poor in-game camera, and its lacking difficulty (playing the game on "hard" helps, barely).
Let's also not forget the ridiculous $80 season pass this game has launched with. And the $53 price tag. The publisher clearly has no idea what it's doing with PC games, especially since I only heard about this game the day before launch.
For $15 to $20, this game is a "steal" - you aren't going to find a mahou shoujo RPG in English anywhere else, and if you are onboard with my three caveats above, you should love this game.
I'd like to see more games like these brought into English, and the game genuinely looked unique, which is why I was comfortable paying close to full price for it. It's not Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest, its battle system is trying to do something different, and I think it mostly works. Plus, the more personal narrative this game offers is something I prefer for a game to have, so I was able to justify paying way above what this game is honestly worth. This is a game to buy when it's really on sale.
This is a budget jRPG trying to do something different so it still deserves props for that.
Now, with that all out of the way, I do have to admonish the game for...Well, it's to be expected, right? A young female character NOT being sexualized in any manner would surprise me more than anything. And the ridiculous amount of lesbian overtones in this game is borderline funny and not offensive. The fact you can go on DATES with your female classmates really takes the cake for me and bridges the comparison to Persona 3/4/5 further.
But was it really necessary to give us bath scenes? Scenes where our protagonist walks in the rain, so her bra can bleed through her blouse? Are details like that really necessary? It's a little creepy, or at least it hurts the serious tone the story tries to take in places. The story here is something you can take mildly seriously, at least for a mahou shoujo, and some of the oversexualization here really undermines that. I mean, mahou shoujo are sexual enough without the additional stuff here, just look at those costumes... I wish they'd exercised a little more restraint, and kept the fan service to a more sporadic level. Instead, it's literally everywhere. But this is an East vs West audience expectation thing. This game was clearly made for Japan, and I'm glad we got a localization of it. That nothing here was censored is great.
If you can handle everything I've described, I strongly reccomend this; it's a unique game.

The Good:
The game has an intriguing atmosphere reminiscent of a post apocalyptic world. You'll explore the ruins of cities, overgrown forests and mysteriously functioning industrial complexes, all while strange tribal figures and mutated monsters try to kill you.
As for gameplay, it has a lot of really clever physics puzzles and timed gauntlet runs, which were fun to this author, though the puzzles were very tedious at the start of the game. They definitely got better as it went on, though.
The Bad:
The aesthetic of the game makes it hard to distinguish hazards from non-descript scenery. The game is also LITTERED with beginner's traps, moments where you're given zero time to take in any information and die for mere lack of psychic clairvoyance. The character you control feels slow and heavy, despite being such a little guy, leading to many moments where I knew the solution to a puzzle but was hindered by the character themselves.
The Ugly:
The game gives you so much to wonder about, so much mystery - who are the tribals that are trying to murder you? What happened to these abandoned cities? Who are we, and what brought us here? NONE of it is explained, it's not even given a satisfying ending to help you feel like the journey was worth anything on its own.
I'm about to spoil the ending. If you care, now's the time to skip to the final verdict.
The game just. Stops. No payoff, nothing learned, nothing gained, nothing you do in the game has any purpose and absolutely all of the interesting creatures, people and environments were left without even one shred of vaguely interpretive meaning. What happens, exactly? You walk up to a random girl sitting by a tree, that's it. She doesn't do anything, he doesn't do anything, they don't even look at eachother and we've never seen her before. There's nothing artistic to me about this, there's nothing being said with any of it, nothing being expressed. It feels like I wasted my time with this game and that depresses me far more than the game's monotone. I wanted to like this game after it had been hyped up for so long, but I feel like I truly took nothing useful from it. Its ending is worse than an old NES style, "conglaturation". At least that acknowledges you DID something, this game just stops. Picture Super Mario Bros. 1 just cutting to black as soon as you see the princess, and the game never mentioning there even was a princess to begin with.
Final verdict: 3/10
I really didn't want to dislike this game, I swear I didn't, but this wasn't worth ten dollars to me. I couldn't get anything useful out of it, and the puzzles - while clever - weren't worth ten dollars on their own. The ending itself was so poor that not only do I feel like the game's not worth ten dollars, I feel like I was ripped off. If you only want a puzzle game, for ten dollars, you could get longer lasting games. If you d care about the story and just want a puzzle game, I recommend waiting for a sale, as there aren't many puzzles to solve.

POST-COMPLETION REVIEW
Pros:
+ Cute waifus
+ God tier artwork (all praise Kishida Mel)
+ Interesting fragment / character growth system (unfortunately rendered meaningless by difficulty level of game)
+ The OST is pretty epic. It lacks variety.. but the boss fight themes are pretty hype (as with all GUST games)
+ Despite my criticisms below, there's a lot to be said about the main character's growth in this story. Watching Hinako change over the course of the story is pretty heartwarming.
Cons:
- Optimisation is meh (gotta use borderless gaming to play in fullscreen windowed, forced to mess with .ini files / resharders etc)
- Interesting combat system bogged down by terrible difficult balancing (unfortunately combat is WAY too easy, especially after you get time warp enemies never get a turn, ever)
- Mediocre gameplay, I was really disappointed with the zones. Only 4 of them, really?
- Also the bosses, really? The first time was epic, then they started recycling them...
- Genuinely melancholic storyline, which is kinda ruined by terrible pacing. Honestly I felt the whole "invite out your friend" mechanic got really old very, very quickly, and the small sub events weren't exactly the most well written or entertaining.
- Side character development is hit and miss. Ako/Mao/Sarasa/Riko were pretty interesting to me... some storylines like Sanae/Yuri felt like they were forced in to just to tick checkboxes. On the whole, it's pretty bad. At the end of character storyquests you're forced to fight generic mobs. We couldn't have unique bosses for those, really?
- Fanservice can be a bit too intrusive at some times
- Translations aren't the most accurate at times (lost nuances + spelling mistakes + mistranslations)
Conclusion:
6/10
It's a pretty nice stress free gaming experience with cute waifus. The first few hours of the game are pretty promising, with an interesting battle and growth system. The repetitiveness of the game is stretched out meaninglessly for absolutely no reason. If anything, this game would have been made better by being shorter and more story focused. Should have done away with the generic heart meter grinding and fetch quests and actually written more event storylines to develop the side characters further. Would have been better if it tried harder to be a VN and had less combat, given how poorly that aspect of the game was taken care of.
TLDR: BUY IF ON DISCOUNT

This is easily my favourite game for this year. The art and music is wonderful, I even bought the soundtrack and have been listening to it almost non stop which I have never done for a game before.
Controls are tight which is a must as you'll be splitting your attention across multiple things that you need to avoid all at once.
The levels I feel are the weakest point. There are only six and they aren't particularly interesting. However, this game was built for the boss battles so it's not too important.
The bosses vary considerably in difficulty, but for the most part the easier ones are at the start of the game. It's great discussing it with other people, you'll find one boss you were stuck on for hours other people beat in minutes or that you beat a boss on the first try and people spent days stuck on them. For example most people find the flying bosses insanely difficult or a complete push over.
Biggest negative for me were the platforming bosses. Whenever you die it feels like it was your fault - you know what you did wrong and you learn from it, makes it feel like a real achievement when you defeat a difficult boss. However, against the bosses with random platform spawns this isn't the case. It feels more like you just got unlucky when loosing and lucky when you finally win, that there was no actual progression as sometimes you just died to platforms not spawning where you needed them.

First off, for those who read both good and bad reviews, if any of the negative reviews only have less then an hour of gameplay, just ignore them. Why? Like everyone has said, once you can get used to the bugs and clunky Ui, it's really not that bad of a game.
What makes this a game that I highly recommend is the community. Many people there are very nice and willing to help if you are willing to ask for it. Within the first few hours of playing I was able to get some help and make a couple of friends. As a veteran of another MMO, Mabinogi, having played for almost 7 years, that didn't happen there in my newbie days. At all. I find a friendly community to be invaluable when it comes to mmo's nowadays. This game is rather aged, a diamond from the past in a sense, however, but if you think about it, it was almost ahead of it's time back then. The graphics are decent given it's age.
As for gameplay, well. It can get grindy, especially with the loop quests but that's ok, the fun part is getting into parties to wipe bosses out. And there's about 15 different classes but once you hit level 10, you literally can choose whatever you want and not be bound to them. There's also the option to make a secondary class as well, which means, let's say you want to be a doctor but also a dancer. You can train your doctor skills for the healing then you can switch classes and have the doctor class be the secondary, with your healing available.
And so my TL;DR version:
Pros:
- Decent graphics and animations for it's age
- Friendly community
- 15 classes to choose from without being bound to any of them
- Decently large maps
- Faster traveling with "flying"
- Pet system/Taming system
Cons:
- Clunky UI
- Some bugs and crashing
- No option to turn the "Red thread of Fate" effects off
- Quirky flying controls
Now I'm only lv 17 in game atm, but from what I've seen this is my review, even on short term, I recommend giving it a try if you can be patient enough with the bugs and ui.

The guns and specials shoot and respond really well, hats off to the developers for the constant updates and patches to continually improve the game. Playing as the monster can be quite difficult. The movement takes a while to get used too. It is definitely a rush to go up against four hunters who are tracking your every move. After a while, the movement becomes natural and once you settle into the abilities that you like, it becomes easier to take out the squad of hunters. Certain monsters are stronger than others at various stages. You have to play them all and try all the combos with the different abilities for this game to reach its true potential. It's quite hard to beat a team who is communicating and coordinating. This game is terrifying at times. I haven't played anything that had me on the edge of my seat for the entire match.
You can play a quick round against humans or bots or you can go for evacuation and play a dynamic campaign that lasts for five maps/days. Each day/map change the dynamics favor the hunter squad or the monster. Apparently there are over 800,000 different combinations or permutations in this mode which makes for great long-term playability.

Dungeon of the Endless is a terrific blend of RPG, RTS, TBS and Tower Defense elements that forces you to evolve not just your gameplay strategy, but your thinking paradigm as you advance. It also carries the inevitable 'pondering a potentially deadly situation' and 'permadeath punch' of a true roguelike.
The core mechanic is exploring a dungeon level to find a rare resource 'dust' in order to power rooms to carry your crystal from a central location to the 'exit'. Dust is always in short supply, and so you will find yourself forced to leave rooms unpowered. Unpowered rooms allow a variety of incresingly powerful monsters to spawn, who will attack towards your crystal.
You can use module slots located in each of the rooms to power either major modules (which give a resource boost); minor modules (which assist your chracters) or turrets, which defend the rooms. Balancing these out will be key to  a successful run. After you're done placement, you choose which door/room to open next, and a wave of monsters spawns from the unpowered rooms. If you survive, you major modules produce resources, allowing you to build more... and you either open another room, or make a break for the exit with the crystal. Deciding when to quit the floor becomes a critical strategic decision with a well-balanced double-edged risk vs. reward mechanic: milk a floor for all the resources it's worth and risk being overrun enitrely, or cut loose and make a panicked run for the exit?
The characters trying to escape are varied and range across a variety of skills and playtypes, and finding a combination that plays to your micromanagement style (or lack thereof) is one of the game's brilliant design features. Especially when a key character dies and you're forced to substitute them with someone you're not as comfortable with/have to learn, or make do without.
A lot of love has gone into the level and character design, and the pixel art is terrific. Sadly, the music from the launch trailer vastly outstrips anything in the game itself (and is also not on the soundtrack, for some unfathomable reason).
This is a great game to experience core elements of different genres at the same time, without getting bogged down in the trappings of each (it allows the player a great deal of freedom in how to approach the game, at least initially). Highly recommended, but also fair warning: this will not be an 'easy' win for the casual or AAA gamer--mistakes come swiftly and are fatal.
btw: The music from the 'Rogue Life' trailer for the game is the track 'On and On' by Tom Hillock. You can buy the album off Bandcamp. You're welcome :)

A lot of games benefit from having random or procedural elements, but it never occurred to me to apply those principles to a stealth game. I always thought stealth games needed to be tightly tuned, with carefully-designed levels and sharp AIs on patrol routes and such. Sir is very much a stealth game that benefits from randomness, but not without some significant drawbacks.
Sir drops you into the middle of five randomly-generated islands, each populated by murderous metallic monsieurs out for your human hide. A mysterious device brought you here, and is now scattered into 16 pieces across the archipelago. Each piece must be returned to the standing stones at the center of the center isle if you are to return home. To aid you in your task, there's a whole host of items to scavenge up, some useful, some not. As you find more pieces, the robots step up their efforts, including robo-dogs, scarecrow sentries, hot air balloons, and more monstrous machines to hunt you down.
The robots are the heart of this game, and they are at times terrifying. Sure, they make conspicuous beep-boop noises as you draw near, but once they spot you with that heart-stopping bleep, you're in deep trouble. The 'bots are almost as fast as you, but they have guns and are pretty good shots with them. They're also intelligent about chasing you, following as far as they saw you go and then making educated guesses about where to search from there. Most robot patrol the islands in groups, paying close attention to structures that can be scavenged but following and suspicious leads they find. Other robots mill around the artifacts you need to recover, making sure you have to deal with some of them to get home. Getting caught can spell disaster if you can't get away fast enough, or if they plug you with a lucky shot that leaves you bleeding out.
You have two important numbers to keep track of, Health and Vitality. Either one bottoms out, you're done. Health regens slowly unless you've been shot, in which case you need to bandage yourself up using an item. Vitality drains over time with activity, and must be restored with food. And THAT means risking patrols to sneak into abandoned villages and churches to loot. You can't enter any structure in the game; the doors to buildings serve as loot containers. It's a bit of a blow to immersion and options for hiding, but other than that the loot system is solid. You have limited space to store weapons and traps, food and bandages, and any other interesting odds and ends you find. It's up to you to figure out what use some items have, which adds an element of mystery and experimentation to the game.
You can only save at the standing stones or the boats to other islands, so you really have to think twice about risky moves. Stealth in this game is tricky... it seems more based on proximity than action, and the robots are good about looking over their shoulders. Proper sneaking takes a long time given the distances, and waiting for patrols to move on is the safest but most time-consuming route. I'm still learning how to deal with them, but honestly I've been able to run by and grab a few artifacts right in front of them without being murdered. Getting caught can be frustrating though, given how hard the robots are to lose. You can fight back if you find weapons, but combat is not a focus and can be pretty fiddly. And in terms of navigation, you have a compass that marks the boats, but if you want to get any additional use out of it you have to find a map and mark it up yourself with points of interest.
Is it a good game? Yes, but one you have to put time into. Finding 16 fragments across 5 islands is going to take time, even moreso if you play the stealth game right, scavenge diligently, and use your map to the fullest. The randomization keeps the game fresh but can lead to situations where you're trapped between patrols for extended periods or find artifacts in nigh-impossible locations. It's not a particularly attractive game either, with some low-poly models and muddy textures. But if you can settle into it and give it some time, it'll keep you busy for a good long while.

Recipe: Rotisserie Chicken
Prep Time: 15 minutes/ Cook time: 1h 30min / total time: 1h 45min
Ingredients:
- 1 tbsp Salt
- 1 tbsp Paprika
- 1/4 tbsp of black pepper
-  1 (3 pound) chicken
- Pinch of Salt
- 1/4 cup butter, melted
Directions:
Season the inside of the chicken with a pinch of salt. Place the chicken onto a rotisserie and set the grill on high. Cook for 10 minutes.
During that time, quickly mix together the butter, 1 tablespoon of salt, paprika and pepper. Turn the grill down to medium and baste the chicken with the butter mixture. Close the lid and cook for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, basting occasionally, until the internal temperature reaches 180 degrees F (83 degrees C) when taken in the thigh with a meat thermometer.
Remove from the rotisserie and let stand for 10 to 15 minutes before cutting into pieces and serving.

The core gameplay is playing the neverending whack-a-mole with these three relentless furies, while you are probably also becoming cold. That is if you have food, water, shelter and fuel. If not, you will probably die miserably very quickly. I was not having fun playing the game.

The game feels stressful, pointless and boring at the same time. I can understand some people like it. I certainly did not.

I'm a huge fan of true survival games, like don't starve. where it's hard to survive and, if possible at all, even harder to thrive. During the winter sale I was looking for a new survival game to play, and this always proves to be a difficult task because there are so many fake survival games, games that with enough grinding you can easily thrive.
So I decided to give project zomboid a try, and the game positively surprised me.
It is a really hard game where if you be careful enough, you'll be able to survive, but a minor screw up can and will kill you. Wasn't prepared for that zombie in the bathroom of a house you thought was empty? He can scratch you or bite you, giving you a high chance of zombification, an illness with no cure in the game. Yes, you a zombie manages to scratch or bite you, there's a big chance that the game over timer will start ticking.
And even if you isolate yourself from the huge amounts of zombie in the forested areas of the huge (HUGE) map, you'll still will have to deal with food and water. Food can be preserved for more time in fridges, but guess what? After a random amount of days, the power will be cut out. You can drink water from sinks and toilets, but just like the power, water will also be cut out after a random amount of days.
The character creation is fantastic as well, and the trait system reminds me of old fallout games. You have good and bad traits that give you negative and positive points, respectively. You can only start the game if you have 0 or more points so you'll need to balance your character accordingly.
And it has multiplayer! I had loads of fun playing with two people, scavenging the city for supplies, reinforcing a place to call home...
And finally, another thing that really surprised me was the amount of zombies in the game. Depending on your luck and area in the game, you can stumble upon hordes and hordes of zombies. This feels just like the walking dead, and in fact it's one of the games that feels most like the series, apart from the telltale's ones, of course.
This game is still in early access and it's loads of fun. I can't even think of how it will look and play when it's done.

If you like strategy games, this ones for you.
I have to say...I'm into it. Im not a huge strategy gamer but the developers behind this game are phenomenal. Their work here is sleek, simple, and properly designed. This game is not complex and yet you are still left feeling stumped from time to time. It's like you know the answer to the puzzles are simple, but for whatever reason you just cannot figure them out. After electrocuting yourself a dozen times you think to yourself, "whatever it is that I am doing, is definitely not the answer." I think all good puzzle games should present a certain level of challenge. With this game, however, you get so much more.
Now after scouring the web to see what others think about Playdead's products, I realize that people have a tendancy to read into games like this. And maybe, it's for good reason. If you are looking for a dialogue packed story, however, this is not the game for you. Instead, the developers decided to weave a story by putting you through a curious and fascinating physics engine and testing your problem solving ability. Believe me when I say there is definitely a story in this game. Now I am not so bold to try and explain my thoughts about what that story is, because ultimately the story is not cemented in undisputed fact. This game is certainly not a crude adventure or science fiction novel. This game, and the story included, is refined. There is no definitive structure to a story like this one. It means what it means; and what it means is for you to decide.
Limbo also incorporates a lot of sensory input to improve your gaming eperience.  To a point this almost reminds me of a black and white silent film. But dont be mistaken; it is far from it. There are many sounds, which almost create a texture to the game. It is almost as if you can feel the game as you play through it. It's intuitive and bold. Sometimes the game is stressful, sometimes it's oddly peaceful. Interestingly enough, it is somewhat indicative of it's title. I think it's brilliant. As for the game play, it's certainly not a tolling game. The playthrough is roughly three to four hours, depending on if you have played it previously, or if you are a completionist trying for all the achievements. All this, means you dont have to be dedicated to it; which i find refreshing.
Now this game is not perfect, but it is damned close. To be honest, I don't see myself playing this more than twice. It does not really lend itself to a high replayability value. With such a short playtime however, I dont really think that was the point. It's more like going to the theatre really. It's an experience! Of course, you could play through it again and again to try and get your time down. Although, with so many games to play, that is not really my goal. But some people enjoy that kind of thing. It seems, by today's standards, it is difficult to produce a game that people can latch onto and that does not dissapoint scrupulous gamers such as myself. Indie developers like this, however, are doing some incredible work.

Limbo is a 2D platform game. You play as a young boy lost in the forest, then later in a derelict urban environment, solving puzzles and struggling to stay alive.There are no coins to collect or mushroom power-ups in Limbo’s monochromatic, eerie world. There are no limits to the number of lives you can have. That latter point is crucial.
Many platform games are about learning a few moves perfectly so you can race through level after level. Limbo deliberately messes with that mechanic. There are places where doing the same thing twice in a row will simply get you killed.As you play through Limbo, dying becomes a fact of life – dying in ever more gruesome ways. Sometimes it will be the result of terrible accidents, other times you’ll fall into the clutches of giant monsters. Other children occasionally appear to thwart your character’s progress by luring him into traps.
It’s a game that will haunt you long after you’ve switched off your pc.

I have now completed Blue Reflection so I am coming back to leave an open and honest review about my full experience.
First and foremost, the most breathtaking aspect of this game is the soundtrack. I am not normally one to rave about soundtracks, but this one is expertly done. If they sold a physical soundtrack I'd buy it in a heartbeat.
The game itself was excellent. There's an excellent story here that really helps you better understand the trials and tribulations of a highschool student. Nothing was too cringy or over the top, everything with the story was fairly believable based upon my personal highschool experience many years ago. There were quite a few shower and bath scenes, however they were tastefully done. It wasn't like your typical anime groping competition. The girls were showering because they needed to, and for the most part they were entirely to themselves. This isn't an 18+ eroge type of game.
The turn based combat was very well done. The combat animations were smooth and beautiful to look at. I enjoyed the combat enough that it never felt like a chore doing it. Unfortunately the difficulty of this game was fairly low due to the fact that you can accidentally overlevel early on. It's not really a flaw with the game, because this game doesn't have a typical leveling system. You level through speaking with other students and forming bonds with them. As you form bonds you collect fragments, these fragments are what levels you up. It's a very nice break away from the typical JRPG leveling system.
Performance wise, the game is pretty great. On my system (4790k, 290x), my framerate was always locked at my monitors maximum refresh rate. 1080p 75hz. My experience was very smooth with no frame drops.
As a game, this game is perfectly playable an enjoyable. There are minor issues with the port mostly, but it shouldn't interfere with your ability to play the game in the slightest.
Koei Tecmo was on top of this one. The crashing issues were resolved within a week of the games release. I only experienced one "crash wall", but it was about 20 hours into the game and it was patched about a day after I reached it. The game severely lacks graphical options, specifically Anti-Aliasing. You can easily upscale the game through the games .ini file, removing the need for such, so that's nice at least. The pre-rendered cutscenes run at a low resolution and are a framerate nightmare, but they're typically 20-30 seconds long and there's only a handful of them. So no big loss there. Nothing game breaking here, just nitpicks that could have easily been resolved by such a large company.
This game is easily an 8.5/10 for me. It's not perfect, but it's still a great game.

Big part of the people who are interested in this game, are going to want it because of Red Faction: Guerilla. So I'll be adjusting my recommendation with that in context.
As comparisons go, the first one is as simple as this: The story is now lineair and you are no longer in a free-roaming world. With that, means that the walls surrounding your path are unbreakable. However, this doesn't mean that desctruction is very absent.
On the contrary, destruction and debris play a much bigger role than they did in Guerilla. In said game, your sledgehammer served for nothing to break down buildings, maybe kill those inside.
In Armageddon, debris is a potential weapon. The Magnet gun is the tool of the trade now. It's functioning is two-staged: You attach/shoot first what you want moved, then attach the second magnet to where you want it to go. This can be structure parts, pickups or even enemies (all but the biggest Behemoth).
This makes for some fun and unique gameplay. And while the tool is powerful and relatively fast, you'll still be needing some firearms. Because the Alien swarm is fast and massive.
Besides that, the weapons array is pretty much classic. Shotguns, Assault/Sniper rifles and two sets of dual pistols. The Sniper rifle does feature a heat-mode that allows you to see and headshot through surfaces, which is the only reason the sniper is not obsolete, as vantage points are nigh unexistant.
I won't spoil the story because... it's not that extraordinary. Saying anything about it may as well spoil it all. It's classic, a little bit cheesy but not too annoying.
S.A.M. however, that's a new box of toys. S.A.M. is your wrist-mounted A.I. that serves a guiding purpose in the story, and a more practical one in combat. You start out with a repair functionality. Anything destroyed can be repaired by the nano-forge that is built in.
Which means, you now have a new renewable weapon in debris, as well as a renewable cover source. Too bad there's no cover mechanic. Just crouching, and that's it.
The Impact skill basically serves as a short-range air bash that pushes back any debris in it's path. Of course, this makes the sledgehammer pretty obsolete. (which can now be swapped out)
It also makes for a nice punching weapon, though eventually you'll want to power it up with upgrades.
Besides that, you have three classical 'extra' skills you can get through the upgrade station. Berserk ups your damage and fire speed, Shockwave (that I didn't even bother to try) is a typical Nova ability, and the Shell works as a projectile shield (great for when you're almost dead) and DoT for enemies that are inside of it.
As per enemies go... it's a good thing your toys are more destructive rather than precision based. AFAIK 25% of the enemies you encounter are human. And they tend to be pushovers, even at Hard difficulty.
The real threat are the Alien creatures. They all come in several ranks, and tend to just swarm you late-game, with the low-rank creatures coming in masses and tending to be very melee based.
But, even on Hard mode, the only real threats are the Berserkers are the Behemoths. Berserkers are quite tough and are hard hitting on both ranged and melee. But they can just be punted around with the magnet gun and melee'd to death once you've taken care of the other critters.
Behemoths, when not encountered while in a vehicle, tend to be mini-boss fights. The area is locked off and you need to use your weapons or available debris to kill them. They're real bullet spunges and hit pretty hard in ranged and melee.
And they can't be punted around.
While in a vehicle, they are the only types of enemies that really pose a threat if not paid any attention to.
Eventually though, you'll find a gimmick that works for you and they just become a nuisance. Much like the other aliens, really.
This is a game with a gimmick that plays it very, very well. But sadly, it can't lean on it to justify a full price. Maybe if it had been free-roaming. But regardless, the game is not something you should avoid simply because of that.
Harsh, unforgiving - but a genuinely rewarding game. Forces you to make choices, some of which you'll live long enough to regret.

Cuphead has so much going for it! It is one of the most polished games in recent years, and it boasts such a unique artsyle that will set it apart for what I believe years to come. The controls are sound even though you don't have dual directional aiming. My only gripe with the controls is that when I ducked on a platform and jumped, it seemed unintuitive that I fell through instead of jumping which caused more than a handful of deaths. Similar to the aiming, I got use to it though, but only because the game punished me for thinking. The loadouts are all useful despite me thinking otherwise at first and gave several different approaches to taking on the bosses. Speaking of which, after beating the game on expert, I came to realize that very few of the bosses are plain unfair (especially when trying to S rank), but a majority just require the player with learning the bosses moveset. This gives an artificial difficulty spike that diminishes when the player does learn the patterns. This can be considered rewarding, but when the whole game is like this, it starts to become a grind. A way to alleviate this grind would be to implement a system where you could choose to practice certain phases of the boss, but instead you have to start from the beginning each time. The good does outweigh the bad in this case though as the feeling of overcoming the boss and/or achieving an S rank is satisfying in the highest degree. Overall, Cuphead is probably somewhere between an 8 and a 9 as it gives a fun but frustrating experience that is definitely worth the asking price if you have the perseverance to overcome the bosses.

Dungeon of the Endless is a terrific blend of RPG, RTS, TBS and Tower Defense elements that forces you to evolve not just your gameplay strategy, but your thinking paradigm as you advance. It also carries the inevitable 'pondering a potentially deadly situation' and 'permadeath punch' of a true roguelike.
The core mechanic is exploring a dungeon level to find a rare resource 'dust' in order to power rooms to carry your crystal from a central location to the 'exit'. Dust is always in short supply, and so you will find yourself forced to leave rooms unpowered. Unpowered rooms allow a variety of incresingly powerful monsters to spawn, who will attack towards your crystal.
You can use module slots located in each of the rooms to power either major modules (which give a resource boost); minor modules (which assist your chracters) or turrets, which defend the rooms. Balancing these out will be key to  a successful run. After you're done placement, you choose which door/room to open next, and a wave of monsters spawns from the unpowered rooms. If you survive, you major modules produce resources, allowing you to build more... and you either open another room, or make a break for the exit with the crystal. Deciding when to quit the floor becomes a critical strategic decision with a well-balanced double-edged risk vs. reward mechanic: milk a floor for all the resources it's worth and risk being overrun enitrely, or cut loose and make a panicked run for the exit?
The characters trying to escape are varied and range across a variety of skills and playtypes, and finding a combination that plays to your micromanagement style (or lack thereof) is one of the game's brilliant design features. Especially when a key character dies and you're forced to substitute them with someone you're not as comfortable with/have to learn, or make do without.
A lot of love has gone into the level and character design, and the pixel art is terrific. Sadly, the music from the launch trailer vastly outstrips anything in the game itself (and is also not on the soundtrack, for some unfathomable reason).
This is a great game to experience core elements of different genres at the same time, without getting bogged down in the trappings of each (it allows the player a great deal of freedom in how to approach the game, at least initially). Highly recommended, but also fair warning: this will not be an 'easy' win for the casual or AAA gamer--mistakes come swiftly and are fatal.
btw: The music from the 'Rogue Life' trailer for the game is the track 'On and On' by Tom Hillock. You can buy the album off Bandcamp. You're welcome :)

Dungeon of the Endless is a top-down roguelike dungeon exploration & tower defense game with many unlockable elements set in the Endless game universe.
The player uses a squad of up to 4 characters to explore a multi-floor dungeon one room at a time while protecting a power crystal. Like other Endless games, the four resources are Food, Industry, Dust, and Science (FIDS). With each door opened, more FIDS accumulate, but dangerous monsters may spawn. Players eventually discover a dungeon floor exit and carry the crystal to a new dungeon floor, continuing on until the game ends at the 12th floor.
Characters may be discovered in-game and unlocked after completing a certain number of floors with that character. Characters have different strengths as might be expected, including attack power, defense, movement speed, and "wit", which in this game translates into better module operation bonuses. Certain secret combinations of characters lead to different in-game events.
Food, Industry, and Science increase in a predictable fashion with each door opened, but Dust is less predictable and cannot be saved between levels. Dust may sometimes be discovered in new rooms or obtained after defeating monsters.
Rooms adjacent to the crystal may be powered (or "lit") subject to a limit based on the current amount of Dust. Lit rooms do not spawn monsters. Given enough industry, different "modules" may be built in a powered room based on the characteristics of that room--not every room can hold a module, no room can hold more than one "major module", and different rooms have different limits for "minor modules".
Items may be discovered in new rooms and are bought and sold for FIDS at merchants which may be discovered in new rooms.
A special Research module may appear in a new room, allowing for Science to be invested to unlock new modules or higher levels of existing modules.
Modules may be removed, for example removing an unneeded Research module to make room.
Like any great game, Dungeon of the Endless presents the player with many interesting choices, for example:
- leave a room dark to spawn more monsters and the chance for more Dust, or light the room to reduce monster spawn and provide room for modules?
- invest Industry in FIDS-producing modules (longer-term payoff) or defensive modules (immediate payoff)?
- spend Food to recruit a new character, or save Food to see if a better choice is available later?
- take the exit as soon as it is found, or open a few more doors to try to gain more Food, Industry, and Science for the next level?
- invest Science now, or remove the Science module in favor of a different major module?
Tactical elements include: positioning of characters when unlocking a door, character movement between rooms during combat, activation of special abilities, healing (which takes Food), and resetting abilities (which takes Science) in combat. Combat may be paused for easier micro-management, but some players will find it more fun to do without pausing (there's even a Steam Achievement for beating a dungeon without pausing).

Sinister City is a small hidden-object point-and-click adventure game about vampires.
Let me get the first thing out of the way; the graphics are terrible, the voice acting doesn't match the movements of the characters. I often found the main character standing in places that made no sence (Ie, outside of the hotel, floating in the middle of the door, or standing on top of the garbage can) That is the only bad things I am saying about Sinister City in this review - so if you can't over look those, you can move along now.
Now to the good points: It's very, very original. I love the storyline, I adore the characters, and despite not lining up correctly, I love the voice acters. You do enough moving around the game that it doesn't get boring easily, although at the same time I would love if it had some more variety to it - although that's not a big issue. It can be slightly hard to find your main objective objects in scenes if you're not sure what you're doing, so I reccomend playing on beginner's mode first.
Now the main conclusion... Even if you can't or don't want to get through this full game on your own, I promise it is worth it. It is a fairly short game (Maybe about 2 hours for me to complete), but the ending scenes are so funny, and really make a nice tie-in for the end of the game. Over all, I reccomend this game - more so to those who have good patience- and am definately going to play it again. A wonderful deal for $1.09 (Or .99 like I got it) or whatever else the price may be for you. Buy this game. You won't be disapointed for long

This is, in my humble opinion, the greatest Star Wars strategy game of all time (and the second-best Star Wars game after Star Wars Battlefront II). I'll give you a quick overview and then launch into a more detailed breakdown of the various pros and cons of the game. (And check the bottom of this review for a couple of handy links)
Quick overview; The game is a grand strategy game, based in the Galactic Civil War period (but mods can be used to get the Clone Wars, or the aftermath of the Battle of Endor or pretty much any other time period). There's a campaign for both the Empire and the Rebels (and the Zahn Consortium if you have the gold pack), or skirmish battles (land or space) and Galactic Conquest. The campaigns can take a while, and there's huge replayability with Galactic Conquest and skirmishes... you won't get bored easily! The graphics are the biggest downside, but for a 2005 game they've aged quite well. Land units are undeniably blocky, but the space fights (relatively unaffected by graphic because ships are blocky anyway) look remarkably good for an 11 year old game.
Pros:
The space battles are the jewel in Empire at War's crown. No game before or since had managed to capture the magic of Star Wars space warfare so perfectly. There's even a 'Cinematic' option that hides the HUD and views the battle as if it were a film.
The Galactic map spans the entire galaxy - all the planets from the canon films and many more. All of them have their own beautifully detailed land and space maps, and many have local life (eg. Wookies on Kashyyyk) who aappear on the land battle and, depending on their circumstances, will fight for either the Empire, Rebels or Zahn Consortium.
The game manages to give each faction not only unique units, but also a unique gameplay without giving any one side an insurmountable advantage. For example, obviously the Empire has Star Destroyers to the Rebel Mon Calamari cruisers, but the Empire gains technology by building research labs, and the Rebels gain it by sending R2-D2 and C-3PO to steal it from the Empire. The Zahn Consortium has various criminal methods at their disposal - such as bribery and extortion - to compensate for their weaker spaceships and (debatably) weaker land units.
The campaign is fairly extensive, and the Galactic Conquest means virtually infinite replayability. The skirmish also means you can easily hop straight into a battle without having to build up tech or anything first.
Heroes. Ah, heroes. Both sides have all the main characters from the original triliogy; Lord Vader, Luke, Leia etc, but also have some more minor heroes, such as General Veers and Captain Antilles. There are also a few from the Extended Universe, such as Mara Jade (the Emperor's hand) and the Zahn Consortium have quite a few bounty hunters (IG-88, Bossk etc). Each has unique powers and some have unique disadvantages (the Empire cannot retreat from any battle if they have Grand Moff Tarkin "Evacuate?! In our moment of triumph? etc)
Grand Strategy - the campaign and Galactic conquest have a heavy emphasis on the grand strategic overview. You have a population cap, and you need to decide how your planets will be defended. Will you have huge defenses over a select few worlds and all but ignore the others, risking losing them to even a small enemy force? Will you have only a few infantry on each  planet, relying on your massive fleets to stop any enemy incursions? Each planet also provides a unique bonus, so some  planets will be more valuable than others - while some will be vital because they are on a hyperspace lane and if you can hold that planet nobody can get to your core worlds.
The Death Star. You won't get this until late in the Imperial campaign, but there are few endgames as sadisfying as literally destroying the few planets yet hiding rebel fighters one by one until the Empire reigns supreme over the galaxy.
Cons:
Land battles. They are very 2005, I'm sorry. There's no getting around it. This game has lots going for it, but nobody plays it because of the terrific land battles. They are somewhat like the battles in Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds (remeber that Age of Empires rip-off?). The graphics are forgivable, but the most annoying thing is you can't build your own base. You can only build on pre-designated build pads, which kind of damages the flexibility of the game.  The good news is they are generally skipable, aside from a few campaign battles.
Multiplayer. If that's your thing, I'm sorry, but once again, old age is hurting this game. As of May 31, 2014, online functionality, including network multiplayer and wireless chat is no longer available due to Glu Mobile purchasing GameSpy and shutting down all game servers. Hey, there's still mods being developed, so the community is far from dead.
The gameplay can be a little frustrating at times, and the AI often appears to be nigh-omniscient during Galactic Conquest. But really, is a challenging AI that bad a thing?
Summary:
As you no doubt have figured out, I love this game. To rehash what I said at the start, it is by a long shot the best Star Was RTS out there, and the way games are going these days, it probably will be for a long time to come. The space battles and the 'grand' part of 'grand strategy' really define the greatness of this game.  Buy it. Buy it now. I promise if you're a Star Wars fan (or even if you're just a casual RTS fan) you won't regret it.

It is time to set these haters to rest my friends.  This game has had way to much unwarranted negative press and it is time to debunk the negative reviews and I will go over the pros and cons concisely without wasting your time.
PROS:
-Evolve is a great game.  It is exactly what it looks like, you teaming up with some friends or online homies and hunting down an uber-powerful monster in an epic showdown of teamwork, bravery, and reckless, unchecked crazy.  It is very satisfying to take down the monster as a team, especially when you and the monster are all down to no life and it's anybody's game.
-Beautiful game... nuf said.
-Character types are all very unique compared to each other, providing critical skills to support the team, and traditionally boring roles like med/support are actually some of the most in-depth-not-so-average characters they have.  All characters within each role are also unique, playing any of the medics followed by another medic feels like a complete gameplay change and is exciting, not just a skin change.
-The grind is short, but rewarding.
-Not pay2win
-You are a freakin' beast tearing up people using cunning and skill, and thus feel very rewarded when you play a round with the monster.  Even when you lose it can be a satisfying round.
-Great after game review!  The map is the best part, where you watch little dots run around signifying the position of all players throughout the game, and can see where the monster juked you, and how well you chased him down.
-Looks like TurtleRock plans on giving us good updates and more content, they seem dedicated to the players, and hopefully remain this way for a while.
-Nice and fair role picking system, no angry instalockers (shout out to LoL).  You rate you pick preference, and the game tries to do its best to make sure you play what you want to play.
-The balance to this game is amazing.  Although the hunters start with and advantage, the monster certainly can win at lvl 1, and when the monster has the advantage at the end, the hunters can win.  There is nothing broken about any class, there is just skill and understanding when to strike, when to evolve, or when to run for your dear life.
CONS:
-DLC, I feel that some of it should have been included, or at least they should lower the prices, because they are pretty steep...
-Some people are running into a loading issued which is EASILY solved within the game.  During the loading screen people get stuck, usually at like 95% (ikr frustrating), by turning off VSYNC in the advanced graphic settings, it solves this problem about 19/20 times.  Worth it to check your drivers too.
-Addicting
-Being the monster is jumping in the deep end for a particular kind of person.  There will be those who find it frustrating to have to fight against a team, while they are solo.  I think these people can learn to enjoy monster after playing the hunters and realizing how they work, their potential, and how they can be taken down.  Learning = better playing = happy :)
-Because of negative reviews this game has suffered on potential player base, but I haven't found it much of a problem when trying to find games to join, so not too bad.  It is a sad fact though.
In summary:
Evolve is a fantastic game that is well worth your time, I hope if you enjoy it you can help write good reviews and beat down these haters.  The game isn't perfect, but what is?  All that matters is that it is a blast to play, and that it can only get better!

I thought KT were up to their old tricks again after hearing about the 720p fiasco shortly before release but as I gathered more information I became more interested in the details of what's going on. I'm going to try to focus on specifics here since other people have already mentioned stuff like editing the ini file (in My Documents, KoeiTecmo folder) to bump resolution and possibly enable AA though I haven't tried the latter through the ini yet.
To start off with a tl;dr: This is a decent port that is most definitely NOT the Vita version, which that version has much of its visual effects cut.
If you want to see screenshot comparisons between PC and PS4, there is a Steam Discussion thread made for this: "PC vs PS4 comparison screenshots"
I played through the first hour or so on PC while directly referencing a video of the game running on PS4 (Youtube "Blue Reflection Gameplay Longplay", video ID: X4J4iZTf1-g) and will comment on graphics with timecodes below (this overlaps with where the screenshots comparisons mentioned above cover but a bit more):
- Bloom is present on both (3:05, 4:33, 7:52 for some reason more visible on PS4)
- Depth of Field is present (togglable option on PC)
- Shadow bugs are present in both but are at times slightly to significantly more visible in PC (5:48 hallway walking, the shadows under the windows shifting as well as some aliasing on the windows to the classrooms which are much more visible on PC, 24:30)
- Shadow LOD popping present on both
- Stair railing shadow map aliasing much more visible on PS4 than PC (7:29)
- In ONE case I saw shadows missing on PC that are present in PS4 (12:04 and visible in one of the discussion screenshot comparisons)
- It should be noted in that case there are some severe issues with shadow LOD on the PS4 anyway as they disappear in horizontal strips as the camera moves.
- Otherwise every shadow that I've noted match between the platforms, including character dynamic shadows (53:10), self shadows (13:00, subtle), and background dynamic shadows (17:10)
- The small outline around characters looks worse with PS4 though I suspect this is something that looks better as rendering res scales (37:55)
- Generally texture quality seems to be equal on both platforms
This game doesn't have Borderless Windowed though seemingly works flawlessly with BorderlessGaming. Note that if you launch as Windowed at full monitor res it may require some finagling to actually force the game to be visible as it launches in a strange non-display state. In my case with multiple monitors it appeared on my higher resolution monitor and I had to use BG to fullscreen it, then remove the fullscreen to make it visible. From there, I simply dragged it into the correct monitor and re-fullscreened it. Single monitor users can likely just immediately use BG to fullscreen.
The game runs smoothly at 60 fps, this seems to be higher than the PS4, though that may just be an issue of referencing from Youtube rather than the actual console. From what I can see it seems like the 720p 2D assets referenced were mostly pre-rendered video (to save download size on a purely digital platform I suspect), tutorial/encyclopedia screenshots, and possibly some of the UI icons.
That all said, other people are reporting the usual gamut of issues such as instability. While I have not experienced this myself it isn't an uncommon occurrence so I can't say definitively that this port doesn't have major issues for everyone, but so far as I am able to tell it seems above average for KT, especially if we can get a few patches for people who are experiencing stability issues.
Edit: After just over 2 hours, I did run into a crash while transitioning areas right after completing a mission so holding for a patch does def seem prudent, save often
Edit2: On 10/5, there was a patch that boosted the 2d assets to 1080p res as well as a stability fix but I can't currently personally confirm the latter.
